chapters.title: Parvatisham's Origins
paragraphs: Many people who have read Parvatisham’s book often ask me, “Who is this fellow, anyway?” or, “On whom did you base this character?” or, “How did you ever come up with the idea to write like this?” I am constantly bombarded with such questions. Not only that, but recently the radio folks too said, “Please tell us a few words about this man—Parvatisham—his origins and background.” The answers I gave them, and the gist of what I usually tell all those who question me in this manner, are as follows.

Our people say that everything is born with a destiny, or that a face is written by fate. Sometimes, just by looking at a face, you feel like planting a kiss on it. Of course, not everyone gets to do that, but at least you feel like seeing that face, or getting acquainted with the person who owns it. Some faces, on the other hand, make you want to shout; you wish you could go through your entire life without ever seeing them. In the same way, the moment you hear certain names, you are seized by an urge to know all about that person’s background and ancestry. Such a fortunate soul is our Parvatisham. His lotus-like face, its radiance, his birth star and fate—all these are his own. Otherwise, why would so many people know his name? And why would no one know mine? Everyone is eager to get to know him, to learn about his story; not just eager, but positively burning with curiosity.

Why, you ask? Among all those who know my son, is there even one in a hundred who doesn’t know my name? Yet, among those who know me, not a single person has ever asked, “What about you, sir? What are your antecedents, your origins?” I must admit, this bothers me a little. Occasionally—especially when my friends introduce me to their friends, or at some gathering—when they say, “This is Mr. Narasimha Shastri,” I see questioning faces, as if to say, “So what?” But the moment someone says, “He is the creator of Parvatisham,” I see a look of satisfaction dawn upon them, as if to say, “Oh, now you should have said so! In that case, we can tolerate him to some extent.” I can’t deny that such moments sting a little! They say, “He who desires a son will be defeated,” but who knows? I’d say, to accept such defeat—even at the hands of one’s own son—is a great thing. Not that I consider myself a great man, but I made peace with the idea long ago that it’s fine if nobody knows my name. I have bid farewell to my ego. I have counted myself among those who never make it to the majority. After all, all the elders call me “Subbarayudu’s younger brother.” Elsewhere, I’m known as “Shivashankar Shastri’s son-in-law,” or “Teerthulu’s father-in-law.” I’ve grown quite accustomed to being identified by my relations to others. So, whenever someone says, “He is the author of Parvatisham,” and the other person bursts into a big laugh and says, “Is that so! You should have said so!”—even if I can tell he’s thinking, “So that’s why he looks like that,” it doesn’t bother me in the least. In fact, these days, it makes me happy. Why, you ask? Well, in some way or other, being talked about by people, being recognized by a handful, is a good thing, isn’t it? Something to be happy about. Many even think it’s something to be proud of.

But who cares about me! What you want to know is Parvatisham’s story, isn’t it? As for his origins, I can hardly say anything. According to his own account, he is an “ayonija”—a self-born, one of the mind-born sons of Brahma himself.
Parvatisham claims his residence is Mogalturru (though, truth be told, he only lived there; his actual birthplace is Gumm...

Let me tell you, in confidence, about Parvateesham’s birthplace. He was born in a village called Looru. Now, if you ask why Parvateesham had to be born in that particular village, it’s because that’s my mother-in-law’s native place. Naturally, I have a special fondness for that village.

In those days, traveling to that place was no easy task. There were no roads leading to it from any direction—not even a proper mud path. When it rained, the plight of travelers was known only to Lord Parameshwara himself. Yet, for some reason, I always found it enjoyable to go there.

Once, during Diwali, when it was raining cats and dogs, I set out for Gummalooru. With every step forward, I would slip two steps ahead, drenched and struggling, but somehow, I managed to reach the village. As usual, my brothers-in-law, sisters-in-law, and the boys from the neighboring house all gathered around me. They looked at me with the reverence one reserves for a leader. Unable to contain myself, I regaled them with tales—stories of my journey by boat, the hardships, the jokes, and a few of my experiences. They were thoroughly entertained.

They unanimously insisted that I write it all down as a story. At that time, I had never even dreamed of writing a book. In fact, I didn’t have the slightest confidence that I could write one. Up to that point, I had written only three stories: “Pilaka” (“The Seed”), “Nenu Maa Avida” (“Me and My Wife”), and a couple of others, which were later published in the magazines Sahityalokam, Lakshmi, and Bharati. I am, without a doubt, one of the foremost among those who gained literary fame at the lowest possible cost. “Pilaka” and “Lakshmi” caught the attention of many and won the affection of quite a few readers. But knowing myself, I thought it best to stop writing altogether and maintain my dignity. It was at this point that the meeting ended.

The elders say, “A child’s word is as sacred as the word of Brahma.” For some reason, when the youngsters asked, I too felt a sudden enthusiasm to write. I started by invoking Lord Rama on the page and took a young man from Sarsapuram all the way to Nidadavolu. Once there, not knowing what to do with him, I took him to Madras. At that point, I hadn’t even named the young man, nor had I thought of sending him to England. Whatever I wrote, I read aloud to the youngsters. They unanimously certified that it was excellent. Those youngsters...

This news filled me with such joy and enthusiasm. That young fellow had remained in Madras, hadn’t he? I thought, “Why not bring him back home again?” For a story to satisfy me, its beginning, middle, and end must all be in proper order. So, I had no choice but to settle that young man’s affairs. Suddenly, an idea struck me: “What if someone like him were taken abroad? Wouldn’t that be quite amusing?” The thought delighted me. No matter the expense or the trouble, I resolved to send him to England.

In those days, going to England—or studying to become a barrister—was considered a tremendous achievement. The moment I decided upon this young man’s future, I immediately wrote down his birthplace, family name, education, and all the other necessary background details. From that point on, my responsibility ended; the rest of the tale, Parvateesham himself took over.

Just as, in our ancient epics, the storytellers—Soota, Shaunaka, and the other great sages—would hand over the narrative, or as Vaishampayana would recount the story to Janamejaya, so too did I pass the tale along. At that point, my role as narrator receded into the background.

There was once a famous English humorist named W. W. Jacobs. He wrote many stories, describing the life of sailors in all its variety and with great humor. All his stories would begin with, “The night watchman, sitting on the deck, said thus—” and only then would the story proceed. Without that, he felt, a story could not even begin.
Just as in an autobiography, I begin: Ours is the Mogaliturru family, our surname is Vemuru. But from that point on, the rest of my story seems to have unfolded entirely without my own involvement.

From the very beginning, my mind—much like my feet—has always lacked steadiness. Rarely did I stay in one place for long; I was always wandering here or there, unable to settle anywhere for any length of time.

I left this young lad (myself) in Madras, while I myself set out from Gummaluru to Guntur. There, I gathered a few of my friends—Tallavajhula Shiva Shankara Shastri, Nori Narasimha Shastri, Varmu Baburao, Srinivasa Shiromani, and others. Just as young poets gather an audience and recite their verses, I too assembled them and narrated my story.

Their delight knew no bounds. They blessed me, saying this would become very popular. Nori Narasimha Shastri declared, “This will be a unique work, it will gain tremendous public acclaim!” The rest of my friends praised me in various ways.
A couple of friends, who had previously doubted whether I had any sense of humor or was merely a man of timely speech, now concluded with certainty that I was indeed a humorist.

This is your fate, that you must while away your time writing humorous stories like this— so said a few critics, sprinkling a dash of sarcasm upon me. Be that as it may, the President insisted that this story must be completed right here and now.
“How so? I cannot write quickly,” I protested.
“Does that mean the story will stop, sir? Dictate whenever inspiration strikes you; this humble scribe will write it down…” Thus assured Srinivasa Shiromani, offering me his protection.
Taking his words as sacred, I managed to finish the whole story within a week and read it out to my friends. They all said it was very good.
“Barrister Parvateesham— that would be a fitting title,” declared our President, Shivashankara Shastri, christening it then and there.

This happened in the first week of December, 1924. By the end of the second week, the book was completed. I had it printed at Sharada Press in Bezwada, and, bless them, they managed to finish the printing within a month.

Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri’s *Barrister Parvatisham*—there is hardly anyone in Telugu land unfamiliar with this character. Recently, his story even made it to the silver screen. Parvatisham is a young man from an orthodox Andhra Brahmin family, brimming with enthusiasm and ambition to travel to London and qualify as a barrister.

But along with English education, he lacked many other essential qualities expected of such an endeavor in those days. The ways of modern civilization were entirely new to him. This was a man who had never even boarded a train before. From the very moment he set out from home, he encountered one bizarre predicament after another. At every turn, circumstances conspired to make him appear a fool, and the world seemed to turn upside down in his eyes.

His awkward gait in the train, the troubles he faced in Madras, the ordeals he suffered on the steamer, the entanglements in strange new places—all these must be read to be believed, for they defy mere description. The author has painted each episode with such humor that one can hardly keep from splitting their sides with laughter, moving from one hilarious scene to the next. In doing so, he has gifted Telugu literature with an unparalleled work of comedy.
When we encounter something unfamiliar, unsure where its head is and where its tail, if we do not make fools of ourselves, who else will?

Even now, we laugh at our past follies, though tinged with a hint of regret. This very principle runs through the story of Parvateesam, from beginning to end, weaving humor into every page. Everything appears unnatural at first, but by the end, we realize it is, in fact, the most natural thing of all.

One mistake leads to another, blunders piling up and entangling themselves like a string of mishaps, each more absurd than the last, driving the story into unexpected twists and turns. The character himself is not, by nature, a fool. Rather, it is the circumstances that make a fool of him, mocking and ridiculing him at every step. The predicaments that befall Parvateesam—more laughable than anything—are ones we ourselves have experienced at some point in our own lives. That is why we feel such affection for this character. Admiration, sympathy, and fondness—all these emotions arise for him. He is a figure that has become part of our national heritage.
We cannot tolerate someone like Girisham. But Parvateesam—

It is no exaggeration to say that Parvateesham stands as the sole comic character in this field. The author has written numerous humorous essays and stories as well, and everywhere, he has delivered delightful humor. His distinctiveness lies in his ability to create comic characters. These characters, too, become dear to our hearts.

In this manner, all those who have reviewed modern literature—whether in their essays, lectures, or radio talks—have continued to praise Parvateesham. I never went to any of them and requested such praise; those are their own opinions, and I feel there is no need for me to say anything further. Now, why have I had to say all this so far? Because, as the saying goes, “Tastes differ from person to person.” Depending on their upbringing, people interpret literature in various ways. That is all I wished to convey! This is the third type of criticism.

Unless an individual or a society has attained a certain level of spiritual and mental maturity, it is difficult to properly appreciate true humor. That is why the appreciation and discussion of humor flourish best among those of similar culture and background, but may not succeed everywhere.

Now, the fourth type: There are some respected elders who, upon first hearing or reading this story, declared it to be excellent. But after a few days, when they constantly heard people around them praising Parvateesham, they could not bear it any longer. They would grumble, “What’s so great about this? He just copied Don Quixote. His intelligence is nothing to boast about.”

This is the criticism that almost every Andhraite makes. If someone writes a fine book or paints a beautiful picture, and if that someone happens to be one of our own, our people will never accept it, even if it kills them. The reason is, every Andhraite firmly believes that no Andhraite can accomplish any work requiring intelligence or skill. So, whenever they come across a rare work of excellence, they convince themselves that it must be plagiarized from somewhere else, and only then are they satisfied. If they do not think so, they feel as if they have not eaten that day—poor souls. Well, what can we do? Even a world-renowned figure like Tagore—

Only the poet is free from this accusation. What about people like us? Well, whatever anyone may say, Parvatisham, born of an unpremeditated impulse, has become a figure of wide renown and affection. That is a source of joy for me. Why, you ask? Because some rays of his fame, both directly and indirectly, fall upon me too, tickling me from time to time—even now.

But along with this joy, certain doubts have troubled me, leading me to a bit of self-examination. I never once thought that I should write a great book and make everyone ecstatic with delight, nor did I ever think I was fit for such a task. Yet, whether some deny it or I myself refuse it, this has become a great book. It has won undying fame. Even today, I am recognized by that name. Because of this, I am constantly plagued by the suspicion: am I not deceiving people, making them believe I possess some power I do not truly have?

While that is so, a chain of questions begins within me: What is so special about Parvatisham? Why has he become the object of such universal affection? Why do people burst out laughing at the mere sight of him? We wrote something. They are laughing, they are happy. Then why do I still have these foolish doubts? Though I sometimes answer myself thus, I am not one to be easily satisfied, so I probed a little deeper.

Then another thought arose: Why do we laugh at others? What qualities in them make us laugh? This is a vast question—if one were to answer it fully, it would fill a hundred thousand books. So I shall state it briefly. In the features, gestures, dress, and speech of people, whenever there is any excess or deficiency compared to what we are accustomed to, we find it amusing.

If someone is unusually tall or short, fat or thin, has a big nose or none at all, if their eyes are oddly set or drooping, if their hair is sparse—whenever we notice such differences, we laugh. That is, whenever there is any deviation from the ordinary standards, it strikes us as odd and makes us laugh. Moreover, in every person, there is a certain movement—

I believe that qualities such as alertness and discernment exist independently. If any person lacks these traits, he appears uncivilized to us, and we laugh at him. Therefore, in storytelling, if such peculiarities are shown in the hero’s speech, actions, and attire, readers are bound to find it amusing and burst into laughter.

Isn’t it commonly believed that the English are far more civilized than us in many respects, and that their dress and language are exceedingly elegant and refined? Don’t we all try to imitate their manners and their style of dress as much as possible?

Now, imagine this Parvateesham setting out, clad in a crisp dhoti, a bright red shawl, a rose-colored silk scarf, and a marigold-yellow turban, equipped with all sorts of flashy accessories—wouldn’t everyone laugh and think, “What a ridiculous, foolish fellow this is!”?
And Also Women’s Hats

When I bought one near the dining hall, When I used knives and forks, When I didn’t, in a French shop, When I walked on the carpet, When I tried to walk on the polished, waxed floor Thinking it was fine, and slipped and fell— People laughed, wondering, “Is it possible to be so inept?” But, in truth, there is nothing to laugh at. Let me tell you, all those who laugh— If they were in those situations, In those very scenes, In those circumstances, They would have behaved just like Parvatisham, Or perhaps even more foolishly. I can say this confidently.

Once, when a distinguished gentleman came to Madras to study for his B.L., He confided to me in secret that he had the very same doubt as Parvatisham did in the barber shop. A great man, who had gone to England and returned after passing his medical exams, Told me he too, in a shop, Avoided walking on the carpet, And ended up tumbling head over heels. He asked, “How did you know about my mishap?”

Man is ignorant in many matters, And so, many blunders arise from ignorance. Even if it seems like an exaggeration to gather a few such incidents and show them in one person, It turns out to be undeniably comical.

To these ignorant blunders, we must add another common habit of ours: never admitting our mistakes, but instead pretending as if we did everything knowingly and deliberately. Many of us are afflicted with this very disease. When Parvateesham, not knowing what a lady’s hat was, bought one and was laughed at, he immediately claimed he had bought it for his lady friend—just to save face. This, too, is a sign of ignorance.
The irony is that the ignorance, confusions, chaos, and blunders that lie hidden within us—when we see them displayed openly in someone else, we cannot help but laugh.
Or else, one might even get angry.
Why do we laugh, you ask? I think I can give just one answer to that. No man ever recognizes his own faults, does he! In fact, he is quick to accuse others of those very faults.
“If someone else had made this mistake, what a fool he would be! But me? Never!”—he pats himself on the back and feels pleased.

That is exactly what happened in the case of our Parvateesham. All the cleverness and follies that dwell within us, we see in Parvateesham and, thinking, “What a silly fellow, to have done such things!” we laugh at him with self-satisfaction, secretly assuring ourselves, “But I would never do such a thing!”

This, in English, is what a philosopher once called “superior edastation”—that is, a kind of prideful delusion. Whatever the reason, Parvateesham has found a permanent home in the hearts of the Telugu people. He may lack the heroic qualities extolled by the poets—he is no great leader. Nor is he the celebrated hero of every drama. But, for all that, he is a man just like us. In him, we see ourselves. That is why Parvateesham has become one among each of us.

No matter how much anyone laughs at him, Parvateesham does not mind. In my view, he is the very embodiment of all the ordinary human qualities—courage, rashness, foolishness, ignorance, arrogance, and the lack of patience to acquire the means necessary for success. What do you say?
I hope you will not mind my speaking so frankly. For, after all, truthfulness is the chief aim and duty of a writer of humor.
As always, may Parvateesham remain the beloved child of the Telugu people, may he live forever, and may he flourish—this is my blessing to him.
—Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 1971

I hail from Mogalthur, you see. Now, you might be wondering—what sort of place is Mogalthur? Let me tell you! It is a city of great renown in history. Just a glance at its towering fort bastions and vast walls is enough to understand what a grand town it is, how famous, how many wars it has witnessed, how many enemy armies it has vanquished. Strangely, though, no one who truly understood all this has ever written its story. If only some real historians had sat here and penned the chronicles of this place, imagine how many secrets would have come to light! How many hidden tales would have stepped out of the shadows! If someone had properly understood and recorded all this, the history of our Andhra people, the valor of the Mogalthur kings, their systems of governance, the charities and good deeds they performed—so much would have been revealed! The whole of our Narasapuram taluk would have rejoiced with pride!

Even today, during the chariot festival at Antarvedi, our kings go and, unless they lay their hands on the chains to pull the chariot, it simply won’t budge—no matter how many thousands try! Did you know that? Such is the greatness that remains in their hands even now; imagine what they must have been in their heyday! To be born in such a town is a matter of great pride for me.
Our family name is Vemuri. The Vemuri family, too, traces its roots to the rulers of Mogalthur.

In that royal court, our family was renowned as a learned and distinguished household. In shaping that kingdom, in guiding all the lords onto the right path, in making them perform acts of charity and righteousness, in identifying and supporting the poor and needy—our people played a significant role. Even now, there exists great mutual respect, affection, and regard between us and them.

Whenever they faced any doubt—be it in matters of scripture or worldly affairs—they would promptly hitch up their horse-drawn carriage and come to my grandfather. They would sit before him with reverence and awe, present their queries, receive his clarifications, take their leave, and depart. I have heard many people recount this with admiration. They extended the same respect to my father as well. And everyone around me used to say that once I grew up, I too would be honored in the same manner. Well, let that be. That is something destined to happen in the distant future.

As for me, I studied there up to the fifth or sixth class during my childhood. Though my teacher had many students, he was especially fond of me. I vividly remember how he would seat me close by and teach me the alphabet with great affection and fun.

After I completed the fourth class, my father tried to send me to Narasapuram for further studies. But my mother, unable to bear the thought of parting with me and worried that I wouldn’t have proper food arrangements so far from home, insisted I not be sent away. Because of her persistence, I spent another two years idling away in Mogalturru itself.

No matter what my mother said, the thought of leaving that village filled me with a strange anxiety and fear. I had so many friends there. All of them had an affection for me that is difficult to put into words.
Affection

“Hey Parvateesam! How can you just leave like that? We can’t live without you! We’ll come along with you!” my friends would say. I would laugh and reply, “Stop your nonsense and study, all of you. I’m not going anywhere. Don’t act so silly. Suppose I go from Narsapur to some big city like Rajahmundry or Madras for higher studies—how could you possibly come along? People should stay where they belong; it’s not as if everyone can go everywhere.”
“Why can’t we come?” one friend challenged.
“Look at your face! Let’s see if you can even try. I’ll jump straight into this canal and swim across from this side to that. If you can, try and catch me!” Saying this, I dashed towards the canal.

“Don’t, please! Don’t go!” they shouted. “He’s only joking, but who could ever beat you in a wager?” Not listening to their pleas, I kept running towards the canal. All of them ran after me, and just as I was about to get into the water, they grabbed me tightly.

“Don’t, please! What’s the point of a bet with you? Your case is different, your situation is different. If you jump into the water for this silly wager, your father will kill us all. He won’t let us live in this town. Come on, let’s go home,” they pleaded, half-laughing, half-scolding, as if they were heroically dragging me back. Amid laughter and cheers, they escorted me merrily all the way to my house.

They all had such affection for me. Not just them—even the rest of the townsfolk, for some reason, seemed to have a great fondness for me. In any game, I was always the winner. Whether I went to a guava orchard or a mango grove, even if the owners or their workers were present, they would pluck plenty of fruit and give them to me. If any of the boys with me tried to pick a fruit by mistake, they would be scolded and chased away.
It wasn’t just the men—even the women of the village were very fond of me.

chapters.title: Childhood Mischief
paragraphs: Even now, when I think back on it, I feel terribly embarrassed. On my birthday, all the women from the neighboring houses would come for the celebration, and when they left, every single one of them would insist on kissing me before going. I found it utterly disgusting and irritating. Once, I even said to my mother, quite firmly, “What is this, Amma! It’s so revolting, all these women smothering me with kisses—my skin crawls. Do they think I’m a little girl or something? If this goes on, I swear I’ll never be born again. Don’t celebrate my birthday anymore. Do you know how childish it makes me feel? And why do all those silly women have to kiss me anyway? Is it even allowed for them to do that, Amma? They’re all such fools! Let them keep their distance,” I blurted out one day. My mother and the others burst out laughing, and then, just to tease me, they kissed me even more. In my childhood, everything happened with such fun and mischief.

Leaving that village was hard for me, and for my mother, leaving me behind was even harder. But for the sake of my studies, there was no choice but to go to Narsapur. They had decided that there was no use staying in our village any longer, so on an auspicious day, they took me to Narsapur, handed me over to my aunt’s house, and got me admitted to the first form at the Taylor High School there.

Until then, though it was not far from us, I had never seen Narsapur. When I saw the houses, the buildings, the court, the high school, the canal, the Godavari—everything—I was overwhelmed. If Narsapur was like this, I wondered what Rajahmundry and other big towns must be like, but I couldn’t even imagine it. Seeing the school, the teachers, and their ways, I felt nervous for quite some time. None of the teachers showed me any special affection. Unlike in my village, no one put their arm around my shoulder or made me sit close to them. I thought, “What kind of place is this? Is this my village? Is this some street-side school? No, this is a big institution.” For a while, I tried to console myself with such thoughts. Here, unlike in my village where we sat on mats or wooden planks on the verandah, the children all sat at desks.

Master sat far away on his chair, and so, unlike in our village school where the teacher would be close by, here there seemed to be a great distance between the master and the children. Still, the teachers here were very good people. They would keep a thousand eyes on us, constantly watching to see if the boys were listening attentively to what he said or not, making sure no one misbehaved. Yet, no matter how carefully he watched, there were always some boys who managed to be naughty. They would shake this way and that, making all sorts of noises. When school was dismissed, all the children would rush outside, whistling loudly as they went.

As soon as we came out, instead of heading straight home, groups of boys would gather together, shouting, running, pushing each other down for fun, and making a racket. Some would play games like hopscotch and marbles. Others would play ball. With all this laughter, shouting, and play, I used to feel very cheerful.

For a few days, I didn’t join any of these groups. I would stand aside or sit on the steps, simply watching the festivities and enjoying myself. But those days didn’t last long—the other boys wouldn’t let me just sit there. They would drag me into their games by force. One boy would grab the ball and throw it at me. I would be compelled to throw it back at him, and as I ran away, the ball would come flying and hit me on the back again. In this way, I was forced to play ball with them. If it wasn’t the ball game one day, the next day they would pull me into hopscotch. After a week of this, I was ready for the games even before anyone called me.
Of all the games, I enjoyed marbles the most. So, every day, I would join the marbles group, and after two or three months, I became quite a good marble player.

The funny thing is, I discovered something new here that I had never seen in our village or in our school there. At the end of the year, before giving us the December holidays, they would hold competitions in all these games along with the class exams. The winning team would get a prize. And even within the team, the best player...
Barrister Parvateesam
They used to give a special prize to the best player.

The year I joined, not only did our team win, but I also received the first prize. I had never imagined such a thing would happen. For the prize distribution, all the school children were made to sit in the examination hall, a grand assembly was held, and our district Collector was invited to present the prizes. As each name was read out, the boys would walk up to the Collector, receive their prize from his hands, offer him a respectful bow, and return to their seats—such was the arrangement. Our teachers had rehearsed this entire procedure with us two days in advance. Because of that, everything went smoothly for me, without any nervousness.

Whenever a student's name was called and he went up to receive his prize, the whole hall would erupt in thunderous applause from the assembled students. I don’t know how it felt for the others, but when my name was called and I stood up, the sound of those claps made my heart swell with pride. I felt as if I were floating in the air as I walked towards the Collector. Even now, I’m not sure whether my feet actually touched the ground. The Collector looked at me, smiled gently, said “Good boy,” and patted me on the back. That was too much happiness for me to contain—I was so overwhelmed that, still floating in the air, I stumbled and nearly fell into my seat.
All the boys sitting next to me hugged me right there. I feel a little shy to say this, but it must be told: that year, not only in sports, but I also received the first prize in academics.

River. I had no idea about that until then. And that day, another thing happened that brought me immense joy. At that meeting, my uncle and the schoolmaster from our village—though I had no idea when they arrived—managed, as soon as the meeting ended and everyone stood up, to slip away from the crowd and come straight to me. They lifted me up and showered me with kisses. All the children nearby clapped and laughed, which made me terribly embarrassed, and yet so happy that tears welled up in my eyes. In this way, two or three years passed by, filled with such happiness.

While I was in the third form, a funny incident occurred. As the school year was drawing to a close, the school inspector came to examine our school. The day before, our master had repeatedly told all of us to come dressed in our best clothes and to comb our hair neatly. That day, even all the teachers wore freshly laundered clothes and, not forgetting, came with their headscarves tied properly. The whole school was unusually silent; we were even afraid to sneeze or cough. Our master paced gravely up and down the classroom, warning us again and again to be careful, and to answer any questions without fear.

Just as he was doing this, the inspector entered the classroom quietly. Our master hurried over to him, greeted him with folded hands, and gently pulled up a chair for him. As soon as the inspector arrived, following our master's instructions, all of us students stood up and greeted him respectfully. The inspector sat down in his chair, draped a shawl over his shoulders, removed his headscarf and placed it on the table, and looked every bit the dignified elder. He spoke softly with our nervous master for a couple of minutes, and then began to question the students.
Barrister Parvateesam
He began to speak.

He was quite dark-skinned and somewhat stout. Not content with the darkness of his body, he had also donned a black coat. On his face were spots, as if his mother had sprinkled them there, looking like the marks left by a spinning top. As if that weren’t enough, one of his eyes drooped noticeably. When he looked around the class, we couldn’t tell which way he was actually looking, and though we felt like laughing, we suppressed it with effort and sat in fearful reverence.

He turned to one boy and asked a question from the science lesson. Not knowing whom he had addressed, the boy sitting next to him sprang up and answered. The inspector was furious, turned to him and shouted, “You fool! Who asked you?” The boy trembled and shrank in fear, while the other, still standing with folded hands and shivering, stammered, “Sir, I didn’t utter a word!” At this, the whole class burst out laughing.

Our teacher, caught between anger and fear, grabbed his cane and, gritting his teeth, marched to the middle of the class, shouting, “Shut your mouths!” The inspector, losing his temper, stood up, banged the desk, and thundered, “Silence!” At that roar, we all froze in terror and sat without a word.

Still seething, the inspector fired off a few more questions. This time, to avoid confusion, the teacher called out the name of the boy to whom the question was directed, and the right boy gave the right answer without any mix-up. That seemed to calm the inspector a little, and he continued asking questions, now in a more pleasant manner.

Then he turned to me and asked a question. I was sitting there, a bit lost in thought. The teacher noticed my absent-mindedness and said, “Parvateesam, they’re asking you something—answer!” I hurriedly stood up with folded hands. But I hadn’t heard the question.

The inspector, with a gentle smile, said, “Look here, boy, when a ray of light falls on any object, it is reflected. That is, it bounces back.” I was still not fully attentive. Oh, I forgot to mention—he was bald, and his head shone brightly.

chapters.title: School Days
paragraphs: At that very moment in our class, it was as if the sun, shining through the frog’s cup, had fallen right onto the heads of the warriors and bounced back. The inspector repeated his question, and without a second thought, I blurted out, “A bald head, sir!” The whole class burst into laughter. Our teacher’s face fell. The inspector clutched his stomach, wrapped his scarf around his head, and walked out of the classroom. The entire class fell silent.

Our teacher slumped into the chair the inspector had just vacated, leaned his elbows on the desk, buried his head in his hands, and groaned, “Parvateesham, you’ve ruined me! How did you come up with such wickedness at this hour? All these days I was proud, thinking you were a clever boy, and now you say something like this! My fate is sealed. I knew these were bad times for me.” His lament was so heartfelt that it nearly brought us all to tears.
Just then, the bell rang for lunch. Our teacher, still dejected, remained seated as we quietly slipped out of the room.

Thus, passing the time with games and songs, I made my way into the fourth form. School life was very pleasant. The teachers used to say I was clever in my studies as well. However, word somehow reached my father that, though I was bright, I was spending too much time socializing and neglecting my studies. There was truth in that—no denying it. For some reason, all the children had developed an inexplicable fondness and respect for me. Every year, whether in mischief or in merit, I would win prizes.

As soon as the exam results started coming in, I was always either first or second in class, regularly winning prizes. This earned me great respect among all the students. On one hand, the teachers’ affection for me grew, and on the other, my circle of friends expanded day by day. When I thought about the fondness and admiration they showed me, I must admit, a certain pride crept in. Along with that, a bit of arrogance, stubbornness, and carelessness—both towards people and my studies—began to take root in me. I cannot deny this fact. As a result, the teachers’ previous fondness for me diminished, and their irritation increased a little.

In the evenings, after school, when games and mischief weren’t enough, I took to exercising at a gym near the village—doing push-ups, lifting weights, and even started learning a bit of wrestling. Then, in the village, there were frequent gatherings: meetings, lectures, Harikathas, bhajans, and so on, all taking place after the lamps were lit in the evening. I would, without fail, attend all these events with my classmates, purely for the fun of it. Amidst all these activities, it’s only natural that my studies suffered a little—I must admit that too.

Meanwhile, marriage proposals began to arrive from various places. My mother was overjoyed. She was eager to see me married soon, and to watch her younger daughter-in-law bustling about the house. She was quite taken with the idea. And who else but me could fulfill her wishes? There was no one else to take up that responsibility, after all.

So, as the first step towards my marriage, my uncle immediately arranged for my upanayanam (sacred thread ceremony). For that auspicious occasion, all our relatives came from far and wide. Two or three of my teachers, and about twenty-five or thirty of my classmates, also attended. My group of friends, seeing the affection and respect shown towards me, made my mother swell with pride—she couldn’t have been happier. She took special care to host them all.

With a loincloth tied, hair in five tufts, the sacred thread around my neck, a staff in my hand, another leather strap, and a begging bowl in the other, my friends and the young men among my relatives gathered around me, and the mischief they got up to was no small matter. All the relatives who came were delighted to see me thus. Never before had I seen so many relatives gather at our house for a happy occasion.

So far, this has always been the beginning. In our village, people of all castes would gather at our house, feasting for four days and merrily passing the time. I found this immensely exciting. I wondered, “Is it only among our people that such things happen? Do celebrations elsewhere also take place with such grandeur and joy?”

After those four days ended and all the relatives departed on their own ways, our house felt deserted, as if it had shrunk to nothing. I returned once again to Narsapuram. My friends, overjoyed by the honor bestowed upon our family, spread the news far and wide among the other students. The day I returned to school, the entire student body greeted me with applause and a warm welcome.

Two of the younger boys grabbed me, hoisted me onto their shoulders, and carried me off to seat me on a chair. Some others brought flowers from the school garden and showered me with a floral rain. Then, one fellow, feeling inspired, delivered a grand, solemn speech for ten whole minutes. His irrelevant ramblings had the boys doubled over with laughter, clutching their stomachs, and shouting cheers.

As soon as this was done, another stepped forward, declaring he would recite poetry in my honor. He managed to recite—well, stumble through—a few verses, some with mistakes, some with forced rhymes, but somehow he got through them. No sooner had he finished than two more boys came forward and announced, “We shall perform an Ashtavadhanam!”

Just two or three months earlier, a pair of poets had visited our village and performed impromptu poetry and an Ashtavadhanam, which had inspired some of the boys to try it themselves. Now, in this auspicious moment, they decided to put their plan into action. The audience was bubbling with enthusiasm as the two boys paced back and forth, reciting lines—one line each, here and there, as they pleased. Someone from the crowd would ask a question, and regardless of its relevance, they would answer with whatever came to mind.

This grand spectacle was in full swing when some of our teachers, followed by the headmaster himself, arrived and stood at the back. At first, no one noticed, but the moment the students realized, everyone panicked and scattered in all directions, running for their lives.

chapters.title: The Decision
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam
“What’s all this commotion, Parvateesam?” they asked.

“I have no idea, sir. I just arrived at school this very moment, after being delayed by some chores. The moment I entered, all the boys started cheering for me, made me sit here, and asked me to give a speech. Then someone else recited some poems, and now they say they’re going to hold an ‘Ashtavadhanam’ competition. Ah, very nice. I’m glad. But it seems your felicitation was interrupted midway by this avadhanam,” said my uncle.

“Never mind, we’ll arrange for another speech some other time when there’s leisure,” he said, patting my back affectionately and giving two gentle knocks on my bald head. “For now, be content with this honor,” he said, and went away.
Smiling to myself, I went on my way.

Because of all the goings-on in the village, my studies at school fell behind. The good opinion my teachers once had of me changed. Determined to teach me a lesson, they kept me in the fifth form itself. This was the first time in my life I had to repeat a class for a second year. I felt terribly ashamed and afraid.
When my father heard this auspicious news, he scolded me in every possible way: “No studies, no prayers! Four years you shone as a student in Narsapur, and now look at you—”

Enough of your mischief! If you stay at home and look after the farming, it will be a help to me, and the land will come in handy. Besides, you know a few Sanskrit verses—recite what you know. They might be useful for something. So, go to Narsapur, fetch your box and bedding,' he said.

I pleaded in every possible way, 'Let me at least somehow struggle through this year and pass Matriculation. After that, I’ll stop. I’ll be more careful from now on.' My mother, too, took my side and said, 'He only got into this mess because of the company he kept, but does he lack intelligence? Is he dumb? What mischief can he get up to sitting here at home? Let him study until he finishes that Matric class he’s talking about, then we’ll see what to do next.' She gently persuaded my father.
He sat there in silence, unable to say anything.

My mother signaled for me to go. Without wasting a moment, I set off for Narsapur in a single breath. But as soon as I arrived, I felt terribly embarrassed to go back to school and sit in the same class again. However, some of the fellows who studied with me last year were still there this year, which gave me a bit of courage.

The headmaster, instead of scolding me as before, said, 'So, Parvatisham, have you finally come to your senses this year? Have you decided to bid farewell to village affairs and study diligently? Whether you’re here or not, the meetings and events in the village won’t stop. They go on every day, whether anyone is there or not. You’ve realized by now that you gain nothing from them, and your studies here are suffering because of it. Lectures and Harikathas are not for you right now, my boy. You’re a clever lad, meant for greater things. From now on, take care and focus on your work.' He gave me this friendly advice.
I thought, 'Ah, I’m saved!' and bowed, saying, 'Yes, sir.'

My return to school was not at all to my father's liking. Unable to refuse my mother, unable to scold or beat me, he sat there in the twilight, probably brooding over me and my future. After much thought, he decided that if I got married, I might become more responsible and enthusiastic. Then, perhaps, I would remember my duties and either study carefully or—

Whether to give up and stay at home, or to make my own decisions—I imagined I would decide for myself. He must have whispered this matter into the ears of two or three people. From then on, without any effort from him, marriage proposals began to pour in. Whenever a good day was thought auspicious, someone or other would come as a prospective bride’s party, and my uncle would summon me home. I would go, they would look me over, and there would be some polite conversation. What happened afterward, I never knew, but my uncle could never finalize any alliance. The bridegroom being liked by the bride’s family was the only certainty. Why wouldn’t they like me? A youth as plump as a fruit, a man of property, with no one else to share that property. On top of that, I was in the fifth form, intelligent, clever—there was no question of them not liking me. It must have been that the girl wasn’t up to the mark, or their family customs didn’t suit us, or there was a dispute over dowry and gifts—whatever the reason, every month or two, someone would come and go. This went on for several months.

I thought this wasn’t good, and decided that somehow this business must be stopped. If I absolutely had to get married, then at least the girl must be to my liking, and for that, I insisted that I must see the bride myself. My mother agreed that this was best!

At last, as fate would have it, a bride’s party came from some village in our own district. When my uncle inquired, their circumstances and background seemed agreeable, and they promised to give a handsome dowry and gifts. The horoscopes too matched well, so after discussing, they sent me, my mother, and my maternal uncle to go and see the girl. We traveled part of the way by boat, part by cart, but even by sunset, we couldn’t reach the village. After finding out the bride’s house, we went there quietly. I don’t know whether they had been informed beforehand of our arrival, or if they simply didn’t care, but the bride’s father, it turned out, had gone off somewhere on some court business, to Eluru or somewhere else. This struck my mother as a bad omen. They seated us in the house, and my uncle went out into the street to make some inquiries about the family. The girl’s maternal uncle and aunt, who lived opposite their house, and others, seated us respectfully,

The girl's father, though delayed, would surely arrive by night, they assured us, and in the meantime, there was no objection to our seeing the girl. So, in a quarter of an hour, they adorned the bride and brought her out, seating her in the front verandah.

As we gazed upon the girl, our nerves grew weak with anticipation. The girl was slender as a reed, tall, with a dusky complexion that shone with a gentle luster. Her eyes, smaller than tamarind leaves, sparkled with a certain charm. Though she lacked the pair of ear ornaments that ought to have adorned her ears on either side, her face did not appear diminished, thanks to her broad mouth, and nostrils that occupied only half their rightful share. She wore a black skirt and blouse that matched her complexion, swaying as she moved.

To those assembled, it seemed as if we were about to faint from the suspense, when the girl's maternal uncle, a veritable army officer, brought forth a harmonium and sternly instructed the girl to sing. The girl, displaying great courage and without a trace of hesitation, raised her voice boldly and began the javali, "Ee virahamu saipajaalara" ("O friends, bear this sorrow of separation").
Oh dear! All our expectations were dashed in an instant. My uncle rushed forward and quickly clapped his hand over my mouth.
"Enough, uncle! The axe has fallen."

There was no need for my mother to say anything. Those two minutes felt like an age, weighed down by unbearable heaviness and din. Afterwards, my mother, who never spoke much, remarked, "The girl is good, son. Don't trouble her any further. What do I know of music or literature, anyway!"

“Shall we leave now, father?” she asked. At once, that girl’s maternal uncle said, “Why leave now? Brother-in-law will come tonight. See him and then go. In the meantime, you can eat and rest. When did you last eat, anyway? Get up.”

My uncle laughed and said, “Uncle, brother-in-law, have you forgotten that if you bathe after eating, the food won’t digest?” “I haven’t forgotten at all,” he replied. “That’s why I’ve made arrangements for you at our house. Please, get up now, don’t delay any further.” He led us to the house opposite and provided water for us to wash our feet and so on.

Even before we finished washing our feet, we were called for the meal. We sat in a row, with the master of the house at the head. He didn’t eat; he just sat at the leaf, serving us. The rice and curries had already gone cold. We looked at each other’s faces. Sensing this, the master of the house glared at his wife and said, “In our house, the cooking and serving take a long time, so the food is probably cold. Please don’t mind.”

My uncle, seeing the cold bottle gourd curry, raw banana curry, and ginger chutney served on the leaf, bowed his head and began eating without a word. Halfway through the meal, from inside, an old woman’s voice rang out: “Poor things, you didn’t even serve them two pieces of ariselu! You’re always like this—can’t you at least serve something sweet to the guests who’ve come to see the bride?” she scolded her daughter-in-law, and we could hear it all.

I, too, am very fond of chutney. I almost asked, “If you have any, please serve a little more,” but I swallowed the words and stuffed a big mouthful of rice instead. That made me choke and panic. My mother rubbed my back, saying, “What’s wrong, dear?” In a blink, my panic subsided, and somehow, we got up from the leaves and went outside.

They had arranged a separate room for us at the bride’s house. You might wonder why I’ve described the meal in such detail. The secret is this: the day we were fed at that house was the annual death ceremony for the master’s father. Since we arrived unexpectedly, the daughter-in-law, thinking we wouldn’t understand, served us the leftover food from the midday ritual. Except for the garelu, which were omitted—whether she didn’t know how inauspicious that was, or assumed we wouldn’t know, I cannot say. Whatever the case, that was the outcome.

chapters.title: Wedding and Departure
paragraphs: No matter how late it got into the night, the bride’s father never showed up. At dawn, we woke up and set off back to our home. They couldn’t say a word to us. Around two in the afternoon, we reached Mogalturru. All along the way, we kept recalling the incident and burst out laughing until our sides ached. My father, upon hearing everything that had happened, became furious and was about to set out to that village to curse them, but we stopped him with great difficulty.

After that, they never wrote us a reply, nor did they ever come to see us. I, relying on the support of my mother and uncles, told my father, “I won’t marry for another four years. Whatever you may think, that’s my decision. If you don’t give up on this marriage business, it’ll be very hard for me.” I said this boldly. Perhaps my father too thought it was for the best, for he didn’t say another word about it. The next day, I went to Narsapur.

This year, the exams gave me a good thrashing. I felt I couldn’t stay here any longer, nor could I bear to sit in the same class again, enduring the teachers’ endless nagging. The very thought of it made me wish I could bid farewell to my studies for good. It seemed my father, without even consulting me, had come to the same conclusion. As soon as the school reopened, I sat there one morning, torn between whether to go or to quit.
Hearing my father call, “Parvatisham, my boy!” I went out to the verandah. “What are you doing?” he asked. “School has reopened, so I was getting my things ready,” I replied.

“Listen, I’ll tell you something. You’ve been studying. I thought you’d rise up and do well through your education. But for some reason, your initial enthusiasm has faded. So, for now, give up this year. If, at some later time, your desire to study becomes strong again, you can start afresh. I say, let it go for this year. But don’t think I’m telling you to loaf around like a donkey! This year, learn two pieces of Sanskrit somehow, and read Telugu well too. After that, we’ll see. Right now, there’s no shame in stopping—after all, unless you pass B.A. and become some kind of master, there’s no real benefit, is there? When you have patience, you can continue.”
Barrister Parvateesam

As I was returning from the fields, my father said, “Come and help me a little, keep an eye on things.” Sensing my reluctance, I stood there hesitating, unable to say a word or make any decision. While I was still wavering, he said in a single breath, “Go to the field. I’m thinking of threshing a heap of grain now. Not our calves, but check the other pen, see if there are two calves there,” he told Venkata. “Go see what he’s doing,” my father said. Realizing that my schedule had been decided for me and that I had no need to think about it, I went to the field without another word.

Thus, two or three months passed by, somewhat sluggishly, but peacefully. I didn’t feel like doing anything, but I wasn’t exactly restless either—just a bit irritable now and then. In the evenings, I would stroll around Narsapur for a while. If nothing else, I’d wander about with my old friends for a bit, then sit on the banks of the Godavari, and as soon as the lamps were lit, I’d return home. But before long, days didn’t continue in this fashion.

Soon, meetings and lectures started increasing day by day in both Narsapur and Palakollu. My old friends and some elders, one morning, arrived at my house in Mogalturru in full force. Luckily for me, my father wasn’t home at the time. Among those who came was a middle-aged pleader, who said, “Well, Parvateesam, you seem to be enjoying yourself! Why have you disappeared altogether? Are you living like a retired official, or perhaps like a newly initiated householder who’s taken up asceticism, keeping away from all of us and from public life? How can that be? There’s so much work to be done by young, enthusiastic people like you. The time has come for future citizens like you to unite, pool your energies and abilities, and step into the field of action. The circumstances are very favorable for us now. The swaraj movement is surging in Bengal and sweeping across the country. Great leaders like Bipin Chandra Pal are coming to us, seeking our support. All our local leaders, starting with Bode Narayana Rao and others, are making every effort to create a suitable atmosphere to honor them and welcome them properly. Meetings are being organized in every town for public awareness. So, without the help of people like you, none of this can happen! Such a great task cannot be accomplished with mere words! All this is for shaping your future, for your...

Lives are meant to be made happy, but not for our sake, oh no! Our days are nearly over; now, your days are coming—days for you, for your happiness, for the fortune of the country. If you four join together, we are eager to stand behind you, to push you forward, to see you lead the way. All the leaders like Narayanarao Garu have come to know your name and how it became known. They have especially pleaded with you to form a voluntary service corps under your leadership, with at least a hundred members, and to give them a month’s training at once. They have sent us word to this effect. Now, there is no room for you to make some excuse and turn away. If I say I have come here solely for your sake, imagine how urgent this matter must be. If you come to Narsapur at four o’clock in the evening, we can meet and discuss how to accomplish our task, and make the necessary arrangements. I must leave in two or three days,” he said, rising to his feet. The five or six who had come with him also stood up.

I did not know what to say, what to think, or whether I even needed to express my consent. I felt as if I were suddenly growing taller, as if I were floating in the air. I stood up with them, offered a silent namaskar, and remained quiet. With a gentle smile, they placed a hand on my shoulder, led me up to the street gate, and said, “You must come exactly at four in the evening, dear. There is no room for delay. The very first thing we must learn is to begin every task at the appointed hour, without a moment’s difference, as if it were an auspicious wedding time.” With that, they climbed into their carriage.

For about five minutes, I stood there absent-mindedly, motionless, without a single thought, simply watching the departing horse-cart as it disappeared from view. Only when I heard my mother’s call from inside did I come to my senses and, as if descending from the sky, return to our house.

For the next three days, I went every evening to Narsapur to meet Pleader Ravana Rao Garu. Each day, when I arrived, ten or fifteen elders and youngsters would be sitting with him, listening with great attention to his words and advice. As I sat and listened to what they said, my mind felt as light as the wind, as if it had spread across the sky.
Barrister Parvateesam

His words would tickle you. Sometimes, he would tell stories that made everyone laugh. He would poke fun at people considered to be great elders. Listening to the variety of topics he spoke about, I would often wonder in amazement—how did he acquire such vast knowledge in just a few years, when it would take most people a lifetime? He would constantly speak about historical events and patriotic ideals.

He would insist that we must never forget our own culture. He would warn us not to blindly imitate Westerners in dress or speech. He would passionately declare that the prosperity of our country lay in the boycott of foreign goods, in fostering love and respect for indigenous products, and in increasing their use.

One day, he gathered me and about ten other young men of my age and made us sit down. He said, “We must form a volunteer corps. There will be no salaries here, nor any compulsion. Those who have a firm resolve and a spirit of service, those who are inspired to work for the nation, should come freely and join our group.
If you work, you will become the first step in building the edifice of Swarajya.

The work you have to do will not be too difficult. Your first responsibility is to organize meetings frequently in this town and in the nearby villages, and to ensure that they are conducted successfully. As for whom to invite to those meetings, and who should deliver lectures, I will take care of all that. If you are with me, I feel as strong as a mountain. If you listen attentively to the speeches of the elders from our Mahwa, you will gain a great deal of patriotism and some wisdom as well. Later, you should set up street schools here and there, at night or during the day, and teach both adults and children who are eager to learn, free of charge. I will arrange for all the expenses involved in that.

Tomorrow, let us set out, visit ten villages, and recruit a few more young men into our group. Tomorrow, Mr. Bode Narayana Rao will be coming from Brundar. He will give a lecture here. Therefore, after you all have had lunch tomorrow, come here to help with the necessary arrangements for the meeting. Now, off you go. We have to travel far, it seems," he said, dismissing us.

By the next afternoon, about ten or fifteen of us went to the pleader's house. He gave a few invitation cards to four or five people and sent them to distribute them in the village. The rest of us were sent to the venue of the meeting to arrange some chairs and tables, and to bring some mats as well. He assigned four laborers to us and told us to supervise all these arrangements carefully.

By four o'clock in the evening, we had poured four buckets of water over the ground at the meeting place, arranged the chairs and tables in one area, spread two large mats on another side, and laid out the mats. We set up ten tables near the dais, as the pleader had instructed, placed five or six chairs, a table, and two gas lamps on top of them.

From five o'clock onwards, people began to gather. Ravana Rao, seeing all these arrangements, was very pleased and said, "Parvateesham, well done! I knew you could do this. That’s why, the moment I saw you, I guessed your capability and wanted you to be the leader of this group. Now it has been proven that my guess was right. In the future, you will surely become a great leader."

All the signs of greatness are visible in you. May Lord Parameshwara bless you,’ he said, placing his hands on my shoulders, nodding once, and then, like a magician casting a spell, flashed a mesmerizing smile before walking away. I was so overwhelmed with joy, so lost in delight, that I stood there, frozen and bewildered, wondering, “Why did he say that to me? What did he see in me to speak so? Did he say it just to encourage me, or does he possess some divine vision and glimpsed my future?” Lost in such thoughts, I remained standing there for a few moments, until the increasing crowd and the rising chatter of people brought me back to my senses, and I finally moved from that spot.

Just then, Narayanarao Pantulu, whom we expected from Bandar, arrived with a retinue of fifty or sixty followers. Ravana Rao and a few other elders seated several more people on the dais, and amidst the applause of the crowd, garlanded another gentleman who had been elected as the president of the gathering. Once everyone was seated and the commotion in the hall had somewhat subsided, Ravana Rao climbed the stage, introduced the speakers to the audience, and declared the meeting open. He urged everyone to listen attentively and in silence to Pantulu’s speech, to take to heart the lessons he would impart, and to conduct ourselves accordingly, assuring that if we did so, the nation would have a bright future. With that, he stepped down from the dais.

The meeting began with the chanting of the Vedas. Narayanarao spoke with such gravity and resonance that his words seemed to echo through the entire town, holding everyone’s attention for more than two hours. The audience listened in such rapt silence that not even the faintest whisper of a fly could be heard, and at the end, they erupted in thunderous applause like the roar of the ocean. With that, the meeting concluded.

As for me, I had no idea what I was doing. Once again, I rounded up ten young men and some laborers, shouting instructions to pack up the tables, chairs, and other items, and sent everyone off to their respective homes. It was nearly nine o’clock by the time I reached home. How I got there—whether by cart, on foot, with my eyes open or closed, walking in my sleep, or floating in the air like a yogi flying through the sky—I could not tell. My mother and father had been anxiously searching for me, wondering what had become of me and why I hadn’t returned. The moment my mother saw me, she exclaimed with great relief and joy, “What happened, dear? Why are you so late?” My father, as usual, said nothing.

chapters.title: Farewell
paragraphs: I didn’t say anything; instead, I recounted the details of the meeting that took place in Narsapur, summarizing the speech delivered there. My father listened to everything without uttering so much as a “Hmm” or “Ah,” and then, without a word, got up and went to bed. I went for my meal. As I was eating, my mother said, “Why do you keep running to all these meetings until late in the evening, my boy? You should either focus on your studies, help with the household, or assist your father with the farm work.” I guessed these were my father’s opinions, relayed through her, so I quickly finished my meal and went to bed without saying a word. That night, I lay awake, turning over the day’s events in my mind, recalling every detail, pondering everything, until I didn’t know whether I was awake, asleep, or dreaming—so passed the night.

The whole night went by in a haze of thoughts and dreams, and I couldn’t tell if I had slept or not. By dawn, I got up, finished my morning ablutions, and saw that my father had already bathed and was about to sit down for his prayers. Seeing me, he said, “Ah, you’re up? Listen, go to the fields today.” And from that moment, for the next fifteen days, he kept me so busy with one task after another that I barely had time to catch my breath. From then on, I guessed, the message was clear: I was to give up meetings and gatherings and stay put at home. I said nothing. He sat in silence, chanting his prayers. I sat down for my breakfast, and as soon as I finished, I set off for the fields.

But though my body was in the fields, my mind was nowhere near the work. My head was still back in Narsapur. I sat there, half-heartedly supervising the workers, my thoughts drifting to yesterday’s speeches, the leaders, and the events of the day before. Try as I might, I couldn’t shake it off.

Barely a week had passed in this fashion when one day, Mr. Ravana Rao came by and told me, “Open Chandrapal, a great leader from Bengal, is coming. We need to make grand arrangements for the meeting. There are indications that at least ten thousand people will attend, so unless you come and take charge of the preparations, the meeting will be a disaster.” Hearing this, my throat went dry. Should I go?

To go or not to go? If I went, all the work here would be neglected, and my father would surely be angry. If I didn’t go, poor Mr. Ravanarao, who was waiting for me with so much trust and hope, would be disappointed. Never mind disappointment—if I didn’t go, who else would take care of all the arrangements there with such care? These thoughts kept swirling in my mind. One morning, after entrusting all the farm work to a servant and eating a hearty meal, I slipped away to Narsapuram without telling a soul.

I met Mr. Ravanarao and poured out all my troubles to him near his house. He listened with great sympathy and said, “My boy, once you’ve taken up such a responsibility, you must never turn back. We can think about everything else at leisure, but this meeting will only be successful if you take it up yourself. So, you must come and fulfill your duty, no matter what. Such difficulties are bound to arise. There’s not much time left until the event, so let’s meet every day at some hour and make the necessary arrangements. Go on now,” he said, patting me on the back and sending me off.

With a surge of enthusiasm, thinking that if we didn’t face obstacles and shoulder responsibilities, the country itself would be doomed, I hurried home, filled with both excitement and fear. From then on, every day at some hour, I would go to Narsapuram, consult with Mr. Ravanarao, and continue making arrangements there. My father kept a watchful eye on all this, but not once did he ask me what was going on. I didn’t tell him either.

At last, the day of the meeting arrived. Early that morning, I ate my rice and told my mother I wouldn’t be home until night. She started to say something, but I didn’t listen and dashed off to Narsapuram. Reaching there in a flurry, Mr. Ravanarao, I, and the other committee members toiled away until evening, making grand arrangements.

At noon, I ate a few mouthfuls at Mr. Ravanarao’s house itself. Then, returning to the meeting venue, we finished the preparations by about five o’clock. There wasn’t even a moment to catch my breath; we had to work non-stop. Still, I managed to complete all the arrangements most satisfactorily.

chapters.title: The Journey Begins
paragraphs: The leader, whom we expected to arrive by around six o’clock, only came and started the meeting at seven. The estimate that ten thousand people would attend, as predicted by Mr. Ravanarao, was utterly surpassed. It looked as if fifty thousand, or even a hundred thousand, had gathered—the entire field, as far as the eye could see, was packed so densely with people that not even a grain of sand could have found space to fall. Mr. Paul delivered a magnificent speech. Never in my life had I heard such an address! In fact, I doubted I ever would again. I felt that the echoes of that speech would ring in my ears for the rest of my life.

For nearly two hours, Mr. Paul spoke in a language unknown to the crowd, but another Telugu leader translated as he went along. Yet, not a single person stirred, not a whisper was heard, not even a breath seemed to escape—so solemn was the silence with which those thousands listened to the speech. It was an unforgettable, indelible scene in my life. For about ten minutes, the air was rent with applause so thunderous it seemed the very sky had drawn near, and thus the meeting concluded.

By the time I reached home, it was about ten o’clock. My mother was sitting at the entrance of the street, waiting anxiously for me. As I walked home, seeing the crowd following behind me, it felt as though the entire village had attended the meeting. I came home, bathed, and ate my meal in silence, answering none of my mother’s questions, and went straight to bed. My father, who usually stayed awake until then, did not get up to see me. He did not speak a word to me. Deciding that thunder, lightning, and storms would not arrive until morning, I slept peacefully.

Morning came. I woke up, bathed, and finished my breakfast of curd rice. My father, having finished his prayers, was waiting for me. Everything seemed calm, but the gravity on his face was quite terrifying. In his usual slow manner, he asked, “You were nowhere to be seen last night. Where did you go?”
“I went to Narsapuram,” I replied.
“Why?” he asked.
At that point, I realized there was no escaping the explanation, and so, two or three...

For years now, I have briefly described the meetings and events that have been taking place in Narsapur under the guidance of Mr. Ravanarao. I then spoke openly and without any pretense about my acquaintance with him, the affection he had for me, the encouragement he gave, and the work I was doing in these meetings.

My father listened to all this in silence for a moment, then said, “Have you really thought this through, this work you are doing? What benefit is it bringing you? All I can see is loss. Your studies have been neglected. Instead of sitting comfortably at home and minding your own business, you’re spending your time organizing these meetings. It’s high time you realized there’s nothing in it for you. Just because they praise you a little, you get puffed up and start dancing to their tune. After all these years of running after them, you’re only good for arranging tables and chairs—nothing else. If you had thought about this even a little, you would have realized this secret long ago.

So, even now, if you can bring yourself to your senses and reflect on all the work you’ve done in the past three years, you’ll see that every word I’ve said is true. Working for the country, uplifting the nation—

I do not deny that such lofty matters are indeed noble ideals. However, without higher learning, greater intellect, broader imagination, and a certain degree of perseverance, even the smallest task becomes impossible to accomplish.

Whether you wish to take up a job, serve the nation, or even if you simply desire to expand your knowledge for its own sake, never forget that education is absolutely essential. I have always hoped that, sooner or later, you would come to realize this truth on your own. But seeing you still wandering about like this, I am now telling you plainly: if you continue in this manner, you will never understand it. Even now, awaken yourself, decide for yourself what kind of education you desire, and make an earnest effort to pursue it.

You are an intelligent young man. There is no need for me to say more than this.” So saying, my father, without another word, without even asking for my opinion, quietly went off to the fields. I abandoned my intention to go outside, sat at home, and, lost in thought, could not bring myself to read any book. I did not see my father again. Thus, sitting and pondering, on the fourth evening I went to visit Ravana Rao garu in Narsapuram.

“Well, Parvateesham, what news? The other day, the meeting was such a grand success—don’t think I’m praising you to your face, but I have been watching all your efforts. You worked yourself to exhaustion, got entangled, and were nearly cut in half,” he said. “So, what else is new? Why are you so silent? Say something!” he added with a laugh.

I told him everything that had happened at home and asked for his advice. He paused for a moment and said, “Everything your father said is true—how can I deny it? Without education, how will knowledge come? I have long intended to explain these matters to you calmly and kindly one day. Your father has relieved me of that duty. He is an elder, a scholar, and knowledgeable in many matters. That education is essential is beyond dispute. The only question is: what kind of education? In my opinion, it would not be good for you to rejoin high school. Instead, study some Sanskrit and Telugu at home; afterwards, I will give you some books on social and political subjects. You can read those as well, and then, gradually, we can consider other subjects.”

chapters.title: Voyage to England
paragraphs: They said so. After exchanging a few more words, they took their leave.

When I reached home and pondered over all that they had said, I realized just how far-sighted my father’s advice had been. Following the method suggested by both of them, I began my new studies. I would frequently travel to Narsapur, meet with Mr. Ravanarao and other friends, and learn about new things. I was able to read many different kinds of books given to me by Mr. Ravanarao. I came to know about many topics that I had neither known nor imagined before. Whenever I had doubts, Mr. Ravanarao would clear them up for me.

Reading all these books on politics and society only increased my restlessness. When I read some books about religion, I developed a certain tolerance towards other faiths, but at the same time, a bit of anger would also arise. In Narsapur and the surrounding villages, Christian proselytizing was both rampant and, to me, quite distasteful. Their words, their teachings, and their methods of preaching were all deeply troubling. Many such small and big incidents combined to stir up unrest within me, and day by day, my mental turmoil only grew. In this way, about one or two years passed.

Four or five times, when I went to see Mr. Ravanarao, I had the chance to meet four distinguished gentlemen who had come there from Guntur. Through them, I first heard about going abroad, about studying there, and the various benefits that could come from it. I would often think about these things. Finally, one day, at Mr. Ravanarao’s house, I met a pleader. After speaking with him, and on his advice, I resolved to go to London to study law and become a barrister. From that moment, my determination only grew stronger with each passing day. At last, I made up my mind, and one fine day, I arranged for an auspicious time to set out on my journey.

[Our home is at Mogalithurru, near Narsapur. Our family name is Vemuru. My name is Parvateesam. I studied up to the fifth form at Taylor High School. For one or two years, I had to remain in the same class due to various reasons. After that, here—

The education at the local school was hardly satisfactory. The teachers themselves had no real understanding of what they were teaching. In my opinion, it was a waste of both money and time. So, I gave up my studies. Since my elders had already amassed some property, I thought it best to live comfortably and idly at home, pondering the changing times and the state of the world.

While I was thus occupied, one day a friend of mine came by and, in the course of conversation, earnestly advised me to go to England for further studies. After he left, I spent a long time thinking about the prospect of traveling to England—its advantages and disadvantages, the hardships and comforts. I reasoned with myself in every possible way and concluded that traveling abroad would be beneficial. Moreover, I thought that visiting the land of our rulers, observing their customs and ways, and secretly learning their methods would be useful for attaining self-rule. With that in mind, I resolved to go there and study law to become a barrister.

My father was a farmer; he was uneducated—a simple, uncivilized man. I felt that if I told him about my plans, he would not grasp their significance. So, without telling him, I borrowed some money from a friend, told my family I was going to Narsapur and would return in four days, and set off.

My knowledge of the journey to England came from a chapter I had read in a book as a child, and later from my study of geography. So, I knew the route to that country. But as for what things I should take with me, or how I should conduct myself there, there was no one to tell me. I considered asking one of the English officers in Narsapur, but then thought they might laugh at my ignorance, so I abandoned that idea. Instead, relying on my natural shrewdness, I decided to take with me whatever items seemed necessary, thinking that anything else I needed could be bought on the way or after I arrived there. Thus, I resolved not to waste money unnecessarily here, but to carefully consider and decide what was truly essential.
Barrister Parvateesam

No matter how long I thought about it, I couldn’t come up with anything definite. I figured that if I started somewhere, everything else I needed would fall into place. So, as soon as I woke up, I wrote down a list of necessary items.
For brushing my teeth: ten sticks of ground tooth powder, and for scraping my tongue, a few pieces of palm leaf. A brass tumbler. After brushing, of course, comes bathing.

For that, I’d need two towels for wiping myself; after the bath, a little coconut oil in a bottle to apply to my head; a local wooden comb for combing my hair; a bit of sandalwood paste in a coconut shell for putting a dot on my forehead; a small mirror, bought for a quarter rupee, to look at my face.
Next, I had to think about clothes! For that, I thought I’d need four twill shirts; two ties; two pairs of woolen socks; one and a half pairs of boots—
