Since suits were necessary there, and as it was a cold country, even after spending ten whole rupees, because the cloth was of slightly better quality, the tailor kept back a little for himself, and as a result, the two pairs of trousers and suits I got were barely enough for me. Even so, I wondered why, after going all the way to England, I should completely abandon our traditional attire. So, as far as possible, I decided to stick to our native customs. For use as a turban, I bought eight yards of bright red Japanese silk. As for the rest of the clothes, I thought, “What’s really important is food, isn’t it?”

For that, I needed a brass tumbler to drink water. After reaching there, I thought it would be best if I cooked for myself, rather than eat food prepared by others and risk breaking my Hindu dietary rules.

After all, rice wouldn’t be easily available there! Since I’d have to make do with rotis, I packed some wheat flour, a little ghee, some mango pickle to go with the rotis, a small griddle for making them, a stove, kerosene for the stove, and a small bottle of spirit. Once I had sorted out the cooking supplies, I turned my attention to bedding. Since I was going to a cold country, sleeping on the floor would be difficult. So, I took along a folding cot from Narasaraopet, and for it, the pillow I usually used at home—homemade—and an orange-colored shawl to cover myself.

Then I wondered if there was anything else I might need. It struck me that it would be nice to take a folding chair for sitting during the day. Since I had no intention of acting against my Hindu faith after reaching there, and fearing I wouldn’t find them abroad, I thought it absolutely necessary to take along six sets of sacred threads and three silk waistbands.

No matter how much more I thought, I couldn’t think of anything else I needed to take. Some people might find all this a bit excessive, but after all, I was going to a distant land. If I forgot even the smallest thing, it would be a real nuisance there. Being a person who’s always been extra cautious from the very beginning, I packed all these things after much deliberation.
Now, to carry all these items—whether I found a porter or not wherever I went—I had a small tin trunk made, painted with marigold flowers, so that it would be easy for me to carry everything myself.
Barrister Parvateesam

I had my hair dyed. I packed all these items carefully into a box, chose an auspicious day, made sure there were no taboos, and waited at the threshold until the omens turned favorable. Then, I climbed into the cart and set off for the boat jetty.

Except for Mogalituru, Narsapuram, and two or three nearby villages, I had never traveled anywhere before. Even though I had lived in Narsapuram for so long, I had never needed to board a boat. Today, sitting in the boat as it moved along, I felt a great thrill. I thought to myself, “So this is what traveling by steamer must feel like!”

At night, on the journey, I munched on black gram rotis and fried chickpeas, wondering whether they would have black gram rotis in England or not. As I ate, I pondered how I might serve my country after returning from England, and with these thoughts, I fell asleep. By dawn, the boat had reached Nidadavolu.

As soon as I woke up, I remembered the great mission I had set out upon, heaved a long sigh, got off the boat, and hurried to the railway station. There, I approached a distinguished-looking man standing nearby and said, “Please give me a ticket quickly.”
“What’s the rush? Where to? For which train?” he began to question.
Why should he care where I was going? If I told him all my business, my secret would be out.
“Never mind all that now—just give me the ticket quickly,” I replied.
He looked at me with a smirk and said, “The ticket clerk hasn’t arrived yet. Wait a little.”
After some time, when I learned that the ticket clerk had arrived, I went over and asked for a ticket. He too asked, “To where?”
“I’ll tell you, just give me the ticket,” I said.
“What’s this nonsense! Where are you headed, man?”
Everyone nearby started laughing.

“Where do you think you are! You behave as if you’re in some backwater village! If you don’t say where you want to go, how on earth am I supposed to give you a ticket? Off with you, you seem to have no sense at all. All these people are waiting,” he shouted.
Everyone nearby began to scold me.

“This train travels a long distance, sir. It stops at many places. That’s why, if you tell them which town you want to go to, they’ll give you a ticket to that place,” an elderly gentleman advised me calmly and kindly.
His words seemed reasonable to me. So, turning to the man issuing tickets, I said, “I want to go to Chennapatnam.”

At once, he glared at me and said, “What’s this, man? Where have you come from this morning? You’re behaving just like a dumb animal! Go on, get moving! Everyone’s waiting. Why are you standing there gaping like that when I tell you to go? The city train won’t come till evening, man. Until then, go find a place to sit and doze somewhere,” he said.

The people around me all pushed me aside. Well, I thought I’d wait until the crowd thinned out a bit and try again. But just as I was about to go back, the train bell rang. Then I asked again, “Sir, when will the city train come?”
“In the evening,” he replied.
“Oh, so I have to wait till evening! But I have urgent business!”

He looked at my face and said, “Oh! You’re back again? If you’re in such a hurry, why don’t you walk?” With that, he shut the ticket window and went off in style. Maybe he was angry with me, so this time I decided to ask slowly and find out the truth. I went up to him, stood right in front of him, and opened my mouth to speak, but even before I could, he started off: “You’re back again to find out when the city train comes! If I tell you once, isn’t that enough? Don’t you have any sense?”
I already have a dislike for people who shout, and on top of that, his face was covered in ugly black pockmarks, making him look even more unpleasant. I didn’t even know how to respond.

As I slowly began to ask him about the matter, I grew irritated, thinking he might speak without any manners. For a moment, I considered saying, “I am going to England. Be careful!” But then I thought it wouldn’t be right to make him cry any more than this.
So instead, I said, “Oh no, I didn’t come here to ask about the train at all, sir. I just came to tell you what your face reminds me of.”
“What does my face remind you of?” he asked.
“When I look at your face, I’m reminded of a stone that’s been chiseled by a mason. And when I look at your head, I’m reminded of a lump of lime,” I replied.
The servants standing nearby burst into laughter. The man, embarrassed and angry, came at me to hit me, but I ran away.

From there, I quietly made my way to a nearby hotel, had my meal, and took a short nap. After waking up, I thought I’d take one last look at the bazaar before leaving. As I wandered here and there, I suddenly remembered I’d forgotten two essential items: a small brass lock for my room, and a coir rope to hang my clothes after bathing, along with four large clothespins to fasten them.
I bought these three items, returned to my lodging, and as evening fell, had a hearty meal and went to the station. It was time to buy the tickets.
Once again, I bought a ticket to Chennapatnam. As I reached the platform, a train arrived. I spotted a porter and asked him, “Can I board this train?”
“Where are you going?” he replied.
“What’s it to you!” I retorted, walking away briskly.

There was a distinguished-looking gentleman nearby, so I asked him, too—can I board this train? He posed the same question: “Are you going to that town?” Annoyed, I decided not to waste any more words and quietly went up to the station master himself.

He, too, asked, “Where are you going?” I explained that unless I told them the name of my destination, they wouldn’t even sell me a ticket. But why all these interrogations even after I’d bought the ticket? To put an end to their pestering, I said, “Rajahmundry.” He replied, “Yes, you can board.”

So, I got on. The train was about to move. The station master was still standing there as the train started to pull out. I called out to him, “Sir! You must be punished for this. I’m not going to Rajahmundry—I’m going to Chennapatnam!” I said, laughing.
He immediately blew his whistle and stopped the train, telling me to get down. I refused.
“Hurry up and get down! You’re causing a delay.”
“Why should I get down?”
“This train doesn’t go to Chennapatnam. Another one will come. You’re standing there like a fool. Get down!”
“Don’t call me a fool or a ghoul! I won’t get down,” I insisted.

At this, everyone in the compartment burst out laughing. Just then, the guard arrived and forcibly made me get off. The train left. Tears welled up in my eyes. The station master, feeling a bit sorry for me, consoled me by saying that the train to Chennapatnam would arrive in another quarter of an hour.
Sure enough, in just about the time he said, the train arrived. With many stops and starts, I hoisted my luggage onto the compartment directly ahead...

I tried to climb up with my luggage. I had just stepped onto the first step and was about to place my foot on the second when someone from behind gave me a shove. Startled by the sudden push, the luggage I was carrying on my head tumbled off, landing first on the head of the person behind me, and, not stopping even there, crashed down with a thud onto someone’s feet below. I turned around to check on my luggage, but in that very instant, my hand slipped and I fell onto the person behind me, who, along with me, toppled onto the people behind him.

Instead of feeling sorry for us for having fallen, everyone started scolding us. Some even walked right over me and boarded the train. I got up, calmly gathered my belongings, and thought to myself that I could check later on the train where all I had been bruised, so I boarded first.

Once inside, I was trying to stow my luggage overhead when, with a sudden jerk, the train started moving. I lost my balance and fell right into the lap of a woman sitting on the bench behind me. She leapt up with four blessings (of the choicest kind) and sprang forward. In the process, I landed on a gentleman on the opposite bench who was blissfully smoking a cigar, his eyes half-closed in contentment. The cigar jabbed my cheek, making it sting sharply. I let out a yelp. The gentleman, roused from his state of bliss, seemed to wonder why his happiness had suddenly become so heavy. With a loud yell, he shoved me away as one would push off a snake that had fallen on them.

I nearly toppled onto a little child in front of me, and, fearing I might crush her, somehow managed to avoid her and instead landed on her mother. When that lady too tried to push me off, I clung tightly to her neck. By now, everyone in the compartment had started laughing so hard their sides must have ached.

That girl’s husband was sitting right beside her. He jumped up in fury, separated me and his wife as if we were two squabbling children, and began scolding me. I pleaded, trembling, that it was not my fault, that I had no idea she was his wife, and that I would never do such a thing again. I joined my hands and begged his pardon.

The rest of the passengers, taking pity on me, began to scold the girl’s husband instead, saying that it wasn’t my fault, that I had only hugged her by mistake, that mistakes can happen to anyone, that today it was me, tomorrow someone else might (by mistake) end up hugging someone. For such a small matter—
There was really no need for Kayan to get so angry, and with a few words meant to soothe his temper, we managed to calm down that great man.

Perhaps fearing whom I might embrace next if I kept standing, they finally gave me a little space to sit. On the upper berth, I placed my box, spread out my folding bed and mat, and, seeing a chain nearby, I tied everything together with the rope I’d bought that evening, pulling it tight and securing it well. Now that my luggage was safe, I sat down comfortably, thinking there was nothing more to worry about.
Just then, for some reason, the train came to a halt.

Everyone peered out curiously. In another moment, two guards entered our compartment and asked who had chained up their luggage. No one spoke. They looked up, spotted my belongings, and, pointing at them, asked, “Whose luggage is this?”
My heart skipped a beat, wondering what new trouble I had landed myself in now. Trembling, I replied, “It’s mine.”
“Why did you chain it up like that?”
“So that, with the jostling of the train, it wouldn’t fall down. I tied it up carefully to keep it safe.”
Everyone in the compartment burst out laughing for no reason. The guard said I would have to pay a fifty-rupee fine. “I don’t have anything with me, I can’t pay. Please forgive me,” I pleaded.
In the end, after much back and forth, they finally let me off with a warning, telling me to untie my luggage and remove the chain.
After they left, the person next to me explained what my mistake had been.

I found out by asking. I wondered, “If you pull the chain a little, does the train really stop like that?” After a while, the train stopped again. Some people got off at my compartment, and a few others got in. After waiting a bit, the train started off once more.

Next to me sat a Brahmin widow, about forty years old, with her back turned toward me, her legs stretched out onto the bench. After a while, she began to nod off. As I pondered over our country’s poverty, the ignorance of the people, the miserable plight of widows, and such matters, I kept wondering when this nation would ever improve. Still, I consoled myself that better times were approaching. I would return home in three or four years and rid the country of these troubles, I thought, and with such noble intentions, I too fell asleep. I had all sorts of dreams.

After some time, I woke up. I realized that the Brahmin widow beside me had slid over and had been sleeping soundly all this while. She was still asleep, I suppose—how would I know? As I stood up, she toppled over onto me. She tried to get up, muttering, “Govinda, Govinda,” but fell back again. As she made another attempt to rise, I, fearing she might fall once more, placed my hand gently on her back and helped her up a little.

Instead of being pleased that she had managed to get up with my help, she snapped at me angrily, “What’s this, boy? Can’t you sit a little farther away? What if you hadn’t moved? Don’t you have any siblings? Isn’t it enough that I set out from home alone? My whole life has been like this—always alone. I set out for Tirupati today, thinking at least I wouldn’t run into anyone I know on the way, but now I have to endure all these troubles!”
If only that Maharaja were still alive, I wouldn’t be suffering like this! But alas, he’s passed on to heaven.

Whenever you travel by train at night, if you don’t take care, you’ll fall ill. “Somehow, make yourself comfortable and try to rest your back,” she said, alternately adjusting her spectacles and wiping her nose, before resuming her dozing and fidgeting.
I felt the urgent need to relieve myself. But where to go, what to do—I had no idea. If only the train would stop for a moment! I thought I could get down, go, and return.

I considered pulling the chain, but then remembered the five-rupee fine and quietly went near the window, shouting to the guard to stop the train for a moment. My cries fell on deaf ears, and my stomach was about to burst. I was at my wits’ end.

A gentleman sitting nearby noticed my distress. I told him my predicament: “I shouted, but no one responded. What should I do?” He laughed and said, “My boy, you look like a complete novice! There’s a room right here in the train for such needs. Whether you need to go for number one or number two, you can use that room,” and he pointed it out to me.

I went, returned, and after sitting for a while, dozed off. By dawn, the train was stopping nicely at every station; there was ample convenience for both those boarding and those alighting, so that passengers didn’t have to get down unnecessarily. There was a lavatory in the train itself, and at every station, all the essential items for travelers were being sold. All these arrangements were excellent, I thought. No wonder the English have become so great!

While I was thinking thus, at about nine in the morning, we reached a station called Basin Bridge. I stood watching the people getting off at the station. A black sahib came up to me and asked for my ticket. I handed it to him. He looked at it, said nothing, and put it in his pocket. What’s this? He’s taking my ticket away! Should I at least ask him firmly—though he’s dark-skinned, he’s still a sahib! What about me? In my confusion, I followed him and pleaded, “Please give me back my ticket!” He...
He told me to get lost, quite angrily. No matter how much affection I had for him, the ticket had already ended up in his hands. So, swallowing my pride, I followed him.
At last, it was time for the train to depart. Another four or five Englishmen joined us. “Please, help me get my ticket back,” I pleaded.
“Get away, man, you seem to be a fool,” one of them said.
“Sir, just get me my ticket and you can call me whatever you like. They won’t give me my ticket, and on top of that, they’re abusing me!” I said, my temper rising.
The train whistled.
“Get in, man! You have no bloody fear. Nobody will ask you,” he said, pushing me into the compartment.

The train started moving. There was nothing else I could do. All those Englishmen at the station were clutching their stomachs, laughing heartily. I tried to get down, but the gentleman next to me stopped me and asked what the matter was. I explained to him how my ticket had been taken and not returned. He laughed and told me that the next station was Channapatna, and everyone would get down there, so there was no need to worry. All the tickets would be collected at this station itself.

He assured me that there was nothing to fear. Since he said that everyone had already handed over their tickets, I thought, “Why should I be scared when no one else is?” and sat down with renewed courage.
In no time, we reached Channapatna.

As soon as the train screeched to a halt, a hundred porters swarmed into the compartment, shouting, “Any luggage, sir?” Balancing my trunk on my head, I too clambered down. Instantly, a crowd of twenty porters surrounded me, each insisting, “Let me carry it!” and began tugging at the box on my head. They started quarreling among themselves, and after a brief scuffle, one fellow managed to snatch my trunk and bolted off. Fearing he might run away with my luggage, I dashed after him and caught up. He wouldn’t stop when I asked, nor would he say how much he wanted. Calmly, he carried the box to the bullock cart stand and set it down.

Now, about twenty cart drivers gathered around me. “Where to, sir? Come with me! I’ll take you quickly!” they clamored, each one grabbing at my luggage, trying to drag it away. I had no idea where to go. I didn’t know a soul in this place. I thought perhaps I should go to a hotel, but I didn’t know the names of any hotels or even the streets. Deciding it was best to escape this chaos first, I sat down on my trunk and declared, “I’m not going anywhere. I don’t need a cart.” Still, they seemed convinced that I would eventually need one. They simply wouldn’t leave me alone.

“Why are you so angry, sir? Take whichever cart you like. How long will you walk in this heat? We’ll take you safely, sir,” they pleaded, standing their ground. Meanwhile, the porter who had carried my luggage was pestering me for his wage.
“How much should I give you?” I asked.
“What, sir? You’re asking me? Don’t you know?” he replied.
“I told you I don’t know,” I said.
“Come on, sir, don’t joke. Just pay and let me go,” he insisted.
Thinking half an anna wouldn’t suffice, I took out two annas and told him to take it. He looked at me, then at the money, and—
“What’s this, sir? What do you mean? Do you think I’m a miser or something? Why are you handing me just two annas as if I’m a beggar?” I said.
I was dumbfounded and thought, “Well, if I give him more, he’ll call me a miser anyway! Do these misers in this town get only coins and quarters? What’s going on here, tell me!”
“Well then, how much do you want to give?” he asked.
“One rupee.”

My heart shattered; but I took out another two annas and put them in his hand, saying, “Fine, take it and go.” He tried to pawn his service to me, insisting that he wouldn’t take even a damidi less than a rupee. I told him, “If you don’t want it, just leave it.” I thought, “He’s acting so high and mighty, maybe he’ll refuse to take it.” But no, instead he started abusing me. The cart drivers standing around began to pass judgment. I thought, “Why argue with this fellow?” and gave him yet another quarter anna.

At first, he refused to take even that, and proceeded to insult me, my face, my nose, my mouth, my character, all other Andhras, and the entire Andhra region in one sweeping tirade. Then, after all that, he pocketed the half-rupee and strutted away.

I was relieved to have shaken off one misfortune. Now I wondered how I would enter the town. Some of the cart drivers were still standing around me. I asked them, “Is there any hotel or choultry in this town where I can stay?”
“There is, sir, right nearby—the Ramasami Mudaliar Choultry, sir.”
“Do they have rooms and such there? Is it convenient for bathing and so on?”
“Everything is there, sir. It’s very comfortable, sir.”
“And what about meals?”
“They’ll cook rice and serve it right there, sir.”
Meals

I asked, “If I bring my own rice, will they cook it for me and serve it? Or what do they do?” He replied, “That’s not it, sir. Even the meal hotels are close to the choultry, aren’t they?” I said, “Is that so? Please explain.” He elaborated, acting it out for ignorant fellows like me to understand: “That’s what I was saying, sir. In the choultry, they serve rice too. But you have to bring your own curry.”

I then asked how much I should pay for the cart. “Three rupees.” “How far is it from here?” “About two miles.” “Three rupees for just two miles? I won’t pay that.” “Have mercy, sir. We only quoted the usual fare. Tell me how much you’ll give.” “I’ll give one rupee.” “Oh, sir! How can you say that? Do you think this is a village town? Do you think it’s like the countryside? Sir, that won’t do. Did you see the horse? It won’t even walk properly.”

We still had plenty to do, so I said, “Let’s not waste time, I’ll give you another half rupee if you go quickly.” “Sir, are you giving just half a rupee extra just for bringing you from the train station to here? It’s two miles, sir. Both the horse and I have to survive, you know.”
“How now, sir! Why bargain with me, sir? Don’t you know the fare? Just give me two rupees. Where are you from?”

Even as I was thinking of refusing, he tossed my luggage into the cart and told me to get in. I considered that what he said was reasonable, so without a word, I climbed in. No sooner had I sat down than the other cart drivers began to shout that they would take me for just one rupee. Realizing I’d been tricked, I thought of getting down, but my cart driver, cursing the others and warning me never to trust such people, set off at a furious pace. The road was rough, and after a morning of fruitless bargaining, and fearing that the others might throw me out, I decided to stick with him. Pondering my misfortune, I pleaded with him to go slowly, but in ten minutes, he dropped me off near the choultry.

I wondered if we had really covered two miles already, but then consoled myself that, in a city, distances are hard to judge. The horse had brought me swiftly, so I was pleased and handed the cart driver two annas. He begged for another anna for a long while, then, growing angry, cursed me roundly and left.

The choultry was teeming with people. I wondered why so many outsiders had gathered here. I went inside. There, squatting on his haunches, knees drawn up, hair tied in a knot, oil streaming down from his head onto his face, black and stout as a stone idol, sat a man. He fixed his legs to the left, stared at me askance, and asked, “Enna venum?” (“What do you want?”)
“I don’t know what you just said, but first, I need a room,” I replied.
“Oh, is that so! Are you a Brahmin or not? Where are you from? How many days will you stay? Where are you going? Why have you come to this town?” he began his interrogation.
“We are Brahmins. As for the rest, why do you need to know? If you have a room, give it to me. If not, tell me whom I should ask.”
“You seem to be a rather stubborn fellow! How can I give you a room if you don’t say how many days you’ll stay? No room for more than three days!”
“I won’t stay even three days. In fact, I’ll be leaving this evening or tomorrow.”
“Alright then. You can stay in this room,” he said, showing me a room.

I entered the room, secured my belongings, and came out. After bathing, I draped myself in my traditional attire, adorned my forehead with a bindi, picked up my brass tumbler, and walked into the dining hall. There, everyone was eating in shirts and coats. Some of the servers were even serving food in their vests. Witnessing all this impropriety, I lost all appetite for food. But with no other option, I went and sat at an empty spot.
Both the diners and the servers began to snicker at me. I thought, “Why bother about them?” and took my seat as usual, preparing to eat.

Even as the serving was still going on, the Tamilians sitting in my row began to eat pieces of curry directly with their mouths. As soon as the serving was done, a man hurriedly went around, serving each person two ladles of ghee. Some of the Tamilians sitting next to me grabbed the ghee with their hands and gulped it down. I wondered, “Why are they drinking it like that?” Some mixed it into a single morsel and ate the rice with just that ghee! I tried it too. The ghee had such a foul smell, yet they were drinking it as if it were nectar; I thought, “If they ever got a taste of homemade clarified butter, they’d probably gulp it down like cool water from a tumbler.”

While the ghee was still being served, another man brought in sambar. No one mixed it with dal. No one mixed it with curry. No one mixed it with chutney; nothing at all. First, they poured sambar over their rice, then mixed in some dal. They ate plain rice without ghee, and mixed the curry and chutney right into it. What kind of wild food is this! Poor fellows, they don’t even know how to eat properly, I thought, feeling sorry for them. I, on the other hand, neatly mixed my dal; when it came time for sambar, everyone turned pale and stared at me. They say a crow in a cuckoo’s form looks quite odd and its voice is harsh. In the same way, to these Tamilians’ eyes…
I appeared to them as nothing but a complete barbarian—what’s so surprising about that! To a madman, the whole world seems mad.

Afterwards, I mixed my rice. Once I had done so, I asked the server, “Please bring me some ghee.” Is it a crime to add a little ghee to one’s rice? He brought it over and declared, “That’s extra, sir!”
“This ghee?”
“What’s extra about it, you rice-monger!”
“Now you’re taking another spoonful, aren’t you? That’s one anna extra, sir.”
“Is that so? And what do you say to that?”
“Shall I serve it, sir?”

“Of course, serve it! Or did you think I called you over to admire your dazzling beauty rather than to get some ghee?” What I said seemed to go completely over his head. The poor fellow just smiled a little and said, “Oh sir, why are you teasing me so much?”

He must have thought I was praising him somehow. It reminds me of a story: once, a Deputy Collector told an innocent clerk, “You look just like a fool.” The clerk, thinking he was being complimented, replied, “As you wish, sir! What a blessing to receive the favor of my superiors! All the great men say the same about me.” That’s exactly the sort of fellow this server is.

Once everyone else had finished eating their curry and rice, they served themselves some rasam. I couldn’t help but laugh at their sequence of eating—curry or rasam, one or the other, but both? What’s going on in their heads?

Well! Why should I care how they eat? I quickly stuffed two more mouthfuls into my mouth and got up. Looking around at the whole scene, I felt as if I hadn’t eaten at all. Everything seemed so improper. Eating rice with their hands, dipping their fingers in the ghee and buttermilk, and then, with those same hands, pouring themselves drinking water. The place where they washed their hands was littered with grains of rice—it was all so unhygienic and disorderly. I wondered how these people could stand such filth.

After finishing my meal, I returned to Nagad’s place, rested for a while, put on my shirt, and set out towards the town. At that time, I used to have a hair knot and wear a giraja (sacred thread). I had them removed, bought a hat like the Englishmen wear, and decided to look into the matter of trains afterward.

As soon as I stepped onto the street, I saw trains running down the middle of the road without any engines. In the morning, I had asked the cart driver what those were, and he told me they were “tramcars.” Apparently, they didn’t have stations or anything of the sort; they stopped wherever one pleased. I thought this arrangement was quite excellent.

I called over an important-looking man and asked, “Where can I find good shops?” He replied, “They’re on Mount Road.” “So how do I get there?” I asked. He said, “Just get on a tram there, and it’ll take you straight.”

While we were talking, a tramcar came by. It had “Royapuram” written on it. Without stopping, it began to move away. Oh no, it’s leaving! In my anxiety, without even listening to the rest of what the man was saying, I started shouting, “Stop! Stop!” and ran after it. The tram stopped a little distance ahead. Good, I thought—my shouting must have been heard, and it will wait for me until I catch up. So I slowed down a bit. But then the tram started moving again. “Stop! Please stop!” I yelled, breaking into a run once more. This business of the tram stopping for a moment, then moving off again, and me running after it—this went on for about a mile. In the end, somehow, I managed to catch up and climb aboard, barely having a moment to catch my breath.

No sooner had I boarded than a fellow appeared, looking like a sour-faced lump, dressed in a coat and trousers of some unknown color, a hat perched atop his hair knot, and a leather bag slung over his shoulder. “Ticket, sir! Ticket, sir! Where to?” he demanded. I placed a quarter anna in his hand and said, “Mount Road.” He asked, “Why, sir, why did you run all this way? You’re a strong fellow, aren’t you? Get down, get down, there’s another tram coming. Take that one.” Even as he was saying this, another tram came from the opposite direction. Not wanting to miss it, and thinking I’d already wasted enough time and that this tram wasn’t going any faster, I ignored the ticket man’s protests and jumped down.
In my hurry, I landed face-first and nearly smashed my nose. The tram driver—

The men came, lifted me up, and scolded me for getting down in such a hurry, giving me a few sharp words before going their own way. As I was coming out onto the street, that same dark, middle-aged man from earlier came towards me. I thought to myself, “It’s because of him that I’ve had to endure all these troubles.”

Today, I resolved not to board the tram again. Instead, I decided it would be better to travel quietly by some other vehicle, so I could take my time and observe everything at leisure. I managed to hire a bullock cart and set off.

Chennapatnam is truly a large town, and a beautiful one at that. The breadth of the roads, the elegance of the shops—I saw it all and was greatly delighted. “Oh, what a city!” I thought. “Are there such grand towns in England? Is London bigger than this? Or smaller?” I wondered. But how could it be bigger? After all, isn’t England just a small island? Perhaps all of England put together is only as big as Chennapatnam, I reasoned, swaying gently in the cart as these thoughts wandered through my mind.

At one place, I saw a sign: “Parisian Hair Cutting Salon.” I remembered that I needed to get my birth hair removed, so I told the cart driver to stop and got down. I stood near the entrance and peered inside. My feet wouldn’t move forward. My heart began to pound rapidly.

I had never, until now, had my hair cut after a meal. Today, that moment had arrived. On top of that, to do it in these clothes, without even bathing, and to touch everything—my mind found all this very troubling. What could I do? Was it wrong? But after all, this wasn’t for mere mischief, was it? Wasn’t it for the good of the country that I had set out on this path? How could any task be accomplished without enduring such hardships? Thus, I consoled myself.

When I peered inside, I was greatly astonished. The whole room was as clean as a mirror. Electric lights hung from above. Set into the wall were large, white porcelain basins, each with a small tap. Above them were vertical mirrors, and in front of those, comfortable beds and chairs. Near the entrance, a gentleman sat at a table, writing something. There was a large cupboard filled with bottles and small boxes of various kinds. Directly opposite the street entrance, on the wall...

A beautiful, colorful glass curtain was hung up. One wall had hooks for hanging clothes. Looking at all this, I began to wonder if I had entered a barber’s shop by mistake. For a moment, I worried—had I accidentally wandered into some office? Or perhaps this was some grand chemist’s shop. But then, why was there a bench placed up above like that? I thought perhaps the barber’s shop was upstairs, so I went back to check the bench in the foyer. But no, the bench wasn’t upstairs; it seemed to belong right here.

Still unsure whether this was a barber’s shop or not, I considered asking the man sitting there. Perhaps sensing my confusion, he greeted me first. Maybe he thought I didn’t know English, so he spoke in Urdu. I replied that I didn’t know Urdu.
“Oh, you don’t? So you’re a Telugu man. Come in, what do you need? A shave? Why are you standing here? Come inside,” he said.
With that, I was certain it was indeed a barber’s shop. Still, I was surprised, and as I stepped inside, I worried that my feet might dirty the floor. I went in, cautiously, and stood there.
“Sit down,” he said, pointing to a chair facing a mirror. Nervously, I sat down on it.
Barrister Parvateesam

Just then, from behind the curtain by the wall, a man appeared, dressed in spotless clothes and wearing a coat. He came over, picked up a bar of soap and a brush, asked me to lean back in the chair, tied a white starched cloth around my neck, and began to rub soap onto my beard with the brush. I was astonished, wondering why he was doing all this, but decided to see what would happen. “Why bother asking?” I thought, and surrendered myself to his care, suppressing my curiosity.

He lathered my face with soap as he pleased, then brought out a razor and, without even sharpening it on a stone, began to shave me. I thought of asking, “How can it cut if you don’t sharpen the blade?” but decided to wait and see—if it didn’t cut, I could always complain then. But, sharp or not, the razor glided smoothly and shaved me beautifully. It didn’t even feel like I was being shaved; it was over before I knew it. I couldn’t tell whether to credit the soap or the razor for this marvel.

Back in my village, whenever I got a shave, our barber would hack away at me as if he were carving a jackfruit—turning my head this way and that, never caring for my neck veins or the sight of my blood. He would never let go until he had left a memory that lasted at least a fortnight. But here, the shave was so comfortable, it suited the room perfectly.

After the shave, as usual, I thought of showing off my native manners and asking for a massage. But then I worried—what if he got angry? So I abandoned that idea, suppressed the sorrow welling up inside, and, holding back the hot tears threatening to fall, closed my eyes and told him to cut my hair. The hair I had so carefully grown and cherished since childhood—he snipped it off in two swift strokes. My face in the mirror looked utterly unfamiliar to me. Swallowing my sorrow, I stood there staring at my reflection.
“Shampoo, sir?” he asked. I had no idea what that meant. But having come this far, what could I do? Steeling my heart, I nodded, “Yes.”

He wrapped a large cloth around my neck, bent my head over a basin, and turned on the tap. Water flowed over my head. Then he poured something on my scalp and began to rub it in. After that, he thoroughly washed my head again.

After washing and wiping myself, I applied a little fragrant oil and combed my hair. “Ah, finally!” I thought, and got up. The first person who had summoned me handed me a receipt and demanded three rupees. I was dumbfounded. I had grown hair as long as a yardstick, and yet, not even a quarter, not even half, but three whole rupees for a haircut? I thought about arguing with him, but decided it was pointless to get into a debate right at the start. Like a dog with its tail between its legs, I silently handed over the three rupees, put on a long face, and walked away.

By the time I reached the carriage, the coachman had started grumbling that I was late. I promised him an extra anna or two to pacify him, got back into the carriage, and thought I might as well buy a hat if I spotted a big shop called “Whiteaway Laidlaw.” When I saw the shop, I got down there. Just looking at the shop from the outside filled me with bliss. All the goods in that shop were arranged so beautifully and attractively, displayed behind a large glass wall like a showcase. Anyone passing by on the road could stop and see if there was something they wanted. Even if you had no intention of buying anything, you’d be tempted to stand there for hours just gazing at those items. Civilization, it seems, belongs to the sahibs; what do we have in comparison?

Thinking thus, I stepped into the entrance. Inside, it was nothing short of Indra’s palace! I, a mere mortal, am not capable of describing such splendor. Everywhere I looked, there were sahibs and memsahibs; the salespeople were all English, and so were the customers. The floor was covered with soft carpets for walking. Across the length of the shop was a slender counter. The salespeople and the goods were all behind it, while the buyers stood on the other side. To be honest, seeing that shop, those goods, and those memsahibs, I was struck with fear. I stood there like a fool, eyes wide, mouth agape, gawking in all directions. After a while, an elderly sahib came up to me and asked, “Have you come to buy something?”
“Yes, I want a hat,” I replied.
“Hats are upstairs. Don’t be afraid,” he said.
I cautiously went upstairs. That entire floor was filled with hats of every kind. In one place, a man was selling; in another—
Mother is a woman, after all. I went to the gentleman and asked for a hat.

“What kind?” he asked. How was I to say what kind? In Chennapatnam, there were hats that suited everyone. I couldn’t think of any particular one to ask for. As I kept looking, I noticed that the hats sold by that woman were a bit larger and more elegant. I told the sahib that I wanted one of those hats. He politely took me over to the memsahib and said, “He wants a hat, see to it.”
“What size?” she asked. I had no idea what to say. I wondered, what size could a hat possibly have? I said, “My size.” Both of them burst out laughing. I felt so embarrassed.

“What kind?” the memsahib repeated. She showed me a large hat woven with palm leaves. I said I wanted that one. She took it, placed it on my head to check the fit, and said, “This one fits, take it.” She put the hat in a paper bag and gave it to me. I paid the price, took the hat, and without saying another word, head bowed, I walked out. Behind me, the sahib and memsahib were still laughing together.

Coming downstairs, I thought, “We’ll be on the steamer, won’t we? Without a watch, how will I know the time?” So, for two and a half rupees, I bought a clean “Tempus” watch. Who knows how many days it would be before I could get off the steamer again? If I let my beard grow without shaving, it wouldn’t look good, and there might not be barbers on the steamer. So, for a rupee and a quarter, I bought a small safety razor and stepped out.
It was three o’clock. I was hungry. I gave money to the cart driver...

I sent it off. This time, at least, he didn’t make me wait. I went into a coffee hotel nearby. Though I had lived in the city for a long time, I had never once set foot in a coffee hotel. This was my first time. There were chairs and tables. Many people were eating snacks. A man, probably the proprietor, was sitting on a chair near the entrance, collecting money. There were all sorts of snacks. I went and sat on a chair near the snacks counter. A dark, barrel-shaped young man came up to me and asked what I wanted. I had no idea what to ask for. Without pausing for breath, he rattled off the names of some twenty items, none of which I could make out clearly. I simply pointed at the counter and got the items I wanted, and ate them.

I asked for coffee. He brought two brass cups and began the process of cooling the coffee by pouring it back and forth. The whole procedure struck me as extremely comical. He started pouring the coffee from one cup to another, lifting it as high as he could. I sat there, terrified that the hot coffee would spill all over his feet or my head. But in the end, without any such mishap, he expertly poured the steaming coffee, creating a fine spray, and handed me my cup.

After taking the coffee, I asked, “How much is it?” “I’ll tell you, sir. Please give it to the gentleman sitting over there,” he said. “Alright,” I replied, and walked over to the counter. He followed right behind me and, in a voice loud enough for the whole town to hear, shouted, “Pay at the counter!” Embarrassed, I turned around and said, “Why are you braying like a donkey?” He didn’t understand a word, and simply walked away. A couple of people who knew Telugu burst out laughing. The proprietor called me over, took the money, and sent me on my way.

I hired a horse carriage and returned comfortably to my lodgings. In the morning, I asked the dark Brahmin about the train. “To where?” he asked. “I’m going to England. When is the train to Colombo?” I replied. He told me it was at three in the afternoon and that I should go to such-and-such station. Noticing the paper bag in my hand, he asked what it was. “It’s a hat,” I said. “Show me,” he said, so I showed him. He burst out laughing. Thinking he’d lost his mind, I asked, “Why are you laughing like that?” He said, “What’s the matter with you, man? You look like a madman. That’s a hat women wear!”

Hearing this, I was taken aback. I put on the hat once, took it off again, and looked at him. I thought perhaps that’s why the people in the shop were laughing at me. Well, whatever it was, I decided I must not appear inferior in front of this fellow from Aravada.

“So, what do you say?” I asked. “Why do you need this, boy? This is a woman’s hat,” he replied. “Oh, you mad fellow, I have acquaintances in Colombo. I’m taking it as a gift for them,” I said. But it didn’t look like he believed me one bit.

Taking the hat, I went into the waiting room, arranged my luggage, and headed to the train. By the time it was half past five in the evening, I reached the Beach Station. They said there wasn’t much time left for the train to depart. I asked how I could get to Colombo.

“If you travel second class, I’ll give you a ticket straight away. You can go comfortably, but if you travel third class, you’ll have to suffer a lot,” he said. I wondered what people going to England had to think about buying a second-class ticket. “Alright then, give me a second-class ticket,” I said.
Handing me the ticket, he said, “You’ll reach Tuticorin by tomorrow evening. Get down there, and if you board the steamer, you’ll reach Colombo by the next morning.”

“So, do I have to spend a night on the steamer? Can’t the train go straight to Colombo?” I asked. Looking at my face, the tone of respect with which he had been speaking to me until then suddenly changed.

“Oh, no, sir, it doesn’t go. In the old days, when Lord Rama’s bridge was in good condition, it used to go, they say. But now, since that’s broken and the sea is in the way, the train doesn’t go anymore. If we want to repair it, we’d have to send word to Lord Hanuman, but we don’t know his address. In fact, we too wish the train would go straight to Colombo,” he said.

Without another word, I took the ticket and went to the train. The porter himself came and helped me into the second-class compartment. He told me I’d be comfortable, that usually no one else boards here, and that I could sleep peacefully. As he was leaving, he added, “No one else will get in here. If any troublesome people start getting in, I can’t stand it. I hate having to travel with all sorts of people. For me, traveling with just anyone...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 77

There is no such thing as respect anymore. These days, no matter how much distance you keep, it doesn’t count for honor. Even people of the highest stature are mingling with us. They don’t think that the disrespect is ours alone. Such etiquette—well, it simply doesn’t exist. That’s why our people are in such a pitiable state. All that respect and honor is reserved only for your white sahibs. Just see for yourself. Did you consider my dignity or honor before speaking to me so casually? Look at the station master. Because he’s a native, he spoke without a second thought, with very little intelligence. I was furious. I wanted to give him a fitting reply and put him in his place. But then I thought, why create unnecessary trouble? I remembered the proverb my grandmother used to say: “If you throw a stone in the mud, it’ll splash back on you.” We dismiss the wisdom of the elders as ignorance, but no one else possesses their worldly knowledge. All their scholarship is packed into their words and proverbs.
As I was about to continue this philosophical discourse, the gentleman said, “I’ll see you again,” and began to leave.

My grandfather used to say, “Money is the root of this world.” I’ve heard from many that if you have money, you can get any work done. In my own experience, if Lady Lakshmi smiles upon a lowly schoolmaster, he can easily get promoted to a higher class. There’s a belief that some policemen assist thieves for a fee. I’ve heard that some unjust magistrates accept bribes from defendants and dismiss cases as a matter of routine. At the registration office, if you slip a ten-rupee note, your work is done in a minute. If you give the railway staff their usual tips, no matter how many illegal dams you build on the canal, they won’t see a thing.

Understanding all this, if a poor guard, a family man, someone like us, doesn’t receive a rupee, they’ll ignore us. Their salary barely keeps their household running. After all, he did me a small favor, so, thinking of his hardships and my own, I called the departing guard and gave him a rupee.
But after handing it over, I began to worry—what must he be thinking of me now? I gave it without knowing his true nature. Who knows what trouble I might have brought upon myself?

Well, at least we didn’t give the man two or three rupees like the others—just a single rupee. But then, my mind began to worry in all sorts of ways, wondering if I’d done wrong by giving too little. The guard glanced at me, looked at the rupee, and, without a word, slipped it into his pocket and walked away with a chuckle.

I thought, “So this is the world!” While I was fretting over what he might think of me, he, without a care, had pocketed the rupee and gone off cheerfully. Ah, what wonders money can do! Well, let the poor rupee go—at least I felt at ease.

The train started moving. After about ten minutes, it stopped at Egmore station. When I asked the porter, he said this was all still Chennapatnam. I was amazed at what a grand city it was—the train ran right through the middle of town! I thought, “How safe it must be for the people here.”

Just then, four noisy fellows barged into my compartment. “Are you going to Chilakaluripet, sir? Please move aside,” I said politely. They paid no heed to my words and began opening the door without a word. “Gentlemen, you don’t know—this is second class. If you get in here, you’ll be fined. Please go to another compartment,” I said.

One of them looked at my face and said, in broken Telugu, “You’re sitting here, but you look like someone who should be in a fourth-class compartment. Please be kind.” I was astonished at their audacity. “Your home must be the birthplace of impudence and beauty alike. If you lack for anything, it’s not for words. Don’t talk too much—please, have some mercy,” I said.
It seemed they didn’t quite understand all I said, so they pretended not to hear me.

“All right, sir, don’t talk too much—we understand,” said one of them. Just then, I saw the guard walking by. I shouted, intending to tell him to throw these fellows out of the compartment. But he paid no attention to me.
He was thoroughly deceived.

Just then, another gentleman joined their group. The newcomers narrated the whole episode to him. They must have thought I didn’t know English. Perhaps they were thinking, “He looks like a rustic simpleton from some backwater village. He must have slipped a rupee or two into the guard’s hand. Poor fellow, he probably thinks the whole compartment belongs to him now.” I wondered how they knew I had given a rupee to the guard, and said, “There’s no need for such unnecessary talk. Even if my town isn’t as big as Chennapatnam, I did study in Narsapur. I didn’t give anything to the guard. Seeing your attitude, I thought you might have mistakenly wandered into the second class, so I told you for your own good. If you have the same tickets, you’re welcome to stay here. I have no objection.”

I thought to myself, “The guard has coolly pocketed my rupee and cheated me. On top of that, why should I get into a pointless argument with these people?” It didn’t seem like there was anything to be gained from a quarrel. I’m not the sort who picks fights without reason. Once I realize there’s nothing to be gained, I don’t even step into a quarrel. If by chance I do, I immediately withdraw with dignity, just as our teacher used to say the English do in battle when they see things aren’t going their way—they retreat politely and sensibly. I too, in such tricky situations, take a step back.

But I was deeply upset about giving that rupee to the guard for no reason. You see, although I may appear otherwise, I am a very cautious man; I don’t like to spend money unnecessarily. That said, I’m not the sort to back down when the time comes. Still, whether for good or ill, I am a man who thinks ahead, so I have adopted a single strategy: “Cast one to catch ten.” That’s my way. So, whether the guard thought I was a fool, or I thought he was a rogue, I gave him a rupee.

Even though I lost a rupee, I thought, “Since it’s a long journey, at least I can sit comfortably alone in a compartment meant for four.” But in my whole life, this was the one time I was truly cheated. Never before had I seen such a scoundrel.
Barrister Parvateesam

Now, I no longer felt bad that someone else had climbed into my compartment. What really bothered me was—why would he betray me for no reason? If he had simply asked, “Please give me your seat,” would I have refused? Am I someone who doesn’t know the pains and pleasures of life? Of course not! How much wickedness there is in human nature! And especially in him—he shouldn’t even be allowed near. It’s only because such cheats exist that they have managed to build such an empire. Otherwise, is it their own merit? Or their ancestors’? That’s why all the great men, like Bode Narayana Rao and others, are trying to drive these people out of the country.

Anyway, they’re not people like us. I didn’t lose anything because someone climbed into my compartment, except for the rupee I gave the guard. Still, if those who climbed in were Telugu people, at least I could have exchanged a few words, shared my troubles and joys. But with none of that, and with these faces that only appear in dreams, and their conversation sounding like village lions arguing in court, and then these shouting fellows joining in—it was all too much for me! I can’t even begin to describe it!

Just then, the guard blew his whistle for the train to depart. Of the four or five people who had come, only the last gentleman actually entered the compartment. The rest seemed to have come just to see him off. Since he was alone, he couldn’t talk to himself, could he? If he wanted to talk, he’d have to talk to me. Otherwise, he’d have to sit quietly. So, I thought, either way, it didn’t matter.

The train started moving. For quite a distance, there were many small stations, one after another. The train didn’t stop at most of them. I wondered why they had built so many stations if the train wasn’t going to stop. I thought of asking the gentleman in the compartment, but earlier, at the village station, he had already said something. I hesitated, thinking, “What will he say if I ask another question?” But finally, I couldn’t help myself and asked him to tell me where the boundary of Chennapatnam was.

He replied that all these small stations were still part of Chennapatnam. I concluded that Chennapatnam must be even bigger than England! If relatives and friends in this town wanted to see each other, it would be like traveling to a neighboring village. I imagined that if government employees lived at one end and the office was at the other, going there would be...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 81

I thought to myself, “Well, at least there are plenty of stations.” But the train doesn’t stop at every one, does it? And as for tram cars, you don’t see them all over the town either. If these people have to ride some bullock cart or jhatka, when will they ever reach the office, when will they work, and when will they get back home? Just going back and forth would eat up half their salary—and half their life as well! How on earth do they manage, I wondered.

Let’s leave aside the matter of work for a moment. Among these people, there are big officers and small clerks too. How does a clerk who earns fifteen rupees a month manage to live? Does he walk this far every day, twice a day? Or does he take a cart? If he does, all the money he sweats and toils for in a month will be gone in a single day’s cart fare! This morning, the cart driver tried to fleece me, demanding a rupee per mile. If these people spend whatever little they earn just on the cart, what will be left for their wives and children? I wondered about that too. Even if all they eat is pulusu, charu, and rice, that still costs something, doesn’t it? No matter how long I pondered, I couldn’t come up with a solution. Though I consider myself a man of subtle intelligence, this problem was beyond me.

Unable to think of anything, I decided to take a look at the elderly gentleman traveling with me. He had been gazing outside until now, but now he turned and looked at me. Our eyes met. “Where are you from, sir?” he asked. “Narsapur,” I replied. Strictly speaking, my village isn’t Narsapur, but if I said Mogaliturru, he wouldn’t know it. Then he’d ask where that is, and I’d have to explain, and what’s the point of all that? Narsapur is easier to say and sounds familiar, so that’s what I told him.

“Where are you going?” he asked. I replied in a way that made it sound like I was a frequent traveler, “Oh, I’m just going up to Colombo.” He looked at me slowly and said, “You’re not going all the way to England, are you? Judging by your appearance, it doesn’t seem so. I can’t imagine any business you’d have in Colombo beyond this.”
“Is that so, sir? Why doesn’t my appearance suggest otherwise? What deficiency did you find in me?” I asked.
“My boy, there’s a short story in your Telugu land,” he began. “Once, a learned man was traveling to a village. A mischievous boy, seeing him, called out, ‘Hey, Thimmanna garu...’”
Barrister Parvateesam

He said, “How long you are being so kind!” “Son, I can’t seem to remember who you are. Where do you know me from? Did someone else tell you about me?” he asked. When he asked this, the other man laughed and said, “Sir, I have never seen you before. But just by looking at your face, I guessed your name must be Mr. Thimmanna. My guess turned out to be right!” He said this with great confidence. “That’s how you should ask, my boy!”
“All right, let that be. But what exactly did you figure out?” I asked.
“Shall I tell you? If I tell the truth, you might feel offended,” he said.
“No problem, please tell me,” I replied.

“Looking at your suitcase, it’s clear you are from a village, and that you have never traveled far before. When I tried to put my things in your compartment and you told me not to, I realized you’ve never traveled by train before. Or, if you have, you’ve never traveled in second class. It’s also obvious you’ve never mingled with important people. That’s why I thought, ‘He’s such a rustic fellow—can he really be going to England?’ Otherwise, I can’t see any reason for you to be going to Colombo. And then, looking at your head, with that freshly shaved patch where your hair used to be, I can tell you’re not used to tonsuring, that you used to have hair, and that you only had it shaved off today. If you were only traveling as far as Colombo, there’d be no need to shave your head. So I concluded you must be going further. I also suspect you’re leaving home without telling your family. Otherwise, why would you go to Colombo instead of Bombay? Tell me, am I right or wrong? Speak honestly—did you tell your people at home?” he said.
As I listened to each of his words, I felt my heart...

They soared high above. I have seen many people in this world, but never have I come across a man like this. Even though he is an “Arava” (Tamilian), he is built like a mountain, and he speaks Telugu quite well too. Perhaps he spent some time in the Telugu region! Otherwise, where would an “Arava” get enough money to travel second class? Unless he earned it in the Telugu land, right? That’s what I thought. But what intelligence! He figured out everything about me in a matter of minutes, as if reading an open book. I felt that nothing dangerous could come from him, but still, who is this man, what is his story, what is the situation? I decided I should find out by asking him. In any case, it would be best to befriend him a little. Otherwise, if he writes a letter to my family at home, I’d be in trouble. It’s always better to be a bit cautious, I thought.

So, I said, “Your guess is mostly correct. I am going to England. Where are you from? You speak Telugu very well too. Have you ever lived in the Telugu region?” As I asked, he smiled slightly and said, “Oh, my boy! I am from Tiruchirapalli. I have lived in the Telugu region since I was a child. My father was a station master and worked for many years in towns like Rajahmundry, Nidadavolu, Eluru, and so on. I studied in England. After passing my engineering exams, I spent a long time in your Dhavaleswaram, Settipeta, and Bezwada. That’s why I am quite used to Telugu,” he said.

With that, my legs cooled down. Until then, my heart had been pounding with anxiety, but now it calmed for a moment. Now he would find out my family background, my father, and write a letter home. I thought my goose was cooked.

If it were someone else, their eyes would have popped out in fear, but I am a bit braver, so I got my stalled heart beating again and resumed my conversation with him. “So, that’s how it is, sir. Thank you for your kindness about England. Are there any of our people there? Is accommodation available? Is the food convenient?” I asked.
He replied, “Ah, yes, there are a few of our people there. Overall, it’s quite comfortable.”
Barrister Parvateesam
He asked, “Son, do you have any friends over there? Have you bought everything you might need? Do you know how to conduct yourself there, or what the customs of that country are?”

At that moment, I thought, “Well, he’s an elder, so perhaps I should speak to him with some respect.” But instead, he tied me down as if I were a little boy, and whenever he spoke, he kept calling me ‘son’ as if I might run off somewhere if not watched. What’s so great about him, and what’s so little about me? He went to England before, and now I am going. That’s the only difference. For that alone, is there any need to treat me with such disrespect?

So I decided it would be better to end this conversation with him. To everything he asked, I replied with a curt “yes” or “no,” and when he kept on asking questions, I leaned back, closed my eyes, and pretended to fall asleep, like someone who could no longer hear.

That seemed to trouble him a bit. Perhaps he felt a little awkward and was silent for a moment. But alas, how long can such a mouth remain shut? As the elders say, “A tongue that turns cannot rest for a moment.” That saying is true. After just a minute of silence, he said, “Son, you seem very sleepy. Why don’t you lie down, dear boy?”

I thought, “What does he mean by that? Does he think I’m some little child?” I considered asking him, but then thought, “Why start an argument with him for no reason?” So, without answering, I took my bundle and set it aside. Seeing this, he started laughing to himself quietly. But what does it matter to me who laughs? If they laugh, their own mouths will twist, not mine.
Then I thought, “Should I show him that I even have a folding bed, just to prove myself?” But then I worried it might be a bit cramped, so I gave up on that idea and just sat on my bedding.
He asked, “Son, are you taking this bundle with you as well?”
“Yes, I am. Why else would I bring it? Not to throw it away halfway, surely. I see nothing here that should surprise you,” I replied.

He looked at me sharply and said, “Just be careful, you might forget it somewhere by mistake. Don’t ever forget it. If any landlord over there sees this and asks you to give it as a gift, even if your life is at stake, don’t give it to anyone. They don’t have things like this there. That’s why many people will ask for it. Be careful, guard it with your life. If you like, you can—”

On the way home, he suggested that I could donate myself to the British Museum, and once again burst out laughing. “Enough, sir, I do not require your well-intentioned advice in this matter,” I retorted, putting an end to his amusement. Yet he sat there, eyes half-closed, staring at me and chuckling to himself. I made myself comfortable, lay down, and soon fell into a deep sleep. But inside, I was still a bit anxious. What if I rolled off that folding bed, or fell from the upper bunk? Still, not wanting to appear afraid, I pretended to sleep soundly, though I kept waking up now and then to check on my luggage.

Once, when I woke up to check, he was nowhere to be seen—he had already gotten down somewhere, and was not in the compartment. All my belongings were safe and sound. “Ah, the troublemaker has left,” I thought with relief. After that, no one else climbed into that compartment.

By the time I woke up again, it was broad daylight. I attempted to brush my teeth, but wondered where I would find water. In the corner of the room where I was sitting, there was a door labeled “Lavatory.” I thought I’d see what it was. Perhaps there would be water inside. I opened the door and went in. The room was very clean. There was a small tap fixed to the wall, and beneath it, a neat little brass basin to catch the water. Beside it was a chair-like seat with a hole in the middle. There was no unpleasant smell at all. The whole arrangement was excellent. I resolved that, after returning from England, I would have a similar setup installed in my own house.

I went over to the tap and tried to turn it. No matter how much I twisted, it wouldn’t budge. Puzzled, I thought I should try turning it harder. As I did so, my hand slipped and I fell forward onto the tap. The tap, which had stubbornly refused to move all this time, suddenly yielded to my weight, and water gushed out, drenching me from head to toe. That put an end to my attempts to get up. “What kind of magic is this?” I wondered. Upon closer inspection, I realized that if you press the lever inward, the water comes out.

Having completed my morning ablutions and brushed my teeth, I ate the four pieces of idli my mother had packed for me at the station, drank a little coffee and some water, and sat gazing at the countryside as the train sped along.
Arabia, too, is a very beautiful land. Who would have thought it would be so lovely...
Barrister Parvateesam

I never expected such a thing. Everywhere I looked, there were beautiful orchards, fertile farmlands, magnificent temples—everything looked just like our Delta region! I wondered, why would people from such a land of abundant grass, wood, and water live in such poverty, yearning for eight or ten rupees, and travel to far-off countries?

At noon, at one station, the guard came and asked if I wanted lunch. I thought, why is he concerned about my meal? Is he going to provide it, or what? Then I wondered, maybe he asks because we’ll be eating on the train, so I told him, “No need.” “Then what will you do?” he asked. “Oh, I’ll manage somehow,” I replied. He looked at my face, curled his lips, raised his eyebrows and shoulders, and walked away with a smirk. Not knowing what else to do about food, I bought a little snack, ate it, and lay down for a nap.
By evening, around five o’clock, I reached Tuticorin.

On the platform, porters were shouting, “Toothukudi! Toothukudi!” Some were yelling, “All passengers for Colombo, get down here!” Wanting to look dignified as I got off from second class, I wore my new suit, wrapped a red silk turban around my head, and left behind the Englishman’s hat I bought in Channapatna in the train, taking the rest of my belongings as I got down. A porter came and offered to carry my luggage. I agreed, bargained with him, and moved ahead.

As I approached the gate, the ticket collector looked at me and politely showed me the way. As I was going, a big official sitting there asked me to show my luggage. The porter had it on his head. “Can’t you see it?” I asked. “No, you must put it down and show it,” he insisted. “Why?” I asked. “Why are you going to Colombo?” he questioned. My heart shattered. How did he find out that I left home without telling anyone? Still, being a man of some courage and composure, I didn’t put on a foolish face and said, “Why do you want to know?” “Alright—”
“Let it be, I don’t care,” I said. “But at least let me check your luggage,” he insisted.
“Why?” I asked.
“It’s the rule here,” he replied.
“What rule is that?”
“We have to check if you’re smuggling any taxable goods.”
The moment I heard this, the weight on my heart lightened. I even felt a little amused. “Alright then, go ahead and check,” I thought to myself.
Just then, the porter carrying my luggage called me aside and whispered, “If you slip half a rupee into that big man’s hand, all these rules will be forgotten. Otherwise, you’ll miss your steamer.”

Missing the steamer was the last thing I wanted. But looking at their shamelessness, I couldn’t help but laugh a little. As soon as I dropped the half-rupee into his hand, the man who had been sitting there with a face as sour as a tamarind suddenly stood up, saluted me, and said, “Thank you, sir!” He grabbed my box and asked, “Are there only clothes in this, sir? Then you may proceed, sir,” and let me go.
Feeling as if I had survived a great ordeal, I walked calmly towards the steamer.

Just then, a railway porter came running from behind, holding the English lady’s hat I had left in the train, and handed it to me. With no other choice, I took it. But the fellow didn’t leave; he stood there, rubbing his hands together. “Alright, the hat is mine now, you can go,” I said. He just sat there, waiting for something. As I was getting late for the steamer, I handed him a pice, thinking that was the price of the hat, and moved on.
Barrister Parvateesam

The sea, the shore, the lights there, and all that bustle—seeing it all filled me with great joy. But when someone told me that this was the steamer, I couldn’t bring myself to board it. It was so small—nothing like the usual riverboats, let alone what I imagined a steamer to be. Was it not dangerous to cross the sea in such a tiny thing? If I had to travel on this, perhaps it would be better to just go back home, I thought. As I stood there lost in these thoughts, the porter hurriedly put my luggage inside and urged me to get on board.
“Is this really the steamer to Colombo?” I asked.
“No, sir, the big steamer is five or six miles out at sea. This one will take you there. Hurry up!” he said.
Relieved, I got on. I sat down on a bench inside. After a short while, the boat set off. Altogether, there couldn’t have been more than twenty-five fellow passengers traveling with me.

For the first five minutes after we set off, it was all quite delightful—the spray of water hitting us, the land receding farther and farther away, the lights on the shore twinkling in the distance, darkness closing in from all sides, the blue sky above, and in it, stars dangling like drops of mercury, and below, wherever I looked, the fathomless sea. The waves rose and fell, rocking us as if in a cradle. Everything seemed magical. If only I had the gift of poetry! If another fellow like me, lacking poetic talent, were to set off on such a journey, the poets of Andhra would not be able to bear it.

But after a little while, perhaps because of the lack of food since morning, or for some other reason, a terrible headache began to torment me. I looked for a place to lie down, but there was nowhere to stretch out. As I sat there clutching my head, nausea started to set in as well. Oh God, what is this? Am I going to fall sick with fever now, of all times? After coming this far, will I have to turn back? But if I went home now, wouldn’t I become a laughingstock among everyone? With that thought, I closed my eyes and sat quietly.
While I was suffering like this, another thought struck me, and it made me even more anxious. If only this idea had occurred to me at the very beginning—who knows what might have happened!

Well, let it be. Whether people laugh at me or scold me, I was determined to return home quietly on the train without uttering a word. What could I do now! There was no way to turn back. If I moved forward, I saw no hope of survival. Going ahead felt like a precipice; going back, like a pit. I was at a complete loss. I didn’t even feel like asking anyone else for advice. Suddenly, thoughts of home flashed through my mind. Ah! What a foolish thing I had done, I thought. I cursed the person who had advised me to go to England. I wondered how much my parents, who had pinned all their hopes on me—their only son—would grieve. But what use was there in thinking such thoughts!

The real issue at hand was that I was unsure how to get from this small steamer to the big steamer. For a while, I couldn’t think of anything. Suddenly, I remembered something I’d once overheard some people from my village discussing. They were talking about the method of transferring from a small steamer to a big one, and I happened to hear it. Apparently, from the big steamer, they let down a rope ladder to the small one. Because of the waves, the small steamer is always bobbing up and down—sometimes rising, sometimes falling. So, the ladder is not always within reach. Therefore, passengers must seize the right moment: when the small steamer is lifted by a wave, they must leap, grab the ladder, and climb up. For those who can’t manage this, they tie a rope around the person’s waist, lower a sort of basket from the big steamer, attach the rope to it, and haul the person up.

If the rope around the person’s waist snaps, or if the knot comes undone, the person will most likely fall into the small steamer below, and not anywhere else—unless, of course, they miss and fall into the sea. But even if they do fall into the sea, there’s no need to fear for one’s life, as they quickly cast a net and pull the person back up—so I had heard. These last words gave me a little courage when I first heard them, but now, when the moment had actually arrived, I didn’t feel so brave. What if I fell into the steamer and cracked my skull? Or suffered some other injury? And if I fell into the sea, before the people above could cast their net and fish me out, the waves might carry me far away. Who could guarantee that I’d stay in one place? And even if I did, would I survive that long? And if I did survive, what if, in the meantime, a big fish came along and made a snack out of me?
Barrister Parvateesam

What happened next? I spent the time pondering in all sorts of ways. Now I regret not having learned to swim as a child. For a moment, I even thought of quietly turning back and returning the way I came, but then I wondered, “Why be in such a hurry? If I just wait a moment patiently, everything will become clear. If possible, I can act then.” With my heart pounding and my breath held, I anxiously waited for the steamer to reach its destination. I forced myself to suppress the surge of sorrow that came over me as I thought of my family back home, and sat chanting the name of Lord Rama for comfort.

The steamer was dashing through the sea at great speed, but the noise of the engines, the roar of the ocean, and the chatter of the people around me only made my headache worse. When I opened my eyes, the whole world seemed to spin like a top.

Just then, someone shouted, “There it is—the steamer! There’s the steamer!” All I could see were its lights; nothing else was visible. I wished our little steamer would slow down a bit—otherwise, I feared we might crash into it in the darkness. As if reading my mind, they did reduce the speed a little. Slowly, we drew closer to the other vessel. Compared to ours, it was enormous, looming before us like a mountain. Our steamer, now trembling with caution, crept up to the big one and stopped right alongside it. Looking up, the large steamer appeared as if a tall black wall had been erected beside us.

Headache, nausea, fear—none of it mattered; my whole body was trembling. Whatever little courage I had left until then was now shattered. No matter what anyone said, no matter how much they laughed, I decided it was best to just go home. Let them laugh if they want; after all, it’s my life at stake, not theirs. If I die, none of those who laugh will give me my life back. I’ve seen enough, experienced enough. Is this the only house in the world? Just because of this whim, I’ve landed myself in this mess. I resolved to stay in Chennapatnam for another week or so, see everything at leisure, and then go back.

Meanwhile, there was a flurry of shouting and conversation between the people on both steamers. After much commotion, they finally lowered a ladder. The ladder rested neatly against our steamer. At the top of the ladder...

There was a large lamp. The staircase, too, was not some flimsy rope ladder, but a proper, wide set of steps, with sturdy handrails on either side—just like the stairs in any respectable house. Even our steamer, contrary to my fearful imagination, was not leaping over the waves into the heavens and plunging into the netherworld, but was moving along quite steadily, with only a gentle rocking motion.

Just seeing all this made it clear that everything I’d heard until now was nothing but lies. Now, I felt no fear for my life and grew more confident. I thought to myself, “There’s no need to turn back and go home now, is there?” With that, I mustered some courage. Though my headache still troubled me, I got up along with everyone else.

I stood up, went over to where my luggage was, and was about to take it with me. Just then, someone told me that I could go ahead, and that the luggage would follow later. I was afraid—what if I left all my belongings behind and everything was lost? I asked him again, “Will the luggage really come safely?” He assured me confidently that it would.

It wasn’t just me—everyone else was also leaving their luggage behind and going up. So, thinking there was nothing to worry about, I clutched the English lady’s hat, which I’d been holding all this time, and calmly went up along with the others.
As I reached the top step and peered inside, I was greatly astonished.

I had thought it would be just a little bigger than the usual country boats, with two or three large halls and perhaps some tables inside. But when I actually saw it, it looked like a grand palace—a veritable royal mansion!
Inside, the place was resplendent with beautiful lamps, carpets on the floor, grand sofas, chairs, and tables—everything was there.
I imagined there must be separate rooms with beds and cots for sleeping, bathrooms, toilets, kitchens, and dining halls, all distinct and apart from each other.
But then again, how big must a steamer be to fit all these things? Perhaps they arranged these chairs and tables just in this one room to make a grand impression as soon as you enter.

As I stood there, marveling at everything, a distinguished-looking gentleman approached and greeted me. He asked where I was headed, learned of my destination, and told me that he had traveled to England many times, that travel was a very good thing, and went on talking about this and that. But because of my headache, nothing he said registered in my mind. On top of that, after a whole day of wandering without food, my stomach was burning with hunger. I had neither the patience to toast bread nor the strength to labor for it. Even if I wanted to make an effort, I found myself incapable. Nothing came to mind. I regretted not bringing at least some idlis or bananas with me. But then again, what use would that have been? When you can’t see the way ahead, what’s the point in thinking about such things? That England-returned fellow was chattering away on his own path. I thought that if I could, I’d just keep my mouth shut and sit quietly for a while.

Our steamer gave a loud whistle and set off. Just then, a bell rang somewhere. I wondered what that bell was for. The England-returned brother beside me said, “Come, let’s go eat.” I could hardly believe his words. “What? Where?” I asked again, twice as eagerly. “To the dining hall, to eat,” he said. Hearing those words was like nectar poured into the mouth of a dying man. My departing soul returned to my body. I thought, “God still has some mercy left for us.” I had never considered who would feed us on the steamer, why they would feed us, or what they would feed us. At that moment, I thought, “If I can just get some food inside me and keep my life inside me, I can think about the rest later.”
Without further ado, I followed my friend, walking briskly. Now, what I saw—
