If you think my previous room was odd, this one is even more amusing. In the middle of the room stood a large, long table. It was covered with a white cloth. Upon it were arranged fine porcelain plates, glass tumblers, knives, spoons, and all sorts of other things whose uses I could not fathom. In small glass bowls, there was butter. Chairs were set around the table. As we entered, a few people had already arrived and taken their seats. We too went and adorned a couple of chairs ourselves.

After sitting down, I turned to my friend and asked, “Why are there so many knives and daggers in a place meant for eating?” There seemed no way to find out unless I shamelessly asked; otherwise, I would be left in the dark. In a minute, the serving would begin, and we would have to start eating. If I made a fool of myself then, it would be most embarrassing. So, thinking it best to learn beforehand, I cleverly asked my friend in a way that wouldn’t make him suspect my ignorance. When I asked, that good man kindly explained the use of those items.

Now, the serving was about to begin. I wondered whether I would be able to handle these knives and implements. I picked up a knife in one hand, and with the other, I gripped the spoon meant for fruits as if I were about to dig a pit in the ground. I tried to stab the bread with the knife just as one would drive a crowbar into the earth.
“Not like that! Be careful, or you’ll break the plate,” my friend whispered softly, still calm.
But I paid no heed to his words.
What danger could possibly come of this? Is it really so difficult, or is this some great secret art? With such thoughts, I aimed the knife at the bread...

To the best of my ability, I struck the blow with great force. Everyone seated around held their breath, watching anxiously to see what would happen. Perhaps because I already had a headache, my aim faltered—the morsel of bread struck the edge of the plate, slipped off, hit the side of the dish, slid further, and finally landed on the table.

In that commotion, the piece of bread leapt up a good half a cubit, like a goat kid snatching something from the table and making a run for it. It bounced over four plates beside me and finally took refuge next to the fifth plate. The plate itself must have seen many like me in its time. Still, startled, it came rolling into my lap. I was relieved that no real mishap had occurred so far. Had the plate fallen to the floor, it would have broken into two pieces. No matter its price—whether an anna or a rupee—they would have come and demanded two or three rupees for it, and I would have had no choice but to pay up as if I were dying. But nothing of the sort happened; it escaped unscathed. I thought to myself, "Today, at least, my luck holds."

Everyone sitting beside me began to laugh. Why do people laugh at such things, whether they are worthy of laughter or not? "Even the wise make mistakes in times of danger," they say. Anyone can make a blunder—what’s so strange about that?

I took off my napkin and placed it back on the table. The hunger gnawing at my stomach, combined with their laughter, made me angry. I thought, "If I give up now, it will be a defeat." So, taking another piece of bread in my hand, I decided, "As long as God has given me hands, why bother with these wretched knives and forks? If I eat as I please, will they beat me or scold me? Let me assert my independence." I smeared some butter on the bread and began to eat it with my hands.

The man next to me kept advising me not to do so, but I paid him no heed. Those who had been laughing until then now began to glare at me as if I had done them a great disservice. Did I care? I glared back at them with even greater anger and continued with my business.
I put two pieces into my mouth. Before they had even fully gone down my throat, I reached for a third...

I clutched my stomach as if mixing something inside, and a great commotion began to rise, swelling up like a thick rope. With a piece of bread in my hand, I quickly covered my mouth, dropped the bread into the plate, and stood up. I had no idea where to go or what to do. The turmoil within kept surging up, unstoppable. I took two steps towards the door, thinking to leave the room. But the force from inside pushed past my hand and some of it escaped outside. Again, I tried to block it with my hand.

A servant, noticing my distress, hurried over, grabbed me by the arm, and dragged me into a room. There, arrangements had been made just like the washbasins on the train for washing one’s face. I vomited completely. Though I hadn’t eaten all day, I don’t know where so much matter came from—enough to account for a whole week’s worth of meals. I washed my mouth and hands thoroughly. My stomach and intestines ached all over. My head felt as if it would split open.
My eyes were spinning. When I opened them, the whole world seemed to whirl around me. My legs felt weightless. I was afraid I might collapse right there.

The servant who had brought me in was still there. He gently took me by the hand and led me back into the room. The room was quite small, but there was a little bed in it, neatly made with clean sheets and a pillow at the side. He told me to lie down on it.

Whose bed is this, I wondered? Poor fellow! Usually, I struggle and end up sitting in a chair in the hall. Or, if someone shows me a place, I lay out my own bedding and sleep there, I thought to myself, planning to say as much.
But not a word escaped my lips. There was nothing to be seen in the room. I collapsed onto the bed just like the fellow who had been drinking in silence. I didn’t even bother to take off my shoes.

I thought perhaps all this was due to the evil eye of those who had sat with me at dinner. I lamented that there wasn’t even a single person to offer a word of comfort. Seeing this headache, I wondered if I might be coming down with a fever of some kind.
While I was thinking such thoughts, my eyes grew heavy and closed. After that, I lost all awareness of my body.

After some time, the night attendant came and woke me. When I opened my eyes, it was already dawn. We had reached Colombo. “Get up, it’s time to disembark,” he said. I got up. The headache had subsided. I felt light. There was no fever or anything of the sort. I thought to myself, “I’ve recovered splendidly.” The attendant asked, “Are you feeling well?” I replied, “Marvelous!” I got up, straightened my turban, and asked, “Where is my luggage?” “It’s already gone down, before you. Please come along,” he said. I hadn’t checked on it during the night. I worried whether my luggage was safe or not. Perhaps, thinking he could answer for any missing items if I checked from above, he had sent it down already. As I stood up to look around, I saw the English lady’s hat I had bought in Chennapatnam sitting on a table. I assumed the attendant had brought it and placed it there during the night. Without inspecting it or saying a word, I went upstairs.

It was nearly seven o’clock. By then, all those who had to disembark had already done so. I was the last. I got down quietly. Below, everything was in utter commotion. People going this way and that, those who had come to receive passengers from the steamer, those who had come just to watch the spectacle, porters—what a crowd! The whole seashore was abuzz with activity. The harbor was full of steamers. Watching all this commotion, I quietly made my way to my luggage. Everything was safe and sound. Not a single item had been squashed or damaged—credit to their sense of duty!

I was coming from a laborer’s quarter, shouting for a coolie to carry my luggage on his head to the carts. Suddenly, I heard someone calling from behind. At first, I ignored it—who would be calling me here, after all? I kept walking ahead. But when the shouting grew louder, I stopped and looked back. There he was—the steward from the steamer last night, running breathlessly, waving that wretched memsahib’s hat in his hand.

There seemed to be no way to rid myself of it. If only I had thrown it out of the train at the very beginning, this whole ordeal would have ended. But then again, why waste it for nothing? I thought if I left it in the train, someone else might take it, but that plan didn’t work out. Now, wherever I go, the hat follows me relentlessly. Never before did I realize that there was so much justice in the world. Many people have told me that if you forget something somewhere, it’s nearly impossible to get it back. Now I know that’s not true. Only when you experience something yourself do you truly understand.

From now on, if anyone claims there is injustice or theft in this world, I won’t believe them. Even if I forget this hat somewhere, it seems determined to chase after me. So, without a word, I’ll take this cursed hat and, when no one is looking, fling it into the middle of the sea at midnight. Otherwise, if I throw it away during the day, some unfortunate soul might spot it, fish it out, and return it to me yet again—that thought terrifies me. The very sight of that hat fills me with utter disgust! Not only does it cost a fortune, but if I try to get rid of it, whoever finds and returns it expects a reward, and I’m supposed to act delighted as if they’ve saved my most beloved possession from being lost.
Enduring this much is already too much to bear. Since I have no choice, I handed a quarter to the man who brought it back, took that wretched hat, and went to the cart.

The same predicament I faced in Chennapatnam has come upon me here. The same question arises: where should I stay? Here, too, the poor souls don’t know Telugu. Thanks to my experience in Chennapatnam, I managed to spot someone who looked like he knew a bit of English, called him over, and asked. He told me there was a rest house nearby, where one could get a room and meals. I learned the way and told the coachman to take me there.

The rooms were quite spacious, and there were good facilities for bathing. There was no crowd at all. Pleased with how nice it was, I took a room, had my luggage brought in, and dismissed the porter. Unlike the fellow at Chennapatnam, this one didn’t try to swindle me. He seemed a bit more dignified. But then, he was a sahib, after all, so perhaps that’s to be expected.

Now, at my leisure, I opened my trunk, took out some dried fruits and such, brushed my teeth, and had a bath. By the time I finished and sat down for a while, it was already ten o’clock. I had my meal. I’d already given up trying to tie my dhoti tightly, thinking that if people laughed at me in Chennapatnam, they’d surely laugh even more here. All through my meal, my heart felt quite heavy. I had no idea what to do next. Which steamer goes to London? When does it leave? Where do I buy tickets? I knew none of this. And I didn’t know a soul here to ask! If only I’d thought to find out last night whether the steamer would go all the way to London, I might have learned something. But now, what’s the use of sitting here and worrying? So, I put on my suit, wrapped a scarf around my head, and stepped out into the street.
I didn’t know a single road. I didn’t know the language to ask anyone for directions. Well, I thought, let me leave it all to fate and set out boldly, nose to the wind.

After walking some distance, I saw a gentleman coming toward me—dressed in a suit, clean-shaven, a hat perched on his head, sandalwood paste smeared in three or four lines on his forehead. Surely, I thought, this man must know English. I stopped him and asked, “Do you know English?” He said he did. “Where are you from?” I asked. “Kumbakonam,” he replied.

The moment he said “Kumbakonam,” a little fear crept in. Would he answer my questions properly or not? After all, aren’t all Kumbakonam fellows known for their trickery? But then, what could he possibly gain by tricking me here? “Sir, please help me a little,” I said.

The gentleman misunderstood my request, looked at me suspiciously, and said, “What can I do? I’m just a poor man,” and was about to walk away. I stopped him again, assured him that I didn’t need any financial help, and said, “There’s just something I’d like to ask you.”
“What is it?” he asked. I—
I told him, “Just don’t tell anyone what I’m about to say.”

He agreed. “I’ve set out to go to London. My family at home knows about it. If you know when the steamer to London departs, or where to get tickets, I’d be grateful if you told me. I was afraid that if my folks at home found out about this, they wouldn’t let me go, so I slipped away. I don’t know anyone here. That’s why, if you know anything, please tell me,” I said.

“Oh, is that all? There’s nothing to it. If you go to such-and-such a place, you’ll see a big company called Thomas Cook & Son with a signboard. If you just walk in there, you’ll get your ticket and all the information you need,” he said.

“Alright, that’s good. Now that I know this much, I can say I’m practically on my way to London,” I thought, and confidently went to the company. But as soon as I saw the company, I was overcome with fear at the thought of going inside. I’d traveled so much in this country, but I’d never seen such a tall building anywhere. And what if, after all this, I go inside and they say there’s no steamer? Or that it won’t come for another week? Or worse, that steamers have stopped leaving from here altogether? If they say there are no more steamers from here, I’d have to go home, feeling as if I’d died. That would mean a delay of another week or ten days, and in the meantime, my family might somehow find out about my situation and come here to drag me back. Not only that, but I’d brought only a little money with me, just enough to get by without anyone noticing. What if it’s not enough here? What would become of me then? Who here would even give me a cup of water? With all these worries swirling in my mind, I hesitated a little before going inside.
But then I thought, after coming all this way, what’s the point of standing here hesitating? Whatever happens, let it happen! So, bracing myself, I went into the company.
There, a servant appeared and asked, “Where to?”
“Inside,” I replied.
“Why?” he asked.
“No reason, just like that,” I said.
“In that case, please turn back,” he said.
“Why should I turn back?” I asked.
“When there’s no business ahead, you should go back,” he said.
“But I do have business ahead,” I insisted.
“What business?” he asked.
“Why should I tell you everything?” I retorted.
“Alright, tell me,” he said.
“Why?” I asked. By then, he was getting angry, his eyes turning red as he glared at me, and he looked as if he was about to say, “I won’t let you go inside…”
Barrister Parvateesam

He said, “What’s stopping you from leaving?” I replied, “If you don’t want to let me go, what can I do?” He retorted, “If you’re so keen, go ahead and try.” I said, “I’ll leave whenever I wish. What authority do you have over me?” For a minute, he stood silent, saying nothing. I too pretended to be deep in thought, staring at the walls and the staircase, hands shoved in my pockets, standing there as if lost in contemplation. But inside, I was trembling with fear. If I dared to step forward, what if he suddenly pounced and dragged me back? It would be just like the humiliation I suffered when I was leaving for England. That would not do at all. Still, I decided to see what he would do, and took a step forward.

From behind, as if firing a gun, he shouted, “Stop!” I turned around and said, “What! You got startled, didn’t you?” He could no longer contain his anger. He came up to me quietly, put his hand on my shoulder, and said, “Enough of your silly antics. Leave decently and respectfully.” The moment he placed his hand on my shoulder, I too was filled with anger. I brushed his hand off and said, “You seem to have forgotten that you’re just a servant. All this while, I’ve been patient and polite with you. I’ve seen thousands like you—if you continue like this, I’ll be forced to report you. If you lose your job, don’t come crying to me. So be careful,” I said, and tried to walk ahead.
Without another word, he grabbed my hand, gently led me out into the street, set me down, and said, “Say whatever you want where there are witnesses.” When I thought about it...

There seemed to be no way out. I began to fear that if I got into a scuffle with this ruffian, the whole affair would go awry. It struck me that there was no use in making friends with this fellow. So, I went back to him, quietly slipped half a rupee into his hand, and said, “It’s true that I have to go to London. I came here for a ticket. Otherwise, what business would I have here? If you want, look, here’s my money,” and I took out the cash from my pocket to show him.
Then he believed me, apologized for the misunderstanding, and showed me the way inside.

I walked in politely. The room was lined with large photographs of steamers and maps on all the walls. There was a sahib sitting there. I went up to him and said, “Sir, I want to go to London. When does the steamer leave? How long does the journey take? How much is the ticket?”

He looked at me with a hint of mockery and asked, “Are you really going to London?” “Yes, I am,” I replied. “Why?” he asked. “To study,” I said. “What will you study?” This question seemed unnecessary for a ticket clerk, but then again, he was a sahib, and he could even issue tickets. What was the use of arguing with him? So I said, “Barrister.” “Have your people agreed to send you?” he asked. I hesitated a little and said, “Yes.” “Or did you come without telling your family anything at all?” he pressed.

I stood there, a little frightened, wondering if he knew something about me, unable to think of what to say. He said, “Come now, did you really come without telling the truth at home? You can tell me, you needn’t be afraid. There are plenty who leave without telling their folks.”

At those words, I mustered some courage and said, “Yes, I came without telling them, because if I had, they wouldn’t have let me go.” “Then, if they get angry, won’t they refuse to send you money? Have you thought about that?” he asked. “It’s all right, they’ll send it,” I said. “If they don’t, you’ll be in a real fix! Think it over beforehand.” “I’ve thought it all through, sir. I set out only because I’m sure they’ll send it. Is there a steamer leaving today?” “There are no steamers to London for another week. But tomorrow, there’s a French steamer going up to Marseilles. From there, you can go by train.”
“If that’s the case, it will be cheaper for you, and you can reach your destination sooner. Do you have any objection to traveling that way?”
“I have absolutely no objection. Please arrange a ticket for the French steamer.”
“In which class do you want to travel?”
“Is third class comfortable, sir?”
“It’s reasonably comfortable. It’s fine, you can travel in it.”
“Then please get me a third-class ticket.”

He agreed and handed me the ticket. “Our company has an office in Marseilles as well. In fact, we have offices in every city. If you need any assistance anywhere, just go to our company’s office—they’ll help you as much as they can. There’s no need for you to worry,” he assured me.

Well, I thought, that settles everything for me. “If you have a lot of money with you, you can either hand it over to us, or keep it with yourself. As soon as you arrive in Marseilles, our company people will return your money to you. If you want your family to send you more money, just write to them and give them our company’s address. Whenever you receive money or letters, we’ll make sure they reach you safely,” he said.

“Alright, alright, this arrangement sounds excellent,” I replied, and handed over all the money I had to him. He told me to keep about fifty rupees with me for expenses, and gave me a cheque for the remaining amount. He also gave me a receipt with the Marseilles company’s address on it. “Come here tomorrow at three in the afternoon, and we’ll send you to the steamer,” he said. I took my leave from him.

Ah, what a wonderful company! They have offices in every city, and they’re providing so much help to people like me. I wondered, do they gain anything from all this? Or are they just doing it out of sheer goodwill? Pondering this, I walked towards the gateway of the street.
Just then, the porter who had earlier carried my luggage came up and asked, “Have you got your ticket, sir?”
“Yes, I have,” I replied. He saluted me. I felt pleased that his arrogance had diminished a little.
From there, I asked for directions to the bazaar and set off. The bazaar in this town was also quite impressive.

In the city, I spotted a company that looked like a proper company. The one I had bought earlier had proved useless, so I bought another hat. Then, as I reached the choultry, another thought struck me. Wouldn’t I need a lamp? What if there were no lamps on the steamer? Even if there were, would they keep them burning all night or not? The idea of sitting in the dark frightened me. Last night, there were lamps on the steamer when I boarded, but with my headache and nausea, I collapsed without knowing what was happening and slept till morning. Because I didn’t wake up during the night, I couldn’t remember whether the lamps were kept burning till dawn or not. If there were none on the steamer, I wouldn’t be able to get one at that point! Anyway, I’d need a lamp at some stage, if not now, at least after reaching England. So, thinking it would be a good way to pass the time, I bought a lamp stand and two dozen candles.

Then another doubt arose. Would I be able to get milk or buttermilk on the steamer? What if I couldn’t get any? I saw a sign on a shop here saying “condensed milk available,” and thought it would be wise to buy some if the shop was nearby. So, I bought two tins and returned to the choultry feeling quite pleased with myself.

After dinner that night, I thought I’d leisurely write a letter home. But when I opened my box, I couldn’t find any paper or pen. Well, I thought, I’ll just have to go to the bazaar and buy them tomorrow. With that, I slept comfortably that night.
The next morning, I went to the bazaar and bought writing paper, envelopes, a fountain pen, ink for the pen, a pencil, and a small exercise book to keep track of my expenses. Then I returned home.
I thought I’d write the letter first and post it before doing anything else, so I began writing.
WELL-BEING

To the revered Veda scholar, Brahmashri Vemuri Ramachandraiah, my father, His son Parvateesham offers many salutations and submits the following humble requests. I hope all is well with both families. Seeing the above address, this Colombo...

What is this place, you ask? Where is it? You might well wonder what reason I had to come here. This is the chief city of Ceylon. That is, in ancient times, we used to call this the Lanka of Ravanasura—the very same Ceylon. The entire race of rakshasas perished in the war with Ravana. So, at present, there is no fear of demons here.

For a long time, I have been watching the pitiable state of our country, and it has made me very sad. I could no longer bear to merely witness and endure it. I thought deeply about how to remove this misery from our land. What occurred to me was that if I could go once to the country of our rulers and learn some of their secrets, it would be of great benefit. Therefore, I set out with the intention of going there at least once. Since people are anyway making the journey, why shouldn’t I? It’s not as if this is a matter that can be settled in a day or two. I would have to stay there for some time—perhaps a year or two. So, in the meantime, if I studied for the barrister’s exam and passed, then after returning to my homeland, I could live independently, without having to bow my head and work under someone else. With that hope, I resolved to study for the bar there.

As for the expenses I would incur there, I will write to you in detail after I reach. For now, to cover my expenses, I have borrowed five hundred rupees at 1 rupee and 14 annas interest, through Mr. Gazavalli Narayana, who plays the role of the king in the Narsapuram drama company. He said that, owing to his friendship with me, he managed to get me such a low interest rate, and he asked me to send the money back quickly. So, I immediately handed over those five hundred rupees to him, and sent another five hundred rupees by telegraphic money order through Thomas Cook & Son, to be collected for me at the village of Marseilles in France. If you do not do this, I will face great difficulties in a foreign land.

You may think all this is foolishness, and that I am spending so much money unnecessarily. But I am going with great foresight. If I pass the bar and return, I will be able to earn as much money as I need. Please do not make any attempt to call me back home.
Do not try to stop me. I will not return home until the task I have set my mind upon is accomplished. I am boarding the steamer today itself. Please do not trouble yourself in vain.

I feel deeply sorry for leaving without informing you and without your permission. You know well that I have never before acted against your wishes. But in this matter, I was compelled to do so, for I knew that if you found out, you would never allow me to go. I am undertaking this daring venture because I firmly believe that, in the future, I will not only earn a great deal of money but also be of great service to our country. I am aware of how much distress this will cause you. Even so, I had no choice but to act thus. Please tell mother not to worry about how much hardship I might face in a foreign land, or what dangers might await me at sea. Forgive me for causing you all this pain.
I will write a letter as soon as I reach Marseilles. Please convey my respects to mother.
Kindly oblige.
Yours obediently, V. Parvatisham
P.S.: Please send money immediately through telegraphic money order, as much as possible.

It was very difficult for me to write this letter. The moment I thought of my mother’s words, tears welled up in my eyes. My hand began to tremble. The pen refused to move forward. Somehow, I managed to finish the letter, put it in an envelope, wrote the address on it, went to the post office, and dropped it in the post. I returned home, bathed, and sat down for a meal. I could not swallow a single morsel. Somehow, I forced down a couple of mouthfuls, got up, packed my things, lay down for a while, and after two hours, set out with my luggage for Cook’s Company.
From there, they sent a porter with me to the seashore. Our steamer was a little way out in the sea.
Barrister Parvateesam

The steamer before me looked even grander than the one I boarded the other day. The attendant who was with me led me to a small boat nearby and told me to get in; he climbed in as well. There were already quite a few sahibs and memsahibs in it. There were two or three more such boats, each ferrying people to our steamer. The man with me told me that all these people were to board the same steamer as I.

Quietly, we reached the steamer. Just as before, we were helped up from below. We climbed up one by one. It felt as though we were standing atop a tall building, looking down. While I stood there gazing, the man with me took my luggage and stowed it somewhere inside.

All of us stood there, quite a crowd, looking out at the sea, at the other steamers, and at the buildings on the shore. Just then, a bell rang. Those who were to disembark were told to hurry down. Many who had come up now climbed back into the little boats, waving their hands and looking up at those on deck as they left. I realized they had all come to see off their loved ones.

I remembered how, back in my village, whenever someone set off on a journey, even if my mother and father protested, people would still come a long way to see them off. But now, there was no one for me. I thought to myself, “Here I am, an orphan, without a soul to care for me, venturing into a new world.” I wondered how my mother and father would grieve when they read my letter from home. As these thoughts crowded my mind, an unbearable sorrow welled up within me.

Our steamer set off. In the small boats, people were still waving handkerchiefs to those on the steamer, even though they could hardly make out the faces. Who knows how many years it will be before I return to this land? And who can say if I will return at all? What if I die in a foreign land? Fear gripped me. The land was fading from view, now visible, now gone. I offered a single prayer to Mother Goddess, begging for her mercy. Unable to contain the rising tide of sorrow, I stood there, weeping like a little child.

I have no idea how long I sat there like that. Suddenly, someone came and placed a hand on my shoulder. I started as if waking from sleep and turned around. On one side, a sahib was looking at me as if to say, “What childishness is this?” On the other side, another sahib and a memsahib looked at me with a kind of sympathetic understanding of my sorrow. The man who had put his hand on my shoulder gestured for me to come along with him. Without knowing why, I wiped my eyes and followed him.

He led me down two flights of stairs, through a hall, and into a small room, where he pointed out my luggage. I supposed this must be the room where I was to stay. The room was very small. On one side, there were two or three long bunks stacked one above the other, each made up with bedding. Against one wall was a small set of porcelain basins with a tap, and beside it, a bar of soap. On another side, there were two towels. In the wall near the head of my bed, there was a round hole with a glass door—that was our cabin window. Through it, the sea was clearly visible. There was a small ladder to climb to the upper bunks.

By the time I entered the room, two Chinese youths were already sitting on the top bunks, arranging their belongings. I pushed my box and bedding under my bunk and sat gazing at the sea. Darkness had fallen. As in the previous steamer, electric lights were switched on in the room. The suit I was wearing felt tight, so I thought it would be better to loosen it. Quietly, I took off the suit and, from the box I had brought from home, pulled out my comfortable dhoti and tied it on, sitting there in just my shirt. The two boys above turned pale and stared at me. Why should I care who looks at me?

Then I wondered about dinner. Do the steamer people provide food? What kind of food do they serve? How much do they charge? I had forgotten to ask the company people about any of this. The previous night, the steamer staff hadn’t charged me anything. Perhaps they had forgotten to ask me.
Barrister Parvateesam

Maybe someone else ate it, or perhaps they left it untouched out of pity. In all the commotion, I forgot to ask what had happened. Anyway, there’s still some wheat flour and other things I brought from home, aren’t there? I thought, “Let’s make some rotis,” and began taking out the utensils one by one. Just then, a bell rang. The two young fellows upstairs came down and gestured for me to come along as well. I gathered from their signs that they were inviting me.
But I couldn’t understand a word of the language they spoke.

Thinking I’d see where they were headed, I went along with them. In the hall in front of our room, a white cloth was spread over a table, and all sorts of regular porcelain plates, knives, and forks were neatly arranged.

Seeing that, I felt a bit more confident. “Well, looks like I’ve escaped having to cook for myself today,” I thought, and put the ingredients I’d taken out back into the box, preparing myself for this electric meal.

There were about thirty or forty gentlemen present. Ten or fifteen ladies as well. Everyone began chatting away cheerfully. I couldn’t tell what language they were speaking. Since they mentioned “French steamer,” I guessed it must be French. Everyone looked me up and down, perhaps wondering about my appearance, and asked me something in their language. I replied in English. They all made funny faces and stared at me as if I were mad. I thought, “Should I try Telugu?” But then, if they don’t know English, how on earth would they understand Telugu? Realizing there was no use, I sat quietly while they continued their lively conversation. I began to feel a bit anxious. It seemed there wasn’t a single English-speaking person on this steamer.
It seemed there was not a single soul here who would talk to me. I wondered how I would ever pass the time.

In another moment, the serving of food began. Their serving style was quite amusing. One person would bring the food around to each person. Whoever wanted some would take as much as they liked and put it in their own plate.

Judging by the shape and smell of the dish they brought, I thought, “This is not something a Brahmin would even touch.” In our country, even those who eat meat cook it with vegetables and mix it with rice before eating. But here, they seemed to eat only meat, without any rice at all! The man brought the dish to me. I told him I didn’t want any. He stared at me in surprise. I didn’t care. What a strange, barbaric language he spoke! Couldn’t he converse in pure English? I thought. But what’s the use of telling him? It’s like talking to a wall! He wouldn’t understand unless I started crying!

It seemed my fate was to starve like a hermit and roast chapatis at midnight. As I got up to leave, the man gestured for me to sit and went to fetch another gentleman. The new arrival began speaking in some language or other. I grew irritated. Looking at the first fellow, I thought, “Why did you bring this ogre along as well? Are you trying to torment me further?” I said this in Telugu.
Well, if he couldn’t understand me, what did it matter what language I spoke? Telugu or otherwise? I assumed the newcomer might know at least a word or two of English.
Barrister Parvateesam

He asked, “Whether it’s through gestures or through that incomprehensible English language, can’t you eat?” I replied, “No, I cannot.” He asked, “Why?” I said, “I do not eat meat.” At that, he seemed to understand my predicament, gestured for me to sit, and took the waiter aside. Soon enough, he sent over two nice loaves of bread, a little butter, and some boiled potatoes. Well, what more could I ask for to fill my stomach? I ate those. By the time I finished, they brought sago pudding for everyone. I thought, “Alright, this is good,” and helped myself to a little more, thinking I might even grow fond of it. If every day went like this, I thought, it would be enough. I got up with the others and went to my room. Since the steamer staff themselves had already made the beds and arranged everything, there was no need for me to fuss over my own bed. I simply lay down on that bed, and in the darkness, wondered how the steamer found its way across this vast ocean, and drifted off to sleep.

At dawn, I woke up. I felt the urge to relieve myself, but was unsure where to go. There was no one around to ask. Should I wake the boys in my room and ask them? But they wouldn’t understand my language. I didn’t know what to do. So I sat there, holding it in with great difficulty, waiting for daybreak. If I tried to sleep, sleep wouldn’t come. Every minute felt like an age.

Somehow, morning arrived. I got up and went to the hall. I went up to one person after another and asked in English, “Where is the toilet?” But they couldn’t understand my language, and I didn’t know how to say it in theirs. I tried asking four or five people, but none could make sense of me. I was unable to express my distress. I feared that if I waited another moment, my stomach might burst. Should I try gestures? But how to gesture such a thing! And even if I did, what gesture would they understand? Based on our country’s customs, I held up one finger. No one understood. I showed two fingers. Still, no response. I wondered if, in their country, they might use three fingers, so I showed three. That didn’t work either. Growing desperate, I showed all five fingers. That too was of no use. In the end...

How I managed to signal them, or how I made my predicament known to the servants, I myself do not know. In the end, one of them took me and showed me the lavatory. He opened the door to the adjoining room and told me that it was the bathroom. I lingered there for a while. As for bathing, God alone knows—first, in my haste, I dashed into the lavatory, relieved myself, then returned to my room, brushed my teeth, and finally went into the bathroom and took a bath.

By the time I finished my bath and returned, everything was set up neatly for breakfast. Everyone else was served eggs and fish. For me, however, they brought some kind of porridge, bread, and butter.

Every day followed the same routine: waking up in the morning, attending to nature’s calls, wandering here and there for a while, having lunch at noon, taking a short nap, sipping tea, and then sitting around, waiting to see when help might be needed. Eating, sleeping—such was my daily program. Four days passed in this manner. Whether it was due to the constant rocking of the ship or the unfamiliar food, I always felt queasy and had a headache. All the comfort of rice was lost to me. By “comfort,” I mean that bread is no substitute for rice. Ever since we left Colombo, I hadn’t even set eyes on rice.

Thus, four days passed. On the morning of the fifth day, the steamer, which had been racing day and night, suddenly slowed down. Wondering why, I peered out of the window and saw land in sight. The man who supplied my meals came and told me that the steamer would soon stop at the port, and that I could go ashore and have a look around.
He said it, but after actually going ashore, what if the steamer suddenly sailed away without warning?
Barrister Parvateesam

After traveling on water for these four days, the very sight of land felt as if life itself had returned to me. The two young Chinese fellows in the cabin were putting on their clothes and gestured for me to join them. I too felt an urge to go ashore. Donning my suit and the hat I had bought in Colombo, I set out looking every bit the English gentleman.

I had no idea where the town was, but right by the seashore stood a large shop and a hotel. In the distance, I saw a couple of people with black bodies, thick lips, faces like monkeys, and hair like sheep’s wool, twisted into tight rings. Around their waists, they wore long leaves, and in their hands, they carried lizards as they wandered about. Seeing them, my mind recalled the geography lessons of my school days, and I guessed this must be an African country.
After wandering here and there for a while, I ate at the hotel and returned to the steamer by three in the afternoon. The ship set sail again at six in the evening.

No one on the steamer could pronounce my name. Since I had boarded at Colombo, they began calling me “Colombo Sahib.” With no one to talk to, not eating the food they ate, not drinking the liquor they drank, I felt quite out of place. It seemed as if everyone pitied me, seeing my predicament. Eventually, someone began sitting near me in the evenings, trying to strike up a conversation.

After this departure, my nausea and headache grew worse. I didn’t even have the strength to go to the dining room. They would bring me some bread or porridge to my cabin. One day, I felt so ill that I couldn’t sleep at all that night. My head felt as if it would split open. Memories of home flooded my mind. I thought, “If only I had a bit of turmeric root!” Who would apply sandalwood paste for me here? Tears welled up in my eyes. Wiping them away, I looked around and saw the lady’s hat I had bought in Chennapatnam hanging on the wall. An immense anger seized me. I thought perhaps throwing it away would ease my pain. In that fit of misery, I got up, grabbed the hat, crushed it, and flung it out the porthole.
After coming and lying down, I managed to get a little restless sleep. Dawn broke. The headache hadn’t lessened at all. In fact, I felt a bit feverish as well.

On the third day after the steamer had departed from the previous port, at one o’clock in the afternoon, the sahib came and announced that everyone had to be examined by the doctor, and that we should dress and be ready. At three in the afternoon, a bell was rung. The young fellows in my cabin signaled for me to come along. Though I had no energy even to move, I slowly made my way to the hall. We were all told to stand in a line. A doctor came, called out names one by one, gave each a brief examination, and told them to move along.

After a while, he called out, “Mr. Colombo.” Thinking they didn’t know my name and had told the doctor this instead, I promptly replied, as I used to during school roll call, “Present, sir!” Everyone burst out laughing. The doctor said, “Not you.” Then an old sahib, about seventy-five years old, came forward. I realized his name must be Colombo.

After the doctor left, I called the steward who served me food and asked, “What’s all this commotion about?” He said the steamer had reached Suez, that it was routine here for a doctor to examine everyone, and that anyone found sick would be put ashore. I asked, “Suez? As in the Suez Canal?” He replied, “In another fifteen minutes, we’ll be entering the Suez Canal. If you wish, you can go up and have a look.”

With the help of one of the young fellows from my cabin, I slowly climbed up to the deck. This was the first time I’d come up here since the ship had set sail. The cool sea breeze made me feel as though life had returned to me! I sat there, watching the Suez Canal, until the lamps were lit. As a child, I used to wonder what the Suez Canal was. It looked just like an ordinary canal for boats. Only, it was a bit wider and deeper. On the banks, there were palm trees just like the ones back home. Some said those were date palms. There were plenty of camels to be seen. Everything looked quite beautiful. As soon as the lamps were lit, I went back to my cabin and lay down. By dawn, we had reached Port Said.
The young men in my cabin were getting dressed. They told me to as well.
Let’s go into the town, they signaled. Well, what’s the point of sitting here? I thought I’d bear it with some patience, stroll around for a while, and then return. So I dressed up and set out.

The town was quite large indeed. There were many fine shops and such. But, looking at the goings-on there, it seemed to me that wickedness was in abundance. They had tramcars there too. But the remarkable thing was that they couldn’t run on their own—they were pulled by horses! That struck me as rather odd.

As I wandered along the bazaars, I spotted the office of the Thomas Cook company. Seeing it felt like running into an old friend. I strode in confidently. The clerk there looked at me and asked, “What do you want?” “Nothing,” I replied.
“Then why have you come?”
“I’m your passenger.”
“So what?”
“Nothing at all. I just came to see how your company is doing here,” I said. He didn’t say a word. I made some remark, glanced around, and then walked back out onto the street.

Nearby, I saw a post office. I went in, picked up a card, wrote a letter home saying I was safe, dropped it in the post, and came out. In one shop, I saw some fine, broad woolen scarves, about two hands wide, made right there. Wasn’t I heading to a cold country? If I bought one of these, I could wrap it around my neck or ears—it would keep me warm, and it looked quite elegant too. So I bought one.
I spotted a coffee hotel, went in, had a little snack, and then calmly made my way back to the steamer. At seven in the evening, the steamer set off.

That whole night passed pleasantly enough. But from dawn, my troubles began. It wasn’t exactly nausea, nor was it vomiting—just a constant churning inside, as if something wanted to come up but never did. Ever since we left Colombo, I’d never suffered like this. Until now, I’d been enjoying myself, but now even the young fellows in my cabin had collapsed onto their beds. I didn’t open my eyes once after I shut them. No food. I didn’t even bother to get up for a sip of water. Like that—

I have no idea how long I slept. The room was sealed tight, with the windows and doors bolted shut, not a breath of air allowed in. When I asked why they did this, they said there was a storm raging outside. If the windows were opened, water would come pouring in.

For about a week, I suffered like this, losing all sense of day and night. With nothing else to do, I would stare at my watch, thinking it would help pass the time. I’d turn it upside down and keep looking at it, hoping for some distraction. In the first few days, the watch worked well enough. I was quite pleased, thinking it was a fine piece. But as time went on, I noticed something odd: it would keep perfect time all day, but by morning, it would be a quarter of an hour slow. There seemed to be no reason for it to lag like this, and if it had happened just once, I could have ignored it. But day after day, it kept falling behind, and I grew increasingly irritated. I began to suspect that the fellow who sold it to me had palmed off a dud, thinking I wouldn’t notice. It became clear to me that even the English, when they get the chance, aren’t above cheating you.

I wondered why I’d even bothered to bring this wretched watch along. Yet, I couldn’t bring myself to throw it away, no matter how much I considered it. Well, I thought, at least it’s only half an hour off—better a blind well than no well at all. So I gave up on throwing it away and put it back in my trunk.

Then, one morning, the commotion of the sea finally subsided. The sahib came in while it was still dark, woke me up, and said, “We’ll be disembarking today. Don’t worry, we’ll reach Bengal—or perhaps some other port—in an hour or two. Land is in sight!” He spoke with unusual warmth, telling me to get up, have a little breakfast, and come up on deck to see.

After four or five days without food, my stomach was in knots. My body felt utterly drained. When I tried to stand, my legs trembled beneath me. Nevertheless, I got up, brushed my teeth, and was just pulling on my shirt when the sahib sent some breakfast to my room. I ate a little, felt somewhat better, and made my way up on deck. It was about eight o’clock. The sky was clear, the sea looked beautiful, and the sun seemed to have just risen. The early rays danced across the waves, turning them into a field of sparkling gems. In the distance, the mist was parting like a curtain, and the mountains along the shore began to appear.

A little could be seen. Most clearly of all, atop a mountain, the golden spire of a temple shone resplendently in the sunlight. As we drew closer, I saw that the harbor was crowded with steamers—so many that I lost count. For a moment, I wondered if every steamer in the world had gathered here at once. The sight of it all filled me with a strange kind of fear. My mind was unsettled, lost in anxious thoughts, trying to guess what fate awaited me ahead. Around eleven o’clock, we finally reached Marseilles.

Just as a train pulls into a platform, our steamer drew up to a platform built out into the sea at Marseilles. The platform was teeming with people, bustling and jostling. Those on the steamer waved down to those below, and those below waved up to those above. There was a flurry of handkerchiefs, garlands tossed, kisses blown and caught. It seemed as if all the friends and relatives of the passengers had come to greet them. I alone had neither friend nor kin there. Whenever I returned home to Narsapur, if I wrote a letter in advance, my mother—no matter how busy she was—would stand in the street, waiting for me to arrive. My father, pretending to have some errand, would come out of town to meet me on the way. But today, there was no one here for me. A wave of sorrow swept over me. I was stepping into a new world, utterly inexperienced, a young man with no one to lean on in this foreign land. How would I manage to compose myself here, all alone? Fear gripped me.

One by one, the passengers disembarked, embracing those waiting below, shedding tears of joy. I, too, felt my eyes fill with tears as I stood there watching. Except for me, everyone else had left. Just as the last person was leaving, an Englishman came up to me and greeted me in English. My spirits revived. I thought, “At least I can exchange a few words with this gentleman, even if he is a stranger.”
“Are you coming from Colombo?” he asked.
“Yes,” I replied.
"Where is your luggage?"
"Downstairs."
"Do you know anyone here?"
"No—who are you?"
"I am a man from Thomas Cook Company. If you need any help, I can assist you. Where have you decided to stay?"
"I have no idea. This country is new to me. If you hadn’t come, I don’t know what I would have done. If you don’t mind, I’d be very grateful if you could kindly take me to a hotel," I said.
He looked at me for a moment, almost mockingly, and asked, "Shall I take you to a big hotel?"

I thought to myself, “What’s the point of coming all the way to England and going to a small hotel instead of a big one?” So I told him to take me to a big hotel. He glanced at me again and, hesitantly, said, "It will be very expensive in a big hotel." Though I appeared as I did, I wanted him to think I was a man of means, so I smiled and said, "No problem, don’t worry. Please take me there."
"Alright, if you tell me where your luggage is, I’ll have it brought up," he said, in a lordly manner.

As soon as I told him the place, he had my luggage brought up and said, "Please, let’s go." We disembarked from the steamer, came outside, got into a carriage, and smoothly arrived at the hotel. I thought, "A hotel here must be like the ones in Chennapatnam or Colombo, or perhaps a little better." But this building looked enormous even from the outside. I had never seen such a grand building before.

As soon as the carriage stopped, a man dressed in a comical outfit came and opened the carriage door. The moment he saw me, he lifted his head a little and began to look away to the side. Then, glancing at me once more, he looked at the man from Thomas Cook as if to ask, "Why have you brought someone like this?" That look made me shrink halfway into myself.
As soon as we both got down, he glanced at my luggage and, without waiting any longer, walked straight to the hotel entrance.

We walked in right behind him. The moment I stepped inside, my feet refused to move forward. It looked just like Indra’s palace! I was afraid he might take me to some grand hotel, and I wondered how much it would cost. But then I thought, “What’s the use of acting like a fool now?” and decided to walk in with all the dignity of a man who had spent his whole life in such hotels.

The Englishman who came with me spoke to the clerk standing there. The clerk took out a big register and asked me to sign it. My Englishman handed me over to a porter, told him to take me to my room, and after making sure I was safely delivered, he went off to his office.

The porter carried my luggage and put it in a small room. In front of the room were iron-barred doors that could be locked. The room itself was extremely small. There was only a tiny bench inside. I wondered how anyone could stay in such a small room. There wasn’t even enough space to lay out a bed, and even if I wanted to sleep on the bench, it wasn’t long enough for me to stretch out. There was at least a lamp burning in the room, but I couldn’t see a single window for air. In such a big hotel, how could there be such tiny rooms? If all the rooms were like this, how did the other guests manage? Maybe, seeing I was a native, they gave me a useless room that no one else wanted. What was my status, after all? I decided I wouldn’t enter that room.

The porter, after putting my luggage inside, beckoned me to come in. I refused. He kept gesturing for me to come in. I didn’t understand a word of his language. No matter what, I insisted loudly, “I won’t come in!” He stared at me with a bewildered look, not understanding a thing. To get to the bottom of this, I called the clerk. The clerk too asked me to go inside. I said, “If this is the room, I don’t want it. I’ll go to another hotel.” In my broken English, I told him I didn’t want the room and would rather throw my luggage out than stay there.

The other guests in the hotel—gentlemen and ladies—started laughing when they saw me. I repeated to the clerk that I didn’t want the room and asked him to throw my luggage outside. Perhaps realizing there was no use arguing further, he grabbed my hand and forcibly dragged me into the room.

He pressed a button and the door closed. As soon as he did, the room, with a jolt, shot upwards into the sky as if it were flying through space. I was so startled that I let out a loud yelp. In a moment, the room came to a halt.
The attendant opened the door and asked me to walk out. I didn’t understand a thing. I wondered what other strange things awaited me and, full of curiosity and amazement, I followed him.

The attendant picked up my luggage and politely asked me to come along. He led me into another room and showed me inside. Only then did I breathe a sigh of relief, realizing that this was a clever way to reach the upper floor without any effort. I felt embarrassed, thinking of how much everyone must have laughed at me.

This room, too, was befitting of a hotel. It was spacious, with a large bed in the center—two mattresses on top, each as thick as two palms. On one side, there was a sofa, two chairs, and a table with a large mirror on it. On another table, there was a big porcelain jug, two pitchers of water, a bar of soap, a bunch of jasmine flowers, and two freshly ironed towels. As for the walls and the decor, words could not do them justice. I stood there, eyes wide, taking it all in, while the attendant set down my luggage and quietly went on his way.

I sat on the sofa for a minute, taking a rest. I thought to myself, “What comfort, what luxury! When will our country ever reach such a state?” Near the door, there was a sign in English: “Press the bell.” I wondered why they had written that. Maybe everyone who comes in is supposed to press it, I thought, so I pressed it.
Within a minute, an attendant came running and said something in French. For no reason at all—
Barrister Parvateesam

Hunger was burning me up. The moment this fellow came and started speaking that language, I felt a surge of irritation. “If you can speak proper English, then speak. Otherwise, walk away without making a fuss,” I told him. He seemed to know a little English. “Why did you ring the bell?” he asked. “I didn’t ring the bell. If it sounded like someone did, that’s not my doing! Do you need anything?” he asked.

“Yes,” I replied, “I need to eat. Where is the dining room?” Suddenly, as if remembering something, he looked me up and down and asked, “Will you be dining in your room or in the hall with everyone else?” Why on earth would I eat alone in my room instead of with everyone in the hall? “Take me there,” I said. “Please, sir, this way,” he said, and led me into the hall, seating me in a corner.

Everything here was stranger than the last. Of all the towns I’d seen so far, this hall was by far the most beautiful. There were tables, and on them cloths as white as jasmine flowers, and on those, vases of all shapes and sizes filled with colorful flowers, and gleaming white plates that dazzled the eyes. What beauty, what luxury! I sat there, wide-eyed, marveling at it all.

The hall was filled with many English gentlemen and ladies, all seated for their meal. Just looking at their attire, you could tell they were people of great importance—nothing like the likes of me. Some glanced at me, then quickly averted their eyes, keeping to their own business. The way they looked at me reminded me of how, during a Brahmin meal, if an untouchable were to appear, everyone would stare at him. That’s how they looked at me. I thought to myself, “Why did I come here at all?”

A servant came and placed a dish of meat curry in front of me. I indicated that I wouldn’t eat it. “What do you want?” he asked. “I’m a vegetarian,” I replied. He took away the dish and brought back a fish. When I refused that as well, he brought two boiled eggs. Astonished, I told him I wouldn’t eat those either. He looked at me as if he were seeing some strange new animal, then, with great indifference, brought me a few boiled potatoes, some beans, and other plain vegetarian fare, and set them down carelessly.
I felt even the servant now looked down on me. I finished my meal. Once again, I decided to go to the Cook’s Company to see if any money had arrived from home.
I set out. Wanting to call for the servant to help me down the stairs with my luggage, I hesitated, unsure how to summon him, and so I simply descended the steps as usual and came downstairs.

Seeing me, everyone burst into laughter. I wondered, “Why are they laughing at me like this?” Glancing down at my clothes, I thought, “It must be this seven-and-a-half rupee suit that’s the culprit.” Resolving at once to buy myself a new outfit, I stepped out onto the street.

But as soon as I was outside, the cold began to make my teeth chatter. Even though my plans were sharp, they were no match for the biting cold. Thinking, “It’s so chilly out here,” I hurried back to my room, fetched the muffler I had bought at Port Said, wrapped it around my neck and ears, put my hat on top, and ventured out again.

Previously, when people saw me, they would stifle their laughter, giggling discreetly. But now, everyone who caught sight of my face burst out laughing openly. As I walked, a crowd of twenty or thirty young fellows trailed behind me, whistling and laughing, making quite a spectacle.
Fortunately, the Cookwari Company Hotel was very close by. As soon as I entered, the clerks inside broke into peals of laughter. I was so embarrassed that tears welled up in my eyes.

I pleaded with them in distress, “Why are you all laughing at me like this? If there’s something wrong with me, please tell me so I can correct it.” Taking pity on me and understanding my predicament, the very clerk who had checked me into the hotel in the morning explained kindly, “The muffler you so affectionately bought and are now wearing to ward off the cold—here, in this country, only women wear such things. It’s not customary for men to wear them. That’s why everyone found it so amusing. Please forgive us for laughing.”

“So this is the reason for all this commotion!” I thought, relieved that it wasn’t anything worse. Grateful for their explanation, I took off my muffler and, as a token of thanks, offered it to anyone among them who wanted it as a gift.
I asked if there had been any telegrams for me. “No,” replied the clerk. “Alright, perhaps it will come tomorrow,” I thought.

I complained, “The cold is really unbearable.” The clerk asked, “Didn’t you buy an overcoat?” “No,” I replied. “Well, if you don’t get one soon, you won’t be able to withstand the cold,” he said. “Please, if you could...
Barrister Parvateesam

I requested him to take me to a clothing store. Poor fellow, he seemed like a good man, one who had seen both hardships and comforts, and perhaps even had children (though he hadn’t said so, I imagined he must have). So, without delay, he came along with me.

The two of us entered a large shop. It was quite grand. The shop looked just like the ones in Chennapatnam, only even bigger, if you can believe it. There was a beautiful carpet spread across the floor. It looked so fine that I thought it would be better to walk beside it rather than on it, so I stepped onto the bare floor. But it turned out that it wasn’t the floor at all—my foot slipped as soon as I set it down. In my attempt not to fall, I tried to grab hold of the air, but since I couldn’t catch hold of anything, I ended up falling flat on my back. The moment I fell, all the clerks, assistants, and everyone else present burst into laughter at once.

The Englishman beside me helped me up and asked if I was hurt, then advised me that if I walked on the carpet, I wouldn’t slip and fall. Until then, everyone had been laughing, but as soon as I got up and looked at them, they stopped laughing and stood there pretending as if nothing had happened.

The Englishman who came with me bought me a new suit and an overcoat shaped like a barrel. I put them on right there in the shop. What a difference between the suit I had brought from home and this one! Anyone who saw the suit I had worn until now would surely have laughed! The cold also became much more bearable. The clothes were quite good, but when I saw the price, I was taken aback—even I, who had seen so much, was surprised.

From there, the Englishman’s clerk and I set out to see the town. To describe the beauty of that city and the wonders we saw would require a book as big as the Mahabharata. In all the foreign lands I have visited...
I have decided to write about all the strange things I saw in a separate book. Moreover, I felt that a personal memoir should not be overloaded with descriptions, so I have not included them here.

However, there is one incident that I feel compelled to recount. Of all the sights we saw, the most amusing was a house of mirrors. It was filled with large standing mirrors—not ordinary ones, mind you. What fun would there be in ordinary mirrors? The peculiarity of these mirrors was this: in one, a person appeared just as he was; in another, he looked four times fatter than in real life; in yet another, he appeared thin and shriveled, as if he had been squeezed through a wringer. In one mirror, he looked like a tiny doll, as if seen through the pupil of an eye; in another, he appeared as long as a furlong. There were all sorts of such variations...

Accompanying us was a rather portly Englishman and a slender English lady whom, by all appearances, was his wife. The Englishman looked especially comical in those mirrors. The lady could not stop laughing. Seeing them, I too burst out laughing. As the two of us laughed together, the Englishman grew visibly embarrassed. Noticing this, I quietly walked away. From there, we returned peacefully to the hotel. The Englishman who was with me bade me good night, saying he would see me in the morning, and took his leave. I went to my room.

But I must say, I was greatly surprised by the courtesy shown by that Englishman. If he were in our country, he would not pay the slightest attention to anyone. Here, however, everyone treats me as if I were a minor zamindar. To have Englishmen do my bidding and receive their salutations—what joy it brought me!
The afternoon had been quite an experience. So, for this meal, I had my food brought up to my room and ate there.

Then, preparing to sleep, I took off my shirt and, as usual, wrapped myself in my native dhoti. But it was so cold I could not bear it. There was no way to endure it. So, without removing my suit or overcoat, I simply took off my shoes and approached the bed.
Barrister Parvateesam

Looking at the silk quilt on the bed, I felt no inclination to lie down on it. The quilt looked so new and pristine that I was afraid even a touch would spoil it. I couldn’t bear the thought of it getting creased. I considered taking my own quilt and lying down on the floor or on a sofa. But then, after paying so much money, what was the point of sleeping on the floor? So, I carefully folded the quilt from the bed, placed it on a chair, wrapped myself in my shawl, and lay down, all the while worrying if my money would arrive the next day or not. What would become of me if it didn’t come? With these thoughts swirling in my mind, I finally drifted off to sleep.

Early in the morning, a servant came and woke me up. He took one look at me, said something, and burst out laughing as he walked away. Moments later, another servant arrived, peered into the room, and left giggling. In this manner, all the servants in the hotel came one by one, peeped into my room, and ran off laughing. Watching all this, my body burned with embarrassment.

I quietly went and told the manager, who brought the head clerk upstairs. By the time we arrived, four or five servants were still standing there, doubled over with laughter. As soon as they saw us, they stopped laughing. The head clerk scolded them, apologized to me, and then left, still chuckling to himself. I wondered if all this laughter was because of my shawl.

After finishing my morning ablutions, as I was having some fruit, a man from the Cook & Co. company arrived and informed me that my money had come. The moment I heard those words, an indescribable joy filled me. I went, collected the money, and returned to the hotel. Learning that the train was leaving that very day, I quickly packed my things and came downstairs.

The head clerk handed me the bill. I do not wish to disclose the total amount now, but I am convinced that if any zamindar were to hear it, his heart would skip a beat. As I was paying the bill, two servants came and stood nearby. Thinking it would be proper to give them a tip since I was leaving, I gave each of them an anna. Did they look pleased? Not in the least! They turned the coin over and over, sniffed it, borrowed a lens from the head clerk to examine it, then wrinkled their noses, tossed the coins aside, and walked away with an air of supreme disdain. Their arrogance was simply astonishing.

By this point, I was thoroughly angry. Did they think money just falls into one’s lap? Who would pay more than I already had? “Keep it, do what you will!” I muttered to myself, and made my way to the railway station.
The cook’s man handed me a ticket to Folkestone and told me to change trains at Paris, and then, after getting down at Boulogne and boarding the steamer, I would reach a place called Folkestone.
The train was, by and large, much like the ones back home. Only, the compartments were a little more spacious. Even the third-class compartments had berths.

By dawn, we reached Paris. There, I got down, brushed my teeth and washed up, and went to the platform for my connecting train. The place was swarming with people. Only two compartments were empty. Thinking they must be third-class, I went and sat in one.

A minute later, a memsahib arrived, saw me, and called out to a porter, seemingly instructing him to remove me. The porter came and told me to get down. He said something in French, in a hundred different ways. Whatever he said, I refused to budge. He went and brought the guard. Even when the guard told me, I didn’t get down. He pointed to the window and showed me a sign. On it was written “Des Dames.” I had no idea what that meant. “Looks fine to me,” I said, feeling quite pleased. He told me to get down. “Why?” I asked. He didn’t know how to explain, so he brought the station master.
Since it was a ladies’ compartment, the station master politely requested me to get down and seated me in another empty compartment.

By noon, I reached Boulogne. I got down and boarded the steamer. The steamer was quite small. The sea was terribly rough. Because of that, everyone was feeling sick and vomiting. Though I had traveled by steamer many times before, I had never suffered so much. Everyone lay in their corners as if their lives were ebbing away. I kept wondering when this misery would end. All in all, it didn’t take more than two hours. But those two hours felt like an eternity.
By the time I got down at Folkestone, it was about five o’clock. Remembering that I was stepping onto English soil for the first time, I made sure to put my right foot forward.

A strange anxiety began to stir in my heart. My chest tightened with apprehension. Until now, I had stubbornly pushed my way through everything. But now, thoughts of what lay ahead vanished from my mind. I simply bowed once, trusting that God would take care of everything.
End of Part One.
Sixth Edition – Final Word

It has been forty-six years since Barrister Parvateesam first made his appearance. In another four years, he will celebrate his Golden Jubilee. If I am fortunate enough to be alive and well by then, I shall witness that celebration with great joy.

It has become a universal custom to write a preface or introduction for every book and to print it at the very beginning. But, to be honest, I have never liked this practice from the very start. In my opinion, readers should first read the book they have chosen, from beginning to end, and form their own judgment. Only after that should they compare their opinion with what others—be it the author or someone else—have expressed in the preface or introduction. If their view matches or differs, they can weigh and consider it. I think this is a beautiful approach. Even today, I believe that forming an opinion beforehand, based on someone else’s words, is not a very good habit.
Barrister Parvateesam was my very first publication. Even back then, I held this opinion, and so, at that time too, I wrote my final word at the end of the book.
Here, I present a few lines from what I wrote then:

Our elders believed that only a work adorned with all eighteen types of descriptions could be called a true poem. Similarly, an English author once said, “A book cannot be a book without an introduction.” It adds...

“Weight to the book,” remarked another gentleman sarcastically. Be that as it may, these days, unless a book has a foreword, it seems incomplete. Of late, this has become something of a tradition among us. One must seek out some eminent Andhrite, or even a non-Andhrite, and have them write a foreword in Telugu or English. Whether that eminent person is from Andhra or not, he usually lacks the time or patience to read the whole book; and even if he does read it, he may not like parts of it but is reluctant to say so. Not knowing what to write, he either heaps praise on the author and the book as he pleases, or, after all that, his praise may not match the quality of the book as the author had hoped. This is quite common. For this reason, I did not wish to trouble someone else to write a preface for this little book.

Therefore, so that critics may all express their opinions without hesitation, I have decided to write this preface myself, stating my own views. Whenever a new movement begins in the world, it first attracts young and impressionable minds, filling them with enthusiasm and propelling them into action. But enthusiasm alone is not enough; at that age, it does not occur to them that one must also consider the consequences, look before and after, and weigh the options. Especially in a country without freedom, there is always a rush to immediately achieve self-rule, forgetting that such haste can lead to missteps. I do not know how things were among the Andhras before, but ever since the so-called Andhra movement began, a peculiar new nature called “Andhra individuality” has emerged. This has manifested most strongly among the youth. That very spirit is embodied in our Parvatisham.

The young man is naive. He has heard the elders’ speeches and learned that the state of the country is not as it should be, that some change is necessary. But what exactly should be done? The elders did not say, and his limited understanding could not grasp it. Yet, they did not leave him at that, either. He considered it beneath him to ask others and find out the full details. He thought it unworthy to seek clarification from others about something even the greats could not define.

He thought he alone could carry on. He believed that if he did not undertake this journey, there would be no salvation for the land of the Hindus. There are many ways to convey a message. Of them all, the method that appeals to everyone is humor. Even the most dejected and disheartened soul is enlivened in body and mind by laughter. That is why, taking only the humorous aspects of the present-day Andhra character and embodying them in a single individual, I wrote this story. Until now, there have been very few works in our language that are primarily humorous. The absence of such books in our tongue made me wonder whether our language was perhaps unsuited for humor. Though Sri Veeresalingam wrote a few farces, I do not think they are entirely conducive to laughter. In the same way, Chilakamarti Lakshminarasimham, Sripanuganti Lakshminarasimha Rao Pantulu, and Sri Gurajada Apparao have written humorous works and shown the way. The poets of old might have thought that humor lay only in bawdiness and abuse.

Taking some trivial matter from daily life and narrating it in a witty, laughter-inducing manner—this art was taught to the Andhra world by Sri Chinta Dikshitulu alone. From the time I read the stories and sketches he wrote in magazines like Sahiti, I realized that humor could indeed be well expressed in Telugu. With that intention, I wrote this book as my first attempt. Just as you read it for amusement, I wrote it for amusement, with no other ill intent.

For some reason, the Andhra public heartily enjoyed and especially appreciated me. As punishment for that first mistake, Parvateesham got stuck in the country. What can I do, you tell me? Since then, I have not hurried to write such things again. Still, who knows when inspiration might strike? Even if I write something by accident, I am fully confident that the readers who have supported me since then will not abandon me even today. With that, I say Namaste and nothing more.
Barrister Parvateesam
I am unable to write any more. Namaste.

The lines above are mostly from the first edition. At the end, these few lines are from the new edition. Now, I feel it would be good to add a few lines to this edition. As soon as the first edition was published, many people read the book as long as they could get hold of it. I presented it respectfully to some people myself. Among them, some did not like my opinion on Sri Veeresalingam’s farces and stopped reading the book. They were quite angry with me too. Others criticized that the book was not good. A book, among the public, attracts some and draws them close, while repelling others who dislike it. Whatever happens, the writer’s responsibility ends with the writing itself. Whether a work is considered good or bad depends on the reader’s culture, sympathy, and diverse perspectives. Everyone has their own opinion. That’s why it is said, “People have different tastes.” Just because some say it is not good, the writer should not be disheartened. As our Devulapalli Krishnasastri wrote, “Let them laugh or not, what is it to me?”

Long before this, a great storm arose over the English novel “The Picture of Dorian Gray” by Oscar Wilde. Countless voices argued about it. Seeing this commotion, a friend asked Wilde, “What a great man you are! With so much uproar and thunder, while we are all shaken, why do you remain silent?” To this, Wilde laughed, gave some answer, and in the middle said one striking thing: “When critics disagree, the artist is in accord with himself.” In other words, let them fight and die if they wish—what is it to us? I found this answer truly wonderful.
By nature, I am averse to quarrelling with anyone about anything. Moreover, if two or three Brahmo Samajists are angry with me, I do not feel any distress. My customs, my beliefs—

I have never harbored any anger towards the Brahmo Samajists who tried to mix oil and fire, nor towards people of other religions. Being one who is content to let things be, I have never been one to answer back to anything. I do not even attempt to do so. Now, after more than thirty years of effort, I feel it is appropriate to share a few of my thoughts on the nature of humor, and so I include them in this final note.

First, a word about the farces of Sri Veeresalingam. The laughter or satisfaction one experiences while watching a farce is not truly related to the essence of humor. In English, this is called satire. That is, it is a form of ridicule. This is an attempt by those who wish to reform society, to highlight and mock the vices and abuses present in it, writing farces in a satirical manner with the noble intention of social reform.
Comedy is lifted above the plane of amusement and sensation and becomes an intellectual experience.
One laughs, but having detachment of mind he sees his potential self in the object of his laughter, and thereby he is laughed at as well as laughing.
Thus laughter must be finely tempered, searching, corrective, yet always humane, if it is to rise to the noble pretensions of a spiritual therapeutic, and comedy be realized to the highest.
Only when an individual or society has become emancipated morally and intellectually can he or it withstand the fusillade of that laughter with remedial effect—

The above sentences were written long ago by George Meredith. Their meaning is that humor intended for social reform must be delicate, corrective, and above all, suffused with compassion. Otherwise, the very idea of using farce for social reform becomes futile. Whether it is an individual or a society, unless they are morally and mentally...

Only when a certain level is attained in society can one endure the ridicule and laughter that comes from the public as a result of farcical performances. In the farces of Sri Pantulu, disgust, anger, and cruelty are more prominently visible. Therefore, I feel that farce lacks the essential quality of humanity. Western philosophers opine that a humorist must possess the ability to view life as a whole with a calm and gentle perspective. To what extent our writers possess this quality, readers themselves may judge.

It seems that many people have concluded that Parvateesham, Girisam, and Ganapathi are all of the same kind of comic character. I am at a loss as to what to say about this. Girisam, in the play, is neither a villain nor a virtuous man. He represents those few in life who are neither here nor there. The chief quality of humor is common humanity. I cannot agree that Girisam’s traits are universal and common to all mankind. Therefore, there are always very few people like Girisam in society. Yet, one cannot but admit that he is ever alive, immortal, and, even if in different disguises, always among us.

Now, Ganapathi is a different kind of person. He belongs to a particular class—uneducated, impoverished, lacking any qualification to earn a livelihood, and, worse still, born a Brahmin but incapable even of working as a laborer. Still, he must live, mustn’t he! Thus, suffering all sorts of troubles, sometimes as a jester, sometimes as a village cook, sometimes as a corpse-bearer, appearing in various such avatars, he has led his unfortunate life. I cannot accept that such a man is the very embodiment of humor.

For a man who ought to be the recipient of everyone’s compassion, justice, and mercy, Sri Lakshminarasimham, in those days, incorporated into his life some humorous sayings and incidents popular among the people, and thus created Ganapathi as a comic character. But I believe that the misfortunes of others should evoke our compassion, not become fodder for humor. This is also the opinion of the elders.

Now, a word about myself. What can I say about our Parvatisham? Except for a handful, he has become beloved to all of Andhra. He has become a name to remember forever. From children to elders, everyone, at some point or another, brings him up as an example. In his book ‘Humour in Telugu’, Sri Mutnuri Sangameshwar Rao wrote, “We cannot tolerate Girisham, but we cannot live without Parvatisham.” I believe this is the voice of the people.
