The power to laugh, the power to imagine—these are gifts that Lord Parameshwara has bestowed only upon mankind. Our rhetoricians have defined why we laugh: whenever we see or hear something grotesque, distorted, or out of the ordinary, we laugh. That is, when our eyes and ears refuse to accept some strange novelty, all we can do is laugh and move on.

The Westerners have gone a step further. They say that not only in sound and form, but if we observe life closely—both in its broad strokes and its subtleties—we find countless humorous incidents in every matter, every single day. The only requirement, they say, is that we have the ability to see, recognize the oddity, imagine the reality behind it, and enjoy it. Generally, human weaknesses—greed, pride, arrogance, ignorance, lust, passion, hatred, and so on—are all sources of humour. Many stories, farces, and comedies in both ancient and modern literature are based on these. You must have noticed that even in the future, these themes will continue to appear in new forms.

Man is, by nature, arrogant. That is why even those great souls who walk around as if they are above all humanity become objects of ridicule. Unable to deny their own flaws, and imagining those flaws in others, they attempt to mock others, only to become the butt of jokes themselves. As the saying goes, “Who is this blue man, Vichi?”—it is nothing but this. It is neither pride nor malice. Man, succumbing to his own weaknesses, fails to recognize the spiritual greatness hidden within himself, buried somewhere deep inside...

A man who wanders about without self-knowledge and the necessary effort inevitably becomes a laughingstock, said Chesterton. In other words, it is the lack of self-awareness and the absence of earnest striving that renders a man ridiculous. Setting all this aside, some have claimed that there is but one true cause for humor: sorrow. Man alone is acquainted with the essence of suffering, experiences boundless anguish, and is subject to pain; it is he who, in order to forget this, invented laughter, said Nietzsche, the German philosopher. Whatever anyone may say, humor is the property of mankind; it has never parted from man. Humor is a perspective through which one can observe and understand human life, and it is also a commentary on that life.

If a poet or storyteller creates a living character—not just alive, but one who breathes the air of everyday existence—and if the writer feels immense sympathy for that character and is able to evoke the same sympathy in readers, then to some extent, the work attains the highest aesthetic flavor. Characters like Nigamasharma, Girisam, and Parvateesam belong to this category. Regardless of their morals, rules, virtues, or vices, we find ourselves inexplicably attached to these individuals. That is why they have joined the ranks of the immortals.
What more is there to say? Any further discourse on humor would be untimely, so I conclude these final words with a sense of trepidation.
Lokāḥ samastāḥ sukhino bhavantu—May all the worlds be happy.
— Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri Sahiti Samiti, Pirapuram

chapters.title: Arrival in England
paragraphs: Whatever the case may be, I can at least say that I have set foot in England! And let me not forget to mention, I made sure to step with my right foot first, just as I had resolved. Despite my meticulous care and scientific precision in placing my right foot forward, London itself seemed utterly indifferent to my arrival. It stood there, cold and unwelcoming, like a wilted face holding a burnt-out ceremonial platter. After all, if fortune favors you, it doesn’t matter which foot you put forward. If luck deserts you, any foot will do—it’s all the same.

No sooner had I landed here than half my enthusiasm seemed to wither away, or rather, it was thoroughly chilled. I cannot quite say why. The moment I set foot in London, my barometer of spirits seemed to plummet. Slowly, I gathered my luggage and stood on the platform. I had no idea what to do next. I didn’t even know which way to go! Everything felt utterly confusing.

If only this were Mogalturru! The moment I returned home from school after a long journey, all the folks at home and the neighborhood boys would come running, crowding around me, playing and joking with me for hours. There’s no need to even mention my mother. “Oh, you’ve come, my boy! First, wash your feet and face, your eyes are sunken, your cheeks are hollow—how are you, my dear?” she would fuss, hurrying me along. After I washed my feet, she would set out some snacks for me. Sometimes, she would even ward off the evil eye. I always felt so embarrassed. “Oh mother, what is this nonsense? You and your superstitions! How much longer are you going to keep doing this?”

"Do you still think I am a little boy?" he had said, feigning a bit of anger. Remembering all this, I suddenly felt a pang of sorrow. Rubbing my eyes, shivering in the cold, I was wondering whether to take the shawl from the next seat and wrap myself up. Just then, as if someone had kicked me up from the netherworld, like a Cook Company’s agent emerging from the depths, he appeared before me—no, not like that, rather like a goddess descending from the heavens to rescue me.

He glanced at me with a mischievous look and said, "Ha Ha! Ah! Good evening. What is your name? Ah! Let me see. You are the Great Mr. Parvatesam, aren't you? Fine, we were hearing a lot about you. Good, fine day. Bit chilly, what?"

(Good evening! Your name is—ah—yes, you must be that great man, Parvatesam. We've heard so much about you. Ah, that's good. It's a bit cold, isn't it?) he greeted me with a pleasant smile, and it felt as if my soul had returned to my body. But he called me “Great Parvatesam.”

He said he had heard a lot about me. How strange! How could he have figured out that I was an important person? I had barely set foot in London, not even half an hour had passed—how could he have heard about me already?

Puzzled by this oddity, and not wanting to appear any less than him, I replied in English, “Yes Sir, I Parvatesam, how you know me, Cook-garu?” I do know English, mind you! I wanted to warn him that if he tried any silly tricks, he wouldn’t get away with it with me.

“Good, lad! Clever, aren’t you? Come, hurry!” he said, grabbing my hand and starting to drag me along. “Yes, coming, my samans, sir,” I kept saying, but he paid no attention. What sort of deaf fellow is this, I wondered. With a single yank, I freed my hand and said, “My saman there, I go and get saman and come.” I turned back and pointed at my luggage. (What’s all this rush? My luggage is still there! I’ll go get it and come.)
“Oh oh! You and your bloody saman! What do you mean, saman?” he said, exasperated. (What’s with your wretched ‘saman’? What do you mean by ‘saman’ anyway?)
“My box, sir, and bed, sir,” I replied, pointing to them.

“Oh, that!” he said, letting out a big laugh. He repeated “saman, saman” four times, then said, “Alright, your luggage isn’t going anywhere. I’ll tell someone to bring it. You go ahead.” He called a man to fetch my things. “He’ll bring them. We need to hurry and catch that train,” he said, pointing to the train nearby.
All the people who had disembarked from the steamer were rushing toward that train and boarding it in a hurry.
“We’ve come to England, haven’t we? Why do we need to take another train? Where are we going now?” I asked.

“This is England, true, but this is just the beginning of England. London is still a few miles away from here. It’s about a three-hour journey. We’ll reach there by around eight o’clock. Once I drop you off there, my responsibility ends. After that, you’ll have to find your own way,” he said, walking briskly. All this time, he didn’t let go of my hand, poor fellow.

This entire conversation took place in English, mind you. Don’t start wondering how he knew Telugu! Even if he spent thousands of years in penance, he wouldn’t be able to utter a single word of Telugu. Even I, born and raised in Telugu land, still have plenty to learn…
Barrister Parvateesam
If there are words that are unclear, words that cannot be spoken clearly, tell me, how does he manage? Is that what you call pure English? Anyone and everyone can learn it in a year or two!

We reached the railway station, and as I was about to climb into a compartment, I found—without knowing who brought them or when—my box and bedding already inside. “Here you go, sir—your, your, whatever-you-called-it…” he said. I looked at him and laughed. He was laughing for one reason, and I was laughing for another.

By then, it was five or half past five, and it had grown quite dark. Whether it was smoke or fog, I couldn’t tell, but it was so thick that you couldn’t see people even ten feet away. It wrapped around us like a heavy curtain. The cold was intense. I began to wonder if trains would even run in such pitch darkness. No sooner did this doubt arise than I started to worry—would the train really go in this utter darkness, without fear? As if voicing my inner thoughts aloud, and not in the way his companion had said, he looked at my face slowly and said, in a grave tone, “No need to worry—there’s nothing to fear for us—or for the train. A pair of men walk ahead of the engine with lanterns, making sure it doesn’t go off the tracks.”

Still, I suspected he was making fun of me. I thought it was a mistake to have voiced my doubts aloud. Then I remembered how I had traveled by train at night from Nidadavolu to Madras, and again from Madras on another night journey, and I laughed at my own lack of sense. But still, I was a little annoyed, thinking he might laugh at me for it. So I gathered myself, and when he tried to say something once or twice, I pretended not to hear and didn’t bother to reply. I maintained my silence all the way to London.

By God’s grace, we reached London safely without any trouble. When the train arrived at the London station, it felt as though we were entering a house rather than a railway station. I couldn’t tell why. When my companion suggested we walk, I hesitated, suspecting he might make fun of me again, and so I stayed quiet.

As the train screeched to a halt, all the passengers began scurrying out in a flurry, like mice darting from their holes. I, along with my companion, stood up to disembark. I glanced once at my luggage. He noticed and said, “I’ll take care of that, you go ahead and get down.”

No sooner had we both alighted than, at his signal, a man entered the compartment and brought my luggage outside. Looking at him, he seemed just like any other English gentleman; I never would have guessed he was a porter. In our villages, a porter is easy to spot from a mile away. Even if we were dying, we wouldn’t dare address such a man as “Sir.” But here, why should one even bother?
TO BE OR NOT TO BE.
Barrister Parvateesam

As soon as I stepped outside, I looked around in amazement on all four sides. I had seen many stations like Madras, but I had never seen a station this enormous anywhere. It seemed to stretch for miles. I thought, at the very least, it must be a mile wide. The reason I had earlier felt that the train was going not into a station but into someone’s house, I now understood. The entire station, so wide and long, was covered on top with glass. I wondered how these people managed to get so much glass. I was also puzzled as to why they had put up all that glass in the first place. What if a coconut fell on it, or if the boys from the neighboring house, in their games, threw a piece of tile or a stone at it—what would become of such a big station then? Still, I realized that to such questions, one must imagine and figure out the answers oneself; if I asked these sorts of silly questions to people here, they would think themselves very clever and mock me. I regretted why I had such thoughts. After all, what did it matter to me if the station’s roof broke? With that, I answered myself and let the matter rest.

Just then, the cook beside me—not a kitchen cook, but a man from the Cook Company—caught me by the hand and led me forward, saying, “Let’s go outside.” After walking about ten yards, I saw a section in the middle of the platform moving on its own, with some people standing on it. That moving path, along with the people on it, was proceeding forward. I couldn’t tell where it was coming from inside or whether it had an end at all. While I was pondering this, the man beside me grabbed my hand and pulled me onto it with him. He stood there as steady as a goat, but I nearly fell backward. He supported me with his hand behind my back so I wouldn’t fall. We were standing on a moving platform. It kept advancing. It looked very strange to me. After traveling some distance this way, I saw what looked like stairs ahead. Even on those stairs, the movement continued. People were standing there without falling. I wondered how they managed to stand without tumbling down, and just then, the section we were on began to climb the first step. I almost fell back again, but with his support, I steadied myself. As if climbing stairs, he told me to climb too, and I thought, “All right then,” and—

Learning the technique, I managed to climb up in a moment, without any mishap, and everything happened in the blink of an eye. After a while, as the train was running across a flat stretch, my friend moved aside and pulled me along with him. The platform path was moving away as if it were a conveyor belt.

We walked another ten yards and stopped near a large room. He opened the door, and I entered. Somehow, my luggage had already reached there before me. Inside, about ten people were sitting on chairs in front of tables, taking out the belongings of the arrivals from their boxes, inspecting them, handing over a slip, and sending them outside.

The man who was about to inspect my boxes looked at me with a frown and said to my friend, in a half-whisper, “Who is this darkie?” My friend, signaling him to keep quiet by pressing a finger to his lips, replied, “This young prince is my friend from India, come to study here,” and gestured for him to hurry up with the inspection.

He opened the suitcase and, with his fingertips, lifted each item and tossed it far away onto the floor. I was furious. Sensing that I was about to say something, my friend gripped my hand tightly, signaling me not to utter a word. Then the inspector unwrapped my bedding. Upon seeing my orange-colored shawl, he was so startled that he clutched his chest, closed his eyes, and slumped back in his chair as if he had fainted.

For a moment, I was alarmed, thinking, “What’s this? Has he collapsed right in front of our eyes? Is he going to cry out ‘Hari’ now?” In a second, he recovered, opened his eyes, and asked, “What is this?” “My shawl,” I replied. “Your what?” he asked. “My shawl,” I repeated.
He looked at me with great pity and said, “Can’t you speak English, my lad?”
As I was about to answer, my friend interjected, “What do you mean, he can’t speak English? He speaks it very well. On the train—”

All along the way, he kept talking to me. “This is a rug they use in their country,” said one of the men standing there. “Oh, is that so? Very nice. Well, maybe he’ll sell it—find out,” I said. My friend signaled to me as if to say, “Enough already, let it go.”

Honestly, if this fellow ever intended to sell such a thing, it would be better for the government to buy it and display it in the British Museum than for me to take it. That would at least be profitable for him. But why on earth would I need it?

After inspecting everything else and just as we were about to finish, the man’s eyes fell on my bundle containing my tooth powder and betel leaves. He opened it and asked, “Is this something to eat? Or is it medicine? Or is it poison?”

My companion burst out laughing. My irritation, which had been simmering, cooled down a bit. “No, nothing like that. This powder is for cleaning my teeth. These leaves are for scraping my tongue,” I explained. He didn’t quite understand, but simply said, “Well, suit yourself,” and quickly wrote us a permit to leave and walked away. I folded everything back up and packed it away as if my life depended on it.

We stepped outside, my luggage following right behind me. The moment we came out, I saw an enormous crowd in the street, people hurrying in every direction. Tram cars, motor cars, horse-drawn carriages—thousands of them were racing by. What was all this rush about? Where were all these people going? I wondered, completely bewildered.
Where do I go from here? Maybe this Cook’s man will just leave me here. What then? As I was worrying, I asked him, “Can you send me to a small hotel, if that’s enough?”

He replied, “No, not to a hotel. Everything will be new for you, and there won’t be anyone to advise you. Here, there’s a place called ‘India House’—the government has set it up as a hostel. All your countrymen stay there. I’ll drop you off there, and you can make your own arrangements from then on.”
He hailed a horse carriage, told me to get in, climbed in beside me, and instructed the driver, “To Tavistock Road, please,” making sure I wouldn’t catch a chill from the cold wind.

He shut the doors. In about a quarter of an hour, or perhaps half an hour, the carriage halted near India House. We got down and went inside. My friend must have introduced me to the landlord there. Entrusting my responsibility to him, he shook my hand and, with a brisk “Goodbye and good luck, young man, I wish you well,” he strode out.

I didn’t even notice my luggage being brought in; it was right behind me. The landlord gave me a slow, deliberate look and asked, “Which part of India are you from?” “Madras,” I replied, with great dignity. He gestured for me to sit down. I sat.

“Why have you come here?” he asked. What a foolish question! Did he think I had come all this way just to gaze upon his radiant countenance? “I have come to study,” I replied. “What are you going to study?” he asked. “What else is there to study but law? My intention is to become a barrister,” I declared. “Here in London?” he asked. “Most likely in Edinburgh,” I replied. “Then how long will you be staying here?” he asked. “Not more than a day or two at the most,” I said. “You haven’t eaten yet, have you?” he asked. “No,” I replied.
“In that case, go to the dining room and have your meal. Meanwhile, I’ll arrange a room for you,” he said.

Before I could even wonder where the dining room was, he pointed out a man who had just entered, as if he had read my mind. “He’ll take you there. Tell him what you want for your meal, and he’ll arrange it for you,” he said, and walked away.

This new man—probably a servant—led me inside with great respect. It was a large room, very spacious. Down the middle, from one end to the other, ran a long table surrounded by chairs. A group had just finished their meal, it seemed; the table was covered with plates, all bearing the remnants of food. Glasses of water, spoons, knives, and other implements were scattered everywhere. A few young men, all male, stood around in groups, chatting. They all turned to look at me at once, as if they were beholding some new species of animal. They were, no doubt, true city folk.
Barrister Parvateesam

It’s as if I were an untouchable, or perhaps just a country bumpkin! Not a single soul came near me. No one greeted me. What strange behavior is this? Back home, if a newcomer is spotted, people immediately ask, “Where are you from? What brings you here? The day is almost done—why don’t you eat here before you go?” They’ll make the stranger feel welcome, introduce themselves, and send him on his way without any trouble. That’s our custom, isn’t it? But here? It’s as if everyone has taken a vow of silence. Not a word from anyone! Would pearls fall from their mouths if they spoke? Do they think their dignity will be tarnished just by talking to a stranger? Do they fear I’ll ask them for something, or beg for help? I can’t make sense of it; it all feels so peculiar to me.

Just then, the man who had brought me inside cleared some things off a table, made space, and kindly asked me to sit on a chair. “What do you need?” he asked. At that moment, perhaps feeling a pang of compassion, an elderly man from the group slowly approached, sat beside me, and asked, “Where have you come from? When did you arrive in this town?”

“I’ve come from Godavari district, in Madras. I am a Telugu man,” I replied. Hearing this, another man from the group called out to someone, “Hey, this gentleman is from your district—poor fellow, see if you can find out what he needs.”
But the man he called to said, “I don’t know who he is. I’ve never seen him before. No one has introduced us. How can I speak to him?”

The elderly man beside me chuckled and said, “Yes, that’s true, my friend—even though no one has introduced us, I’ve forgotten myself and started talking. But don’t worry, this gentleman won’t mind.” As he was saying this, the other man hurriedly turned and walked away.
The elderly man next to me asked, “Sir, what would you like to have? Are you a vegetarian or a non-vegetarian?”

“I am strictly vegetarian,” I replied. He turned to the servant standing behind us and asked him to arrange a vegetarian meal for me. The servant brought a little rice, some sort of curry, and placed it before me. Then he brought some bread, butter, and what looked like jam. Since I was hungry,
As the saying goes, “One who hasn’t known hunger cannot appreciate taste”—without uttering a word, I devoured the entire meal in just two mouthfuls.

After that, they brought out pudding—sago rice payasam—served so thick it resembled a lump of dough. Along with it, they placed a jug of hot milk and some sugar for me to add as I pleased. I took my share and stood up. The servant offered to carry it to my room. “I’ll meet you tomorrow morning. If you need any advice, I’ll be happy to help,” said our new acquaintance, introducing himself as Menon. With a “Good night,” he took his leave.
The servant led me into a small room and provided everything I needed.
Barrister Parvateesam
Having arranged all the bedding, he said, “Good night, sir. Sound sleep,” and left quietly.

My luggage had already been brought into the room. I sat on the bed, took off my coat, and began to slowly remove my boots and socks. Suddenly, I remembered that I hadn’t washed my hands and feet before dinner. I thought to myself, “Perhaps there’s no need to follow such customs in this country.” My mother’s scolding echoed in my mind: “Will you eat with those dirty rags, without washing your hands and feet?” I even took off my shirt, wrapped myself in my dhoti, and reclined on the bed. “What does the future hold for me?” I wondered, but in the very next moment, the goddess of sleep claimed me.

Out of habit, I woke up early in the morning, before six o’clock. I got up, drew aside the curtain, and looked out through the glass doors. Everything outside was pitch dark. There was not the slightest stir in this boarding house either.

Looking at these buildings, the strict orderliness, the chairs and sofas everywhere, the carpets on the floors for walking, I was filled with amazement. In all the years since I was born, I had never seen such things anywhere. Every door and window was adorned with beautiful, expensive curtains.

For some reason, I couldn’t understand their purpose. Why so much arrangement to block out the breeze and keep out the air? I couldn’t imagine. Later, I noticed that here, and in France too, all the houses and shops have glass doors. Perhaps they have no fear of thieves here. Maybe they don’t have mischievous boys who throw stones at houses for fun, as we do back home. Thinking such thoughts, I lay back down on the bed for a while.

Why is it still so dark? Why hasn’t it become daylight yet? Has the sun forgotten to rise? When do people here get up? When do they wash their faces and perform their daily routines? When do they get to their work? If men and women both rise only after the sun is high in the sky, when do they ever get anything done? As I pondered these questions, a wave of drowsiness swept over me again.
I dozed off. For another hour, I did not wake up.

When I finally got up and thought I should quickly wash my face, I realized I had no idea where to go. I opened the door and looked outside, but there was no one to be seen. I went back inside and was pondering what to do, when I noticed a spot on the wall that said, "Press Button - Servant." Curious to see what this was, I pressed the button just as it was written.

As if summoned from thin air, a man opened the door and entered the room. Looking at his attire and the way he stood, I wondered, “Is this some high official?” As I stared at him, he bowed his head slightly, smiled, and said, “Good morning, sir. Had sound sleep?” Then, seeing the way he was dressed so smartly, I thought, “Perhaps he is the master of the house, or at least a big officer,” and was at a loss for words, astonished at what to say. While I was still thinking, he asked again, “What can I do for you, sir?”
At last, my slow mind realized he must be a servant. I also remembered the writing on the wall: “Press Button - Servant.”
So, standing up with great dignity, thinking, “Isn’t this their custom?” I extended my hand for a handshake. He smiled, said, “Thank you, sir,” and touched my hand ever so lightly before letting go.
“I want to—lavatory where?” I asked.

“Oh, this way, sir,” he said, and, walking ahead like a royal attendant, led me to the adjoining room. He opened the door and said, “You can wash here, sir,” pointing to a porcelain basin on the wall with a tap above it. Then, showing me a large porcelain tub, he said, “You can have your bath here, sir—hot or cold,” and demonstrated the two taps. From one, steaming hot water gushed out, and from the other, icy cold water flowed with a whoosh.
Then, pointing to another wall nearby, he said, “Meet you later, sir,” and left gracefully.

Everything I saw seemed utterly strange. There was not a single thing in which our country and this country bore any resemblance. If I were to describe how long it took me to finish my business in that room, and how I managed to get out, it would take quite a while, and apart from being a bit tedious, it would serve no purpose! But, in a word—
Barrister Parvateesam

I must admit, whenever new customs appear, only those who can quickly grasp their context, pros and cons, and usefulness can adapt with ease. For the rest—for ordinary folk—such times become a real test. They struggle quite a bit.

There’s another thing I must mention here. At first, I thought I should go to my room and fetch my own towels. Just then, I noticed a bundle of towels, soap, and other items brought by the housemaid, laid out in front of me. Why are these here? Are they for me? If they are for me, am I the only one receiving such honor? Or do they provide a fresh towel for every newcomer? This doubt inevitably arose in my mind. Still, seeing those towels, as white as jasmine flowers, I couldn’t resist. I thought, let me use them first; I can clear up my doubts later.
Even after entering my room, I realized that everywhere—beds, pillows, blankets—everything was provided by them. There was no need for me to bring anything of my own.

Just then, I heard someone knock on the door. I opened it, and the same servant who had come earlier entered, carrying a large tray with tea, some slices of bread, butter, sugar, milk, and so on. He placed it silently on the table and left without a word. What is this courtesy? These royal honors? I wondered, as I had my breakfast. Then I sat, pondering what to do next, where to go, whom to ask for information.

After a while, Mr. Menon, an elderly gentleman I had met the previous night, gently knocked on my door from upstairs. As soon as I opened it, he entered with a smile and said, “Good morning, sir! Did you sleep well last night? Did you get your morning tea and all?” Before I could answer, he glanced at the tea cup and other items on the table and said, “Ah, looks like everything’s been taken care of!”

I was thinking of asking him if he could take me around the town and show me the sights, when he himself said, “You’ll be here at this hour, won’t you? What will you do? Are you planning to go anywhere? If not, why don’t you come with me? I’ll take you around the town once. It’ll be a bit of an adventure for you.”

Delighted at how I had so easily guessed his intentions, I said, “You are a very good man indeed! I was just thinking of asking you to take me into town, and here you are, offering to do so yourself, as if you read my mind. I’m very happy—shall we set out at once?”
“Let’s go, but first, freshen up a bit. We’ll go to the dining hall, have a little refreshment, and then head out,” he replied.
“But didn’t we just have refreshments?” I asked.

“Oh, that’s not enough,” he said. “That’s just to give us a bit of energy to start the day. The real benefit comes only when you eat a proper, hearty meal. Otherwise, our carriage won’t run until one o’clock in the afternoon!” Saying this, he led me into the dining hall.

It was the same hall I had seen the night before. The table was laid out with all sorts of fruits, sauces, knives, forks, and various other items. A few people were already having their refreshments. The Telugu gentleman we had seen last night noticed us, nodded his head, and greeted us with a “Good morning,” before returning to his meal.

Finding an empty spot, the two of us sat down. “You’re a Brahmin, aren’t you?” asked Menon. I wondered how he had figured that out, when he added, “You’re a vegetarian, right? That’s why I asked.” Without waiting for my reply, he told the attendant standing behind us to bring me vegetarian food and the usual fare for himself. Immediately, the attendant set before me a plate full of delicious, steaming dishes—milk, sugar, bread, butter, and so on. He placed something else for Menon.

For a moment, I felt it was odd to sit beside someone eating such things, having to bear the smell while I ate my meal. What would my mother and father say if they knew about this, I wondered. As I was lost in these thoughts, Menon urged, “Come on, let’s finish up quickly and go outside.” We both finished our refreshments and stepped out.
Barrister Parvateesam

The moment I set foot on the street—though it was only ten o’clock, or perhaps not even that—the entire road was bustling with people hurrying along, horse-drawn carriages, motor cars, and tramcars. There was such a commotion and flurry everywhere. Here, the roads are not laid flat as usual, but paved with stone blocks like bricks. Because of this, the clatter of the horses’ hooves, the rumble of the carriages, and the rattling of the tramcars all resounded so loudly that it seemed as if my ears would be battered by the noise.

My friend glanced at me, as if reading my thoughts, and said gently, “You’ll get used to this noise in a couple of days.” He led me to a tram and helped me board. From there, our tour of London began.

Everywhere I looked, there were buildings of no less than four stories, and all of them had large glass doors for the windows facing the street, with curtains behind them, and people peeking out from within. On the ground floors, for the most part, there were big shops. On the pavements on either side of the road, crowds of men and women hurried along. Watching this throng was quite a spectacle. All the men and women wore boots on their feet. Everyone seemed to be in a rush from the break of dawn. I sat there wondering, “Where could these thousands of people, in such a hurry, be going?”
My friend beside me kept explaining various things. Some of it made sense to me, some of it did not.

Just then, I saw a river flowing through the middle of the city, with a bridge across it. “Look, look, that’s the Thames,” my friend said. “This bridge is called Waterloo Bridge,” he added. “It’s very famous and historic.” The impressive building nearby, he said, was the Parliament House. Even from the tram, it looked magnificent. Though the river was not as large as our Godavari, he explained that it was very important, and that from its mouth, goods essential to daily life are exported all over the world, especially to our own country.

The river, the ships on it, the Parliament House beside it—all of these looked just like the pictures I had seen in my geography books as a child. There was no difference at all. If he hadn’t told me, I would have asked myself, “Isn’t this the Parliament?” He kept on explaining something or other, while my mind wandered.
It felt as if my mind had wandered off somewhere, crossing the boundaries of the present and drifting into some distant past, into some unknown era.
A strange sensation came over me, as though I had seen all these sights before, as though I had roamed these places many times already. The same feeling had once visited me in France as well.
Whatever my friend was saying did not reach my ears. My memory had slipped off somewhere into the past.

I even wondered, “Did I truly come here in some previous birth?” Perhaps realizing that I was not listening to him, my friend placed his hand on my shoulder and, laughing, said, “Hey, are you asleep? Or are you dreaming?”

I replied, “No dreams, my friend! Even while awake, my imagination is carrying me away, beyond country and time, to some unknown place. I feel as though I have seen all these things before. It is very strange indeed.” My friend looked at my face for a moment—
Barrister Parvateesam
Case looked at me intently, and for two whole minutes, he didn’t utter a word.

In this manner, we sat in the tram until about one o’clock, gazing at countless buildings. We saw a few theatres. We saw some famous churches. But we couldn’t get down anywhere or examine anything closely. “If you want to see each one leisurely, it would take several months, my dear fellow,” my friend said. So, he had no choice but to be content with just this much.
The clock struck one somewhere. “Let’s get down now,” my friend said, and led me outside.

“Are you feeling tired at all? Shall we have a light meal somewhere nearby and continue our wandering? Or shall we go back to our lodgings, eat there, rest a bit, and then resume our assault on the city?” he asked, laughing.

“We’ve only been sitting in the tram since morning—what’s there to be tired about? Let’s eat somewhere nearby, as you suggest, and then continue our lunar expedition. Anyway, I’m thinking of leaving tomorrow,” I replied.
“Alright then, let’s go,” he said, and led me to a small hotel.

By the time we arrived, it seemed as though several thousand people were already packed into that tiny hotel. For such a small place to attract so many people, it must be a good hotel indeed, I thought. We circled the room a few times and managed to secure two chairs. We had barely settled into our seats when a waiter arrived and handed my friend a card listing the day’s dishes. He took it, marked what he wanted, and told the waiter that I was a vegetarian and to bring me whatever was suitable.
“What’s that card?” I asked my friend.

He explained, “In every hotel here, they print a list of all the food items available that day and keep it ready. When guests arrive, they’re given the card, so they can indicate what they want and have it brought to them. That’s the system here, in every hotel.”
In Madras hotels, what do we do? We ask what’s available, and someone shouts in a booming voice, “Idli, sambar, vadai!”—all jumbled together, and half the time we can’t even hear it properly.

Ordering something or the other. After eating, without telling us how much it cost, he would shout from the back, “Anje kalana!” Remembering that, I thought this arrangement was quite good. As I was thinking this, the waiter brought a plate and set it before my friend, and another plate before me. The moment I looked at my plate—a mistake!—a strong smell hit my nose. When I looked closely, I saw a beautifully cooked Matsyavatara (fish incarnation) laid out before me. I began to worry—would he now bring out the rest of the Dashavatara one after another? In fear, I asked, “What is this?”
“Fish, sir,” said the waiter.
“But I’m a vegetarian, aren’t I?” I said.
He replied, “Well, isn’t this vegetarian too?”
“What do you mean, vegetarian?” I asked.
He explained, “Sir, when you kill this, it doesn’t bleed red blood. Only the flesh of animals that bleed red is considered non-vegetarian.”
Even so, I told him this wouldn’t do for me. Immediately, he took it away and brought back a boiled egg—either a hen’s or a duck’s.
“What is this, a donkey’s egg?” I exclaimed.
The poor fellow didn’t understand and replied, “It’s a hen’s egg, sir.”

“Is this really vegetarian food or what?” I asked. “Yes, sir, and it’s a very fine kind too,” he replied. “I don’t want this,” I said. “Then what else do you mean by vegetarian, sir?” he asked. “If you don’t eat fish or eggs, what’s left for you to eat, sir?” he said.

At that moment, our friend intervened and said, “Bring them some rice with potatoes or cabbage, or something like that.” Hearing those words, the waiter looked utterly bewildered, as if thinking, “How do these people even survive eating such things?” He gave me a pitiful look, shook his head from side to side as if to say, “This is a hopeless case,” and in two minutes brought me a plate with a handful of rice and two more plates with two kinds of curry, and set them before me.

Thinking, “Ah, at last, something to keep body and soul together,” I ate it up as if it were a feast. Immediately, he took away those plates and brought another plate with thick sago pudding and milk, and served it to both of us.

I thought, “Well, at least this is palatable,” and finished it off, wondering if perhaps another plate would be brought. But my friend, guessing my thoughts, shook his head and signaled that nothing more would be coming. Our meal was barely finished when the waiter brought the bill on a plate. My friend paid the full amount and, in addition, gave him two shillings as a tip, I suppose. The waiter received it with great satisfaction and left.

We stepped outside. From there, we boarded another tram and resumed our city tour. We saw enormous shops, business establishments, newspaper offices, bookstores, and countless other places. In every shop, the goods on display were arranged so attractively that they were a delight to behold.

But in one shop, and one shop only, what I saw was so horrifying and disgusting that my stomach turned and I felt as if I would vomit. In that shop, the carcasses of cows, sheep, goats, and pigs, skinned and gutted, hung vertically for all to see. Even now, the very memory makes my skin crawl.
Why do our people say that eating meat is like hanging corpses around your neck? I thought, “Wouldn’t it be better if such ghastly displays didn’t exist at all?” Just then, we got down and—

I even thought of going into the shop and scolding the proprietor, asking, “What sort of business is this?” I considered sweeping the floor with all four limbs, just to show them they had no shame. But before I could act, those shops were already behind us. As soon as that scene faded from view, my anger subsided. Is this our village? Is this our country? Would they listen if I said something?—these thoughts occurred to me. “Good thing I didn’t act rashly and cause a commotion,” I thought, and felt relieved.

After that, he showed me a place called ‘Trafalgar Square’, with a statue of Nelson in the center. Then he mentioned something called Piccadilly Circus. I asked, “Are there circus companies here as well?” He laughed and replied, “Apart from the animals you see on the street, there are no circus companies here. This place is just called ‘Circus’. I don’t know why it got that name.”

By then, it was four in the evening. Again, he suggested we get off at a stop. Menon got down with me and took me to another small hotel nearby, where he again arranged for tea and refreshments. But refreshments here aren’t like our pakoras, punukulu, or mirayi. Instead, there’s bread, butter to go with it, something called ‘jam’ made from fruits, and some sweet cakes—these are their refreshments.

After a light snack, we stepped out again. This time, instead of taking the tram, we walked a distance, looking at the shops with great delight. There was a place called a ‘picture house’. My friend stopped there. On large posters above, there were strange pictures of men and women. “What is this?” I asked. “Come, let’s go inside. I brought you here to show you this. Inside, you’ll see a play of moving pictures on a screen. It’s very good.” He led me in, bought us each a ticket, and took me inside. It was quite dark inside. Someone brought us a lamp—

He showed us our seats, and we sat down. We couldn’t see who was beside us, nor how many people were inside. Directly in front of us was a large white screen, upon which the shadows of men and women moved about, expressing themselves with gestures. After a while, I realized that this was a play being performed in this room. I was astonished. Without a single word spoken, without any sound to be heard, without a single person visible, they managed to present a play for nearly two hours using only the shadows of people! How marvelous it seemed!

There were no words to describe it. Once or twice, the lights came on in between, and the entire auditorium became visible. It was very large. At least a thousand men and women were seated there. I didn’t know then if there were any distinctions among them. That so many people could be captivated by this shadow play, without any commotion, made me think the performers must be truly talented.

As soon as we finished watching the play, we quietly got up and went outside. The show continued on the screen. People kept coming in, and those who wished to leave kept leaving. Unlike in our village, where the play ends and people make a great racket, pushing and shoving each other to get out, there was no such practice here. As soon as one performance ended, another would begin without pause. So, whenever people had time, they would come in, sit down, watch from whatever scene was playing, and leave when that scene came around again. No one sat through the whole thing just to watch it again from the beginning.

Throughout the performance, the hall was utterly silent. Could such a thing ever happen in our country? I couldn’t believe that people would leave as soon as they finished watching, making room for newcomers. Who would even ask us to leave if we didn’t go immediately? If the play was good, why not watch it again? In such a crowd, no one could catch us! I suppose it’s our nature to think, “What does the theater owner lose if we stay a little longer?”
By then, it was about eight o’clock at night. We walked out onto the road.

We went upstairs. “Well then, shall we end today’s sightseeing and head back to our lodgings?” said my friend. I agreed that was for the best. After sitting in the tram all day, my body was feeling a bit weary.

Once we reached our lodgings, we finished our dinner and other evening routines, wished each other good night, and each retired to our own rooms. I changed my clothes in my room, lay down comfortably, and reviewed the day’s events in my mind. What a good man my friend is! Not a single Telugu person here has even bothered to greet me, but this man, out of sheer kindness, spent the entire day with me, showing not the slightest sign of inconvenience, and kept me company. Why can’t our own people be like this, I wondered, and without realizing it, I drifted off into the arms of sleep.

In the morning, after completing my daily ablutions and getting dressed, my friend Menon came again. Smiling, he wished me good morning, sat down, and asked, “Did you sleep well last night? You’re not feeling tired, are you?” He inquired after my well-being.
“Will you be here at this hour? Where are you going from here? What plans have you made?” he asked.

I confessed my secret: that I had made no plans, had no idea what to do, had come here without thinking anything over, without making any decisions, without telling anyone. He laughed and said, “From the way you behave, I guessed you must have done something like this. People like you have only just started coming from your region. Anyway, what have you come to study? Do you have enough money? Will your people send you more? Or will you go back home from here?”

I told him that I had written to my family from Colombo, that they had sent me money to Marseilles, and that they had written pleading with me to come home. But I had no desire whatsoever to return like that. Somehow, my people would manage to send me money, and so my decision was to get admitted somewhere and continue my studies. I said, “If you could advise me on where it would be good to enroll, where it would not be too expensive, and how I might get there, I would be grateful. I want to study for the barrister’s examination. Back home, I finished high school—”
I stopped with my studies. I asked, “Now, please tell me what I should do next.”

He replied, “Good, very good! I’m glad you’ve come to me and told me everything plainly, without any pretense. Looking at you, it’s clear you’re very young and innocent. I feel a brotherly affection for you. It’s difficult for someone like you to get ahead in a place like this. If you go to Edinburgh in Scotland, you can stay there and study. Living there is more comfortable than here, and it’s much cheaper. There are plenty of our countrymen there as well. Since the town is much smaller than this, you’ll have more opportunities to meet our people frequently. Since you said you finished your high school studies at home, you’ll have to sit for the entrance exam here. You can stay there for three or four months, get private coaching from someone, and then take the exam. After that, you can study for the barrister’s exam as you planned. If you have the patience, you can even prepare for the M.A. exam at the same time. What do you say?”
I replied, “What is there for me to say? Whatever you suggest, my only job is to say, ‘So be it!’”

“Well then, at this moment, I can’t come with you myself. There’s a lady who manages this India House institution. This afternoon, she plans to take some of the newcomers, like yourself, to the zoological gardens. I’ll introduce you to her now. Go along with her. You’ll all return here by four or five in the evening. By then, I’ll try to come as well. Let’s finish our refreshments now and then meet her. After that, I’ll go my own way.” With that, he led the way towards the dining hall.

After we finished our business there, we went over to the manager lady. She welcomed us with a smile, but seeing her, I felt a twinge of fear. My heart thudded for a moment. She looked to be about fifty years old—quite stout, tall, and imposing. My friend introduced me, saying, “This is so-and-so, he just arrived last night, and he’ll be leaving today or tomorrow.”

chapters.title: First Acquaintances
paragraphs: She extended her hand in greeting and said, “It is a great pleasure to meet you. If you are not in a hurry, there is no problem staying here for another four days. You can see all the beauties of this town, or you can simply stay here and study if you wish.” My friend took leave of her and departed. She asked me to sit down and inquired about my village, my name, and everything else. After a couple of minutes of this and that, as soon as lunch was over, she said, “Some friends and I are planning to take a few newcomers from your country to the zoological gardens. Would you like to come too?”
“Of course, I would be delighted to come,” I replied.
“In that case, let’s meet at two o’clock,” she said. I stood up, wished her good morning, and returned to my room.

After finishing my lunch, I sat waiting, ready by half past one, wondering when they would call me. What exactly is a zoological garden? Why have they arranged such a thing? What is there to see? Back home, we see all kinds of animals everywhere, brushing against our eyes and feet! Would there be tigers and lions here too, just like in a circus? As I pondered these questions, with just two minutes left for two o’clock, someone came and told me to get ready to go out. I immediately got up and followed him outside.

In the main hall, about ten or fifteen of our countrymen, all a little older than me, were standing there. As I looked at their faces, not a single one looked like a Telugu man. While I was still scrutinizing their faces, the lady manager who had spoken to me in the morning entered, dressed up, wearing a hat adorned with some kind of feathers on her head, and a long coat that reached down to her feet, holding a stick in her hand. After seeing that coat, I thought perhaps everyone has to wear such attire here. When I looked at the others, I saw that they too were all putting on similar coats. Everyone’s...
Barrister Parvateesam
All eyes were on me. Realizing this, I quickly excused myself, saying, “I’ll be back in a moment,” and dashed into my room. I hurriedly put on that coat as well and returned. Immediately, we set off.

By the time we reached the street, there was a car ready, large enough to seat ten or fifteen people. As soon as we all got in, it started off and, weaving smoothly through the town, took us to the exhibition hall. We all got down there and went inside. Even to enter, we had to buy tickets. The manager lady herself bought tickets for all of us.

As we went inside, I thought it would be like our big cattle sheds back home. But instead, it looked as if it stretched over several hundred acres. In one part, there were buildings with iron bars, like houses, and inside them were some animals. By animals, I expected only cows, buffaloes, oxen, bulls, goats, sheep, donkeys, horses, and, if they were feeling extravagant, maybe an elephant or two, or perhaps a few sparrows—nothing more than that.

These don’t exist at all—there are no such things here. There are foxes, wolves, a few kinds of horses, and some types of braying donkeys that have come from Africa, it seems. Those must be the zebras. They look just like horses, but with big stripes all over their bodies—stripes like those of a tiger. Not that I’ve ever seen a real tiger, but I’ve heard elders say that tigers have stripes. Besides, in our village, during the Peerla festival, people dress up as tigers, and I’ve seen them paint stripes on themselves. Here, these zebra-like creatures with stripes looked quite beautiful. After returning home, if necessary, I thought I might travel via Africa, buy a pair of zebras, harness them to a cart like two horses, and take them to Madras or somewhere. People would flock to see them and be delighted! Anyway, I decided that I must take them along.

There were local pigs and wild boars too. Though they looked like ordinary pigs, they had two large tusks sticking out of their mouths. But even more peculiar, beautiful, and fearsome was something else—a true crown jewel of the pig family, and the smallest among them—the porcupine! What a strange creature! Its entire body, except for the face, was covered with black, Telugu-colored (dark), six or seven-inch-long quills, so densely packed that you couldn’t even poke it with a needle. I wondered whether these quills were there from birth, or if they grew later, or perhaps if the exhibition folks had dressed it up in this spiky armor just to amuse the visitors! As I was pondering this, an attendant from the exhibition, who was with us, poked one of the porcupines through the bars with a stick. The porcupine, as if to say, “You wretch! Just wait, I’ll teach you a lesson,” made a peculiar sound and leapt at him. The strange thing was, at that very instant, just as our hair stands on end when we’re startled, all the quills on the porcupine’s body stood up straight. In that state, if it fell upon anyone, what would happen then? As I was thinking this, the attendant began to lecture us about the creature. He said that this was God’s great gift to the porcupine, to protect itself and escape from enemies. I, without thinking, asked about the other animals. He turned to me, sharply and—

Afterwards, looking on with a touch of sympathy, he said, “God grants every creature the necessary means to protect itself, suited to its nature.” A gentle smile appeared on our manager madam’s face. We moved ahead.

Next, we went to the place where the monkeys and baboons were kept. There, hundreds of monkeys—big and small, of every kind—were chattering away, baring their teeth, watching us with mischievous curiosity, leaping about, swinging from the bars, climbing up and down, and playing among themselves in all sorts of amusing ways. Of all the enclosures, it was here, at the monkeys’ cage, that the crowd was thickest. Everyone who came—men, women, young and old—had brought along some fruits, nuts, or vegetables especially for them. As people tossed these treats inside, the monkeys would scramble and scuffle, snatching food from each other’s hands, eating, grinning at us, while some stretched out their hands, begging for more. It was all so strange and delightful to watch. No one seemed in any hurry to move on. Some women and children, holding out fruits and nuts in their hands, would offer them directly to the monkeys, and when the monkeys took them, they would laugh and play with joy.

One girl reached out her hand to offer something, but just as the monkey was about to take it, she quickly pulled her hand back to tease it. The monkey glared at her in annoyance and sulked. The girl, not to be outdone, stretched out her hand again. In a flash, the monkey grabbed her hand and wouldn’t let go, while the girl shrieked in alarm. The monkey, grinning, held on tight. Just then, a zookeeper arrived, scolded the monkey, and threatened to hit it. Only then did the monkey release her hand. A crowd had gathered to witness this commotion, and laughter rippled through the onlookers. Some showed sympathy for the girl. While a few people moved on, others—especially the women—remained, gossiping and recounting the incident with great relish.

Near the cage stood a stout woman—somewhat advanced in age—waving her hands and talking animatedly, clearly in high spirits. We decided to move on, but noticed that inside the cage, a monkey had been watching this lady’s performance for quite some time, listening to her speech and grinning broadly. In the midst of her lively conversation, the lady, without realizing it, had...

Without realizing it, she had come too close to the cage. In the blink of an eye, that monkey snatched the hat from her head with its nimble hand. The lady let out a startled cry. Everyone stood there, dumbfounded, staring at the scene. Along with the hat, the artificial hairpiece she wore on her head also came off! The lady was overcome with an uncontrollable grief. In her agitation, she tried to strike the monkey with the stick she held in her hand. The monkey, grinning mischievously, dodged and retreated inside.

From behind the bars, the monkey, unable to pull the hat all the way in, simply dropped it right there. The lady picked it up, but now she was pondering how to put it back on her head in front of such a crowd. Just then, an attendant came running, scolded the monkey, consoled the lady, and took her by the hand...
Barrister Parvateesam

Nearby, there was a room specially arranged for women to adorn themselves. She was taken inside. Looking at her, I felt a surge of pity. But when I saw that monkey’s mischievous antics, I couldn’t help but laugh. Perhaps that’s why, when children make mischief at home, people say they have monkey-like qualities. That’s what I thought.

As I had expected, there were also some elephants. There, in the circus, they had brought two or three elephants that had been specially trained, and the keepers were letting children climb on them and giving them rides. Besides those, there were six elephants roaming freely outside, without any chains. I was told that this animal is very gentle and harmless. It doesn’t harm anyone. Whatever anyone gives it, it takes with its trunk and puts it in its mouth. There was no need to stand there for long.

Nearby, I saw ostriches. Until then, I had only seen them in pictures, never in real life. Their long necks, their beaks, and those faces! Of all the animals, this one struck me as the strangest creature I had ever seen.

I couldn’t stand there for long. After walking another ten yards, I saw another peculiar animal from Africa—a giraffe. Its long legs, slender body—it looked quite good in its own way, but I can’t describe how tall its neck was! I thought it could easily reach the top of a palm tree and pluck its leaves. Apparently, it lives by eating leaves and twigs. That’s why, the servant who was with us said, the Creator gave it such a long neck so it could reach the highest branches and feast on them. Even with such a long neck, it looked rather charming. Its face looked as innocent and timid as a lady’s. After standing there for a couple of minutes, I followed my companions a little further ahead.

There, I saw a large well surrounded by a high wall, and inside was an animal. They called it a rhinoceros. On its nose was a strong horn—that was its weapon, they said. Whatever enemy it faces, it splits apart with that horn. Its skin is as tough as iron plates—so much so that even lizards can’t get through it. It spends some time in the water and some time on land, they said. I heard that this too had come from Africa. On our side, the large...

The Bobbili bull was just as formidable. It looked rather frightening. After that, we saw tigers and lions as well. Even though they were let loose, they were enclosed within a vast compound, fenced off with very tall iron bars, within which they roamed freely. There were also tiger cubs—tiny little things, and they were quite adorable. The lions, meanwhile, were both majestic and terrifying, though they did not appear quite as beautiful. There were a few leopards too, and those were truly splendid to look at. Besides these, we saw all manner of other animals as well.
After leaving the menagerie, we went on to see the aviary. Oh, the variety of birds! So many kinds, so many colors, so many shapes, so many sounds—it is impossible to describe them all.

Among them were birds familiar to us: crows, kites, cranes, and sparrows. There were also red parrots among the lot. One particular species of parrot was nearly ten times the size of our ordinary parrots, measuring about three or four feet in length. They said it had come from Japan, or perhaps from somewhere else—I cannot recall exactly. Then we saw peacocks, which brought even more beauty and ornamentation to the aviary. Most remarkable of all were the flamingos, the likes of which I had never seen or heard of before. They are quite tall and sturdy, and, it seems, they even eat burning hot coals! The feathers on their wings are so beautiful that the local ladies use them to decorate their hats and other ornaments, or so our guide told us.

We also saw swans, which are believed to live in the Himalayas back home, as well as many varieties of ducks and cranes. There were even white parrots, which, they said, had come from Burma. In this way, hundreds of species of birds from all over the world have been brought here, confined and raised for our enjoyment and for the sake of knowledge. How did they ever discover so many varieties? How did they manage to capture and bring them all here? I was greatly astonished.

As we continued our tour, we entered a large hall, something like a great chamber. It was filled with glass cases, behind whose vine-covered doors we saw all sorts of snakes. I had never known there could be so many varieties of snakes. I had never heard of such a thing, nor had I ever seen it.

chapters.title: Culture Shocks
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

Just looking at them sent chills down my spine and filled me with fear. But as I observed them more closely, I felt that even in those things, there was a certain beauty. How strange! Why did the Creator mix such venom and grotesque forms with beauty? After wandering for a while longer, looking at various other kinds, my legs began to give way. Having spent two or three hours patiently roaming about, and seeing that there was still much left to see, we decided to call it a day and turned back. Our manager, taking pity on us, led us to a nearby tea shop and treated us to tea and snacks.

After finishing our refreshments, we stepped outside and got into our car. I felt that I wouldn't be able to set foot on the ground again unless I went home and took off my shoes. But my far-sighted manager, as if to say that this little excursion wasn't enough, took us to the great park in the city—Hyde Park, as it is called—and made us stroll there for a while.

Here, there were all sorts of trees and flowers, and many strange plants with leaves of vivid colors, all arranged beautifully and appearing here and there. It seems that for recreation in this park, all the great and important people come, riding in carriages or even on horseback! To see it all thoroughly would take a whole day or two, I thought. With so many places to visit in this city, if one were to see each spot, it would take days on end. Especially this city of London—from one end to the other, just to see it all, it would take a whole year, I felt. Therefore, I decided that I would have to see the rest of this city at leisure, some other time.

With these thoughts, dragging my feet, I walked slowly. Then my wife—no, my mistake—our manager, came up gently beside me and said, “What is it, dear? Are you having trouble? Are your feet hurting? Is it difficult to walk? Your face too looks tired and worn out. Never mind, let us end it here for today and go home,” she said, placing her hand on my shoulder and looking at me kindly.

For some reason, I felt rather sad at her hospitality. Outwardly, I put on a grave face and said, “It’s quite all right, madam. If the others who came with us still wish to see around, please show them. I’ll just sit here for a while,” I added, feeling embarrassed.

“Oh no, not at all! What are you saying? I have work to do at this hour. I’ve seen enough for now. We can come another time. Let’s head to the lodging,” she said, leading the way to the car. We got into the car and reached our lodging in about half an hour.

There, my friend Menon was waiting just for me, sitting patiently. On seeing me, he smiled and quietly came with me into my room. As soon as I entered, I first took off my college shoes and put them aside, then removed my socks as well. Sensing my discomfort, Menon went into the bathroom and advised me, “Wash your feet with hot water and keep them in the warm water for a while. The pain will be drawn out. I’ll wait here until you’re done—take your time.”

Agreeing, I hobbled slowly to the bathroom, unable to put my foot down properly. Following Menon’s advice, I soaked my feet in hot water for about a quarter of an hour. By the time I finished, I felt much better—the pain seemed to have been washed away for the most part. I dried my feet and returned to my room.

“How are your feet now? Are you feeling any better? Has the pain subsided?” Menon asked. “Thanks to your kindness, the pain has reduced a lot. If I rest tonight, I think it will be much better by tomorrow. But I was planning to travel tonight, wasn’t I?” I replied.

“Even if you’re delayed by a day or two, nothing will be lost. There’s still some time before you have to join college. So don’t rush—you can leave tomorrow. Let’s think if there’s anything else you need to buy here. Sit down,” he said. After I sat down, he paused for two minutes and then asked, “Do you have enough clothes? Can you manage in this cold? You’re not facing any trouble, are you?”
“It’s quite cold, sir. It’s hard to bear,” I replied. “I’m asking about your clothes—what do you have?”
Barrister Parvateesam
“Tell me honestly, did you have that suit stitched in India?” he asked.

It certainly looks like it. It won’t do here. No matter how cold it gets, if you wear a suit stitched in that style, everyone here will laugh at you. Then he asked, “Is there an undergarment beneath your suit?”
I didn’t understand what he meant. I turned pale and looked at him questioningly.
“Did you wear the suit directly on your body? Is there nothing underneath?” he said.
“There’s nothing else,” I replied.

He was taken aback. “That’s a big mistake. In a country like this, it’s very risky. The undergarments here are made to cling to the skin, like a vest. You must wear them on your body and legs too. Otherwise, it’s quite dangerous. So, first, you must see to these clothes. Tomorrow morning, I’ll come and take you to the bazaar. You can buy whatever you need. Tomorrow, or at the latest the day after, have a hearty meal, sleep comfortably, and you’ll rest well. This discomfort will go away. I’ll come and meet you in the morning. Good night,” he said, and left.

Just as he said, I ate my meal right away and lay down. I didn’t even have the patience to sit up. What will I have to buy tomorrow? How much will it cost? I started worrying. So far, I’ve been giving my share of the daily expenses to Menon. He would accept it with a smile and a “thanks.” Today, the manager lady paid for everything. She didn’t ask anyone for anything, nor did anyone offer her money. I don’t know if all this will be added to the final bill, or if the government is providing it free of charge. Before I could finish worrying about how much this would all add up to, I fell asleep without even realizing it.
In the morning, by the time I finished brushing my teeth and washing up, Menon’s friend arrived.
“Well, brother, are you ready to set out?” he asked.

The two of us went to the dining hall, finished our tea and snacks, and stepped out onto the street. After walking about a furlong, we turned aside, passed through a large gate, and went inside. Within two minutes, Menon...
He came back with two tickets.

“Why tickets now?” I started to ask, but before I could finish, he grabbed me by the arm and dragged me through another gate inside. The moment we set foot inside, the gate slammed shut with a bang, and in the blink of an eye, we descended into the underworld with a whoosh. All of this happened so quickly, I barely had time to utter a sound. Just as I was about to shout, the gate opened again with a clatter, and Menon, still holding my arm, pulled me outside. “What’s all this?” I began to ask, but before the words left my mouth, the train arrived, and we found ourselves seated inside.

At that point, Menon patted me on the back and said, “No need to be afraid. You were quite anxious just now, weren’t you?” There was hardly any time to talk in that place. “Just now, when we bought the tickets and entered through the gate, that was a ‘lift’. You see, you stand inside, the door closes, and with the press of a button, it carries people either up or down. You’ve been observing these streets for the past two days, haven’t you? See how efficiently everything runs! To reduce the congestion, and to allow people to travel from one place to another quickly, they’ve built this railway deep underground.”

By the time he finished his explanation, the train had already stopped. Without giving me a chance to speak, Menon grabbed my hand again, led me out of the train, and into another lift. The lift shot upwards, and before I knew it, we were out again. Oh, Lord! All these things happened so fast, there wasn’t even time to catch my breath.

Once again, without a word, Menon led me forward. My mind was flooded with thoughts, doubts, and fears. The first time we descended into that underworld, I thought my heart had stopped. Even when we came back up in the lift, it felt as if my heart was in a vice. At such times, I thought, wouldn’t these arrangements be dangerous for both children and adults? If so, why were such contraptions made at all? But then, neither in Marseilles nor here today did anyone shout “Help!” Everyone emerged safe and sound. After that, I realized that even deep underground...

How on earth did they dig such tunnels so deep! Isn’t it terribly dangerous? What if, all of a sudden, there’s an earthquake and it collapses—what would happen then? And then, how do they get air and light down there? But I had no time to ask my friend these questions. He didn’t seem to be in any state to answer them, either.

We hurried along and entered a clothing shop. Inside a glass wardrobe, I saw all kinds of suits, neatly tailored and ready. I thought to myself, “Perhaps someone had these custom-made and left them here.” As we stepped inside, my attention remained fixed on that wardrobe, and I stood there, staring at it. I didn’t even notice when a gentleman inside came over to Menon and started talking to him.
After about four or five minutes of my gawking, that fellow came over to me and began measuring my height, arms, and so on. Ah, so these are for stitching clothes, I realized.
“Will he have them ready by this evening?” I asked. “I must leave by then, you see!”
“Don’t worry, sir,” he said. “He’ll have it ready in five minutes. Just pick whichever one you like from these here.”

To tell you the truth, what do I know about all this? I couldn’t tell the quality of the cloth or its value even if my life depended on it! I didn’t know if bargaining was possible here or not. No matter how bad he might be, even if he’s just a clothes-selling Komati, here he’s a lord!

Wondering why I was being put through all this trouble, I nonchalantly said, “My dear Mevan, you know better than I do—why don’t you take care of it? You’re more familiar with what’s good and bad here than I am.” Mevan was delighted. “Alright, come this way,” he said, leading me to another table where he showed me four or five varieties of neckbands, or what they call ‘ties’ here. Apparently, every man here must wear one of these around his neck, as if it were a sacred thread! For the life of me, I couldn’t understand why. There was neither the opportunity to ask nor the means to find out. It felt as though death itself had descended upon me.

Next, he had half a dozen collars brought out. After that, he ordered two sets each of those undergarments worn beneath the suit—what they call “vests”—and shirts. Then, two pairs of what they call “drawers.” Watching all this, my heart nearly stopped. What sort of Mevan is this, acting as if he’s some zamindar, and making me out to be an even greater zamindar, ordering one thing after another with his eyes closed! Who’s going to pay for all this? Neither he nor his father is going to shell out a penny! Surely, this shop wasn’t established to provide charity to the likes of me! And what’s with all these drawers and ties—why so many? Wouldn’t one or two suffice? When they get dirty, can’t I wash them at night and have them clean by morning? If all this comes to a hundred or two hundred, where am I to find that kind of money now? But how could I say no?

While I was still pondering this, the shop assistant took everything we’d selected, arranged them neatly in a small, beautiful cardboard box, placed the suit in another box, tied them up prettily with something like a ribbon, and brought them over, setting them before me.

Mevan handed me the bill. Swallowing back the tears that threatened to well up, I managed to hand over the money to Mevan without a word, not even asking how much it was. If you heard the amount, you’d be shocked. I tucked the boxes under my arm and walked out.

For a moment, I paused outside and asked, “There’s nothing else left to buy, is there?” I held my breath for a second, fearing he’d say there was still a lot more to get. Mevan looked at my face for a moment—
Barrister Parvateesam

After examining the case, seeing the fear and doubts on my face, he laughed and said, “That’s enough for today.” “So, does that mean I have to come back tomorrow, dragging my bundle of accusations behind me?” I asked. It didn’t seem like he understood what I meant. “No need for all that. You’re leaving today, aren’t you? For now, I don’t need anything else,” he replied. If I needed any small items, he said, I could get help from someone and buy them after reaching Edinburgh. With that, the day’s business was concluded, and we immediately set out for our lodging. This time, instead of taking a train or a tram, we hired a horse carriage and reached our place. I wondered if we had suddenly become so fortunate to deserve such a conveyance. Now was a busy hour. In this town of ninety thousand people, everyone was bustling about their own affairs. The trains and trams were all terribly crowded. He explained that, in such circumstances, without anyone’s interference, even if it cost a few extra coins, it was better to reach our destination quickly. By the time he finished telling me all this, we had already arrived at our lodging. “Come, hurry up,” he said, and, seeing me standing there watching the crowds running back and forth, he pulled me inside.
“I still have work to do. I must go into town. You pass the time however you like until evening. I’ll come back in the evening, meet you, and put you on the night train.”
Saying this, and without waiting to hear my words of gratitude, he went off to his room.

I went into my room, placed all the things I had bought on the bed, sat down, and began to open them one by one. Looking at them, I was delighted—never mind the money wasted, where would I ever find such things back home? I thought.

No matter what the item or its quality, do they pack everything so beautifully in such lovely boxes for every customer? Or do they only do this for foreigners like me, thinking we are important people? I wondered. Whatever it was, everything here—the arrangements, the customs—looked so beautiful and elegant. Perhaps this is what they call civilization, I thought. Of all these things—

chapters.title: Lodgings
paragraphs: After that, I couldn’t understand how that fellow managed to stitch the suit and hand it over to me in just five minutes. Or perhaps, among the ones already there, he picked out one that had been stitched for someone else, and since I was in a hurry, he thought he could just give it to me and make another one for the other person later! With this suspicion in mind, I wondered if that’s what he had done. But then I thought, “Why should I care how he manages? My work is done, isn’t it?” Satisfied, I folded everything neatly, carefully put it back in the box, and stored it safely. After resting for a while, I got up at one o’clock and prepared for lunch. At that hour, there was no one to be seen in the dining hall except me.

I assumed that everyone here must have gone off to their own work and probably eat at some hotel or the other. The attendant immediately served me some refreshments. After finishing the snacks, I went back to my room and lay down. I didn’t wake up from that bed until four o’clock. I wondered what sort of mad sleep had overtaken me! After washing my face and wandering about for a bit, I decided to step out onto the street. Afraid that I might lose my way if I went too far, I confined myself to that street, observing the shops, the passersby, the people rushing about, and the various vehicles. Without even realizing it, six o’clock had come around. I immediately returned to my lodging. Just then, Menon arrived.
“Is all the packing done? We’re traveling tonight, aren’t we?” he asked.
“I’m not late at all. We’re traveling tonight,” I replied.
“In that case, let’s have dinner. Come along,” he said. We finished dinner in fifteen minutes and returned to my room.
“Have you packed all your things carefully?” Menon asked.
“Yes, everything is packed,” I replied.
“Are the clothes all right?” he asked.

“Would you buy them if they weren’t?” I retorted. But I must tell you about my little predicament! I’m dying to know how that fellow managed to stitch the suit so quickly, I said. Menon burst out laughing and said, “They always have some ready-made ones—”
Barrister Parvateesam
They stitch and keep them like that. When new arrivals come, they give each person whatever fits them.

Generally, for a person of a certain height, the arms will be this long, the chest this wide, the neck this length, the waist this size, the legs this long—there’s a calculation for everything. They stitch accordingly. Except in rare cases, these standard sizes usually fit most people. With this explanation, he cleared my doubt.
“Did you put on the baniyan-like thing you bought this morning underneath?” he asked.
“No,” I replied.
“Then why did you buy it, my dear fellow? To wear, or just to keep in your trunk? You’ll be traveling at night. It’ll be much colder then. Put those on first,” he said.
“Will just one baniyan suffice, or should I wear something like a shirt over it as well?” I asked.
“You should wear both,” he said.
“Good heavens!” I exclaimed. I had to untie everything I had just put on and tried to wear those underclothes. They wouldn’t go on easily. It was like trying to pull on a pair of tight socks.

They were so tight, it almost felt like they were pricking my body. “What’s this? Why did you give me such tight ones?” I asked. “They’re supposed to be like that. Wear them for two days and they’ll loosen up. When they cling to your body, you’ll know how warm and comfortable they are! It feels as pleasant as embracing a woman,” he said with a laugh.
“Look at this fellow, spouting nonsense as if he spends his days hugging women,” I thought to myself, feeling a bit embarrassed.

“All these things you’ll understand in time,” he said, and then, “Let’s get going.” I quickly finished dressing, packed my things again, and came outside. Menon called the servant who was there. The man brought my luggage and placed it on the street. We walked into the hall, and there I went up to the formidable lady manager.

“I’m leaving for Edinburgh now. If you tell me how much my bill is, I’ll settle it,” I said. The bill, already prepared—how or when it had been made ready, I couldn’t tell—was handed to me from the table. I paid the amount at once. She handed me the receipt with a gentle smile. “Wish you good luck,” she said, wishing me well, and then, “Goodbye,” she bid me farewell.
By the time I stepped out onto the street, Menon had called for a horse carriage, loaded my luggage into it, and told me to get in.

We arrived at the station. Menon bought my ticket and helped me board the train. Even in this train, all the compartments had those beds with benches. I put my luggage under the bench and was about to take out my blanket when Menon stopped me.
“No need to take that out now,” he said. “But how’s that? Won’t it get cold at night? Shouldn’t I at least take my shawl?” I asked.
“No need. Just watch—I’ll perform a magic trick and get you pillows for your head and two rugs to cover yourself,” he said.

Before he could finish speaking, a railway porter arrived, carrying two pillows in white pillowcases and two rugs as heavy as myself, and placed them on the bench. Menon slipped a shilling into his hand. I stood there staring like a simpleton. The servant who brought them left. People were starting to board the train.
Barrister Parvateesam
Meenan looked at me and laughed.
