“In this country, the railway company rents these out every day, every minute, even at night. When we get down, we simply leave them in the train, and they collect and take care of them. They keep them clean at all times,” he said.
“So, does that mean everyone here is as honest as us? No one ever steals these?” I asked.
He laughed again. “This isn’t our country! Here, no one does such things. Even our own people who come here don’t stoop to such petty acts,” Meenan replied.

“You don’t need to worry. If the train isn’t crowded, you can lie down comfortably. Otherwise, just wrap yourself in these rugs and sit at your place with ease. No matter how crowded it gets, more than three people never sit on a bench. A fourth will never come. Travel in comfort. Once you reach safely and settle in, write me a detailed letter about how you managed everything. I’ll take my leave now,” he said.

Thinking of the kindness and help he had shown me over these two days, my eyes filled with tears. In this distant land, where I knew neither face nor name, he had given me such selfless assistance, such genuine affection—how great! What a generous heart! Bowing to him, with a slightly trembling voice and tears welling up, I managed to express my gratitude in a few words.

Just then, the train whistled. He gave me a quick hug and said, “Don’t be afraid, brother. Everything will go smoothly on its own. Don’t worry, stay cheerful. The Lord’s grace will be with you.” He shook my hand and quickly got off the train. As he waved goodbye, the train started moving.

Left standing there, I felt completely lost. For a moment, I couldn’t see the people or things inside or outside the train. Wiping my eyes, I sat down. The two people sitting opposite me at the table looked at me with puzzled, half-amused expressions.
"Are you new here?" asked one of them. I nodded, unable to get a word out.
"You have nothing to worry about. It’s comfortable here. Just lie down and sleep well," he said.
"Thank you," I replied, as the train picked up speed. My mind, however, raced homeward even faster.

As Menon had said, the train was quite empty. I spread out my bedding, wrapped myself in the rugs, and lay down comfortably. For a moment, I wondered whether I should change out of this suit and so on. But then I thought, why bother with all that trouble in the train? If I just lay down like this, it would be fine. I felt there was no need to even take off my shoes and socks. The bedding was so soft and comfortable. I had never seen such soft bedding anywhere before.

To tell the truth, the bedding in our house was as hard as rocks. We would put a brick at the head, cover it with a blanket, and call that a pillow. I thought to myself, perhaps the cotton in this country is just that much softer! With such thoughts, my eyes began to close.
Just as I was about to fall asleep, the man sitting on the opposite bench, who had been watching me all this while, smiled and said, "Good night, sir. Sound sleep. Pleasant dreams."
I smiled back and said, "Thank you," then closed my eyes. I must have fallen asleep as soon as I closed them, for I remember nothing after that.

When I started to regain a little consciousness, there was a commotion in the train. I realized the train had stopped. The brothers who had been sitting opposite me had disappeared. I didn’t know where to get off. For a moment, I worried that even my luggage might have vanished. I looked under the bench, but my belongings were still there, sleeping as soundly as I had been.
The train had stopped, and everyone was getting down. "Is this Edinburgh?" I asked a fellow passenger.
"Yes," he replied.

As Menon had advised, I rolled up the rugs, placed them on the bedding, and got down with all my luggage. Now what should I do? I was pondering this when a railway porter approached, smiling, and greeted me with, "Morning, sir," tipping his hat.
"Had sound sleep, sir? Where are you—"

“Going, sir? Can I help you, sir?” he asked politely, his manner full of humility and deference. Seeing his respectful attitude, I felt quite pleased. The truth was, I had no idea where I was supposed to go. I was pondering whether I should go into town and look for a room first, or do something else.

He said, “There are rooms available right here at the station, sir. I can put your luggage in one of them. You can have some refreshments at your leisure, and then go into town. Your belongings will be safe here. If you wish, you may even stay in the room for a day or two, paying a small rent.”

I felt as though I had been thrown a lifeline. “Thank you,” I said. He took me, along with my luggage, into a room. After placing my things there, he showed me a small adjacent room and said, “You may attend to your personal needs in here. If you press the button on the wall, someone will come and bring you refreshments or anything else you require.” With a respectful salute, he quietly closed the door behind him and left.

I was quite astonished by all this. I thought to myself, “Well, I can give him something when I leave.” I took off my coat and other clothes, attended to my needs, and within half an hour, dressed again and pressed the button as he had instructed. In less than a minute, as if he had sprung up from the ground, a man appeared before me and stood respectfully, saying, “Good morning, sir. What would you like?” with great reverence.

I asked him to bring me some refreshments and tea. In these past four or five days, I had become quite accustomed to such procedures. “I shall bring it at once, sir,” he said, and true to his word, returned in a moment with everything arranged neatly on the table. He told me, “If you need anything else, just press that button,” and quietly closed the door behind him as he left.

I enjoyed my refreshments comfortably and, as I was preparing to go out, pressed the button again. The same man returned. I said, “This town is new to me. I have never been here before. I have come to study, so I must stay here for some time. I need a room to stay in. Where can I find one? How should I go about it? What should I do?” I asked him frankly, without any hesitation.

chapters.title: The Boarding House
paragraphs: I remained standing. He too was still standing. I said, “Please, you be seated,” and pointed to a chair. But he alone continued to stand.

“It would be convenient for you if you stayed near the university, wouldn’t it? Here, if you get on this tram and get off at the street I mention, you’ll find yourself in a neighborhood full of boarding houses. On every street there, you’ll see boards and signs in the windows saying ‘Room to let.’ If you press one of the buttons by the door—either on the right or left, depending on where the sign is—they’ll open the door for you. If the sign is on the left side of the door, press the left button. If it’s on the right, press the right button. If it’s on the ground floor, press the lower button; if it’s on an upper floor, press the button for that floor. Then, in whichever street you prefer, at whichever rent suits you, you can choose a room as you like,” he explained.

He conveyed all this information with great patience, leisure, and humility. I thanked him and stepped outside. I noticed that after I left, he gathered up the fruit peels and leftovers from my snack, closed the door, and came out as well.

As I walked down the street, I noticed many people staring at me, and a couple of them even smiled. What do I care if they laugh? I thought, “Let them twist their mouths as they please,” and went to the tram stop after finding out where it was. When the tram with the number he mentioned arrived at the station, I boarded it and got down at the place he had told me.

There was a small park there. Many children, some alone and some with their mothers, were playing in it. Watching them filled me with affection; for a moment, I stood there, lost in their games. Without realizing it, a smile crept onto my face. Some of the children, seeing me, moved away to a distance. A couple of them, braver than the rest, came closer, their eyes wide with fear and wonder, and stood staring at me.
A little way behind me, a few children, after glancing at me, ran off to their mothers, hugged them tightly, and cried, “Mummy, mummy, there’s—”
Barrister Parvateesam

"Is black mummy (Is that a black man, mother)?" one of them said. Another asked, "Mother, will that black man carry away children?" Yet another piped up, "Mother, does he never take a bath?" Their mothers pressed their mouths shut and warned, "Don’t say such things. If you ever say that again, you’ll get a beating. Be careful."

I was pleased by the courage of the children who came near me, and I greeted them with a "Hello." The children, startled, ran away in fright. Chuckling to myself, I continued on my way. I hadn’t gone very far before I saw, on a street, boards just as the station master had described: "Rooms to Let."

I went up to one such house, pressed the button at the door, and waited. An old woman opened the door, took one look at my face with great distaste, exclaimed "Oh!" and promptly slammed the door shut. Amused, I went to another house. There, a middle-aged woman opened the door, looked me up and down suspiciously, and asked, "What do you want?"
"I want a room," I said.
"There are no rooms available, very sorry," she lied politely and closed the door.

At another place, the lady of the house made it quite clear from her expression that she had no desire to rent her room to someone of my complexion, and quoted an exorbitant rent. Understanding her meaning, I left.
At yet another house, an old woman opened the door and asked, "Which country are you from? Africa?"
"No, India," I replied.
"Oh! India. How wonderful. Are you the son of a Maharaja there?" she asked.
I laughed and said no. "I’m no Maharaja, just an ordinary man. I’ve come here to study. I need a room," I said.
She smiled, expressing both amusement and regret. "There are no vacancies at present. In about a week, a room will be free. If you come then, I’ll give it to you," she said.

Pleased with her words, I continued a little further when, to my great relief, I saw a countryman of mine coming towards me. It felt as if my soul had returned to my body. I thought, "You have saved me, my friend!" I stopped him, greeted him with a "Good morning," explained my predicament, and asked him to advise me on what to do.
"Alright, come with me," he said, and led me to a place nearby.
He took me into a large house with a signboard reading "Indian Association." Inside, he seated me in the hall, sat down opposite me, and said in English, "Now, tell me about yourself."

Many of our countrymen could be seen coming in and going out of that place. I narrated my entire story. He listened patiently. He told me he was a Bengali. As he was about to say something more, a man who looked unmistakably Telugu entered the room.

The Bengali sitting before me called out, "Hello Raju, come here!" The man came and stood by us. "Sit down. This fellow is from your region. He’s come here looking for a room. Poor chap, he’s been wandering about. Why don’t you show him a room somewhere and help him settle in?"

chapters.title: New Routines
paragraphs: Otherwise, it would be quite troublesome. If we don’t support each other here, how will we survive? What do you say?” he asked with a gentle smile.

“Oh, certainly! I’ll keep an eye out for you. You go ahead,” said Raju. He stood up and said, “Well, let’s meet again. This Raju is from your region. He’s a very good fellow—he’ll help you with anything you need. I have some work to attend to, so I’ll be off now.” With that, he shook my hand and left. Raju then moved into the chair he had vacated and sat down.

“So, my friend! Where are you from? When did you arrive? Tell me all about yourself—your background, your circumstances,” he said, introducing himself as being from Bhimavaram, a Telugu man, and a Kshatriya. “Now, go on—tell me about yourself,” he urged.
Without skipping a single detail, I narrated everything that had happened to me up to that point. “And your luggage—where is it?” he asked.
“I left it at the station,” I replied.

“All right then, let’s go. We’ll fetch your things and come back to my place. You can stay with me until you find your own room—don’t worry, you won’t face any trouble. You’ll be quite comfortable,” he said.
So, I set out with him to the station, collected my luggage, paid the porters the usual fee, and then arrived at Raju’s room.

I rested there comfortably for a while. At four in the evening, without my even asking, the lady of the house brought me tea and some bread, setting it all neatly on the table. After I had eaten, I sat in the room flipping through some books. Not long after, Raju returned from college.
“Well, did you have a good rest? Did you have tea?” he asked.
“Oh yes, everything’s taken care of. I feel so at ease here,” I replied.
Raju tossed his books aside and went to the washroom to freshen up. By the time he came back, the lady of the house had brought tea and snacks for both of us again. “I don’t want anything,” I said.
That was when he taught me my very first lesson here: “In this country, whenever anyone...

Even if you don’t want it, you mustn’t refuse at least a cup of tea. In our country, just as you’re offered water to wash your feet and cool drinking water as soon as you enter a house, here in this country, at all times—whether in hardship or in comfort—they first offer you tea. You mustn’t refuse it,” said Raju.
After we had our tea, Raju asked me to narrate my story in detail. “So, where exactly are you from?” he asked. I replied, “Mogalturru.”
“What! Mogalturru! That’s quite close to where I’m from. We have many relatives in those villages. Our ancestral home is actually in Poduru,” he said.

After that, I explained my situation in detail, and he listened attentively. I requested him to help me find a room and get admitted to a college. “Of course, I’ll definitely do that. What’s so great about this help? If we don’t help each other in a foreign land, who else will?” he replied. “Let’s go out for a while, sit in the park, and have a chat. Tomorrow morning, we’ll look for a room,” he said.

The two of us set out and went to a nearby park and sat down. By then, it was around six o’clock. It had grown quite dark, yet the place was bustling with people. Men and women, so many of them! All the children who had been playing there until then were now scampering home, running as fast as their little legs could carry them. Among those who had come to the park, many were young men and women—couples, some sitting on benches, others sprawled on the grass—laughing, chatting, and, every now and then, engaging in such passionate embraces and kisses that they seemed to have forgotten this world and entered another altogether. Because of this, no one paid us the slightest attention. They all behaved as if no one else existed in the park but themselves, lost in their own happiness. So, we too sat comfortably on the grass, at ease.
“What’s your name, young man?” Raju asked. “They call me Parvateesham. My family name is Vemuri,” I replied.
“All right, very good. But here, I must tell you briefly about the customs, manners, and ways of this place. If you learn these ways and adapt to them…”

If we behave as we do back home, only we will have to face difficulties. The first thing is, if anyone asks you your name, just say “Parvateesam.” That’s enough. No need to add “I am called,” “they call me,” or “I am known as.” No need for all those extra words.

Now, the next matter. I must tell you about renting rooms here. All those who let out rooms for rent here are called the “lower middle class.” That is, people of a slightly lower status than our own middle-class families. Usually, they are widows. But sometimes, they are elderly spinsters who have never known marriage, or couples with low incomes, who rent houses with one or two rooms more than they need, and let out the extra rooms. These rooms are furnished with chairs, sofas, and so on. That means three or four chairs, a sofa, a table, a bed, a mattress, pillows, a side blanket, rugs to cover yourself, and towels to wipe yourself with. The rent for the room includes all these things. Not only that, they also provide towels and soaps.

Next, in every room—you must have seen it in my room—there is something called a fireplace. It’s a stove built into the wall, where they stack coal and light a fire. There is a pipe to let the smoke out so it doesn’t fill the room. This fireplace burns day and night for seven or eight months of the year, like Ravana’s sacrificial fire. Especially in winter, people pull up chairs and sit around the fire. The whole room stays warm, and you’ll notice it when you come to my place.

Here, there is a secret worth knowing. The people of this country, especially those of the lower classes, don’t even wash their faces. He said this. I was shocked. “They don’t even wash their faces?” I asked. “No one washes,” he replied. “Then what do they do?” I asked. Wherever you go outside, you’ll see rolls of paper nearby. After relieving themselves in the commode—a porcelain contraption—they take a piece of paper, wipe themselves, and throw it into the commode. There is a chain you pull, and water flows in...

She comes specially and cleans up all this filth so thoroughly that she takes it somewhere far away, down to the last speck. Since this is a cold country, the stench doesn't rise up so quickly. As for washing their faces—well, people here don't even bathe every day. Why spell it out any further? he said.
"Then what about us?" I asked.
"If you wish, you may also stop bathing," he replied.

"What is this, sir, how can you say such a thing? I am a Brahmin, and moreover, a Vedic one. I am already troubled that I cannot perform my daily Sandhya Vandanam and other rituals, and now you ask me to give up bathing as well? If that is the case, I cannot stay here even for a moment. Whatever you may say, I will see the country and return home, but I cannot live in such utter disregard for custom and tradition. Do as you please," I said.
"Alright then, as you wish. I never said you must stop. If you want hot water for your bath, just tell the people of the house and they will supply it. No problem at all," he said.
"That is good, at least," I replied. "But for cleaning my teeth, it would have been better if I had brought some chewing sticks and palm leaves!"

He turned pale. "What? Chewing sticks and palm leaves? Did you bring them? All this time, between us, did you bring nothing else? Are you following the customs of this country to the letter or what?" he asked in dismay.
"Then, did you not ask anyone for advice before coming here?" he said.
"Who do I have to advise me, sir, in Mogaliturru? Don’t you know?" I replied.

He looked at me for a moment, slowly and thoughtfully. "Yes, that's true. Not only there, but nowhere in the surrounding areas either. Well, never mind, it's good you brought them. But since those things dry out, be careful to keep them safe. Use them as you need, and when we go to the room, I’ll buy you the tooth-cleaning things they use here," he said, poor fellow.
After that, we never had to go to a hotel for meals. If we told the people of the house what we wanted, they would prepare it accordingly.
Barrister Parvateesam

They charge a certain fee for this. No matter how much they take, it still costs less than eating at hotels. Since you are Brahmins and Vedic scholars, and since you do not touch the meat and fish that I eat, you can simply tell the householders that you are vegetarians and list out the rice, salt, and other ingredients you need—they will bring everything for you. If you know how to cook, you can instruct them. Otherwise, you’ll have to eat whatever they prepare. After ten days, you’ll get used to everything,” he said.

“Oh, there’s no need to worry about that! I’m quite used to all this. Back home, whenever my mother was away or my father went to the fields or to a neighboring village, I had to cook for myself. My mother even praised me for doing it so well. Just wait until I settle down somewhere; I’ll treat you to a meal cooked by my own hand one day,” I replied.
He laughed and said, “I’d be delighted! That would make me feel as if I’d gone home for a visit.”

From there, we slowly made our way to the room. There, he had his usual meal, while I was given a little rice, some potato curry, and milk. As for the curry, it was simply boiled potatoes mashed up and served. My friend suggested that I sprinkle salt and chili powder on top as I liked. “I have already grasped this subtlety of dharma,” I said.

After dinner, the lady of the house brought two pillows and two blankets and laid them out on the sofa, just as she had done on the train. My friend courteously said, “I’ll sleep on the sofa tonight. You take my bed.”

“Oh, no, not at all! I can sleep on the sofa. I’m quite used to it,” I replied. Much of my life has been spent sleeping on sofas, so even though he insisted a little, I did not agree. The sofa was actually quite comfortable. After chatting idly for a while, I lay down on the sofa and he on the bed. Thus, I spent my first night in ‘Edinburgh’ dreaming sweet dreams.
That night, I slept soundly at Raja’s house. So many strange...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 187

Strange dreams visited me. I felt as if I were floating away to far-off places. In the sky, I saw something like a giant fish soaring above. The stars appeared so close, as if I could reach out and touch them. Many other oddities and wonders presented themselves to my eyes. But by the time I woke up, nothing remained. Not only were those visions gone, but I couldn’t even recall them well enough to tell anyone about them. As usual, I woke up near the house to the familiar clamor of morning. Raju was still fast asleep. I thought of waking him, but then wondered what purpose it would serve to rouse someone so early, so I let him be.

I went to the window and looked outside; there was no sign of people moving about yet. It was still quite dark. So I came back and lay down again. But this time, sleep eluded me. Instead, a jumble of vague thoughts and dreams began swirling in my mind. What is this country? Who are these people? What are their customs and ways? Without knowing any of this, I set out blindly, like a bull let loose in a field, and managed to arrive here without a single clear thought.
It’s been a whole week since I arrived, and yet, I still haven’t figured anything out. Even though I am new here, and just a young man, everyone addresses me as “Sir” with great respect.

Here, wherever I look, there seem to be more women than men. They don’t seem to have any shyness or fear at all. In the middle of the streets, in the shops, in the trains—they stride about boldly, pushing past everyone. Watching them, I feel both afraid and amazed.

Tomorrow morning, when I go out into the street or join the school, these women will surely be there too. Even from a distance, just seeing them makes me feel a little nervous and a little embarrassed. If they come closer, if they sit here and there in the classroom, how will I listen to what the teachers say? How will I keep anything in my head? Somehow, these women are bound to cause me some trouble. Well, let’s see what happens. Why worry about the taste before eating the meal? After all, God is up there watching over me.

Will I find a room at this hour or not? If not, what then? How long can I keep sitting on Raju’s head? But what if I don’t find one? In such a big city, with so many buildings, will a bachelor like me not find a place to stay? Even if they refuse to take in bachelors, I doubt they have such strange rules here.
Barrister Parvateesam

While I was being tormented by all sorts of strange thoughts, morning arrived. There was a gentle knock on our door. Forgetting that I was in this country, I shouted, “Yes, I’m coming!” just as I would have yelled at home. At this, Raju woke up with a start and, laughing, said, “What’s the matter? Why are you shouting?”
I replied, “It’s nothing. I just heard someone knocking on the door and, out of habit, shouted that I was coming. Sorry if I disturbed your sleep.”

He said, “Oh, it’s no problem at all. It’s already morning anyway. The lady of the house knocks on the door to wake us up. That’s her usual practice—not just today. The custom here is that whether it’s a family member or a stranger, they never bang on the door. Instead, they gently tap twice with their fingers—‘tuk tuk.’ At that time, we should say ‘Yes’ or ‘Come in’ if it’s someone from the house. If it’s someone from upstairs, we should say ‘Come in, please.’ That means, ‘Please come inside.’ Here, regardless of whether someone is young or old, for everything, people say ‘please’ and ‘thank you.’ They’re very pleased by such words. We’ll be considered very polite if we do the same,” he explained. Then he said, “Come on, let’s wash our faces.”

I hadn’t noticed properly at night, but now I saw that Raju was wearing a loose, long robe, something like a dressing gown, over his pajamas. Now that he had gotten up, he put on a large gown that reached down to his feet. It had no buttons. Instead, he tied a silk cord around his waist. It looked rather odd to me. As I stared in surprise, he said, “This is called a dressing gown. The clothes worn underneath—shirt and pants—are called pajamas. If we stayed in our suits all night, we wouldn’t be comfortable. Besides, they’d get wrinkled. Here, there’s no facility to press suits every day. People like us usually get one or two suits tailored for winter and one or two for summer, and they last a year or two. While at home, whether it’s day or night, we wear these pajamas. No matter how we sit or sleep, there’s no discomfort. Suits are made of wool; pajamas are made of cotton. We can wash them whenever we want, or send them to the laundry. You should also buy two sets like these.”

When you buy these, whether it’s your family members or the people upstairs, if any women come by, you mustn’t be seen in these pyjamas. The moment they knock on the door from upstairs, you must swiftly grab this dressing gown, wrap it tightly around your waist, and only then open the door. Another thing: as long as you’re inside the house, there’s no need to wear shoes or slippers. But they sell these Japanese sandals—rather like our leaf slippers—thin, light, and warm. You mustn’t walk around the house without them. These are the customs here.”

As we were exchanging such tidbits while brushing our teeth, a servant girl—though calling her a girl is a stretch; she must have been about twenty—came into the room. She went over to the bed where Raju was still lying, pulled off the blanket, dusted it, and put it back again. She cleaned the whole room. Even the way she cleaned was peculiar—no sweeping with a broom or bending over. Instead, there was a four or five-foot stick with a brush at the end, and she cleaned while standing upright. The strange thing was, it seemed like she was cleaning just for the sake of appearances.

chapters.title: English Lessons
paragraphs: He only said he had swept, but there wasn’t a speck of dust anywhere. In our villages, no matter how many times you sweep in a day, there’s always enough dust to go around. No one knows where it all comes from. After about ten more minutes, without us saying a word, the lady brought us some snacks and tea, serving us with a smile. Once we finished that ritual, we changed into our street clothes and stepped outside. As we were leaving, he carefully closed the doors behind us.
Once we were out on the street, I asked Raju quietly, “Aren’t you going to lock the door?”

“Oh, it’s not necessary. Here, if you lock the door, people take it the wrong way. They think you don’t trust the people in the house, or that you’re insulting them. So, there’s no need to lock up. If you must lock something, it’s usually just the front door, not the rooms inside.”

Then we set out in search of my own lodgings. Every house with a “To Let” sign, upon seeing us, would say, “Sorry, there’s nothing vacant! Very sorry, I regret it.” No matter which house we went to, it was always the women who opened the door, greeted us, and answered our questions. I supposed the men must have gone out somewhere. In some places, the rooms were so tiny and cramped that I didn’t like them. In others, both the house and the housewife were so disagreeable that I had no mind to stay there. In one or two places, though everything seemed fine, Raju said the rent was far too high.

So, we wandered about like this until one o’clock, our legs growing heavy as lead, and by lunchtime, we could barely drag ourselves back to the house. I began to lose hope that I’d ever find a room. Poor Raju noticed my discouragement and said, “Don’t worry, don’t rush. If you don’t find something today, you’ll find it tomorrow. If not tomorrow, then the day after. You can stay with me for a week if you need to. I only worry that you might be inconvenienced.”
I replied, “I’m not troubled at all. The only thing missing is an extra bed for you,” said Raju.
“That’s no problem at all. Come on, let’s go.”
“I feel bad that I am causing you so much trouble,” I said.
After reaching home, we finished our meals and rested for a while.

After wandering around like this for two or three days, I finally managed to find a room—quite a good one at that. Attached to the sitting room was a small bedroom. In it, there was a large bed with two mattresses, two or three rugs, blankets, and two towels for washing up—everything was right there. In the sitting room, there was a sofa, two cushioned chairs, a dining table with two or three chairs beside it, and a small cupboard-like thing to keep books and such. There was even a fireplace built into one wall to keep the place warm. Everything looked so elegant. I was amazed to see that things like these mattresses, sofas, and chairs—which even the wealthy in our country rarely possess—could be found in every ordinary person’s home here.

The landlady had two daughters, both a little older. With Raju’s help, I immediately brought my belongings and performed my “new house entry”! Even though it had only been a week since I arrived in this country, I noticed that I was already changing in some ways. I completely forgot to check whether the time was auspicious for entering the new house. Even when I remembered later, whom could I ask here? Who would tell me? If I asked anyone, they would just laugh. Besides, it doesn’t seem like they have almanacs or anything of the sort here, so one must simply adjust to everything, just like everyone else. If my uncle found out about this, what a fuss he would have made! There’s no use living in a country and not following its customs as much as necessary, I thought, and laughed at myself.

Raju advised me not to unpack my mosquito net, saying I wouldn’t need it as long as I stayed in this country. The poor fellow even took me to the market himself and bought two bed sheets, slippers, and a dressing gown for me. “Since you have to wear a dressing gown on top anyway, can’t I just wear my usual dhoti underneath?” I asked. “Let it be! Why bother with all that? There’s no way to wash and dry your dhoti every day here, is there? If you give it to the laundry, who knows what will happen to it, or how it’ll turn out? Even the laundryman will be bewildered, not knowing what to do with it!”
Barrister Parvateesam
...will fall. So, if you stick to this way of life here, you’ll be just fine,” said Raju.

From that day, a new chapter of my domestic life began. I told the lady of the house that I was a vegetarian, and so, for my meals, I would need rice, dal, a little tamarind, chilies, and so on. Raju and I together made a list of all the necessary items and handed it to her. She turned pale after seeing the list. With a hint of doubt, she asked, “What am I supposed to do with all these?”
“If you bring them, our friend here will explain everything. He’ll even show you how it’s done. You must watch our cooking sometime, and perhaps even taste it,” Raju said with a laugh.
The lady left, and Raju stood up as well. “Well, I’ll be off now. If you need anything, just ask me. I’ll tell you what to do. Good luck to you!” he said, shaking my hand, and departed.
The lady of the house brought all the groceries and asked, “Now, tell me what to do with these.”
“Can you cook rice?” I asked.
“That’s no problem, I can cook rice,” she replied.
“In that case, for the dal, just add a little water and boil it until it’s soft. Then mash it well and add a little salt,” I instructed.

Next, I told her that after chopping and boiling the vegetables, I would explain how to make the curry. But I didn’t know how to say “curry” in English. No matter how many ways I tried to explain, she couldn’t understand. Then, when it came to “pulusu” (tamarind stew), I had no idea what it was called in English either. Again, my explanations were in vain.
Finally, I said, “Just put two kinds of chopped vegetables in water and boil them.”
“Oh, you mean soup!” she exclaimed. “That’s easy, I can make soup.”
“Alright, but I’ll check it later,” I said.

At noon, at twelve o’clock, she brought my lunch. She’d forgotten to call me for adding the tempering to the dal. The dal was as hard as pebbles, each grain separate. She’d also forgotten to add tamarind to the pulusu.
Oh, Lord! How am I supposed to eat this? I thought.
“Which one is the ghee?” I asked.
“What’s ghee?” she replied.
“My fate!” I muttered.
“What’s that?” she asked.
“Oh, nothing, sorry,” I said, and asked her to bring a little butter instead.
For that meal, she placed everything on the table, including something called “pudding,” which was supposed to be a sweet dish, and left.
The rice was a bit like glue. The dal was like gravel. In both the curry and the pulusu, she had forgotten to add salt.

I couldn’t help it. Even though my stomach was burning, I somehow swallowed it. That evening, as I was having tea, Raju came over. Smiling, he asked, “So, how’s your married life going?” I replied, “It’s a brand-new marriage, you see. I have to explain everything to the lady of the house from scratch, step by step.”

Raju laughed and said, “No need to explain everything—just teach her cooking, that’s enough.” After a while, we went out to see the college, and since there was a park nearby, we sat there chatting. In the midst of our conversation, he asked, “What about your studies?”
I countered, “What’s your advice?”

He said, “Since your knowledge of English is quite limited, it’s best if you first hire a private tutor here and study for three or four months. After the summer holidays, there’s an entrance exam. If you pass that, you can join the M.A. course right away. After that, depending on your patience, you can also prepare for the Law exam—the barrister’s exam.”

The next day, I began trying to teach the lady of the house how to cook. I sat nearby, attempting to explain—using my half-baked language skills—how we prepare food in our tradition, describing things I myself barely understood. The lady and her daughters sat there, bursting into laughter. When they laughed, their mouths twisted in odd ways. I didn’t care; I carried on with my task.

I taught them how to cook rice properly, how to make it fluffy and just right. I demonstrated how to prepare mudda pappu (plain dal)—that’s a birthright for us Godavari district folk. Next, I had them cook a curry with Bengal gram and potatoes. After boiling it, I told them to add chilies and mustard seeds, but when I checked, there was no oil.
“How can you cook without oil?” I asked.
She replied, “You can’t get ghee or any regular oils here.”

“Alright, let’s think about tomorrow’s meal,” I said. That day, I melted a bit of butter, and as the saying goes, I used the ghee I’d just prepared to fry the seasoning. The pungency was too much for them—they were left gasping for breath.

After that, I had them boil pieces of fish, add tamarind water, and as I was mashing it all together, it seemed strange to them. The lady of the house asked, “Instead of mashing it by hand, can’t you just press it with a spoon and extract the juice?”

“You can,” I replied, “but it’s hard to get all the juice out that way. This is the easier method.” Still, they didn’t like it at all. In any case, none of the dishes we prepared that day were particularly appetizing to them.

As far as possible, they intended that I should cook without touching anything with my hands. Well, somehow, I managed to finish cooking that day, and after pretending the meal was ready, I invited them to taste the dishes too. I served some dal, curry, and pulusu to them as well, and managed to fill my own stomach in the process.

Gradually, she herself learned to prepare food in some fashion or the other. “Our dal is quite good,” she said. “The pulusu is also nice, but for that reason, we cannot eat it. And besides, eating so much tamarind here is not good for us. If we want, we can make a thin soup with just the leaves and add a little lemon juice to it.” I thought that was a good suggestion.

For a few days, though I struggled like this, since we were all used to different tastes, my attention turned to our hometown pickles. I asked my friend Raju for advice, “Tell me if there’s any way to get them.”
“I sometimes write home and have them send me some,” he replied. “They should arrive any day now. As soon as they come, I’ll give you a share.”
Remembering the new etiquette I had just learned, I said, “Thank you.” Raju laughed and nodded.

The next day, Raju and I went into town to see the university. I was utterly spellbound by the sight. Words failed me. I was overcome by a sense of awe, as if some sacred feeling had taken hold of me, and I stood there, rooted to the spot. After a couple of minutes, I regained my senses and, with Raju’s help, went inside. We explored the classrooms, the library, the examination halls, the assembly rooms, the administrative offices—each place seemed grander than the last. Drowning in this sea of wonder, I returned home.

That evening, Raju quietly arranged a private tutor for me. The tutor spoke to me very gently and patiently. He assured me that he would do his best to help me pass the entrance exam. He said, “If you gain a good command of English first, everything else will become easy.” And so, every day, he gave me two or three hours of special English lessons. The other subjects, he would teach a few topics one day, a few more the next. Thus began my studies—not exactly at an auspicious hour, but they went along quite well.

A couple of days later, one morning, Raju came in laughing and said, “Good morning, Mr. Parvateesham! Along with this fine morning, I have some good news for you. Yesterday, a cartload of pickles arrived from home. I’ve brought your share—this bottle has mango pickle, and this one has tokku chutney. Eat to your heart’s content!” He handed them over with a flourish.
I gazed at them with great affection, and resolved that, come what may, I would do justice to them today.

That day, I decided to try my hand at cooking and went into the kitchen. “What brings you here at this hour, Mr. Same?” asked the lady of the house. I forgot to mention—she couldn’t pronounce my name, so for convenience, she started calling me ‘Same’. I told her, “Call me whatever you like, as long as you’re happy.” From that day on, I became ‘Same’ to everyone in that household.
“I’ve just received fresh pickles from my hometown, so I came to the kitchen,” I said. Then I asked her to melt some butter for me. The lady of the house...

While she was cooking, I was clarifying ghee. After the meal was ready, she brought everything and arranged it in my room. As she was about to leave, I called her back and placed a little bit of mango pickle in a small plate. “This is a famous pickle from my region. Try spreading it on your bread with a generous layer of butter, just like you would with jam. Though it’s a bit spicy, it tastes wonderful. But don’t use too much at once,” I warned her. She was delighted and took it with her.

That day, I felt an urge to eat in our traditional manner. These spoons, knives, and forks don’t really suit our style of eating. So, for once, I decided to honor the sacred customs of our beloved India. I pushed the spoons and forks aside, resolved to eat with my hand, and began my meal in comfort. I started with rice and dal. As I was mixing in some mango pickle for the second bite, a piercing scream rang out from the other room.

I wondered what had happened, when I heard someone call, “Oh, Mr. Sam!” Was there some disaster? I quickly stuffed the morsel I had mixed into my mouth, intending to go see what was wrong, when suddenly, with a single wail of “Oh, Sam!” the lady of the house burst into my room, sobbing, followed closely by her daughters.

“What is it, madam? What happened?” I asked. She looked at my plate, as if trying to say something, searching for an answer. Meanwhile, I was still mixing the pickle with my hand. Only then did she seem to realize the true cause of her distress. Upon seeing my hand, she let out a string of “Oh! Oh! Oh!” like a madwoman, staggered backwards, and collapsed into a chair as if she had fainted.

Until then, her daughters had been peering at me with a mix of curiosity and disgust, but now they abandoned their post, squeezed out a couple of forced tears, and rushed to their mother’s side—one fetched some water, the other sprinkled a little on her face. The lady slowly opened her eyes, pointed at me with a trembling finger, and with sobs, kept repeating, “Sam! Sam! You—” as if she was about to faint again.

I, too, went over to her and said gently, “It’s all right, madam, why are you so upset? There’s nothing to be afraid of. Please, tell me what happened.” In my concern, I forgot I still had pickle on my hand, and with that very hand, I wiped her eyes. Well, that was all it took—the house was in an uproar once again.

Her eyes and cheeks began to burn fiercely. “Oh, same! You’ve killed me!” she cried out. “It’s all right, it’s all right. I’m sorry!” I said, and dashed off at once to wash my hands thoroughly. Then, with a damp towel, I gently dabbed her eyes and cheeks, and even applied a little of the snow I use on my own cheeks.

Watching all this, my mother was caught between laughter and anger—she wanted to laugh, but feared it would make the old lady angry; she wanted to cry, but couldn’t. So she simply glared at me, wide-eyed, and stood there frozen, while the other women watched in stunned silence.

After about a quarter of an hour, having exhausted all the cold treatments I could think of, the old lady’s agitation finally subsided—her eyes and face cooled down. She looked at me and said, “Oh, same! Well, you are a bad boy. You really killed me. You are a very naughty fellow!”
“You’ve done as much as killing me!” she said, bringing a little Hanuman’s face to her own.

Yes, madam! What have I done? So far, you haven’t told me what happened to you, or why you were so frightened, or what mistake I made. If I have done anything wrong, please forgive me—I said humbly. “That’s not it, dear. There’s no fault of yours in this. Out of affection for me, you cheerfully asked me to taste your village pickle. Not fully understanding what you said, as soon as you served me food, you put a piece of bread with a bit of butter and some pickle into my mouth, and my throat caught fire. In that distress, not knowing what to do, I ran into your room, only to see you mixing rice with your hand and eating it. On top of that, when that same hand touched me, I nearly fainted. These customs are unfamiliar to us; just seeing them made me lose my senses. That’s all there is to it. I only scared you for nothing. Don’t take it to heart, forgive me,” she said, and walked out. Her daughters followed her, paused at the doorway, turned back to look at me, gave a single laugh, and ran away.

The next day, when I recounted the pickle incident, the commotion it caused, and the trouble my hostess went through, to Raju under the guise of a story, Raju burst out laughing. Remembering that day’s episode, the two of us laughed heartily together. We also told this story to the lady at Raju’s house. They too laughed to their heart’s content. From then on, Raju went around telling this story to his circle of friends for a whole week, making everyone laugh and filling them with delight.
My lessons are going very well. My teacher heartily congratulated me, saying that I was picking up English very quickly and thoroughly. Raju too was very happy to hear this good news.

Every day, I got into the habit of going to the Indian Association, sitting there for an hour or two, and reading whatever books or magazines I could find. Thus, I would spend my leisure time pleasantly. Gradually, I became acquainted with the other members who came there—not just Telugus, but also Tamils, Malayalis, a couple of Kannadigas, Bengalis, Punjabis, and students from various backgrounds. With so many foreigners around, all of whom were, like me, enjoying themselves on equal footing...
I am always very enthusiastic about talking.

One day, our Raju came to my room and said, “Tomorrow, in this town, there is a lady of high status—a memsahib, the mistress of a grand house, and a learned woman. She looks upon people from our country with great affection. From time to time—perhaps two or three times a year—she invites a few of our people and some of the locals, both young men and women, and hosts a small party for them. She has arranged such a party for tomorrow, and she has sent word asking me to bring you along as well. So, let’s go. Be ready,” he said.
“A party? Is that something like a meeting or a lecture, or is it something else? I’m asking you because I want to know what the customs are here and what exactly happens at such events,” I asked.

“Oh no! There’s no business of meetings, lectures, or any such commotion. It’s just about meeting a few people, chatting leisurely, having tea and snacks, then chatting some more. If there are any singers, sometimes there will be songs. Occasionally, if there’s time, they play indoor games—games you can play inside the house. After that, everyone goes their own way. That’s the custom—nothing more to it,” he explained.

So, wearing our usual dress, with an overcoat on top and a hat on the head, we set out for the place. There, by the door, there was something like a chain attached to the wall. If you pull it, a bell rings inside. Then the butler of the house comes and opens the door. As soon as the door opens, we say, “Good afternoon, Sir,” and remove our overcoats and hats, handing them over for safekeeping. The butler leads us into the hall inside.

There, the lady of the house comes to greet us, extending her hand for a handshake and saying, “How do you do?”—which means, “Are you well and at ease?” Then she takes us around and introduces us to everyone present. After that, as I mentioned earlier, the program begins with conversation.
“Alright, let’s go and see how the festivities are here,” I said, “You’ll be there too, right? Then what is there for me to worry or fear?”
“I’ll come and take you along. But if, for some reason, I can’t make it, you must go to the place yourself…”

chapters.title: Social Life
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

He said, “I’ll write down the address and all the details about how to get there for you. Wait for me until half-past three. If I still haven’t arrived by then, just follow the instructions I’ve written. Don’t worry, you won’t get lost anywhere,” and with that, he wrote everything down on a piece of paper, even drawing a little map for me. Poor fellow. As I was about to leave, he suddenly remembered something important.

“Oh, by the way, I almost forgot to tell you one more thing. As soon as we arrive there, either the servant or the lady of the house, or after the usual greetings, they’ll ask, ‘Would you like to have a wash and brush up?’ That means, if you feel the need to wash your face and hands, comb your hair, or freshen up, you can say yes. If not, just say ‘No, thank you,’ and that’s enough. Don’t forget this—keep it in mind,” he said.
I agreed, set off for home, had dinner, chatted a bit with our landlady about this and that, studied for a while, and then went to bed.

The next day, I finished my meal, studies, and everything else by three o’clock, washed my face and so on, and sat waiting for Raju to arrive. But he didn’t show up. Even half-past three passed. Fearing that if I delayed any longer I might not reach there on time, I put the note Raju had written into my pocket and set out. I took the tram for part of the way, and for the last stretch, I had to walk through a lane as described in the directions.

Without any trouble, and without having to ask anyone, I managed to find the lane. When I was about a furlong from their house, I remembered how, after arriving, they would ask me something, and I would have to go to their bathroom. Thinking there was no need for all that, and since the lane was deserted and dusk was already falling, I relieved myself by the roadside and then proceeded to their house.
I was sure it was the right house, so I pulled the chain. The servant came and opened the door.
After greeting me, he took my coat and hat and hung them on the stand in the hall. As he was leading me inside, Raju hurried in, almost running. The two of us went into the hall together.

The lady of the house, her face beaming with joy, was talking to someone but came over to us, greeted Raju, inquired about his well-being, and then, pointing at me, asked, “Is this gentleman your new friend?” Raju replied yes, introduced me by name.
She looked at me with a gentle smile, a hint of mischief in her eyes, shook my hand, and said, “Very pleased to meet you, Mr. Par... Ba... tisan. How do you do?”

The grandeur of the house, the people there, the beauty and grace of the lady of the house—all of it left me so spellbound that I completely forgot everything Raju had told me earlier. When she said “How do you do?” I was at a loss for words, and blurted out, “As usual, like all people,” and then—

Just as I was about to say something, the lady gave a slight smile, and at the same time, Raju pressed my hand. All this happened simultaneously. Realizing that I had already made some blunder, I thought I should at least be careful from now on. Just then, the lady of the house asked, “Would you like to have a wash?” Out of habit, I was about to put my foot in it again, but then, recalling Raju’s advice just in time, I replied, “No, thank you.” But I didn’t stop there. Since I wasn’t used to telling lies, I added, “I did it at the corner of the street.”
That was it! It was as if a thunderbolt had struck. The lady was dumbfounded. Everyone who had been standing and talking nearby froze on the spot, as if my words had turned them to stone.

A little distance away, the butler suddenly clapped a hand over his mouth as if he were about to vomit and dashed off to the other side. The entire atmosphere seemed to chill and settle into a heavy silence. Oh Lord! What on earth did I say wrong? Why have they all turned to ice? I trembled, my eyes filled with tears, and I looked around, blinking in confusion.

The hostess was the first to recover. She quickly regained her composure, glanced at everyone, and with a gentle smile, revived the spirits of the room. “Very good, Mr. — Mr. Same, very good! Come along,” she said, introducing me to everyone there with Raju’s help. In a few moments, everyone returned to their usual manner. But my fear did not leave me. Somehow, I sat through until the refreshments were served. Then, seizing an opportunity, I said, “I have some studying to do. I’ll take my leave now.”
“It’s quite dark outside. Can you go alone, or shall I come to help you?” Raju asked.
“Oh, there’s no need! I’ll go slowly by myself. It’s all right,” I replied, and made my way out, returning to my lodgings.

When I got home, my wife asked what interesting things had happened there. Distracted, I replied that there was nothing special, and picked up a book. Sensing that my mind was not at ease, she quietly left me alone. I realized that I had done something improper at the gathering, though I still didn’t know exactly what it was. Poor Raju seemed to feel very sorry, as if it were his own fault. Well, what could be done? I tried to study, but my mind kept wandering, thinking about the incident.

I sat there for quite some time. As I was thinking that I should go to bed, Raju arrived right on cue. The moment he came in, he exclaimed, “Oh, great man! Parvatisham, you’ve landed yourself in a fine mess! I advised you in every possible way, but in the end, what have you gone and done?”

I, meanwhile, had been so absorbed in observing the scenes there—the cleanliness of the house, the arrangements, the graceful features and mannerisms of the lady of the house—that I had forgotten everything you had told me. Honestly, to this moment, I still don’t know exactly what mistake I made, but I do realize it must have been a big one. What can I do? Forgive me, I said.

“It’s all right. They’ve understood that you’re new here, that you’re young, and that you’re not yet familiar with the customs here. So it’s not a big deal. When she asked, ‘Would you like to have a wash?’ and you replied, ‘No, thank you,’ that was fine. But why did you have to go on and say that you relieved yourself by the roadside? Did anyone ask you where or how you did it—whether you stood or sat? Things like that are considered very improper in this society. But nothing disastrous has happened. Don’t worry about it,” Raju said.
“It’s getting late. I’ll be off now. Let’s meet again tomorrow,” he said, and took his leave.
So, that was how my very first tea party went—what an amusing affair! I laughed to myself as I lay down on the bed.

By the next morning, I had already forgotten all about the previous night’s events. By the time I had finished my morning ablutions, instead of the lady of the house (Mrs. Thompson), it was her younger daughter who was setting my breakfast on the table. I wondered what this was about. That girl, too, glanced at me shyly, lowered her head, and with a small smile said, “Good morning, Mr. Sam. My mother is feeling a bit lazy today, so I’ve brought your breakfast. I hope you don’t mind.” I laughed and replied, “Oh, silly girl, what is there to mind about this? I’m very happy—not because your mother is feeling lazy, but because you brought it!”
She responded, “Why should you be happy just because I brought it?”
Barrister Parvateesam
As if they didn’t know.

“Oh, nothing of the sort! You and your sister both—when you see me, you act all timid and keep your distance. That feels rather strange to me. We’re all young people here, aren’t we? I don’t like it at all when you behave as if you’re scared of me and keep to yourselves,” I said.

“It’s nothing like that for us. We just thought, if we keep talking to you often, you might wonder why we’re being so forward. That’s why we’ve been a little hesitant. Even our mother warned us to be a bit careful. That’s all there is to it,” she replied.
After that, she left.

After I finished my breakfast, Appagaru came back with her younger sister, both of them beaming, and greeted me with a cheerful “Good morning! How are you? Did you sleep well last night?” thus beginning the conversation.

“Please, have a seat. Why are you standing?” I said, pointing to a chair. Meanwhile, the younger sister took away the breakfast dishes from the table, put them away inside, and came back. She wiped the table, set it straight, and then stood there, looking uncertain, as if wondering whether to stay or leave. “If you’re not in a hurry, why don’t you sit down too?” I said. I noticed Appagaru signaling her with her eyes to sit down.
“Don’t you go out anywhere these days?” the younger girl asked.
“Not just yet. I’ll stay in for now. Please, sit,” I replied.
Both of them began to converse with me quite comfortably.
“How is your house, sir?” asked the elder girl.
“It’s very nice. And your house—your family too!” I replied.
“Oh!” she said, laughing.
“Are you getting all the facilities you need? You’re not having any trouble here, are you?” she asked again.

“Oh, everything is fine. No trouble at all. It’s very comfortable. Only, now and then, when there’s nothing to do and I’m alone, memories of my hometown and my house come to mind. At those times, my heart feels a little unsettled,” I said.
“Then why didn’t you ever mention it before? If you’d told us, we could have come and sat with you—”
We were just sitting around, chatting about this and that. “At least it would have kept you entertained and free from boredom!” said the younger girl.

“If you ever have some free time, or if you feel like it, we’ll take you out to see the town, or maybe even to the picture house, if you’d like,” the elder girl added, her shyness finally melting away.
“Oh, so that’s their game!” I thought to myself. If I get too friendly with them, they’ll end up sitting here all day long. My studies will be left hanging in the balance, I realized.

“Alright, that sounds lovely. We’ll definitely go, as soon as you’re free. But until my exams are over, I’ll have to be a bit careful with my time,” I replied. I hoped that would be enough to send them on their way. But there was no sign of them getting up to leave.
“Where did you go yesterday evening? Was it to a picture?” asked the elder girl.
“No picture, no nothing. I went to a party. Someone invited me, and my friend took me along,” I said.
“To a party? Oh my, what a sly fellow! And you didn’t even tell us!” exclaimed the younger girl, her eyes wide with mock accusation.
“Why didn’t you ask me then? If you had, I would have told you right away,” I replied, laughing. Just then, the elder girl pleaded, “So what happened there? Any interesting stories? Tell us, please!”

What was there to tell? Everything was new to me—the people, the customs, all of it. So, naturally, I made a couple of blunders. I did a few things I shouldn’t have, and, not knowing better, I said a few things one ought not say at a party. But the lady of the house, who had invited us, was very gracious. She smoothed things over as if nothing had happened and put me at ease. The others, too, spoke to me in a friendly, relaxed manner.
“Oh, so much happened, did it? If we had been there, we would have told you everything in advance, and you wouldn’t have had any such troubles!” said the elder girl, laughing.
“It’s true—if you had been there, I wouldn’t have had to do that business in the street,” I thought to myself.
“At least tell us what actually happened. Is it right to be so embarrassed over a small mistake? Come on, tell us what really happened,” she coaxed sweetly.
“As if the humiliation I suffered there wasn’t enough, must I recount it to you as well?” I replied.
“You must! We want to hear your blunder for our amusement,” she said, pulling her chair closer with a mischievous smile.
What could I do? What is this childish commotion? I sat in silence for a moment, thinking.
“There’s no need to be so shy, brother. Just tell us, it’s all right,” the younger girl chimed in again.

Oh, what a predicament! If I don’t tell them, they won’t let me be; if I do, I’ll never live it down. With a sigh, I began, hesitantly and with my head bowed, to narrate the entire saga—from the moment I left home to the moment I returned.

Both of them burst into uncontrollable laughter. I had never heard them laugh so heartily before. While they rocked with laughter, mother arrived and knocked on the door. I quickly went and opened it. The girls seemed not to have heard the knock, nor noticed me opening the door. The two sisters were still doubled over, tears of mirth streaming down their cheeks, laughing as if the world itself were shaking with their joy.

Mother, seeing them, smiled gently and said, “What’s this, girls? Have you lost your senses? Did your brother tell you some stories?” she asked, pulling both girls up by their ears. “Do you have any sense at all? How can you behave so rudely in front of your elder brother?” she scolded, her tone tinged with annoyance.

“Oh mother, mother!” the girls cried, wriggling free from her grasp and running away, still laughing. Mother, too, smiled and said to me, “What wonderful stories you must have told, for my children to laugh so much!”
She said, “Please don’t mind their behavior, they’re just children. I’ll scold them myself,” and went outside.

Poor you, you got up and came all the way here. They said you’re lazy in the kitchen. I asked, “How are your girls?” “Oh, nothing much, just the usual. Some aches and pains, you know, growing up! There’s a lot of work, but since both of them are here, it’s manageable. Other than eating, sitting around, and roaming the whole town, they hardly help me with any work!” she said, and left.

For a moment, I wondered if their mother had overheard what they were saying, or if she was suspicious about what the girls were up to here all this time. But then I thought, “Why should I bother? Compared to Josie, these girls are as lively as squirrels.” I considered reading something, so I reached for a book, but just then, a loud noise came from the kitchen.
Curious about what it was, I ran over and knocked on the door.

chapters.title: Indian Friends
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

With a face streaked with tears—though I could not tell whether she was laughing or crying—the old lady came, opened the door, saw me, composed herself, and suddenly embraced me, exclaiming, “Oh! Mr. Sam, Sam!”

The two children, who had been laughing until then, stopped as abruptly as a gramophone record screeching to a halt. They pressed their lips together, stifled their laughter with great effort, and stood up straight.

“So much has happened, Mr. Sam. If only you had told us beforehand that you were going to a party with us, I could have given you some advice! Still, it’s all right, don’t worry about it,” she said, releasing me from her embrace and patting me on the back.

“I’m not thinking anything of it,” I said, and without another word, hurried into my room. I collapsed onto the sofa, realizing that those little imps must have recounted everything I had said, adding their own spices and garnishes. The three of them were laughing together, I thought.
Just then, all three of them came back and said, “Mr. Sam, please forgive our foolish behavior. It was a mistake to laugh like that. Please don’t take it to heart.” They apologized.
“I haven’t taken it to heart at all, so there’s no need for apologies,” I replied.

“Thank you,” they said, bowing their heads and leaving quietly. I thought to myself, “It was a mistake to tell them anything at all. As far as they know, they’ll broadcast it to all their friends. But so what? What’s lost is lost!” I chuckled to myself.

Though at first I had been a bit angry with them, seeing the mother and children pulling such silly faces, looking at me with fear—especially that little one—by the time they apologized, I felt sorry for them. After they left, as I replayed the whole episode in my mind, I realized—what fault is there in them? I was the one who made the mistake. Anyone who heard what happened would laugh. How could they not? Now, with time to spare...

When I think about it quietly, I can’t help but laugh at myself! A lack of intelligence is simply a lack of intelligence. But then, if someone calls you dull-witted, or even just thinks it, what’s the use in feeling hurt or bearing a grudge against them? Isn’t that just another kind of foolishness?

So, from the bottom of my heart, I forgave them. No matter what they say about my lack of brains, when I look at their silly faces, I can’t help but feel a mix of pity and amusement. Isn’t that a curious thing?

Trying to put all that behind me, I resolved to return to my studies. But just as I was about to begin, thoughts of home crept in again. How is my mother doing? How much must she be worrying about me? Even though my father is strict, surely he has a deep affection for me inside. But he never lets it show. Even now, instead of comforting my mother with kind words and easing her worries, is he making her even more anxious by scolding her?

What can I do about it from here? Did my letters reach them or not? But how could they not? This isn’t India, after all, where letters, telegrams, and money orders might go missing! Then why hasn’t Father written back? All this time I’ve been here, not a single reply from him—why is that? If I don’t hear from home, how am I supposed to survive? Will I end up abandoning my studies and heading home, empty-handed? Oh Lord, would that not be the most ridiculous fate for my life? Perhaps I should send a telegram? But that would cost a fortune! What am I to do now? Lost in these thoughts, I sat there, book in hand.

I don’t know how long I sat like that, but suddenly there was a knock at the door. I started, and called out, “Come in.” Slowly, Mrs. Thomson entered, opening the door gently. What could she want this time? I wondered.
With a gentle smile, she said, “You have a letter, Mr. Semgar! Perhaps it’s from your home,” and handed me the letter before leaving quietly.
The moment I took the letter in my hand, I knew it was from home. For some reason, a tremor ran through me. Tears welled up in my eyes. Was it from happiness, or...

I do not know whether it was sorrow or something else. For two or three minutes, I could not bring myself to open the letter. At last, somehow, I gathered my courage and opened it. The moment I saw my father’s familiar handwriting, it felt as if life itself had returned to me.

As I read the letter, the fears and doubts that had haunted me since I first set out began to melt away. His words, filled with compassion, felt so soothing to my eyes, and a flood of emotions—joy, surprise, and more—rose up all at once, overwhelming me.

Nowhere in the letter could I find even a trace of my father’s usual sternness, not in a single line or letter. Perhaps, the farther people are from you, the more their affection grows! Every line he wrote was filled with such warmth! Reading about the pain my mother was enduring, and how helpless he felt at not being able to comfort her, brought me such sorrow that I cannot express it. Instantly, I felt like throwing my books aside, bidding farewell to my studies, sprouting wings, and flying home.

Somehow, I managed to finish reading the letter. Tears welled up and overflowed like a Godavari flood. No matter how hard I tried, I could not stop them. There was no one to say, “My boy, why are you so upset? Why are you grieving like this?” Nor was there anyone to advise, “You shouldn’t be so troubled by this. Just write a reply to your father and that will suffice.” On the contrary, if anyone heard of all this, they would only laugh—so I thought, and read the letter again from beginning to end. This time, I was able to read it without so much pain. Like this, I read it five times over, and with each reading, the initial agitation and sadness faded, giving way to calm. After all, everything my father wrote was true and natural! I had set out knowing they would be distressed! What sense was there in feeling so miserable now?

Slowly, I resolved to write a long letter to my father. With that thought, I sat there for a long time, letter in hand, lost in reverie. Our house, my mother, my father, our fields—everything began to parade before my eyes like the pictures I had once seen in a London cinema. Lost in that whirl of images, I was startled back to reality by a knock at the door.

“Come in, please,” I said. The lady of the house entered with a cup of tea in her hand, smiling, and placed it on my table. Unlike usual, she did not leave immediately; instead, she pulled a chair close to me and sat down.

“What’s the matter, Mr. Same?” she began. “Did you leave the letter at your house? Are your mother and father well? Did they write asking you to come home? Did the letter upset you in any way? I guessed that something of the sort might have happened, so I brought you a cup of tea, thinking it might calm you down a little. First, take this, and then we’ll talk,” she insisted.

Unable to refuse her, I wondered how she had guessed all this. She’s not my own, after all—I’ve come from somewhere else, a foreigner in this land. Why does she have so much affection for me? Perhaps, being a mother herself, she could understand my mother’s pain. Thinking thus, I accepted the tea, drank it, and placed the cup back on the table. I thought she would take the cup and leave, but she did not.

“Why are you just sitting there silently?” she said. “Are all your people at home well? Is your mother keeping well? Poor thing, she must be terribly anxious about you! That’s only natural, isn’t it? I can understand her pain, at least to some extent. You know, it’s always a bit easier when you’re at home. After all, you are her own flesh and blood—how many children does she have, anyway?”

With that, I was once again overcome with sorrow. Gathering myself for a moment, with a choked voice I said, “I have no one else, madam. I am the only one for my mother and father—just me. There is no one else. They have no other children. No one to comfort them. The one who should be with them, I am stranded here, so far away. My mother cannot bear this separation, madam. I—I—I…” Unable to say anything more, I broke down and wept like a child.

She immediately sprang up, came over to my chair, stood beside me, drew me to her heart, stroked my head, and said, “Don’t be so distressed, Mr. Same! You mustn’t worry. There’s nothing to fear. Perhaps you’re eager to rush back home! Don’t do that. All the money you’ve spent so far would be as good as thrown into the sea. Write a long letter home, saying you are safe and well here, that you lack for nothing, and they shouldn’t worry. Back home, don’t you go to the neighboring town for higher studies, since they aren’t available in your village? Don’t you? Does your mother leave house and hearth to follow you even there? This is just a little farther, that’s all—there’s no more danger or difficulty here than there. Write and tell them so. In a few months, they’ll get used to this separation and become courageous.”

Her words, spoken with such sympathy, fell upon my ears like a shower of nectar and brought great comfort to my heart. Then she let me go and said, “If you are brave, they too will find courage. Now promise me you won’t worry anymore. I’ll take my leave now—otherwise, you’ll be late for your meal again.” With that, she quietly left the room.

Oh! How much compassion this lady, a complete stranger, has shown me! When hardship strikes, all humans are one, aren’t they? Perhaps this spirit of humanity is even stronger in women! Thinking thus, I sat there for a while, lost in thought.

chapters.title: Raju's Absence
paragraphs: Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 213

Of late, Raju had completely stopped showing up. I had no idea why. I wondered if he was angry with me for some reason. But I couldn’t think of anything that would have made him upset. I myself was so busy with my studies that I barely had time to breathe here, let alone go visiting. My lessons were going exceedingly well. The private tutor took a special liking to me and showed great attention, teaching me with care. There was a marked difference between his method and the way things were done back home. Every point he explained, he did so in such a way that, even with my limited grasp of the language, I could understand it easily. Realizing that I was making an effort to comprehend and retain what he taught, he was very pleased. My studies, and the progress I was making in them, gave me immense satisfaction.
One day, having nothing in particular to do, I went over to see Raju. He was just about to head out somewhere.
“Hey, what’s this? You’ve come at last! Where have you been all this time? Have you already forgotten me? Or have you found someone to help you forget?” he said, laughing.

“I haven’t had a moment to spare to go around collecting such people! My studies alone are more than enough for me. What about you? Why did you stop coming? I just came to see how you were, since I hadn’t heard from you in so long,” I replied.

He laughed and said, “Believe it or not, I was just about to set out to visit you myself. Wager as much as you like! I too had a few exams and such lately, so I couldn’t make it. Only yesterday did I finish everything. That’s why I was planning to come see you now. Well, since you’re here, let’s have a nice lunch somewhere and then wander about the town until evening. We’ll shake off our weariness and find some fresh enthusiasm. Have you been going out anywhere lately? Seen any pictures or anything?”
He asked as we stepped outside.
“Nothing at all. Haven’t gone anywhere. There’s only one thing of note that happened…”
“That’s a letter from my home,” I said.
“Oh, what’s the news? Are your mother and father keeping well?” he asked, placing a comforting hand on my shoulder.

“They’re doing well,” I began, and proceeded to narrate the entire saga of the day the letter arrived—my wife’s display of affection, the words of consolation she spoke. “My father wrote sternly, asking me to come home. I was at a loss for what to do, so I thought I’d run to you for advice. But I managed to muster some courage from what our landlady said, and I’ve already written another letter home,” I finished.

“You did the right thing. After coming all this way, enduring so much hardship, showing such courage, and spending so much money, it wouldn’t be wise to return without seeing or learning anything. In fact, it would be quite laughable. Besides, we go around talking about lofty ideals and grand ambitions, things beyond our years, and then if you go running home in tears for your mother, all your ideals will be for nothing. You’ll just become one among hundreds of millions of ordinary Indians. Writing back that you’re not coming was the best thing you could do. I congratulate you. Now let’s forget all this. Let’s have lunch and go to a picture house,” said Raju.
“What’s this, man? A picture house now? Like Ankammasivam’s midnight rituals, you want to go to a cinema in broad daylight? What’s so great about that?” I protested.
“It’s perfectly fine! Why wouldn’t it be? I’ll make you see for yourself how enjoyable it is,” he said, brimming with the confidence of a man making a wager, and dragged me along.

“Have you forgotten, my friend, that in this country, picture shows run continuously from 2 in the afternoon till 10 at night? So we can watch a movie comfortably and enjoy ourselves,” he explained, steering us into a small restaurant across the street.
There, as per the usual custom, a waiter welcomed us...

Standing there, being seated at an empty table, having the dishes we wanted brought and arranged before us, and then making those dishes disappear as if by magic, all happened in a matter of moments. We rose, paid the bill, tipped the waiter as usual, and dashed off to the picture house nearby on the same street.

Well, the picture was amusing, lively, and quite good—why deny it! But if you ask whether there was anything particularly noteworthy, it was this: they showed scenes from various sports competitions happening somewhere—badminton (which, in this country, they call shuttlecock), then tennis, cricket, and so on. The images were truly rousing.

After we came out, I bombarded Raju with countless questions about the sports here. He answered everything with great patience, saying, “Why should I explain all this fuss to you? I’ll show you some of these sports in person right here. Anyway, it’s only four, four-thirty now, isn’t it? It doesn’t get dark until nine at night. I forgot to mention—you can watch these amusements till then. You must have figured it out by now: in the summers here, it doesn’t get dark until nine or ten at night. Until then, you can even sit outside and read. There’s that much daylight. And then, at three in the morning, dawn breaks again.

When the season changes, the sun’s influence gradually wanes, and he rises only at nine in the morning, then sets again by three in the afternoon. In winter, in northern Russia and Siberia, it’s even stranger. They have only two seasons in a year. In each of those seasons, for six months there’s twenty-four hours of daylight, and for the other six, twenty-four hours of darkness.”
At this point, I was dumbfounded and asked, “So, do those people stay awake for six months and sleep for the next six?”

He laughed and replied, “Oh no, nothing like that! They’re just like us. During the days of light, they work during working hours and sleep during sleeping hours. And during the dark nights, they sleep when it’s time to sleep and work when it’s time to work.”
“Ah, so their houses aren’t made of gold after all!” I said. We then quietly...

We quietly made our way out of the village. There, we found something like a small club. Anyone could pay a little money and play tennis with their friends. The tennis courts there were very beautiful and of two kinds. Some courts were just like the ones in our country. The others were covered with closely-cropped, lush green grass. That looked especially lovely to me. I wondered how the ball would bounce on such a surface, so I asked Raju.
“Just watch and see whether it bounces or not,” he replied.

Soon, two women and two men arrived and began to play. The ball bounced quite normally. On this kind of court, the ball doesn’t bounce as much as it does on the regular courts. Even if you hit it a bit harder—
...have to be beaten. There’s no other difference,” said Raju.

There, a cricket match was underway. I had only ever heard or read the name “cricket” before, but never actually watched the game. I sat there for over half an hour, observing. To me, it all seemed rather comical. One fellow throws a ball, another stands with a bat and hits it, while ten others stand around like statues, making every possible effort to catch the flying ball—what sort of game is this, I wondered!

It reminded me of the “Kunda Batti” game we used to play in my village during the Sankranti festival when I was a child. At best, you could say this was a more elegant and delicate version of that. Still, I couldn’t see what kind of exercise or excitement it offered to the players or the spectators. With such thoughts, we continued to sit and watch for over half an hour.

“When there’s a match here, you should see the fun! The spectators go wild, shouting and cheering. From that, you’ll understand just how much the public adores this game,” said Raju, gently leading me outside as he spoke.

From there, we took a tram to the outskirts of town, to a hill called, I believe, “Braidhills.” Atop the hill was a small club of sorts. The land there was partly level, partly elevated, and then sloped down again, spreading out in all directions. The entire area was covered in short grass. There, just like a tennis court, a net had been set up.
“We must watch a funny game here. It hasn’t yet taken root in our country,” said Raju. We went up to the club, took a look around, and then continued on our way.
Ahead of us, people were walking—some alone, some in pairs—each holding a peculiar stick in their hands. Behind each of them, a young boy followed, carrying a bag full of various such sticks.
