“That’s called golf, Parvatisham. Just wait and watch the fun,” said Raju, as right then, a gentleman ahead of us placed a small white ball on the ground...

He placed the ball on the ground and, aiming carefully with a stick that looked like a walking cane, struck it. Wherever the ball landed, he would spot it with great attention, and both he and the boy carrying the bundle of sticks would walk over to that spot. Upon reaching it, he would strike the ball again, and once it had rolled further ahead, yet another group of people would begin at the original spot. The two of us followed them, keeping a little to the left.

After the first man had struck the ball two or three times, he reached a small, square-shaped area. With great skill, he hit the ball so that it fell into a hole in the center of that spot. Apparently, there are eighteen such holes. The whole game consists of hitting the ball into each of these holes in turn. One can play alone, or as many people as desired can play together. They even hold competitions for this game. The winner is the one who manages to get the ball into all eighteen holes with the fewest number of strokes.

In this game too, just like in tennis, both men and women can play together. But what beauty there is in this game, why people play it—I could not, for the life of me, understand. To me, it seemed like the sort of game that people weighed down by sorrow might play to lighten their burden of grief. When I said this, Raju burst out laughing. “You get some brilliant ideas, don’t you!” he said.

From there, we strolled back into town and went to another club. In four or five rooms there, there were large tables. On top of them, a cloth like velvet was either glued or stitched on. At each of the four corners of the table, there were holes, and underneath each hole, nets were attached. On the table, a ball made of ivory was placed, and with a long stick with a pointed end, they would strike it. There was another red ball and another white ball on the table. The player’s own ball was also white. For quite some time, I couldn’t make head or tail of this game. But after I learned the rules, it struck me as a beautiful game, one that required great skill and keen observation. Even though there was nothing particularly thrilling or exciting about it, I couldn’t bring myself to leave. We watched for about an hour and then slowly made our way home.

From there, we went to another hill on the other side of town. It was more or less in the middle of the town, and not too far away. Later, I learned it was quite close to where we were staying. Here, there was a large crowd—many people, both men and women, who had come for recreation. Most of them were young men and women. Couples, in pairs, each to their own tree’s shade or behind a mound, sat huddled together, so absorbed in each other that it seemed as if they had forgotten the world above. A little distance away, our own group—about ten or twelve of us, all Telugu people—were sitting together, chatting loudly. By the time we both reached there, they all welcomed us with great cheer. For a while, we exchanged all sorts of stories and gossip. In the midst of this, one of them said, “Why don’t we all play chedugudi or uppattiga here?” Another chimed in, “What a great idea! Let’s play both!”

chapters.title: Growing Fame
paragraphs: At the mention of “Barrister Parvatishan,” everyone immediately sprang to their feet with enthusiasm.

We split ourselves into two teams—one for “Chedugudu” and the other for “Uppatti”—and set about playing. Within two minutes, a dozen or fifteen locals from the surrounding area had gathered. In another couple of minutes, another twenty-five or thirty people came running from who knows where. Five minutes later, more than a hundred young men and women, abandoning their romantic pursuits, flocked around us. Seeing such a crowd, our spirits soared, and we played our games with even greater gusto.

By chance, I ended up as the captain of the Chedugudu team. Since I’d been used to this game from my childhood, I played with confidence. The spectators clapped and cheered, shouting “Hurray! Hurray!” and encouraging us. As soon as the game ended, some of them came up to me, praised me, shook my hand, and bombarded me with questions: “How do you play this game? What are its rules?” They wouldn’t let me go until I explained in detail both Chedugudu and Uppatti. “Will you let us play with you tomorrow?” they asked, a little hesitantly.

“Of course! Come, let’s play together tomorrow. After all, games and songs know no barriers of race or religion,” I replied, feeling rather grand. They all left, delighted, each going their own way, and we went ours. I walked on, feeling as though I had imparted something great about our country to them, my gait solemn with pride. Our Raja clapped me on the back and congratulated me heartily.

You must believe me when I say that for the past month, I haven’t had a moment’s peace. You might think I’ve been out on picnics, playing cards with friends, or arguing and debating! Nothing of the sort, my friend—exams! The entrance exam loomed over us like a dark, menacing cloud, threatening to burst at any moment. Terrified, I clung to my books and chair, not knowing whether I had eaten or not, or even what I had eaten—like a newly widowed woman lost in confusion...
Without so much as glancing at the street or even noticing if a cyclone had swept through, I kept my eyes glued to my books and studied with a single-minded intensity.

Our landlady and her daughters, observing my resolve and persistence, grew quite anxious about what might become of me. The landlady herself came to me four or five times, urging me with great affection to take some rest, warning that such excessive dedication was not good, that it might harm my health, and that I might not even be able to appear for the exams if I fell ill.

Her daughters too joined in, especially the second one—a real mischief-maker. She would boldly enter my room at all hours, without so much as a knock, and sit there even if I paid her no attention. She would leaf through this book and that, giggling to herself as if she found something amusing, or pretending to be frightened by some news in the paper, or making a racket by dropping a book or something else to the floor. Then, with a dramatic “Oh sorry, Sam! I must be disturbing your studies and breaking your concentration. Please forgive me,” she would apologize.
I would feel my blood boil and say, “Would you please go away for a while? Go see what your mother wants. What business do you have here with me, for heaven’s sake?”

Instead of getting angry, the girl would burst out laughing and leave cheerfully. After this happened four times, and with only four or five days left before the exams, when I was in the thick of my preparations, this girl came in again and began her usual mischief. I tolerated it for a long while, but I simply could not get through even a single line. Tell me, how can anyone keep their mind on their books when a girl comes in and sits there making mischief? Even some of our great sages, in such circumstances, lost their focus on their penance!

I was absolutely furious. I felt like grabbing a stick and giving her a good whack. Controlling my anger and my amusement, I caught her by the arm and pulled her up, intending to throw her out of the room.

She was a little frightened, trembling slightly. “Sorry, Mr. Sam! Please don’t hit me. Let me go, I promise I’ll never come like this again. I only came to make sure your health wasn’t suffering and to give you a little break, not for any other bad reason. Believe me. I’m leaving now.”
She turned back, saying, “Let it be.” In her last words, there was a slight tremble in her voice, and tears welled up in her eyes—like the wind scattering the clouds, my anger vanished in an instant.

As I was about to step forward to leave, she caught hold of both my shoulders, turned me around, and said, “I am sorry, dear,” planting a quick kiss on my cheek. Seeing her tears, I was filled with pity. I don’t know what was going on in her mind, but the girl who I thought would leave stood right there, wiping her tears, looking at me with a faint smile.

Oh dear, this treatment seems dangerous, I thought. Pretending to have a headache, I slowly walked towards the door, led her to the threshold, and, fearing she might come back in again, quickly shut the door and locked it. Poor thing, perhaps it’s her nature—she didn’t come back. I thought she might return to bring some food, or perhaps fruits after dinner, but for some reason, she didn’t.

Now, forgetting all about her, I returned to my studies and managed to complete all that I had to read. On the last day, my friend Raju pleaded with me to let him come along, so I went to the examination hall with him.
For the first three days of the exam, I was a little nervous, but then grew confident.

Carefully and without a doubt, I wrote all the papers as best as I could. Like escaping the jaws of a tiger, on the third evening, I finally emerged, returned home in a single bound, and as I entered my room, I called out, “Dhamsanamma garu! Please bring urgent tea and snacks—enough for ten people!”
She was startled. “What’s the matter?” she asked.
“Oh, nothing at all! I’m simply starving. You know, for the past month I’ve been fasting, barely drinking even plain water!” I replied.
“How could I not know, dear? Of course I’ve noticed. But no matter how much you claim to have fasted, the bill I’m about to give you in a little while will prove the truth,” she said, laughing.

Both the children burst into laughter—not in turns, but all at once. I went into my room, sat for about five minutes, then headed to the bathroom, washed my face, and by the time I returned, both the girls were standing by my table, having set out snacks on plates for three people.
“What’s this? Why three plates?” I asked.
“You asked for enough for ten people, didn’t you? But only three are ready, so our mother sent these and told us to bring them,” they replied.
“All right then, go ahead,” I said.
“We’ll go, but since you can’t possibly finish all these by yourself, our mother sent us to help you out,” they said.
“Such terribly mischievous children you are!” I said, pretending to be annoyed. “Well then, please do help.”

They picked up the plates of snacks and were about to leave when I said, “So far you’ve listened to your mother, like sensible children. Now, listen to me for a change: in ten minutes, both of you should get dressed and ready, and then, each of you take an arm and escort me to the cinema.”
“Oh dear! That’s impossible for us!” the younger girl exclaimed.
“I know it’s impossible for you. I also know exactly what happens when you try. That’s why, for everyone’s safety, I’m inviting your elder sister to come along as well,” I said.

chapters.title: Edinburgh
paragraphs: “Alright then, I’ll be ready in just half an hour,” said the elder girl, disappearing inside. The younger one immediately followed her, but paused at the door, turned back for a moment, and with a sly grin said, “My sister says half an hour just for the sake of conversation, but rest assured, we’ll be ready in an hour at the very least.” She stuck her tongue out at me in mockery, and as I made to stand up, she darted into the kitchen on one foot.

Not even a week had passed when our exam results were announced. Our private tutor, beaming with joy and surprise, congratulated me heartily, embracing me with a wide smile as he told me I had passed with a second class. I expressed my gratitude with all due humility, served him a little tea and some snacks, and sent him off. He left in high spirits. “Will I see you again?” he asked. “Certainly,” I replied. “Your job isn’t done yet. You’ll have to help me get admitted to the university, and even after that, you’ll have to guide me for a while until I find my footing.” “Sure, sure!” he laughed, and took his leave.

Upon arriving in Edinburgh, I learned that there was an Indian Association in the city, and visited it on my very first day. However, I didn’t go again for some time. Recently, I took Raju along and went there once more. Raju advised me to become a member, and I agreed. The Association seemed quite a substantial establishment. There were about 100 to 150 members, hailing from all corners of our country. Every day, students would come here—either on their way to the university, or in the evenings after classes, or during breaks between lectures—to sit and chat, read books from the library, or peruse newspapers. Among them, there were about thirty to thirty-five Telugu fellows alone. With so many of our own people around...

Until recently, it seems, they were never members here. This whole business, like a passing craze, suddenly inspired all our Telugu folks with the urge to come here and study at least once in their lives, and so quite a few have managed to make their way here. For passing the time, this library is the only option—there are no other arrangements for games or music or any such amusements. However, from time to time, they do organize lectures by inviting people from our country, from their country, by great poets and scholars.

Once, in this very manner, they invited a gentleman who had served as a district collector in our country, and later as a member of some revenue board, and who had retired from service. They had him deliver a lecture. For some reason, nobody liked his speech. He still seemed unable to let go of the notion that he was a collector, that he was superior to ordinary mortals, a sense of status and self-importance that should have been shed upon retirement, but which he clearly could not relinquish. He failed to realize that here, his status and his former grandeur held no sway, that here everyone was equal, and that among those present, some might, within a few months or a couple of years, attain positions as high or even higher than the ones he had held. It was rather unfortunate that he could not grasp this. After finishing his speech, he seemed to realize that he had failed to win over the audience. The vote of thanks at the end was performed with the barest formality. When he left, only the president, the secretary, and one other person from our association shook his hand and accompanied him as far as the taxi.

So that’s how that went. About a month later, from our country, a great poetess by the name of Mrs. Sarojini Devi came to our association and gave a lecture. I had never heard of her before, though I was told she was such a renowned poetess, and that she had written many books not in our language, mind you, but in English. Her deep, resonant voice, her manner of lecturing, and above all, the poetry she recited—all these captivated us completely. For nearly two hours, we sat as silent as stone statues, not a whisper or a rustle to be heard, listening and delighting in her words.

After the meeting, Sarojini Devi came up to each one of us, shook our hands, asked where we were from, what we were studying, and so on, all the while laughing, tossing out witty remarks, and spent another half hour with us.
Barrister Parvateesam

As we were about to leave after spending some time, all the young men there too came out onto the street, helped the lady into the car, and sent her off with thunderous applause and shouts of victory.

After that, once, the famous Irish poet W. B. Yeats visited. He delivered a lecture for about forty-five minutes on modern poetic forms and also read out some of his own compositions. What he said, the way he said it, and the uniqueness of his poetry—how much of it was understood by the audience, I cannot say, but we listened to his lecture with great attention. He spoke of many profound matters. We all came away with the impression that he was indeed a great poet.

Some time later, another curious meeting took place. Dr. Ananda Coomaraswamy, a distinguished gentleman—though not exactly from our country, but a resident of Ceylon—came with his wife and delivered a lecture on Indian painting, sculpture, and the finer aspects of art. The amusing part was that he brought with him a little box-like device called a "magic lantern." He had a small screen set up right there in the hall, and as he placed each glass plate into the device, images began to appear on the screen, just like in a picture house—various paintings and sculptures came to life before our eyes. As he displayed these, he explained each one in detail, and for about an hour, his lecture captivated me so much that I still cannot forget it. I think it was on that very day that a thirst for beauty awoke within me. Ever since then, my curiosity and eagerness to learn about painting and sculpture have only grown.

After his lecture, his wife—an English lady—performed for a while, demonstrating different styles of Hindustani dance. It was the first time I had ever heard such music or witnessed such dance. I was astonished at how an Englishwoman could attain such mastery in this art. Afterwards, at Dr. Coomaraswamy’s request, our secretary called upon each of us from different provinces to recite one or two beautiful verses in our respective languages. In Bengali, Hindi, Marathi, Malayalam, Punjabi...

The readers were all young men who had come from various regions. Among those from the Telugu region, not a single soul stepped forward to read, no matter how much they were asked, or for whatever reason. The secretary himself was a Telugu man. And who do you think it was? None other than the great Duggiirala Gopalakrishnayya. He sprang to his feet and said, “Look here, so many Telugu people are sitting here, and while all the others from different regions are reciting their poems, is there not a single person among us who can read even a verse, even if it’s just from the Sumati Shatakam, in Telugu? What a shame for us! It’s not that I can’t read, but I wanted to give you all this opportunity first.”
Saying this, he immediately raised his voice and sang a Sanskrit shloka so melodiously and meaningfully that it echoed through the entire hall.

As soon as he finished the shloka, he once again said, “Well, is there really no one? Even now, is there no one who will read?” Then, turning to me, he said, “Parvatisham, you’re new here. Surely you haven’t forgotten your Telugu yet. No matter what, you must get up and read a verse that will make all these people feel ashamed and uphold our honor.” He said this with a disarming smile.
Whether it was enthusiasm or agitation, his words inspired me, and I stood up. It’s true, though, that my legs were trembling a little.

As soon as I woke up, I couldn’t come up with a poem. Gopalakrishnayya noticed this and said, “Well, that’s fine, but it’s up to you. Any poem will do.” At that moment, the words came to me and I recited:

“Softer than lotuses, more beautiful than beauty itself are your feet; like elephants, we plead with you, O our beloved, as we cry out in distress—let us dance and follow you, O Krishna, may your wanderings in this harsh forest not cause heartache to your dear ones.”

For some reason, this verse came to my mind. Though I have no knowledge of music, I recited the poem clearly and simply, and before I could even finish, Gopalakrishnayya, overflowing with joy, exclaimed, “Excellent! Excellent!”

Ananda Kumaraswami smiled gently and asked Gopalakrishnayya, “Where is this poem from, and what does it mean?” Gopalakrishnayya, delighted, replied, “This is from the Bhagavatam. These are the words of the Gopikas when Krishna returns from his wanderings in the forest.” He then translated the meaning into English. By the time he finished, Kumaraswami was very pleased. He stood up and, for five minutes, gave a commentary on the philosophy of Krishna’s incarnation. He then asked if I could recite another poem, and everyone in the gathering turned to look at me.
With enthusiasm and joy, though my heart was pounding, I stood up, a little nervous, and recited another verse from the same episode:
“Your wandering during the day, your playful smiles for your companions—those moments, though fleeting for you, become ages for us…”

This too enraptured Gopalakrishnayya. As soon as he translated it into English, Ananda Kumaraswami was even more delighted. He praised me, saying, “What wonderful verses this young man has recited!” and, elaborating on their meaning, spoke a few more words for another couple of minutes. Afterwards, someone recited in Tamil, and another in Malayalam.

The hall resounded with thunderous applause, and the gathering concluded. Everyone crowded around me to offer their praise. Gopalakrishnayya came, took me by the arm, and led me to Kumaraswami and his wife, introducing me to them. Kumaraswami drew me close, placed his hand on my shoulder, and blessed me.
My joy knew no bounds—I felt as if I might collapse right there.

Somehow, I managed to regain my composure. After steadying myself, I joined everyone else in bidding farewell to the guests, and then returned inside and sat down. All our people gathered around me, saying, “Though you are young, your sense of decorum is truly admirable!” and showered me with praise. I replied that it was only because I was young that I was able to muster such courage. We spent quite some time there, chatting merrily, and then, one by one, everyone set off for their respective homes.

Raju was beside himself with joy. He had sat quietly all this while, but as soon as we stepped outside, he suddenly embraced me tightly and exclaimed, “Well done, Parvateesham! I can’t even express how happy I am. Now, let’s not go back to our lodgings just yet. We must have a meal at a nice hotel here and then go to the picture house!” With that, he dragged me along.

One day, I set out and went to Raju’s place, and together we went to visit our private tutor’s house. The tutor was sitting leisurely at home, reading some book. Upon seeing us, he was delighted, and with great warmth, he invited us to sit down and served us various cakes, biscuits, bread, and other snacks, along with tea.

He began chatting with us in a most relaxed manner. Raju, out of courtesy, said, “I hope we’re not disturbing your work, sir?” The tutor replied, “At the moment, I have no work. Even if I did, if you both came to visit, I would gladly set aside any task to spend some time with you.” Thus, the conversation flowed from one topic to another, until he turned to me and asked, “So, what are your plans now?”

“I have come to you precisely for your advice,” I replied. “The time has come for me to enroll in university, but I have no idea what I should do or what I should study. Only if you guide me onto the right path will I manage. As long as I am here, you must accept the role of my honorary guardian—there’s no escaping it, sir! Even if you wish to refuse, I won’t allow it. Even if you say no, I won’t let go of you,” I declared.

He laughed and said, “Mistake, my boy! Even if you try by any means to escape from me, I will never let you go. You may have managed to run away from your own home, but you won’t so easily slip out of my hands. Don’t even think of making such plans!” And then, still laughing, he said, “Alright then—”
Barrister Parvateesam
“So, what shall we do then? There’s no problem if the patient’s wishes and the doctor’s prescription are one and the same,” I said, laughing.
“Then what do you want to study? How long do you think you’ll be able to stay here?” he asked.

“I want to stay as long as possible. My people back home are terribly worried about me. I am the only child to my parents. They wrote to me, asking me to quit my studies and return home at once, but I didn’t like that idea. I decided to stay here, complete some exam, and only then return. So, you must think and suggest a course that can be finished in two or three years. When I was coming here, the friend who advised me to come suggested that I study for the Bar. Now, if you have any advice, I’d be happy to hear it,” I said.
“Alright, that’s good. For studying the Bar, you’ll have to keep going to London from time to time. So first, enroll here for an M.A.,” he said.
I turned pale and asked, “M.A.? Why M.A.?”
“Yes, of course! What else did you think? Why are you so worried? What do people do in your country after passing the Entrance?” he asked.
“Oh, in our country, there’s enough trouble to last a lifetime for that!” I replied.
At once, he burst out laughing, “What, what, what’s that? Oh my God!”

“It’s nothing, sir, just a saying in our country. In our country, this ‘Entrance’ is called the School Final. After passing that, you have to study Intermediate for two years. Then B.A. for another two years. If you have the patience and the means, M.A. for another two years. In both B.A. and M.A., you must choose your subjects, and the related subjects are introduced right from Intermediate itself,” I explained.
“Ah! That’s quite a hassle! There’s no such trouble here. Once you pass the Entrance, you can join M.A. directly, without any intermediate steps.”

chapters.title: Studies
paragraphs: “That’s all. The studies I’ve described to you are equivalent to your Intermediate course. Therefore, you should join the M.A. program. Now, you must decide whether you want to study Science or Arts. Since you wish to become a barrister, don’t even think about Science. You must choose Arts subjects. In this, you can study various languages and linguistics if you wish. Subjects like History, Politics, Economics, Art, Literature, Philosophy, and so on are closely related. There are twelve subjects in total; you must select them and complete four each year over three years. Then, you will be awarded the M.A. degree,” he said.
“So, that means the exams are only after three years?” I asked.
“That depends on your preference and patience,” he replied.

“In that case, if I study each subject thoroughly, the topics I learn in a given year will be finished within that year, right? Since there’s no need to revisit them, it’s easier to take the exams for those four subjects at the end of each year. Otherwise, if you insist on remembering everything, you can sit for all twelve subjects at the end of the third year. Though that’s a bit more difficult, it’s considered better. That’s called M.A. (Honours). So, you must decide based on your abilities. There’s also the added trouble of the barrister course. Can you handle both? If not, will you sit for the exams each year? Make a decision and go to the university tomorrow or whenever you can. Get an application form there, answer the questions, pay the fees—this is the very first thing you must do. Let me know your decision tomorrow or whenever you’re ready,” he said.

“Alright, sir. I’m very grateful. I’ve troubled you a lot. I promise I’ll keep coming to you with questions and continue to trouble you like this. With that, we took our leave and returned to our lodgings.
Recently, at my house—that is, at our Edinburgh residence—

The whole affair struck me as rather astonishing. Human nature, wherever you find it, seems to behave in much the same way in certain situations. Chief among these, of course, are the habits of cooks and servants.

When I first arrived here, I thought that just as the people’s bodies were so white, their actions too would be pure and spotless. I began to suspect, however, that this was not entirely true—perhaps it was merely my own fanciful imagination. From the very day I set foot in this country—not just in this country, but from the moment I arrived in Edinburgh—I stopped using the bundle of neem sticks I had brought with me, following Raja’s advice. Instead, as an alternative, I went to a local craftsman, spent an hour explaining my needs, and had him make me two silver tongue-scrapers. I kept one safely in a box and used the other daily. After brushing my teeth with paste and brush, I would leave the tongue-scraper in the bathroom.

This went on for some time, until one day, the scraper was nowhere to be found. I searched high and low, but it was gone. I wondered what could have happened to it. That day, I made do with my old neem stick, carefully cleaning it so the landlady wouldn’t see, then chopped it into small pieces and discreetly tossed them into the street.

For two days, there was no news of the missing scraper. At last, I gently asked our landlady about it. She feigned ignorance, claiming she had never seen such a thing before. I described it to her in detail, explaining that it was made of silver and quite valuable. “Silver, sir? Real silver? Oh dear, what a pity! But no one ever comes here,” she exclaimed, feigning surprise.
“I know no one comes here, that’s precisely why I’m asking you,” I replied.
“Oh no, sir, I know nothing about it. I’m not that sort of person. What use would I have for it? In our country, scraping the tongue isn’t a custom,” she said.
“Yes, in your country you don’t scrape your tongue, nor do you wash your face. In your country, it’s not just the face—nothing gets washed at all, does it?” I retorted.
The underlying meaning of my words was lost on the lady of the house.
In any case, I became firmly convinced that she was the one who had made off with it.

“Well, what can we do! Let’s see,” I thought, and tucked it away in my box. I continued to keep the second silver item in the bathroom as usual. One day, when she brought my meal as usual, she casually remarked, “Sir, I think I’ve found the thing you were looking for—it’s right there.”
“Silver and gold shouldn’t go missing, but if they do, who knows when or where they’ll turn up? I’ve already had a new one made,” I replied.
Even after ten or fifteen days, this one too disappeared without a trace.
“This four-legged thing has gone missing again, madam,” I said to her politely.
She acted a little annoyed and said, “What is this, sir! Nothing ever goes missing here except for this one thing of yours? You must have thrown it somewhere yourself.”
“This isn’t something I’d take out into the yard or the street and toss away! It must have gone missing right here,” I said.
“So you’re saying I took it, then?” she retorted angrily. How could I accuse her of that without seeing it with my own eyes! I simply said it had gone missing here.

She seemed quite angry and, with a huff, walked away from me. After that, another suspicion began to creep into my mind. I noticed that the bill for rice and other groceries she bought for me every week kept increasing. Was I eating more than before? I wondered. No matter how much I ate, there was no reason for the bill to rise so much, I thought, and so I brought up the matter with Raju.
“It’s best if we’re a little careful. These landladies have a habit of showing some sleight of hand in such small matters,” he said.
Oh, I thought. What he said was neither a lie nor an exaggeration, as I soon found out in another matter.

Four or five times, Raju sent me some things, and five or six times, I bought some myself—some of our Indian sweets like minapappu laddu, and some cakes and chocolates you get here. I used to bring them and keep them in jars...

I even introduced my housemates to a couple of our country’s traditional dishes once or twice. They seemed to acquire a taste for them. Whenever I brought such things, which would usually last me a week or ten days, they would vanish like camphor in just a day or two. Unable to contain myself, I once asked the landlady, “What’s this, madam? The bottles seem to be getting lighter awfully fast.”

She acted as if she was terribly offended. “If you’re not satisfied with the way we do things or the accommodation here, you’re free to go elsewhere. But it’s not fair to accuse us of such petty thievery,” she said. She even tried to squeeze out a few tears, but failing that, she rubbed her eyes and nose with her handkerchief until they turned red, and then stormed out of my room.

I recounted all these incidents to Vemraju again. He said, “Don’t even think about moving out. Wherever you go, you’ll face the same problems. Here, at least, we’re close to the university. The house is clean. In every other respect, the lady is decent enough. By now, you must have figured out for yourself whether her daughters are good or bad,” he added mischievously.
“Let’s have some fun and teach that old woman a lesson. After this, she’ll never dare do such a thing again in her life,” he said.
“What is it?” I asked.
“I’m not telling you now! You’ll find out soon enough,” he replied.
Two days later, he handed me a neat little packet with my name and a short note on it. “Untie the string and keep this in your room. Then let’s see what happens,” he said.
The packet was a bit heavy. Curious to see what it was, I did as he said. That evening, after our usual stroll, Vemraju and I, along with Raja, came home a little later than usual.

As we entered, we could hear the lady of the house wailing and her daughters trying to console her. Both of us hurried into the kitchen, anxious to know what had happened. The moment she saw me, she began to cry even louder.
“What happened, madam? What’s the matter?” I asked the children.

“It’s nothing, sir. While cleaning and tidying your room, my mother found some sort of box lying there. Not knowing whether to keep it or throw it away, she opened it up. Inside, there was a... a... snake! The moment my mother saw it, she fainted from fright,” the elder daughter recounted the incident, sobbing.
I was dumbfounded and looked at Raju’s face.
With an air of great sympathy and concern, I said to our Parvateesham, “Oh dear, what a terrible mistake has happened! Keep that carefully, my dear, and don’t let anyone touch it.”

“This is a new kind of snake found in this country. It doesn’t exist in our homeland. That’s why I wanted to send it to our college museum. I went through a lot of trouble to acquire it and handed it over to my friend. It seems, in his lack of sense, he left it somewhere within your reach. Anyway, since it’s a dead snake, there’s no need to feel bad even if it’s dead again. We are truly sorry for this mishap. Please don’t take it to heart. Assure your mother that there’s nothing to fear.”
With that, I strode confidently into my room, and the two of us laughed ourselves nearly to death for quite some time.
We all burst out laughing. “Now your precious item has nothing to fear anymore, my friend,” said Raju.
“You’re a good man, truly! What a miraculous treatment you’ve given. In this lifetime, our kitchen will never see this disease again,” I replied.

As it was getting late, Raju took his leave. I, pretending to know nothing, went back into the kitchen, then headed to the landlady’s room where she was lying on her bed. I sat beside her, placed my hand gently on her shoulder, consoled her for quite a while, apologized once more, and as I was about to leave, planted a kiss on her cheek before getting up from the bed. At this, she was filled with a happiness she hadn’t felt in ages; all her anger melted away.

“My dear Sam, you have no idea how frightened I was! I truly thought my life would end right there. For a moment, I even suspected that thing had bitten me. That’s what scared me even more,” she said, dabbing at her eyes again.

“Please don’t worry, madam. I promise never to do such a foolish thing again. I’ll send this thing away from here today itself. If I ever do something like this again, you can throw me out of your house,” I said.

“Oh, no, no, don’t ever say such a thing! Whatever happens, I won’t let you leave. Until you finish your studies, pass your exams, and get your degree, we must all stay together as a family,” she said, hugging me.
“Well, since your anger has subsided, to completely rid you of your fear, I must take you to a picture show now. Please get ready quickly,” I said.
“Our mother never goes out alone, leaving us behind,” said the little girl.

“Yes, that must be true. There’s a small child in this house—what mother would leave her child behind? If you get hungry, who will give you milk?” I teased. At this, the girl looked like she was about to throw something at me, so I quickly ran to the doorway, then took a step back and explained, “When I say ‘mother,’ I mean along with her children.”
“Whatever your opinion is, I have no time for it right now,” she said, pouting. “You—”
“If you don’t make an effort, how will your mother come here leaving you behind? Poor lady! So, at least for her sake, you must put in a little hard work,” I said, cleverly turning the tables.

And so, the day arrived to lay the foundation stone for the grand edifice of my life. Early in the morning, Raju and our private tutor both came to see me off. After offering them some tea, I dressed myself and set out with them.

The university was barely a furlong or two away from our place. Though I had seen those buildings from outside before, seeing them again today filled me with a curious mix of fear and wonder, and I must admit, a slight tremor of nervousness ran through me. My friends led me inside and showed me, one by one, the classrooms, the lecturers’ rooms, the office rooms, the library halls, and the science laboratories. It took more than an hour just to see all these. When I thought of our own village, our schools, the narrow corridors, and the cramped classrooms back home, the comparison was laughable. Where were those, and where were these!

Just sitting in these rooms—no, not rooms, in these grand halls and galleries—made me feel as if knowledge would come to me unbidden. Right next to each classroom was the lecturer’s room for that subject, filled with hundreds of books neatly arranged in cupboards, all relevant to the subject and useful for the lecturers. Before entering the classroom, there was a narrow passageway called a “corridor.” There, an attendant would note down the names of those who arrived in the attendance register. This made it easy for the professor to call roll in class without wasting any time. There were also arrangements for students to leave their overcoats, hats, umbrellas, and such, all neatly organized. Not even a scrap of paper was out of place. In winter, every room was kept warm with steam pipes so that no one would feel cold, and there was nothing to hinder anyone.

After wandering around and seeing everything, we went to the office, collected the application form, and, with the help of our private tutor, filled in all the required details. Then, as instructed, I took the form and went alone to the registrar’s office to submit it. I stood in front of a room, just as our private tutor had told me, and knocked on the door...
I knocked softly. From inside, I heard a “Yes.” But my legs began to tremble, and I couldn’t bring myself to go in immediately.

Then, a little louder, came a “Come in.” Somehow, I mustered up my courage and entered the room. Along both walls, there were tall bookshelves. There were a few sofas and chairs scattered about. Directly opposite me, at the far end, sat an elderly gentleman with a white beard and white hair, wearing spectacles, intently looking at some papers on the table before him. Even after I entered, he didn’t lift his head for a moment. Without looking up, he said, “Sit down.”

Suddenly, my head felt cold, as if I’d been struck by a feverish chill. I stood there, frozen, unable to sit. After another moment, he finally raised his head and looked at me. He didn’t seem to recognize me. Perhaps he thought I was a professor or some other important official from the college. He stared at me for a while, then, with a gentle smile, said, “Well, my boy, what can I do for you?”
I couldn’t speak. I didn’t know what to do or say. Forgetting the customs of this country, I pressed my palms together and mumbled a barely audible “Namaskaram.”

Once again, he smiled kindly, his face full of warmth and compassion, leaning back in his chair as if he had all the time in the world. “Come now, my boy! What is it? There’s nothing to be afraid of. Tell me,” he said.

Hearing his gentle words and seeing the kindness in his face, it felt as if someone had poured nectar over me. Somehow, I gathered my courage and said, “I have just come from India, sir. I have passed the entrance examination here. I wish to join the M.A. class.”
“Is that so? Very good, very good! I’m delighted,” he said. “Show me your entrance pass certificate.”
He examined my marks and said, “Very good! Excellent, excellent! I’m very pleased. To enroll here, you must fill out a form.”
“I have brought it with me, sir,” I replied, showing him the form.
“Good. The Registrar’s office is just next door. Go in there and complete your work. You must have come into this room by mistake,” he said.

By then, I had come to my senses and said, “Thank you, sir. Very, very sorry, sir,” and bowed again, only to realize I was making another mistake. I quickly turned back, went into the next room, and finished my business there. At that moment, I felt a sense of satisfaction and happiness, thinking, “Now I am truly a student of Edinburgh University!” With a beaming face, I came outside, met our private tutor and Raju, and recounted everything that had happened.

“Ah, your house is made of gold, isn’t it? Once again, you’ve put your foot in the dal!” said Raju. All in all, “You haven’t lost your father’s nature,” he added, laughing. Our private tutor said, “It’s all right. The first room you entered belongs to the Vice-Chancellor. That old man you saw is the head of this university—a very good man, with a compassionate heart.”

“It’s already past twelve. Let’s get up and go to the nearby hotel for lunch,” said Raju. “So be it,” I replied, and we set off. But our tutor said, “Why waste money unnecessarily? Why not go to each one’s room?” Raju replied, “Wherever you go, food doesn’t come free, does it? At this hour, let’s enjoy a meal together for fun. Let this be a feast to celebrate Parvatisham joining the university. Parvatisham will bear all the expenses—three cheers!” he said, clapping his hands. The three of us laughed, chatted, and made our way to the hotel.

The next morning, I woke up early, finished my daily rituals, bathed, had some fruit, and, remembering my mother and father for a moment, recited “Gananam Tva” in praise of Lord Ganesha. I thought to check the tithi, nakshatra, and muhurtham, but alas, there was no almanac at hand. I reminded myself that I had to go to my first university class by half past nine, and, not forgetting, set my right foot first as I entered the university grounds. Since it was time, everyone was heading in, and I too made my way towards my class.

All the students began to look at me curiously. I thought, “Perhaps I am the only Indian here,” and went inside. There, the attendant looked at me once, gave a gentle smile, and said, “Good morning, sir. How do you do, sir?” Immediately, I remembered the tea party incident…

As soon as they questioned me in the same manner there, the answer I had prepared came to mind, and I smiled inwardly and said, “Quite well, thank you.” He asked, “Would you please tell me your name?” “Of course,” I replied, and told him my name. Immediately, my name was accepted and he noted it down. He pointed to a place where I should put my coat and hat. Once again, I said, “Thank you,” and, as if shedding some of the weight from my head and body, I placed them there and went inside.

By then, it seemed all the students who were supposed to come had arrived. The hall appeared full. Looking around in all directions, I spotted two or three Indian faces as well. To my surprise, among them was the face of an Indian young woman. There were also about twenty-five or thirty young women of that country present. While I was hesitating, wondering where to sit, a student sitting opposite gestured to the empty seat beside him, inviting me to join. I went over and, saying “Thank you,” sat down. The entire class was silent. For three or four minutes, all of us passed the time by looking at each other’s faces.

Just then, there was the sound of a door opening—the door from which the professor would enter. All of us, displaying a mixture of fear and reverence on our faces, turned to look toward that room. The professor entered, holding a book, and stepped onto the platform. I, flustered and following the custom of our country, was about to stand up. But none of the others moved. The student next to me noticed I was about to rise and pulled me back down by my coat. I was startled and embarrassed. The whole class, though not loudly, laughed at me with a soft chuckle. Even our professor noticed this. Looking at me, he said, “Well, boy, are you new here? Is this your first year? Your first class, perhaps?” Thinking it would not be proper to answer his question without standing up, I quickly stood again. Everyone laughed once more.

“Sit down, my boy. Here, you don’t need to stand up whenever we ask you something. You can answer while sitting. Sit down,” he said. Then he asked, “So, which part of India are you from?” As I was about to stand up again, he gestured for me to remain seated. “I am from Godavari district in the Madras Presidency,” I replied. “What did you study?” he asked. “I passed the Entrance exam here,” I said. “Is your English good?”

“Did you learn it here?” he asked. “I learned it well after coming here,” I replied. “How many marks did you get in English in your Entrance Exam?” he inquired. Feigning a bit of modesty, I said, “I got eighty-five, sir.” “What’s this—eighty-five! That’s good, very good. I’m very pleased. Then, can you recite any poem written by an English poet?” he asked.

Even though I had scored eighty-five marks, the professor kept questioning me calmly and cheerfully, and soon the entire class’s attention was fixed on me. Everyone sat in silence, staring at me. I too felt quite enthusiastic. Once again, forgetting myself, I stood up, folded my hands behind my back, and recited a passage from Tennyson. I spoke without any hesitation or fear, my pronunciation flawless. No one told me to sit down. Everyone continued to watch me intently. I even gave a ten-line explanation of the poem I had recited. The professor was very pleased. All the students were astonished.

“You’re still standing, my boy—sit down. I know that in your country it’s customary to stand and answer. But remember, that is not the custom here. From now on, you need not stand up,” he said. All this while, he himself had been standing. In my delight, I once again forgot myself, joined my hands, and said, “Thank you, sir,” before sitting down.

The professor welcomed all the students and said, “Looking at the conduct of this first student, you all seem to be very intelligent and wise. I am very happy that so many enthusiastic young scholars have come to my class. I hope that all of you, with the same devotion and diligence, will complete your studies by the end of the year and succeed in your examinations. Today, as a formality, I will say a few words about English literature as an introduction and then let you go. I do not wish to frighten you with a long lecture on the very first day.” So saying, he delivered a fine half-hour lecture on English literature and concluded the class.
Listening to his lecture was a feast for the ears, but as for the lesson itself—

chapters.title: Amusements
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

How wonderful it would be if all the lessons here were delivered in this lecture style! If one listens attentively to these lectures, there may be no need to laboriously study textbooks. Even if one does study, there would be no need for the help of a private tutor—one could pass the time quite comfortably. So I thought. The professor turned towards his room. All of us quietly made our way upstairs, without any of the childish mischiefs of our homeland—no chaos, no loud talking, no pushing and shoving each other.

As we were taking off our overcoats and hats in the corridor, a few English students and a couple of Indians approached me. They congratulated me on my courage and my command of the language. One of them, an Indian, asked, “What did you pass in our country?”
“I didn’t pass anything,” I replied.
“Then how did you learn such good English?” he asked.
“I hired a private tutor here and learned from him. He taught me very well,” I said.
“Oh! Is that so? That’s quite surprising,” he said, laughing sarcastically as he walked away.
Thus, my education at the university began.

That afternoon, there were two more classes. I returned home at four o’clock without any mishap, had tea, and went to Raju’s lodging. We chatted for a while, and I narrated the morning’s classroom comedy in detail.
“That’s nothing, it’s all good,” he said. “Don’t worry about anything. Everything will go smoothly,” Raju encouraged me.

After he had his tea, the two of us went outside and, chatting leisurely, climbed up Blackworth Hills, where we had been before. By then, many people had gathered there. Some of our own countrymen were also visible. We all chatted together for a while and then started a game of tag. As soon as the game began, many young men and women from the surroundings gathered in front of us. We played with great enthusiasm. I, recalling the skills I had back in my hometown...

Based on my experience and my performance, they elected me as the captain, just as before. As we played, the spectators grew more and more enthusiastic, their whistles, claps, and “hip hip hoorays” reaching a fever pitch.

No sooner had our game ended than about ten young men from among the audience—our own age—came over and insisted that we include them too and teach them this game, otherwise they wouldn’t let us go. “Alright then,” I said, and we took some of them in, explaining the rules and methods of the game for about ten minutes before stepping onto the field again.

Our team started the chant first. The opposing team, not knowing how to catch us, was a bit confused at first. Eventually, though, they managed to catch one of us and send him out. Then it was their turn to chant. A young Scottish lad came forward. Not knowing how to begin the chant, he looked at us and started off with a “Oh yes, well, well!” We stopped him at once and began to instruct him all over again. No matter how much I tried, I simply couldn’t get him to say “Hari ball” properly. However much I explained, he would say “well” for a while, then “bell” for a while. Finally, I told him, “Forget it, just keep repeating ‘doo doo’ without pausing for breath.” But even if his life depended on it, he couldn’t hold his breath on that syllable.

“Alright, forget that. In English, just pick any letter you like and keep repeating it without stopping for breath,” I suggested. But even that was beyond him. “Well then, just keep saying ‘ooo…’ without pausing,” I said, but he couldn’t manage that either.

“That’s enough, my boy. If you can’t do it, then neither I nor even Brahma, the creator himself, could teach you,” I said. He didn’t understand what I meant, and I had no intention of making it any clearer.

Still, their curiosity to learn the game only grew. They insisted that I must explain it somehow, and pressured me so much that I had no choice but to say something. So I said, “Gentlemen, let’s do one small thing. Just learn to say two short English words quickly, no need to hold your breath. You can take a breath in between. For the sake of the game, just say ‘Welcome’ or ‘Come in’ quickly, let’s see how that works.”
They tried to say “Well come come in” quickly, mixing up all four words, but even that they couldn’t manage.
While this lesson was going on, our own Indians from the north—

Some of the Desasthas came and said they too wanted to join in. When I tried to teach them the same method, they couldn’t pick it up quickly either. So I said, “Let’s just say ‘Welcome’.” Even after ten tries, saying that proved a bit difficult. In “Welcome,” some of them left out the “l” and started with “Come” or “Wek.” So I dropped that too and suggested we say “Come in.” That, too, was hard for some to say quickly.

“This isn’t working,” I said, “let’s just say ‘Time… Time… Time…’” That sounded a bit odd to them. Finally, one of the Scottish lads boldly said, “Don’t mind us, we’ll just say ‘Ta… Tan… Tan…’” I said, “Splendid, let’s leave it at that.”

After that, my game went on smoothly for a while. For several days, they earnestly requested that I give them practice. I agreed and told them to come along, and Raju and I turned our minds homeward. They were all very happy. Thanks to this, all my friends started teasing me as if I had become a big leader.

Thus, every evening, this became a pastime for us. Every day, we would play, and our new disciples would praise the game, saying it was great fun, and played with much enthusiasm. After some days had passed like this, I caught hold of one of them—a Scottish lad who had been just a disciple till then—and said, “Shall I teach you a game from our country?”

“Certainly!” he replied. “Let’s start tomorrow. We can play from early morning till six, and then leave. If you don’t mind a bit of trouble, please do teach us. Or, if you’re new to it, I’ll come and take you along myself. This time, let’s go up to Bread Hills and start with golf,” he said.
“Very good, let’s definitely begin. But for that, don’t we need some stick or club and all that?” I asked.
“No need for all that now. Tomorrow, let’s just use what I have for a bit of fun. If you get interested, you can buy some golf sticks for yourself,” he said.
I agreed, and the next day he came to my house and said he’d take me along, so I set off on my way with him.
…The next morning, by five-thirty, that lad named Jack…

He came and shouted for me. The two of us had some tea and snacks together and set out. He had packed five or six different kinds of hockey sticks into a long, slender canvas bag, slung it over his shoulder, and we set off. In about half an hour, we reached Bride Hills. There, a bungalow served as the golf club. We went in, gave our names, and set out to play. Though these hills were not flat, but rather undulating with mounds and dips, it did not trouble us much.

From the moment we left our lodgings until we reached here, he kept explaining the various methods of playing this game, its rules, and all sorts of regulations. The game begins on a level patch. From there, you must walk about a mile, hitting the ball along the way. The entire area is covered in lush green grass, with not a tree or shrub in sight—truly a feast for the eyes. Along the path, the grass is trimmed every day, as closely as one’s hair is cut at the barber’s. The ground is kept moist with spring water. Just walking on that green meadow feels as delightful as walking on a springy mattress. Only the players are allowed to walk on it—no one else is permitted to tread there.

At the starting point of the game, there is a small ball, about the size of our badminton ball, perhaps a little smaller. But, like a cricket ball, it is very hard. On the green field, a little sand is sprinkled (there is always a box of soft sand ready at hand). The ball is placed on that sand, and with a long stick, curved and padded at the end, you must strike the ball. As you strike the ball and proceed, at every furlong or half-furlong, there is a small square patch with a hole in the middle, sunk into the ground. The goal is to get the ball into that hole; the fewer strokes it takes, the greater the player you are. On that hill, there are eighteen such holes. For the first nine, you must go quite a distance from the clubhouse. From there, taking another route, you complete the remaining nine holes and return towards the club. That is the game.
On the first day—well, not just the first day, but for four or five days—I did not grasp the intricacies or subtleties of the game. In this sport...

Wondering what was so special about it, I began playing. But within a week, I managed to pick up the subtle tricks of the game. I was filled with enthusiasm. This is a very scientific sport. Before striking, one must estimate how much to swing the club, how hard to hit, and how far the ball will travel as a result. All these calculations must be made in the mind before taking the shot. The ball must not touch the ground before it should.

No matter how hard I tried at first, for ten or fifteen days, even up to a month, I struggled. But soon, I became a good player, and everyone began to express surprise at how quickly I had mastered the game.

My own student has now become my teacher. When he told everyone he knew about my progress, they couldn’t believe it. Fifteen of them came one day just to watch me play. They were astonished by what they saw. Afterwards, they started coming one by one to play with me. They all praised my game highly and insisted that I join the club as a member. They brought all the committee members to watch me play, and after seeing my performance, they were thoroughly convinced and admitted me as a club member.

This became a matter of great pride, and all my friends congratulated me. Many of the club members were much older and more experienced than I, but they all played with me and encouraged me further. Not only did they encourage me, but they also took me to all the famous golf courses in the villages around Edinburgh, giving me the opportunity to showcase my skills to everyone. Later, I even participated in four or five competitions and played successfully.

There is a place called North Berwick, a village by the sea. It has some very famous golf courses. One of them is quite small in area, but playing there is extremely difficult. The reason is that there are many mounds and hollows. The starting point is on top of a hill, and the first hole is on another hill opposite. Even if the distance isn’t much, if the ball falls into the valley in between, getting it back up onto the hill is a real struggle.
The day we went, four of us played there. The other three took their shots. One of them...

With the stroke, the ball landed in the hollow. Then it was my turn. I somehow guessed and took a swing. Where my ball ended up, I had no idea. The four of us set off to retrieve the ball that had fallen into the hollow. It took him five or six strokes to get his ball out. Somehow, I managed to climb up the hill on the other side. My ball was nowhere to be seen. The other three slowly brought their balls near the hole. When we finally looked, there was my ball, sitting right in that hole. That means, with the very first stroke I played, the ball had gone straight in! This was extraordinary! Unprecedented, historic, astonishing—they all praised and congratulated me. By afternoon, news of my effortless victory had spread throughout the village.

The next day, all the players in that village congratulated me in various ways, made me an honorary member of their club, and invited me to play on the golf course there. With much happiness, a bit of embarrassment, and some fear, I accepted. Here, the ground was all level—no hills or hollows like before. The sea breeze, the cold climate, and the distant holes made the game a bit difficult. Besides, in the middle of the course, there was a wall about five or six feet high, built right across. Unless one could hit the ball over that wall in a single stroke, it was hard to win the game. From all corners of the country, famous players would come and play here regularly. Among them, the renowned Lord Balfour, who often came to play there.

But, as it happened, even though Lord Balfour had been coming to play there four or five times a year for nearly sixty years, he had never managed to send the ball over the wall in a single stroke. Because of this, the villagers affectionately named that wall "Balfour's Wall." As for me, as if I had stepped on a lucky charm, on my very first attempt, my ball sailed right over the wall. From that moment on, I became a celebrated golfer, and invitations poured in from many places, asking me to come and play in their towns. I participated in numerous competitions and managed to win many prizes. In this way, I can proudly say that I brought fame to our country as well. For I heard that, until then, no Indian had ever achieved such success in this game. This—
My Recreations

My daily routine was packed. During the day, I would go to college; in my free time, I’d visit the library. In the evenings, I’d either go for a walk up the hill, play some games, or, if not, head to the cinema. With such a schedule, there was hardly any leisure, yet my mind was always lively and joyful. Previously, I used to meet my private tutor often and spend some time with him, which gave me the opportunity to learn about many different things from him.

One day, during a conversation with him, the topic of plays and theatrical performances came up. Listening to all that he said was astonishing. At one point, he asked, “Have you ever seen a play performed here?” I replied, “No.” He said, “Tomorrow, there’s a Shakespeare play being staged at the Lyceum Theatre. Go and watch it.” I asked, “Won’t you come along too?” He replied, “If you sit beside me, it’ll be easier for me to explain things to you.” I said, “That would be great.” So, the next day, we went to see Hamlet.

The moment I saw the theatre, I was dumbstruck. The arrangements for the audience inside, the verandas beside the stage, the entire setting—just seeing all that made me feel as if I had entered another world, even before the play began. From the start of the play to the very end, it felt like I wasn’t in this world at all. That day, I truly understood what real immersion means. When the curtain fell, even the explanations my tutor had given me didn’t register in my mind during those few moments.

During the interval, when we stepped outside and sipped tea, I still felt as if I was wandering in a dream, not fully awake! For nearly three hours, I was completely transported to Denmark, several hundred years in the past. Even after the play ended, for quite some time, I couldn’t return from that world to the present day. My tutor was surprised to see me in such a state of absorption.
At first, I couldn’t quite grasp the actors’ pronunciation. But soon enough, I was able to follow. The stage setting, the actors’ demeanor, their makeup, costumes—all were extraordinary.

I do not have enough words to describe my cleverness as a spectator. The master said he had never before seen anyone so engrossed in a play as I was. Mr. Mumeshtaru said, “This is all very strange to me, sir. This performance has given me a rare, unexpected experience. Though I have seen some plays in my own country, I have never felt anything like this. In fact, there isn’t even the slightest possibility of experiencing such a thing there. You see, we don’t really have proper theaters. We are not in a position to develop the stage as an industry, as a business, or even as an art. That’s what I’m beginning to think. After seeing this play, I feel I must learn more about the theater here. Whatever one may say about cinema, these plays—I must see more of them.”

I replied, “Absolutely, you must. Sometimes a new play comes out, and with your enthusiasm, it’s good for you to keep going and watching them. And let me give you a small piece of advice, just my way of doing things! If you want to truly enjoy a play, it’s best to go alone. I, for one, never go with anyone else. The joy I get from sitting alone and watching is something else entirely. If someone’s sitting next to me, whispering some nonsense, it spoils my enjoyment. My attention won’t stay on the play. So, I think you too should get used to watching alone.”

“What you say is absolutely true. That’s exactly my intention as well,” I replied. Taking my leave, I went my way. Even after I returned home, even while eating, my mind was completely filled with the experience of that play. The lady of the house noticed my absent-mindedness and, after warning me two or three times, I finally told her about going to the play and the experience I had there. She was very pleased.

Thus, I got into the habit of watching plays regularly. As a result, I became quite adept at understanding their dialogues and pronunciation. Their costumes and acting styles captivated me. As my master had advised, I always went alone whenever I attended a play.
Social dramas, especially those with a comic flavor, particularly delighted me.

What attracted me the most were the plays. I was someone who could truly enjoy them. Except for one or two of our own people, I never saw anyone from our community attending plays. They say they don’t understand the language. Apparently, the humor in the farces is lost on them. But I, for my part, enjoyed them immensely. One day, I went to see some comedy. I went alone, and as soon as I sat down, a young lady took the seat next to mine. She too seemed to have come alone. On the other side sat a married couple, a bit older. Next to the young lady, on her other side, sat a newlywed couple.

The farce was simply magnificent. With each scene surpassing the last, the wit in the dialogues, the double meanings that sparkled in the actors’ delivery, all had the audience rocking with waves of laughter. From the second act onwards, I noticed that the girl beside me was trying to strike up a conversation, trying to get closer. But I pretended not to notice, acting as if I knew nothing.

Then, at some point in the play, a great joke landed. The audience burst into laughter, some nearly splitting their sides. The commotion was such that we could barely hear the actors’ lines. In that moment, clutching her stomach and laughing, the girl beside me, in a most natural way, as if hugging one of her own, threw her arms around me in her laughter and said, “Oh, sorry, forgive me!”
“What is there to forgive? It’s all in good fun,” I replied, laughing.
“What’s this?” she said, looking at me.
“Oh, the play is just wonderful,” I said.

“Bad boy,” she said, giving my shoulder a playful squeeze. After that, whenever the opportunity arose, this scene kept repeating itself. I didn’t dare say anything, fearing that if I did, it might come off as rude or uncivilized, so I kept quiet.
After the play ended, as soon as I stepped out into the foyer, the girl stood waiting for me. Walking by my side, she began to chat. “So, did you enjoy the play? Did you have a good time?” she asked.
“The play was excellent. I enjoyed it very much. And having you beside me made it all the more enjoyable,” I replied.
“Oh, is that so? You’ve learned to talk well, haven’t you? How long have you been here?” she asked.
“It’s been almost a year and a half since I came here. After coming here—”

“Is there any way to escape without learning the language?” I asked. “If you want to escape, you must do what’s necessary. All your friends have come to the play, haven’t they? Don’t you have any friends? Or, are there no young ladies you know? Haven’t you made a single acquaintance in the past year?” she asked.

“I haven’t made friends with anyone. I haven’t had the initiative to try and make acquaintances. This life is new to me, and I’m not used to the customs here. I feel a bit shy and scared to talk to your people,” I replied.

“Well then, let me help you get over some of your fear. As a token of our new acquaintance, let’s have some tea and refreshments here,” she said, and without waiting for my answer, she led the way to the hotel.

The hotel was packed to the brim with people pouring out from the plays and cinemas. It seemed there wasn’t a single seat available for anyone. Though many of the men and women there must have been used to such scenes, they all began to stare at us as if we were a spectacle. I felt a bit nervous and embarrassed. I suspected they thought, “This girl has bravely brought along this newcomer.” It all felt very awkward to me.
“Shall we go somewhere else?” I asked the girl.

“It’ll be the same wherever we go for the next two hours. Let’s wait and see. We might find a seat here,” she replied. By then, it was already eleven o’clock. Apparently, people keep coming in, eating and drinking, and whiling away the time until two or three in the morning. What is this eating at odd hours! What is this wandering about! When do these people sleep? When do they get to work in the morning? Their whole way of life seems upside down. I came here thinking they were highly civilized, but look at how they are! What kind of civilization is this? I wondered.
Just then, my friend spotted an empty spot. She grabbed my hand and quickly led me there. We had a light snack. All the while, the girl kept chattering away without pause.
She bombarded me with a hundred questions—why I had come to her country, how long I would stay, where I lived, and how I spent my evenings.
BARRISTER PARVATEESAM
Though I had been there for almost a year, she wondered how I managed to remain without making the acquaintance of the other children, and as she ate, she kept firing such questions at me.
She listened to my answers while continuing to eat. Indeed, she never stopped eating as she listened to my replies. Doing both these things at once—eating and talking—felt a bit awkward to me.
Nevertheless, I answered all her questions with great patience and ease. All the while, the girl kept smiling and conversing very pleasantly.

“You seem to have settled here for quite a while, but you don’t look like a newcomer at all. You appear rather inscrutable. I feel one must be a bit cautious around you,” she said, walking slowly beside me all the way to the tram stop. There, too, she paused and continued, “I am very glad to have met you at this hour. I, too, am new to this town. I wasn’t born here. I came here for work and live alone. None of my friends are here. I don’t know what you think, but I am not the sort to take the initiative to get acquainted with everyone. This is the first time I’ve seen people from your country in this town. I am quite curious to learn about your land and customs by making friends, but I am too shy to approach anyone and start a conversation. The people I have met so far are rather brusque and impatient…”
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 253

They looked just like ordinary people. That’s why, even though one or two tried to talk to me, I would quietly slip away without a word. You, on the other hand, seemed to be quite innocent and gentle. That’s why I mustered up the courage to speak to you. I don’t know what you thought of me. Anyway, everyone has their own path in life. I, too, am alone. By now, my landlady must be imagining all sorts of things about why I haven’t come home yet. So, will you let me take my leave now?” she said.

Looking at the girl and listening to her words, I felt that everything she said was true. “I, too, am very glad to have made your acquaintance. Sometimes, without any effort, we come across kindred spirits,” I replied. She said, a little sadly, that perhaps we wouldn’t have another chance to meet. “Why not? Maybe we’ll run into each other again at some cinema or play,” I said, smiling.
“Is that all? Can’t we meet separately, go up some hill or to a park, and chat leisurely?” she asked. “Why not? Let’s do that,” I agreed. Immediately, she eagerly asked, “When and where?”

“That’s up to you. You tell me. Whenever you’re free, wherever you think it would be nice to meet,” I said. The girl, delighted, suggested, “Well then, tomorrow—since I have a holiday too—shall we meet at four in the afternoon? We can watch a movie, go for a stroll, and have a pleasant chat.”

“Alright, let’s definitely meet,” I said, and her face blossomed with happiness. She herself fixed the place and time, shook my hand warmly with both of hers, said, “Good night, thank you so much,” and without another word or a backward glance, dashed away at a run.

I stood there for a while, gazing after her. I don’t know how long I stood like that. It was only when a tram arrived and people began boarding in a hurry that I realized where I was. Deciding it was too crowded to get on, I thought I’d walk back leisurely and started walking towards my lodging. On the way, a couple of children looked at me and laughed. Seeing me walking along, they said, “No good,” and ran off. A couple of others winked at me as they passed.

chapters.title: Theatre and Music
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

As I didn’t respond, they came closer and said, “Hello, Johnny!” “You’re mistaken! I’m not Johnny,” I replied, moving ahead. “Too young!” (meaning, too much of a youngster), they laughed to themselves and walked away. Young men and women, strolling arm in arm along the road, watched this spectacle, laughing and going about their way. Some were lovers in their middle age, some were married couples, and others were just pairs. A few of them tried to greet me, and when I didn’t reply, they attempted to grab my hand and pull me into their group. I gently freed my hand and said, “Sorry, good night,” and walked on. Noticing this, they called out, “That’s right, young man! You’ve got to be jolly careful!” Well done, boy, you must be a little careful with these people, they said as they went on their way. By the time I reached my lodging, it was midnight. The landlady and her children seemed to be in deep sleep; not a sound was to be heard. I quietly entered my room. On the table, the landlady had left a little hot milk and two or three slices of bread with a pat of butter. I drank the milk, changed out of my clothes, put on my pajamas, and, thinking over the night’s events, wished myself good night and went to bed.

The next day, at three in the afternoon, I went to the meeting place the young lady had mentioned. By the time I arrived, she was already there, waiting for me. As soon as she saw me, she came forward with a gentle smile, said, “Good afternoon,” and extended her hand for a handshake. “I’m so glad you came. I was confident you would, but still, I had a little hesitation. After all, your face doesn’t look like one that tells lies,” she said without a trace of doubt. “So, you can judge a person by their face! Please teach me that art as well. Whoever I see, I only notice the good in them. Why is that, do you think?” I asked. She laughed and replied, “You see good in everyone because you are a good person yourself.” Chatting thus, we went to a nearby hotel, had a light tea and snacks, and then went to a cinema.

There, they screened a film starring a certain Charlie Chaplin, which was full of humor. That was the very first time I watched a Chaplin film—words cannot express how marvelous it was. Without a single line of dialogue, without song or verse, the entire story was made clear to us solely through their acting. How skillfully they accomplished this! And Chaplin’s comic performance was simply extraordinary.

For about an hour, I, the girl sitting next to me, and—why just us?—all the audience in the hall were utterly enchanted by that comedic acting. We were so absorbed, so delighted, that we lost ourselves in waves of laughter and joy. The hall resounded with our laughter.
When the picture ended, we stepped outside, had a little more tea, and then, chatting away, we strolled leisurely up a hill for an outing.

By then, it was around six o’clock. By the time we arrived, hundreds—no, thousands—of people, all in pairs, had already come to the hill for their excursion. More than ninety percent of them were young people—young men and women.

All the young men and women, paired up, sat here and there, utterly fearless and unconcerned, embracing each other, laughing, chatting, lost in their own world as if they were the only people atop that hill. Just like in the movies or plays, they seemed to forget the outside world entirely, reveling in their own happiness. Only a handful—some mischievous fellows in one corner, a few girls in another—sat apart, gossiping among themselves. We reached one such spot. Though by now I had grown somewhat accustomed to such scenes, here, apart from romance, nothing else seemed to exist. We sat down as well. For two or three minutes, neither of us knew what to say.
Then, the girl looked at my face and said, “Why are you sitting so silently? Did you bring your friend all this way just to sit in silence?”
I laughed and replied, “You need to correct that a bit. I didn’t bring my friend here—my friend brought me. So, the responsibility of entertaining me with lively conversation falls on you.”

She smiled and said, “Is that so? Then first, tell me about yourself—where you come from, how long you’ve been here, what your experiences have been. Tell me everything, one by one. That should keep us occupied for a good while.”
I said, “I don’t know if it will pass the time or just give you a headache.”
She laughed, “No matter! If a headache starts, I’ll quietly slip away and fetch a headache tablet without even telling you.”

With such introductory exchanges, two or three hours slipped by in conversation—what I said, what she said, what either of us talked about, I couldn’t say. Time sped by so quickly in our mutual acquaintance that we didn’t even notice it passing; it was our stomachs that finally reminded us. Both of us, in unison, suggested we should leave. I stood up first, offered her my hand, gently helped her up, and we strolled slowly towards the hotel.

There, after having some refreshments, we each went our separate ways, agreeing to meet again sometime. I returned home and sat for a long while, lost in thought. That girl was truly intelligent, gentle…

The enthusiasm she had shown in the theater was nowhere to be seen now. She made no attempt to come closer, neither in word nor in deed. It seemed she had come simply to make the acquaintance of a new person, but she gave no hint of expecting anything more than that. I thought she was just like me—alone, come to pass the time.
As I was thinking thus, my wife’s daughter quietly came inside and said, “Well, Mr. Same, what are you thinking about? You’re neither reading nor sleeping.”
I replied, “Why are you still awake? All the children went to bed hours ago and should be fast asleep by now.”

She said, “That’s true, but you yourself said that we’re not little children, so that rule doesn’t apply to us. Anyway, tell me what’s going on with you. Where did you go, what did you do? I can’t sleep.”
I said, “Alright, if you insist, I’ll tell you. But if you get angry, you mustn’t blame me.”
“Why would I get angry? What have you done that would make me angry?” she asked.

“Well, the other day when I went to the play—by the way, I didn’t tell you, did I? I went to the theater the other night. The play was excellent. There, I made the acquaintance of a charming young lady. I thought, ‘What a lovely girl!’” I said, looking at her face.

Her face, which had been bright and eager, now clouded over with a hint of irritation. “So what if she was lovely? Why should I care? What’s it to me if you met someone? Did you go out for a drive with her this evening?” she asked, a bit sharply.

“Yes,” I replied, “First we had some refreshments, then went to the cinema, after that took a drive up the hills, chatted merrily, had more refreshments, and then I came back here and have been sitting, thinking about that girl’s beauty and her conversational skills.”

“Oh, I see! So I’ve interrupted your thoughts—please forgive me. Now I understand your ways. Just wait, I’ll tell my mother and have her write a letter to your family about all your doings. The girl was beautiful, was she? Of course she was! For young men like you, especially those who’ve returned from abroad, every girl here looks beautiful.
