If only you knew what real beauty was, you’d know the difference between true beauty and mere prettiness,” she said, huffing and puffing, spinning around to leave.
I caught her by the arm and pulled her back, saying, “Some girls, even when they’re angry, look beautiful...”

I pulled her close and planted a small kiss on her cheek. “Enough now, I’m happy. You don’t have to do all the things you did with that girl here. Just think of those and go to sleep, poor thing,” she said. If I told you I didn’t even do this little thing there, you wouldn’t believe me.

“Why are you so angry with me, dear?” I asked, laughing. “Who are you, who am I? Why would I be angry with you?” she replied. So, you’re just joking for no reason, is that it? Anyway, let’s leave this quarrel aside. “How wonderful was that Charlie Chaplin picture! I want to see it again, or at least another one of his films. You must take me. What do you say?” I asked.

“Very well, I’m delighted,” she said, mocking me with a single word, and before I could say anything else, she darted off to the other side of the room. What a strange thing! Even this girl seems to be jealous. That’s why they say a woman’s other name is Jealousy, I thought to myself, chuckling as I tried to fall asleep.

In that town—Edinburgh, that is—I believe I was the youngest among all the Indian students. Yet, for some reason, I became the object of everyone’s affection and regard. Why that was, I cannot say. Students from every language and every region, whenever they saw me, would greet me with enthusiasm and joy, always inquiring after my well-being. Even my Scottish classmates developed a fondness for me.

At my encouragement and suggestion, all the Telugu students began to meet regularly. I told everyone it would be wonderful if we celebrated festivals like Ugadi, Vijayadashami, Deepavali, and Sankranti together. Our Raju also supported my idea. All the Andhra brothers unanimously agreed. With Ugadi just a week away, we decided to begin our new tradition with that festival.

On the day, the program did not begin with mango pickle, as is customary, because we couldn’t get any. Instead, we started in the morning with tamarind rice and fruit snacks. Raju and I prepared the tamarind rice ourselves. When it came time to add the tempering, we realized we had no oil. There’s no Indian oil to be found there, and ghee wouldn’t do. So…

After consulting our landlady, we immediately dragged her to the bazaar, got some olive oil, and managed to get things done with it. All my friends congratulated us, saying the pulihora (tamarind rice) was absolutely splendid. When we bought so many chilies, tamarind, anise, and other such items at the store all at once, the shopkeeper was bewildered and asked us why we needed all these things. We told him, “We use these for snacks,” and just with that, he looked alarmed, as if wondering what would become of us after eating such things. He was quite taken aback.

In the afternoon, we organized a small gathering, and there, with songs and poems, we carried out the day’s program without any hitches. Not only our own people, but some from other regions also attended the meeting, appreciated it, and enjoyed themselves. Afterwards, they too decided it would be nice to hold such events themselves.

That day, a couple of South Indians and a Telugu man newly arrived in town. They also attended our gathering. The newly arrived Telugu man, seeing me bustling about, managing the event and mingling with everyone, assumed I was a leader of sorts. At the end of the meeting, he quietly approached me and introduced himself.

He explained that he hadn’t yet found a room anywhere, was staying in a small hotel, didn’t know anyone here, and asked if I could help him in some way. “Of course, that’s no trouble at all. Let’s meet tomorrow,” I said, and sent him off. Memories of the genuine affection and invaluable help that Menon in London and Raju here had shown me in similar circumstances came flooding back to me.

The next morning, I took the young man around until noon, and managed to find him a room not too far from my own. Later, when my South Indian friends came and asked, I was able to help them in the same way. These three stuck to me like shadows, never leaving my side, and became my bodyguards. I taught them, just as Raju had taught me, all the intricacies of how to live here, how to get around, how to speak, and so on, in great detail.

But no matter how much I taught them, the strange thing was that at every step, every single day, they managed to make all sorts of blunders. I used to wonder why they behaved with such lack of sense. From how to walk on the road, to the proper way to eat—

I told all the boys just as I had told the children. Yet, no matter how many times I explained that spitting on the road while walking, picking one’s nose, and such habits were useless here, it never seemed to sink in for them. One of them, it seems, even had a fondness for snuff. He would take out his snuff box, snort a pinch with a flourish, sneeze loudly, and then wipe his hand on the nearest lamp post or, if in a tram, on the tram car itself. Everyone who saw him would be thoroughly disgusted. I brought this to his attention and asked, “By the way, where did you get this snuff from?”
He replied, “I brought it from home, sir.”
I couldn’t help but laugh. “You brought snuff too, my boy? How much did you bring?”
“It’s heavy, so I couldn’t bring much, sir. I brought about a seer’s worth.”
My heart nearly stopped.
“A whole seer! But—”

He interrupted, “Who knows if we’ll find it here or not? If we don’t, at least this will last until we can gather the necessary ingredients to make it ourselves. That’s why I brought a seer. Would you like to see a sample?” he asked, grinning, as he pulled out his snuff box.
“No, no, my boy, keep it. What else did you bring?” I asked.
Bapu

— “A little charcoal powder to clean my teeth, some sambar powder for meals, rasam powder, a bit of pepper, cardamom, cloves, and other such odds and ends. I even brought a little betel nut, sir. Later, we can get them here anyway,” he said.

“As if they won’t be available here! They’ll be available, all right. And if, by chance, they aren’t, you can always go home during some holiday, bring back a whole ton, and open a little shop here for yourself!”

The expenses would be shared, and it would also be useful for your fellow countrymen here, I said. Whether I said it sincerely or just offhandedly, I couldn’t tell from his reaction. Nevertheless, he laughed and said, “Yes, sir, what you said is absolutely right, sir. That’s a good idea, sir,” and thanked me profusely, becoming even more friendly and relaxed with me. They too joined the college. Each began their studies in their own way.

While things were going on like this, one day a Scottish couple who lived there invited Raja, me, another two people, and these new arrivals to tea on Sunday evening. We agreed. I gave these newly arrived friends a thorough briefing again on how to behave there and what to expect.

At four o’clock that evening, we all set out separately and reached the house of our hosts. The strange thing was, by the time we arrived, my tall disciple was already sprawled comfortably on the sofa, legs stretched out, reading some novel in bliss. We were all dumbfounded.
“What’s this? When did you come?” I asked.
“I came in the morning,” he replied.
“What’s this nonsense, coming in the morning when they asked us to come in the evening?” I said.

He, without the slightest hint of embarrassment, replied, “What does it matter when, sir? I had nothing to do. They invited us, didn’t they? They’re good people. I thought I’d make friends with them, so I came in the morning, sir. No harm, sir,” he said, giving me a look of innocent madness.
“Oh, no harm done. They must be very pleased,” I said.
“Yes, sir, they’re truly good people. Treated me with great respect, sir,” he replied.
Just then, the lady of the house arrived. After the usual exchange of “Good evening, good afternoon, how do you do” and so on, I quietly called her aside.

“He came in the morning, it seems. Please don’t mind, and forgive us. It’s just innocence, nothing else. He had no other intention. I assure you, nothing like this will ever happen again,” I promised her.

She laughed and said, “Why are you so troubled by this? It’s all right. It’s just like someone visiting their relatives’ house in a strange village without knowing the customs. What’s the harm in that?”

I thought to myself, “What a broad-minded lady she is!” and said aloud, “We are all very grateful to you for understanding and welcoming us with such generosity. We truly appreciate it.” Just then, we were called in—the tea was ready.

On the table, as usual, there were empty plates and spoons set for everyone, while the food items were placed separately on other plates on the table itself. Each person was to take what they wanted with the help of spoons and forks and serve themselves onto their own plates. As we all began to do this, that long-nosed fellow suddenly grabbed a cake with his hand, took a big bite, and then, picking out a few more things that caught his fancy, filled his plate to the brim and started eating with his hands, biting into everything.

Everyone was dumbfounded. We tried to tell him that this wasn’t the way to do it, but he gave us no chance. At that moment, the hostess intervened, saying gently, “If you try taking things with the knife and fork and putting them in your mouth, you might find it easier. Why not give it a try?”

He replied, “Oh, why bother? Let it be! When God has given us hands, what’s the need for all these things? Eating with one’s hands is the natural and most comfortable way.” What could we possibly say to someone like that? All of us fell silent, swallowing our embarrassment.
As if that wasn’t enough, he continued eating with his right hand. The family members were clearly uncomfortable. The lady of the house asked, “Do you always eat like this?”

“Of course, madam! How else would I eat?” he replied, about to say something more, when I, unable to bear our collective embarrassment and disgust any longer, gave him a sharp kick under the table. He yelped. I shot him a fierce look, signaling him to keep quiet.
I quickly said, “Oh, it’s nothing, madam. My leg slipped while I was stretching it out. Please forgive me.”
Worried about what else might happen, we hurriedly brought the tea party to a close. After some more small talk, we took our leave of the hosts and stepped outside.
Looking around, I noticed that the long-nosed fellow hadn’t come out yet. Wondering what new mischief he was up to, I went back inside.

chapters.title: The Landlady's Daughter
paragraphs: There was no sign of the fellow coming back. The landlady’s face was clouded with annoyance. I was burning with impatience. “What now? Why hasn’t he come yet?” I said.
He replied, “I’m thinking of staying here tonight and going to my room in the morning.”
An immense anger welled up in me. The landlady stood there, listening to our conversation, unable to decide whether to laugh or cry.

“What’s this? You want to stay here tonight? Have you lost your mind? Can’t you see their discomfort, or do you only care about your own convenience? First, you made the mistake of arriving in the morning. Then you committed a few more blunders. And now, as if all that weren’t enough, you say you’ll sleep here tonight, clinging to them like a ghost that won’t let go! Did you think they’d have another bed, mattress, and blankets all set up for you here? Come on, let’s go!” I said.
He replied, “Never mind, if there’s no bed, I can sleep under their bed.”

The landlady couldn’t contain her laughter and ran off to the other room! Without another word, I grabbed him by the arm, picked up his coat and hat, and dragged him outside. He realized there was no use resisting and came along quietly. What more could I say to him? What was the use?

“Don’t you dare turn back and come here again. Go straight home. I’ll come by later to check. If you’re not at home, wherever you are, I’ll hunt you down and break your bones. Be warned!” I said, pushing him ahead.

We went our separate ways and reached the house where we were staying. He went home quietly. I don’t know how this whole affair spread through the town, but after that, no one invited him to any party again. When you’re in a foreign land, if you don’t learn to behave according to the customs of that country, what else can you expect?

One day, there was some sort of holiday. Colleges, offices, factories—everything was shut down. It was an annual holiday, it seemed. On that day, trains would be packed with people going to neighboring towns. Whichever railway station you looked at, it would be overflowing with people. The streets would be filled with crowds wandering about with nothing to do, and hotels, cinemas, picnic spots, amusement parks, sports grounds, hills, parks—everywhere you looked, the ground would be covered with men and women, boys and girls, as if the earth itself was teeming with people.

The strange thing is, even amidst such a dense crowd, there is no jostling, no one bumping into another, no petty squabbles, and not a word of reproach exchanged. Despite the throngs, people here do not lose themselves in a frenzy as our folks do at the holy pilgrimages back home. Even when everyone speaks in unison, not a sound is heard—only the occasional laughter rings out here and there.

The crowds roam about the town in their own way: some wander the streets, others play outdoor games like tennis and badminton, some, taking advantage of the holiday, spend the whole day at the cinema, while others stroll along the roads gossiping about the town’s affairs. Women, in particular, stand for hours before the large shops brimming with clothes and wares, gazing at the beautifully arranged displays behind glass doors, delighting in the spectacle. The roads are abuzz with people like me, solitary souls, simply observing these scenes.

Then there are those of middle age or older, who step into a public house, sip a little liquor with friends, spend some time in conversation, and then move on to another place, and from there to yet another—thus, some brothers spend the entire day migrating from one pub to the next. Yet, even after hours of drinking, you do not see the kind of loud shouting, brawling, or unruly behavior that is so common among our countrymen. Overstepping bounds is rarely seen here.

As for us, meaning our countrymen, we usually while away the time reading at home or visiting friends’ houses. That evening, we decided to set out for the hill. I too set out, and by the time I reached the other side, a few more friends had joined me, and we resolved to play a game of tag. As we were walking, a peculiar incident occurred.

The road was packed with people and various vehicles, all in a jumble. Crossing from one side to the other seemed both difficult and dangerous. Still, we had no choice but to cross at one point, so each of us, separately and hurriedly, tried to make our way across.

Right beside me was a man past middle age, attempting to cross the road, swaying a little as he walked. Fearing he might fall or meet with some mishap, I went close to him, took his hand, and said, “Come, sir; I’ll take you across carefully, nothing will happen to you…”

“No need to be afraid,” I said. He let go of my hand with a hearty laugh, looked me up and down as if to size me up, then steadied himself and said, “Boy, at your age, you shouldn’t be indulging in such spirits. See how you’re already swaying! Walk carefully, I have urgent business to attend to,” and with that, he staggered forward.

The crowd in the streets was immense. Navigating through these vehicles in the pouring rain required the skill of Arjuna steering his chariot in battle. This man took another four steps ahead, nearly slipped and fell, and landed right on top of a woman of about thirty who was coming from the opposite direction. Clutching her tightly to steady himself, he looked at her with a grin and, in the sweetest tone he could muster, said, “Thank you, dear,” as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

The lady, unable to bear the stench of alcohol, tried to push him away in disgust. But he only held her tighter and declared, “If we stick together, we stand. If we separate, we fall!” (United we stand—separated we fall), he said, with great solemnity.

Everyone crossing the road stopped and burst into laughter. The carriages came to a halt wherever they were. The poor woman was mortified. From somewhere, a constable appeared, pulled the man away from her, apologized to the lady, and advised her to proceed carefully.

We, meanwhile, had a good laugh and made our way to the game of “chedugudi.” There, our Scottish friends joined us. They formed one team, and we formed another, and we played chedugudi with great enthusiasm. Hundreds of spectators gathered around, cheering us on, and that day’s match turned into quite an exhibition. We decided to arrange another match soon and parted ways.

Me and Our People: After sitting for a while, chatting and relaxing, we set off on our way back. On the way, we witnessed another curious scene. Here, some people—highly educated, experts in their respective fields—regardless of what job they held for a living, never let go of their academic pursuits. Those who had studied botany would always be on the lookout for interesting plants; those who had studied geology would collect rocks and minerals related to their field. Most notably, those who had studied entomology—the science of insects—would always be on the hunt for new species of bugs and beetles.

Whenever he saw a butterfly with colorful, fluttering wings, or a moth, I have often observed him trying, by any means, to catch at least one of those insects, even if just as a token. That day, as we were returning home, it had already grown quite dark and the street lamps were lit. The crowds had thinned considerably.

As we were walking along, we saw a priest standing near a lamppost. He was gazing intently at the lamp itself and at the swarm of winged insects fluttering around it, with a look of deep concentration. A few others like me, curious to know what he was staring at so intently, also stopped and began to watch.

After a couple of minutes, the priest slowly began to climb up the lamppost. Now, anyone climbing a lamppost in the middle of the street is bound to look comical. But when it’s a priest—a man of some age and religious dignity—doing this, for some reason, it struck us as even more amusing. He, oblivious to our amusement, continued his slow ascent.
Just then, another fellow—a rather hefty man, swaying unsteadily under the influence of drink—staggered over to us, stopped, and looked up at the man climbing the pole.

Realizing that the man was a Father, we couldn’t for the life of us guess why our companion was rushing at him. He paused for a moment, pondering, then turned to us with a knowing smile, winked, and shouted, “Hey mate, come down here—I’ll give you a matchstick!”

Poor fellow, what this drunken soul imagined was that the important man—meaning the Father—had come up to light his cigar, but didn’t have a match, so he was climbing up towards the lamp. Out of great generosity, he offered to give him a matchstick himself. The underlying meaning, of course, was that this wise man assumed the person clinging to the lamp post and climbing up must be thoroughly drunk, and so he was eager to demonstrate his own cleverness. I was nearly doubled over with laughter. The Father, too, grasped the situation and, feeling embarrassed, climbed down, turned to us, and said, “Sorry, gentlemen,” then put his hand on the drunkard’s shoulder and continued, “My boy, you thought I was about to do what you would have done, didn’t you? You’ve made quite a mistake. I wasn’t going up for that. I was trying to catch the colorful-winged moth fluttering so beautifully around the lamp, out of curiosity. Your enthusiasm has killed mine. Now, let’s all walk slowly and get home safely. Can you walk carefully, or do you need my help?”

“No need, Father, I’ll go carefully. Forgive me. I made a mistake. I made a mistake. Good night, Father,” the drunkard said, and hurriedly tried to walk ahead, nearly stumbling. The Father caught him, helped him up, and walked with him for a distance before sending him on his way. In these bustling days, such incidents—strange and wonderful—are quite common, and always provide a good laugh.

There is a custom in this country: whenever holidays are given, whether students, office workers, or factory laborers, everyone leaves their town and goes to some seaside resort, spends a few days there, regains some energy, and then returns to their work. Those who live inland go to the sea; those who live by the sea go to the mountains. This change of air, this change of scene, works wonders in just ten days. It brings such health! Even if it’s only for a day’s holiday...

As far as possible, people tend to leave their own towns and go elsewhere during the holidays. So, this summer vacation, I too was seized by such a fancy and decided to visit the seashore on the Irish side. Without telling anyone, and following my teacher’s advice, I resolved to travel alone during these holidays as well.

By the time I reached the station, it was teeming with people. After securing a ticket, I managed to find a seat at one end of the railway carriage. Next to me sat a young woman, about twenty years old. I wondered if she might feel uneasy sitting beside me. But instead, she smiled, moved aside, and graciously offered me the seat by the window. Beside her sat a young man, not yet twenty-five. The rest of the passengers were also young men and women, each group absorbed in their own conversations. No one seemed to notice me, the young lady beside me, or the gentleman next to her. I had no particular desire to talk to anyone, so I simply sat there, observing the faces around me.

The young lady next to me took out a novel and began reading it with the intense concentration of someone preparing for an exam. The fellow beside her, finding nothing better to do and with no one else free to talk to, seemed disinclined to converse with me. He tried instead to engage the young woman: he smiled, winked, edged closer, and attempted all sorts of little tricks, but none of them succeeded. He sat there, looking quite dejected. I almost felt sorry for him. I thought he might get off at the next station or the one after that. But even after two more stops, he neither got down nor ceased his pining.

After we had traveled a little further, the train entered a tunnel. Suddenly, everything was plunged into deep darkness. It seemed as if everyone was familiar with this route and had been waiting for just this moment. All at once, the sound of about twenty kisses echoed through the carriage. The young lady beside me, without my noticing, stood up and moved near the door. Suddenly, two hands—clearly a man’s—grabbed me in a tight embrace. “You silly!” I exclaimed, trying to free myself from the grip, and just then, as the train emerged from the tunnel into the light...
It arrived.

The girl standing by the door, and the rest of the passengers in the compartment, all witnessed my predicament and, I suppose, imagined the extent of my misery. The whole carriage erupted in laughter, loud enough to drown out even the train’s roar. As soon as the light returned, the man who had tried to maintain his dignity shrank with embarrassment, his face turning as red as a beetroot. Without letting the others hear, he whispered a quick “Sorry” and slipped away to the other side.

The girl sitting between us, as if entirely oblivious to the commotion, without so much as a twitch of her eyelid or the trace of a smile on her face, calmly settled into her seat and immersed herself in her book. I too was seized by an irrepressible urge to laugh, but somehow managed to stifle it and keep a straight face.

Just then, we pulled into a station. The young man sitting next to the girl sprang up, head bowed, and hurriedly got off, making his way into another compartment. Watching him, everyone burst out laughing all at once. This time, I too joined in, blending my laughter with theirs. The girl, for the first time, glanced at me with a gentle smile.
Laughing, I said, “How extraordinary! How clever and quick-witted you are! Did you know the tunnel was coming? How did you manage to slip away so quietly, right between us, without anyone noticing?”

The girl laughed heartily and replied, “Oh, I’ve travelled this route many times. I know exactly when this tunnel comes and what usually happens here. That’s why, with alertness and agility, I quietly slipped away and stood up as soon as it began. There was really nothing for me to be afraid of. I—”
Barrister Parvateesam

“The humiliation that was meant for you has already occurred. For quite some time, I noticed him making gestures, moving closer to me, and about to lay his hand on me. Sensing the impending danger, I became cautious. Please forgive me for causing you this trouble in the middle of your journey,” she said.
“What is there to forgive in this? I didn’t suffer any hardship. I wasn’t humiliated. In fact, this experience was rather enjoyable for me,” I replied.
The girl widened her eyes innocently and, with a laugh, said, “Oh! Was his embrace so delightful to you?”

“Are you now upset that you missed out on that pleasure? My happiness wasn’t because of that. I felt pity for his failed attempt, his lack of wit, and his impatience. He was the one who faced defeat, not you or me. Afterwards, your alertness, your awareness, and your quick thinking made me happy. All in all, would you say that this little incident, which took place over a minute or two, was enjoyable or not?” I asked.
She laughed and said, “Actually, I thought you might be the one to try such a thing.”
“If that were the case, would you have slipped away so easily?” I said.
“Oh no! That’s not what I meant,” she replied.

To be honest, I had no idea that this tunnel would come or that traveling through a tunnel would be like this. “I am a stranger here, from a foreign land. I don’t have enough experience yet. If I did, who knows what might have happened?” I said.

“Is that so! Have you come here recently? Are you here to study at the university? How long has it been since you arrived?” she asked, setting aside her silence, closing her book, and engaging in conversation with me.
“What is this book you’ve set aside? Have you finished reading it? Are you studying for some exam? You were reading with such focus, I thought perhaps you were preparing for an exam,” I said.

“I have no exams or anything of the sort, sir. I’m a stenographer at a business firm. Whenever I get leave, I like to go somewhere and spend a few days. I don’t really have any acquaintances here, so whom would I talk to? I have very few friends near my house, and among them, not a single male friend,” she said.

“How is that? Is it your shortcoming, or theirs? In this country, such friendships are common among both young and old, aren’t they? I find it hard to believe you live such a solitary life. Still, I’m glad that, even if only for the sake of breaking your vow, you agreed to converse with me. If we hadn’t met on this train, perhaps both of us would have had a chance to get to know each other better,” I said.
“So, where are you going?” she asked.
“I’m going to a small village called Lock Ramja.”

“Well, what a coincidence! I’m going there too. It seems our tastes align. As you said, perhaps we can deepen our acquaintance here, as circumstances permit. Have you arranged any accommodation there?” she asked.
“No, I heard there’s a hotel here. I thought I’d take a room there and spend a week in this peaceful place,” I replied.
“All right then. Anyway, everyone comes to the seashore by evening, don’t they? We can meet there,” she said, just as our station arrived. We got down and each went our separate ways.

I went to the hotel I had in mind and asked for a room. They hesitated quite a bit but finally gave me a small one. By then, it was around five in the evening. I put my things in the room and set out to explore the town. After wandering here and there and strolling along the seashore for a while, I returned to the hotel at seven o’clock.

But as soon as I arrived, the hotel manager and the porter came running up to me, looking anxious and terribly polite, and with some fear, they said, “Please forgive us, sir, but we cannot give you the room we promised. It has already been allotted to someone else before. There are no other rooms vacant. Please try somewhere else if you can.”
Barrister Parvateesam

I said. It was becoming clear that what they said was not true. I even told them so. “Your faces themselves reveal that what you’re saying is not true. On what authority do you refuse to give rooms to guests who come to the hotel? Is there any kind of discrimination here? If so, why did you agree to take us in the first place?” As I fired off this barrage of questions, they were left speechless. From there, they shifted their stance.

“There’s a man here in this hotel who worked for a business firm in India and retired. He lives here now. He saw you arrive. As soon as you left, he came to us and insisted for a long time that we must not give you a room. That’s why we couldn’t refuse him,” he said nervously.
“In that case, I don’t like his presence here either. Why don’t you ask him to leave?” I replied boldly. At this, they grew even more anxious.
“He is a permanent resident here, sir. He has no one else, and he has made this place his home. It wouldn’t be proper for us to ask him to leave,” they said.
“Then did it seem proper to you to ask me to leave?” I shot back.
“No, sir, it’s our mistake. Please forgive us and kindly go to another place. Otherwise, we’ll be in a lot of trouble,” they pleaded, holding my hands in supplication.
“Show me where he is. I’ll speak to him myself.”

“He’s gone out somewhere. He’s a very short-tempered man. You were supposed to stay only four days and then leave. You say you’re students—why all this fuss?” said the manager, looking very pitiful. I too began to feel the same way.
“There isn’t another hotel here, is there?” I asked. “If you go up the hill, you’ll find rooms there,” the manager suggested.

“Fine, I’ll go and try. If I get a room, I’ll leave. Otherwise, I’ll stay here tonight and leave in the morning. I thought everyone in this country was a gentleman, a person of honor. Now that I see my judgment was wrong, I am deeply disappointed,” I said, and walked out.

chapters.title: New Lodgings
paragraphs: Without much difficulty, I managed to secure a room in the house of a railway porter. After that, I brought my luggage and took up residence here. Though the place wasn’t particularly clean, it was at least moderately tidy and somewhat comfortable. The landlord and his wife treated me with great respect. When they heard about the incident at the hotel, they were deeply sympathetic. Well, what’s done is done, I thought, and decided to stay here for a week.

The atmosphere here is very pleasant. It is wonderfully peaceful. There are no noises of any kind; it is utterly silent. In this manner, four days passed by in complete ease. Once or twice, I happened to see the girl who had traveled with me on the train to the seaside. She would come by, chatting in a lighthearted, witty, and clever manner—always managing to amuse without offending, and to jest without being the butt of the joke herself.

One night, after returning to my lodgings and having my meal, a rather amusing incident occurred. This isn’t exactly something one ought to broadcast to everyone, but since there’s no way around it, I must tell you.

I was suffering from constipation. I had to spend quite a long time sitting in the lavatory. In the mornings, this would cause inconvenience to the other tenants, so I had developed the habit of conducting my business at night. Now, did the people here discover this little secret of mine?
Barrister Parvateesam

The main difficulty here is that, to go to the lavatory, one must pass through the landlord’s kitchen. Every day, I would wait until they had finished their meals, wrapped up all their chores, and the husband and wife were sitting together, chatting. They would watch my comings and goings with amusement. Since there was no tap in that room, I would take a small jug of water with me, trying my best not to be seen by them.

One day, the landlady happened to notice this and mentioned it to her husband. For two days, they debated why I was carrying water with me. They couldn’t come to any conclusion. Perhaps I had some secret ailment, they thought, and maybe I was taking some special lotion water for it. If that was the case, it might not be good to keep me here. They decided that this matter must be clarified at once.

So, that night, as I was returning from the lavatory, they asked me to sit down. Wondering what this new formality was, I set the jug down and sat. After some small talk, they said, “Are you comfortable here? You don’t have any problems, do you? If you need anything or if there’s any lack, please tell us frankly. We’ll do whatever we can.”

Pleased, I replied, “I have no difficulties at all. Your kindness makes me very happy. I’m even thinking of staying another week or so.” They seemed quite delighted. After a couple more minutes of conversation, the landlord, with a hint of nervousness, said, “I wanted to ask you a question. Please don’t mind.”
“Of course, ask away! Why such a preamble?” I said.
He asked, “Why do you take this jug with you?”
“For water,” I replied.
“But why?” he pressed.

I turned pale, wondering why he was asking this question, and for a moment, I pondered what to say. Then the answer struck me, and I replied frankly, “In our country, we don’t use paper; we wash ourselves clean with water.”
By the time I finished, they both burst out laughing, and, relieved, explained their doubts and apologized for any offense. I laughed along and returned to my room.

Life was moving along smoothly, without any bumps or troubles. My studies were progressing well. I made all the necessary arrangements to prepare for the barrister’s exam and left for Lincoln’s Inn in London. At home...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 275

News reached me that all was well at home. My father had firmly resolved that I should not return until I completed my studies. Having no other recourse, he resigned himself to the circumstances and settled down. Here, too, my studies were progressing with great enthusiasm. I was studying diligently. I had earned a reputation as a bright and intelligent student. Day by day, my circle of friends was growing.
I was even elected as an assistant secretary in the Indian Association. I was participating more frequently in meetings and gatherings there. In this way, my acquaintances were increasing as well.

It has been over a year since I arrived. If, by the grace of God, things continue like this for another two or three years, I hope I can return to my homeland in comfort. Dreaming such dreams, I whiled away my time.
At first, I often consulted with my private tutor. In class, I learned not only from the prescribed textbooks but also began reading many other works—books on social, political, and economic systems.
Barrister Parvateesam

Moreover, I found myself reading more and more books related to literature, the arts, and logic. When I was about to set out, I was happy, thinking everything was going well, but soon I began to see signs that all my dreams were about to be turned upside down. Reading the newspapers, I saw daily hints—sometimes subtle, sometimes blatant—that the world was on the brink of upheaval. In Russia, the Tsar’s empire was teetering on the edge of collapse. Germany was amassing tremendous power and making a colossal attempt to swallow the whole world. Wherever one looked, there was only unrest and uncertainty—no sign of peace or stability. What was going to happen? How would these terrifying circumstances unfold? Everyone, every single day, questioned themselves and each other, spending their time in fear and anxiety.

War was inevitable. Germany suddenly attacked France, advancing over the black soil as swiftly as a chariot on the open road, like the Juggernaut’s rath yatra, moving forward by the minute. One day, I read in the newspapers that Asquith, the Prime Minister of England, was coming to Edinburgh. That very night, England decided to go to war with Germany. They even made an official announcement. The next day, Asquith, the British Prime Minister, indeed arrived in Edinburgh.

A meeting was arranged in a hall called Usher Hall. Though the hall looked ordinary from the outside, inside it was fitted to comfortably seat six or seven thousand people. With great effort, I managed to secure a ticket to attend the meeting as the Joint Secretary of the Indian Association. The British Prime Minister reviewed the state of world affairs, explained the many reasons why they had to enter the war, and exhorted the people not to be afraid but to remain courageous and support the nation in every possible way. I had never heard such a magnificent speech in my life. Everyone present listened in such utter silence that they seemed afraid even to sigh.

When the speech ended, there was not even the usual applause; the audience simply stood up in silence. Immediately, the English national anthem was sung, and the meeting concluded. All the attendees remained standing in their places. The Prime Minister and his entourage stepped down from the platform and exited. They passed right by me. The Prime Minister came close to where I was standing.

As soon as he arrived, I was overcome with excitement and, full of devotion, greeted him in our traditional manner. He glanced at me, gave a gentle smile, and walked away. That smile left me floating in the clouds. Everyone in the hall filed out in a single line, without any commotion. Lost in thoughts of the President’s speech, I wandered into a world of imagination, unsure whether I was walking on the ground or soaring in the sky, and in that dreamlike state, I reached my lodgings without speaking to anyone.

The moment war was declared, the whole atmosphere changed in an instant. From the very next day, it was as if a cold wave had swept over everyone—enthusiasm cooled, joy faded from faces, and each person moved about with anxiety and fear, preoccupied with thoughts of what would become of us in the defense of the nation, and plagued by doubts about who would ultimately triumph. The usual calm, fearlessness, self-confidence, and courage were nowhere to be seen. It was all very strange. We had only read about wars in books—where would we have had any direct experience? For young people like me, the true nature of war, its consequences, and how it could transform daily life—all these things were now becoming part of our everyday experience.

Within a week or ten days, even the city of Edinburgh itself seemed to have changed—its very character and customs transformed, as if the whole town had turned into a battlefield and its people into soldiers. There was no sign of the usual bustle; everywhere you looked, there were only preparations for war. On the hills outside the city, all you could see were military drills. Every young man over eighteen was enlisting for war. Everyone—rich or poor, students or laborers—was abandoning their studies, their intelligence, their wealth, their earnings, with only one thought in mind: to save the country from this danger. The responsibility was ours and no one else’s. We must all go, shed our blood for the country, and even if we are all killed, we must trample Germany so far down that it can never rise again in this lifetime and achieve victory.

Cries of “Long live England! Rule Britannia! God save the King!” were all that could be heard. Smiles vanished from every face. All day long, airplanes began to roar overhead, filling the sky with their thunder.

Until now, it seems, airplanes had never been used in any previous war. Because of this, to everyone, this was something entirely new and, though it brought a certain fear, it also instilled a confidence in people’s hearts that with these very machines, we would achieve victory. The authorities decreed that not a single street should have lights at night. Warnings were sent out that in every house, thick black curtains must be drawn so that no light from inside would be visible through the windows. Even the headlights of cars that moved about at night were dimmed considerably, and the tops of those lights were painted black.

Almost every two or three furlongs, they constructed large underground shelters in a matter of minutes. Since bombs dropped from enemy planes flying above could be extremely dangerous, people were instructed not to panic, not to be afraid, but to calmly take shelter in these underground bunkers. When airplanes approached, a sound like a train whistle would be heard first. As soon as that sound was heard, all women, children, and the elderly were to rush into the shelters. Men on the roads were to drop flat wherever they were. All these arrangements were explained to the public, and the procedures to be followed in times of emergency were rehearsed like stage plays so that everyone would become accustomed to them.

In the big factories, the usual production of goods was halted, and instead, the manufacture of war materials began in earnest. Even elderly people over fifty started pressuring the authorities, insisting that they too be allowed to participate in the war effort, and if that was not possible, that they be put to use in some other way for the service of the nation. Thousands of young women joined the Red Cross to receive training and tend to the wounded on the battlefield. In this way, it seemed as if every living being, every object, every atom existed solely for the defense of the country. Observing these unprecedented, unimaginable, and extraordinary circumstances, I was left bewildered, wondering if such preparation and such indoctrination were truly necessary.

I could not understand why the flames of this war had spread to so many countries. I could not fathom why so many nations had plunged into war all at once. Still, one could not help but observe these events and circumstances as they unfolded. Until then, even those who had shown me great friendship, affection, and admiration...

These Englishmen began to look at us with suspicion and fear. In countless ways, they made it clear to us that we were outsiders here, that there was no place for us among them. No matter how much our people pleaded, saying, “We too will join the war effort, please include us,” not a single one of us was allowed to participate.

All of us began to feel that someone was secretly observing our every move and daily routine, every moment. When we tried to ask why this suspicion had arisen, not one of us could give a proper answer. Any letters that any of us received, no matter where they came from, were all opened at the post office without our knowledge, translated from our native languages into English, and then the envelopes were resealed so cleverly that we wouldn’t suspect a thing, before being distributed to us. There is no exaggeration in this; it is a well-known fact. Wherever we went, everyone looked at us as if we might join the enemy camp, or were about to. It became inevitable that we were seen in that light.

Suppose we couldn’t bear all this and wanted to finish our studies and return home—well, even that required a mountain of permissions and passports, and only after much rigmarole would anyone be allowed to leave.

While things were like this, news appeared in all the English newspapers that all the Indians were ready to join the war and help in whatever way they could. With that, the suspicion towards us lessened somewhat, and a measure of trust began to develop.

One day, while we were all in our classrooms at the college, we suddenly heard a terrifying noise, as if the whole universe had shattered at once. Our entire university shook. We thought it must be an earthquake. But it wasn’t. Then we thought it might be an air raid. But there was no sound of airplanes anywhere. Whatever it was, the whole town was thrown into panic, people sitting with their hearts in their hands, terrified for their lives. Again and again, two or three times, those dreadful sounds echoed.

Our professor stopped his lecture, bowed his head, closed his eyes, and stood as if praying to God. After the last of those noises, there was silence. For another five minutes, everyone sat in utter stillness. Then a servant came in, handed our professor a note, and left. The professor quietly told us all to go home, and dismissed us. We, trembling with fear and anxiety, one by one—

chapters.title: Wartime England
paragraphs: Without exchanging a single word with each other, we set off for our lodgings.

On the way, we discovered the source of that noise. Just a few miles from Edinburgh lies a port called Firth of Forth. All the warships tasked with guarding the Scottish coast were stationed there, poised for battle. Somehow, the Germans managed to discover this, and—without alerting the authorities—slipped in with their submarines. With a weapon called a torpedo, they struck the warships three times, sinking them before anyone could react, and then escaped fearlessly. News of this spread everywhere, sending waves of terror through the city. There was nothing we could do, so each of us simply returned to our lodgings.

Gradually, everyone became accustomed to the routines of wartime life. Even though fear never truly left us, and even though we knew that death was always near—closer than ever before—in these times, with this new style of warfare, death could appear not just on the battlefield, but anywhere, at any moment. Everyone understood this truth. Yet, with a kind of stubborn courage, with a certain resignation, the thought that we must destroy the enemy and protect our country, even if it costs our lives, took root in every heart. Some people did raise questions: Who is the enemy? Why do we consider them our enemy? But the officials who ought to answer these questions maintained a stony silence, declaring that our sole duty was to destroy the enemy. That was our dharma; all other debates and arguments were pointless, and none of our concern.

As we grew used to steering daily life along whatever path we could find, one night, around three in the morning, a signal was heard that enemy planes were approaching. The entire population, deep in sleep, young and old, men and women, jolted awake in terror. Before anyone could decide whether to change clothes or stay as they were, the planes arrived. Here and there, bombs were dropped, and before our own planes could even take off in response, the enemy aircraft had already fled. Many men and women, still in their nightclothes, rushed out into the streets in panic. They ran in all directions, searching for air-raid shelters.

An old man and an old woman were running in the middle of the road. Whether they were husband and wife or not, I couldn’t say, but just as they were dashing along, they suddenly stopped, as if struck by a memory, and in the very center of the road, they both collapsed with a thud, sprawling flat on the ground. People running this way and that paused in alarm—what happened, why have these two fallen like this, let’s hope they haven’t died of fright!—and hurried over to help them up. Within moments, hundreds of people had gathered around. Soon, with the support of those who had come to their aid, the old couple shakily got to their feet. As the crowd cheered “Hip hip hooray!” in delight, a siren wailed to announce that the air raid was over and everyone could safely return home. Hearing that, everyone heaved a collective sigh of relief, burst into laughter, and, feeling sheepish, brushed the dust off their clothes and made their way home.

In this manner, though a new kind of danger had descended upon us, people somehow managed to muster courage and pass the time. To assist the public during these air raids, a new breed of wardens had been appointed, and it was a novel sight to see them patrolling the streets day and night. People had reduced their usual evening strolls up the hills. Though daily life hadn’t come to a complete standstill, it had certainly become crippled in many ways.

We continued going to college as usual, and the lectures went on as before. One day, the whole town began selling small national flags, pinned with needles, in the streets. Everyone, young and old, bought them without exception. It was announced that all the proceeds would go to the war fund. We each bought a flag, pinned it to our coats, and attended our classes. While the lesson was underway, there was a bit of commotion at the back benches. Two young women from the right and two from the left, all dressed in clothes of the national flag’s colors and wearing soldier caps of the same hues, marched to the center of the class and began collecting donations for the war fund. In one hand, each of them held a plate filled with the same kind of little flags we had bought in the street.

With boxes sealed on all sides except for a hole at the top in both hands, they began collecting contributions from everyone. No one could quite tell how they had entered, who had brought them in, or how they had managed it. That was neither the time nor the place to interrogate them about how they had arrived, nor to get angry at them. Each person, as they saw fit, silently chuckled and dropped coins into the boxes.

Our professor, utterly bewildered, stood rooted to the spot, watching this scene as if he had turned to stone. Without leaving a single student out, those children collected from every student in the class, then nimbly climbed onto the platform and approached the professor. Two stood on this side, two on that, all four waving little flags, pinning them to his coat, and, grinning, extended the collection box towards him.

The professor, with a gentle smile, began patting his pockets. When he couldn’t find even a single penny in any pocket, he turned pale and stood there, not knowing what to say. The sharp-witted students, seeing his predicament, began tossing whatever pennies, half-shillings, and shillings they could find onto the platform with a whistle. The children, laughing, gathered up all the coins and sat down.

Our professor, watching this whole spectacle, wore a gentle smile on his face and said, “I think that’s enough for now. Let’s end the class here,” and walked gracefully into the room. All the students, clapping and laughing, some helping the children collect the coins, and the rest of us walked out.

Here, no matter what happens or what mischief occurs, the professors never lose their composure. They do not display anger. Whatever difficult situation arises, they face it calmly and deal with the students without hurting their feelings. When they are teaching, they finish their lecture two or three minutes before the bell rings, so there’s no need to wait for the bell to signal the end of class.

One day, a funny incident occurred. That day, it was the English class. At twelve o’clock, the class is dismissed and everyone goes for refreshments, lunch, or home. That day, the professor was so absorbed in his teaching, delivering the lesson beautifully, that no one noticed the time. It was already past twelve. Some students, growing restless, began to stir and make a bit of noise...

They started it. The noise hadn’t yet reached the professor. The lecture continued for another ten minutes. The students began to stamp their feet on the gallery above. The professor looked at the students with a questioning glance, as if to ask, “What is this noise?” In response, they only increased the racket. Then he understood what was going on and said, “My dear boys, I seem to have lost track of time and kept you here longer than I should have. But I still have a few more pearls left to scatter. Afterwards, do as you please.” (I am sorry, Gentlemen, but I have a few more pearls to throw away), he said with a smile.

There is a proverb in English: “throwing pearls before swine.” If you scatter pearls before pigs, will they know what they are? Will they recognize them as pearls, as precious things? The moment the professor uttered those words, the hall fell completely silent. Not a soul stirred. No one even dared to breathe too loudly.

With a gentle smile, the professor continued his lecture for another quarter of an hour and then said, “Boys, you may now go home.” He added, “Unable to bear your hunger, I became so absorbed in my lesson that I made you sit here and suffer for so long. Please, don’t mind it—go home, and since you’re so late, eat double your usual amount, even if you forget about the war!” With that, he cheerfully walked into his room.

That’s the custom here. This is the kind of affection and respect that exists between professors and students. In our country, it’s hard to even imagine what sort of severe punishment would be meted out to students who behaved so mischievously.

Here, many professors possess a great deal of wit, humor, and presence of mind. The custom here is that if, for any reason, a professor cannot come to class, he writes on a slip of paper, “I am unable to take your class at this hour,” and pins the notice to the board outside the classroom. One day, such a notice appeared for us: “The Professor will not be able to meet his classes today.”
As we saw this and were heading outside, one mischievous fellow—

chapters.title: The Great War
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

A certain boy, thinking himself clever, decided to play a prank on the professor. He went up to the notice board and, in the word “Classes,” neatly erased the first letter, “C.” What remained was “Lasses,” which, as everyone knows, means “girls.”

The next day, the professor saw this, and without the slightest anger, without uttering a single word of reproach to anyone, simply erased the second letter, “L,” and went on with his lesson as usual, unperturbed.

Many students, not having glanced at the notice board, were anxiously whispering among themselves, “Did the professor see it or not? If he saw, didn’t he get angry?” As soon as class was over, everyone rushed in a single file to the notice board. Now, with the “L” gone, only “Asses” remained.

To the professor’s clever move, we had no counter; we hung our heads in shame and quietly slunk away. We were all amazed at how deftly and wittily the professor handled such childish mischief. We went away, inwardly applauding his presence of mind.

Recently, one day, my friend pulled off a prank none of us had ever imagined or expected. He had already made a name for himself in another incident before. Among all the Andhras here, he is the most lively and talkative. Not only that, he is fond of humor and possesses a sharp wit.

He was a man of many talents. He could charm and captivate everyone with his words. A lover of the Andhra language, and something of a poet. He possessed a melodious voice that could sing enchantingly. Yet, he was a thorough mischief-maker. All day long, he would pick on someone or the other, making them cry one moment and laugh the next. With this penchant for pranks, he would keep us all on edge, making us laugh till we were nearly dead. This great man was Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya. He would often come to my room, chat for a while, and then leave. From the very first day he saw me, he held me in great affection and regard. When Sri Ananda Coomaraswamy visited and I unexpectedly recited some verses from the Bhagavatam at the gathering, his fondness for me increased tenfold.

One night, around ten o’clock, as I was studying with great concentration and dedication, Gopalakrishnayya burst in, flustered and anxious, with a most grave expression on his face, and knocked on my door. Who could be coming at this hour? Wondering, I got up and opened the door, and he immediately stepped inside.

“Babu, quickly get dressed! Our Rao has suddenly fallen terribly ill. He’s suffering a lot and doesn’t even know what’s happening to him. You must run there at once. I’ll go and rouse another ten of our friends, and bring the doctor too,” he said, not waiting for any response from me, and dashed out into the street.

I, who had been standing there, collapsed into my chair, utterly bewildered. This Rao was our friend, also studying to become a barrister, and was to finish his studies in a few months and return to our homeland. He was a man of five and a half feet, somewhat stout, and among us all, he appeared the most robust. What could have happened to this thunderbolt of a man, I wondered anxiously. Hastily, I put on my suit and rushed out into the street. I was determined to get there quickly, but I couldn’t go as fast as I’d hoped. Somehow, I reached Rao’s room, and, just as Gopalakrishnayya had done, knocked on the door in a panic. Inside, I could hear voices speaking softly. Someone opened the door. I stepped inside, frozen in place, utterly dumbfounded. There was Rao, sitting and laughing like a black diamond.
Barrister Parvateesam

Meanwhile, he was playing cards with a few others. Around them, seven or eight people stood watching the spectacle. At first, they pretended not to notice, but then someone raised his head and exclaimed, “Hey! What’s this? Isn’t that our Parvateesam? And look at him—so relaxed, as if he’s at home!”

At that moment, Mr. Rao threw down his cards, sprang up, strode over to me, and gave me such a slap on the back that I nearly toppled forward. “Well, Parvateesam bhai! What brings you here at this hour, looking so battered? At your age, when all sensible young men should be immersed in their studies, you seem to have wandered off to some den of pleasure, as if you’ve just come back from a movie! If this is how you carry on, my boy, it won’t do at all. We elders are here precisely to keep an eye on youngsters like you. Your people sent you here with the confidence that we’d watch over you. From the beginning, we’d hoped you’d act responsibly and focus on your studies, so we relaxed our supervision a bit. But now, you’ve taken advantage of our leniency and plunged into these romantic escapades! You’ve given us no choice but to keep a closer watch on you again,” he said, motioning for me to sit down.

I didn’t know what to think, seeing all this. Just then, another young man opened the door and said, “What’s the matter, Mr. Parvateesam? You’ve come in such a rush! Seeing your anxious face, I was quite frightened myself, I must say!”

No sooner had he finished speaking than there was another knock at the door—just as I’d feared. Four or five more people entered, greeted me, and then, as Mr. Rao and the others greeted them in turn, they all turned pale and stood speechless. By then, I’d recovered from my anxiety and asked, “So, gentlemen, have you all come here for the same reason as I have?”

One of them replied, “Yes, sir, it seems so. In fact—” he began, but before he could finish, another chimed in, “Mr. Rao, are you fully recovered now? Poor fellow, you rushed off on your journey, only to end up back in bed! You’ve given us quite a scare, so we came to check on your well-being. Ah, what good people you are!”
At this, everyone burst out laughing. Mr. Rao leaned back in his chair, his belly shaking with laughter, and we couldn’t help but laugh along with him.
“At this hour in April—”

“Is today the first of the month or not?” someone asked. “No, it isn’t,” replied another. “So then, that scoundrel, that rascal, that seven-faced trickster—he’s nowhere to be seen! No matter where he is, even if he’s hiding in the mountain caves or burrowed deep under the sea, we must drag him out, thrash him, and grind his bones to dust!” declared one fellow, his face contorted in rage, as if he were some modern-day Dushasana.

Rao garu, witnessing all this, was brimming with anxiety. He pleaded with the landlady, who, poor soul, was either asleep or in some other state, “Please, call her and make her serve us some tea! Otherwise, we’ll have to leave him to his fate. There’s no sign of any instructions, and if we don’t get our tea, I won’t be able to sleep tonight!” he begged most pitiably.

Though the landlady seemed quite annoyed at first, in the end she burst out laughing, counted the number of souls present, and, just as Rao garu had hoped, within ten minutes—if not five—she brought out some sort of tea and biscuits. What could we do? Whoever brought it, whatever it was, we had no choice but to accept it and make the best of it. After finishing our tea, we advised Rao garu to get a good night’s sleep and warned him that inviting such troubles was not good for his health, then went our separate ways. In English, this is called a “practical joke.”
The next morning, I resolved to catch hold of Gopalakrishnayya as soon as I saw him. But for a whole week, he was nowhere to be found.
Barrister Parvateesam
He survived.

There’s a small incident that happened quite some time ago, which I forgot to mention. There’s nothing particularly special about it, but I’m telling it just for amusement’s sake. After I came here, apart from the naming ceremony that took place during my childhood back in my village, I had to undergo another naming ceremony here—without any auspicious day or grand celebration.

The custom here is that, just as in our country, everyone has two names: a family name and a personal name. However, in this country, the personal name comes first and the family name comes last. In our country, or rather in our state, the family name comes first and the personal name comes last. Moreover, most of our family names are either the names of the villages our ancestors once lived in, or titles earned by our elders. This practice, I learned from the North Indian students here, is also common in some regions of the North, where the personal name comes first and the family name follows.

I noticed that some of our own people, after coming here, started putting their personal name first and moving the family name to the end. At first, I didn’t think I needed to do the same, but eventually, I had no choice. The reason was, whenever I told anyone my name, not only did they not understand it the first time, but even after telling them ten times, they still couldn’t pronounce it and suffered greatly trying. Some called me “Tesam,” others said “Teesam.” A few, in their mischief, called me “Mr. Sam Tea.” My landlady and others couldn’t even manage that much and simply called me “Sam.” Many people got used to calling me just “Sam.” Later, even in the post office, the postman struggled to pronounce my name and had a hard time figuring it out.

So, I thought, why go through all this trouble? It would be better to change my name according to the custom here, putting my family name at the end. So I did just that. But even that change didn’t help the people here. I changed my name to P. Y. Murph. Yet, even then, some called me “Vemar,” others “Morvay,” and some “Moore,” inventing all sorts of distorted versions. Unable to bear these ear-torturing sounds, I thought it over and made another small change. The family name—

Until now, I used to write my name in English as “Vemur.” Then I thought it would be nice to make a small change to it, so I switched to “P.V. More.” But that brought its own set of troubles. Some people started murmuring, “What is this ‘More’?” and others began to ask, “What does ‘More’ mean?” So, this time, I decided to tweak the spelling a bit. I changed it to “Mor,” thinking everything would go smoothly now. But alas, that was not to be. The word “Vemur” kept echoing in my mind, and I was delighted to drop the “Ve” and keep just “Mor.” But I forgot that in English, “More” is pronounced as “Moar.” From then on, some people started teasing me: “So you are now ‘more’—what more?” and “Mister More, we’ll be sorry when you are no more!”

Oh, the shame! Whichever way I turned, there was nothing but trouble. I suppose all this happened because I didn’t consult an astrologer or perform a Ganesh puja before changing my name. These were the thoughts that kept me awake all night.

The next morning, as I was heading to the university, I stopped by a bookshop to look for a poetry anthology I needed. While searching, I came across a book by the poet Dharman Moor. The moment I saw the name on the cover, without even flipping through the pages, I was struck by a sudden inspiration—how to choose a name without any complications! Without wasting a moment, I bought the book, hurried straight to the printing office, and got my new visiting cards printed as “P.V. Moor.” I showed them to my friends, and they all approved, saying, “This is a good one!”

Over time, I realized that such small changes can sometimes be quite beneficial. Whatever the benefit, now everyone here—locals and our own people—can pronounce it easily. Letters are reaching me on time, without any confusion.

Recently, a little prank took place. Nothing much—just that we all got together and made a young fellow cry for a whole evening by playing a trick on him. Still, why lie about such a small matter? I can’t say whether I feel proud or ashamed to admit that I was the mastermind behind the whole setup and the mischief. After all, that’s all we’re capable of, isn’t it? Find someone a little less clever than us, a little more fun for everyone, and—
Barrister Parvateesam
In a moment, we forget how, not so long ago, someone else made us cry in just the same way.

It’s been about a year since a young man from our region—a very clever fellow, yet utterly innocent—arrived here as quietly and neatly as a jasmine flower, without telling anyone at home, either choosing an auspicious day or not bothering about such things. When I first came here, Raju became my companion in adversity; in the same way, I became a friend in need to this young man. I managed to get him a room close to mine and helped him with whatever he needed. Poor fellow, the respect and regard he developed for me is beyond description. I can’t see any particular reason for it. We simply thought it was something special about the time we met and left it at that. The poor chap would tell me everything without the slightest hesitation or reserve. In fact, not just with me—he seemed the sort who would confide in anyone. That was his nature. His people hailed from the Godavari district—wealthy landlords, and he was the youngest of three brothers. Swept here by a westerly wind, so to speak, he settled down and began his studies. I advised him to do what I was doing—to study for an M.A. and become a barrister.

He agreed and joined the college. Since then, time has been passing smoothly, and our friendship has only grown. One day, an envelope arrived addressed to him, its edges smeared with turmeric, at the address of the Indian Association. I found it when I went to the association, as I did every day. Seeing the letter, and recalling our customs, I guessed it must be a wedding invitation. I took the letter and slipped it into my pocket, intending to give it to my friend Ramana later, but then forgot all about it. I spent some time in the association’s library, then went to the university, and after classes, returned home. After finishing my meal and other routines, I went back to the college for afternoon classes and returned again. All this while, I had completely forgotten about the letter. Suddenly, I remembered it, slapped my forehead, and hurried to my friend’s room, where Ramana was getting ready to go out. I made him sit down and said, “I’ve brought you some good news! There’s a wedding in your family—why don’t you go and...?”

I asked, “So, are you going to attend that auspicious event and return, or what?” He turned pale and stammered, “What are you saying, sir! Who is there left in our house to get married now? Even the youngest one—myself—has already been married off,” he blurted out, letting it slip.
“What’s this you’re saying! You never mentioned it all this time. You’re impossible, always so secretive! I thought you were an innocent fellow all along.”

“You’re right, sir. What did I do in this? My people got me married. I forgot all about it and came here, nice and quiet. When I saw you, you seemed like gods to me, and I forgot to mention it. It was a mistake, sir, nothing more—no other misfortune,” he said, putting on a foolish face.

“Then what’s this auspicious letter about?” I asked. “I’m handing you this letter now, but it actually arrived this evening. I picked it up thinking I’d give it to you first thing in the morning, but I forgot until now—don’t think anything of it,” I said.

He took the letter in confusion, tore it open, and sat there in a daze, speechless and lost in thought. I couldn’t understand why he was so absent-minded after seeing the auspicious letter, or why he didn’t look happy. After a moment’s pause, I asked, “What’s the matter, Ramana? Why are you sitting like that? So, who’s getting married after all? You don’t have to go now, do you? Why are you so worried?”
“It’s not worry, sir. I’m not going anywhere, sir. I just don’t know how to tell you,” he replied. “My father wrote this letter,” he said, handing it to me.

I took the letter, wondering what strange news it could contain, and quickly read it. It wasn’t about a wedding, nor about any slaps or scoldings. The gist of the letter was this: My Ramana’s wife, Mrs. Satyavati, has become rajaswala (menstruating). Since the star under which this occurred is somewhat inauspicious, a shanti (ritual for peace) must be performed. So, his father wrote asking him to take a week’s leave and come home immediately.

I burst out laughing. Well, isn’t this something! This is even better news than a marriage for you. The moment you saw this, you must have started imagining the next set of ceremonies in your mind out of sheer joy.

“So that’s the reason for your absent-mindedness. Very well, as they say, ‘Auspicious deeds should be done swiftly.’ Shall I look for a good time for your journey right now? And next time, if your father writes asking you to come home, why not take care of the next auspicious event as well, so everyone will be happy? It’ll save you some expenses too,” I said.

He put on a pitiful face and said, “What is this, sir, even you are making me cry like this? Why did my father even write this letter? He wants me to take a week’s leave and come home. He says I can settle all matters in the village during that week and then return here. How foolish our people are! Poor father, he has forgotten that it took me nearly a month just to reach here,” he said, and was about to tear up the letter in a huff. I stopped him, snatched the letter away, and said with a laugh, “Never tear up a letter, my friend! Leave it as it is, or I’ll have to keep a close watch on you. When I write my autobiography in the future, this will serve as a record, you see.” He hung his head in embarrassment, unable to say a word, as if he himself had become a young maiden.

Still laughing, I said, “Let’s meet again. You seem to be heading somewhere, and I’ve interrupted your journey. But now, you’re not going back to our country, are you?” Without waiting for his reply, I strode ahead. From behind, he called out, “That is for you to decide, sir. I can disregard my father’s words, but your command is one I must obey.”

“Very well, then. I’ll think it over and let you know my decision soon,” I replied grandly and walked away. The journey I had planned to take elsewhere was abandoned, and instead, I went quietly to Breadhills, played a little golf alone, and then sat in a trance on a bench.

Suddenly, like a flash of lightning, an idea struck me. The more I thought about it, the more wonderful and astonishing it seemed—it would surprise and delight everyone! I resolved to carry out this plan without letting a second soul know of it, and, chuckling to myself, I floated home on a cloud of excitement and anticipation.

The next day, I had invitations typed up, politely requesting all my Telugu friends to kindly attend a tea party at Nagadi that evening. I sent these invitations to ten or twelve of my acquaintances. I spent the whole day in a flurry of preparations for the event. Thinking my friends would enjoy it, I even made some pulihora with my own hands. I prepared a sweet as well, and bought two kinds of cakes and biscuits from the shop. This

Seeing all the commotion, the lady of our house turned pale and asked, “What is this, Mr. Same? Why are you making such a fuss? Have you perhaps fixed your marriage, or have you won a prize in the Derby races? Tell me! We too will rejoice.”
I replied in Telugu, “No, it’s not about my marriage, nor is it your concern.”
She looked bewildered and asked, “What? What? What is it? What’s going on?”
I reassured her, “You’ll know by evening.”

By exactly four o’clock in the evening, my circle of friends, eager to find out what this party was all about and why it was being held, arrived promptly, not allowing even a moment’s delay. Before any of them, our Ravana also arrived and, while I was arranging everything, asked, “What’s all this fuss about, sir?”

After I had set the table with everything except the coffee I had prepared, and everyone had finished eating, I brought out a plate of sweet delicacies and placed it on the table. Then, standing up, I addressed them:

“Brothers! You must be wondering about all this commotion and this party. Though it may not be entirely just to keep you in suspense all this while, there’s really no harm done, is there? So, I took the liberty. Trusting that you will forgive me, and fearing that if I don’t tell you now, you might never forgive me—or worse, commit some atrocity—I am now daring to reveal the secret.
The other day, this auspicious letter arrived. I took out the reply that had come for Ramana. He was dumbfounded.

‘Among our friends here, there is a young man who was recently married. This auspicious letter announces that his wife has had her first menstruation. By now, she must have completed her ritual bath. Due to postal delays, this news has reached us a little late. Back home, there would have been feasts and celebrations for the in-laws and relatives. At such a joyous time, the groom too should have been there, rejoicing and celebrating. Instead, he is stuck here, alone among these stalwart men, burning with embarrassment and misery. Feeling that it is our duty to cheer him up, I took it upon myself to organize this event and invited you all here. I trust that you will join me in celebrating and blessing the young lady on her first menstruation.’”

I hope you understand. Especially at times like these, our elders say that whatever sweets are prepared, whether many or few, should be distributed primarily among the married women. Since it is difficult here to distinguish who among the womenfolk is married and who is not, I thought it best not to invite any of them. So, for these few moments, if you all consider yourselves as married women, then the groom here—though feeling a bit shy—can distribute this sweet as a substitute for the traditional treat, and sweeten all your mouths with it. “Come, Ramana,” I said.

He, who was already shriveled up with embarrassment, became even more bashful at this invitation. He looked as if he would melt away and disappear. Seeing his plight, I took pity on him, gently lifted him up, and together we took the plate—yes, the very plate used for the auspicious offering—and distributed the sweets, giving one piece to each person.
“Havva is not available here, so I had to make do with almonds for preparing this sweet,” I announced.

Amidst the applause and cheers of the guests, everyone declared that the party was magnificent, that it would surely have a special place and distinction in history, and that it was a truly original idea. All my friends praised me, patted Ramana on the back, and said, “The next event will be conducted soon, Parvatisham garu, don’t be afraid.” Thus reassured and blessed, everyone cheerfully went their separate ways.

chapters.title: Examinations
paragraphs: Only Ravana and I remained. Tears welled up in his eyes.
“Guruji, is this really fair of you?” he asked plaintively.

“Oh, you fool! There’s nothing unfair in this. It’s only affection and fondness for you that’s behind it. Not just me, but all these people who have come here—however much affection they have for me, they have just as much for you too. So, don’t take it to heart,” I comforted him.
He hugged me, overcome with tears of joy, unable to speak, pressed my hands together in a namaste, and left without another word.
No sooner had he stepped outside than the lady of the house and her daughters came dashing into my room.
“What’s the matter, sir? What’s going on? You must tell us! We’ve been sitting here holding our breath since earlier,” they demanded.

“All right then, sit down,” I said, and set before them the remaining cakes and biscuits, along with a dish I had prepared myself, warning them not to be shy and to help themselves. Then, at leisure, I explained to them in detail the customs of our country, the natural tendencies of our women, the commotion our people make over such matters, and so on. They listened to all this in astonishment, giggling as they left.
At the doorway, the youngest girl turned back, looked at me, and laughed.
“What is it? Are you suspicious about something too?” I asked.
Without replying, she dashed off to their room.

As for victories and defeats in the war, not only is it hard to decide whose side fortune will favor, but even to guess seems impossible for anyone. Many have begun to suspect that, whoever wins, it may not necessarily be the English. In many theaters of war, the English have had to face unexpected and disastrous outcomes. In the Turkish regions, they had to endure a defeat even more crushing than the naval disaster that befell them earlier in Scotland. Because of this, Winston Churchill, who was then the First Lord of the Admiralty,
Barrister Parvateesam

...and so he had to retire from his post. There were numerous criticisms that the entire conduct of the war strategy was unsatisfactory, and as a result, even the Prime Minister, a man named Asquith, had to step down from his position. I believe it was around this time that the political parties had to go to elections. Until then, Lloyd George, who was in Asquith’s own party, began an enormous campaign against him. Never before had such campaigns been seen. I had not even read about anything like it. But witnessing it firsthand today felt like a great enlightenment.

Eager to hear Lloyd George speak, I went with some friends to the nearby city of Glasgow. Compared to the meeting I had attended in Edinburgh for Asquith, this was even more grand. Instead of being held in a hall, this meeting was organized in a vast open ground. People had gathered in countless numbers—so many that it was impossible to estimate. Within a few minutes of our arrival, the meeting began. The chairman spoke for a few minutes and then invited Mr. Lloyd George to deliver his speech.

Judging by the size of the local people, one must say he was a bit short in stature. Behind his white mustache, a gentle smile was always visible.
