As soon as he stood up, the entire gathering fell silent. The silence was so profound that you could have heard a pin drop. His speech flowed like a mighty river. His words thundered like a lion’s roar, reaching far and wide.

In the middle of his speech, while describing the circumstances of the day and the aspirations of the people, he said, “Distant India is demanding Home Rule. I, too, am saying that Wales should have Home Rule.” Up to that point, the audience had been listening in complete silence. Suddenly, from among the listeners, a man stood up and shouted at the top of his lungs, “Home Rule for Hell!” The shout was so loud it shook the entire assembly.

With that, chaos erupted in the meeting. Many voices could be heard shouting, “Throw out this rowdy! This scoundrel! This wretch! This agent of the enemy! This drunkard! Throw him out!” The cries of thousands rang out. Many feared that the meeting might have to be called off then and there. Everyone stood up. Even the chairman was unable to calm the crowd.
At that moment, Lloyd George said, “Ladies and gentlemen! Just a moment—”

Have patience. Why are you all getting so agitated? What is so wrong in what that great man said? Why are you so angry and upset? To me, it all seems quite reasonable. Turning to the mischief-maker, I said, “Sir! What you have said is certainly worth considering. As for the rest, let’s discuss it later.” As I was about to resume my speech, the entire audience burst into laughter so hearty that it seemed their stomachs would split, and even the sky itself trembled with their mirth and thunderous applause. For another half hour, my lecture continued without any further interruptions. As for the mischief-maker, he simply vanished—who knows what became of him. I doubt I’ll ever witness such a meeting again in my life. No matter how great an orator may be, when he is interrupted mid-flow, how many can respond so calmly, so gracefully, striking back at the troublemaker without letting him feel the sting? Only the rarest can manage such a feat. As I walked home, I kept thinking about his witty retort, and thus I returned to Edinburgh.
In the end, in the elections, Asquith—renowned throughout England as a peerless leader—was defeated, and Lloyd George took his place. Such are the strange turns of fate.

The war, day by day, was taking on a monstrous, terrifying form, shaking the entire world. The battles on land were dreadful enough, but those raging in the seas and skies were even more fearsome. Whenever people went out during the day, there was no certainty they would return home alive. At night, there was no telling whether those who went to bed would rise in the morning or remain forever in eternal sleep. With the constant roar of airplanes overhead—never knowing whether they were ours or the enemy’s—our ears rang, our hearts pounded, and every day was spent in terror. Even essential items in the market became scarce, and prices soared sky-high, racing alongside the airplanes.

Each morning, upon opening the newspapers, we would read that the Germans had occupied several hundred villages, or that they had destroyed some towns, or that somewhere far off, their submarines had sunk a few ships.
Barrister Parvateesam

Apart from news that hundreds of bombs had been dropped from airplanes on certain towns, and that thousands of soldiers, sailors, and ordinary civilians had perished, nothing else was visible. It would not be an exaggeration to say that, at all times, the only sounds to be heard were the thunder of cannons and the explosions of bombs—no other noise reached the ears. Day after day, moment after moment, people lived with their lives in their hands, gripped by terror; it was truly astonishing to see how they endured such dreadful, fearsome times.
Such an unbearable, terrifying, and dreadful situation was unprecedented; never before had the entire world experienced such a thing simultaneously, nor had we even heard of such an event.

The strange thing was that, even in the midst of this dire and dreadful state, people seemed to have grown accustomed to these bizarre circumstances. They appeared to have forgotten that death was stalking them every day, every moment, and carried on as if nothing was amiss. Even when some poisonous gas or sudden storm swept in and caused panic and confusion among the populace, as soon as it passed, people treated it as just another incident, and this war too, they believed, would end today or tomorrow. With the conviction that, in the end, victory would be theirs, everyone seemed to comfort themselves and pass the time with courage. Each person, to the extent possible, continued their daily routines without change. Young men still went to their colleges; they continued their sports and games as usual. In the cinemas and theatres, everything proceeded as if nothing had happened.

However, it was noticeable that plays and songs which could help destroy the enemy, inspire courage in the people, and rouse the youth to war, were being performed more frequently. There was no count of how many patriotic plays had been launched to stir national feeling. And, as per their usual habit, in the evenings, as soon as their daily activities were done, young men and women, no matter how dark it was, and even if there were no streetlights, did not refrain from going out. In that darkness, without going too far, embraces and kisses would conveniently take place wherever they happened to be.
One night, around nine o’clock, people were strolling along the roads, chatting cheerfully, laughing, lovers...

Just as lovers were embracing and kissing, a terrifying siren wailed in the distance, signaling the approach of enemy airplanes. People on the street hurriedly turned towards their homes. The lovers, struck with fear and anxiety, clung to each other even more tightly, as if wondering what fate awaited them in the next moment, merging into one another as closely as possible. At that instant, a window on an upper floor burst open with a bang, and the head of an elderly man appeared, craning out. He shouted, “Hey! Don’t you have any sense? If you don’t rush home quickly, you’ll end up dying right here. If you survive, you can resume these embraces later. Do you understand? Are you listening?” he bellowed.

Right below that window, a young man, still holding his beloved in a tight embrace, looked up and replied, “Grandfather, please pull your head back inside, or else the moonbeams reflecting off your bald head might serve as a beacon to guide the airplanes.”

Passersby, as well as those standing nearby, burst into laughter. The old man, furious, shouted, “Just you wait! I’m coming down. I’ll set you straight. Scoundrels!” With that, he yanked his head inside and slammed the window shut.
Some of the young men and women wondered if he might really come down and cause trouble, and began to quietly slip away.
The maiden, still nestled in the young man’s arms, said, “I feel like crying. Your cleverness! Come, let’s go over there. If he really comes, he’ll ruin us. He’s my father, after all.”
Barrister Parvateesam
“It seems you haven’t noticed what’s going on,” he said, startled by those words.

“Oh my goodness, hurry up! Why are you walking so slowly?” he shouted, grabbing the girl by the wing and dragging her along with a flurry of steps. I watched all this from the archway of our street, enjoying the spectacle so much that I forgot to go inside. By the time I remembered, the two daughters of our landlady came out, each grabbed one of my arms, and pulled me inside.

How do these people live so fearlessly even in such terrifying circumstances? I wondered in amazement. But then, what else can they do? Instead of living in constant fear and dying of a broken heart, it’s better to accept such things as a part of daily life and carry on as best as possible. With these thoughts, I sat down.

The next morning, around nine o’clock, an invitation arrived, announcing that there would be a meeting that evening at the Indian Association to review these emergency circumstances, and that everyone must attend without fail. What is this call? What is the purpose of reviewing these situations? What benefit could come from it? Pondering all these questions in various ways, I went to the meeting in the evening, right on time.

All my friends were there, and nearly all the Indians in the area had filled the hall. Just the previous day, the newspapers had reported that a certain barrister named M.K. Gandhi had arrived in London, and that the Indian Red Cross Society was being established to help the Indian soldiers who had been wounded and disabled on the battlefield.

At the meeting, our own Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya presided. He gave a grave speech, broadly reviewing the war situation and declaring that it was foolish, unnecessary, and even laughable for India—a country with no real connection to the conflict—to plunge into war and suffer losses of life and wealth beyond its means. He urged that, even now, we should open our eyes, recognize our true situation, and find a way to extricate ourselves from this war as our first duty. After that, he said, our second duty should be to continue the struggle for our own liberation from servitude.
His speech left many of the young men present there thrilled and inspired. Afterwards, we discussed our current situation and the person called Gandhi—

There was a long and heated debate on whether or not we should join the Red Cross Society being organized and cooperate with them. In the end, the meeting concluded without any decision or resolution being reached.

After this meeting, the atmosphere in the Indian Association also grew increasingly somber. The previous enthusiasm and fearlessness seemed to have vanished from everyone. Each person began to walk around with a face that suggested he alone was bearing the entire burden of the war. News kept coming in that even in the Red Cross, started by Gandhi, not as many people were joining, nor as quickly, as he had hoped. Gandhi, through the newspapers, kept issuing frequent reminders that it was an honor and a duty for all Indians to join this voluntary service corps.

About a week passed like this. Then, Mr. Duggirala Gopala Krishnayya invited a dozen of his close Andhra friends to his house for tea. I am very proud to say that I was one among them. The tea, drinks, and snacks were finished quickly and in silence. None of us were used to such gatherings, and each of us wondered to himself why this great man had called us together. As soon as the refreshments were done and the landlady had come in, cleared away the cups and cleaned the table, Mr. Gopala Krishnayya locked the door. This left us all astonished.

Without sitting down or offering any preamble, he began, “I know you are all wondering why I have called you here today. A week ago, unrest began in our Association. We cannot yet imagine the consequences of this war and its impact on subject countries like India. The seriousness of these circumstances does not seem to have disturbed any of us sufficiently. We are all thinking this is just a passing wind, a storm that will blow over as quickly as it came. Already, we cannot even fathom the horrors of the slaughter that has taken place in Europe. In this carnage, our Indian—”
Barrister Parvateesam

Our rulers even brought sugarcane here and used it as firewood in the thousands, or perhaps even in the hundreds of thousands. Yet, it seems we neither noticed nor cared about this fact. From this distant land, the cries and commotion that began in our own country may not reach our ears. But just because we do not hear them, it is by no means reason for us to rejoice, thinking all is peaceful there.

The intense mental agony I am experiencing now is something I cannot begin to describe. No one else can truly understand this pain. It is unbearable, unfathomable. That is why I have come to a decision. I have called you here to share it with you, to seek your cooperation, or at the very least, your sympathy. The country is calling me—I feel it is absolutely necessary for me to be there. Not that I alone can go and accomplish something great. But I simply cannot stay here any longer. My duty is to go there. If not today, if I live and am well, I can always resume my studies another day.

If any of you are feeling the same mental unrest as I am, I pray that you will come with me. If even one or two of us set out with pure resolve and unwavering determination, hundreds will join us there. With them, thousands, and behind them, lakhs will follow—this is my belief.”
Before he could finish his speech, one of my friends asked, “That’s all very well, but have you at least thought of any concrete plan of action, even a small one?”

“It’s good that you asked. I cannot give you all the details. But broadly, I have an idea. I plan to go, gather ten or a hundred people, and in every town, attack the police stations, seize their weapons, and render them helpless and powerless. That is my intention.”

Some among us laughed. Some remained silent. A few wanted to say something but lacked the courage and simply sat quietly. As for me, being a little impatient, I blurted out without thinking, “Have you considered that after attacking two police stations, you might not even get the chance to reach the third before your game is up?”
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 303

I asked, “Did you anticipate any reaction if things didn’t go as planned?” He looked at me, smiled gently, and said, “You’re a clever one! I almost forgot your point. I’ll answer you later. But shouldn’t you also join me?” I replied, “Would I be so fortunate? I can’t even imagine my circumstances ever affording me such an opportunity. Still, if you go ahead and start your movement, perhaps I’ll come running after you. I can’t say anything for sure now. But do count me as your first disciple. If you lead the way, I doubt I’ll be able to set foot here again.” He said, “Very well! So be it! But all of you, please think carefully about this and let me know any suggestions you have—I have no objection to accepting them. I’m very glad that you all responded to my call and came here today. I hope that, just as you have come today at my invitation, someday in the future, you will also come running to serve our country’s cause. Farewell.”

Everyone rose silently, bade their farewells, and went their separate ways. For a week or ten days, we did not meet again. The war was growing more dreadful by the day. It had become difficult for anyone from our country to come here, and even harder for anyone here to return home. For whatever reason, our Gopalakrishnayya’s journey did not proceed. Along with that, my own eagerness subsided.

Life here, in some respects, appears strange and contrary to our customs. Here, it is common to see young men and women, even those of some age, mingling freely and without hesitation. They make acquaintances with strangers very easily. In large families, it is not considered proper for people to speak with each other unless they have been introduced by someone they both know. But how can such formalities be maintained in middle-class or lower families? We all belong to middle-class families here. Therefore, when men or women wish to speak with someone new, there is no need for a formal introduction—they can simply walk up to the person, say “Good morning” or “Good evening,” and then, with an “Excuse me,” strike up a conversation right to their face.
However, making the acquaintance of women is not quite so easy. For men...

Women seem to have endless doubts. That’s why, when speaking with them, one must be careful—if you don’t want to talk, or if you wish to extricate yourself politely, you have to think a little ahead and behind before uttering a word. Even among the middle class, there are two types: the upper-middle and the lower-middle, who are more or less alike. So, it’s quite easy to make acquaintances among men and women of this class.

Here, rather than with our college girls, it’s common to befriend the young women you see out and about—going with them to parks, cinemas, and plays, spending time together quite intimately. Everyone is used to this. While some of these introductions happen through friends, most occur without any intermediaries at all.

On a holiday or some other leisurely time, if you stroll along the street, some young women will look you straight in the face. Perhaps they think we are foreigners, or maybe they’re simply curious about what it would be like to talk to us. When we look back at them, some bold young women, without any shyness, might themselves take the initiative and say “Hello!” If they’re a bit timid, they might only respond if we greet them first. Once that “Hello” is stretched into conversation, before you know it, you’ve taken ten steps together—like “friendship in seven days”—and you might end up going to the hills or to the cinema together. You can deepen the acquaintance as much as you like. Some people even share certain experiences with each other, or simply confine themselves to exchanging stories. Even if there’s a little awkwardness, no one makes a fuss about it.

Once, during a holiday, I went to a seaside village. There, I became acquainted with a girl. Later, one day here in town, I happened to run into her in the bazaar. We saw each other and exchanged a gentle smile.
“Well, sir! How are you? See how small the world is!” she said.
I laughed and replied, “They say not only is the world small, but it’s also round.”
“That’s why, no matter where we wander, we can meet again in this very place,” she said.
“Are you still working here?” I asked.
“What else can I do? It’s inevitable,” she replied.
“So, have you still not found anyone to take responsibility for you?” I asked.
“Such wise and compassionate—”
I still haven’t found any suitable matches, sir. I keep hoping that someday I’ll come across someone wise like you,” she said with a laugh.
“My goodness, your imagination is running wild! How did you learn to tie shackles to your own feet at such a young age?” I teased.
“Oh, no, no! I have no such intentions at all, don’t worry,” she replied, laughing.
Without realizing it, we had climbed up to a place called Arthur’s Seat.

Until we reached there, I hadn’t planned on coming, nor did I expect we’d have to walk such a distance. But since we’d already come, we decided to make the most of it. We sat there for a while, hands entwined, chatting cheerfully. In the midst of our conversation, we lost track of time. It must have been past nine o’clock. The couples atop the hill had thinned out. Noticing this, we too got up, holding hands, and started heading homeward.
After walking some distance, we stopped at a hotel for some refreshments and tea. Then we walked a bit further, until we reached the end of a street where we each had to go our separate ways.
“Well, good night then, shall we part here?” I said.
She squeezed my hand and asked, “When shall we meet again?”
“Whenever you wish,” I replied.
We decided to meet again in two days and fixed a secret spot for our rendezvous. Even then, as we said goodbye, she held onto my hand for a moment longer, not letting go as she wished me goodnight.
I wondered, “Why isn’t she letting go of my hand?” So I said good night once more.
She laughed and said, “What sort of manners are these?”—my hand still in hers.

I couldn’t make out what she meant. As I stood there, pale and confused, she gave a single laugh, came closer, lifted her head, and in a flash kissed me on the lips. “Ta-ta!” she said, waving her hand, laughing, and without a backward glance, dashed away.

I stood there, frozen like a statue for several minutes, utterly stunned. What a strange experience! I thought to myself, “I have much to learn here. Some of the customs in this country are quite interesting.” With that, I made my way home.
Barrister Parvateesam

This happened the very next day. One of my friends, a young Mohammedan, came rushing to me in a flurry and insisted that I must, without fail, attend his wedding that very evening. He would not take no for an answer and left only after extracting my promise.

I was quite astonished. What’s this? Marrying here, with these people? I wondered. How could someone from our background marry one of them? How would their lives blend together? How would their household run? These thoughts ran through my mind. Still, I decided, let me at least go and witness the ceremony that evening.

When I arrived, I saw that the bride was none other than the daughter of the lady who owned my friend’s house. I was dumbfounded. I had often seen my friend and that girl walking together, arm in arm, chatting away. But none of us ever imagined that their closeness would progress all the way to marriage.
The wedding was completed. Many friends attended. Everyone congratulated the bride and groom, blessed them in their hearts, enjoyed the feast, and then returned to their respective homes.

After I came home, I could not sleep a wink that night. How did this all happen, I wondered. Did my friend, in his haste, make a mistake? Or did the girl’s family, upon learning that he was wealthy, hurry to arrange the marriage by any means?
I thought to myself: haste, no matter whose, always leads to the same result. We shall have to see how successful such marriages turn out to be.

The bride and groom went off on their honeymoon. The next day, as planned, my lady friend and I met at our usual spot, went to a small hotel nearby, had some tea, and, just as before, strolled leisurely up the hill, chatting lightheartedly. By then, the place was deserted. We sat under a bush, and for a while, engaged in idle banter. In the midst of our conversation, she gently took my hand in hers. Placing her hand on mine, she drew me a little closer. Sensing her intent, I moved nearer. She slowly leaned against me, wrapped both arms around my waist, and brought her face close to mine. Smiling, I embraced her tightly. She, in turn, kissed me even more passionately on the lips.

I fell into thought, offering no response. Where was this excessive intimacy leading? We had seen what happened to our friend, hadn’t we? So, I began to think it might be wise to stop this romance before it went any further.

Sensing my lack of enthusiasm, she asked, “What are you thinking about? Are you afraid? Don’t young men and women in your country go out like this, spending time together with hugs and kisses? Do you consider it wrong?”

I laughed and replied, “To us, all this seems quite strange. Back home, young men and women hardly even talk to each other, let alone go out together. And as for hugs and kisses—where’s the chance? Even married couples don’t indulge in such things outside the bedroom, and certainly not in front of others, no matter how close they are.”
She looked a little worried and asked, “So, are you saying I was too hasty? That I behaved improperly?” Her tone was tinged with regret.

“Oh, no, not at all! This is the custom here, isn’t it? I’m just not used to it, so I couldn’t respond with the same enthusiasm. My upbringing raises all sorts of doubts in my mind. That’s all there is to it,” I said.
She slowly leaned into my lap and said, “Then tell me, your—”

chapters.title: Farewell to England
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam
“Tell me at leisure about your country, your customs, your marriages, and all the background that leads up to them. Don’t be afraid that I’ll rush you off to church from here in a hurry,” she said.

“There’s no such fear, madam! I only said this is all new to me, not that I’m a coward! Perhaps, in time, I might get used to these luxuries, but I do worry whether I might get carried away beyond that. Besides, these decisions and their consequences are not entirely in our hands,” I replied.

So, for a long while, she lay in my lap, fiddling with the buttons on my coat, pinching my cheeks, while I stroked her curls and spoke of my homeland, our marriage traditions, and customs. We sat thus for quite some time, and then, calling it a night, I got up. Right there, we embraced and kissed, and then set off for home.

Even after returning home, I felt no inclination to read anything. A peculiar restlessness, a strange anxiety, began to stir within me. What is this state? Is it proper or improper? For a long time, I wrestled with these questions.

This is a habit instilled in me by my father and elders since childhood. Whatever the task, they would always say it’s necessary to weigh the pros and cons, to discern what is right and wrong, to consider the consequences and benefits before acting. That habit has become ingrained in me. Whether I am qualified to make such decisions or not, I do my best to follow this approach. Sometimes, this tendency is a bit troublesome, but on the whole, I think it serves me well.

As I reflected, it felt as if the girl who spent the evening with me was still sitting there within me. Her words from earlier, her latest remarks, her touch, her form, her gaze, the fragrance her body left behind—all these mingled together and cast a kind of intoxication over me. My independence, my imagination, all seemed to have deserted me. While she was in my lap, I couldn’t think of anything at all. This whole experience was entirely new to me. In our country, young men of my age rarely have such experiences, do they?

It’s been nearly two years since I arrived here, yet I haven’t become even remotely close to any girl of my own age. Now and then, the neighbor’s daughter would come over, play some mischief, and once or twice, either she kissed me or I kissed her—purely in the spirit of childish playfulness, nothing more. I would immediately forget about it, never feeling any further excitement or emotion.

But with this girl, I find myself unable to remain calm. I’m in a state where I can’t even guess where this is all heading. I have no idea what her intentions are. Does she simply wish to seize whatever pleasure she can whenever the opportunity arises, or is she trying to provoke me and lead me all the way to marriage? Until now, I’d assumed from her words that she wasn’t just a mischievous girl. But if her only aim was mischief, why would she ignore all the men of her own race and seek me out? I’m utterly confused, unable to make sense of anything.

And as for thinking about my own position—well, in this heat, I can’t seem to think at all. I don’t believe I harbor any wicked intention to simply take advantage of the opportunity and then abandon her. So what should I do in such a situation? Should I make up some excuse and avoid the girl altogether? Or should I just meet her and see what happens, taking things as they come? Or, if the matter of marriage arises, shouldn’t I first make up my own mind about what I want?

In matters like these, should one make decisions alone, or is it better to seek advice from friends? I spent the whole night unable to sleep, pondering these questions. At last, I resolved to consult my friend Raju or someone else, and finally, at dawn, I managed to get a little sleep and woke up the next day as usual.

With sunrise, all my nighttime worries vanished like the darkness itself. Even the idea of consulting Raju faded into the background. Instead, it struck me that it would be better to consult my private tutor, a native of this country. Surely, he would be able to give me the right advice. So, after finishing my morning routine, I went straight to my tutor’s house. He was overjoyed to see me.
“Hello, Sam! What brings you here so early in the morning? There must be something special.”
Barrister Parvateesam

“Though you live here, you’re not in the habit of dropping by like this. I can hardly believe you’ve come solely out of affection or respect for me. Perhaps our conversation will flow better if we both have some tea first—what do you say?” he asked.
“I have nothing to say against that, sir. Our elders always tell us that a teacher’s command must be obeyed without question. In matters such as these, your word is law,” I replied.

Just then, the tea arrived. Smiling, he handed me a cup. After we finished our tea and sent the cups away, we sat in silence for a couple of minutes. Then he said, “Well, Same! What’s the matter? You look troubled. I can tell from your face that something’s weighing on your mind. You know you can count on me for any help I can give, don’t you? Come now, tell me what’s bothering you.”

“That’s exactly why I’ve come, sir—to seek your advice. This is a purely personal matter, not something I can discuss with just anyone. But why should I fear to approach someone like you? So I’ve come to you boldly,” I began, and slowly recounted everything—how I’d recently become acquainted with a certain young lady, how we’d been meeting from time to time, how that association had progressed, and to what extent, without any hesitation, evasion, or concealment. I also told him about the doubts and anxieties that had arisen in my mind because of it.
He listened very attentively, then burst out laughing.
As I watched him laugh at my worries, I wondered, “Why is he laughing so much at my troubles?”

He stopped laughing, came over to me, patted me on the back, and said, “Same! My boy! How innocent you are! There’s absolutely no need for you to be so distressed over such a trifling matter. I may not know your customs, but here, among young men and women of your age, this is entirely commonplace. We don’t see anything wrong in it; we simply consider it a natural development for that age. In our language, we call it ‘flirtation.’ It’s a harmless, spirited pastime—no one ever fell ill from it! In fact, if someone were afraid of such things, we’d suspect there was something wrong with them. So, in all that’s happened so far, there’s neither fault nor danger.”

It’s nothing. If this goes any further and becomes more than just a passing tune, then it’s certainly a matter that deserves some serious thought. That English girl might truly have affection for you—there’s nothing strange or extraordinary about that. The world is growing closer by the day, travel is easier, and as movement between countries increases, such developments become inevitable. Many English women have married men from your country. So, there’s nothing surprising if this girl has the sincere intention of marrying you. However, your religion, your family’s wishes, your customs, and your traditions are all vastly different. Every day, every moment, there will be some differences arising from these. Sometimes, these differences can even grow into conflicts. When that happens, it becomes very difficult to keep the household running smoothly.

All in all, I cannot say with certainty that such marriages are ideal. The final decision is yours to make. You both should express your opinions openly, without any pretense, and decide with a calm mind so that your friendship does not suffer. That’s all I can say. Think it over carefully, he said.
I couldn’t say anything in response, nor could I sit there any longer. I immediately took my leave.

The whole day, I kept pondering over what my teacher had said. A strange anxiety, a fear, a restlessness haunted me. I couldn’t bring myself to do anything all day. I couldn’t sit peacefully in one place, nor could I read any book. Mechanically, I went to college and returned, but nothing said there entered my ears or registered in my mind.

Somehow, I spent two days like this. On the third evening, I met my lady friend again. After exchanging some refreshments, we went to a nearby cinema. On the screen, a love story was unfolding. The entire audience in the hall seemed to be watching with great enthusiasm. Looking at the young men and women sitting near me, their expressions and gestures seemed to confirm what I had always imagined about them. But for us, somehow, it didn’t feel as exciting as it should have. I couldn’t say why.
Barrister Parvateesam

Perhaps it was because we were both lost in our own thoughts and fears. Just as I had suspected, that girl too seemed to have resolved that today, our friendship must be taken to some conclusion, that some decision must be made. Before the picture was even halfway through, she said, “Same, isn’t this film rather dull? However you feel, I’m getting a headache just sitting here. Why don’t we go out somewhere and sit comfortably?”
“Alright, let’s do that. I too am finding it a bit uncomfortable sitting here,” I replied. So both of us got up and walked outside.

From there, we climbed up the hills we had passed on our way. By the time we reached the top, the crowd had thinned out. It wasn’t completely dark yet. We settled down beside a bush in a quiet, deserted spot. For two or three minutes, neither of us spoke a word.
That girl too seemed to want to bring this matter to some conclusion.
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 313

For some reason, I felt she had made up her mind. Suddenly, without a word, that girl came close to me, embraced me tightly, and kissed me without so much as a by-your-leave. I sat there motionless, refusing every kiss, as if I were denying her, and she, noticing my frozen stillness, was taken aback.

“What is this, Sam? Why are you like this? You’re cold as ice, not a flicker of movement in you. Are you unwell? Are you angry with me? Never before, when we embraced or kissed, were you ever like this. Has the fire in your blood gone out today? Don’t you want to hold me tight in your arms, to smother me with kisses until I can’t breathe? I can’t understand your behavior today. This pain is more than I can bear. For the past two or three days, every moment has been filled with thoughts of you, your words ringing in my ears, your kisses lingering on my lips, making me feel as if I’m floating in some heavenly realm, not knowing whether I’m awake or dreaming, night or day. I come and collapse in your arms, pouring out my anguish, but why won’t you speak? I’m telling you of a pain I cannot endure, Sam—these are words that should come from your own lips. No woman ever reveals her feelings so openly to herself. Do you think I am shameless, Sam? I think you are very innocent, a child, with no experience, and even the little you’ve gained from knowing me, you’re too shy to admit. Imagining your suffering, I’ve revealed my own, Sam,” she said, her voice trembling with emotion, tears brimming in her eyes, looking at me as if awaiting a reply. She rose from my lap and sat a little distance away, still gazing at me.

I said nothing. I had melted away, become water. Just as she said, I could never express my pain so clearly. The moment a woman’s touch grazes me, my blood grows warm, rushing through my veins, a tingling sensation runs through me, and when skin meets skin, chest meets chest, lips meet lips, I am swept away, losing all sense of the world, as if wandering in paradise. But beyond that, I could never describe this sweet torment. Without words to express it…
I was someone who couldn’t even speak plainly. Just as that girl said—

“Why don’t you say something? Why don’t you speak?” she exclaimed, grabbing my beard, and with her other hand, caressing my face, eyes, and cheeks. Then, like a mother cradling her child, she drew me into her lap and pressed my face to her bosom.

At that, I became utterly spellbound, as if I were being swept away by a great current to some unknown place. Slowly, I extricated myself from her embrace, sat up, wiped away the tears that had begun to flow, and sat there in silence for another two minutes.

“Look here,” I said, “it feels as though our two hearts are beating in perfect unison. The same thought seems to be turning in both our minds. It’s a strange feeling. Just as you said, I too came here intending to say everything you have just spoken. The moment I saw you, your dignified countenance made me hesitate. I couldn’t utter a word. Even so, the right words to express my feelings did not come to my lips. That’s why I sat there, motionless, unable to say anything. Every word you spoke was the absolute truth.

From the moment I left you yesterday, I have been restless, consumed by a single thought—what will be the outcome of our affection? I have never experienced anything like this before. That’s why, when the possible consequences flashed before my eyes, I was startled. It’s true—I was frightened by that very thought. If not for that fear, I think today our passion would have reached its climax. That very thought terrified me. I suspect my words gave you the same apprehension. That’s why, not knowing what to do or what to say, or even how to say it, I sat there like a lifeless doll. Still, my body was burning, my blood was racing, and I hesitated to take even the next step. Since you too felt the same, it is time for both of us to calmly reflect on our situation and our future.

I suppose you are entirely unfamiliar with our country and our customs. Among us, it is impossible for young men and women who are strangers to meet each other. Even acquaintances, if they do meet, must do so in secret—

There is hardly ever a chance to meet in such places. Even if we do, any touch between us must remain confined to glances, or perhaps, on rare occasions, to words. It never descends into actions. All these are post-marital acts; even then, opportunities for them are scarce. Therefore, I decided that we should calm ourselves, put chains on our impulses, think through our situation thoroughly, and come to a decision.

I have come here from distant shores, having studied far away. For some divine reason, we have met. Our union did not stop at the first introduction, nor at a handshake; it progressed from there to an embrace, and from an embrace to kisses. Now, there remains only one step. In your country, and according to your customs, taking that step—marriage—is not so easy, or so I have come to think.

Between you and me, in terms of race, religion, custom, and culture, there seems to be no harmony. If the two of us unite, will our journey through life be smooth, regardless of everything else? Will there be no friction, no pricks of conscience at every moment?

I am the only child of my parents; I cannot leave them for your sake. But could you live in my country? Even if you agree and come, my people would not allow us to cross the threshold of their home. Let us not forget that. In these circumstances, we must first resolve whether our marriage and our life after marriage are even possible. If they are not, we must let go of our excitement, steer our love onto another path, and consider what will happen if I leave you and go my own way.”

Immediately, the girl looked at me and said, “Everything I feared and suspected has come to pass. For some reason, I had a feeling you would bring up this topic today. That made me reconsider where the happiness of these past few days might lead. The very thought that occurred to you has occurred to me as well. But when that thought struck me, I was shaken. In just these few days, you have established a permanent residence in my heart. Not just my heart—you have filled my whole being. Ever since I left you last time, every moment my body has been tingling with anticipation. Your...

My hands tingled all over my body as if tickled. Your sweet words are still singing in my ears. Your lips are still pressing and tormenting mine. Your hot sighs, mingled with mine, continue to intoxicate me. Even though you are far away, Sam, I can say nothing more—how can I say more, Sam? How can I ever forget all this, Sam? Can I ever forget, Sam? What choice do we have? How can we ever separate? I cannot repeat your words, but I doubt I can remain as I am. Even if I could meet you from time to time while you are here, could I bear to see our love’s end, Sam? You are a man, even if you are but a boy, and you are brave. Though I have lived in this country all my life, mingling with so many men, not once have I ever experienced anything like this—believe me, Sam. What refuge do I have, what do I want? I am losing my mind, Sam—I cannot live away from you, Sam. Oh God! What is my fate? Saying this, she sobbed and sobbed, embracing me, kissing me, clinging to my neck with hiccuping sobs.

I did not know how to console her, how to comfort her. I held her tightly, pressing her close, motionless, not even daring to breathe, and sat like that for a long time. After a while, her hiccups subsided. The tears stopped flowing. As if exhausted, as if her whole body had gone limp, she slipped from my side into my lap like a doll. Gently, I wiped her tears with my handkerchief, stroked her hair and cheeks, kissed her eyes, and spent a few moments thus. Then, slowly, she sat up. “Let’s go home, Sam. I can’t sit here any longer. I cannot bear this closeness. Your touch is unbearable to me. Let us part for today. Let us meet again, calm this turmoil, and decide at last what is to be done. I cannot stay here another moment. You must not come with me.” So saying, she stood up abruptly, without listening to me, without letting me take a step after her, and ran off in a single dash.

I stood there, stunned, like a stone statue, staring after her in the direction she had gone. Some people passing by glanced at me oddly, thinking, “Who is this madman?” and walked on. After a while, I came to my senses, wiped away the tears that threatened to fall, and slowly made my way home.

Our exams were drawing very near. Day and night, I was studying with great effort. Though I had the confidence that I would surely succeed, at the same time, a deep anxiety gnawed at me. Placing my trust in God, I continued my studies without any lapse in effort. Just then, out of the blue, a letter arrived from my lady friend, pleading most earnestly that I must somehow make time to meet her that very evening.

Oh God, what is this? Why this letter now, like a bolt from the blue? Should I go, or not? If I go, I might once again lose myself in her presence, in the spell of her gaze, and fall behind in my studies. If I don’t go, and she comes here instead, what could I possibly do? It was like being caught between the devil and the deep sea—unable to decide, I spent the whole day in a state of agitation, unable to study a single word. In the evening, I finally went and met her.

How can I describe the joy she felt! Yet, behind that joy, faint traces of sorrow seemed to linger, casting a shadow over her happiness. We had some tea at a nearby hotel, and then went to our usual spot and sat down. She sat very close to me, put her arms around my neck, pressed her cheek to mine, and sat in silence for a long time. It was only after a while that I noticed tears streaming down her face.

Only then did I come to my senses. I turned her face towards me, wiped her tears, kissed her wet eyes, and said, “What is this weakness? If you suffer like this, how can I bear it? My exams are very near now. I have come to this country, far from my people, enduring so much expense and hardship—if I don’t finish my studies now, what will my family say? What will become of me if I ignore their words? Who is there here to look after me? Who will feed me? And do you really think it’s possible for me to stay here, marry you, and live off your earnings? After this fever has cooled, won’t you find it unbearable to put up with me? Don’t think I’m saying all this because I want to get rid of you or because I don’t love you. I know your pain. My pain is twice as much as yours—

I do not know. You cannot even imagine how many troubles and torments are plaguing me at this moment. All of this feels like a dream—I told you to forget me, and I said I would forget you. But in life, no matter how painful certain truths may be, we have no choice but to face them. I never thought I would have to utter such words in my old age; do not think I am saying all this just for the sake of conversation. Therefore, I believe it is best for both of us if we remain apart until my exams are over. Somehow, I will force myself to focus on my studies. You too, immerse yourself in your own pursuits and try to forget about me. I cannot say anything more than this. I am sorry that I have to say this—that no matter how painful this separation may be, it is inevitable for us.”

I spoke with great gravity. That girl, nestled in my arms, listened to everything I said without even breathing, then burst into tears once more, kissed me once, and without looking back, walked away gracefully, saying, “Goodbye, Sam.” For a long time, I sat there motionless, eyes fixed in the direction she had gone. I did not even realize that my own eyes were raining tears for quite some time. When I finally regained my senses, I wiped my eyes and thought, “What madness is this?” and quietly made my way home. That night, I could not study at all.

The next day, I tried to focus on my studies without dwelling on the past, though it was somewhat difficult. I forced my mind to concentrate and began to read. Now and then, once or twice, that girl would quietly come into my room without any warning, sit for ten or fifteen minutes without offering any new praise, and say, “Forgive me, Sam. I just wanted to see you one last time, even if only with my eyes.” She would leave without even accepting the tea I offered. I could not say anything.

I completed my studies. I went for the exams. I wrote very well. By that evening, I felt as if a great burden had been lifted, and I returned home lighthearted. As soon as I arrived, my landlady’s daughter quietly came in and said, “Well, Sam, have your exams finished? Did you write well? Mother asked me to inquire.”
“Oh, is that so! I thought you were asking on your own. Poor thing, you wouldn’t have such thoughts, would you!”

“I wrote it quite well, didn’t I?” I said. Just then, mother too arrived and said, “Mr. Same, did you write well? How wonderful! I made this cake especially for you today. You must eat it.” She placed the cake, bread, and tea on the table.
“What’s this, serving it to just one person? This girl came and sat here before me, didn’t she? Will she let me eat in peace? Even if I do, will it digest? Please bring another plate here,” I said.
She laughed as she walked inside, saying, “So, are you planning to take her along with you as well?”

Heavens! Even the god who created me couldn’t bear this demoness. I have a suspicion she’ll follow me when I leave. That’s why I’m planning to pick a good day, in the dead of night, and slip away quietly without a sound,” I said.

“Oh, I know all about you, poor thing. Let me tell you something you don’t know. I’ve written a letter to your home about all your affairs here. I’m just telling you it’s better you know,” she said, and while saying this, she quickly cut a piece of cake and stuffed it into that mischievous girl’s mouth, saying, “Now, keep your mouth shut.”

The old lady laughed and left. The girl, fuming, tried to get up from her chair. “Sit down, dear, don’t be hasty,” I said, and with a peck on one cheek and then the other, I plopped her back into her chair. Then, before she could get hold of me again, I went and sat in the opposite chair, feigning ignorance, and solemnly continued my snack.
Once the girl finished her snack too, I said, “If you and your sister can be ready in a quarter of an hour, let’s go to the cinema. Don’t delay.”
“My sister isn’t here,” she said.

I knew she was at home, but I said, “Stop your silly tricks and get ready quickly. You probably want to sit next to me in the cinema and shake with excitement, don’t you, poor thing? I know your intentions, please.”
Suddenly, she came over, bent my head, kissed me, and said, “You are a very, very bad boy. But all the same, I love you,” and ran off.
Within ten minutes, they were both ready, each grabbing one of my arms, and without even asking me where I wanted to go, they dragged me off to whichever cinema they fancied.

For a few days, with nothing much to do, I spent my time pestering all my friends, occasionally meeting our teacher as well, whiling away the hours with books, and sitting around anxiously waiting for the exam results to be announced.

One evening, as I was thinking of going out for a walk, my lady friend appeared and said, “I’ve come right on time—shall we go?” I agreed, and we set out. On the way, we stopped at a hotel for some tea, and then went to the cinema. While watching the film, we chatted about all sorts of silly things. In the middle of it, she asked, “Are your exams over? Did you write them well? I hope I wasn’t a distraction.”
“I did well enough, I think I’ll pass,” I replied.
“When will the results be out?” she asked.
“I’m waiting just for that. I think we’ll know in four or five days,” I said.
“So, as soon as you know, is it straight back to your country?” she asked.
“Yes,” I replied.

She was very pleased. “You’ve worked hard and studied well. Now you’re passing your exams and heading home. Your future will be a path strewn with flowers. Whenever you remember this country, I suppose you’ll also remember the people here. For us, this is as far as our fate goes,” she said.
After that, until the end of the picture, we sat quietly, side by side, occasionally exchanging glances. When we came out, I asked, “Shall we go to our usual place?”
“Thank you, but no. It’s better we part ways like this,” she said.
I didn’t say anything more. With that, we each went our separate ways.

A week later, the exam results were announced. I passed in the first class, scoring even higher than I had hoped. I was so overjoyed, I could hardly contain myself. But with whom could I share this happiness? First, I ran to tell my tutor and Raju, and basked in their congratulations. Then I hurried home, went straight into our landlady’s room, and announced that I had passed.

She was in the middle of cooking something, but was so overwhelmed with delight that, with her greasy hands, she pulled me into a tight embrace and planted kisses on both my cheeks, just as a loving mother would kiss her own son. She showered me with heartfelt congratulations. I was utterly charmed by this sincere display of affection. Her two daughters stood by, laughing and watching me.
“Why are you just standing there? Aren’t you going to congratulate me?” I asked.
“That’s exactly why we’re standing here!” they replied, stretching out their hands and saying, “Heartiest congratulations!”

“Oh, is that all? I was hoping you’d congratulate me like your mother did, but you just stand there stretching out your hands so formally!” I said, pulling both of them closer and taking matters into my own hands, giving them the congratulations I had hoped to receive. Their mother laughed so hard her stomach must have ached. The elder daughter blushed, her cheeks blooming like roses. The younger one, feigning anger, said, “We know what a mischievous boy you are! Just wait, I’ll tell on you!”
“Fine then, come along,” I said, grabbing her hand and pretending to drag her into my room, but she slipped away and ran off.

As soon as the exam results were posted at the college, and everyone saw that I had passed in the first class, all my friends—and not just them, but even people from other regions—came to my room in droves to congratulate and lift me up in celebration. Among all of them, I was the youngest, and to have gone for the exam so soon and passed in the first class left everyone astonished. Even before this exam, I had played a prominent role as assistant secretary in the “Indian Association,” introducing our country’s customs to the English, and I had quickly learned to play golf, earning a name for myself as a first-class sportsman. Because of all this, I was well-known and well-liked by everyone. All those who came to congratulate me were familiar—
Barrister Parvateesam
I had now become a celebrity and an object of affection. All these visitors not only congratulated me, but also sat down and demanded, “Will you throw us a party, or do you want to die?”

“Oh great ones, I have no intention of dying just yet. So I shall indeed host a party. I’ll arrange it as soon as possible. When the stars are in our favor, such things keep happening. I’ll consider this as interest on the expenses I’ve incurred here. Please, have mercy,” I said, and sent them all away. Then, consulting my friend Raju, the ever-present nose-blower who had just arrived, and the young fellow who had recently become ‘untouchable’ (poor chap, it was his wife who had done the deed), I organized a little tea party at a small hotel with their help.

As we had done once or twice before, Raju and I together prepared a final batch of upma kesari that looked like the sacred offering of pulihora at a Satyanarayana puja. The result was marvelous. Raju fancied that it was all thanks to him, but I made it abundantly clear that if he had merely stood beside me, flapping his elbows, these delicacies would never have materialized, nor would they have tasted half as good. He looked rather crestfallen and said, “Let’s see. This isn’t something to be settled between us. It must be decided in an assembly or a court. Just wait and watch.”

That evening, the party was a resounding success. Everyone was thoroughly delighted. Without my knowledge, someone had secretly arranged for a tabla and a harmonium and hidden them there. As soon as the party ended and the tables were cleared, two or three friends sang songs in Telugu and Hindustani. They asked me to sing as well. I pleaded incompetence. “But you recite poems,” they said. Unable to refuse, I recited a few verses from the Bhagavatam, some from the play Harishchandra, and a few others—an odd assortment, like a mixed rice dish.

One after another, my friends expressed their joy in the manner of public speeches. Some spoke with great wit, their words dripping with humor. A couple of elders, who fancied themselves wise, declared that I would surely journey through life in triumph, and advised me that, upon returning home, I should not forget the proper ways, but seek out a bride who was beautiful, intelligent, virtuous, and learned, and marry her. If I failed to do so, they said, they would see to my transport themselves—offering both advice and assurance.
With everyone shaking hands, the “Hip Hip Hurray!” began—
After the party ended with much fanfare, everyone went their separate ways.

I was so overwhelmed with joy that I could hardly contain myself. Sitting there for a while, I tried to suppress the tears of happiness that welled up inside me, then finally stood up and stepped outside. All my friends, without exception, had left me alone and disappeared. As I walked absentmindedly down the street, I was surprised to see my lady friend standing at the end of the road.
“Good evening! What brings you here? Why are you standing here? My place is quite far from here!” I exclaimed.
She replied, “I knew there was a party at this hour and guessed you would be here. I came hoping to catch you alone and have been waiting here for about an hour.”

“Oh dear, what a mistake! How much trouble I’ve caused you. The party was only for my countrymen and fellow students—no women were invited. If I had invited anyone, I certainly would have invited you. Come, let’s walk,” I said.

We walked a little distance and reached our usual spot. Sitting down, we chatted about the world and its ways for a while. In the midst of our conversation, she asked, “So, your work here is finished, isn’t it?”

“Yes, most likely. The results of the barrister’s exam will probably be announced tomorrow. I received news this afternoon that I have passed. So, my work here is done. In a few days, I’ll have to say goodbye to everyone and leave this country. I can’t even hope—nor do I dare to hope—that I’ll ever get a chance to come back here in this lifetime,” I replied.

As I uttered those last words, my voice trembled a little. Tears welled up in her eyes. Like the saying, “the tamarind tree by the riverbank, the gooseberry in the forest”—where is India, and where is Scotland? Who am I? Who is this girl? Why did we become acquainted? Why must this union end in separation before it could even blossom? Such thoughts began to swirl in my mind.

I did not even notice that I had fallen silent for some time. The girl, gazing intently at my face with a look of deep resolve, asked, “Why have you suddenly become so serious? Are you sad that the time for us to part is near? Didn’t we always know this moment would come? If you become like this, what will become of me?”
Barrister Parvateesam

Are not these unions and separations the very nature of human life? Even knowing this, why does it still pain us? I suppose the true happiness lies in savoring the joy while it lasts, and then parting from it with that very joy in our hearts. It is all rather strange.

It seems I too have fallen into your line of thought—into your mood, as it were. Perhaps the thoughts of those who are closest always run in the same direction. “This is a peculiar experience for me,” she said. I too, regaining my composure, abandoned my grave demeanor after much effort, and slipped back into my usual manner. We chatted for a while, and then, as if prompted by the same impulse, both of us rose at the exact same moment, as though to say, “Shall we go?” Without any display of emotion, we simply shook hands, and lightly kissed each other on the lips before moving on.

Four days later, the convocation took place. The hall was packed to the rafters. With great difficulty, I managed to procure tickets for entrance for the Holland lady and her daughters. All the while I sat in the hall...

At that moment, I felt as though I did not even exist in this world, among these mortals. All my thoughts deserted me and began to wander in the heavenly realms. When my name was called, it sounded as if someone was calling me in my sleep. I rose, walked over to the platform, took the hood they offered me, clutched it tightly, and returned to my seat.

The ceremony ended. We all came outside. While I was looking for a taxi, I noticed, at a distance, my lady friend turning away and walking off with her head bowed, without so much as glancing at me. I had no idea she had come. She hadn’t told me she would. She hadn’t asked for a ticket. Poor thing, how much trouble she must have taken to come, how much affection she must have for me, I thought, surprised and touched. Calling a taxi, I returned home with our landlady and her daughters. Their joy knew no bounds. I was astonished—why did they have such fondness for me?

The next day, dressed in my convocation robes, I had a photograph taken, another for my travel application, and on my way home, I bought a small gift for her and the children and gave it to them. Our landlady, too, presented me with a beautiful silver fountain pen in a lovely box—a gesture that filled me with both surprise and delight. They were overjoyed with the gifts I gave them. As I handed a present to the youngest child, I said, “There’s another gift I must give you in secret. I’ll give it to you later.” That child was a little angel. Sensing my intention, she said, “I don’t need any more gifts. What you’ve given is enough.” “Well, it’s not enough for me,” I replied.

So I said, “Since you’re a clever girl, you must accept the gifts I give you openly—there’s no two ways about it. I say this with your sweet face as my witness—do you understand?” I pinched both her cheeks, teased her, and retreated into my room.

Four days later, my passport arrived. That meant I now had permission to travel. When I came here, I arrived smoothly and quietly, without anyone’s permission, without telling a soul. Now, because of the war, all this rigmarole had to be arranged. After another four days of great difficulty, I managed to secure a cabin on a mail steamer for my journey. As soon as this news reached me...

All the things that were not available there, I bought here at great expense, packed my luggage, and felt satisfied. I wrote a letter to my dear friend, saying, “On such-and-such a day, I will depart by such-and-such a train from such-and-such a station, reach London, and board the steamer there. Forget about me, find a suitable young man, get married, and be happy. Please consider this my farewell.” I believe a few drops of tears fell onto the letter, making some parts illegible.

That afternoon, I took leave of all my friends, and in the evening, after a grand farewell meal, I told my family that I was setting off on my journey. Immediately, one after another, they embraced me, kissed me, and with tears in their eyes, sent me off. The little girl, especially, was weeping uncontrollably. Whenever I saw that child, I felt a mixture of affection, pity, and happiness. Many times, I wished I had a sister like her. With a heavy heart, I sat in the carriage, and as they waved their hands saying “Tata,” the carriage started moving. They were eager to come to the station as well, but I insisted they should not.

As soon as I got down at the station, Raju, our private tutor (unexpectedly), and a few other friends arrived. They bought my ticket and other necessities, helped me board the train, and once I was comfortably seated, they bid me farewell and left. The hour bell and the train whistle sounded, signaling departure. Thinking I’d take one last look at the station before the train moved, I stuck my head out of the window.

To my surprise, my friend came running towards me with a small suitcase. The train began to move. Without hesitation, she jumped onto my compartment. I was shocked and trembling as I asked, “What is this? Why have you come? Why did you board the train and sit here?”

She replied, “Sit down, there’s nothing to fear. You are going so far away, all the way to your country! I thought I’d at least accompany you to London and shake your hand one last time. Don’t be upset.”
She sat right next to me. Neither of us, nor the other passengers, tried to sleep that night. We kept talking all sorts of things, most of which made neither head nor tail.

We spent the night laughing like little children, whiling away the hours until dawn. Early in the morning, we arrived in London, took a small room in a hotel, and then went to the steamer dock to find out when the ship would depart. After gathering this information, we returned and, with the help of our friend, managed to load all our luggage onto the steamer. By the time we finished, it was already one in the afternoon.

We went to a hotel, had lunch, wandered about for a while, and by half past two, we returned to the steamer. As I was about to board, she said she wanted to see my cabin and came inside with me. She looked around, sat for five minutes, and as soon as the bell and siren announced the imminent departure of the steamer, she threw her arms around me in a tight embrace, kissed me deeply, and, gazing into my eyes, said:

“Same, this is the last embrace, the last kiss, my dear Chamu. As long as I live, they will echo in my heart. If, as people say, there is another birth, then even there, this memory, this form, will remain with me. Goodbye. May Lord Parameshwara grant you all happiness and every success. Goodbye, Same,” she said, and hurried away.

I followed after her, coming up to the deck, and stood watching her. Through a veil of tears, with trembling hands and a choked voice, I managed to say, “Tata, God bless you,” and nearly collapsed onto the benches on the deck as if I had fainted.

The fellow passengers nearby caught hold of me, seated me in a chair, and brought me some tea. By the time I had recovered and opened my eyes fully, our ship had already left the London dock and was speeding into the vast ocean.

chapters.title: The Voyage Home
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

By evening, our steamer slowly crossed the Strait of Dover and entered the English Channel. The waves were a bit more turbulent there, but somehow, we managed to escape and entered the vast Atlantic Ocean. By then, darkness had fallen completely. Though our ship had traveled this route thousands of times, it now seemed to be feeling its way forward step by cautious step, as if it couldn’t see the way in the darkness. Everywhere I looked, there was impenetrable blackness—except for the stars in the sky, not a single light could be seen from any town along the French coast. All this, I supposed, was due to the fear of war. Beneath us, the endless, unfathomable Atlantic Ocean. After three years, I was once again sailing the seas, filled with the joy of returning home, and with the thought: “In this lifetime, how many of these people will I ever meet again?” More than anything, I was gripped by a single fear: “Will our ship, which has thus far escaped the ravages of nature and the monstrous acts of enemies, be able to carry me safely across this unknown, boundless ocean and deliver me home?”

Just then, the call for dinner came. I went below. At the table, they served everyone the same food, myself included. I called the waiter over and told him, “This meal won’t do for me. I am a vegetarian. Except for rice and vegetables, I won’t touch anything else, not even eggs.” He asked, “What shall I do now, sir?” I replied, “If necessary, I can wait a little. Otherwise, just bring me a plate with some vegetables, a bit of bread, butter, pudding, milk, and fruit.” He said, “Is that all, sir?” I replied, “That’s enough. I am easily satisfied.” He laughed and went off cheerfully. Soon enough, he brought me potatoes, cabbage curry, bread, butter, sago pudding, milk, and bananas. I told him not to forget to have two handfuls of rice cooked for me for both meals from tomorrow onwards. “Sure, sir! Certainly, sir!” he replied.

After dinner, I went up on deck, strolled for a while, gazed at the endless, unfathomable ocean and sky, then quietly returned to my cabin, changed my clothes, and lay down. No matter how long I lay there, sleep would not come to my eyes.

I could not get a wink of sleep. As I lay down, without any effort on my part, the waves of the sea were tossing me this way and that. Once again, my mind began to wander with all sorts of thoughts—our house owner, her daughters, that mischievous little child, the unexpected affection they all showed me, my private tutor, the young instructor who taught me golf, the friends who played golf with me, the young lady who once tried to flirt with me while sitting beside me at a play, the beloved who was so drawn to me and loved me dearly—so many faces, so many places, all began to parade before my eyes like pictures on a cinema screen. As I watched all these faces and recalled the stories behind them, I eventually slipped into sleep without realizing it.

The next morning, after completing all my morning routines, I leisurely went up to the deck. From above, I heard some commotion. Curious, I looked around and saw that, along with our ship, here and there, airplanes were flying, keeping pace with us. For a moment, a fear struck me—are these enemy planes? But then I reassured myself: if they were enemy planes, would our ship be traveling so calmly? After another moment, I noticed that, a little distance away, on either side of our ship, warships with cannons mounted were also accompanying us.

I called over a distinguished-looking gentleman who was standing nearby and asked, “What are these planes above us? What about the warships below? Are they just passing by, or are they traveling with us?”

He looked at me with a hint of mockery, as if wondering how someone could be so ignorant, and replied, “Ours is a mail steamer—it carries the mail. All the regular passenger ships have stopped sailing. Nowadays, this vast ocean has become a very dangerous place for travelers. Day and night, at every moment, enemy planes fly above, enemy warships patrol the sea, and enemy submarines lurk below the water. For our protection, the government has arranged for two airplanes above and two warships on the sea to accompany us. They will stay with us until we safely enter the Suez Canal.”
That explanation brought some peace to my mind.
Barrister Parvateesam

The old fear did not rear its head again, not even a little. On these ships, for the convenience of passengers, canvas chairs and folding deck chairs are rented out to sit on the deck. After disembarking at Bombay, they collect them back and store them safely. I took one, picked up some book, and began to while away the time reading. Just then, a young man came and stood beside me, greeted me, and asked, “What are you reading?”
“A novel, just to pass the time,” I replied.
“Is it from the library here?” he asked.
“No, it’s my own,” I said. “Is there a library here?” I asked in turn.
“Why wouldn’t there be? Otherwise, how would some of us pass the time? Don’t you know there’s a library?” he said.
“I didn’t know,” I replied.

“Come, I’ll show you,” he said. He took me and showed me the library. He also showed me that there were some indoor games for others’ amusement—ping pong tables, card tables, chess boards. “On the deck above, people even play badminton,” he said. “And if that’s not enough, some enthusiastic fellows even place bets on the ship’s route, how many miles it travels per hour, and how far we’ve come now,” he added.

Chatting away with this new acquaintance, lunchtime arrived. We went down and sat for our meal. I learned something today that I hadn’t noticed before. On the dining table, to prevent the plates from sliding back and forth with the ship’s rocking, they had placed thin wooden bars across every row. Then the servers, carrying dishes of food and fruit in their hands, began to walk as if they were dancing, to keep the food from falling. I wondered what kind of dance this was at mealtime. If it were an English dance, maybe, but why now, I thought.

I quietly asked my new companion about this. “Why are they dancing like that?” I asked. He laughed for quite a while, as if I had made a witty remark. “That’s not a dance, sir. We too will have to get used to walking like that. The ship keeps rocking back and forth, so even if we stand straight and walk straight, we end up swaying in the direction the ship tilts. Those who aren’t used to it often keep falling down. That’s why, on ships—”

If, instead of leaning towards the side where the wind is blowing, we walk tilting ourselves in the opposite direction, then no matter how fierce the storm, there is no chance of us falling down. Therefore, from now on, you too must get used to walking in this manner.
Otherwise, you will have a lot of trouble,” he warned me.
For the rest of that day, I tried, more or less, to get accustomed to this walk that resembled a dance, or perhaps a dance that resembled a walk. I believe I succeeded to some extent.
By 7 o’clock in the evening, our ship entered the Marseilles harbor. Our guardians, the warships, were stationed outside the harbor...
Barrister Parvateesam

...came to a halt. The airplanes had gone off somewhere. I asked a sailor, “Will our steamer stay here all night?” “Yes, it will,” he replied. “In that case, can I go into town?” I asked. “You can,” he said. “Are you sure?” I pressed. “Absolutely, but make sure you’re back within ten hours,” he cautioned. Not knowing what else to do, I thought I’d see how Marseilles looked at night, having seen it by day. With curiosity as my companion, I set off. I walked quite a distance and found myself in the middle of the town. The streets were all shrouded in darkness. People were moving about as usual.

As I walked, I saw a hotel aglow with twinkling lights and the sound of soft music drifting out. I went inside and took a seat. It was fairly crowded. I ordered tea and some snacks. The waiter looked at me with a questioning face. Only then did I realize how clever I was—suddenly it struck me that I was in France, where no one speaks English, and I myself didn’t know a word of French. Remembering this, I managed to convey my wishes through gestures alone, finished my snack, paid the bill, and stepped outside.

Not knowing where else to go, I noticed a cinema hall quite nearby and was seized with the urge to see what French films were like. I went in. The place was packed. An usher showed me to an empty seat. I sat down. After a few moments, I became aware—by the delicate scent wafting to my nostrils—that a young lady had sat down beside me. I turned and looked; she glanced at me and smiled sweetly. I smiled back and sat watching the screen.

Barely two minutes later, another hand reached behind me. In another moment, a soft tickling touch brushed my cheek, and locks of hair fluttered against my face in the breeze. Who was this girl? Why such boldness, and in such a hurry? I wondered. I didn’t know French, so I couldn’t speak to her. Why on earth had I come out like this without thinking? All I could do was sit and watch for a while—what else? In any case, I decided it would be best to return to our ship at once. Without a word, I got up, brushed her hand once as I passed, and hurriedly made my way outside.

That girl, thinking I had invited her, followed behind me. Realizing this, I thought, “Oh dear!” and quickened my pace, heading out onto the road. When I entered the town, I had no idea which way led to the harbor. In fact, I didn’t even know where I was at that very moment.

What was I to do now? It was as if I had become utterly stuck in this foreign, godforsaken land. “Oh God, how will I ever reach the ship?” I lamented in every possible way. After walking a little distance, I spotted a taxi. I called to the driver and asked him to take me to the harbor. He didn’t understand my language, and I didn’t know his, so both of us suffered a great deal.

Somehow, using the dozen French words I knew, I managed to convey my request. He carefully seated me in the cab and took me to the harbor, dropping me off there. I was overjoyed, thinking that it was only by the boundless, causeless grace of the Lord—an ocean of mercy—that I had been brought here in this manner.

But what do you know! The steamer, which was supposed to remain there until morning, was just about to depart. As soon as I set foot in the harbor, the siren sounded, and the gangway for passengers to board was being pulled back onto the ship. I ran up, panic-stricken, with a wild look on my face, and stood there helplessly. A sailor saw me, immediately spoke to someone, and had the gangway lowered again.

“Hurry up! Hurry up!” he warned. Blessing my stars, I wiped away the tears that were about to fall and scrambled up the steps. I hadn’t even planted my second foot properly on the deck when the steamer set off. They pulled the gangway up. My whole body trembled violently. Cold sweat poured down my face.
Barrister Parvateesam

I collapsed awkwardly into a chair nearby, like a dog that’s lost its way. The steamer was quickly picking up speed. No one seemed to notice my predicament. For nearly a quarter of an hour, I sat there motionless, shivering like a man stricken with a cold fever. Gradually, the shivering subsided, my fear ebbed away, and I silently offered a thousand salutations in my mind to the compassionate Lord—He who, hidden somewhere, watches over all and had just delivered me from such peril.

When I slowly got up and went downstairs, lunch was already being served. I hadn’t even heard the bell that must have rung earlier. I quietly made my way to my seat, bowed my head, and began eating in silence. My new friend, seated beside me, had apparently been observing me closely for some time.
He asked, “What’s the matter, sir? Why did you come so late?”
“There’s a long story behind that,” I replied. “I’ll tell you later.”

After finishing our meal, since the cold still lingered, we didn’t go out onto the deck. Instead, we sat in a corner of the hall. I asked, “This steamer is supposed to stay here all night. Why did it suddenly set off so soon?”

“At first, they planned to stay here,” he explained, “but then an urgent cable arrived from the naval authorities instructing the ship to depart immediately for Italy. So they weighed anchor at once. You were nowhere to be seen.”
I confessed, without hiding my foolishness, exactly what had happened. He was astonished.

“Do you realize what you’ve done? Do you know how dangerous that was? If you had disembarked here, lost your way, and wandered about not knowing where to go, the French police might have mistaken you for a spy, thrown you in jail, and only after a lengthy investigation, upon hearing your story, would they have realized the truth and handed you over to the English embassy. They would have taken their sweet time, and by the time all this was sorted out, several months might have passed—perhaps not until the war ended! They might even have kept you here until then. You and your family back home are very, very lucky!” he exclaimed, patting me on the back and giving me a joyful hug.
After chatting for a while about this and that, we each...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 335 We went back to our cabin.

The next morning, when we woke up, our steamer was anchored at the port of Italy. This time, the authorities themselves forbade any of us from going ashore. All day long, everyone sat inside, gripped by some unknown fear, with no games, songs, or amusements to pass the time.

On the steamer, various kinds of trinkets were brought for sale—beautiful little marble carvings, silverware, and other curios. From below decks, a few Italian boys would shout loudly, trying to attract the attention of the people above, urging them to throw coins into the sea. Whenever someone tossed a small coin down, the boys would dive after it, and without letting the money sink, they would catch it mid-water. This was a source of amusement for us and a sort of game for those boys. We spent some time watching the wares above and the antics of the boys below.

As night fell and we were preparing for dinner and bed, the authorities informed us that no one was to sleep tonight. We were to remain alert, sitting up in our regular clothes. Once again, we wondered, “Oh Lord, what now?” and sat anxiously.

After another half hour, we were all told to put on life belts. These are made of rubber or cork. In case of any accident, if one jumps into the sea wearing this, a person can float for a long time without sinking. Such belts were arranged for everyone on board. They distributed them to us now and taught us how to wear them.

All of us were then asked to come up to the deck. We were told that we were in a very dangerous situation, that enemy submarines were pursuing us, and that at any moment our ship might be in peril. Therefore, we were to sit with our belts on, without fear or panic, and listen to the officers’ instructions. There were also small boats enough to take everyone safely to shore, and it was their responsibility to ensure that, as far as possible, no harm would come to anyone.
As soon as we heard the siren, we were told not to panic, not to be anxious, not to rush or push, and that women and children would be sent first into the small boats.

The officer gave a speech, saying that women and children should disembark first, and only then should the men descend; if any men disregarded this order and tried to push ahead, they would be severely punished. Therefore, he advised everyone to remain calm, pray to God without haste or panic, and then he left. But tell me, in such a situation, no matter how many speeches are given, how can one remain free from fear or anxiety? Whose life is dear to whom at such a time! Still, can we ignore the words of the authorities?
