After the captain’s speech, a man of about fifty among us began to narrate an incident: Once, while he was traveling by ship to America, some accident occurred at night. All the sleeping passengers were awakened and told to dress quickly and get into the lifeboats. Women and children were to go first, and until they had all boarded, no man was to move. If any man, in his haste, tried to push the women aside and go ahead, he would be shot. They assured everyone that proper arrangements would be made, and the officer, holding a revolver, stood on the top step of the ladder leading down, calling for the women and children to come first.

Some men, ignoring his words, tried to push forward in their hurry. The officer, angered, declared that if they tried again, he would shoot without hesitation, and sent them back. The women, in a flurry of fear and tears, clutching their children and whatever small belongings they could grab, hurriedly descended. About thirty-five of them boarded three lifeboats and sat down. As the rest continued to rush forward, two old men at the back, yelling and shoving the women aside, tried to slip past the captain and jump into the boat. The officer pointed his revolver and roared, “Stand back!” Even then, they paid no heed and pressed forward. The revolver fired—one man fell dead into the sea, the second collapsed on the spot with a minor wound. No one uttered a word. No one mourned the dead man. The sailors dragged the fallen man back. The remaining women, trembling, quickly got down. Then all the men descended and settled into the lifeboat below.
Within half an hour of the lifeboats being taken out to sea, there was a huge explosion—

Hearing the sound, we learned that the ship we had disembarked from had sunk right there along with all our belongings,” he described. This account filled us all with even greater fear, and we decided that it was best to obey the orders of the authorities without question. Many of us remained standing right there on the deck.
Just then, the ship shot forward at tremendous speed. Never in our lives had we imagined that a steamer could move so fast.

All the lights on the ship were switched off completely. Apart from the churning of the engines and the sound of the sea, there was not a single other noise. None of us dared utter even a word. Not one among us believed that we would survive the night and live to see the sun rise again.

Thus, for several hours, we stood huddled together on the deck, our lives hanging by a thread. At dawn, we reached the British island called Malta. The sun god himself seemed to greet us with a gentle smile. All of us let out a deep sigh of relief.

A Christian priest aboard the ship came and offered a prayer, presenting a hundred salutations to the Almighty on behalf of us all. We spent the entire day there, and as soon as word arrived that the enemy submarines had retreated, our journey resumed. By the following day, we reached the Suez Canal.

The warships and airplanes that had come to protect us turned back without even bidding us farewell. We slowly crossed the Suez Canal and entered the Arabian Sea. After traveling some distance, we received word that enemy ships and submarines were present there as well, and that just the previous night they had sunk two ships. We were told to proceed with the utmost caution.

But what choice did we have except to move forward? So, with a mixture of fear and hope, we pressed on. That night too, many of us spent a long time on the deck. As we were nearing our homeland, there was no cold or fog to trouble us. Life felt much more comfortable and safe. No one spoke to anyone else; each was lost in his own thoughts.
I alone got up and began to pace the deck. Lost in my own musings, I happened to look up at the sky, and there I saw a lunar eclipse. The sight was truly beautiful.
Barrister Parvateesam

Below us, the deep sea; above, the endless sky; and in between, we insignificant mortals, trembling for our lives. For a long time, we stood there, gazing at that eclipse. The memories of all that happens during such eclipses came flooding back. Somehow, that night passed and dawn broke. Continuing our journey, after spending yet another night in the same manner, we would soon be nearing the shores of India. With the courage that we would reach safely, we pressed on, and one morning at eight o’clock, our ship entered the Bombay harbor. Everyone was filled with boundless excitement and joy.
Not a single one among us had truly believed we would reach here alive. Who among mortals can fathom the divine play of the Almighty?
End of Part Two.

chapters.title: Homecoming
paragraphs: The joy one feels upon returning home after spending several years abroad is truly beyond words. If I were a poet, perhaps I could compose a few clever verses and bring some satisfaction to my heart. But, lacking that talent, I am forced to make do with mere words.

When a mother is out of sight for a long time, the happiness children feel upon finally finding her is immense—but the joy I experienced was a thousand times greater than that. The very moment I caught sight of the distant shores of Hindustan, as the steamer drew near to the Bombay coast, I was so overcome with happiness that I rushed up to the deck, stood there, and let tears of joy stream down my face.

All the while I was away from my homeland, I was convinced that our country was the greatest, the most ideal in the world. I would argue with everyone abroad in the same vein. “There is no country on this earth like ours!” I would declare. When you’re away, you either don’t notice your homeland’s flaws, or you forget them altogether. I believed that all the virtues found in foreign lands were present in my own as well. Whenever I spoke in this manner, the locals would look at me with a mixture of amusement and pity. They would laugh at me as if I were a simpleton.
For some reason, it was my misfortune that whatever I expected would happen, the opposite always occurred; whatever I imagined, reality would turn out to be the exact reverse.

The steamer reached Bombay harbor. It hadn’t come to a complete stop yet. No one had set foot on land. At that moment, it became clear that everything I had assumed was wrong, that my words were false, that what others had told me was the truth, and that all my imaginings were merely fantasies.
Barrister Parvateesam

I learned that this was the only reason. Would you believe it, before the steamer had even come to a complete stop, a hefty Sharab (money changer), with a large turban, sweating profusely, panting, wiping his brow with his shirt, looking around at everyone and grinning foolishly, made his way up onto the deck. Now, if one arrives, is it not proper to sit respectfully on a chair or a sofa? But this fellow squatted right on the floor, in the middle of the walkway where everyone passes. Do you know why he came running as if he might collapse any moment? To give change to those who needed it, of course! After all, everyone on the steamer was coming from foreign lands. They wouldn’t have pounds or shillings, only rupees and annas. But without local currency, nothing could be done here. So, for the convenience of travelers, he had resolved to exchange foreign money for local money. A fine idea in itself, but it’s not as if this Sharab had any particular affection for us—his real intention was to make a quick fifty or hundred rupees in half an hour, without any effort, by offering a poor exchange rate for our rupees or annas. I have traveled to many countries, but never have I seen such a practice anywhere else. If you need money, banks are everywhere, ready to serve you in an instant. That’s all it takes—no fuss, no bother. But here, it’s just exasperating.

Meanwhile, another Sharab appeared, ready for business. Perhaps, out of jealousy that the first one was gobbling up all the profits. Seeing this, all the sahibs from the steamer came out, laughing as they passed by. Despite all this commotion, many people didn’t even bother to exchange their money with these fellows. But just looking at them made me feel as if I had committed some crime—I felt so ashamed, I wanted to hide my head somewhere.

Is it over? I have seen many large harbors and railway stations, haven’t I? Nowhere else is there such chaos. People disembark and board quietly, calmly. Coolies load and unload luggage efficiently. But the kind of commotion, panic, and confusion that exists in Bombay Harbor and later at our railway stations is found nowhere else. I doubt even the great European War could produce such a racket. In fact, I’m certain it couldn’t.

Anyway, somehow I managed to keep an eye on my luggage and disembarked in style. I shouted for four coolies and told them to put everything over there. Just then, one of them approached me, bowing repeatedly, trembling as he came near. Why all these salaams for me? Why was he so frightened at the sight of me? Had I become some sort of...

Governor, is it? After doing all this, do you know what he said? He wanted to inspect my luggage—that was the matter. “Why?” I asked. “It’s the rules, sir. Everyone’s luggage must be checked,” he replied. “Well then, check everyone’s,” I said. “I am checking from one side, sir,” he answered. “So, you’ll only check mine from one side?” I retorted. But I suppose he didn’t quite grasp what I meant.

For a moment, he said nothing. “Have you finished inspecting the sahibs’ luggage?” I asked. “Yes, sir, but they are sahibs, after all. Their luggage doesn’t need to be checked so thoroughly,” he replied. Hearing this, my blood began to boil. But what could I do at that moment? Swallowing my pride and this insult, I silently unloaded my luggage for him to inspect.

What did I have, really? Clothes and books—what else would someone like me possess? He began rifling through all my books. “Why do you need to look at those? What could possibly be in them?” I asked. “I have to check if there are any books forbidden in this country,” he said. “Alright then, go ahead,” I replied. He flipped through every book I had, but what would he understand anyway? He even looked at some forbidden books and couldn’t tell the difference.
But then, he picked up a copy of the Bhagavad Gita with Annie Besant’s commentary and declared, “This one is not allowed.” “Why is that?” I asked. “No Annie Besant books are allowed—”
Barrister Parvateesam

He shouted, “Hey, you mad fellow! This is the Bhagavad Gita, a holy scripture—not a political treatise. It does no harm to anyone. Mrs. Besant has worked hard and written many books about our religion. Those books and her political agitation have nothing to do with this.” Only after he explained all this to that officer did my elders finally come down. Somehow, I escaped that calamity unscathed. From there, I hired a carriage and told the driver to take me to a decent hotel.

I have seen all sorts of hotels, big and small, all over the world, but I had never seen one as shabby as this. In Bombay, this place is supposed to be a good hotel, and many people stay here. But after seeing it, I felt that if a man, after seeing a king, looks at a commoner and feels enlightened, then I must have achieved supreme wisdom. The arrangements, the furniture—everything I saw there—oh! I was deeply distressed. Later, of course, I saw places even more wretched than this, so now it almost seems respectable in comparison.

I arranged my luggage in the room and went to the bathroom, thinking I’d have a bath. You know how the English bathe, don’t you? I took off my clothes and stood under the tap. The kind of bathtubs they have abroad aren’t found here, so I thought, never mind, and began bathing right under the tap. I looked all around the room, but there wasn’t a bar of soap in sight. “What sort of injustice is this?” I thought, and shouted for the manager. Thinking some disaster had occurred, a servant came running. He saw me and, startled, quickly retreated. Only then did I remember my predicament and, embarrassed, began searching all around for a towel to wrap myself in. But there was neither a towel nor a cloth of any kind to be found.

How could one dry oneself without a towel, let alone cover oneself? Standing behind the door, I cursed the hotel staff and asked, “Where are the soap and towels?” He replied, “Everyone has to bring their own. It’s not customary for the hotel to supply them.” In foreign countries, wherever you go, the hotel provides soap, towels, blankets, quilts, and so on.
If this is how things are at a place reputed to be a big hotel, just imagine what it must be like in the smaller ones!
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 349
Somehow, with my clothes still damp, I threw on my shirt and stepped outside. I went straight to the shop and bought soap, towels, and a few dhotis and such for wrapping myself after a bath.

Now, what can I say about the food? Even to think of it is revolting, and to speak of it is shameful. The cooked dishes, the serving vessels, the people, the customs—everything is disgusting. If the Englishmen laughed at us after seeing all this, could you blame them? If they were repulsed, would it be any surprise? I, who am so full of patriotic pride and was born and raised here, feel this way—so what can I say about others? From there, I set out to see the “town.”

As soon as I stepped onto the street, it was all chaos, confusion, and anxiety. The cart drivers push their vehicles any which way they please, without rhyme or reason. As for the cyclists, there’s no need to even mention them. Every person seems to be in their own world. As far as possible, no one walks in the middle of the road. They conduct all their business and negotiations standing right in the middle of the road. While walking, every man spits with double force, as if it’s a competition. There’s no sense of connection between people. Even if four people set out together, not a single step matches another.

From the beginning, I’ve been a man accustomed to rules and regulations—especially after going abroad. There, on the roads, you hear nothing but the sound of carriages and the tapping of shoes—no other noise at all. But here, we shout as we please, laugh loudly, and talk at the top of our voices. Is this too a great crime, I wonder? Is there not even that much freedom to speak? Of course, we can talk. But there’s no need to make such a racket that the whole town hears our quarrels. If we get used to speaking softly and laughing gently, life would be so much more pleasant. If we could adopt this habit in hotels, trains, theaters, or any place where people gather, how peaceful life would be!

If you look on the street, you won’t find two people who are alike—not in appearance, of course, for that’s impossible. What I mean is in dress and language. No matter how many countries I’ve traveled, I managed with English. But even after returning to my own country, every place has its own language. Let’s leave language aside—what I’m talking about is attire. In all the countries of Europe and America, wherever you go…
Barrister Parvateesam

Aren’t they all wearing the same kind of clothes? In our country too, shouldn’t all foreigners dress in a similar, uniform manner? Is it only the duty of women to uphold the dignity of the nation by wearing the same kind of attire? Here, at least, the women maintain the decorum of the country by dressing uniformly. But as for the men, I can’t fathom why they insist on these suits and boots. Even little children are made to wear them. For the grown-ups, it’s a matter of fashion. Some, when they don a suit, look as if their eyes are about to pop out—one can hardly bear to look at them! Imagine a man with a pot belly, or someone plump, or with a huge stomach, or hair tied in a knot on his head, wearing a suit—just picture it! I’ve seen plenty of such people. I’ve suffered watching the suit slip off their bellies, and to prevent that, their wives tie an old saree around them, using it as a makeshift belt, leaving the coat buttons open so that the cloth is visible, and a scarf tied on the head. I can’t understand why they put on this bullock-cart disguise.

It’s the same with the houses on the streets. There’s no connection between one and the next. A big mansion stands next to a small house, and beside that, an even smaller hut. Even among the mansions, no two look alike. Each has its own path, and everyone builds as they please. In those foreign countries, it’s not like this. Streets run in orderly rows. The buildings have uniformity and symmetry. There’s equality in their dress and language. There’s unity in their walk and actions. Because of this, one can sense that there is unity in their race, in their society, in their customs and dealings, in their outlook on life. But here, from our attire, our gait, our buildings, it seems that such unity is a rare thing.

As soon as I arrived in Bombay and saw this disparity, I felt deeply troubled. Is this merely an external difference, or are there such divisions within us as well? That doubt arose in my mind. At that moment, I resolved to observe our society carefully from this perspective. So, I set out to explore the city. Everything here is new—the people are new, the language is new, the customs and practices are new. And as for me, I’m completely lost. I can’t make out what, if anything, is not new here.

I thought, if I stay here for four days, roam the city in all four directions, observe the customs, and learn about the ways here, it would be as if I had understood the whole of India. After all, I’ve already spent three years away from home—what harm is there in spending another four days, or a week, here?

I thought to myself, “Whatever happens, let me first reach home safely. But before that, let me write a letter from Bombay to let them know I’ve arrived safely.” With this in mind, I realized I didn’t have any cards, envelopes, or the like with me. So, I quietly went to the post office, bought what I needed, and somehow managed to sit there and write: “I have reached Bombay safely. In four or five days, I will set out and reach home. After all this time, I am eager to see you all again, offer my humble salutations, and receive your blessings.” As I wrote the letter, tears kept streaming from my eyes the whole time. Somehow, I composed myself, dropped the letter in the box, and stepped outside.

Even in this post office, there was such a commotion, such confusion, and so many languages and costumes that I lost count. For a moment, it seemed as if all the people of India had gathered here for some festival. In foreign lands, whether you see a city or a village, everyone’s attire is more or less the same. Even in big cities like London or Paris, if you see people from behind, you’d think they all belonged there. But here, the streets were so crowded it was unimaginable. Even on the broadest royal roads, people were jostling shoulder to shoulder. Everyone was pushing and shoving each other. Men and women would stand right in the middle of the street, discussing politics, mutual rivalries, hurling insults or compliments, or talking about domestic squabbles, completely oblivious to the fact that they were blocking the way for others.

Even when cyclists rang their bells, rickshaw pullers shouted and cursed, and motor cars honked to warn them to move aside, none of these noises seemed to reach anyone’s ears, drowned as they were in their own arguments and counterarguments. In this matter, I was almost impressed by their stubbornness, persistence, and fearlessness.

Hundreds of vendors could be seen, selling all sorts of things—snacks, curries, flowers, fruits, children’s toys, women’s ornaments, and whatnot—piled high on pushcarts, hawking their wares at the top of their lungs. Carefully weaving my way through them, dodging both people and carts so as not to get run over—like a circus performer walking a tightrope—I made my way forward. I went into one or two shops and tried hard to buy some dhotis, shirts, towels, and the like. But not a single shopkeeper would quote a proper price. I had no idea of the value of things here. If I bargained too low, I feared I might be doing something wrong; if I didn’t bargain at all, I’d surely be cheated.

chapters.title: The Train Home
paragraphs: The matter was finally settled. After all that distress, I managed to buy just one or two absolutely essential items and made my way out.

After wandering about, watching the festivities, I went to a hotel for some refreshments. But as it turned out, that place catered only to non-vegetarians. Realizing this, I immediately stepped out and this time went to a vegetarian hotel. There, I managed to put something in my stomach and set off again. Deciding there was nothing more to see here, I resolved to return home that very night and hurried back to my lodging.
That night, I calmly arrived at Victoria Terminus in good time. I asked for a ticket to Nidadavolu.
He asked, “Which country is Nidadavolu in?”

“It’s in our own country, on the eastern coast, in the Madras State. It’s a small station about three hundred miles north of Madras, on the M.S.M. railway line. I don’t have a map with me, otherwise I’d show you,” I replied.
“Oh, I see. No problem. But we don’t have tickets to Nidadavolu. If you want, I can give you one to Madras,” he said.

“I don’t want to travel all the way to Madras and then go back north again. That would be both troublesome and a waste for me. So, please write the ticket to Nidadavolu. Or perhaps you’ve heard of a place called Bezwada? If you can give me a ticket there, that’s fine too,” I said.

“In that case, I can give you a ticket to Bezwada,” he said, and began writing it out. Looking at the ticket, I politely asked, “Could you please make it second class for me?” He glanced at me, a bit flustered, and said, “Excuse me, sir, which place did you want again?”

“Nidadavolu,” I repeated. Immediately, he pulled out the India Guide, looked up the town, calculated how far it was, how much the fare would be, and quickly wrote out the ticket for me. “Why didn’t you mention this at the start, sir? Forgive me for putting you through this trouble,” he said, standing up respectfully to hand me the ticket.

I handed my luggage to a porter and boarded the train. There was still quite a bit of time before departure, so I took out a book and sat reading in the compartment. I had to wait there for nearly an hour.

Gradually, the compartment filled up with people. In my carriage, two Anglo-Indian young women, a couple of Parsis, and a Maharashtrian husband and wife boarded and took their seats. Seeing me sitting all by myself, sprawled comfortably, the Maharashtrian couple came over without hesitation and settled themselves cozily on my berth. The station was bustling with all the usual commotion. The train set off. “Ah, life is moving forward,” I thought.

I was happy, thinking, “In two days, I’ll be home safe and sound.” I wondered what the Mughalpura station would look like now, how eagerly my family must be waiting for me, how they managed all these days alone, and whether any other relatives might have come upon hearing of my arrival. Such thoughts flitted through my mind, making me chuckle to myself, though now and then a shadow of melancholy would creep in, only to be quickly pushed aside. Like a madman, I sat there, forgetting entirely where I was.

The rest of the passengers were conversing in their own languages. The two Anglo-Indian ladies were loudly chattering away, talking nonsense that made little sense, bursting into peals of wild, shrill laughter, and generally creating a ruckus. Through their words, their laughter, and the way they tossed their heads, they made it clear that they considered themselves very clever, as if they had been born and raised only in England and had, by some misfortune, ended up in this wretched country.

Their manner of speaking grated on me. No matter how little our people are educated—even the rickshaw pullers in Bombay or Madras—I’ve heard them speak better English than this. Across from me, the Parsi brothers were deep in some business dispute. The Maharashtrian couple beside me, from the moment they boarded, hadn’t stopped bickering in Marathi for even a second. Suddenly, as if reminded of something, they began rummaging through their bags, pulling out every item as if undergoing a customs inspection, tossing everything onto the seat. The husband would try to repack things, only for the wife to open another bag and dump its contents out again. He would get exasperated, and I found the whole scene thoroughly entertaining.

For over an hour, they turned their luggage upside down, but whatever they were searching for remained elusive. Though I couldn’t understand their language, it was clear that each blamed the other—“You must have put it somewhere!” “No, you did!” “No, you must have put it somewhere!” “Somewhere, you must have put it!” Still, I wondered, how could a woman be so scatterbrained when traveling?
Barrister Parvateesam

The husband expressed his feelings with a touch of fear. “Enough now. You and your endless chatter! That thing is in such-and-such a place. I’ve told you a thousand times to get up and take care of it. If only you’d listen to me! And on top of that, you yell at me. All men have the same disease,” she declared, in a booming voice, with exaggerated gestures.

As I mentioned before, though I did not know their language, from their facial expressions and dramatic gestures, I felt as if I understood their entire conversation, and I was greatly amused. On this lonely journey, I found this way of passing the time quite enjoyable. If only I knew their language, I would have joined in their conversation, perhaps stirred up their quarrel a bit more, or helped to settle it. That would have been even more entertaining.

In any case, by the time it was past midnight, one by one, they reluctantly drifted off to sleep, still muttering half-formed words for a few more minutes, until finally their eyes closed and their mouths fell silent. As for me, I could not sleep for quite some time. I watched their faces, imagined their lives, and thought, “Perhaps their daily routines are always like this.” Without realizing it, I too fell into the arms of sleep.

The next day, after the sun was well up, I reached Hyderabad. Here, everyone was getting down in a flurry—porters shouting, women making a commotion, men grumbling, children crying—the din was so overwhelming it felt as if my ears would burst. I thought perhaps my confusion would subside a little.

I learned that I would have to get down here and continue my journey by another train in the evening. I deposited my luggage in the waiting room, rested for a quarter of an hour, bathed there itself, and, after instructing the attendant to keep a careful watch over my things, I went out for a meal. Never had I imagined that, even after coming so close to my own region in my own country, I would have to eat such wretched food. In the middle of the meal, I abandoned it, quenched my thirst with a little curd, and came outside. I filled my stomach with four bananas and set out to explore the city.

Here, except for a handful of people, everyone else conversed only in Urdu. The streets and vehicles were exceedingly unpleasant. I was a little disappointed, thinking, “Is this the state of the illustrious Nawab’s city?” At least in Madras and Bombay there are tramcars...

I felt no urge to see anything there, nor to greet anyone. So, I bought a few more fruits and retreated to the station’s waiting room, where I lay down comfortably. By sheer luck, the room was neither crowded nor noisy, and I slept soundly.

I awoke around half past two. When I stepped outside, I found the station porter slumped against the wall, dozing and dreaming away. Though I wasn’t particularly keen, I had no choice but to gently wake him, bring him back to this world, and slip some money into his hand. I told him, “First, get yourself a little tea. Then, bring me some bread, butter, and tea.” The man, overjoyed, seemed to forget that his sleep had been disturbed, and acted as if he hadn’t slept at all. He dashed off, washed his face and finished his ablutions, and soon returned with the refreshments, accompanied by a man from the refreshment stall.

Since my stomach was already rumbling with hunger, I made short work of the food and sat back. There, the porter, bringing along a coolie, informed me that it was time for the train. He took charge of me and my luggage, accepted the tip I gave him, and sent me off with the joy of a man bidding farewell to a dear friend.

I found a suitable spot in second class on the train and settled in comfortably. Within another fifteen minutes, the station was abuzz with activity—crowds everywhere, hawkers shouting about fruits and snacks, and a general commotion. My compartment soon filled up as well. Four or five elderly Muslim gentlemen, a man who looked like a government official with his wife, two Anglo-Indian young women, and a Telugu couple with a small child joined me.

The Telugu couple sat right next to me, as if we were all headed to Bombay together. For some reason, the couple seemed to take an immediate liking to me, though I couldn’t fathom why. But what could I do about it? Their child must have been about a year old—large, expressive eyes, a broad forehead, jet-black hair, plump and fair-skinned, altogether a delightful and adorable sight. The child, too, stared at me without blinking and flashed a sweet little smile.

A sudden, irresistible urge seized me: I wanted to pick up the child, cuddle and kiss it, tickle it, make it laugh, and play with it. But how? How could I ask them to let me hold their baby? What would they think of me? I hesitated for quite some time, my desire growing stronger by the minute, until I could bear it no longer. I turned to the child sitting next to me...
I greeted the man, “Sir, where are you from?” “Bandar,” he replied. “Are you working here?” I asked. “No, not here. I came to attend an auspicious event at a relative’s house,” he said.

After another ten minutes of idle chatter, he asked, “Where are you from?” “I’m from Narsapur,” I replied. “Do you live in Hyderabad?” he asked. “No, I went to England to study. I stayed there for three years and have just returned. I boarded the train in Bombay yesterday. Now I’m on my way home,” I said.

The moment he heard that, he looked at me in astonishment, as if my stature had grown by several feet. His wife, too, glanced at me with a look of great respect, her eyes and face lighting up with a gentle smile. Even their little child looked at me knowingly and burst into laughter.

What’s this, madam? Do you know me? Have we met before? Are we old friends? I stretched out my hand and said, “Come here, come!” “Why, sir?” the man started to say, but before he could finish, the child tumbled from her father’s lap into my arms. I received her with great affection. In that exchange, my fingers must have brushed against the mother’s hand, for she shrank away shyly.
I cuddled the child, showering her with kisses as I sat there. After a while, she began playing with me and, right in my lap, relieved herself. “What a mischievous little one!” I exclaimed.

Her parents noticed and the father cried, “Oh dear, what a mess you’ve made, you little rascal!” He pulled the child away from me, and then the mother snatched her from his hands, about to give her a smack.

“Don’t hit her,” I said. “Don’t hit her, I can’t bear it. The child has done nothing wrong. What does a little one know?” I went on, as if I were an expert in child-rearing, as if I had raised ten children myself, spinning tales. The mother, still angry, hugged her daughter to her chest and began kissing her instead.

So, chatting away with them, recounting tales of foreign lands, I slowly drifted off to sleep. By morning, we had reached Bezawada. They got off there. Once more, I asked for the little girl, took her in my arms, kissed her, and said, “Will you come with me, little one?” I pinched her cheeks playfully as I laughed. She shook her head, “No, no.” “Well then, you may go. Your parents’ burden is now lighter. I’ll take your daughter, marry her, and send you the wedding invitation. You must come without fail!”

“Alright then,” I said. They were delighted and agreed at once. “Once she grows up a little more, if you’re still unmarried by then, we’ll give her to you ourselves and arrange the wedding. Why go through all this trouble?” they said, half-afraid that I might actually take the child with me. They quickly took her from my hands and went their way. The little girl kept turning back to look at me as they left.

I stood there for a while, lost in thought, before collecting my luggage and heading to the waiting room. After attending to the necessary business, I bathed and changed my clothes. By the time I was ready, I learned that our train heading east was about to depart, so I dashed to the platform once again. The thought of food didn’t even cross my mind. That little child’s image lingered before my eyes, filling my heart and, strangely, my stomach as well.

As the train set off and the journey continued, my thoughts drifted back three years. I remembered that night when, without a care or a clue, with the innocence of one who knows neither good nor bad, I boarded a train for the first time and traveled to Madras. Some of these stations looked familiar. Nothing seemed to have changed. My fellow passengers today looked just like the people from back then. However, since this was second class, there were a few higher-class folks among us, unlike the common crowd of before.

Somewhere along the way, my stomach began to grumble. I bought a few fruits and a couple of guavas, ate them, drank some water, and managed to suppress my hunger. By evening, I reached Nidadavolu. As I stepped onto the platform, old memories began to stir in my mind once again. The quarrel with the station master over the ticket, stumbling backward with my luggage as I tried to board the train, getting on the wrong train heading in the opposite direction, stubbornly refusing to get down when told—all these memories and more held me rooted to the spot for a while.

Regaining my senses, I handed my luggage to a porter and, despite the meager fare, tasted Telugu food for the first time in three years at a nearby hotel. Then, collecting my things, I went to the ferry. Just as before, I took a room on the boat and settled in. Soon, with much shouting and commotion, the boatmen pushed the ferry into the river and we set off toward Narsapur. Night fell.

chapters.title: Arrival in the Village
paragraphs: Like the gentle sway of palm trees, the boatman’s whistling tunes and the various conversations of my fellow passengers shattered the tranquil silence of nature. Yet, my heart felt an inexplicable delight. With every mile we drew closer to my village, I imagined my home, my people, standing before my eyes. It felt as though I was speaking with them, reminiscing about childhood tales, wandering in a world of imagination, forgetting myself and even sleep, gazing into the breaking dawn, sitting hunched on the boat.

By about six in the morning, we reached Narsapur. Alighting from the boat, a sense of longing for my homeland, suppressed for three years, surged within me. The imminent joy of seeing my parents, and countless other thoughts, made me restless. In a hurry, I hired a horse-cart, pestered the cart driver to go faster, and finally reached Mogaliturru.

It was about eleven o’clock by the time the cart entered Mogaliturru village. Seeing the cart, and spotting a new face—myself—inside it, a wave of speculation swept through the onlookers. Many wondered, “Who is this gentleman?” Some opined that I must be a Tahsildar or perhaps a Calcutta official. “But if he’s really a Tahsildar or from Calcutta, why isn’t there a Daftari or a peon in front?” an experienced elder was heard asking. “Well then, who could he be?” The debates and arguments continued, but my cart sped ahead before anyone could resolve their doubts.

A few youngsters ran after my cart for some distance but couldn’t catch up. As the cart turned into our street, the local gossips, who had been standing at the street corner exchanging news, caught sight of my face. “Isn’t that Chattulugaru’s boy?” someone asked. “Why has he come from Seema?” wondered another. “If he’s come from Seema, why isn’t there a sahib’s hat on his head?” a third questioned. “Whether he has it or not, shouldn’t there at least be a memsahib with him?” another chimed in. “You and your cleverness! If there were a memsahib, would she ever come to Bapan’s house?” someone retorted. Their questions went unanswered, and they stood there, puzzled and silent, as my cart finally stopped in front of our house.
None of my family had really expected that I would return that very day.

The moment the sound of a cart stopping in the street was heard, my mother, with the hope that it must be me, came running out in a flurry and flung open the door. My heart was pounding like a steam engine, and I stood at the threshold, trembling with excitement, my whole body tense, eyes wide, staring at the doorway.

As soon as the door opened and my face appeared, my mother too stood frozen for a moment. “Oh my child! You’ve come?” she cried out in a wild, ecstatic shriek, forgetting even the sari she had draped over her shoulder. Without pausing to think whether she should touch me or not, whether she should let me inside or not, she rushed forward and embraced me tightly, unable to utter a word, tears streaming down her face in an unbroken flow.
I was even more bewildered than she was, standing motionless as my mother’s tears soaked my shirt, while my own tears, welling up like a flood, rained down upon her head.

My father, who had been performing his daily worship to the gods, must have heard my mother’s cry. For the first time ever, he abandoned his devotions mid-way, and in a single stride, came out to the verandah and stood before me. He was struck dumb, unable to speak, holding back his tears with great effort, as if damming a river, his eyes wide and unblinking, as though all his life breath was concentrated in that gaze fixed upon me.
For several minutes, we all stood there, unmoving, frozen in that moment.

Meanwhile, the cart driver unloaded my luggage and brought it inside. From the end of our street and from the next one over, all those who had been speculating about my return came hurrying to our doorstep, tossing their betel leaves aside, and with their feet—

Leaving their slippers right there on the street, they stopped a few paces behind me, watching us. At that moment, I was still spellbound, but my mother, regaining her senses before anyone else, took the lead and said, “Come, son, come inside.” My father stood there and remarked, “We were wondering if you’d come tonight or tomorrow.”

The people who had followed us came inside the doorway, bowed to my father and me, and said, “Sir! Your son has returned—you are truly fortunate. We had all but given up hope of seeing the young master again, thought he’d be lost to Calcutta forever!” Four or five of them exclaimed in unison, “Would he ever have come back if he’d settled in Calcutta?”

I stood there with a smile, saying nothing. My father, with a serene composure, replied, “At last, after three years, the Lord has blessed us and brought our boy home safe and sound, even in these dreadful times of war. As long as we have His grace, we shall never lack anything. I see you all are on your way somewhere. Let the boy rest a while, bathe, and refresh himself. We’ll meet again at leisure this evening—what say you?” His tact, eloquence, and presence of mind left me in awe.
All the visitors bowed and said, “As you wish, sir, please excuse us,” and took their leave.

Meanwhile, my mother went inside, bathed, changed into a fresh cotton sari, adorned her face with turmeric and a half-rupee-sized bindi, and returned, radiant as Annapurna herself, shining with joy like Mahalakshmi.

“My dear! You’ve returned safely! You didn’t face any dangers on the way, did you? I was certain nothing could happen to you, that Lord Shiva was watching over us. That’s why, with a steady mind, I counted the days, waiting for your return,” my father said, standing a little distance away, speaking gently. I sat down on the bench nearby, and as I was about to get up and bow at his feet, he guessed my intention and said, “First, you go and bathe, son. Mother—”

“There will be hot water ready for you there. Meanwhile, I will finish my worship to the deity,” she said, and went inside. I sat there for a moment, gazing at the soot-darkened walls of the kitchen. I don’t know how long I sat thus. As my father completed his worship, the bell rang out loud and clear as a signal. I was startled, and stood up as if I had been shaken awake from a trance. The *Mantrapushpam*—which I had heard so many times until three years ago—now, flowing once again from my father’s throat, sent a shiver down my spine. Instinctively, I joined my hands in reverence and stood there.

As soon as the *Mantrapushpam* ended, I took off my clothes for a bath and picked up a towel. A new habit, this—one I never had as a child. I even took soap with me, but hesitated, unsure whether I should go through the kitchen or not. So, I slipped out through the passage beside our backyard shed and made my way to the well. The bathroom, the tub, the English-style bath I’d grown used to over three years—all that had to be forgotten now. For a moment, I hesitated, then threw my towel over the pole nearby and bathed as I used to in days gone by. Remembering my old habit, I soaked the towel, wrapped it around my waist, dipped my *pancha* in water, wrung it out on the pole, and went inside.

All this while, my mother stood by the door, utterly absorbed, as if she had forgotten the entire world and I was the only soul in this creation. Her eyes followed my every movement, every gesture, brimming with life and joy. I went back the same way, into the backyard, put on fresh clothes, slipped into the fine lace underwear I’d bought in Bombay, combed my hair, and sat down. My father seemed to be preparing to eat.

My mother brought a mirror and sandalwood paste with turmeric, placed them before me, and said, “Put on your *bottu*, my boy! You’ll have to eat here again tomorrow at this very hour. What can I do, son? I had to say it, though it pains me.” With that, she went inside, set up a low wooden stool for me in the backyard, spread out a leaf plate, and served me food in the traditional, scriptural way.

As I was about to sit down to eat, she said, “Son, take off your shirt before you sit.” As I was removing my shirt, she came a little closer and asked in a hushed tone, “Are you wearing your sacred thread?” I replied, “Yes.” I had anticipated such a situation and had made sure to be prepared. After I sat down by the leaf plate, my mother peered through the door to see whether I would perform the customary rituals or not.

Mother kept watching me the whole time. Until I finished my meal, she kept asking me every little thing ten times over, bustling back and forth between the living room and the kitchen. As soon as I finished eating, with tears in her eyes and a choked voice, she said, “Take away that leaf and throw it out in the street, dear.” Then she added, “Let me sprinkle some cow-dung water here and wipe it with my hand, son. What a miserable state this is! It’s come to this, that you have to do these chores yourself.” She lamented so much.

I laughed, picked up the rice grains, folded the leaf, and said, “Why, mother? Why do you act as if this is something new for me? When I was little, whenever you were out, how many times did I do this myself? I haven’t forgotten the habit yet.” I said, laughing. “No, my dear, I haven’t forgotten. I still remember, my silly boy,” she replied, smiling tenderly through her tears, her lips curved in affection.
Just then, my father too finished his meal and came out. He sat on the same bench where I was sitting, putting his legs up. I prostrated before him with full devotion.
“Why now, boy? Why all of a sudden?” he asked.

I stood up, my voice trembling, and said, “Won’t you forgive my offense, father? Was what I did such an unpardonable act? People kept saying that if one studies abroad, one gains great knowledge and civilization, and later can get a big job and a high position. Hearing this repeatedly from some elders, I was swept away in a moment’s impulse and hurriedly left.

From the moment I left till this very moment, I haven’t forgotten you. I have felt so much longing and pain for you—can you believe that, father? If I had asked your permission that day, would you have agreed? Staying at home, caught in this predicament, with no way forward or back, living like an eyelash on an eyebrow—there was no other path I could see. I didn’t like the studies here. That’s why I made up my mind and, not fearing even your anger, quietly left. Is that still an unforgivable crime, father? I made you spend so much money. I caused you so much mental anguish. But I still have the courage that I can make up for that fault. The education there, the teaching methods there, have made me so enthusiastic and opened up so many unknown vistas—”

I suppose education is what has shown me new worlds before my eyes. At any rate, my outlook has broadened. My arrogance has diminished, and the pettiness of man has become clear to me. I have come to understand the place and value of truth in life. Ultimately, it is only God who is capable of shaping the future as it ought to be. Father, if you would just bless me and say you forgive me, with that one word, I would feel such satisfaction and enthusiasm, as if I had gained the strength of a thousand elephants. Please say that one word, Father,” I pleaded, standing before him with folded hands.
For two minutes, he did not lift his bowed head. I could not tell whether he had heard what I said or not. His face never betrayed any emotion, and now was no different.

After a while, he raised his head and looked straight into my face. “My son! Why do you plead so much for my forgiveness? I bear no anger towards you. It is true—and I do not deny it—that when you first left, out of selfishness and pride, I was pained that a son who should have been by my side at my age was going far away. As for what you have done, and whether it was good or bad, even now I am unable to decide. The one who must make that decision, the one who must either forgive or rejoice, is God Himself. That you have completed your studies victoriously in those foreign lands, have not strayed from the path, and have returned home safely in these turbulent times—this makes me feel that God has been pleased with you and has protected you every moment. Seeing you gives me only joy, not anger. Now, for two more days, you must remain apart from us, according to our tradition and customs, to perform the necessary rites of atonement. This evening, after consulting with the priests, I will make the arrangements. Until then, we must continue to stay apart. You have returned after a long journey. Rest for a while,” he said, and went inside.
Though I was eager to lie on the cot and chat with my mother, I hesitated to go inside and lay down. In that state of uncertainty, I drifted off to sleep. I must have slept for about four hours.
Barrister Parvateesam

As usual, I didn’t wake up early. I thought perhaps Mother would make tea, but then remembered—there are no such habits in our house! How could she possibly do that today, I wondered, when suddenly my mother brought me a little fresh water and some light refreshments, set them down, and said, “Son, go to the well, wash your face and feet, then come and have your snack,” looking at me all the while.
I got up with a gentle smile and asked, “Mother, why have you done all this now?”
“I’ll tell you later. First, go wash your feet,” she replied.

With great happiness, I got up, thinking how strange it felt to suddenly give up the tea I’d been drinking four or five times a day for the past three years. I went, washed my feet, and returned to eat the snacks lovingly prepared by my mother’s divine hands. I was so delighted that I completely forgot about wanting my usual Murphy tea.

A little while after this ritual, our family priest arrived. My father and he consulted for some time and decided that the expiatory rites should be performed the next day. My father then went out to gather the necessary items. After another ten minutes, the priest inquired after my well-being and then took his leave.

The next morning, I woke up, took the brass vessel for the leftovers, and, feeling a bit nervous, went outside. It was already a little late in the morning, which made me feel even more embarrassed. I lamented that even this small change hadn’t come over me yet, but having no other choice, I walked quite a distance away and, on my way back, decided to bathe in the village tank.

Without delay, I plunged into the tank and swam for a while. Suddenly, I noticed men and women, both in the water and on the bank, standing still and staring at me in astonishment. The moment I realized so many people were watching me, I felt as if I’d done something terribly wrong and, blushing with embarrassment, got out and began drying myself.
A couple of elderly villagers remarked, “Well, even after three years away in a distant land, you haven’t forgotten how to swim! That’s wonderful.”
I was quite pleased. There, without any cold, just like this, there were ponds and such, and in them...
They asked, “Do you swim while bathing?”

I laughed and replied, “There are different arrangements for bathing over there. There aren’t any open ponds like these. Even if there are rivers or canals, the cold won’t permit you to bathe in them like this. And the people there wouldn’t tolerate such half-naked displays either.”
“Ayyo! Oh my! Is that so! Hmm! Well, never mind, don’t think anything more of it. But then, how do they go out?” they asked.
I laughed and said, “If they don’t even bathe, how will they go out?”
“Then—for these three years—however those people may be, but how did you manage without bathing? How do people live without this?” they exclaimed, astonished.
“Don’t worry, I didn’t say there’s no bathing at all. Every house has arrangements suited for it,” I said.
“Ah! That’s what you should say. So, it’s like the backyards in Narsapuram,” they said.

“Not quite like those. There’s no need for separate people to clean them, and there are different arrangements to keep them clean. I’ll tell you about it later,” I said, and, fearing what other questions they might ask, I quickly climbed out of the pond.
“But then, son—” they began, but without waiting for them to finish, I dashed off at a speed that would shame a startled deer and reached home.

On the steps of our street, about forty or fifty village elders of all castes had gathered, holding a meeting and waiting for me. Oh Lord, I thought, I escaped there only to be trapped here. These people will surely torment me with all sorts of tricky questions! As I trembled with anxiety, they all stood up, greeted me, and smiled politely.
“Please sit, I’ll be right back,” I said, and hurried inside, changed out of my wet clothes, wrapped a towel around myself, and was about to put on my shirt when my mother—

Even without being asked, she brought four delicious pesaratlu, golden and crisp, arranged on a silver plate, along with a tumbler of cool water and a bowl of milk. She set them all down on a low stool before me. I rose from my bed with great delight. After three years, to eat pesaratlu like these—words cannot describe the joy I felt. Afterwards, taking the milk with me, I went out to the street-side platform where the village elders were waiting to meet me.
As soon as I arrived, all of them stood up again, shifted a little to one side on the platform to make space for me, and invited me to sit.

As I was about to sit down, our household washerman piped up, “Just a moment, sir, I’ll bring a mat for you to sit on,” and started to go inside. But I said, “No need for that! Everyone else is sitting as they are. Why should I need anything special?”
He turned pale and quietly retreated.
For a moment, everyone seemed uncertain how to begin the conversation, and there was a brief, awkward silence.

Then, one of the elders, a respected raja, spoke up. “Babu Parvateesham, when did you arrive? Last night, by the time I returned home, it was very late. Everyone was saying that you’d just come, that you were a new man now. I was eager to see you, but my family said you’d probably be asleep by then, so I shouldn’t disturb you. So, though my heart was impatient, I waited and came first thing in the morning.”

“I’m truly delighted,” I replied, “that all of you have set aside your morning work just to come and see me. It fills me with happiness. What news is there? Even though I left this village, left all of you, and went far away to a distant land, my heart was always wandering here—seeing you all, speaking with you, roaming these very streets, these fields, these canals. Are you all well? Are the seasons and the crops favorable?”

chapters.title: Family Reunion
paragraphs: “Ayyababai Babu! Our Parvatisham Babu knows everything—he hasn’t forgotten any of us,” said one of our former tenants. “Is everything there completely new, sir?” a young man asked. “Yes, yes, everything is new over there,” I replied. “Then how do you manage, sir?” he asked.

Just then, someone else asked, “Does everyone there speak only English, or do they have our language too?” “Ayyababai Babu! What childish questions! Of course, those people know English,” another fellow chimed in.
I laughed and said, “Children only learn what their parents speak. Don’t we have a saying: ‘The words of elders become the songs of the young’?”

“Then, are the houses there like ours?” someone asked. “They’re not like ours. It’s a cold country, so you won’t find street platforms or people sitting on them chatting away, or sleeping right there,” I said.
At this, someone clutched his chest as if heartbroken and exclaimed, “No street platforms at all, sir?” “No, there aren’t,” I replied.
“Then how do they wash their faces and all that?” he asked. “I don’t really know, but perhaps that’s why many people there don’t wash their faces every day,” I said.

“What’s this, what’s this!” cried one of the Rajus, who had been slouching against the wall but now sat up straight. “They don’t wash their faces? Oh, these people’s faces! If they don’t wash their faces, what else do they wash? And they eat and drink with the same mouth! May their faces burn!”
Barrister Parvateesam
“Oh Parvateesam Babu! What sort of trouble have you landed yourself in now?” Desamayyah exclaimed, clutching his heart in distress at the thought of my journey.

“Every country has its own customs, you know. Why worry about what happens where? Our neighboring Tamil brothers don’t wipe their tongues, but does that mean we should burn their faces? Or cut off their tongues? Among them, aren’t there so many scholars, intellectuals, learned men, and Vedic pundits?” I said.
“Then, are there no open fields to go to?” asked one man, pitifully, as if he suddenly felt the urgent need himself.
Suppressing a smile, I replied, “There are plenty of fields, hills, and mountains as you wish, but over there, you can’t do such things. No one does, nor is it allowed.”
“Oh, what kind of death is this!” exclaimed another. “If you can’t do either of the two things one must do in the morning, how do they survive? How did you manage to live and come back alive?”
Before I could answer, another fellow chimed in, “They say you can’t go to the fields, nor can you bathe in the canals or rivers. Then what is left to do?”

As if these three were the only things to be done in life! I said, “I only said you can’t do certain things outside. I never said you can’t do them at all, did I? I only said you can’t do them in public. If you do nothing at all, how would anyone survive? Each country and time has its own arrangements for people’s needs. They too wake up in the morning, relieve themselves, eat their meals, and stay in their houses.” I hadn’t even finished when—
“Then what about marriages and such?” interrupted someone.
“Ah! They do get married. After that, everything happens as usual, and they have children,” I replied.
With that, some of them stopped their questions, but one man—
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri,

“Sir, forgive us if this sounds foolish, but we’re asking out of pure ignorance. How do people live over there? What are their customs and ways of life? How do they run their households? If you could elaborate a bit, we’d love to hear it,” he said, his curiosity plain.

“I have no objection to telling you all about it. But if I start that story now, it’ll go on as long as the Kondaveedu chains—it’ll stretch out till evening! Unless we’re ready to skip our meals and sit patiently, I don’t mind telling it all,” I replied. At that, half the enthusiasm in the room died down. Still, one persistent fellow couldn’t hold back:
“Sir, are all the people there white-skinned, or are there people like us too?” he asked.
“Except for our own people who have gone there, the rest are all white,” I said.
“So, the children there are all white too, then?” he asked.

“Oh, you silly fellow! If white people didn’t have white children, how would black people be born? And if, by chance, a black child is born there once in a hundred or a thousand, you can be sure something fishy has gone on!” I replied. The whole room burst into laughter. The poor soul who asked the question couldn’t grasp the hidden meaning in my answer.
Everyone was about to get up when one of them quickly piped up, “Sir, what about food? What do they eat over there?”

Before I could say it’s not rice, another interrupted, “Oh, leave it! They eat some kind of grass, what’s it to us? If they didn’t eat grass, why would they come here and sit on our heads? If they had food, why would they come here at all? Whether it’s an Englishman, an Arab, a rat, or a Yanadi, they all come here because they have nothing to eat there! Isn’t that why our Parvateesham went so far, and why so many of our people go there?” declared the future village accountant.
“Let me tell you, slowly! I’ll tell you everything. Just put your work aside for a bit!”
Barrister Parvateesam

From now on, let us not gather on the porch in the evenings, nor on Raju’s verandah, nor even in any field. Instead, let us sit together every day for an hour or two, chatting leisurely. I will tell you all sorts of stories—so I said, and got up. Everyone was overjoyed and said, “Agreed! Agreed! This is a wonderful idea.” Raju said, “This way, we’ll have a delightful pastime.” All of them, praising me and showering me with compliments, went off to their respective tasks.

The next day, there was quite a commotion. As soon as I woke up in the morning, after finishing my dental ablutions and just as I was about to bathe, our family priest arrived in grand style. The moment I saw him, I remembered the atonement rituals that were to be performed at this hour. As he entered, he asked, “Well, Parvateesam, have you finished your remaining rituals?”
“Most of them are done, sir. I just need to bathe and perhaps have some light refreshment—” I began, but before I could finish my sentence,

“Wait, my boy, just a word. For now, put aside your bathing and forget about your stomach. Unless you do exactly as I instruct, your father won’t let you live. Even now, after much argument, I spoke on your behalf and tried to reduce your burden, and for that, your father has heaped a mountain of curses on my head,” he said. “If there are any more complaints at this hour, all of them will fall on my head. I haven’t told you anything that would get you into trouble,” he added.
“But why, early in the morning, on an empty stomach, did my father heap so many curses on your head?” I asked.

“Oh, it’s nothing. Your father insists that everything must be done strictly according to the scriptures. So, first and foremost, he told me to perform the purification ritual for your head. He believes that young people these days, especially those who have been abroad like you, have no sense of such things, and that even if the ritual isn’t performed, nothing untoward will happen. I tried to convince him of this, but as a result, I’ve ended up with a head full of curses. What can I do?”
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri,

I won’t do it. But once you’ve done it, can you escape the consequences? That’s how it is. So now, I spend my time at home with the lady of the house, and outside with people like your father,” he said.

“In that case, it seems I’ve narrowly escaped a calamity. But I have a request. If only I could complete the impending atonement chapter as soon as possible, and have my Brahminhood restored to me, I’d be most delighted,” I said.

To this, he replied, “What should take three days can be done in one. Somehow, I’ll pull you out of this with the utmost subtlety. But beware—be ready soon for those five dreadful days. Still, there’s a little catch here: whatever strange foods you’ve eaten in those foreign lands, a bit of their sting will remain on your tongue. There’s no denying that,” he said.
Indeed, sir, how could it be denied? Only after you’ve burned my tongue, I replied.

“That’s not it, boy. Don’t be alarmed and stop there—there’s plenty more to be done before that. Our people, for everything, have devised all sorts of shortcuts and simplified procedures for the likes of you. Before the event, fellows like you will pester us, saying this won’t do, that won’t do, but when it comes to the three-night affair, not a soul utters a word. If possible, they’ll even ask for a five-night version,” he said.
“I wouldn’t say such things, sir. Anyway, whether it’s three nights or five, there isn’t a fool alive who would stop with just that,” I said.

Unable to contain his amusement, he burst into laughter, lost in memories. “Enough, you’ve learned plenty of tales. After all that travel, you’ve gained a fine wisdom. Now go, bathe quickly—if your father arrives, he won’t let us live in peace. Go on!” he said.

With that, he went inside. He and I have known each other intimately since childhood. So, I know he always speaks in this easy, witty manner, and that provoking him with words and making him talk has always been my favorite pastime.
This sort of gossip was quite familiar to me. In fact, I rather enjoyed listening to such tales.

By the time I finished my bath, our family priests had arranged everything for the atonement ritual. My father, ever the foresighted one, had long ago procured and kept ready for me a silk dhoti, which now lay spread out there. They asked me to put it on. Although I had fallen out of the habit lately and the silk dhoti kept slipping off, I managed to tie it securely with great care.

Just then, my father arrived, accompanied by ten of the most prominent Brahmins from our village. Following them came a few notable Kshatriya gentlemen as well. With mantras, rituals, and Vedic chants, the atonement ceremony was completed after about an hour, somehow or other.

Within another half hour, everyone was graciously invited to partake in the meal. Besides the elders who had come, several other Brahmins from the village also kindly joined the dining line. I, too, was asked to sit and eat with them. The meal was served, and after the customary offering of dakshina and betel leaves, everyone returned to their homes.

But by that very evening, a certain commotion began to stir in the town. I heard that some people had started grumbling that this atonement was insufficient, that it was not in accordance with the scriptures, and, above all, that there could be no atonement for a sin committed knowingly! Thus began a chorus of protests and arguments among some villagers.
Of course, there was no one with any real authority in these matters. But then, human nature never does change, does it? Well, I thought, let’s see what happens, and went to bed.

Four days later, word reached us from all quarters that not only our family, but also all those who had dined at our house, were to be excommunicated. My father was furious. He consulted many elders, scholars, and those in authority, and arranged a meeting.

The very same scholars who had advised us and personally conducted the rituals at our house, now, making some excuse, left without partaking of the meal, and later claimed that the ceremony had not been performed according to the scriptures, which is why they had not eaten. We also learned that they had gone around spreading malicious rumors through certain people.
My father was a man of great composure, but once he set his mind to something, he would not rest until it was resolved. His determination only grew stronger by the day.

Later, on the occasion of a family death anniversary, the usual guests who would come to eat at our house refused to do so. “Never mind,” we said, and brought someone from the neighboring village to perform the ceremony.

My father finally brought the matter to a close. With that, the Brahmins of our village split into two factions. This stubbornness spread to the neighboring villages as well. The Brahmins from our village were no longer invited to any ceremonies or feasts by the people of nearby villages. Because of this, our rival group found themselves in quite a fix, struggling to get by, until at last they came crawling back, begged my father for forgiveness, and made peace. Thus, our village’s “scholarly” elders dragged out this whole affair to a pitiful end.

After this atonement was completed, I too spent two or three days at home, roaming about as I pleased, eating in my father’s row at mealtime, whiling away my afternoons with some book or the other, and generally lounging about. By evening, I would sometimes go out to the fields and return. Every morning and evening, without fail, not just one or two, but at least ten people would come and sit down, saying, “Babayya! Tell us something about your experiences over there.”

Every day, I didn’t know what to say. I didn’t want to disappoint them by saying, “Please, have mercy, I have nothing left to tell.” So I would say, “What can I say, sir! If you ask me something, I’ll try to answer it.”
Immediately, someone would ask, “Well then, how did you manage your meals there? Were there any of our own cooks over there? Or did you cook for yourself? What did you do?”
“There were no cooks from our village, and I didn’t cook for myself either. I managed to hire a cook,” I replied.
“What! Our own people, you say? Or was it a woman?” he asked, eyes wide.
“No, sir! Not that fortunate, alas! Neither our own people, nor a woman from home.”
“Listen here! Don’t tell anyone, but I managed to hire a lady sahib,” I said with a wink.

“Ayyo baboy! Oh my! You’ve become a real lord, haven’t you? So it was truly a lady sahib? Well done! Even the big shots in our village can’t get such a thing! And you managed to catch one, eh? Well, well! You’re a real hero, that’s all I’ll say!”
For a while, as I was laughing to myself, the people around me too began to chuckle. “It’s true, absolutely true!” exclaimed a young man.

“Yes, it’s the honest-to-God truth. I found a real lady, and that too without much effort or expense. For as long as I was there, she would always have a hot meal ready for me, right on time. When I was coming here, she even said she’d come along. I thought of bringing her, just to show you all. But then, I was afraid that if I brought her, all of you would drop your own work and just sit around gawking at her, not letting us mind our own business. So, I didn’t bring her,” I said.
“Oh dear! Oh dear! What a thing you’ve done! You’ve deprived us of a good sight, sir,” they lamented.

“We too would have been happy to see her, wouldn’t we?” said one, sounding terribly disappointed. Another piped up, “So, all the time you were there, was it just that one woman for you, or—” but before he could finish,
“One is enough for my life, isn’t it?” I replied.
“Oh, but you’re both young and look like a lord and lady! What’s lacking for you?” he said.
“Nothing for me, nothing for you either, I suppose,” I said, and just then another interjected,
“So, does she know how to cook our food?” the lawyer asked.
“Do they eat our kind of rice there?” another asked.

“They don’t, my dear fellow, not at all. How would they get our rice? Our rice, our dal, our curries—unless they’re born here, even if they’re reborn a hundred times, they’ll never taste them. That’s why, after much effort, just as I taught her everything else, I patiently taught her all about our food too.”
“That’s all there is to it, sir,” he said.

“That’s all there is to it. I just learned whatever little I could and managed to get by. That’s the way for all of us. It’s customary for the people in the house we rent to help us with these things. Even our landlady has two children,” I said. That seemed to dampen their enthusiasm a bit.
“So, what’s the difference between our food and their food, sir?” one of the youngsters asked.
“Well, first of all, we’re strict vegetarians, aren’t we? But over there, from the youngest child to the oldest adult, everyone is a meat-eater,” I replied.
“In that case, do they cook your food with the same hands?” another fellow piped up.

“Do you think they’ll go out and get a brand new pair of hands just to cook for us, attach them specially, and use them only when needed?” I shot back. Everyone burst out laughing, and that Friday fellow shrank a little in embarrassment.
“So, do they get up early in the morning and bathe like we do?” someone else asked.

“It’s hard to say everyone does that. After all, it’s a cold country! Nobody bathes in ponds or canals there. In fact, they can’t. So, people have to bathe indoors, using taps or hot water. But that’s not something everyone can manage easily. Only those living in big houses can do it comfortably; for the rest, it’s not so simple,” I explained.
“Well then, what about you, sir?” another asked.

“I somehow managed by tying a special cloth for the purpose and didn’t give up bathing,” I replied. And so it went—one silly question after another, pestering me endlessly. From the moment I woke up in the morning until I went to bed at night, they had doubts about every little thing I did.
“They must have mats to sit on there, right?” someone asked.
“What kind of mats? Palm-leaf mats? Jute mats? Or those made from woven grass?” another chimed in.
Barrister Parvateesam
“Are there palm trees, date trees, or coconut trees over there?” one fellow asked, full of doubt.
Another simpleton wondered, “Do you sleep on a bed or on the floor?”
“I sleep on a mattress placed on a bed,” I replied.
“So, they have beds and mattresses and all that over there too, then?” he said, as if he’d uncovered a great truth.
“Blankets are what we use to cover ourselves!” exclaimed another, astonished.
“Not just one,” I said. “You have to pile on three or four, sometimes even more, and even then, in winter, the cold doesn’t let up until you’re buried under a heap of them.”
“Is it really that cold?” another asked.

“It’s not just cold—it’s a kind of cold you can’t even imagine. In winter, sometimes it snows. And by snow, I don’t mean dew drops like we get here. It’s as if someone up in the sky is shaking out white cotton, and it floats down, soft and silent. When it lands on the ground, it melts away. But sometimes, it piles up in layers several feet thick, and a kind of icy wind blows, turning everything solid—hard as stone. At such times, even rivers and lakes freeze solid. If you go further north from where I was, it gets even colder. There, for six months, it’s nothing but darkness—no sunlight, only night,” I explained.
“Goodness gracious! Six months in the dark, without getting up, without answering nature’s calls, without food or trouble—how do people live in such darkness?” one man exclaimed.

“Why would anyone stop eating or doing their business just because it’s dark? Did we stop doing anything just because it was night? Everything goes on as usual, whether it’s dark or not. You’re not asking if people get married in the dark, are you?” I replied.
One man, thoroughly bewildered, asked, “Are there women there too, in such cold?”
“Where there are men, how could there not be women?” I said.
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 377
"Ah! So, over there too, there are villages, weddings, and families, is that what you’re saying?" he exclaimed, clutching his heart.

"Enough of your foolishness and lack of sense, you dolt. How else would the race continue? If there weren’t marriages and children for those people, then where do you think all these white sahibs came from, you idiot? Why do you think we’re seeing them everywhere? Before you ask such a question, you should think a little ahead and a little behind," said another, answering on my behalf.

The one who asked the first question hung his head in embarrassment and sat down, thoroughly chastened by this blow. Another old man, who had been sitting quietly through all this, looked at me, folded his hands, and said,

"Sir, I have a small doubt I’d like to ask you. It’s a question that shouldn’t really be asked, so I’m a bit afraid. Not that I’m scared of you, but I worry these young fellows here might say something or laugh at me," he said.

"You are an elder. I’ve known you since I was born. None of these people are wiser than you. When we’re all chatting amongst ourselves in a relaxed way, why should there be any fear or hesitation?" I replied.
He folded his hands together as if in prayer, lowered his voice conspiratorially, and said, “Over there, women are just like our men.”

While I was still reeling, wondering what he might ask next, he continued, “Just like our men, their women also stay outside for months at a time.” Everyone gasped in unison. The fellow shrank a little in embarrassment.

I said, “My dear fellow, you’re grown up now; you should ask questions befitting your age. It’s not just among us—no matter which country a woman is born in, after a certain age, this is the way of the world.”
But he wouldn’t let it go. “In such cold weather, how do they manage to stay outside?” he pressed on.
“I forgot to mention,” I replied, “even if they’re ‘outside,’ they’re still indoors. Just like our women, they don’t sit far away; they usually stay inside the house.”
“But for those three days, they do all the cooking and other chores, sir,” he said.
I knew about the cooking part. As for the other chores, I had no idea whether they did them or not. “You shouldn’t be asking such things,” I told him.
“All right, I won’t ask. But tell me, sir, if your wife cooked for you during those days, would you eat it?” he asked.

My wife never told me anything about those days. Who knows what would have happened if she had! If you keep asking such questions and someone at home overhears, my mother would throw you out of the house this very instant. Just to atone for such sins, my family made me perform penance the other day. If they hear about this, they’ll imagine even worse things, and not only throw me out of the house but out of the country as well!
Everyone burst out laughing at once. Then, another clever young man, emboldened, asked, “No matter what happens to you, even if you learn everything here, will your people…”
When I said, “Let’s go,” they replied, “We won’t agree to that, that’s our final word,” and gave me their assurance.
For a moment, I placed my hand on my chest and said, “Thank you, it’s enough that you’ve given me at least this much assurance.”
All of them stood up, laughing, bowed respectfully, took leave of me, and departed.

Before they had all completely left, about ten young men—some of whom had studied with me—arrived from Narsapur, greeting me with a loud, “Namaskaram, Parvateesham garu!” and chanting “Jai Rama, Ramana Govindo Hari!” with great commotion.

“What’s all this ruckus?” I asked, laughing. “Are you all so carefree? For three years, I haven’t seen a single one of your faces here. What happened? Even if you were busy with some wretched work, why hide your faces for three years?”
They burst out laughing.
One of my friends said, “Our Parvateesham, even after going all the way there, hasn’t changed a bit—he’s come back just as he was, like an unpolished coin.”
Everyone laughed again.

“What is this?” I said. “Why have you all gathered here like this? Are you the morning rain, or the midday drizzle that vanishes as soon as the sun comes up? If you all want to stay here tonight, I won’t object, boys. After that, do as you please.”

“Oh, let’s think about that later,” they said. “Just seeing you has filled our stomachs. We’ve come to prove that the proverb you quoted is false. You must be getting up to go for your meal, right? But we’ve come for another reason. We wanted to give you a small warning.”

“The news that you, Dayakeshara, have returned to the country spread through all of Narsapur like wildfire four days ago. As soon as the news broke, people started discussing whether you’d return wearing coats and turbans. Some have grown older and more cunning, and others are whispering—”

We have heard about it, but we cannot officially confirm it. Leaving all that aside, the matter at hand is this: our high school has decided to honor you grandly on behalf of the past and present students. The pleaders are also planning to organize a similar event on behalf of the Bar Association. We rushed here just to give you this good news in advance. Perhaps the function will be held tomorrow, or maybe the day after. At the very least, one of them will definitely take place. To invite you to our school’s function, our illustrious and renowned headmaster himself, with great effort and after swallowing two grains of rice to steady his heart, is planning to come in person. This is to inform the distinguished Barrister Parvatisham, who has brought such glory to us,” said my friend, who had studied with me since childhood and had helped me through many misadventures and troubles.

Another old acquaintance, with folded hands, added, “If our headmaster is kind enough, he will come himself; otherwise, the president of the Narsapur Bar Association is also likely to do us the honor.”

“Now that we have properly fulfilled our purpose in coming here, we are delighted to have had the good fortune of seeing you. With that, we shall take our leave,” said the third member of our old trio, who was always the least of us, offering his salutations and giving me a military salute before turning back. Everyone laughed.

I was very pleased. “Now, swear before fire, the sun, and the moon that you will never again put on such mad performances. Sit here until I return. Otherwise, if you come again talking about honors and felicitation, I’ll tell our headmaster not to come at all,” I said.
“We’ll come and see for ourselves what you’ll say,” they replied, laughing as they went on their way.

chapters.title: Public Reception
paragraphs: As a rule, I am afraid all of them will end up with a headache. I suggested that it would be much better if I simply showed them my face once and we could have a small gathering among ourselves.
