“Your suggestion is quite good, but since we have already made all the arrangements, let us finish this assembly first. Afterwards, I will arrange a special meeting with the teachers. That too is a very good idea. Therefore, the day after tomorrow at four in the evening, either our student leader or a teacher will come with a carriage to fetch you. You must come with them. I will come as well,” he said. When I bowed to him, he placed his hand on my shoulder, led me out to the street, took his leave, and rode away in his carriage.

What is this assembly? What is this felicitation? Why has it come to me, O Lord? I sat there pondering these questions, when once again I heard the sound of a carriage stopping at the doorstep. I was just about to get up and go out to welcome the visitors when they entered inside. This time, it was two pleaders. I learned who they were—both senior to me, so I was not very well acquainted with them. As soon as they arrived, we exchanged greetings and sat down. They immediately stated the purpose of their visit.

“We have heard of your return. Among the people from our region who have gone abroad, you are the first. You are the very first to have studied overseas and returned as an M.A., Barrister. It is a matter of great pride for us that you are so closely associated with us in every way. Therefore, on behalf of our Narsapur Bar Association, we have come personally to request you to kindly honor us by attending a meeting and sharing some of your experiences abroad. Our president himself wished to come and meet you, but we told him not to trouble himself, that we would certainly persuade you and bring you along. He will preside over the meeting that day.”
They said, “You will surely be kind enough, won’t you? This evening, one of us will bring a cart and take you along.”

“Oh no, you needn’t—” I began to protest, but before I could finish my sentence, they stood up abruptly, cutting me off. “Please, do not say another word. Kindly forgive our insistence. We must take your leave now,” they said hastily, and hurried away.

That day, I was certain there was no escaping this yajna in Narsapur come evening. So, at three in the afternoon, I got up, bathed, dressed in my usual five-yard dhoti, put on a laalchi, and even arranged a shawl to drape over my shoulders. Expecting some students and teachers from our school to arrive, I was ready and waiting by a quarter to four, sitting prepared for their arrival. They had said they would come at precisely four o’clock. The clock struck four. Then half-past four came and went. I began to wonder if I had made some mistake, or if perhaps they had changed the date. Still, thinking I should at least check if a cart was coming, I stepped out to the street gate—just as a cart pulled up at that very moment.
From the cart alighted a student and a teacher. Smiling gently, they greeted me with folded hands.

“Forgive us, Parvateesham garu, we are very late. After you so kindly agreed to come, we tried our best not to delay, but by the time all the arrangements were made, it was already this late. If you’ll just change your dress, we can leave at once,” said the teacher who had come.
“I’m not late at all. I’ve been waiting for you for nearly three hours,” I replied. He turned a little pale.
“Aren’t you going to change your dress?” he asked.
“What is there to change? Other than the freshly laundered dhoti, shirt, and shawl the washerman brought, what other clothes do I have?” I said. He hesitated a bit.
“Oh, oh, I see. I thought, perhaps, you might leave these behind and come in something else,” he said, joining his hands nervously.
“Master! How can I go to a meeting without any clothes?” I replied, with great seriousness.

With an innocent face, he stammered, utterly flustered, “Yes, yes, that’s right, sir. I mean, I never thought you would dress like this, sir. I always assumed you’d never step out without a suit and a hat and all that, sir,” he said, trembling with fear.

“So, did you expect me to come out into the street with nothing on at home, and then suddenly put all those on right here? What a fine fellow you are! Come on, let’s go,” I said, putting my hand on his shoulder and leading him out into the street.
The young man beside us was caught between wanting to laugh and trying to hold it in; he clutched his stomach, doubled over, suffering in silence, and followed right behind us.

With great respect, they asked me to get into the carriage first. The young man sat behind me, and the teacher took the last seat. By the time we reached Narsapur in that carriage, both my clothes and my face had acquired a slight yellowish tinge. I consoled myself, thinking, “Well, surely there won’t be anyone in Edinburgh to ask whether I’ve washed my face or not,” and though my body shivered at the thought, I had no choice but to get into the carriage and sit down. The carriage had barely gone ten yards when—
“Sir, Panditji, could you please move up a little?” said the carriage driver.
Smiling, I moved forward a bit. After we’d gone a little further—
“Sir, you still need to come up a bit more,” said the driver again.

“My boy, with so little acquaintance, you already seem to have developed such affection for me, asking me again and again to come closer. You’re the only one I’ve seen like this. Very gratifying. Is this enough now?” I said, shuffling forward a bit.
“That’s enough, Maharaj,” he replied.
“Oh, your house is made of gold, isn’t it! You’ve already made me a Maharaja now,” I said.
“Of course, sir, you’ll always be like a Maharaja to us,” he said, laughing, and with a whistle, he urged the carriage forward with great gusto.
With that enthusiasm, he managed to get us to Narsapur in less than half an hour.
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 387

Stopping the cart at the gate of our high school, the driver called out, “Now get down, Maharaja,” warning both me and my entourage. He then swiftly jumped down himself and, making sure the cart and horse didn’t drift away, held them firmly in place.

The three of us descended slowly. Right in front of us, the headmaster, along with all the teachers and a whole crowd of students, stood waiting to welcome me. The moment I got down, I was greeted by a spectacle the likes of which I had never seen before. A few students from each class, one or two from each, dressed in khaki uniforms with caps on their heads and blue cloths tied around their necks like ties, stood in two neat rows on either side. As I began to walk forward, their leader shouted “Attention!” and the whole group stamped their boots in unison and saluted me like soldiers.
I smiled at them, feeling for a moment like a Field Marshal, while the headmaster beamed with pride.
“They are Boy Scouts,” he explained enthusiastically. “We have just started this training in our school this year. The students are all very excited about it.”

Meanwhile, some teachers, like town criers announcing the curfew, were warning the young boys not to get too rowdy, telling them to sit quietly in their places. I, walking beside the headmaster who looked every bit the grand vizier Timmarusu, couldn’t help but wonder if I was some sort of king as we entered the hall.

The hall was buzzing with activity. Not only students, but many prominent townsfolk and officials had also gathered. As I entered, everyone hesitated, unsure whether they should stand up or not, and whether this man in a dhoti, shirt, and shawl was really Parvateesam or not. After a moment’s uncertainty, they decided it was better to be safe, and the entire assembly rose to their feet in unison. The headmaster, with great respect and decorum, led me to the seat of honor. Once they saw that, despite my traditional attire, I was indeed Parvateesam, the whole gathering erupted in cheers and applause.
Barrister Parvateesam

With great solemnity, without so much as a smile or a twitch, I stood for a moment like a person of great renown, casting a compassionate gaze upon all the members of the assembly, as if to say, “Please be kind.” I gestured with my hand in a manner beseeching their indulgence, and then sat down. All the members took their seats as well.

The teachers seated below made sure the students were properly settled, and those who had no benches to sit on were made to sit cross-legged on the floor, facing the platform. The teachers warned everyone to remain silent, and at once, the noise in the hall subsided. The headmaster, adjusting the cloth on his head and the scarf around his neck, ascended the platform. He politely requested that a young student come forward and offer the opening prayer.

All the members rose to their feet. The student recited a Ganapati hymn in Sanskrit and a Saraswati prayer in Telugu, bowed to us, and, feeling as if he had achieved some undying honor, descended from the stage beaming with satisfaction. The headmaster stood up again, adjusted his coat and scarf once more, looked at the assembly with a gentle smile, cleared his throat, and with folded hands, began:

“Respected members, dear students, fellow teachers, today is a most auspicious day for all of us. This is an extraordinary, unforgettable, and momentous occasion. One of our own, who studied at this very school, has accomplished a feat that, until today, only one or two among all Telugu people have managed. With remarkable courage and skill, our Parvateesam has achieved what others could not.

Several years ago, he was my student. That fact alone is, if I may say so, a source of both joy and pride for me. In my overwhelming happiness, I forgot myself and addressed him with the familiar singular pronoun, as I used to in the past. I trust he will not take it amiss—at least, that is what I felt from his expression. I responded with a silent bow and a gentle smile in his direction.

He acknowledged it with a smile of his own and continued: ‘Our Parvateesam, as I requested, without any patronage, without anyone’s assistance, at such a young age, crossed thousands of miles of ocean, traveled all the way to Scotland, which is part of the homeland of our rulers, Great Britain, and at the University of Edinburgh, secured his M.A. and Bar-at-Law degrees with first-class honors. I am sure you have all heard of this and rejoiced in his success. Now, a grave responsibility...’

The great war raging in Europe is well known to all of you. These days, with submarines prowling the seven seas day and night, with terrifying warships patrolling the ocean’s surface, and with airplanes in the skies above keeping watch over our every movement and stirring with a thousand eyes, it is only with immense courage and utter fearlessness that our Parvateesham managed to evade all these dangers and return safely and in good health to his homeland. We must all raise our hands in prayer and beseech the Almighty to grant him long life, health, and prosperity,”—no sooner had these words been spoken than everyone in the assembly, without a trace of reluctance or complaint, raised their hands in unison.

Once more, our headmaster cleared his throat, and, without losing an ounce of his vocal gravity or dignity, continued, “I would dearly love to speak at length about Parvateesham’s virtues, his learning, his wisdom, and his intelligence. However, as we have already exceeded the allotted time, I shall conclude my introductory remarks here. I now request our Parvateesham to rise and share his experiences with us. I beg your pardon for this rather late start to our gathering, and with that, I take my leave.” With these words, he sank into his chair, wiping the beads of sweat from his brow, the visible marks of his exertion, while the audience erupted in prolonged applause that echoed in all directions.

As the applause subsided, I rose to my feet, glanced around with a gentle smile, and, following our headmaster’s example, pressed my palms together and began, “Respected assembly, dear fellow students, to our former and present teachers, and especially to our headmaster, who introduced me to you with such affection, admiration, respect, and, if I may say, a touch of exaggeration—I offer my heartfelt gratitude and a thousand respectful salutations, with all humility and devotion. When he kindly came to my house the other day and personally invited me to attend this gathering, I accepted with much hesitation. The reason is, I too was once a student in this very school, just like you. My education was under the same teachers who are here now, and I still bear the marks—sometimes from their anger, sometimes from their affection—of the canings they administered. I have not forgotten those stripes even now.
I must confess, I was quite a mischievous boy in those days. Even if I did not realize it at the time of punishment, later on...
Barrister Parvateesam

I was able to understand. Now and then, the mischievous pranks my classmates and I used to play would come to mind. Only much later did I realize how much these antics must have tested our teachers’ patience. One particular escapade from those days comes to mind at this very moment.

One day, a peculiar incident occurred. When I reached school that morning, I found forty or fifty students struggling to herd the washerman’s donkeys from the street into the school compound. They somehow managed to drag them in, tied their heads and legs, and were making them run back and forth. The donkeys, with no way to escape, were running around in a panic, braying loudly.

Just then, I arrived with a few friends. Seeing the door closed and hearing the commotion inside, we called out, but no one opened the door. So, we climbed over the compound wall and jumped into the fray. We asked the boys what all the ruckus was about, and after learning the story, we enthusiastically joined in their game.

The hero of the tale, who had been getting thoroughly trampled by the donkeys all this while, called out to me. “Not like this, boy! I’ll show you the proper way,” I said. At this, everyone clapped and shouted, “Tell us, tell us!” brimming with excitement, urging me to hurry before the teachers arrived.

“First, someone go and fetch two strong ropes. Let’s tie up these donkeys and put on a circus!” I declared. Two or three boys dashed off in search of ropes. One boy, however, stood there, scratching his head and watching the scene unfold.
“How will they do a circus just because we tell them to?” he asked.

“Your intelligence is truly something to behold,” I replied. “Since we’ve brought them here anyway, and since today is Panchami Thursday, let’s start their training today itself. First, you go and fetch some ink. We’ll mark their tails or faces, so we’ll know which are our donkeys. From today, we’ll…”

If we put in some effort and bring them into the school, we could teach these fellows circus tricks for an hour in the morning, and, if possible, another hour in the evening. That would be entertaining for us, and a good way to pass the time. Moreover, instead of carrying laundry bundles in the future, we’d be giving them a chance to join a circus company and live in style. What do you say? I asked. He, and the others present, unanimously and with a round of applause, expressed their agreement.

Just then, two boys somehow managed to drag in two donkeys, each holding a rope and a tamarind switch, huffing and puffing as they ran in. In the midst of these students, the donkeys had no way to escape, nor did they seem to have any thought of saving their own lives—if they had, how could they be donkeys! They stood there, drooling, gazing at all of us with a mixture of fear and a hint of happiness, braying as if to say “Hurrah!”

As I wondered how to tie up the donkeys with those ropes, one particularly clever lad, like someone catching a goat kid or a calf, grabbed a donkey by its ears. The donkey, in response to this playful mischief, twisted its body, tried to bite those in front, and kicked out at those behind. The boys, startled, ran for their lives. The second donkey, though it hadn’t done anything so far, decided to show solidarity with its companion. It spun around and began kicking at everyone in sight—and even those out of sight! In English, you wouldn’t call this a “sympathetic strike,” but rather a “sympathetic kick.” Remembering that it’s wise to stay away from mischief-makers, all the spectators quickly retreated to a safe distance.

Somehow, four boys managed to subdue the first donkey and tied up all four of its legs. I picked up a tamarind switch and, recalling the circus method I’d seen in this very village, gave the donkey a gentle tap and shouted “Up! Up!” But it was a donkey, after all. On top of that, all this commotion had driven it half-mad. That donkey, who had only ever heard washerman’s commands and no other language, how could it possibly understand “Up!”? I tried coaxing, threatening, and every trick I could think of. When it still wouldn’t listen, I gave it two more taps and said, “Hey, you crazy donkey! When I say ‘Up,’ you’re supposed to lift your front legs. Got it?” and gave its front legs another two taps. We were trying to teach it to “march” in the circus ring—
Barrister Parvateesam

Slowly, I told one boy to hold the rope tied around its neck and to lead the donkey forward. Until then, I had assumed it was a donkey, never once imagining it might be an elephant. No matter what I did, I couldn’t make it take a single step. Determined to accomplish at least this one feat today, I persisted with all my might.

After some time, I noticed that the earlier commotion had died down, and an unusual silence had settled over the place. Looking around in all directions, I realized that the entire crowd of students who had been there before had vanished into thin air. Puzzled by this strange turn of events, I turned around—only to see, from the other side of the gate, our headmaster and a few other teachers watching us intently.

A chill ran down my spine, and I was about to bolt. Sensing my predicament, the donkeys, cleverer than I, seemed to smirk at me mockingly and dashed away, as if to say, “You’re on your own now!” By then, I too regained my senses and tried to make a run for it. Just then, our headmaster called out to me in the most affectionate tone, “Parvateesam, my boy, would you please open this gate? We’d like to come in and perhaps offer you a little help.”

I couldn’t quite grasp the meaning behind his words, but somehow, dragging my feet, I went and opened the gate. The headmaster placed his hand kindly on my shoulder. The teachers behind him were struggling to suppress their laughter, nearly bursting at the seams. The headmaster’s hand on my shoulder felt like an iron weight, growing heavier with every passing moment.

He gently led me into his office. The other teachers went off to the common room, where, I was sure, they were laughing and talking about us. The first bell rang. The headmaster sat down leisurely, removed his hand from my shoulder, and said, “Well, Parvateesam, as if our own donkeys weren’t enough, you’ve brought in some new ones and are trying to start a donkey convention of your own! What’s all this about?”
I couldn’t tell whether he was angry, mocking, or affectionate. An indescribable fear gripped me—my heart pounded, my legs trembled, and tears welled up in my eyes.
“Well, Parvateesam, why don’t you say something?” he asked again, ever so gently.
By the time his words reached my ears, I heard a great rumbling noise, like thunder. Trembling all over, I folded my hands and stammered, “N-n-nothing, sir. The donkeys…”
Still shaking, I managed to say, “They, sir… I mean… those donkeys, sir… somehow they came here, I wondered why they came. We all thought the same thing, sir.”
“That’s nothing. Perhaps they just came to see you,” he said softly. “When we told them to go outside, they didn’t listen. They didn’t listen to anyone.”
“What’s this! Didn’t they listen to anyone? Not even to you in the end? Very strange indeed. So, what did you say to them?” asked the Headmaster.
I couldn’t make out his tone at all.

“By the time you arrived, they were making a mess of everything here, so I told them to go outside. When they didn’t listen to me—well, they are donkeys after all—I gave them a couple of whacks with this stick. Just then, you kindly arrived,” I said.
“Oh, so that’s it. Nothing more to be done, then. But one of the donkeys seems to have bandages on its legs? Did it tie those on itself and come inside?” he asked sarcastically.

“No, sir, poor things, how could they tie bandages themselves? Some of our boys must have done it. While they were leaping all over the compound and ruining the plants, I told them to tie them up. Four of the boys, despite being kicked by the donkeys, bravely managed to tie them up. I thought we could either hand them over to you or have Bantrotu Veeraswamy drive them out to the shed,” I said.

“Alright, alright… That’s it… It was a mistake, just a mistake. It’s my fault. The other day, I saw a circus that came to this town. In it, the man made horses, donkeys, and all sorts of animals do all sorts of tricks…”
Barrister Parvateesam

He got a shawl made, you see. I thought I’d try to do these things too, so I started shouting just as loudly as they did. That’s all there is to it. I haven’t said a single false word, I swear it,” I said.
“Oh, come now, why would you swear on that? I trust your word. So, it seems my arrival didn’t interrupt your lessons. At least you didn’t ask me to come again tomorrow, my boy,” she said.
“It’s true I didn’t say that, but honestly, I did think that if I met them again, I might try a bit harder and perhaps win them over,” I admitted.
“Well done! Just as I suspected, you thought the same as I did. Now, who helped you with this training, my boy?” she asked.
“What do you mean, just one person? All hundred people here cooperated with me,” I replied.

“How’s that? When I arrived, there was no one here but you. Were there really a hundred people before? Hmm, well, whatever the story with those new donkeys, we must settle the matter of these old donkeys. Tell me, who are your fellow students?” she demanded.
My heart nearly stopped. Whom could I name? I had no idea. I pleaded with her just as I had with the others.

“Madam, I really can’t say. When I arrived, there were some young fellows chasing these donkeys. I just suggested, ‘Why don’t we do it this way instead?’ and they all gathered around me. How can I possibly tell you who was who?” I said.
“Yes, poor thing, it must be hard if there really were that many,” she said.
“It’s true, madam, I swear as many oaths as you like. I never lie, madam. It’s not in my nature. I never have,” I said, joining my hands together.
She burst out laughing again.
“Oh, you silly Parvateesam, how innocent you are! When I look at you—”
He was showing mercy. “I cannot shirk my duty, can I? Give me the cane, and hold out both your hands,” he said.

Trembling, I stretched out both my hands. On each hand, two strokes—four in total—landed with a sharp crack. Unable to look at his face, unable to hold back the tears welling up, I squeezed my eyes shut tightly. “Now go, my boy,” he said. As he spoke, his voice quivered a little. That such a kind-hearted, compassionate man was forced to punish me—imagine how much I must have troubled his mind! Even as I said this, my own voice trembled a little.

Once, people believed I was clever, energetic, and one of those students who would pass every exam in the top class, bringing fame and prestige to our teachers and school. I shattered the hopes of my elders and teachers, who dreamt such dreams for me. One day, I managed to provoke even our headmaster—who was the very embodiment of peace and compassion—into anger and agitation, and earned a caning from his own hands. Such a mischievous, wayward fellow as I, on some auspicious day, took the advice someone gave in passing, without a thought for the consequences, without weighing my abilities, and without so much as a word of reply to those who advised me, packed my bags and bundles and set off from Mogalturru, thinking I was perhaps going to Narsapur or Sakinettipalli or Antarvedi, but ended up traveling all the way to England! When I think of all the troubles I faced on the way, and how foolishly I behaved at every turn, I feel ashamed even now. I do not think it proper to waste your time by recounting all those incidents in detail. Besides, at some point, the wicked idea did occur to me that I should one day recall all those memories and write them as a story.

Today, I do not understand why you are honoring me here, someone who is known to you all as a notorious mischief-maker. I do not know in what way I am worthy of this honor. Yet, I am very happy to be the recipient of your extraordinary affection and respect.
Now, regarding the social life and educational system over there, there is so much for us to learn. Even in their daily life, their customs are many...
Barrister Parvateesam

There are many things here that we must emulate. In their daily lives, in their dealings and businesses, there is so much decorum and fairness to be seen. In their food items, in their milk, you will never find the adulteration we are so used to back home. Whether it is a child or an adult who goes to buy something, there is never any cheating in the weights. In fact, it makes one wonder if they are even capable of telling a lie. For as long as I have been here, I have not witnessed a single instance of injustice in any of my daily interactions.

But the strangest thing happened to me one day. I had gone to a railway station in a nearby town on some errand. After finishing my work, I stopped by a bookshop at the station, bought a few magazines, and hurried outside. Unbeknownst to me, my purse slipped out of my pocket. Without realizing it, I walked away. It was only after I boarded the tram and reached into my pocket that I discovered the loss—nothing was there. I informed the conductor, got off midway, and walked home.

About a week or ten days later, I happened to go to that same station again. As I was passing by the bookshop, the shopkeeper recognized me and called out. I went over to him. I was about to buy a newly arrived magazine and pay for it when he said, “There is a small gift I have for you today.”
“At this hour? No, thank you. Perhaps on my birthday, or when I come by specially, I’ll let you know. Then you can give it to me,” I said, trying to leave.

But he stopped me insistently. “This gift is a very small thing. When those auspicious occasions you mentioned come, I’ll give you something else according to my means. For now, please keep this with you,” he said, and placed my purse—the very one I had lost that day—into my hand. It had every single coin in it, not missing even a penny.
I was astonished.
“What is this?” I asked.

“That day, in your enthusiasm, you dropped this here. A porter picked it up and brought it to me, gave me your details, and told me to return it to you when you came by. Since then, I’ve been waiting for your return,” he said, laughing.
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 397
With delight, I said, “Thank you! By the way, where is that porter? Where can I find him?”
“How can I say that, sir? I don’t know when he’ll be on duty or where he’ll be. But I’ll let him know that you came and what your purpose was,” he replied.
“In that case, could you do me one more favor? Please give him these ten shillings, convey my thanks, and tell him how happy I was for the help he gave me,” I said.
He was about to protest, “That’s not necessary, sir. He won’t accept it—” but before his words could reach my ears, I hurried away.
Have you ever heard of or seen our porters back home doing such things as a matter of course? I doubt it.

There, every custom is something we must learn and follow diligently. From the time children are infants up to their student years, the patience and skill with which they are raised, the methods by which they are taught—these are things we must especially observe. One thing that always struck me as peculiar during my time there: not once did I hear a child crying, anywhere, at any time. Here, in our country, there is hardly a moment when our children are not wailing. Our elders even have a proverb to justify it: “A child’s cry is its strength.”

Another curious thing: you never see mothers constantly carrying their children on their hips, wandering about, walking long distances with them, or stopping now and then to breastfeed them in the middle of the road—such scenes are simply not to be found there.

From the time a child learns to walk, they believe a little sun and fresh air is good for health, so they take the children to parks and let them roam freely. Once schooling begins, they teach them everything: how to walk on the road, how to dress when going to school, when and how to say “Good morning,” “Good evening,” “Thank you,” and “Sorry” to the teacher, the appropriate occasions for each, how to enter and leave the classroom quietly and in line—everything is taught. To elders, with words—

chapters.title: The Speech
paragraphs: They teach one to cultivate propriety in conduct. Throughout their lives, in every matter, they give utmost importance to this sense of decorum. Our people too have written a great deal about propriety. But all those writings have remained buried in palm-leaf manuscripts, on scraps of paper, and in printed books—never seeing the light of day.

If I continue in this vein, there are many more things I could say, and many more you would have to listen to. But by now, I must have already wearied you all with my long-winded lecture. It would not be proper—nor would it be courteous—to trouble you any further. Therefore, I take my leave, offering my heartfelt thanks to you all for having listened so patiently and attentively to everything I have said thus far. I wish you all the very best.”
With these words, I sat down.

The felicitation held at the high school caused quite a stir. The whole town was abuzz, everyone talking about it—some saying it was splendid, others simply marveling at it. My fellow students exclaimed, “Our Parvatisham spoke so magnificently! Imagine, even with the headmaster present, he spoke without a hint of fear or hesitation—how did he manage that, eh?”

Others said, “Oh, that’s not it! He’s one of us, isn’t he? He used to play and sing with us, just like anyone else. We’ve seen him as he was—how did he become such a person? I simply can’t fathom it.”
Yet others remarked, “What’s the big deal? If you burn through ten thousand rupees and make a single trip to London, any fool can become like that!”
And so, within twenty-four hours, all these comments had lifted me to great heights.

Though they raised me up so high in their enthusiasm, I, for my part, felt rather dizzy and uncomfortable. As long as I was on solid ground, nothing anyone said bothered me, but now, being hoisted so high, even the slightest slip in balance could spell disaster.
Now, with the lawyers’ felicitation ceremony approaching, I wondered how I would manage to hold my own there…
I sat there, pondering whether I should step outside or not.

Just then, my mother brought me a little snack she had prepared with some effort. Poor woman, how much trouble she takes for me! I thought to myself, “If only I had a daughter-in-law, she wouldn’t have to suffer so much,” and chuckled inwardly as I finished the snack. By the time I was done, the clock struck four. “Oh, it’s getting late,” I thought, and quickly washed my face, tied my turban neatly, and came out to sit in the front yard.

No sooner had I settled down than two lawyers from Versapuram arrived to take me along. Just as I had thought no one would come—just like those days when I used to go to high school—they appeared at the exact moment and kindly asked me to come. They were very pleased to see that I was ready on time.

We set off immediately and reached Narsapuram in half an hour. As soon as we got down from the carriage near the court, I saw that the whole court compound was bustling with people. I had imagined this would be a small gathering, that only lawyers and their clerks would attend, and no one else. But many people who had heard about the meeting at the school the other day, though they had nothing to do with the court, had come out of curiosity to see me, even without any invitation.

Because of this, the meeting, which was originally planned to be held in the bar room of the court, had to be hastily arranged outdoors in a public space. But the lawyers were capable men, and despite the chaos, they managed to organize the meeting quite well.

As soon as we got down from the carriage, two more senior lawyers came up to us. When I got down and greeted them with folded hands, they returned the greeting warmly, each taking a place on either side of me, and led me into the bar room. There, they introduced me to the court’s head clerk and the other lawyers who had already gathered and were waiting for me. They insisted that I join everyone in partaking of the refreshments that had been laid out on the tables.

Having no choice, I quickly finished that ceremony, and then we all walked together to the meeting. The head clerk stayed by my side, chatting away about something or other. But my attention was entirely on the gathering. I was anxious about how to speak before these dignitaries, and what to say. I barely listened to the head clerk’s words, lost as I was in my own nervousness, and thus we entered the assembly. As soon as we arrived, we were seated in two chairs.
Barrister Parvateesam

The secretary of the Bar Association ascended the stage and, with utmost humility, requested the president of the meeting—the venerable Munasabu garu—and today’s distinguished speaker, the honorable Sri Parvateesam of the Bar, to kindly grace the dais and adorn the seats reserved for them. When such dignitaries themselves are so earnestly entreating, it would be discourteous for us not to promptly mount the stage. So, following Munasabu garu’s lead, I too went up.

No sooner had we taken our places than a pleader called upon the association’s clerk to come forward and offer a prayer. The clerk sang four verses in a melodious sequence, in a style reminiscent of a stage play, delighting the audience before quietly stepping down. The secretary then requested Munasabu garu to conduct the proceedings as per the established program and left the stage.

Munasabu garu stood up gracefully, gathering the folds of his angavastram in both hands, cleared his throat in a single motion, and surveyed the assembly on both sides. “Ladies and gentlemen! Today is indeed an auspicious day! I know why you have all gathered here with such enthusiasm—” he began, when some wag in the crowd called out, “If you really know, then tell us why we’re here!”

“That’s exactly what I’m about to tell you, my friend. For the very first time from our region, someone has ventured forth so boldly to foreign lands, pursued his studies there, and, with great success, passed the M.A. and Bar-at-Law examinations in the first class. Even as the terrifying war in Europe raged on, he remained fearless and safe, and has now returned securely to our country and our region. We have all gathered here, both you and I, to celebrate and rejoice at the return of our Parvateesam garu.

“He is a very young man, who had never before left even our taluk. Such courage is beyond my imagination! At such a tender age, to travel thousands of miles away, to a strange land, separated from his parents and all his relatives, to a place with none of our customs, none of our traditions, and yet to live there for three years without fear or anxiety, passing his days in comfort and peace—when I think of it, I myself am filled with awe. This is truly an extraordinary feat; it speaks volumes of his courage, determination, and unwavering mind. The secretary—”

chapters.title: Train Journey
paragraphs: For example, it is our foremost duty, our minimum obligation, to invite them among us, to welcome and bless them. Even after living for so many years in those distant lands, seeing how they have not forgotten our dress and language, and how kindly they behave, I felt assured that our dharma, our culture, and our nationality can indeed be preserved. Just by seeing them, I gained the courage to believe so. I hope that, in this regard, they can become role models for us. There are many things we must hear from them, learn from them, and put into practice. Therefore, without prolonging my speech and wasting time, I now conclude my address, requesting the young Sri Parvateesham to share his experiences, opinions, and ideals with us. Saying this, he adjusted his coat and other garments and settled comfortably into his chair. The audience broke into applause.

Amidst the thunderous applause that shook the entire hall, I thought to myself, “Now I must stand up—oh Lord!” To stand before this crowd, in front of these learned men, in the presence of such scholars, and to adjust my shirt and scarf like a great intellectual, put on a grave expression, and begin a solemn speech—just imagining it made me want to laugh at how ridiculous it would be. Remembering this, I sat quietly until the noise in the hall subsided, then composed my face into seriousness and stood up. As soon as I rose, the audience again burst into applause. This made me even more embarrassed, and, pushing aside my growing cowardice, I said, “Sabhaayainamah!” (Salutations to the assembly). Instantly, the hall fell completely silent.

“Just the other day, I trembled at the thought of speaking before the students who studied with me and behind me in high school, and before the teachers who taught me. I somehow managed to mumble a few words that came to mind and escaped. But today, to stand before these great scholars, these experts in law, these elders seasoned in age and experience—what can I possibly say? What right do I have to speak on any subject before them?”
Barrister Parvateesam

What is it? What could I possibly know more than you?—I’ve been asking myself this question since earlier, sitting here. But then it struck me: “There’s nothing to it! This is just a peculiar custom of the day. The people who invited you don’t know your true worth, do they?” As soon as this answer flashed in my mind, I’ve been quietly laughing at myself and trying to muster up some courage.

Since you are the ones who made me do this, I hope you will forgive the incongruities and blunders in my childish games, just as elders enjoy watching children’s play, with all its mishaps and mischiefs. Perhaps, before long, I too will be one among you, practicing law right here in this very court. Then I will have to learn many things from you all. At that time, I hope you won’t say, “Back then, you gave us a grand lecture as if you were some great man. What can we say now?”—I sincerely hope you won’t say that.
As soon as I finished, the hall resounded with applause.

Three years ago, my studies here came to a standstill. For some reason, the enthusiasm and energy I had at first dwindled away. I had come here with all sorts of fanciful notions about education, soaring in the skies of imagination. My father, noticing my state, told me to leave off my studies for a while, stay at home, help with the farm work, and try to learn Telugu and Sanskrit. He said that if I regained my interest in English education, I could always resume my studies later.

I was caught in a predicament, unable to say anything, and was feeling quite miserable. At that time, by some stroke of luck, I became acquainted with the illustrious and prominent Sri Ramanarao. You might wonder how such an acquaintance came about. One day, he himself came looking for me and said, “I need your help. Only you can do this—no one else. We are planning to organize some political meetings here. You must take charge of all the arrangements. When I inquired about you, everyone said you are very capable, and that you are the only one in your school fit for this responsibility.”

He flattered me thus and drew me into that field of work. I didn’t realize it at the time, but after some years, when I thought back on it, I realized that in our school, I was the only one who, having lost interest in studies, wandered about aimlessly, with a bit of muscle, enthusiasm, and determination. Whatever the case, I became his disciple and began organizing meetings and assemblies.

Not only did I learn a great deal from them, but I also read countless books on various subjects that they recommended—books I would never have encountered in school, nor even known existed. I take great pride in saying that, thanks to them, I became far more knowledgeable than my fellow students. It was they who encouraged me not to remain here in school, but to go abroad, to study law and become a barrister. Following their advice, I resolved to travel to foreign lands, pursue my studies there, and, upon passing my examinations and returning home, to seek their blessings. But alas! Just as I was about to fulfill that wish, I received the sorrowful news that they had passed away. Their absence today leaves a great void in my heart.

Still, upon seeing our esteemed chairman—who is older, wiser, and a judge to boot—my cowardice took flight and I managed to summon a bit of courage. Before him, I am but a child. I trust that he, in his wisdom and good humor, will forgive my shortcomings. With that confidence, I must confess that, for quite some time now, I have been wandering off-topic, unsure of what to say next. I am sure you have noticed my digressions.

I am a man who had never crossed the boundaries of Narsapuram. Other than a bullock cart or a boat, I knew nothing of any other means of travel. I had never even seen a train in my life. The very idea that I, of all people, should set out on a daring journey to foreign lands is, in itself, so laughable and comical that I need not say more. I could never have imagined, even in my wildest dreams, the extent to which civilization has advanced in cities, especially abroad—the countless comforts, inventions, and conveniences that scholars have devised to make life easier for people. Raised in such utter ignorance, was it not an act of sheer recklessness for me to set out boldly for foreign shores? Or was it not? The experiences I had after setting out, the sights I beheld—if I were to describe them all to you, one by one, it would take a very long time indeed. I doubt I am even capable of such a task. Therefore, I shall content myself with a few brief remarks, so as not to weary you with my ramblings.
The first marvel of travel I encountered was the machine that could carry hundreds of people, day and night, across hundreds of miles with utmost care and efficiency…

The means of travel was the railway train. Many of you must have seen it. You must have traveled in it. As for me, having had no such experience, the troubles I faced that day at Nidadavolu—while buying tickets, while boarding the train, and even after taking my seat—are too many to recount. But by the time I had spent that one night traveling and reached Madras, I had become aware of so many new things that, without any effort, I felt as though my knowledge and civilization had increased.

Then, in the short time I spent in Madras, the problems I encountered, the wonders I witnessed, and the special things I learned were endless. There, I saw for the first time another mechanical means of mass transport—the tramcar. Not only that, I also saw another machine, the motor car, which was suitable for wealthy individuals to travel alone or with their families over long distances. Among all the students at Taylor High School with me at that time, I believe I was the first to witness such marvelous human-made inventions. I must admit, I felt a little proud about that.

Until then, I had only heard that, apart from English and Telugu, there were other languages and peoples in our country. But it was only when I heard the sound of Arabic in Madras that I realized how difficult it is to manage in a place where one does not know the language. I wondered how it would be when traveling to many countries in the future.

In Mogalturru and Narasapuram, I would stand in awe before the buildings, the mansions, and the temples. But when I saw the grand buildings and the towering temple spires in Madras, my joy and wonder knew no bounds. I wondered if, in any country, there could be palaces more spacious and grand than these, temples more beautiful, or royal roads more magnificent. As my journey continued and I saw more and more new places, I realized that there is always something greater than what has come before. No matter how much beauty I saw, I felt there was no limit to it, no final pinnacle. In the countries I visited, among the people, in human creations, and even in nature itself, the variety and beauty I witnessed were beyond description. Even things that seemed similar always had some subtle difference.

I did not see anything like it anywhere else. One day, when I went to see the sacred ruins of Melrose Abbey in Scotland, I noticed that all the windows there were carved out of stone like intricate lattices, allowing the wind to pass through. No two windows were alike. In one window, half of it appeared in one design, the other half in another. Curious, I asked the guide who accompanied us, “What is this?” He replied, “That’s just it, sir. The sculptor who created these was a great genius. He always showed something new; he never repeated what he had already done. Genius does not repeat itself.”

Hearing those words, I thought—if human intellect can display such variety, is it any wonder that the Creator of the universe, who is the cause of all existence, produces before our very eyes an endless array of forms, never making one exactly like another, and crafting even subtler differences within each one every single day?
As I traveled from one country to another, I saw that civilization, customs, manners, and languages differed endlessly. There isn’t enough time now to describe all of them.

Let me say a few words about their way of life and civilization there. None of this will be unknown to you; you must have read such things in books or heard them from others. Still, when someone who has just recently returned from there shares his experiences—what he saw and lived through firsthand—it is always more exciting.

They have a social system. We have four castes; they too have divisions equivalent to four castes. Their society is divided into four classes based on economic status: the aristocrats, the upper middle class, the ordinary middle class, and the poor. Our divisions are based on cultural knowledge and tradition, while theirs are founded solely on material wealth and economic superiority.

I cannot now discuss the merits and demerits of each system. Because our rulers are foreigners, the constitutional system we follow does not quite suit our way of life, and our social structure has become somewhat disordered. There, since the rulers and the ruled are of the same nationality, their way of life and their constitutional system fit together seamlessly and proceed smoothly.

The moment you see the orderliness here, you realize this is a country that has embraced civilization. Observing the people and their customs, you understand how closely intertwined life and civility are. Wherever I went, the first thing that captivated me were the meticulously laid-out streets, the buildings, and their elegant designs. Then came the cleanliness, and after that, the people who moved about in such a disciplined manner. The vehicles traveling on the roads, the pedestrians walking along the pavements—there is a sense of order and method in everything.

No vehicle can dash about as it pleases. All vehicles going in one direction stick to one side, and those going the other way keep to the opposite side. Nowhere do you see cows, donkeys, or other animals obstructing the path of these vehicles. Nor do you find crowds gathered in the middle of the street, standing around discussing politics, household secrets, or amorous affairs. Even the people walking on the pavements must do so in an orderly fashion. No one walks haphazardly. When two or three walk together, their steps fall in unison.

Nowhere on the roads do you see any kind of litter, rubbish, spit, or phlegm. This is not just in the cities—even in the smallest of villages, these same practices are observed. In fact, their villages are almost indistinguishable from their towns. In our country, it is quite the opposite.

The people here have a greater sense of beauty. It seems to be an integral part of their lives. Our elders have said, “Truth, Auspiciousness, Beauty.” The auspiciousness may be known only to Lord Shiva, but at least beauty is undeniably a part of Western life. Once upon a time, beauty was also woven into the fabric of our lives—but now, it has become a mirage.

Just as the Westerners have made beauty an essential part of their existence, they have also resolved that truth must be followed at all times. From the common man to those in the highest positions, everyone observes truthfulness with great care. They practice it in their daily lives and even in business dealings. I have seen this myself. Not that I am claiming everyone here is a modern-day Harishchandra! In large transactions and big businesses, there is certainly deceit—how could it be otherwise? Our belief is that commerce and business are nothing but deception, and that it cannot be any other way.
When it comes to employment, our people are not content with just their salary—if there is any way to get a little extra…

The question arises beforehand as to whether such a thing is possible. From the lowly clerk to the highest official, each, according to his position, is constantly engaged in this pursuit. But the most astonishing thing is that even in the courts of law, among the judges themselves, this weakness is said to exist here and there. In that country, I have never heard of such frailty among those who hold such positions.

I have heard that those who occupy such high offices conduct themselves in their daily lives in such a way that no one among the public ever has the opportunity to point a finger at them. There is a story I heard about a judge in London—a bachelor, a man of great integrity and virtue, devoted to righteousness. One day, in a moment of weakness, he had an illicit relationship with his cook. Realizing his mistake the very next moment, he was filled with remorse, took leave the following day, and immediately married her to set right his wrongdoing. Such integrity—how far is it possible in our country? It is something to ponder.

Thus, by making truth, beauty, and such ideals an integral part of life, only those who possess such qualities can truly be called civilized—so our teachers used to advise us. There are many more wonders and peculiarities I have observed here. If I were to sit and recount them all, it would amount to wasting your time here. I believe that it is only because of my three years in a Western country that I have learned so many things and acquired so many noble ideas. In reality, there are countless things—ranging from the smallest matters to the greatest—that we must learn from them. To forget all these and be content with merely imitating their dress or appearance, thinking ourselves civilized, is nothing but self-deception, in my opinion.

Above all, what we must learn from them is how greatly and in what manner they respect their own country, their education, and their culture. You are all aware that many Westerners, experts in these matters, come to our country to teach us lessons. What more can I say to you than this? Hoping that you will forgive any shortcomings in what I have said...

chapters.title: Starting Practice
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

Thanking you all for having listened to my insipid speech with such patience and attention, I concluded my address with heartfelt gratitude. Uttering a solemn “Vande Mataram” and bowing, I sank into my chair, feeling as if I had accomplished some great feat, while the audience’s applause thundered around me.

Once the applause had died down, the president of the gathering rose and, on behalf of the audience, expressed their delight and blessings for my grand oration, thus bringing the proceedings to a close. Afterwards, the organizers and the secretary of the Lord Council too conveyed their appreciation and gratitude, formally ending the meeting.

When the hustle and bustle of Narsapur had finally subsided, for about a week, students, teachers, lawyers—whoever found the time—would come to chat with me, ask about my experiences there, and then take their leave. In this manner, I managed to while away some time. But gradually, even this pastime faded away. With nothing to occupy me, I would go to the fields, but there, not knowing how to converse with the workers or get any work done, and at a complete loss, after two days I decided I must go somewhere—anywhere—for a change.

Since returning from abroad, that is, from foreign lands, I had not seen any of my extended family. Not far from Narsapur, in a small village, lived my maternal aunt. Curious to see her, I told my mother and set off early in the morning to visit.

It was a remote village, with very little in the way of civilization. Someone had informed the villagers that I was coming. The moment they heard this, the entire village poured out onto the street. Especially the womenfolk—eager to see what a man who had crossed the seas looked like. Did he, too, turn as fair as a white sahib? What did he wear? Did he dress like us, in a dhoti, or had he adopted the sahib’s style with suit, hat, and boots? Did he speak our language like us, or had he forgotten his mother tongue and now spoke only English? All sorts of wild questions plagued their minds, and they hoped that by seeing me, at least some of their doubts would be put to rest.
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri,

Meanwhile, everyone was eagerly awaiting my return, placing bets on how much my appearance and speech might have changed. Whether someone actually told him or not, a solid rumor had reached him that I had married a lady from the zamindar’s family in the Rayalaseema region, brought her here, and hidden her away in Madras. Apparently, some clever fellow had started this gossip, and so everyone was even more anxious for my arrival. Who knows, perhaps that lady herself might accompany me! Would she be fair-skinned? Or, after marrying an Indian, had her complexion faded a little? How would she dress? Would she be just like our own women, or completely different? In any case, the young men’s hearts were pounding with excitement at the thought of seeing her, even if just once. All this, of course, I only learned later.

That day, I reached my village at about eight in the morning. In a village, the arrival of a stranger is immediately noticed. Someone spotted me at the outskirts and, running ahead into the village, spread the news of my arrival faster than salt dissolves in water. As soon as I set foot in the village...

As soon as I set foot there—oh, what a sight, my lord! It was as if some Collector or Governor had come to visit. The whole village had turned out, lining up in rows along the roadside. All the women of a certain age, from both sides of the family—that is, both the present and former daughters-in-law—were standing on the verandas. The young girls and new brides were peering out from doorways and windows. At first, I had no idea why so many people were standing there like this. Some people were walking alongside and behind me, keeping pace. Still clueless as to why such a crowd—men and women alike—had gathered, I turned to the elderly gentleman walking beside me and asked, “Are some officials coming here today, sir? Why is the entire village lined up like this?”
“Who else would be coming? They’re all here just to see you!” he replied.
Hearing that, my chest swelled with pride, and I felt as if I’d grown four inches taller. Accepting the villagers’ respectful greetings as grandly as I could, I somehow made my way to our house.

Inside, after inquiring about everyone’s well-being and washing my hands and feet with the water they offered, I came out into the front hall. There, the entire porch and every veranda were packed with people of all kinds and ages, sitting shoulder to shoulder, chattering away. I wondered why they were all sitting there like that. For a moment, I feared they might ask me to give a speech right away. But, true to their nature, they just sat quietly, watching me intently, without uttering a word.
After two or three minutes, an old man slowly cleared his throat and began, “Shastrulu-garu (meaning my father) is truly a fortunate man.”
Another chimed in, “To have such a son as him…”
“And that gentleness, that wealth of good qualities!” added a third.

In this manner, they spent some time showering me with praise from all directions. Half of me wanted to laugh, the other half was dying of embarrassment. Somehow, clinging to life like a royal bridegroom about to faint, I sat there, stiff as a log.
From there, everyone began to ask some ridiculous, foolish question or another.
“So, sir, is it just like here over there too?” asked one fellow. “Do they wear clothes there as well?”
“They do wear clothes, of course! If they didn’t, we wouldn’t be able to look at them, and they wouldn’t be able to bear the cold—they’d die,” I replied.
“Ah, but do they wear dhotis and sarees like us, or do they wrap themselves in something else?” he asked.
“Oh, my dear fellow! How could they possibly manage without?” he exclaimed.

“What can they do if they don’t? I myself was shivering with cold. Immediately, I had two suits and coats stitched according to the customs of that country. To tell you the truth, there are indeed some places in the world where people go about without wearing anything at all,” I said.
“Oh, dear me! So, over there, both men and women are like that?” he asked, clutching his heart as if in distress.

Seeing his attitude, I laughed, suspecting he was secretly planning to find out the name of that place and make arrangements to travel there. It is a very hot country, inhabited only by tribal people—savages, uncivilized folk, who do not even know that certain parts of the body ought to be kept covered out of modesty. Therefore, they feel no shame at all, I explained.
Wishing to steer the conversation in a different direction, an elderly man interjected, “But, my boy, does it rain there?”
“Yes,” I replied.
“Then, just like here, they must have paddy fields and crops, isn’t it so? Is that right?” another asked, expressing his amazement.
“Well then, my dear fellow, I am an ignorant man from Erramunda, so forgive me if I ask a silly question. But tell me, do they also get married over there?”

I felt a burning sensation in my stomach. “They get married, have children, and do everything else just like us. Even their children are born,” I said.

“Then I suppose even those children speak only English. But how do they manage to speak such perfect English from the moment they are born, as if they were all born lords?” he asked. At this, everyone, along with him, looked astonished.

All these questions were asked by people from my own village. Wherever I went, I realized, I would probably be bombarded with such questions. Amused by their innocence, I allowed myself a small smile. There were still many more questions they ought to have asked, but for that day, they all took their leave.
If this goes on every day, as long as I stay here, they’ll torment me like this. What is this? I thought, feeling a bit flustered.

The next morning, I got up and went to the tank for my bath. By then, a few young women, each with a pot balanced gracefully on her hip, came sauntering along. Seeing me, they blushed, paused a little distance away for a moment, and then slowly stepped into the water. Watching their graceful movements, their beauty, and their modesty, I was enchanted. I marveled at how much charm and delicacy our village maidens possessed. Lost in wonder, I began to swim gently back and forth, floating and diving, and even started doing some water exercises.

The women finished their baths, chatted among themselves with gentle smiles, and slowly set out for home. Seeing them, so young and yet carrying such heavy pots, my heart was moved. I thought, “Why don’t I help them with their pots?” But how many pots could I possibly carry? How many girls could I assist at once? So, feeling a bit helpless, I just stood there silently, watching them with sympathy, standing in the water.

All of them had climbed up the bank. One girl, about sixteen years old, slender and delicate like a figurine made of gold, was struggling to lift her pot. Poor thing, she was having a hard time. She called out to her friends for a little help, but they paid her no heed and walked on ahead. Seeing her plight, my heart went out to her. Without thinking, I took a step forward.
"Wait, let me help you," I said.

The girl's face turned as red as a yam with embarrassment. She tried to say, "No, thank you," but the words wouldn't come out. Her lips moved silently, but no sound emerged. Pretending not to notice, I picked up the pot from one side and helped her lift it onto her shoulder.

With no other choice, trembling, the girl accepted my help and balanced the pot on her shoulder. As I was lifting the pot, my hand accidentally brushed against her. Poor thing, she shivered as if struck by lightning. I was terrified she might drop the pot right there. The other women, noticing the commotion, all turned around at once to see what was happening. When they saw me helping with the pot, they were utterly dumbfounded. It felt as if the whole world had suddenly come alive with excitement.

Just then, one of the girls let out a shrill cry, "Sita!" addressing the girl I had helped. Flustered, the girl lowered her head and hurried away. And what next? In a flash, the news spread through the village like wildfire. The villagers' good opinion of me took a slight dip.

With this, the village split into two factions. The elders—both men and women—formed one group. The youngsters formed another. The young folks were on my side, needless to say. They all developed a certain fondness for me. Among the young men, many took to spending time with me. When I regaled them with my stories—especially tales about women abroad—they would listen with rapt attention, thoroughly entertained.

A day or two after this incident, I was at the tank again with a few other young men, bathing. The women, mostly elders, were finishing their baths quickly and carrying water home. I was drying myself off when a widow, about twenty-five years old, turned towards me, let out a loud call, flashed a sly smile, and, feigning shyness, said, "Could you please lift this pot for me, son? My arm is completely out of commission," she said, half in jest.
All the while, with so many women around, I wondered why she wouldn't ask one of them for help.
"I'm coming," said another woman quietly.

For a moment, I was at a loss, hesitating. “Oh, boy! In my hour of need, I turned to this good-for-nothing, didn’t I? Couldn’t you lend a hand? Or do you think I’m a child? Or perhaps a delicate damsel?” she said, pressing her words like a string of pearls. “Mother, what a thing you’ve said!” I thought to myself, and, swallowing my pride, I helped her as she had asked. Later, I learned that she was quite a famous woman in the village, renowned for her learning and wisdom. Well, what more is there to say? Thanks to this incident, my fame spread to all four corners of the village.

But my friends did not abandon me. Impressed by my courage and boldness, they became even closer to me. At their encouragement, I even delivered one or two lectures. In that village, the women too requested that I give a special lecture just for them. Since there were many things I wished to tell them, I suggested that a separate meeting be arranged for the ladies. My friend tried his utmost to organize such a gathering, but none of the elders would agree to send their young women. “Well then, I have no special Vedantic discourses to deliver to the old women. Let it be,” I said.

During my stay there, a young man named Satyam never left my side, shadowing me day and night. Whenever I went to his house in the evenings, he would accompany me. He had passed his B.A. and was full of modern ideas. His wife was a real beauty, and he loved her dearly. He gave her a great deal of freedom. Though his mother did not like it much, both husband and wife treated me with great warmth and without any reserve.

One afternoon, I was sitting in their house. That day, the young lady was preparing to visit her parents’ home. An ox-cart stood waiting in the street, loaded with bundles and bags, while she was inside, getting ready. Her husband and I placed the luggage in the cart. “Why trouble yourself, sir?” he said, embarrassed at my help. There were still one or two items left to bring, so he went inside to fetch them. The young lady, ready to leave, stepped out into the street toward the cart.

She arrived. My mother-in-law stood near the back doorway. A handful of neighbors, women from the houses opposite and beside ours, had all gathered, each standing on their own thresholds. I was standing right next to the cart. The girl tried two or three times to climb into the cart but struggled and failed each time. My mother-in-law, raising her voice, called to her son inside the house, “Bring a chair here!”

“Why, madam? I’m right here—let her climb up,” I said. Without a moment’s hesitation, and before my mother-in-law could protest, I reached from behind, grabbed the girl by the waist, and hoisted her into the cart. No one there could have imagined such a thing would happen. I, too, acting thoughtlessly in the Western manner, considered the girl as if she were my own sister or a close relative, and felt compelled to help her in this way.

She was a girl living in her in-laws’ house. Even if she had been my own sister, lifting her up and putting her into the cart like that was against our customs—a fact I completely forgot in that moment. That was my blunder. The girl, mortified and frightened, could not utter a word. My mother-in-law turned into a blazing fire. The neighbors, in unanimous chorus, exclaimed, “Oh, what audacity from that fellow!”
The old woman spat fire, saying, “Parvatisham, may you never prosper!”

Realizing my mistake, I was so flustered I couldn’t even open my mouth to explain that I had no ill intentions. I couldn’t look anyone in the eye, so I hung my head and slunk back home. But the news reached my house before I did.

My mother, upon seeing me, began her lamentations: “After traveling to so many countries, after all these years, after spending so much money, is this what your education has taught you? What a thing to do in broad daylight! Have you no shame? How will we ever face those people again? Where shall I hide my face?” She poured out her grief in a continuous wail, making sure I’d never forget it.
A little later, my friend arrived, erupting like a volcano. Upon seeing me...
I never imagined you could be such a scoundrel. If you so much as smile now, I’ll kill you!” he shouted, and ran off without looking back.

I didn’t know whether to laugh or cry. I thought, “How strangely this story has turned!” Who would have guessed that this small, thoughtless act would create such a commotion? In a single moment, they all heaped so much blame on me. Mulling over this, I wrote a detailed letter to my friend explaining my side of the story, and that very day, I packed up and left the village. They say, “When you set out for good, evil meets you on the way”—perhaps this is what they mean. This is how our people’s affairs always seem to go.

Should I then make peace with village life? But then, are the city folk any more refined in their thinking? I recalled the honors showered upon me in Narsapur the other day, and now, today, these humiliations here—perhaps this is what life is.

By evening, I slowly made my way back to Narsapur. I didn’t have the heart to go home right away. Even now, I cannot bring myself to believe that what I did in that village was wrong, or even blameworthy. In a moment of innocence, without the slightest ill intention, I acted thoughtlessly, thinking it a simple, natural thing—who could have foreseen it would lead to such disastrous consequences? Three years—is that all? In these three years, perhaps I have attained a level of progress that our civilization, after thousands of years, may not achieve for another century. How could I possibly explain this to the people of that village? If I were to recount the incident today, they would think I’d invented the whole story, but they would never understand my true feelings.
How disturbed my mind was by these events! Even I was surprised at myself. Never, in any circumstance, have I experienced such mental anguish. What do the villagers make of this story? I do not know.

What can I do? I have lost the right to set foot in my own village—death itself would be preferable. As for me, I shall never return! What’s done is done; I must simply endure the consequences. I have no objection. Even if I did, it would make no difference. But that poor girl—like a goddess—her innocent husband, her foolish mother-in-law—how many ways will they torment her! And those village women, even more foolish, will circle her like crows...

He was overjoyed to have me. Amidst our long conversations late into the night, I managed to forget my troubles for a while. The next morning, when I said I’d be leaving, he clung to me, pleaded with me in every way possible, and made me stay back. Thanks to my friend, I had become almost normal again. At last, somehow, after convincing him, I made my way back to my native village.

The great deed I had performed in my aunt’s village—despite our village not having the luxury of a telegraph—had, somehow, reached my family before I did. How many people in our village already knew about it, I couldn’t even estimate. After I had bathed and settled down, my father returned from the fields.

“Hey boy! When did you come back from the town? Are your aunt’s people all well? Did you come straight from there? Nothing special happened, right?” he rattled off, barely pausing for my answers, all the while eyeing me sharply. From his facial expressions and his tone, I could guess that he already knew something of what had happened. For a moment, I wondered what to say, and how to say it. Then I remembered the English proverb, “Honesty is the best policy.” In situations like this, it’s best to tell the truth as it happened—so I decided to stick to that approach.

“I’ve just come from Narsapuram, Father. It’s been three days since I left my aunt’s village and arrived there. I had planned to stay another week at her place. But four days ago, a strange incident occurred…” I began.

Until then, my father had been standing, but now he sat down in silence. Without leaving out a single detail, I narrated everything, from the moment I set foot in that village to the moment I left it. My father sat quietly for a moment, without any response, and then said,
“So, you’re still under the impression that you’re in London?”

That’s all. As for returning to my homeland, to my native village, I haven’t forgotten a thing, you know,’ I said.

‘No, father, I remember everything. How could I forget? The only mistake I made was this, father. In these three years abroad, I assumed that the civilization I saw there would be found here as well. The very moment this incident occurred, I realized my mistake—that we are still several centuries behind in modernity. That is the only error I committed. Whether I deserve forgiveness or not, you elders must decide. If I am to be punished, whatever punishment or penance you prescribe, I am ready for it all, by your grace,’ I said.

My father paused for a moment and said, ‘What is there in this for punishment or penance? What you did was a mistake, yes, but how can I call it a crime? Even lifting that girl and seating her in the cart—I cannot call that a crime either. But the only mistake was in thinking that your mental development and transformation had come to everyone here as well. At that moment, I didn’t have time to imagine all this. That’s all. Centuries of civilization, customs, social rules—they cannot change across the whole country in a single day, or even in a century. There’s no leisure to think so. Well, what’s done is done. You need not dwell on it or worry about it,’ he said, and immediately got up to go for his bath.

For about a week, I stayed indoors, not showing my face on the street, passing the time with books. One afternoon, around three o’clock, I was reading something when my father suddenly called out to me for some reason. Wondering why, I picked up my book and went out to the verandah, saying, ‘Did you call me, father?’ There, besides my father, two other elderly strangers were seated.
“I’ve called you. Come here! Sit down for a moment,” said my father.

Who are these people? Why have they come? I wondered, as I sat down and glanced at their faces. They, in turn, were examining me from head to toe with great scrutiny. For some reason, my father said, “Here he is—this is my son,” to them. “These are the Surya Narayana Shastris. They have come to see you. They are wealthy householders, belonging to a highly respected and scholarly lineage. They themselves are learned men. With the intention of giving their daughter to you, they wish to establish a relationship with us. Out of that desire, they have kindly come here today. According to their means and our eligibility, they are prepared to give dowry and gifts. I have told them that we have no particular demands in such matters.”
“Sir! Shastriji, what do you say?” my father asked, addressing the visitors.
Without uttering a word, Surya Narayana Shastri gestured to the elder gentleman beside him, who spoke up:

“What is there left to ask, sir? We have already heard of your name and reputation, your virtuous conduct, your wealth, your son’s education, intelligence, and good qualities. Having heard all this, we have come here today. Now, having seen your son’s features, his graceful bearing, and gentle manners, we are overjoyed. On an auspicious day, as soon as possible, please do us the favor of coming to our village to see our daughter. That is our humble request.”
My father replied, “Of course, let me think about when we can make it convenient, and I will inform you.”
Shastriji expressed his great happiness.

After coming here and witnessing your hospitality and respect, and after seeing your son, I felt that seeing the girl is merely a formality—the alliance is as good as settled. When we were about to leave, they remarked, “It is a special day for us, and a stroke of luck for the bride.” Both of them stood up, bowed to my father, and gave me another thorough once-over before leaving.

Now, please grant us leave. We will make our own arrangements and await your arrival," they said, turning onto the street. My father walked ten steps with them, escorting them, and then returned. I stood rooted to the spot, thinking, "Oh Lord! What is this that has now landed upon me?" It seemed as though, with this talk of marriage, another round of conflict was about to erupt between my father and me. Pondering how to handle this, I quietly slipped into my room.

No sooner had I sat down in my room than I found myself unable to read a book. My mind was racing in all directions. Memories of the marriage proposal that came before I set out for foreign lands, my uncle and I going to see the girl, the embarrassment that ensued—one by one, all these recollections came flooding back. I sat there for a long time, laughing to myself. Ever since then, the very thought of going to see a prospective bride has filled me with a certain dread. Back then, the journey to see a girl was tinged with curiosity. Now, all that enthusiasm has vanished.

For two or three days, nothing was decided about this matter between my father and me. He busied himself with his own affairs, and I passed the time with my books. Four days went by. One afternoon, after lunch, my father spoke up.

"Well, my boy! To those marriage people who came the other day, I wrote a letter yesterday saying that we would come to see the girl the day after tomorrow, provided all is well. If we like the girl, let us proceed. As for the dowry and gifts they might offer, we have no need for any of that. What we want is a virtuous and beautiful bride, not the burdens that come with her. So far, they have not boasted to me about any such things, nor have I asked. All I have heard is that the girl's father is a worthy man, a Vedic scholar, and a bit of a traditionalist. His old-fashioned ways are his own concern; they won't come into our house with the girl, will they? It is only proper for them to invite us to see the girl, and it is also proper for us to go and see her for our own satisfaction. What do you say?" he asked.
What could I say! For the past four days, I had been wondering when this conversation would take place and what I should say. But what—

I simply could not come to any decision. Before I could even imagine what answer to give, my father posed the question. Thinking that I must say something, I replied, “Oh, let it be for now. What’s the hurry? It’s not as if I’m a girl to be rushed into marriage! I haven’t even decided yet what I want to do—whether it’s farming, pleading, or taking up a job. I haven’t made up my mind about anything yet.”

“What does that have to do with this?” my father asked. “In the course of your life, your wife is meant to be your companion, to walk beside you in your chosen path—not to make decisions for you or to change the ones you’ve made.”

“Well, perhaps that’s the tradition,” I said. “But don’t you think the way people think these days has changed a little? A girl leaves her own family and comes to ours, to live with us for the rest of her life, to be one with us in everything. Shouldn’t she know about our thoughts and our ways? When deciding what’s good or bad, isn’t it right to ask her opinion, or at least, even if we don’t ask, isn’t it fine if she offers her advice of her own accord? Don’t you ever ask mother? Don’t you ever consult her about anything? Or does she only get to make decisions about what to cook for meals?” I asked, a little hastily.

“Ah, is that so? Truly! It seems your education has seasoned you in more ways than one. I’d forgotten. Well, fine, all those things can be thought about later. First, you can at least see the girl, can’t you?” he said. After sitting in silence for two or three minutes, I asked how old the girl was. My father, who was never at a loss for words, was taken aback and stared at me for a while in silence. Then, recovering himself, as if he had understood my intention, he said, “Your intention, is it?”
“What intention do I have? It’s just as you guessed. I’m twenty-two or twenty-three now, am I not? And for that girl and for me—”

I wondered aloud, “What difference could there be?”

“There will certainly be some difference, that’s for sure,” my father replied. “You might remember, before you went abroad, you tried once before.
