Back then, we didn’t have all these newfangled ideas. But now, inevitably, there will be some changes. Anyway, I haven’t asked them yet. First, we must like the girl, then the horoscope must match. If both are agreeable, only then comes talk of any differences.” He looked at me for a while, then fell silent, as if to say further arguments were unnecessary, and got up and left.

My father made sure I had no chance to get the last word in. Despite all these years, and all the countries I’ve traveled to, I still haven’t mustered the courage to say, “I’ll handle my marriage as and when I wish, if at all I wish.” With nothing else to do, I resigned myself to see what would happen.
On the third day, after finishing lunch in a hurry, we were about to set off to see the prospective bride. I suggested we take my mother along as well.

“There’s no need for that now,” my father said. “If I like her, your mother will like her too. Besides, we’ll have to walk a fair distance there. No need for your mother to tire herself. Once everything is settled, she’ll see the girl when we go to present the ceremonial betel leaves.” With that, he shouted, “We’re off!” and strode out.
Whatever work my mother was doing, she wiped her hands on her sari, smiled, and came to the doorstep to see us off, saying, “May it be auspicious.”

Around two in the afternoon, we reached the village. They had made all the preparations for our arrival and were sitting on the veranda, waiting expectantly. As soon as they saw us, they called out to the household, announcing our arrival. The lady of the house brought water for us to wash our feet. We went inside, sat down, and after some small talk, the host called out to his wife, “Well, shall we bring the girl in?”
The priest who had come to our village the other day was also present, sitting in the courtyard. A couple of others were there as well. Just then, the priest’s wife brought in her daughter.
“Sit here, dear,” she said, seating her on the mat spread out nearby.

Standing behind the girl was her mother. Inside the doorway, two or three elderly women were watching the proceedings. The moment I saw the mother on the street, I felt a twinge of suspicion. Now, upon seeing the girl, my doubts were confirmed. The girl could not have been more than eleven years old—thin, very childish, and extremely dark-skinned. The only thing striking about her were her eyes. After seeing her, I lost all curiosity to see “my bride.” For a moment, I glanced at my father. Judging by his face, he too did not seem pleased. Within another moment, as if he had no further reason to stay, he said, “Very nice, Shastriji. We are very happy. Now, if you’ll excuse us…” No one asked the girl a single question—not even her name. I suppose our feelings were clear to everyone present. No one spoke a word.

By evening, though it was a bit of a struggle, we reached Mogalthur. All along the way, my father did not utter a single word. What could I say? As soon as we got home, my mother seemed to understand everything just by looking at our faces. She too offered no praise. From the moment a daughter is born until she is sent off to her in-laws, parents of girls have only one thought in their minds! They do not sleep peacefully, nor do they let any eligible young man sleep in peace. Before a month had passed, another proposal came up, and it was decided that we should go see the girl again.

This time, the girl’s father was not a scholar, but he seemed very worldly and shrewd. Just as we were about to set out to see the girl, a letter arrived from somewhere, describing the girl’s father as utterly unscrupulous and saying that this match was not suitable for us. The planned trip was canceled for that day. My father went off somewhere and returned home in the evening, looking quite exhausted. He spoke to no one. After bathing and sitting down to dinner, he brought up the topic.

“It is our boy’s good fortune that this alliance fell through,” he said. Over the next few days, I made inquiries and gathered plenty of information about them. To understand just how worldly and unscrupulous the girl’s father was, let me tell you one thing: not only did he promise a certain amount of cash as dowry, but also two or three acres of land, and that land…

To the south of the village, and with such-and-such a number, without my even asking, he told me all the details—even though I had already said we did not require any dowry, he wouldn’t listen. The matter that came to light today was this: that land turned out to be a cremation ground, and the so-called “barren village border” was its only distinction. What sin would it be to do to such a man? Did he think this secret would never come out? Such wickedness, such devious plotting—I have never heard of anything like it in my life. They say our boy’s horoscope is excellent, and that a very good match will come; but only when the time is right, it seems. “Ayyo, this house is not for us,” said my mother. I didn’t say anything. I felt just enough to smile a little. Thanks to this experience, for a few days, the marriage discussions came to a halt.

One day, my friend Raju from Bhimavaram wrote to me, saying he had arrived and that I should drop everything and come immediately—since there are no airplanes in our country, I should strap on wings and fly there at once; if I failed to do so, he would come himself, break my wings, and drag me back. Not wishing to trouble him, I told my mother and set off for Bhimavaram at once. Though I didn’t exactly fly as Raju had written, I did travel with nearly that much speed. Raju, expecting me only by evening, was astonished to see me arrive so soon; he rushed out into the street, and before I could even get down from the cart, he hugged me tightly and pulled me inside.

After we went in, he showed me every courtesy, inquired after my well-being, quickly took care of his remaining business, and then said, “Let’s go somewhere outside.” He took me to the banks of the Upputeru. The two of us sat comfortably in the shade of a tree on a sandy spot, and began to reminisce about old times. Starting from our first meeting abroad, up until the day I boarded the train at Waverley Station to return home, we recalled all the adventures of our lives there—the mischief we made, the blunders, the times we made others cry, the times others made us cry, and all the delightful incidents in between. We spent hours lost in this lion’s gaze at the past, oblivious to the passage of time.
Though we didn’t notice the march of time, being creatures of flesh and blood, our stomachs eventually reminded us it was time to get up and head home.

That evening, I thought of returning home, but Raju put his foot down and declared that I was not to budge from there. I protested, saying I had come only with the clothes on my back and had nothing else to wear.

Without delay, he dragged me to the bazaar, bought two sets of dhotis, towels, and other necessities, and even had two shirts stitched for me on the spot. Then, with a stern face, he ordered, “Keep your mouth shut and stay right here until you say you want to leave.”
And so, quite against my will and without even realizing it, I ended up staying there for a whole week. Still, I insisted, “I must go home tomorrow, my dear fellow.”
“There are still twelve—no, fifteen—hours left until tomorrow, aren’t there?” he replied.

I said nothing more. After we finished our evening snacks, we were about to step out somewhere when two Brahmins entered the front porch and began conversing with Raju’s father. He asked us to sit for a moment. I wondered, “Who are these people? What’s going on?” For some reason, a suspicion crept in—could they be here to discuss my marriage?

Soon, the elder Raju introduced his son and me to the visitors. Then he explained that one of the guests was Achyutaramaiah, a Brahmin from our own sect, a renowned lawyer in that town. As he spoke, the man who had accompanied Achyutaramaiah turned to me and said,

“We have heard much about you, your father, your family’s reputation, and your studies abroad. Achyutaramaiah and I have been trying to visit you and your father for the past fifteen days, ever since we arrived from Mogalturru, but court work kept us too busy to come sooner. Achyutaramaiah’s eldest daughter is very beautiful and intelligent. She is currently studying for her school finals. Though the girl herself is eager to pursue higher studies, her mother and grandmothers are pressing to have her married as soon as possible. It was only yesterday evening that I learned you were here and had been staying here for five days…”
Barrister Parvateesam

So, we have taken the liberty to come here now. I would be delighted if you could kindly see the bride just once this evening. If you have no objection, tonight you may go to your village, consult with your father, and tomorrow, please request him to come here. Then, you may return here again in the evening, and by dawn, we shall convey your decision to you," he said.

All this while, Achyutaramaiah garu had been sitting without so much as a twitch or a word. "Dear sir, please forgive me for saying this, and do not take it otherwise, but kindly visit our home just once. See our daughter. If you find her even the least bit attractive, we shall go to your father. We have the hope and confidence that, after learning our good and bad points, he will surely oblige us by coming here tomorrow. Come, let us go. Your friends may accompany you as well," he said, standing up before I could even answer. Raju took my hand and pulled me up. We had no choice but to follow them.

Achyutaramaiah garu’s house was a large mansion built on an expansive plot. In front, there was a small garden, beautifully maintained. As soon as we entered, we saw that the hall was furnished in Western style, with chairs, sofas, and the walls adorned with eye-catching paintings. By the time we arrived, a few people were already sitting in the front verandah, perhaps waiting for our arrival as part of their party. We quietly followed Achyutaramaiah garu inside and sat in the hall. It seemed that all arrangements had already been made, for as soon as we entered, Achyutaramaiah garu went inside and told his wife to bring the bride. The girl, already adorned and ready, was brought in by her mother within a couple of moments.

Some women were inside, and another little girl and two boys—presumably Achyutaramaiah garu’s children—came into the hall and stood there. As the girl entered, she immediately caught my eye. Our glances met quite unintentionally. Without my knowing, my mind and heart were filled with her. All the castles I had built in the air over the years vanished into thin air. As the girl was about to sit down, she looked at me once more with her large, expressive eyes. With a gentle smile, she sat down. Her mother stood beside her.

“She is our eldest daughter, currently studying and soon to be married,” said Achyutaramaiah. The girl, as if to indicate that not everything her father said was true, nodded slightly and lowered her head in embarrassment.

“If you wish to ask the girl anything, please do. There’s no need for you to feel shy or hesitant. She is also learning music—within a few moments, she can sing you a song she has learnt,” Achyutaramaiah continued.

For some reason, as if someone had cast a spell on me, I was struck dumb. All these years, whenever I went to see brides, I would ask countless questions, make the girl speak, try to gauge the sweetness of her voice, her wit, and all sorts of other things. But now, not a single question came to mind. Just sitting there, gazing at that figure, seemed more than enough.

Since I said nothing, the girl’s father prompted her to sing a song. With that, I, who had been wandering in some heavenly realm, was suddenly brought crashing down to earth. Why all this now! “When my father comes tomorrow, you may see him,” I blurted out, standing up without even realizing it.
The faces of everyone present blossomed with smiles. The answer they had hoped for, the words they wished to hear, had slipped out of me unintentionally, without any effort or awareness on my part.

chapters.title: Marriage Proposal
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam
The words stuck in my throat.
As soon as Raju and I stood up, everyone else there also rose to their feet.

That girl, too, stood up. Once again, our eyes met. She smiled shyly. But I—unable even to return her smile—could not manage so much as a grin. Like a bashful bride, I lowered my head in embarrassment and stepped out onto the street.
Achyutaramaiah garu came along with my sister and escorted us up to the road. “I’ll let you know first thing in the morning what your father has to say. I’ll be here,” he said.

Without a word, I folded my hands in farewell, leaned on Raju for support, and trudged forward as if walking in my sleep. We reached the end of the street and turned the corner. Suddenly, Raju burst out laughing.

“Parvateesam, your game is up! This is the end of your freedom. I thought you were some great hero, a man of courage. After traveling through so many countries and seeing countless beautiful women, how is it that the moment you set eyes on this little girl’s face, you turned into a nervous wreck? Where has all that bravado you used to spout gone now?” he teased me mercilessly all along the way.

I didn’t utter a single word in reply. My heart was still back there, fixed on the eyes of that girl, who stood at a distance, looking at me with a smile, her gaze following me as I walked away. Raju practically dragged me along until we reached the place where we had sat the previous night, but that daze did not leave me.

Raju patted me on the back. “Well, my boy, have you come to your senses yet? Or should I fetch you a bed, a blanket, and a pillow so you can sleep right here? If you want, do so—your father will come tomorrow and wake you up anyway. I’ll be on my way,” he said, getting up to leave.
With that, the spell was broken. I returned to my normal self.

“Why are you standing? Sit down!” I made Raju sit again, and we slipped back into our usual chatter. In the midst of our conversation, a stray word or two from Raju’s mouth revealed to me that both he and his father were, in fact, the root cause of the entire episode that had just transpired.

The next morning, just as we were finishing our ablutions and breakfast, a message arrived from Achyutaramaiah’s house. The messenger informed us that my father had given his consent, and that they would be coming over before three o’clock that afternoon. He added that we should be ready, as they would bring us the news as soon as they arrived.
Raju and I exchanged glances and burst out laughing.

“Parvateesham, your father will come today, and while you’re still lost in your daydreams, they’ll have that girl tie three knots around your neck. By the time you regain your senses, you’ll find a fresh, green turmeric thread dangling from your neck, and a brand-new mangalsutra sparkling away. So, if you want to avoid this calamity, you’d better stop daydreaming right now, stay alert, and keep your wits about you. Otherwise, for the rest of your life, you’ll be gazing at that girl’s face, losing your mind in her gentle smile, fluttering about in the shade of her eyebrows, serving her like a slave, forgetting all your studies and ambitions, and spending your days basking in the divine glances of that goddess—happy and contented,” Raju said.
I sprang up, grabbed my towel, and stuffed it into his mouth.

“I’m glad. It was clear to me yesterday evening that you were the mastermind behind all this. Well, I suppose you did it with good intentions. But don’t push your luck—I won’t tolerate too much of this nonsense,” I said.
With a broad grin, Raju pulled the towel away and smacked me in the face with it.

“Parvateesham, have you completely forgotten your Edinburgh lady friend? Did just one look at this girl bring you such joy? Don’t you want to see anyone else? Looking at you, I’m reminded of that song: ‘If this is how you are for just one word, what will happen next?’ To be honest, this girl is—”

I must admit, she is indeed a fine girl. I have known her since childhood—very clever and intelligent. Recently, I came to know that Mr. Achyutaramaiah is actively seeking a marriage alliance for her. After you arrived, it occurred to me that it would be good to inform them about you at the earliest opportunity. In this entire district, Mr. Achyutaramaiah is a very famous lawyer—so gentle in nature, and even while being in the legal profession, there is no one else as upright as him. It would be difficult to find another like him. Even your father must have heard of his reputation. That’s why, as soon as this idea struck me, I whispered it into my father’s ear. He was delighted and immediately did everything necessary to facilitate this alliance. As a result, I suspect that this very evening, the formal betrothal ceremony might even take place. I suppose this is what our people call an “incident.” Otherwise, I know you are firmly against marrying a young girl. I also heard that this was one of the reasons you rejected previous proposals. But the moment you saw this girl’s picture today, you forgot all about that, didn’t you? For whatever reason, if your father does not approve of this match, would you simply let it go? Tell me the truth. I am sure he will like her. The marriage will happen. This girl will become your divinely ordained wife. I cannot express how happy that would make me. In such situations, all our plans, our ideals, our stubbornness—they all get swept away," he said.
"Enough already! Stop your philosophy," I replied, feigning annoyance.

Thus, we chatted away until nearly eleven o’clock. Afterwards, we satisfied Atmaram’s hunger and took our meal. Exactly at two o’clock, a message arrived from Mr. Achyutaramaiah’s house, asking us to get ready and come over.

Within half an hour, we reached Mr. Achyutaramaiah’s residence. It seemed my father had already arrived. The whole front yard was bustling with the pleader’s friends. Everything looked as if it had already been decided—festive garlands were hung at the entrance. Two elderly men stood in the street, as if waiting for our arrival, and as soon as we alighted from the carriage, they warmly ushered us inside.

They took us inside. Achyutaramaiah, who had been chatting with friends in the front hall, came up to us and shook hands. All those seated there rose to their feet with gentle smiles. We, too, went inside with Achyutaramaiah. My father greeted me with a soft smile. They were about to serve us refreshments.
My father said, “Let us first see the children, and then, at leisure, we can go through these formalities.”

Achyutaramaiah agreed and brought in the bride, seating her before us. Once again, I became spellbound, my eyes wide as saucers, staring at the girl. I have no idea what the girl was thinking, but with a gentle smile, she too glanced at me. What happened after that, I cannot say. Apparently, even the betel leaves were exchanged at that moment, but I have no recollection of any conversation that took place.

Raju sat there, grinning at my foolish expression. Achyutaramaiah came over, draped a shawl over my shoulders, and placed betel leaves in my hands. That brought me back to my senses, and I looked around, startled, wondering what was happening. My father chuckled quietly to himself.

Meanwhile, Achyutaramaiah presented my father with a precious zari shawl and betel leaves. Though the people present did not break into applause, they expressed their enthusiasm in other ways. When I tried to look at the bride, I saw nothing less than a full moon shining before me. As I gazed, entranced, at that moon-like face, the priest’s blessings fell upon my ears, and sacred rice rained down on me from all sides.

Achyutaramaiah and his wife, overjoyed, came up to me and showered rice grains upon my head. My father, too, approached, blessing me with deep emotion and sprinkling rice. Seeing him, my eyes filled with tears. I rose and bowed at his feet. He placed his hand on my shoulder and drew me close.

I also bowed to my in-laws. Joy danced on my mother-in-law’s face. Sandal paste and betel leaves were distributed to all the relatives and friends who had come. Everyone began to exchange glances, recognizing one another. In two minutes, the hall was empty. Only Raju, my father, and I remained. Achyutaramaiah stood up and...
Barrister Parvateesam

After paying my respects to my father, I said, “Shastriji, I am at a loss for words to express my happiness. You have blessed us and made us fortunate. All the elders will truly be delighted with this alliance—there is no doubt about it. Many astrologers have said that our girl’s horoscope is excellent, that she is very lucky, and that she will be happy herself and bring happiness to others. Today, I am overjoyed to see that it has all come true. All this has come to pass with such unexpected speed that I can hardly believe it. The one responsible for making this happen is our Raju—your Parvateesam’s friend. I have never seen such a clear example of divine intervention. I am left speechless,” he said, his voice trembling with emotion.

My father took both his hands, made him sit down, and said, “I am very happy indeed, sir. Truly, this is nothing short of divine will. Your name has been familiar to me for a long time. Even so, this outcome is purely the work of fate. They say my son’s horoscope is also excellent, that he will rise to great heights, that he will have a wife of exceptional beauty, virtue, and character, and that she will bring prosperity to our home. The elders have said this, and I too have been convinced of it for a long time. I have cherished those hopes, dreamed those dreams, and passed the time waiting for them to come true. Last night, when you came and expressed your opinion, and today, seeing your daughter’s radiant face here, all my dreams have come true. My penance has borne fruit—I cannot express how happy I am.

Above all, what delights me most is that my son insisted on marrying a young girl, one who has not yet come of age. He made it clear to me that he did not want a girl who had already reached womanhood. Today, just by seeing your daughter, all his doubts and hesitations have vanished into thin air. He has become utterly captivated by her. Yesterday evening, when my son went to see her alone, I don’t think he asked a single question about her name, age, or education. Is that not so, my boy?” he turned to me and asked, “Isn’t that right?”
This unexpected question left me flustered and embarrassed. Like a bashful bride, I hung my head and could not utter a single word.

“My future father-in-law’s guess is absolutely correct,” he said with a gentle smile. I felt a bit awkward at the direction this conversation was taking, so I tried to change the subject. “It’s not good that my grandmother couldn’t come. I feel quite lonely and uncomfortable,” I said, glancing at my father.

“Oh, you silly boy! Why trouble your mother for nothing? In two or three days, your future father-in-law, mother-in-law, their daughter, and other relatives and friends will come to our place and perform the betel-nut ceremony there as well. Your mother won’t feel satisfied until then, so I arranged it this way. Aren’t you happy now?” he said.
My joy knew no bounds. My father stood up and said, “Well then, brother-in-law, please excuse me now. If I don’t leave immediately, it will be difficult to reach home by night.”

Achyutaramaiah said, “There’s no need for you to hurry. After you finish your ablutions and have some refreshments, the same motorcar that brought you here will take you back and drop you at your doorstep in no time.”

My father laughed and said, “So, from the very moment the alliance was fixed, we’ve been provided with a vehicle! From now on, it seems we’ll be riding in cars all the time, startling everyone with our car horns!”
Everyone burst out laughing. I never knew my father could speak so wittily.

Soon, after finishing the refreshments, my father prepared to leave. “Son, are you coming with me, or will you stay another day, take another look at the bride, check her age and all that, and then come?” he asked, laughing.
Unable to reply, overwhelmed with joy, I bowed my head and stood there, unable to contain my happiness. My father, noticing my feelings, smiled knowingly.

"Alright, as you wish. Come two days earlier, not with the wedding party. If you want, you can go with them when they leave our village, drop them off, and then return," said Achyutaramaiah garu, and hurriedly went out to sit in the car waiting at the porch. The car immediately started and sped away.

As soon as my father left, Raju and I took leave of Achyutaramaiah garu and walked away. I had no mind to go home. We wandered the streets of the village aimlessly, without any purpose, without even a proper conversation, and finally ended up at the riverbank, as usual. We sat there, lost and silent for a few minutes.
Then I asked, "Raju, why did you come up with this idea?"

"Why, what can I say? There’s no special reason. Didn’t you ever wonder if you’re taking on too much, marrying so young? I couldn’t help but suspect that there would be a big clash between your father and you over this matter. I kept thinking about how to avoid that."

"Just the other day, someone came to our house and was talking to my father. In the middle of the conversation, I overheard them say that Achyutaramaiah garu was trying to arrange a marriage for his daughter, and that soon he would finalize some alliance and get her married. After they left, the thought struck me like lightning. I discussed it with my father. He was delighted, and wondered aloud how, despite this boy staying here for so many days, neither of us had thought of this before. It’s very strange. Anyway, now it’s settled. ‘Auspicious things should be done quickly,’ he said. Without further ado, he put on his shirt, threw a shawl over his shoulders, and rushed off to Achyutaramaiah garu’s house. What more is there? At a time when Lord Parameshwara himself was pondering who should be the instrument to bring about this auspicious event, my father took up the task, and it was as if all the three crore gods unanimously said, ‘So be it!’"
"But Parvateesam, at that moment, seeing you and that girl together, it seemed as if..."

Strange thoughts raced through my mind, as if to say, “This is not for you, young man!” and left me in a state of utter delight. Nowhere else, I believe, is the idea that a suitable wife is destined for a man from birth proven as clearly as it is here. The girl, it seems, is just fourteen years old. She has not yet reached puberty. Because of this, her mother and her elders are pressuring her father to have the three knots tied at once. But the father and the daughter are both determined that the marriage should only take place after she completes her education. They have resolved not to let anyone else's plans interfere with their own wishes.

The moment my father mentioned this alliance, their family came to see me, and immediately agreed—as if they had been waiting all these years just for me, and had never considered anyone else! Is it not astonishing? Parvatisham, you are a lucky man. I am using a phrase today with complete conviction, which I never really believed before. The moments when we first met were delightful, but the moments of your first sighting were a thousand times more joyous. Believe me! He laughed and said, “I must sound like an old man, talking to you like this. But these feelings have settled in me only now, and I feel intoxicated with happiness just looking at your foolish face.”
I stood up, intending to give him a smack. Sensing my thoughts, Raju sprang up and ran off in a flash. I had no choice but to chase after him.

The next evening, I went home. As soon as I entered, my mother rushed out to the porch, warded off the evil eye, told me to wash my feet, and hugged me like a little child. Tears of joy streamed from her eyes. My own tears fell upon her. For a few minutes, the world ceased to exist for both of us. Holding me tightly, she led me inside with unsteady steps, her voice trembling with emotion.

“My dear child, my joy knows no bounds. Son, all these days, your father and I have been anxious about what would happen with your marriage, what obstacles might arise. But as of yesterday, all our worries have vanished. We have no more troubles. May you both live a thousand years in happiness!”
Barrister Parvateesam
A couple of days later, Achyutaramaiah garu arrived from Bhimavaram, accompanied by relatives, friends, and the bride-to-be. Here, they performed the betrothal ceremony.
Achyutaramaiah garu, his wife, and the bride’s parents—all elderly—were filled with boundless joy upon seeing our home, the customs here, and the virtuous conduct of my parents.

Once the betrothal was done and they returned to Narsapuram, I cannot begin to describe the happiness my mother experienced. At any given moment, she seemed not to walk on the ground but to float in the air. Just looking at her radiant face filled me with an indescribable joy. I wondered if, in any other country, any mother could ever feel such happiness, even for a single moment, when something auspicious was about to happen to her son.

I thought, “Do all mothers in our country feel the same way?” But then, the saying came to mind: “It’s the joy of the son’s marriage, not the thought that a daughter-in-law is coming.” That made me chuckle a little. Whatever my mother’s feelings, as for me—I didn’t know whether I was on the earth or in the air or where I was wandering.

My mind was awash with all sorts of fancies and waves of delight, so much so that at times I felt as if my head was floating away from me. I couldn’t tell how many days had passed, whether I had eaten during the day or slept at night, or even what was day and what was night. In this state, my uncle arranged the wedding date within a month and wrote to inform me that the auspicious time was fixed in Narsapuram.

With that, the thought struck me like a gunshot: “How will I get through this month?” Immediately, it was as if someone patted me on the back and warned me not to get carried away imagining that from the very next day my wife would come running from Edinburgh like a little girl, sit in my lap, wrap her arms around my neck, and shower me with kisses.

That’s when it struck me—my wife is still a child! Once again, for a while, my mind and my heart seemed to be in two different places, wandering in the world of imagination. “How many days more?” That thought settled heavily in my chest.
It’s strange—despite having spent a year or more in Edinburgh in such close proximity, with such enthusiasm, with that girl...

Here, without any such special reason, I was overcome with such boundless, unbearable joy that I began to wonder what could be the cause of it. Perhaps this is what our elders mean when they speak of bonds from previous births, I thought, and thus consoled myself with that answer. I spent my days muddling through, losing count of the days as they passed.

Without any prompting from me, without my uncle asking me for any help or assigning me any task, he arranged for the auspicious invitations to be printed and sent, took care of everything from setting up the wedding pandal to erecting the festoons, all on his own—or perhaps with help from others, though I was unaware of it. I didn’t even know whether the month was over or not, and one morning, before I could make sense of anything, my mother woke me up at dawn and said, “Quick, finish your chores. Today we must perform your ‘Pellikoduku’ ceremony.”
Startled, I jumped up and blurted out, “What’s this, Mother? Aren’t there still ten or fifteen days left?”—forgetting myself in my confusion.

She laughed and said, “Oh, you silly boy! The wedding is the day after tomorrow. Today is the ‘Pellikoduku’ ceremony, tomorrow is the sacred bath, and the day after, we leave for Narsapuram. It’s all quite simple. Our relatives haven’t even noticed the dates, you scatterbrain!” She said all this so lightly, as if it were nothing at all.
With no room for argument, I hurried through all my morning routines and, in about an hour, was ready.

I had no idea what this ‘Pellikoduku’ ceremony entailed. I thought perhaps it was just a matter of oiling my hair and putting on new clothes. I had never seen such a ritual before. My mother called in a group of married women and made quite a commotion over something or other. I thought to myself, “What is all this madness?”

The next day, again before sunrise, they woke me for the ‘Snathakam’ ceremony, which my father conducted with some elaborate rituals. This was mostly a men’s affair; the women came only to watch the festivities. After a while, they told me to put on a new pair of sandals, handed me a palm-leaf umbrella, slung a small bundle over my shoulder, and said, “Now, walk forward.”
“Where are you off to?” I asked.
The band struck up their instruments with great gusto. “It’s inauspicious to ask such things when the journey has already begun,” said one fellow.

“Hey, you madman! Are you saying the dowry isn’t enough, or the bride isn’t good, or you have no need to go through with this wedding, and so you want to set off for Kashi right now with all this music and fanfare? Perhaps you haven’t noticed that your father-in-law or brother-in-law has just arrived—if you rush off in such a hurry, they’ll stop you with a plea as sweet as a lump of jaggery pressed under your chin, and beg you to stay,” he said.

“My dear brother-in-law, how can you be angry with me and suddenly say, at this auspicious hour, that you’ll up and leave for Kashi? We’ve made all the arrangements to marry you to my sister, haven’t we? How can you say such a thing now? Did you say this only after accepting the ceremonial betel leaves?”—and so, with these words, my brothers-in-law, their kin, and my mother-in-law’s people surrounded me, making a commotion, not letting me proceed even ten steps forward. One snatched my umbrella, another grabbed my shoes—
“Enough, man! Go if you must, see if we care!” said my uncle-in-law, and dragged me back to the dais and plonked me down again.
I thought to myself, “What is all this drama?” and chuckled inwardly.
“My dear brother-in-law, when they pressed the jaggery under your chin, didn’t it stick properly?” teased one brother-in-law.
“And you didn’t bite your tongue, did you?” said another young man.

“Maybe he did bite his tongue—that’s why all the jaggery is still stuck under his chin,” another chimed in, and the teasing continued from all sides. To be honest, I found the whole thing rather amusing.

Just then, they brought out the ceremonial panasa leaves for blessings. The blessings and the auspicious aarti were completed. I got up from the dais and went inside. After another hour, it was time for the meal. There, once again, all the young men gathered around me, saying—
“It looks like Parvateesham garu has lost all appetite for food today!” said one.

chapters.title: Wedding Preparations
paragraphs: "What's this, dear? Has he been sitting near the mat all this time? He must be thinking we're somewhere far away," remarked one.
"How will you spend another twenty-four hours, boy?" asked another.
When someone came to offer ghee for the meal, yet another would say, "He's finished eating, don't force him again and again just because you think he looks frail."
When the sweets were served, someone else would protest, "Oh dear, please don't trouble him! He can't tolerate anything sweet at all, believe me!"

Thus, in all sorts of ways, with banter and laughter, they somehow made it seem as if the meal was finished. Once everyone had taken their betel leaves and gone their separate ways, even the relatives from Narsapuram—my aunt's people—left immediately. After that, all our extended family, with all the necessary commotion, household chores, last-minute packing, gathering the children, and everyone talking over each other, began preparing for the journey. There was as much bustle and noise as one could wish for, with trunks being packed for the trip. I had no idea what was happening, who was doing what, or what anyone was saying.

Since I thought the journey would begin only after dawn, I couldn't sit still in the midst of all this chaos at home. So, taking along a couple of young cousins, I wandered off towards our fields, chatting away. By the time we returned home, it was quite dark. My mother and the others were worried, wondering where I had disappeared to. The entire street was filled with bullock carts—two for every household. Some carts were already loaded with luggage. Some newlywed couples, each having been allotted their own cart, had even spread out their bedding inside, ready for the journey. Some of the elders, unable to grasp the excitement or perhaps having simply forgotten, were muttering, "How will this work, dear? At this rate, we'll need a hundred carts for ourselves!"
Still, it wasn’t enough.

Without any sense of shame or hesitation, they even spread out mattresses. Are these supposed to be benches, or are they birthing rooms? Costumes! Are these costumes or what?” Shouting thus, they began to raise such a commotion that the whole street echoed with their cries.

Amidst this chaos, I and the young fellows who had come with me managed to reach home. Even at the end of the street, those shouts were still audible to us. I had completely forgotten the present situation.
“What are these benches, man? What’s all this racket that can be heard from here to Narsapuram? What’s this birthing-room hullabaloo?” I asked.
“Why do you ask like that? In another half hour or so, or an hour at most, we have to set out for Bhimavaram, don’t we?” said one of the youngsters. Only then did my senses return.
“Are we leaving right now?” I asked anxiously, and dashed into the house. The moment my mother saw me, she came running—

“What is this, my boy? Where did you go? Why are you so late? Everyone else has finished eating. The benches are ready for you to get on. Quickly wash your feet and at least put a couple of morsels in your mouth, dear,” she said, not even finishing her sentence before I rushed into the backyard, washed my hands and feet in a hurry, and by the time I returned, a meal was already served for me in a plate.

But I was so full of excitement and agitation that I couldn’t bring myself to eat. Not a single item, not even the delicious sweets, felt pleasant to me. Just as my mother had said, I somehow managed to force a couple of mouthfuls down and got up and went outside.

Just then, someone started shouting, “Have the palanquin bearers arrived?” My heart nearly stopped. What new commotion is this now? After all these years, they must be thinking I’ll sit in a palanquin and be paraded all the way to Bhimavaram, I suppose, I muttered half to myself, and ran to my mother.
“Amma!” I called out, my voice rising with agitation.
“What is it, son?” she said, dropping whatever she was doing and running over in alarm.
"Mother, what’s all this talk about palanquins and gig-carts? Who are these people, anyway?" I asked, a little irritated.

"What’s this, you silly boy? How can there be a wedding without a palanquin? All the wedding guests will come in carts, but the groom must go in a palanquin, my dear. After all these years, how can you still be so innocent? If anyone hears you, they’ll laugh their heads off," said my mother, and she rushed off.

Without my knowledge, she had already had a new dhoti and a new shirt stitched for me, a velvet coat, a grand zari-bordered shawl, a velvet cap with a shimmering border—all of these she brought out, arranged on a silver plate. She told me to take off the clothes I was wearing and put these on, all the while suppressing her laughter.
My legs began to tremble. I was afraid I might collapse right there. To be safe, I flopped onto the bench nearby. My mother looked a bit worried.
"What’s wrong, dear? Are you feeling unwell?" she asked.

"I’m perfectly fine, Mother. Absolutely fine. It’s just that, as soon as I saw these theatrical costumes, my eyes went wide, my heart started pounding, and I collapsed like this. Did you borrow this coat and cap from some merchant’s house or a royal family? Or are they ours? Heaven forbid, are these the priceless garments worn by my grandfather or your grandfather on their wedding day? If so, after this auspicious event, it’s your responsibility to preserve them carefully for my son and grandson," I said.

My mother burst out laughing. I had never seen her laugh like that before. In a moment, she composed herself and said, "These are for you, dear. I had them stitched without even telling your father. I knew if I told you earlier, you’d make a fuss. So, from time to time, I saved up money from my little boxes and spent it on these. I kept imagining how handsome you’d look in them, and every day, I’d take them out and look at them, so happy, and I’ve been hiding them carefully for a whole month so you wouldn’t see them."
Barrister Parvateesam

I am very happy, mother, to know how much affection and fondness you have for me. But let me say just one thing—don’t take it the wrong way. This coat and hat—none of our people ever wear such things, mother. I’d only put them on if I were acting as a king in a play, that’s all. Otherwise, if there’s a wedding in any of our villagers’ homes, you can give these as a gift to the bridegroom. They’ll be delighted. That way, at least, they’ll be put to good use, I said.
My mother was struck dumb.
“While we’re at it, let me say one more thing. You mustn’t get angry. I cannot travel in a palanquin. I simply won’t, no matter what anyone says,” I declared, firmly.
All the fear and trembling that had come over me before now seemed to descend upon my mother. She collapsed beside me in a heap. Tears welled up in her eyes.

“What is this, my son? Why are you uttering such inauspicious words, like the saying ‘Auspicious beginnings, but ill omens follow’? If not in a palanquin, where else would you sit for your wedding, my boy? You don’t understand, son. Don’t say such things. If anyone hears, they’ll burst out laughing. Is this some great sin? Is this something no one does? Why do you refuse the palanquin, you mad fellow? If your father hears of this—”

Now she started a big commotion. All the wedding folk will each have their say and pester you endlessly. “Whatever it is, at least the palanquin is unavoidable, dear,” she said, placing her hand on my shoulder, drawing me close, pinching my cheeks with both hands, pressing them against her temples, spreading her fingers, and with a choked voice and tear-filled eyes, she pleaded, “Son, at times like this, it’s best not to be stubborn.”

I didn’t know what to say. “Mother, no matter how much you say, no matter what you tell me, I’ll listen, I’ll obey. But I will not wear that coat and hat. I will not sit in the palanquin. Let’s just happily go in the bullock cart,” I said, solemnly, as if there could be no argument.
Without another word, she trembled, swayed, and went inside. She must have told my father, for he came to me at once. As soon as he arrived, his eyes fell on those clothes.
“What’s all this? Who gave you these?” he asked.
“Just for fun, as my wedding gift, my mother gave me this maternal alms,” I replied, laughing.
He too laughed, took away the coat and hat, and told me to put on the rest. “And what’s this about the palanquin? Your mother seems to be talking about it,” he said.

“It’s nothing, father. I simply cannot bear the thought of people carrying me in a palanquin all the way to Bhimavaram. Even if it were someone else being carried like that, I couldn’t stand to watch it,” I said.
“All these honors performed at weddings are the ancient customs of kings, my boy,” my father said.
“That may be so, father. But when those kingdoms and those kings are all gone, why should we cling to their customs?” I asked.
“Then will you not even agree to the procession?” he asked.

“I’m wondering what the need for a procession is at all—it’s unnecessary, isn’t it? If we skip that, the palanquin problem disappears. And if there’s no procession, no one loses anything. In fact, it would be quite comical—”

chapters.title: The Wedding
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam
“It’s not something forbidden by the scriptures, nor is it against dharma. So, just because we stop this, no one will blame us. And even if they do, we needn’t bother about it,” I said.
My father, without saying a word, paced back and forth for five minutes. Then he said, “Alright, as you wish.”

Feeling as if I’d been granted a new lease on life, I let out a huge sigh of relief. My father then went and found a good cart among those available, arranged it so that my mother and two others could sit comfortably by spreading hay and laying a mattress and blanket on top, and brought it to the doorway.

Meanwhile, I went around inspecting all the carts to see what had become of the carts of the couples who were about to leave when I arrived. Ten or fifteen carts had already set off. I heard that the couples had seated themselves, and the cart drivers, eager to help, had driven off without telling anyone. In four or five more carts, bedding had been spread and they seemed to be waiting for the couples. In any case, after a while, all the carts moved ahead. My father and another man made sure all the doors and locks at home were secure, checked that nothing was forgotten, left reliable caretakers and villagers to look after the house, and finally came in the last cart.

It was still a little dark when the carts neared Bhimavaram. The carts were stopped for a while outside the town. All the men and women got down quickly to relieve themselves. Then, after moving a little further, the carts stopped again near a pond. Here, everyone got down to brush their teeth.

As soon as we got down, the cart I was in, my father’s cart, and our priest’s cart were led ahead to their house. Hearing of our arrival, they took us into our quarters. We all walked together, chatting as we went. Our carts followed behind us.

By the time we had finished brushing our teeth and such, all the remaining carriages had arrived. Many villagers—women, children, and elders with no urgent work—came running in haste to see these carriages and the wedding party. Everyone got down from the carriages, arranged their luggage, and began preparing for their baths and ablutions.

Even here, the energetic, modern young couples, as far as possible, had their belongings placed in separate rooms and promptly locked their doors. However, as this was a very large house, and perhaps even that was deemed insufficient, another house next door had also been vacated and cleaned for our use. Because of this, there was no need for the young couples to hurry so much. No matter how many couples there were among the wedding guests—young or old—there were enough rooms for each to have one to themselves if they wished.

Once everyone in the wedding party had bathed and adorned themselves, milk was first served to the little children. A quarter of an hour later, fruits and snacks were brought for the adults. For all the boys and girls who were accustomed to eating early in the morning, those arrangements were ready as well. The aunts and the favorite elders also received an immediate invitation to come at once.

No sooner had the invitation reached them than, in a flurry, all the men under twenty, some mothers with children on their hips, some elders from both sides who could not wait until the usual meal time, those who observed ritual purity and those who did not, and the young men and women who had no such concerns—all of them, each with a plate in hand, made their way to the wedding house for breakfast.

As soon as they arrived, all the women forgot the reason they had come and, gathering together, rushed to see the bride. While the bride was being bathed and adorned, so many people, with laughter and chatter, crowded into the room that those already inside were startled, imagining that, seeing so many faces, they might faint away. Immediately, someone spread a mat and invited everyone to sit down.

The bride, blushing deeply, shrank into herself and became a bundle of shyness. Yet, she kept looking at them all with wide, smiling eyes. All those who had come, without even asking the bride’s name, now wondered what to say next.
Barrister Parvateesam

Without uttering a word, with unwavering determination, nearly a hundred pairs of eyes there were scrutinizing the bride from head to toe, inside and out. The womenfolk, too, were silently continuing to adorn her. Just then, as soon as the call came that the meal was ready to be served, this whole flock, like the offspring of Shakuntala, swooped down upon the dining area in a single instant.
Now, there was a flurry of leaf plates, food, chaos, and mockery as the meal commenced.

Someone remarked, “The mango pickle is excellent!” and immediately the young crowd seized upon the pickle. With so many people, and everyone asking for it three or four times at once, the pickle on that side seemed to be running out. Sensing this, all the youngsters unanimously began a chorus: “Aavakaya, Ma’am! More aavakaya!”—their voices rising in unison.

Inside, a trusted maid, having hurriedly bathed and left her wet clothes in the pickle room, scooped up a heap of pickle in a large shell, forgetting her own state, and with the shell in her palm, rushed out—since the commotion in the courtyard was growing louder.
Everyone seated at the leaves raised their hands and cried out, “Govinda! Govinda!”

The poor woman had no idea what was going on. She wondered what all this uproar was about. As she served pickle to ten or so young men and moved forward, the women seated in the row stopped her right there, and through their expressions made her realize her predicament. Only then did she catch a glimpse of her true state.
“Oh, you wretches! May your faces be cursed! Why all this racket for nothing?” she muttered, running off in embarrassment.

Just then, an elderly woman grabbed a colored sari and rushed over, wrapping it around the maid from head to toe, sending her off to the other side of the courtyard, taking the shell from her and starting to serve the meal herself.

The old maid, cursing and wailing, ran to the well, washed her hands and face, poured two pots of water over herself, went inside, discarded her wet clothes, and, so that no one would see her for the rest of the day, lay down in some corner—poor thing. Meanwhile, even before the meal was finished, the bride’s party began to depart from the guesthouse...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 447

The sound of drums and cymbals came floating towards us, as if the very air was vibrating with their rhythm. At once, everyone hurriedly washed their hands and dashed off to the guesthouse. There, the groom’s party had just arrived, their luggage in tow. The bride’s party, not to be outdone, met them at the entrance, stopped them with due ceremony, performed all the necessary rituals, and then led the groomsmen inside.

The wedding pavilion was a sight to behold—adorned so beautifully, it was a feast for the eyes. The entire hall was bustling with people, while servants stood at intervals, fanning the guests with large hand-fans. The chanting of Vedic hymns echoed throughout the pavilion, lending an air of sacredness to the occasion.

Here, after completing the Ganesh Puja and other preliminaries, the priest, along with a few other Brahmins, made their way with great eagerness to the bride, who was busy performing the Gauri Puja. Her parents and other elders, waiting anxiously for the groom’s arrival, were informed by the priest, “An extraordinary groom, the one destined for your daughter, is now waiting in the wedding hall. His lineage, gotra, and ancestry are such-and-such.” The bride’s lineage and gotra were then recited by their own priest, and after formally agreeing to the match, everyone returned to the main hall.

The band struck up their instruments. Within two minutes, the bride, resplendent in all her finery, was seated in a basket of rice and carried in by her maternal uncle, who bore her with great pride. The moment the bride caught sight of the groom, her relatives, fearing she might lose her composure, quickly drew a curtain between them to shield her from his gaze. The bride, still in her rice basket, was seated in the hall, and the assembled guests showered her with rice grains as a blessing.

At last, the curtain between the bride and groom was drawn aside. The two of them, as if by mutual agreement, completely forgot the crowd around them and gazed at each other with shy, delighted smiles, lost in their own world. For a few moments, even though the priest repeatedly urged them to pay attention, the groom simply could not tear his eyes away from the bride.

“My boy, for these four days—no, these five days—your gaze must remain fixed on us as well. Only then will this marriage be complete. And for the next two or three years, no one will dare come between your glances. But even then, don’t forget the importance of timely meals!” the priest admonished.
I, overcome with embarrassment, bowed my head…

We have now become a household! For this auspicious occasion, it is customary to send off all the dear ones—who have come from near and far, after much effort—with gifts of new clothes. Immediately after, it is tradition to take the bride and groom, their parents, and other close relatives to the groom’s house, and on the following day, to finalize all the rituals of this blessed event, conduct them with great pomp and circumstance, and then worship our chosen deities, who have been blessing us from above. This marks the conclusion of the entire affair.

On the third day, the bride’s parents and their relatives, who had brought her, returned to Bhimavaram. I settled down at home, reminiscing and savoring every little detail of those five days of joy, not forgetting a single thing. After another four or five days, my father-in-law arrived, saying it was time for the customary return visit, and whisked us all away to Bhimavaram once again.

“May all auspiciousness be yours. May you have everlasting prosperity. May the whole world be happy.” These blessings continued to echo in my ears for days on end. I took immense pride and joy in the thought that this auspiciousness was unique, unparalleled, and purely Hindu in its nature.

For several months, time seemed to stand still for me. I had no inclination to do anything. No matter how long I sat with a book in my hands, I never felt like reading. Not a single day passed productively. I could not understand why such a lethargy had overtaken me. I could not imagine that every newlywed groom suffers in this manner, devoid of any spirit or enthusiasm. I had seen many newly married couples, but I never noticed any of them in such a state.

All the dreams and fantasies I had cherished for years were now scattered and changed beyond recognition. I had resolved never to marry a girl who was not yet of age, but the moment I saw this bride, my decision changed without any effort on my part. That girl, as if casting a spell on me, made a challenge—“Let’s see whom you’ll marry if not me!”—and managed to get her way, triumphantly returning to her village. Now that she has won, shouldn’t she at least leave me alone? Why does she stand before me, twenty-four hours a day, staring at me without blinking, and smiling mischievously? Whether in my own country or abroad...

No young woman ever attracted me the way Mrs. Proud did. I do not know whether this pain can still be called longing or not, but I felt that unless I found some excuse to go to Bhimavaram, there was no way out. My friend Raju, as if he had read my thoughts, sent someone to tell me that he had some urgent work with me and that I should come quickly.

Mother, this fellow’s house is made of gold! How did he manage to guess what was on my mind? What urgent need could he possibly have for me at this very moment? With these thoughts swirling in my head, I told my mother, and without waiting even until I reached my father’s house, I took off for Bhimavaram as if by airplane. Not that it was a real airplane, of course, but I lost count of how many hours I actually traveled. Still, I convinced myself I had reached Bhimavaram in about five and a half minutes.

I lingered outside the town for a moment, wondering if I should go straight to Raju’s house, thinking it would be best to avoid any fuss. No sooner had I arrived at Raju’s place—having responded to his invitation, which seemed to have anticipated my own desires—than a most astonishing event occurred within the hour.

I had just finished my coffee and snacks and was chatting with Raju when a man arrived from Achyutaramaiah’s house—that is, from my uncle’s place—saying, “Parvateesham garu has come, it seems. If he is here, please ask him to come to our house.” I was utterly surprised. How did they know I had arrived?
“Raju, did you send them any word?” I asked.
“Heavens, no! I didn’t say a thing,” he replied.
“Then why did you feel the need to call me here at all?” I asked. “I might have written to you casually once, but there was no hidden meaning in it,” he said.
“Then what was this urgent business you mentioned?” I pressed.

“There’s no business, really. But the strange thing is, for the past two days, I’ve had a strong feeling that I must see you, and that you ought to come here. I couldn’t shake the thought. I sent for you just to find out what it might mean,” Raju replied.
Curious to see if such a strange notion had also occurred to Achyutaramaiah garu, Raju was about to say something further, when—
No, I’ll come again, I said, not even bothering to notice Raju’s smile, and quietly made my way to Achyutaramaiah’s house.

Achyutaramaiah was surprised to see me, but also expressed great happiness at my arrival. In his words, there was not the slightest hint that he was the one who had sent me this message. I thought of asking him, “How did you know I was coming?” but as I absentmindedly lifted my head, there, just beyond the threshold, stood the bride, adorned and waiting for my arrival, smiling as if she had been expecting me all along. She put her hand to her mouth, signaling me not to say anything, as if she had guessed my thoughts. With that, my tongue was tied. The question I had intended to ask retreated to the back of my mind.
Achyutaramaiah called out, “Well, well, the son-in-law has arrived! Bring him inside!” he shouted.
The girl who had been standing by the door ran inside, laughing.
I, with my head bowed, marveled at this supernatural web of anticipation. As soon as I stepped inside, my mother-in-law came to meet me, bringing water for washing my feet.

“Did you come straight from home? Are your mother and father well?” she asked, inquiring after my family’s welfare, and placing the water there, she called out, “Bring the towels, dear!” and disappeared inside.

Before the words had fully reached the girl’s ears, she appeared again, towels in hand. Once more, I stood there like a fool, gazing at that divine, beautiful figure. She laughed, tossed the towels at me, and said,
“Wash your feet and then come inside, please. This way,” and led me to her room.
I followed her mechanically, as if walking in a dream.
Once inside her room, as soon as I entered, she pointed to a chair for me to sit and stood a little to the side. After a moment’s pause, I asked,
“Is it a rule that we must keep such a distance?”
She replied, “There is such a rule, but the need for it hasn’t arisen yet.”
"Then why are you sitting so far away now?" I asked.
"This is closer than Mogalthur, isn’t it?" she replied.
"You’re like a parrot that’s learned to talk," I said.
"A parrot only imitates the words of others, but never says anything of its own," she retorted.
"Alright then, I’ll admit you’re a parrot with originality. Now, let me ask you something," I said.
"I can hear you from here as well. Why should I come closer just to answer a question?" she said.
"If you come closer, you’ll find out for yourself," I replied. She lowered her head and smiled a little.
"First, ask whatever it is you wanted to ask," she said.

"That day, I came running to see our Raja. Not half an hour after I arrived, I received a message at his place, inviting me to your house. It turned out that your father hadn’t sent that message. So, how did the news of my arrival reach you so quickly, dear lady—no, dear girl?" I asked.
Instead of answering, she simply started smiling to herself. I sat there, looking at her. After a while, perhaps realizing my silence, she raised her head and looked at me.
"Why are you sitting there, staring at me so quietly?" she asked.
"I was waiting to see if you’d answer the question I asked after you finished laughing," I replied.

"I really don’t understand why you’re asking that question at all. You’d been sending me word for a week that you were coming, hadn’t you? And besides, even today, when you set out, you sent a message. I just took you at your word and sent for you with confidence. That’s the truth," she said, laughing. Then, suddenly changing her tone and sounding a little plaintive, she added, "Are you saying I did something wrong?"

chapters.title: Married Life
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

My astonishment knew no bounds. Could it be that my desire, my imagination, both so powerful, had managed to send a message not only to the king but also to the queen of my heart? It was something unbelievable, something almost impossible to accept. Yet, all this had truly happened before my very eyes—how could I possibly deny it? Perhaps human imagination and resolve possess such strength after all. Speechless, I gently took my beloved’s hand and drew her closer to me. The moment my touch reached her, every nerve in her body seemed to come alive. Her body grew warm. She stood still, as if a little afraid to come any closer. I pulled her just a bit nearer, brushed back the curls that danced across her face, and caressed her cheeks as I said:

“All these seven days, you were wishing I would come, weren’t you? You kept sending me silent messages, day and night! How strange it is. In this short span of time, though we are so far apart, we have become one. This feeling fills me with such wonder that I cannot even express it to you, my dearest,” I said, and with that, I embraced her tightly and kissed her even more deeply. In that moment, the two of us became one.

After a while, she gently freed her hands from mine, moved a little to the side, and said, “Did I really call you? Did my call truly reach you? I too am greatly surprised. Outwardly, I said nothing. I don’t even know what I wished for in my heart. Perhaps this outcome is because I chanted your name a hundred thousand times. With the power of that mantra, my lord has appeared before me in person,” she said, covering her face with her hands and leaning on my shoulder. I was at a loss for words. What an imagination! What a beautiful description! I wondered if my Saraswati would become a great poetess. At that moment, I even said aloud, “If you become a poetess, then I have no role in it. Every thought, every response comes to me only from you. The one who makes me speak is Ramabhadra—no, Parvateesam!”

She laughed and, like a dragonfly, flitted away to the other side. “It would be good if you bathed now—my father has to leave for court. My brother-in-law will be getting ready for the meal with the family. Let’s continue this conversation after lunch,” she said.
“Well then, Saraswati! My clothes and all are with Raju. I’ll go and fetch them,” I said.

“I didn’t want to trouble you again after you came here, so I had them brought here for you. No matter how shy you feel, it seems to be your custom, as a son-in-law visiting your in-laws’ house for the first time after marriage, to stay somewhere else in the town. No one here has ever heard of such a thing,” she said, noticing that I was getting up. As if she hadn’t seen me rise, she leapt away to the other side and ran off, while I stood there like a stone statue. Thinking, “What great fortune is mine!” I was overcome with joy and went off for my bath, unable to contain my happiness.

I have no idea how long I was there. I thought I’d been there for about ten minutes, perhaps. Suddenly, a man arrived from my house with a letter from my father, saying it had been fifteen days since I’d left home, and there had been no news of me. He asked me to write back, letting them know that I and everyone at my in-laws’ house were well. My heart skipped a beat when I saw that letter. “Has it really been fifteen days since I came here?” I wondered. I went and asked Saraswati.
“How long has it been since I arrived here?” I asked.
“How would I know that? Days? Maybe half an hour, maybe an hour, I suppose. But why are you suddenly wondering about this?” she replied.

“My father sent a man to remind me that it’s been fifteen days since I came here. Hearing that, my heart nearly stopped for a moment. Has it really been that long? Couldn’t you have told me at least?” I said.
“This is rich! How would I know the passage of time that you yourself are unaware of? Has it really been fifteen days? Your father—”

The lies wouldn’t stop. It must have been fifteen days, truly. Haven’t I been right here before your eyes all this time? How did fifteen days pass by, I wonder? “It must be some mistake,” she said, bursting into peals of laughter. Not knowing what else to do, I joined in her laughter.

For these fifteen days, except for spending an hour every evening with Raja, I sat at home the rest of the time. I didn’t go anywhere else. I didn’t talk to anyone. I didn’t read a single book. Yet, those fifteen days raced by as if they were fifteen minutes. What a strange thing! We weren’t cowards, nor did we behave in any improper or uncivilized way. My wife is a maiden, not someone else’s, after all! What did we talk about? We didn’t play hide and seek, chess, or even marbles or spinning tops. How did the time pass for us? I don’t even recall her speaking much. In fact, what did we even talk about? Yet, neither of us felt bored. Not a trace of irritation. We didn’t know what a headache was. With so few words, without noticing the passage of time or the weight of our bodies, how did we find such joy? Tell me, girl, can you explain how our time passed, how such rapture and delight came over us? Surely you haven’t learned any enchantment spells from those Ekoi people, have you? Whatever happened, happened. From now on, I’ll be careful. Put my clothes over there—I’m going to the village. If I don’t leave now, I won’t get another chance,” I said.

She replied, “How can you leave the moment you think of a journey? I have to search for the clothes you asked for, wherever they are. I need to check if today is an auspicious day or not. There’s so much ritual to be done! How can a journey begin in an instant?” Saraswati said, putting on a most innocent face.

I don’t need all those guest-star constellations, or those good and bad omens. I’ve gone abroad and learned a great deal; now I must go. Even if you don’t find my clothes for me now, it doesn’t matter—I’ll take them when I get the chance,” I said.
“Let it be, then. If you’re in such a hurry for everything, how will that do?” she said.
“I’m not in a hurry for everything. Only for the journey,” I said.
“I know that not everything happens just because you hurry,” I replied.
She gave me a mocking look and darted off to the other side.

After about five minutes, I went inside and said to my aunt, “Auntie, I’ll be going home this time. It’s been many days since I last visited. My friend Raju sent word asking me to come urgently for some reason, so I came. All this time, he hasn’t told me what the matter is. Now I’m stuck here in the middle,” I said.

Softly, from somewhere, a sweet “Poor thing” drifted into my ears. I looked around, but couldn’t figure out where the voice had come from. Why someone with such a melodious voice would hide behind a door was even more puzzling.

My aunt, perhaps having heard her daughter’s words, stifled her smile and said gently, “What’s the rush? After all, how long has it been since you came? You could stay another couple of days and then go, couldn’t you?”

“Oh, no, it’s already been fifteen days. There’s plenty of work at home. My father is struggling all alone. So, I must go. I’ll come again. It’s not as if I won’t return,” I said. Without realizing it, my tongue slipped and I hinted at the magnetic pull that seemed to exist here. I hoped my aunt hadn’t caught that.

From behind the door, a peal of laughter as sweet as a mountain stream reached my ears. As I was about to turn and leave, my aunt said, “If your journey is unavoidable today, at least have your meal before you go. Anyway, traveling at this hour will be a bit inconvenient.”
Without giving any reply, and pretending not to have heard, I hurried off to the other side.
By the time I entered the room, the mischievous girl was there, taking out my clothes, folding them, then unfolding them again, laughing and playing as she did so.
“What’s this? Why are you messing with my clothes?” I asked.
“I’m looking for something among them,” she replied.
“Well, hurry up. I’m getting late,” I said.
Barrister Parvateesam

“My mother said you shouldn’t leave until you’ve eaten and rested. Besides, the dhoti and towel you used for your bath are still not dry. How will you take wet clothes with you?” the lawyer’s daughter questioned.
“So, have you spoken to my father yet or not?” she asked.
“Why? Isn’t it enough if you and your mother tell me?” I replied.

“How can that be proper? Leaving from here without even saying a word to the people sitting in the hall—what sort of manners is that? If you’re in such a hurry, do you think they’ll refuse? If you go without telling them, they’ll surely say, ‘Why did he leave without a word?’” she said, smiling gently.
“Is that so? Wait a moment, then,” I said.
“I’m arranging your clothes here. Even if you speak from there, I can hear you from here,” she said, without lifting her head.
I was at a loss for words to counter her. I started wondering how I would argue in court tomorrow if I couldn’t even manage with her now.
“If you want someone to respond promptly in court, you should take me along too,” she said.

“In that case, you should study for your B.L. degree. Until you pass that exam, I’ll keep urging you to come to our house. Then, we’ll practice together as partners,” I said. She lifted her head and, for a moment, looked innocently and slowly into my eyes.
“What did you say?” she asked.
I got up, flustered. Like a lady, she quickly darted to the other side. Suppressing my happiness, I went into the verandah and gently broached the subject of my journey with my father-in-law.
“What’s this? You’ve just arrived, and you’re already leaving?” he said.
“It’s been quite a few days since I came. I even received a letter from my father,” I replied.
"Alright then, let us think about it after I return from court," he said.
"But by then, it will be too late, and the journey will become difficult," I replied.
"Why are you worrying about all that? I’ll come and make all the arrangements myself," he said, his eyes still buried in his papers, completely absorbed in his work.
Unable to say anything further, I hung my head and, counting my steps, walked into my room. As soon as I entered, I found my beloved already there.
"So, you’re leaving right now? Didn’t you tell my father to inform the coachman?" she asked, in a tone of great gravity.
"Your father said he would take care of all the arrangements," I replied, with even greater gravity.

She sat in silence for a moment, then said, "Ah, so it’s settled that the journey is not happening right now. Would they ever listen if I said anything? The saying goes, 'Even a child’s words may be wise,' but who cares about such things here!"
With no other choice, I ate my meal and took some rest.
Perhaps because I was to leave either tonight or early tomorrow morning, my mother-in-law, in that short span, even prepared special rice dishes for me.

Lunch ended up being a bit late. I thought I’d rest for a while, but how could my better half allow me to rest? When half of my very being is beside me, weeping and wailing with sobs and hiccups, how can rest even be possible?
Barrister Parvateesam

Therefore, amidst all that cheerful, tinkling laughter, I could not help but be swept along by the mood. I have no idea how many hours passed like this, but suddenly, realizing that my other half had fallen silent, I glanced to my side—she was nowhere to be seen. I was about to get up and search for her, thinking to bring her back, when, just as a celestial maiden might enter the court of Indra with a platter of fruits in a graceful dance, my better half appeared, swaying gently, carrying a silver plate of fruits and a silver tumbler of fresh water.

Though I felt a bit heavy at heart, I could neither refuse those who had sent her nor disappoint the enthusiasm of the one who brought it. So, I quietly got up and sat down, and together we finished off the fruits.

After this ceremony concluded, and after washing my face and such, I was about to go tell Raju that I was leaving, when my father-in-law returned from court and said, “My boy Parvateesam, I have decided that it would be best for your journey to begin at dawn tomorrow. I have also arranged for a car by then. You can leave quickly in it.”

What could I say to that? Without a word, I bowed my head and quietly walked over to Raju. Around eight o’clock, I bid Raju goodbye and came home. After dinner, I thought, “Well, what’s the use of all this fuss?”

At dawn, I woke up to the bustle in the house and brushed my teeth. My mother-in-law brought me fruits and milk herself and served me. By the time I finished, my father-in-law brought out new clothes and handed them to me along with betel leaves.
“Why are you giving me all this now? If you keep giving me such things, I might feel like coming back every week,” I said.
“That would be wonderful, my boy! That’s exactly what we wish for. Not just once a week—even if you came every other day, we would be delighted,” he replied with a laugh.

I bowed down and touched his feet. He blessed me and went inside. I heard the sound of the car at the doorstep, and my Saraswati came and stood beside me. I bid her farewell in the usual manner. I saw tears in her eyes. Unable to stand there any longer, I stepped forward. She wiped her eyes and...
“Remember what your uncle said,” she whispered softly.
“What is it?” I asked.
“He told you to come every other day, didn’t he? We must heed the words of our elders,” she replied.
I gave her a playful pinch on the cheek, but fearing that if I lingered any longer the journey might be delayed, I hurried out onto the street.
As soon as I stepped into the porch, my uncle and aunt both accompanied me all the way to the car. Just as I was about to get in, my uncle placed his hand on my shoulder and said,

“Listen, my boy! There’s no need for any formalities or ceremonies between us. Don’t ever doubt that I didn’t write to invite you. It is the wish of us all that you set out and come here whenever you can. From now on, whenever you come to this town for any reason, it wouldn’t be proper for you to stay anywhere but here. If you can manage to come again soon, we can sit down at leisure and talk about matters relating to your enrollment and other professional affairs. That’s something that must be done sooner or later, isn’t it? Auspicious things should be done quickly, as they say. Whether you join immediately or not, whenever you come, stay with me for ten or fifteen days. By observing, you’ll gain some understanding of our profession and the ways of the world. So don’t hesitate—keep coming. Give my regards to your father and mother,” he said.

No sooner had I sat in the car than the door was shut and the car set off at once. As we drove away, I looked back towards the house. There, at her favorite window, she stood rubbing her eyes, gazing wistfully in my direction, and waved her hand gently. My heart ached. What could I do?

We reached Mogalthur before dawn. As the car turned towards our house, I saw my father coming from the fields on the opposite side. He had just bathed and was about to step onto the threshold when he noticed the car approaching, and, wondering who it might be, paused at the doorway. In a moment, the car stopped at the entrance, and as I got out, my father, seeing me, broke into a slight smile.
"Ah, you’ve arrived, my boy! Did your father-in-law arrange a vehicle for you, or what?" he asked, laughing.
"Yes, Father. He wouldn’t take no for an answer," I replied.

"Of course, my boy, it’s all new to them! For a while, they’ll keep up these formalities. But why did you come running in such a hurry? I only wrote to ask about your well-being, not to summon you home," he said. Just then, my mother came out from inside.

I handed five rupees to the car driver. He protested, but accepted it with great delight. As my mother approached, she said, "Son, ask the driver to have a meal before he leaves. Otherwise, he’ll be late reaching home."
Hearing this, the driver declined, saying, "No, madam, I’ll be at my place within twelve hours. I don’t mind the delay. My master will be waiting for me, too," and with that, he took his leave.
"So, my boy, did your wife give you permission for this journey? She just tied you up so tightly, and now she’ll probably insist you stay home forever," my mother said with a laugh.
"Why would you say that, Mother? Did I insist on anything? Did I demand this match?" I said, walking inside.

"You didn’t insist on anything. I myself, understanding your heart, made the decision. I was convinced that this girl is most suitable for you—beautiful, virtuous, and of good character. I agreed, confident she is a perfect match for you in every way. There’s not the slightest doubt. I am certain that, with her arrival, you will have all happiness, all comforts, and all joy," he said, and went off to perform his prayers.

My mother’s face blossomed like a lotus. I was filled with delight from head to toe. The scene in Bhimavaram, where she looked at me from behind the window with half-shy glances and waved her hand, played before my eyes. Lost in that memory, I sat down, absorbed. Suddenly, I remembered that my father had gone for worship, so I got up to bathe.

chapters.title: Return to Practice
paragraphs: Once again, I had to spend two or three months in utter idleness. Nothing appealed to me. I had no inclination to do anything. I didn’t even feel like reading a book. My body was in one place, my mind in another—such was my condition. Now and then, I would go to the fields. There, as I gazed at the lush green paddy fields, the banks of the lake, the ridges between the fields, the flowering plants, and the blossoming creepers, my mind would settle there, while I wandered off to who knows where. I used to wonder, “What madness is this?” Is this experience common to all, or is it my unique fate? I would ponder.

All the dreams I had as a child, all the resolutions I made abroad—once this village girl came into my life, everything turned upside down.
