She settled into my heart, became my everything, and made herself at home. What a strange thing! Until then, whenever I read about the pangs of separation between heroes and heroines in poetry and epics, they always seemed exaggerated, even a bit comical. Now, though I am not a hero, nor do I possess their delicate sensibilities, I am surprised to find such feelings, such pain, arising in me as well.

To pass the time, I would occasionally visit Narsapur. There, the young men at the bar enrolled me as a member of their club and would invite me to come by now and then. When I went there, I would while away the hours with chatter and games, but upon returning home, everything reverted to its usual state.
While I was in this state of confusion, one afternoon, as I was eating some fruit—

“Well, what are you doing? I have good news for you. Your wife has come of age. The stars and all are favorable, it seems. This evening or tomorrow morning, someone will come to take you there. Your elder brother will arrange for your transport. There’s no escape,” my mother said, and I could even hear the smile in her voice.

As soon as I heard this auspicious news, I was overcome with an inexplicable joy. Though I was sitting, I felt as if I were floating. “Did you hear, boy?” she said, coming over to me with great delight to share the news.

The words, spoken in joy, fell upon my ears. Determined not to let my happiness show, I suppressed it deep within and asked, “Why all this commotion and excitement, mother? Isn’t this what happens to every woman after she is born? You only waited this long for a daughter-in-law, but did you think things would remain the same even after the wedding?” I said this as if I knew nothing.

“Oh, enough of your nonsense! You and your prattle! She’s grown up now. My daughter-in-law is coming home. I’m so happy, I just want to see her walking around the house like Goddess Mahalakshmi herself.”

“Well then, mother, let me ask you something, if you don’t mind. Is she more beautiful than you? To my eyes, you look just like Goddess Parvati herself. Is Mahalakshmi more beautiful than Parvati, mother?”
“Your doubts are endless! No matter how old you get, you never change. Once she comes here, I’ll know who’s more beautiful—no need for you to tell me. You should come with me tomorrow, you hear?”
“Why should I come, mother? If I wander into that crowd of women and end up becoming one myself, it’ll be a disaster,” I replied.
She laughed, saying, “You’re a madman! Always the same!” and bustled away.

Just as my father had predicted, by late evening, a car arrived from Bhimavaram. In it came a relative from my aunt’s side, along with his wife, to take my mother with them. My mother hurriedly cooked, served them dinner, and arranged their beds for the night. They were to leave at dawn. They tried very hard to persuade me to come along as well. I flatly refused. I said I had urgent work in Narsapur in the morning. When they couldn’t get a proper answer from me, they finally gave up and went to bed. I too lay down.

The others fell asleep in an instant, but for me, sleep vanished from that very moment. Countless thoughts began swirling in my mind like whirlpools. I couldn’t have explained a single one of them, even if you’d asked.
At three in the morning, I got up, tidied up all the household chores...
...then, my mother came and arranged hot water for the relatives’ bath and all such necessities. Once they had finished their ablutions and breakfast, they got ready for their journey.

Once again, my uncle and aunt insisted, over and over, that I should at least wake up properly and accompany them, even if only for a short distance. They pleaded so much that I almost felt compelled. But I explained to them that I didn’t have the time to come now, and promised I would visit them at leisure another time, and sent them off. In the morning, I told my father that I had work in Narsapur and slipped away neatly. Poor father, he had to cook for himself and struggle.

On the third day, at sunrise, my mother returned from Bhimavaram by car. Along with her came my aunt’s fifteen-year-old son to help. By then, my father had already left for the fields. I was in the midst of brushing my teeth when I heard the sound of the car and came out into the street. The moment I opened the door and saw my mother standing before me, my heart was filled with relief. If just two days apart made me feel like this, how did I ever manage to spend three years abroad, away from my mother? That very thought struck me, and my heart skipped a beat.

“My dear, I’ve come back,” she said. “They insisted so much that I should stay another day, but I thought you’d be troubled here, so I couldn’t stay. Your uncle arranged a cart for me, even though I said no. What good people they are, don’t you think? How much respect they showed me! Did you know how much they missed you because you didn’t come?”
“Who, mother?” I asked, secretly laughing to myself. My mother didn’t catch my meaning right away.
“Who else, your aunt and uncle, of course,” she replied.
“Yes, of course, who else could it be?” I said. By then, my mother caught on to my joke and burst out laughing.

“Oh, so you meant that! You didn’t ask about her, did you? She’ll come and tell me herself, it seems. What a mad fellow you are! There’s no need for you to ask about her, and no need for me to tell you either. The moment the car’s sound was heard, even the children playing far away pressed their faces to the gate, peering to see who had arrived...

She sat there, staring unblinking. When she saw that only I had returned, how disappointed she looked! Poor thing, her face was so forlorn that I felt a surge of pity for her. “By sheer luck, without any effort on our part, God has blessed us with a gem of a girl,” she said.

“Yes, Mother, that’s exactly what I was thinking. You are indeed very fortunate, and because of your good fortune, your son has found such a worthy bride. I am truly happy,” I replied, rising to my feet and trying to put on a dignified expression.

“Oh, silly Nagamma! You’ve always been the same, never changing. If this new wife can make you happy and make you feel, ‘I am a lucky man,’ then that alone is my good fortune. What greater blessing could I ask for, my boy?” she said, and then disappeared inside, absorbed once more in her household chores.

I asked the young man who had come with her to sit down and wash his face. After I finished my own bath and other ablutions, my mother too—though I have no idea when or how she managed it—had already bathed in a hurry. She brought some snacks and a little milk, and served them to the young man who had accompanied her, as well as to me. She even took some out to the man waiting with the cart on the street. Poor fellow, how delighted he was! After finishing the snacks, the young man, despite all our requests, refused to stay until my father returned. He climbed into the cart and sped off to Bhimavaram.

With my mother’s return, my mind once again became restless. I thought perhaps it would have been better if I, too, had gone to Bhimavaram, just for a change. What next? Should the usual ceremonies proceed in the usual way, or…?

As I was lost in such foolish thoughts, my father arrived in his usual brisk and bustling manner. Not knowing that my mother had returned, he seemed worried that the cooking would be delayed! As soon as he entered the lane leading to our house, he noticed the freshly drawn rangoli at the doorstep and heard the commotion of my mother bustling about inside.
“Has your mother come home, boy?” he asked.
“She’s come, bathed, and even started cooking. Everything is going quite well.”
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 467
“It’s done,” I said.

He went inside, thoroughly satisfied. I, meanwhile, sat down, book in hand, holding it up to my face as if engrossed, but in truth, my mind was wandering the skies, strolling along the Milky Way, and I was making a herculean effort to drag it back to earth. Just then, my father finished his daily worship, and my mother called out to summon me for lunch. I flung the book aside and prepared myself for the meal.

Again, for two or three months, I drifted along with a restless mind, a lifeless body, a heavy heart, and a vague, inexplicable anxiety. I had neither the desire to go anywhere nor to do anything, and time dragged on tediously. At such a moment, a piece of advice from my uncle came to mind. He had once suggested that if I sat in on the proceedings at the court now and then, I would gain some understanding of court procedures and the temperaments of those who frequented the place. The idea struck me as a good one. Sitting idle at home, not even touching a book, I feared my mind would grow dull and I’d become utterly useless. So, I decided to discuss this with my father and thought it might be a good idea to spend ten days in Bhimavaram. Without coming to any conclusion about the merits or drawbacks of this plan, I suddenly heard the postman’s shout. I stepped out to the verandah, took the letter he handed me, and noticed, in the usual fashion, that the handwriting on the envelope looked distinctly feminine. For a moment, I wondered which woman could possibly be writing to me. Then I decided the mystery would be solved if I simply opened the letter. With deliberate care, I tore open the cover, pondering all the while, and slowly drew out the letter. The moment I saw the salutation inside, I was struck motionless, tingling with delight, swept up in boundless ecstasy. For a moment, I simply basked in that joy. Then, in a rush, I ran inside, sat on my bed, and read every word, every letter, with the utmost attention, affection, and happiness. Just then, my mother—
“Why, my dear boy, where is this letter from? No matter how many times I called you, you didn’t respond. Wherever you’ve come from, I hope all is well?”—hearing these words, I was startled.

“All is well, mother. It’s from Bhimavaram. Last time, when I was leaving, my father-in-law advised me that if I occasionally came and sat with him during his work, I’d learn all about court affairs. Now, recalling those words, I wondered whether I should say the letter came from my wife, but thinking I’d lied enough already, I decided to admit the truth. My father-in-law had my wife write the letter. She wrote, ‘Your wife sends her respects to you and to father as well,’” I said.

“Oh, so that’s what it was! No wonder you didn’t hear me calling you four or five times. But why so much hesitation just to say that, my boy? What else did she write? Or never mind, why should I care?” she said, laughing as she went inside.

I didn’t even realize my mother had called me. I thought I’d read the ten lines in that letter only once, but perhaps, like the Gayatri mantra, I must have chanted them a hundred and sixteen times—well, maybe only a hundred and eight times. Still, for some reason, I felt like reading it once more, and after reading it, I seemed to have sunk into a trance. I don’t know how long I sat like that, but my mother came in and said,
“What’s this, my boy? Are you asleep? You’re sitting there as if you’re dozing off. Get up, wash your hands, feet, and face, and that laziness will go away. Come, let’s have some fruit.”

With that, I snapped out of my reverie and returned to this world. Just as she said, I washed my hands and feet and had my usual fruit. My mother, who never did this before, stood there watching my facial expressions, trying to read my thoughts.
“Did your father-in-law write anything else?” she asked.
“What else is there for him to write?” I replied.
“Did he give any further instructions or suggestions?” she asked.

“That’s nothing, mother. Unless she’s out of her mind, if he truly had such intentions, wouldn’t he write in father’s own hand, using his own name? Would he have his daughter write it? There’s nothing of the sort. Besides, there’s no urgency for that now,” I said, feigning ignorance. My mother, chuckling to herself, gathered up the tray of fruits and snacks she’d brought and went inside.

Once again, I found myself pondering the strangeness of it all. The very moment I resolved to go there, I received a summons, as if fate itself wished me to appear. It struck me as quite odd. Just as I was seized by a curiosity to go and see my wife, perhaps my Saraswati there too was possessed by a desire to see me once more. After all, she’s no heroine from some ancient poem, but a modern maiden—innocent, yet studying English. Perhaps, forgetting her innocence, she had taken it upon herself, as a lover, to choose an auspicious moment and write me her very first love letter.

Thinking thus, I took out the letter again and read it ten times, from top to bottom, savoring the elegance of her handwriting, the beauty of her script, the cleverness of her words. Rather than sit idly at home, I thought it better to go outside, to sit in solitude on the bank of some tank or canal, to gaze upon the beauty of nature and, in that tranquil setting, bring to mind even more vividly the beauty of my wife. Resolving thus, I stepped out.

By the time I returned home, it was quite late. Darkness had fallen thick and deep. The whole village was hushed and still. By the time I arrived, even my father had finished his meal. He was washing his hands and coming out as I stepped inside.
“What’s this, boy? Why are you so late? I thought you’d gone off to Narsapur and finished my meal too,” he said.
“Why would you need to wait for me, father? I didn’t go to Narsapur. I was just sitting by the tank in the village, lost in thought,” I replied.
“It’s not good to sit in such places till it’s this dark. Worms and insects come out at night, searching for food. They wander about…”
Barrister Parvateesam
“If that’s the case, we shouldn’t stay there,” he said.

“It’s nothing, really. As long as we don’t go looking for trouble, trouble won’t come looking for us, right?” I replied, lost in thought. Only then did I notice it had grown dark. I had been sitting there all this time, and suddenly, realizing how late it was, I hurried in.
“What was the serious matter?” he asked.

“Oh, nothing much. It’s about my future. When I went to Bhimavaram recently, my father-in-law advised me to come and stay with him for a while, learn a bit about the pleader’s profession, and then enter the field. I’ve been thinking about that all this time. Should I go? Should I give it up? Or should I abandon the idea altogether and stay here, helping you as your right-hand man? I sat there pondering all this for a while. I couldn’t come to any decision, but time doesn’t wait for me—it just kept moving on. By the time I opened my eyes and looked around, I realized how late it was, so I came,” I said.
“So, you haven’t come to any decision yet,” my father began to say, but before he could finish—
“Come, dear, I’ve served dinner. It’s already quite late,” came my mother’s call from inside.
As I was about to go in,

“The advice your father-in-law gave is quite sound. If you spend ten days with him, observing his work, you’ll get a sense of the ins and outs of the profession. Based on that, it’ll be easier for you to decide. If you feel like going, set out tomorrow,” my father said, getting up.
I went inside for dinner.

After that, I lay down comfortably, but my thoughts wouldn’t leave me alone. They continued to torment me through the night. With my mind weighed down by endless, unresolvable thoughts, I must have fallen asleep at some cock’s crow hour—otherwise, how would my wife appear in my dream? Not only did she appear—
“To come here, why so much hesitation? You’re going to come anyway, aren’t you? Still, I thought you might feel shy, so I wrote the letter myself…”

chapters.title: Court Cases
paragraphs: “You’re writing too, aren’t you! If I do the work you’re supposed to do, what’s the point of more thinking? Please, stop these pointless thoughts and hurry up. Are you still drowsy, or have you finally come to your senses? Our people are waiting for your arrival. Get up now. Even now, aren’t you men ashamed?” she said, laughing, and pinched my cheek, gave my neck a playful twist, and as I was about to get up, she scampered away as if frightened and startled. I truly woke up with a jolt and sat up. I quickly got off the bed and looked around all four corners. Where was my beloved? Only then did I realize it was just a dream. I flopped back onto the bed, chuckled to myself, and thought, “This is a warning to hurry up and get going.” So I got up and began preparing for my journey.
My mother noticed my haste and asked, “Are you leaving already, son?”
“Yes,” I replied.

She left without another word. As I was getting dressed, she quickly brought me some snacks and milk. By then, my father had already woken up and gone to the fields. I told my mother I was leaving and set out. She blessed me, and if anyone there tried to ask about my business, she would say, “Don’t say anything now or later—just keep quiet,” and, laughing at my reply, she slipped inside.

“If you’re so eager to bring your daughter-in-law home, you go ahead and bring her. I have no objection. I’ll take care of myself,” I said, stepping out into the street and setting off for Bhimavaram.

By the time I reached Bhimavaram, it was nearly two in the afternoon. My uncle had already eaten and gone to court. As the cart stopped at the gate, my Manohari was standing at the end of the street, looking out for my arrival. As soon as my cart stopped at the gate and I got down—
Barrister Parvateesam
She beamed at me like a blossoming lotus and settled down contentedly.

After the usual formalities and inquiries about each other's well-being, I finished my bath and meal, and then went to my room. There, I sat down, and until three in the afternoon, the room was filled with a ceaseless clamor. I can't recall whether she alone did all the talking, or if I too contributed, or even what exactly was said. At some point, as if someone had called her, my wife hurried inside, brought out some refreshments, and set them down before me. After finishing that, I changed my clothes and went to see my friend Raju.

The two of us wandered here and there, and by the time darkness had truly fallen and I returned home, my father-in-law was already searching for me. Both of us had dinner, and then spent a long time exchanging stories—this and that—whiling away the hours until late into the night, before finally retiring to our respective beds.

I was utterly charmed by my father-in-law's wide-ranging knowledge, his mastery of language, his worldly wisdom, and above all, his gentle demeanor. Thinking about all this, sleep eluded me for a long time. Only much later, without my realizing it, did the goddess of sleep finally take pity on me, and I slipped into deep slumber.

I woke up a little later than usual, performed my morning ablutions, and went to sit with my father-in-law, determined to observe his way of handling affairs, his understanding of the world, and to heed his advice. As I stepped into the veranda, my father-in-law, just about to sit in his chair, looked at me and said,

"Come, Parvateesam, sit down like that. In another two or three moments, our clerk will arrive, and trailing behind him, a flock of birds—some feathered, some not—will descend. Watch and listen to their conversation, their skill with words, their sharp wit. This is your first lesson. It will be both enlightening and entertaining. At some point, you may feel an urge to jump in with a clever reply, but restrain yourself. With people like these, self-control is essential," he said.
Even as he was speaking, the clerk entered, respectfully saluted his master, threw a mild smile in my direction, picked up a bundle of papers, and went into his room.

As they were about to leave, a group of three men arrived, followed by another set of four or five, each entering in their own little gang. They greeted us with folded hands, some lingering hesitantly, while the bolder ones made themselves comfortable on the chairs. Among them, one or two looked like big landlords, but the rest appeared to be ordinary farmers or agricultural laborers. Though there was a certain humility and apprehension visible in all of them, I could also clearly see another emotion flickering across their faces: “We are the ones paying this pleader, feeding him with our money, so why does he act so high and mighty before us?” That sentiment was written plainly on every face.

I supposed this must be a typical trait of the newly prosperous. In English, they call it “the new rich.” Just as my uncle had described, for nearly three hours, people kept coming and going—some seeking the pleader’s advice, some offering him their own, some arguing haphazardly, and some even quarreling among themselves. A few tried to speak with great arrogance, only to be utterly deflated by the pleader’s sharp words, their faces crumbling in defeat. Whenever the pleader revealed some subtle secret of the case, or when he unraveled in a single sentence a knotty problem that had left them banging their heads in confusion, all of them would gasp in amazement: “Oh my goodness! Look at that! This fellow untangled such a complicated matter in just one word. Did you see that? That’s why he’s a pleader. We’ve been breaking our heads over this for six months now—what fools we are! What kind of brains do we have, just lumps of clay! How could we not see something so simple? Let’s get out of here.” With that, everyone would rise to their feet.

Just then, the clerk appeared as if he had sprung up from the ground itself, briskly grabbing two of them by the arm and leading them into his room. There, with the gentlest touch—so that they felt no pain, as if extracting a tooth without the patient even noticing—he quietly relieved them of the pleader’s fee and his own customary charges from their pockets, and then released them. The two of them, rubbing their heads in confusion, muttered, “Come on, let’s get out of here, whatever happens. This is more than enough for today,” and as they made their way out onto the street, the whole crowd silently dispersed without even a word of farewell.

During those three hours there, countless people of all sorts—big and small merchants, employees, the unemployed, people of every stripe—came with their bundles of troubles, poured them out, received the pleader’s sympathy and advice, and left, satisfied. As my uncle said, it was truly both entertaining and enlightening.

After some time, while my uncle was bent over, writing something, I quietly slipped inside. Half an hour later, we met again at the dining table. Smiling, he asked, “Well, Barrister sir, how was your first lesson?”
“It was quite an eye-opener, uncle,” I replied.
“Very good! I thought you might complain of a headache,” he said, and after that, he didn’t speak again until the meal was over.

After eating, he went off to court. To pass the time, I picked up a book and began to read. Not long after, the book suddenly flew out of my hands and landed on the table opposite me. Startled, I turned around to see my dear wife standing behind me, looking as innocent as could be, as if she’d just been fixing something.
Ah! So this is her mischief, I thought. “What’s this, girl? Such naughtiness, with no regard for age or decorum? Who do you think I am?” I said, with a frown on my brow and a smile on my lips.
“That’s exactly what I was wondering,” she replied. “Who is this brave soul who’s become so bold at such an hour?”
“Don’t tease me. I’m glad, but please, have mercy,” I said.
“Who are you to command me so, sir? In our family, we don’t have the custom of going wherever strangers invite us, no matter how politely. So, you be the one to show mercy,” she said.
“Alright then,” I said, and as I stood up hastily, she was even quicker—she darted over and plopped herself into my chair.
“Mother’s daughter!” I exclaimed—and for the next fifteen or thirty minutes, we chattered away...

While I was whiling away the time with idle chatter, gossip, and banter, my wife suddenly sprang up, shook herself free from me, and dashed inside. When I looked up at the clock, it was three o’clock. “Why is this wretched clock running so fast? What’s the hurry that only this clock seems to have, which no one else does?” I wondered.

At one point, as I stood by the mirror adjusting my cravat, my mother-in-law quietly entered and stood there. She never comes in like this—what brings her here now, and why is she just standing there? I thought. “Please, have a seat,” I said.
“It’s all right, son. I just wanted to say a word in your ear, without my daughter overhearing,” she said.
“What could be so secret that even your daughter shouldn’t hear?” I muttered softly, just as I thought to myself. I don’t know if she heard me or not, but—
“Listen, son. The girl has come of age. So, I thought it would be good if you finished the formalities quickly and took her to your home,” she said.
“Is that so?” I replied.
“What does she know about all this? She’s just a child,” she said.
“That’s exactly my point, madam. She’s still young. If she stays here for another two or three years, she’ll finish her studies. By then, she’ll have matured properly,” I said.

“What’s this? Why does she need more education? Isn’t this much schooling enough? Even among our people, very few have studied this much. Why go for higher studies, son? Is she going to take up a job or rule a town?” she said.

“Just because someone is educated, does it mean they have to get a job or rule a town? She’s only going to rule me, isn’t she! As long as your daughter has an interest in studying, let her study, poor thing. As you said, another—”

Even after two years had passed, she still appeared to me as nothing more than a child. That is why I am of the opinion that there is no need to rush things. Only when both age and mind have matured is it truly appropriate to burden children with the responsibilities of family life. Otherwise, I feel it may not be such a good idea," I said.

"That may well be true. But for a woman, it is inevitable at some point, is it not? And after all, she is not such a little girl anymore. She must be at least fifteen by now. Tell me, how much longer can we delay? We somehow managed in our time, but the world will not wait, will it?" they replied.

"Let the world be! The world will neither save us nor condemn us. It is not the world that will marry off your daughter, but me. Therefore, we must look to our own convenience. If we sit around worrying about what the world thinks, we will never be able to take a single step forward, nor live a single moment in peace. So, I earnestly request you: do not stop your daughter's education now. Do not send her off to her in-laws just yet. This is my humble plea, and your wife too has expressed the same sentiment. I told her as much—let the poor girl continue her studies," I said.

She could not reply, only bowed her head and said, "What do I know about all this, my boy? Who knows what your father-in-law will say, or your father? We women are always in a hurry about such matters," and as she was leaving the room, my wife entered, carrying a plate of fruit. She glanced once at her mother, once at me, her eyes full of questions, then smiled, nodded, set the plate down, and was about to leave when I caught her by the arm and made her sit beside me.
"There are matters of utmost importance that I must discuss with you—matters far sweeter than fruit. Listen carefully and attentively," I began.
"Sorry, I have no attention to spare right now. I’ll come back later," she said, and in a flash, darted out of the room.

That evening, I went to see our Raju, spent some time chatting with him, then wandered all over the town until it was quite dark before finally returning home. After dinner, I sat down beside my father-in-law for a while...

He narrated the court stories in a light, easy-going manner. Without my noticing, this conversation went on for a whole hour. Afterwards, he dismissed me, and sat for a while longer, poring over some papers.

When I returned home, my wife was sitting primly beside my seat, passing the time by reading some book. After I sat down, we chatted idly for a quarter of an hour, maybe half an hour, exchanging this and that.
“In the afternoon, you said there was something very urgent we needed to discuss,” she reminded me.

What was that again? Oh yes, it was something urgent, but not exactly the sort of topic to be raised and discussed at this moment. Such matters might lead to some agitation and hasty decisions, so I decided to postpone that discussion until tomorrow afternoon. With that, the court too was adjourned.

But just as she was about to leave, that darling girl cast a slow, enchanting glance at me, then turned away with a twirl. I lost all self-control, caught her by both shoulders, turned her towards me, pulled her close—so very close—and embraced her tightly, planting a kiss on her cheek.
She laughed once, her face blooming like a bouquet of roses.
But this is neither the time for excitement nor for enthusiasm, I must respectfully submit to the court. And while I am at it, I would like to make another small submission to the court.
I am not yet a woman, nor am I a man. According to the laws of the body, I may be considered a person, but I have not yet developed a personality of my own.
Even though I stand before you now, at all other times, I am still a maiden.

chapters.title: Building a Reputation
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

I am wavering. My obsession with studies, which has gripped me from the very beginning, has not yet shifted towards family life. What does my future hold? Should I bid farewell to my education and embark on the journey of domesticity, or should I continue my studies for a while longer? I found myself caught in this dilemma. My mother, my relatives, and my circle of friends—all of them are urging me to do what everyone else does, and to do it quickly. It has become the popular verdict that my education will not redeem me, nor will it be of any use to me.

In this time of uncertainty, I was filled with both curiosity and anxiety to know what advice the court would give. With her head bowed, leaning slightly towards me, she stood there tracing patterns on the ground with her toe.
Listening to that girl’s words, I felt a surge of affection and pride for her. “Is this innocent girl speaking truly my wife?”—the pride swelled within me like the rising waves of the sea.

“Very well, the court has heard your plea attentively. After careful consideration, the verdict will be delivered tomorrow,” I said, pulling that innocent girl once again into my embrace, kissing her lotus-like face, and sitting there for a long time. Neither of us spoke a word. In that midnight silence, in that utter stillness, it was as if we could not even tell whether we were breathing. Time itself seemed to have forgotten to move, and after a while, Saraswati gently slipped from my embrace, left without a word, and did not look back.

I sat there, afloat on the waves of emotion that surged within me, forgetting myself until dawn. Leaning back, or rather, not even leaning back, I just sat there until some commotion in the house reached my ears and, seeing the light streaming through the window, I realized that it was morning and got up to attend to my daily routines.

I stayed in Bhimavaram for about a week or ten days. Every morning for an hour or so, and again for another hour after dinner at night, I would spend time with my father-in-law. The rest of the time, I would immerse myself in books. In the evenings, I would stroll through the village with Raja. This was my routine.

The plan. For these ten days of the week, my beloved would remain away from me. So, I decided that in another day or two, I would return home. I hadn’t mentioned this to anyone yet. That afternoon, after lunch, as I was sitting leisurely, Saraswati quietly approached me, perched herself on the arm of my chair, placed her hand around my neck, turned my face gently towards her, and said, “The request I made to the court a week ago—they said they would consider it carefully and give a verdict. So far, it seems their deliberation hasn’t concluded. Judging by their pace, it looks like they’ll hoist the flag any day now, without a word of warning. That’s why, if you’d share your opinion, I’d be delighted,” she said, running her fingers through the hair falling on my forehead.
I sat there, surprised at how this girl had already guessed about my impending journey, and for two minutes, I pondered how to broach the subject. She then grabbed my beard, lifted my face, and said,

“Well, sir, have you still not reached a decision? Why such prolonged contemplation? I’ll act according to your wishes. You needn’t have any doubts about that,” she said, pressing her cheek against mine.

“You’re able to read my mind and innermost feelings so easily, aren’t you? Yet, in this matter, you haven’t figured out what I think? Even before you asked, I had made up my mind. When I was about to leave for this town, my mother praised you and gave her opinion. A week ago, your mother too expressed the same view. I gave both of them my answer immediately.”
“What was that? Tell me,” she said, softly wrapping my hand around her waist and drawing a little closer.
“Oh, come now, how would I know all your thoughts? But if you whisper them in my ear, I’ll feel satisfied, as if I’ve heard them from your own lips,” she said.
“All right, then listen. As soon as I returned home from abroad, my father began searching for a bride for me. At that time, Raj—”
Barrister Parvateesam

I had clearly stated that I was not in favor of marrying an uneducated girl, and for that, I had incurred their wrath. But the moment I saw you, I forgot all my opinions and ideals. Not just those—I even forgot myself. There is some magic in your eyes. Your words seem to possess a kind of enchantment. That is why I have become yours. Now, having regained a bit of sense, as my old ideals come back to memory, I have resolved not to approach you until your studies are complete, to keep my distance. I am restraining, with great self-control, the strong desire to make you wholly mine. I have told this very thing to my mother and to your mother as well. I believe that our fathers too will abide by this decision. So, you need not be afraid of anything. Study at ease, with peace of mind. Forget everything except your studies. In the list of things to be forgotten, do not include me at all, my girl," I said, looking into her eyes.
To my surprise, a veil of tears appeared in that girl's eyes. Hearing my words, for the first time, I gained self-awareness.

After dinner that night, as usual, I sat in the office room for a few minutes, and after the usual small talk was over, without launching into the usual court gossip, my father-in-law, with some hesitation, broached the same subject with his daughter. I was surprised. Had the father and daughter already discussed this? Or did each want to clarify the matter for themselves? Thinking so, I hesitated for a moment, and though not as boldly as I had spoken to the girl, I said with some confidence that I was of the opinion that the girl should continue her studies for another two years, and that in the meantime, I might find a place to set up my practice and establish myself, so they should not hurry me or press me into haste.
I wondered what he would say, but with a sigh of relief and happiness, he said,

"Your decision is good, my boy, between us. That is my opinion too. I too know that my daughter wants to continue her studies, though she hesitates to say so openly. But you know how our womenfolk and relatives are—bound by old customs. Everything must happen as in the olden days..."

they said. “Alright, but let’s see,” and after chatting about the usual court matters for a while, they dismissed me. By the time I got home, as usual, my wife was waiting for me. The moment I told her the good news, she was overjoyed, and unable to express her happiness in words, she showed it with her hands instead.

The very next day, despite everyone unanimously telling me not to, I stubbornly set out for Mogalthur. As soon as I reached home, my mother looked at me with a questioning gaze. I suppose she didn’t get any answers.
That afternoon, during snack time, noticing that my uncle wasn’t at home, she asked me eagerly, “What happened, my boy? What’s the news?”
“What could have happened? I just went and came back as usual,” I replied.
She laughed, as if she didn’t understand my answer, and said, “Enough of your stubbornness, you and your ignorance. Poor thing, you know nothing. I’m asking about your business.”
“What business! Nothing happened there,” I replied innocently.
“You rascal, you,” she said, glancing around angrily, as if looking for something to throw at me.

“That’s not it, Mother. Now you know the truth. Why should I run around the house and yard, while you search for some stone or stick to hurl at me? My mother-in-law, just like you, had some thoughts. I gave her the same answer I gave you that day. She listened and let it go. She didn’t go searching for a stone to throw at me, nor did she try to beat me. To tell you the truth, even my father-in-law later praised me for it. Though a bit reluctantly, I suggested that if they allowed their daughter to continue her studies freely for another two or three years, and gave me a chance to start my practice and get settled, it would be best. He agreed that this was reasonable and was quite pleased with my intelligence,” I said, laughing.
“Pleased, indeed! A son-in-law to match the father-in-law, and a father-in-law to match the son-in-law—”
Barrister Parvateesam
Well, you’ve found a suitable son-in-law, whatever the means. But tell me, did my daughter-in-law also sing your praises?” she asked.

“No, mother, let’s call a spade a spade. She’s just a simpleton, an innocent soul of this very age, just like me. She’d say the same thing I do. Tell me, did you think she’d ask me what my opinion was in this matter—about our business here? Or that she’d ask me what you thought? What kind of fool do you take her for, mother?” I replied.
My mother glared at me in anger, said not another word, and stormed off muttering, “So this is what you’ve learned, after burning through all that money and traveling to foreign lands.”

I quietly added, “Mother, one more thing. Your daughter-in-law asked me to tell you something. She wants to study for a few more years, but she said, ‘Whenever you call me, I’ll come, mother-in-law. Please tell her that.’”

“Is that so, my boy? That poor girl, such a simple child. I thought as much—she’s just like me. All this is the handiwork of you and your father-in-law, that’s all. Anyway, why should I bother with all this? Your father is still around, isn’t he?” she said, her irritation subsiding as she walked away.

I quietly got up and went for a stroll towards the fields, returning home only after night had fully fallen. By then, my father had finished his evening prayers and was about to begin his meal. I washed my hands and feet, changed into fresh clothes, and slowly joined him at the dining line.
After dinner, my father sat on a bench in the courtyard and asked, “So, what news from Bhimavaram? Is your father-in-law keeping well? Did he say anything about your practice?”

As if I knew nothing, I replied as usual. Every morning, I would sit with him for an hour, observing the court proceedings, the methods, the people who came with lawsuits, their natures, the pleaders, the skill of those who could persuade others, the stubbornness of some—all of it I watched closely. Then, after dinner at night, for another hour, he would tell me about the cases, the complications in them, the tricks clients played, the lies they told, the troubles faced by the judges who had to deliver verdicts, and so on.
He would narrate everything in great detail, with empathy and a sense of fun. I said, “I thought these ten days of lessons were enough for now, so I came home.”
“That’s good. Very good. But it seems they didn’t ask you to start your practice in that town, or insist that you do so. Well then, did they say anything about sending the girl with you?” he asked.

“They did, sir. Both my father-in-law and mother-in-law praised me for it. They couldn’t help but do so. However, my mother-in-law immediately tried to send her daughter along with me. My father-in-law, though, hesitated a little, raised the matter of praise, and seemed to suggest that their daughter should study for a while longer. Still, he said, ‘You may do as you think best.’”

His words carried a hint of stubbornness, as if their opinion was the same as mine. Afterwards, the girl herself, expressing her own curiosity to study further, put the responsibility on me, saying she would do whatever I decided.
“Oh, I see! So the father’s stubbornness has clearly rubbed off on the daughter. So, did you come to a decision yourself?” he asked.
I replied, “It seemed reasonable that she should want to study a little longer. Meanwhile, I can start my practice, get established, and take care of other matters as well.”

“Ah, well then, what more is there for me to say? You respected my wish and opinion, and married according to the scriptures. For that, I am pleased. As for when to proceed with the next step, no scripture prescribes a date. Consider it yourself, learn the girl’s opinion, and whenever you both wish, I shall be happy,” he said.

Hearing those words, I was greatly surprised. His generosity, the breadth of his heart, his empathy towards others, his ability to understand their feelings—all these overwhelmed me. In my heart, I offered him countless salutations. Without saying anything further, he got up and left. I too went to my room.
I don’t know how long I sat there, lost in these thoughts.
Barrister Parvateesam

I have no idea whether I actually slept or not, or when I finally drifted off. But at dawn, I woke up feeling utterly at ease, free from worry, and surprisingly light-hearted. In this manner, two or three months passed by—doing nothing, thinking of nothing. This way of living was not good, I realized. I thought, if I went to Madras just once and observed the workings of the High Court, I would gain a thorough understanding of court procedures. With this in mind, I broached the subject with my father. He too encouraged me to go. Not only did he say so, but he added, “If you think it’s necessary for your profession, you must certainly go.” Within two days, he himself fixed an auspicious date for my departure, and that very evening, without my even asking, he handed me a hundred rupees, saying, “Will this be enough for your expenses, my boy?” “It will suffice. If I need more, I’ll ask you again,” I replied.

At the appointed hour set by my father, I set out, first traveling to Bhimavaram. There, I informed my father-in-law and my wife about my plans. Immediately, I went to Raju as well, and arranged for him to accompany me on the journey. Returning home, I called my wife and asked, “How is your education going?” She replied, “There aren’t any colleges nearby, as you know. Since our people didn’t want to send me alone to Rajahmundry or Kakinada, they arranged for three private tutors here. My studies are progressing well, and I’m feeling very enthusiastic.” Hearing these words, I too felt happy, and the very next day, taking Raju along, I set off for Bezwada.

There, I had a friend named Ramachandra Rao—a very easy-going fellow, with not a care or occupation in the world. I thought if I took him along, the journey would be more comfortable, entertaining, and lively. After much trouble, we finally reached Vijayawada at about two o’clock in the night. By the time we arrived, Ramachandra Rao appeared to be a very wise and capable man. From inside the house, some mantras could be heard. As soon as we pushed open the door and went inside, we saw, seated among the Brahmins who were chanting the mantras...
—That was Ramachandra Rao. On seeing us, he was so overjoyed that he even forgot he was wearing a dhoti tied up for ritual.
“Wait! Wait, don’t go away like that!” he called out, ignoring the Brahmins chanting mantras and his wife’s repeated warnings, and came running to embrace me.

“Hey Parvateesham! Where did you drop in from like this? And what’s this—you’ve even brought along a royal-looking fellow! If I’d known you were coming, I’d have seated you both as honored guests for the feast,” he said.
“What are ‘honored guests’?” asked Raju. I couldn’t help but laugh.
“Today is our foster father’s annual ceremony. He’s not one of those madly orthodox Vedic types. So, whoever sits as a guest, he wouldn’t mind,” he said.
Just then, the Brahmin reciting the mantras came running over.
“Sir, you must immediately pour water from two vessels, tie up your dhoti again, and return. There’s no more time to delay,” he pleaded, almost begging.

“What’s this—another bath, another dhoti? Our Parvateesham is a pure Brahmin! Moreover, he’s a true Vedic scholar, always pure. Anyone who touches him—man or woman—becomes pure, not impure. Why, in foreign lands, he’s purified countless English maidens! If you don’t believe me, ask him yourself. Or else, ask that royal fellow standing there like a statue. He’s even purer than him!” he said.
The Brahmin, at a loss for what to do, tried to suppress a laugh, but stood frozen, worried that our Chandra might get angry.

“Hey, you good boy, go take a quick bath! My stomach is starting to grumble,” I said, sending Chandra inside. Whether he actually bathed or not, he went in and came out in half a minute, having changed his clothes.
The household servant put our luggage in a room and politely asked us to bathe. By the time we finished our baths, our Chandra...
The Brahmin who was to recite the mantras was having some sort of argument.

“Look here, sir, I have no particular urgency. But you must make up your mind and stick to your word. I’m not the sort to obey if you point the darbha grass this way and then tell me to throw it that way, or twist your hands and ask me to turn my face away and bow. I have no use for all these words. After that, do as you please,” he said.

“No, no, that’s not it, son,” the Brahmin began to say, but was interrupted—“Alright then, do as you wish. Recite the mantra or not, as you please. If there are any irregularities to be done, you do them yourself, but don’t expect me to say one thing and do another. In fact, from now on, let’s do away with all these mantras and quarrels. You just come, eat comfortably, take your honorarium, and be on your way. If you want compensation for missing out on the mantra squabble, take a couple more rupees as honorarium. If that’s not enough, come once a month, have a meal, and go,” he said.

We were sitting there, bursting with laughter. The rest of the ceremony—meaning the meal for the participants, the offering of rice balls, and so on—was all wrapped up in ten minutes. They sent the Brahmins off and hurried the household to serve us quickly, pleading, “Please, the real guests, have mercy!”

Thus, we spent that day and the next in leisure there, and the day after that, no matter how much I wailed, “I won’t come,” they wouldn’t let me go. They dragged along Chandru as well, and we set off for Madras.

Arriving in Madras, we went to George Town and the three of us took a room together in a hotel. Three or four years ago, during the rush of my England trip, I had only stayed in Madras for two meals, but otherwise, I had never really seen or known Madras. Even then, I had found Madras thoroughly disagreeable. Poor Madras, it’s still the same—even now, perhaps the population has grown by ten or twenty-five thousand, perhaps business has increased a bit, perhaps the number of loafers wandering the streets has gone up. But all that’s resulted is more confusion, more noise, more filth in the streets, more shouting and quarrels. Other than that, no remarkable change is visible. Now, as for our stay—

There’s hardly any need to describe the hotel we stayed in. On the day I returned to India, I had felt sorry seeing the hotels in Bombay, thinking how half-baked and shabby they were. But now, this hotel was ten times more miserable than those. The stench, the torment of mosquitoes and bedbugs, and all sorts of discomforts—yet, people assured us there was no better hotel than this, so we listened and arrived here, thinking it must be excellent. Once we had arrived, there was nothing to do but grit our teeth and make peace with it—after all, what’s the use of complaining once you’re stuck?

For four days, with no other thoughts in mind, I wandered about the town, marveling at its oddities and festivities. There are indeed a few sights worth seeing here. Setting out at dawn, whenever we felt the need, we’d stop at whatever hotel we could find for a little sustenance, and then walk until our legs nearly gave out, finally reaching the seashore by evening. Sitting on the sand, feeling the cool breeze off the water, listening to the song of the sea—it was so soothing to the soul that we’d forget all the day’s exhaustion. Watching the thousands of men and women who, like us, had come to enjoy the shore, and seeing the long road running alongside the beach lined for miles with all sorts of horse-drawn carriages—such a royal parade of horses, especially the small, beautiful breeds called “Pegu” and “ponies”—we’d sit speechless, struck dumb by the sight, and gaze at it all in silence for hours.

After a while, we’d notice the carriages on the road and the people sitting below them beginning to head home, though we never realized when they’d decided to leave. After a little longer, we’d find ourselves the only ones left, and the sound of the sea would seem to say, “Aren’t you going to move yet?” That’s when we’d come to our senses and slowly make our way back to the hotel.

After four or five days of this, one day I spent wandering all around the High Court, observing the lawyers’ attire and mannerisms, watching the various types of people who came to court, and carefully studying the procedures of legal inquiry that took place there. I spent two days like this. Afterwards, I went alone to meet one of the prominent locals of Madras, the renowned lawyer Mr. Peri Narayanamurthy. I introduced myself to him and expressed my wish to learn about the procedures of the High Court here.
Barrister Parvateesam

I mustered up the courage to approach him, thinking I should seek his advice on where it would be best for me to set up my practice. I humbly expressed my request. He was very pleased and insisted that I stay for lunch that day, saying he wouldn’t let me leave otherwise. He spoke with me at length, with great warmth and affection, for two or three hours, discussing all sorts of matters. He earnestly urged me to stay at his house whenever I was in that town. I told him, as if confiding in a close friend, that I had come with two other friends and that I would certainly stay at his place the next time I visited. I left, reflecting on the kindness, affection, and genuine concern for others that is so often found among our elders—where else could such qualities be found? Brimming with enthusiasm, I recounted everything to my friends. They were very pleased.

After that, I spent two days in the town and then returned to Baladur. I had heard that a Telugu barrister named Tanguturi Prakasham was rapidly gaining fame there, so I decided to visit him as well. I went the very next morning. Compared to Sri Narayanamurthy, whom I had met earlier, Prakasham Garu seemed quite different. Narayanamurthy Garu was elderly, while Prakasham Garu appeared to be under forty. Narayanamurthy’s face radiated gentleness and warmth. But just seeing Prakasham Garu would make anyone feel a bit intimidated—his face was so stern and formidable. I had heard someone say that he looked like a tiger. His speech, too, was as grave as his expression. When he spoke, his voice seemed to come from somewhere deep within the earth.

When I arrived, he was busy looking through some papers. No clients had come in yet. As I walked up to his desk and stood there, he glanced at me sharply. I had just begun to say, “Namaskaram, sir,” when he snapped,
“Ah! Who are you, boy? Where did you drop in from so early in the morning? At such a young age, what criminal case have you gotten yourself tangled in? Though, you don’t look the type.”
I was left wondering what on earth I should say.
“Sit down. Anyway, you’ll have to stand in the dock later. For now, sit.”
Suppressing my laughter, I slowly took my seat.

“I haven’t come here to stand in the dock, sir. I don’t think that necessity will ever arise. In fact, I can confidently say such a misfortune won’t befall me so soon. I too wish to enter the noble profession and spend my life in it,” I was about to say, when, like a gunshot—
“Aha!” he exclaimed, sliding back in his chair and bursting into loud laughter. “What! You’re going to be a vakil? Did you study here? B.L. first grade? Why did you study law, my boy?”
“Neither, sir. I have passed Bar-at-Law. Among our Telugu people, I heard you are the foremost and most distinguished to have earned this degree, so I have come to pay my respects,” I replied.
Once again, he looked at me in astonishment at my answer.

“Oh, you rascal! Impossible fellow! You too are a barrister? Want to compete with me, do you? Well, let’s see,” he said, sliding back in his chair again, placing his pen on the table. “Now then, tell me—where are you from? Where have you set up your table? How long since you started practice?” He was about to ask something more when I quickly interjected,
“Sir, who am I to compete with you? Whoever tries would be like trying to climb a mountain,” I said. He smiled a little.
“Oh, that’s all right. You’re a sturdy fellow. Even if the bird is small, its song is mighty. So, have you started your practice here?”

“No, sir, not yet. I haven’t decided anything. I’m from Mogalturru, sir. So I’m thinking of starting practice somewhere nearby, perhaps in Narsapur or Bhimavaram. But I haven’t made any decision yet.” He smacked his lips and said,
“Let it be. What’s there in those places? No matter how long you stay or how hard you work, you’ll never get ahead there. You might make some money, but your talent, your intelligence—”

chapters.title: Legal Career
paragraphs: There is little chance to rise to the top and shine in the lower courts. Here, if you practice in the High Court itself, you’ll gain the acquaintance of eminent people and as much experience as you need. When you take up appeals that come here from the lower courts, you’ll have the opportunity to display your intelligence and wit, to show your sharpness of mind. You can think over your convenience and circumstances and make your decision. If you decide to stay here, you may, if you wish, join me as an apprentice. Later, after careful thought, you can make your own choice,” he said.
After another ten minutes of this and that, he dismissed me.

I returned to my lodgings in great delight and met my friends, to whom I recounted all that had happened. They too were very pleased and said, “Whatever it is, you should begin your practice right here. If someone like Prakashamgaru himself says he’ll take you as an apprentice, what more could you possibly want? Don’t even think of anything else. Living in Madras is inevitable for you. Whenever you need a bit of moral support or a cheer, we’ll come visit you from time to time—so you have nothing to fear.” Thus, both my friends unanimously gave me their assurance.
Since my business was done, I packed up my things and decided to take the night mail train for my return journey.

After I came back from Madras, time began to crawl again. Nothing came to mind, nothing passed the time. If I tried to talk for a while with anyone in the village, they would immediately say, “Tell us some stories about London,” and then bombard me with all sorts of ridiculous questions: “Do they have weddings there, sir?” “Do children and all get born normally over there?” “How do they know English as soon as they’re born?” “Did you come back without marrying anyone there?”—and so on, asking all sorts of silly questions, trying to trip me up and get me to reveal some secret or other, as if I were hiding some great mysteries from the world.

Their intention was that I must be hiding some secrets, and that, by asking clever questions, they would somehow coax them out of me. They would ask me all sorts of questions. Observing their attitude, the way they posed their queries, their restraint and skill, I realized that even if these people had no formal education or intelligence, they had thoroughly mastered the art of carrying their own burdens—and others’—on their shoulders, spending all three hundred and sixty-five days of the year circling around the houses of pleaders. This eloquence, this knack for asking any question necessary to get the answer they wanted—they had learned these things well. I resolved never to go anywhere unnecessarily, nor to indulge in idle gossip with anyone.

When I returned from Madras, I bought many kinds of books—some new, some old. Among them, I managed to find, though somewhat battered, the invaluable work by Savarkar, *The Indian War of Independence*. I also acquired books about Annie Besant’s Home Rule movement, as well as works by Indian luminaries such as Gokhale, Malaviya, Lajpat Rai, and Naoroji. In addition, I purchased a variety of literary and cultural books. With all these spread out before me, I began to read with the same dedication as I had when preparing for my M.A. exams, burning the midnight oil. The more I read, the more inspired and enlightened I became, and the greater my thirst to read further grew. Thus, several months passed.

But how long can one keep reading books that have no immediate practical use? So, once again, I was plagued by doubts—what should I do, where should I stay? These dilemmas began to stir within me. Meanwhile, without my knowledge, my mother had written a letter through my uncle, asking that my wife be sent here to stay with me for ten days. And so, one morning at dawn, she appeared before me quite suddenly. I was so startled that I stood frozen, wondering how the moon could rise at sunrise. As I gazed at her, dumbstruck, a sweet voice gently asked if I was still not awake. By then, I had fully regained my senses and was about to display my newly acquired alertness, but, sensing my intentions, the girl quickly ran off to my mother. The enthusiasm that welled up within me—
Barrister Parvateesam
Half of it cooled down.

After a few days, time once again gathered speed and began to race ahead. Ten or fifteen days slipped by as swiftly as fifteen minutes. Many times, I wondered how it would be if I wrote down my words and actions in order. With that intention, I would take up paper and pen, but all that came to mind were scattered, blossoming salutations, unopened rosebuds, unreachable depths, the blue lotuses that reveal themselves, the parrot’s chatter, the cuckoo’s song, and suchlike. I saw and heard many things, but none of them came clearly to mind to write or speak about. So, giving up in frustration, I would toss aside the paper and pen and slip back into my own waking dreams. As soon as those fifteen days were over, the person who had stirred up all those dreams and hopes vanished without a trace.
One day, at sunrise, only darkness remained.

For another fifteen days, with nothing else to do, I spent my time wandering along the banks of canals, tanks, and fields. By then, my mind had settled, and though my parents were not entirely pleased, I decided to set out for Madras. There, I arranged for lodging in a house at Mylapore, and resolved to begin my pleader’s profession on an auspicious day.

I say I made a firm resolution, but is everything else so easy and swift? As soon as I entered Madras, I went to see the renowned Narayana Murthy garu and explained that I had decided to stay in Madras for some time. Whether or not it would be permanent, I requested that he take me on as a junior in his office for the time being.

“Very happy, babu! I always thought you would come someday. Now you have come—very happy indeed. For now, you need not exert yourself too much. Come here every morning and sit until nine o’clock. Observe every case that comes in with attention. Try to understand each case thoroughly. Learn what facts are required for each case, and in what books you can find previous judgments in similar cases. After that, whatever ideas or opinions you have about the case, write them down on a piece of paper and, in your spare time—”

“At night, come and observe a case with me sometime. On the day of the trial, listen carefully to the arguments of both parties. If you patiently and diligently follow this method for five or six months, you will gain a good understanding of the procedures here. If you feel enthusiastic in between, you can even sit with me in court and help me with references or relevant points as needed. What do you say? Do you like this method? This isn’t the usual way things are done, you know. I am arranging this especially for you, so that you may quickly develop independent thinking and ideas. Otherwise, if you have any other suggestions, let me know. We’ll do as you wish,” he said with a smile.

I was utterly charmed by his kindness and affection. “This method is excellent, sir. As you said, I feel I will soon develop the ability to think independently in all matters. I’ll start coming here from tomorrow. I am grateful for your sincere care and regard,” I said, bowing and taking my leave.

That entire evening, I remained lost in a world of imagination. At dusk, I set out slowly, familiarizing myself a little with the bazaar and the streets, and by evening I reached the seashore. Thus began my life in Madras. In all the three years I spent abroad, and even after returning here, I never felt loneliness. But in this vast metropolis, I suddenly felt completely alone. There was not a single soul I knew to talk to. Even the clients who came to the office didn’t seem likely to become acquaintances or friends. I had become a householder now. I had a wife, my household goddess, who gave me encouragement and joy, and yet, while she was in one place, I was living like a mere log in another. How long would this go on, I wondered, as I sat on the seashore, struck for the first time by such thoughts. A certain sadness crept in.

After it grew dark, I turned homeward—or rather, hotel-ward—ate a few mouthfuls with sambar and rasam for company, and returned to my lodging. Until I fell asleep, which was well past midnight, my mind was troubled—not just a little, but quite a lot.
Barrister Parvateesam

I woke up early in the morning and by seven o’clock, I was present at Sri Narayanamurthy’s office. By that time, he had just finished his morning ablutions and was perusing some papers. A few parties were already seated, prepared and waiting. Narayanamurthy garu accepted my respectful greeting, blessed me, and with a gentle smile, invited me to sit comfortably. From that very moment, my career as a pleader began.

I sat there like a model student, observing every little thing that happened, paying close attention, and absorbing it all. That day, they insisted very strongly that I stay and have lunch with them. Afterwards, they took me along with them to the High Court in their horse carriage. Not only that, they even took me into the Bar Room and introduced me to many Telugu lawyers, a couple of English solicitors as well, saying, “He is a new barrister from London, a very energetic young man, destined to rise swiftly.” As they introduced me, everyone received my greetings and shook my hand as if blessing me. I felt a strange joy at this. That entire day, it didn’t feel like I was walking on the ground at all—I felt as if I were floating on air.

Just then, as previously mentioned, Pantulu garu came bustling in, caught sight of me, and said, “Ah! Well, Parvateesam, you’ve come? Are you going to stay here? Good, you’ve done the right thing,” and patted me on the back in a friendly manner. Narayanamurthy garu, seeing this, laughed and said, “Pantulu garu, I was just thinking of introducing this young man to you, but you’re already speaking to him like an old acquaintance. That’s a very auspicious sign for him.” Prakasham garu too laughed heartily and said, “Once he’s fallen into our hands, what’s this about being a young man? The moment he showed up here, it’s as if he’s left the minority behind. From today, he’s one of us. Isn’t that right, Parvateesam?” “Yes, sir,” I replied, not knowing what else to say.
And thus, my career as a pleader began.

For four or five months, I was so absorbed in this profession, in this apprenticeship, that I scarcely had time to breathe or to entertain any other thought. Letters kept arriving now and then from home and from my father-in-law. Though my better half continued to write letters, she had become a silent partner in my life, and, being absent, remained so in every sense. Regarding this matter, both my father and my father-in-law wrote to me two or three times, warning me that I should come as soon as possible and take my wife with me, so that she would not have to suffer there alone. But I hardly had the leisure to pay much attention to that issue or even to think about it.

During this training, I read countless books. I learned innumerable things. I realized that advocacy was not merely about words and arguments and emphatic assertions. I encountered all sorts of people and all kinds of temperaments. I came to understand, at least to some extent, how hard one must work, what rigorous tests one must endure, to practice law and to do justice to the legal profession. I also realized that if one could withstand all those trials and perform one’s duties properly, one could bring great distinction to the profession and even reach the highest pinnacles of success. It felt as if a vast, new world had opened before my eyes. Whenever such a vision filled my mind, I was overcome with boundless joy.

In these six months, I became a favorite pupil of both Narayanamurthy and Prakasham. From Narayanamurthy, I learned everything about civil court procedures. With Prakasham, I had the opportunity to learn mostly about criminal work. Both of them had attained the highest ranks in their respective professions. Among the two, Sri Narayanamurthy was extremely gentle and peaceful by nature. Prakasham was very grave and dignified. With a single word or a single glance, he could make anyone tremble. Even judges, no matter how eminent, were said to be wary of Prakasham. On two occasions, I myself witnessed proof of this.

One day, I believe it was a major forgery case that was underway. It was noon. Prakasham’s grave arguments were in progress. His words, like thunder, his arguments, like a lion’s roar, echoed in the ears of the opposition. At such a moment, as if it were a lullaby, the judge’s head...
Barrister Parvateesam

Drowsiness began to set in, and noticing this, Prakashamgaru, without even finishing the sentence he was speaking, suddenly slumped heavily in his chair. For two whole minutes, the entire court was silent. The judge, perhaps wondering if a lullaby was being sung, opened his eyes and, feeling a little embarrassed, said, “Let it be, Prakashamgaru, you may sit down.”

Prakashamgaru immediately stood up and said, “I only sat down because I did not wish to disturb the court’s slumber. Since your honor was taking a nap—” As everyone there burst into laughter, he picked up the sentence he had left half-finished and continued his argument. Until Prakashamgaru completed his submission, the judge, whether out of shame or stubbornness, did not move a muscle. Poor man! I realized then that even judges, who command so much authority, sometimes have to submit to such situations.

I heard of another strange incident of this sort. Either Prakashamgaru or someone else was arguing in court, and the judge began to nod off. It was the peak of summer, and for the judge’s comfort, a servant would be assigned to pull the fan. That day, even though the servant did not enjoy the same cool breeze as his master, he too was overcome by sleep. I learned that there are two or three established methods to wake up a judge in such situations without incurring his wrath. One is to “accidentally” drop a valuable book with a thud, another is to drag a chair back and forth to make a noise, or to have a client or servant let out a loud sneeze as if by accident. I heard that any one of these tricks is sure to rouse even the most eminent High Court judge.

That day, it seems, Prakashamgaru turned his attention to the fan-pulling servant. “Hey fool, are you sleeping too? What’s your job? Who do you think you are, a High Court judge?” he shouted. By the time he finished yelling, the judge himself woke up with a start, and, along with everyone else, joined in the laughter. “It’s all right, we are not really sleeping. Now and then, we pretend like this to give the lawyers arguing for and against a little rest,” the judge said, smiling. Everyone in the courtroom burst into laughter at once.
That day, I wrapped up my work and slowly made my way back to my lodgings. As I opened the door and stepped inside, I saw that my father—

The letter written by my father was inside. I took the letter from beneath, placed it on the table, changed my clothes, washed my face and finished my ablutions, then sat down comfortably and opened the letter to read it. Everything happened just as I had expected. The gist of the letter was this: It is no good for me to be here, eating hotel food and ruining my health, nor is it right that my wife should be pining for me back in Bhimavaram. Therefore, I must return home at once, make arrangements, and settle down with my wife in Madras. This is my father’s stern decree, and there is no choice but to obey it. Looking at that letter, I didn’t know what to think or what I ought to think. Whenever my father issues a decree, it is never something to be defied, nor is it something that ought to be defied. In ordinary law books, there is always scope for differences of opinion about any statute, but the decrees that come from my father’s lips are unique in that there is never any possibility of such a thing. Thinking along these lines, I sat there, silent and motionless, wondering what I should do. After a while, it seemed to me that his decision was quite reasonable. The reason, perhaps, was that, without realizing it, I myself had come to the same decision a few days ago. Well then, what’s the use of thinking about it any further? First, let me go and have a cup of coffee; perhaps if I lie down for a while, the lethargy will leave me and I’ll be able to make some decision. Resolving thus, I set out for our Iyer’s place. Even after drinking more than my usual amount, I still couldn’t come to any decision, so I went to the beach. With an empty mind, I sat there for nearly two hours. Alone, by the sea, the cool breeze blowing from near and far, the sweet nothings carried by the wind to my ears, the laughter behind those whispers, the comfort behind that laughter, and the happiness behind that comfort—all these stirred a strange vitality within me. Why had I forgotten all this for so long? Or was I only pretending to have forgotten, deceiving myself? With this thought, I started and looked all around. Everywhere, I saw only couples lost in embraces and kisses, intoxicated with each other—there was not a single solitary soul, not a pairless person in sight.
Barrister Parvateesam
No one could be seen except me. My state of uncertainty had finally left me.

As always, I came to the firm conclusion that my father's commands must certainly be obeyed, and so I quietly went to our pleader-guru. Feeling a little embarrassed, I asked him to grant me leave, saying I had some urgent business at home and would be away for a week or ten days. He looked steadily at my face for a moment, then, with a gentle smile, said:

"Well, let me ask you this. Has Achyutaramaiah's daughter not come to your house yet? Tell me, sir, whose fault is this! No matter whose fault it is, go at once, set that affair right as soon as possible, and after you’ve forgotten all about it and are left alone, remember—her name is Saraswati, isn’t it? Take her with you. In your profession, without Saraswati’s help and grace, it’s hard to rise up. Shubham Bhavatu—may all be well!"
I, now three times as embarrassed, could only bow in silence and leave, unable to utter a word.

The next day, without letting him see me again, I busied myself with all sorts of thoughts and errands, finally reached the lodging, somehow managed to put a few morsels in my mouth, made sure not to forget anything I had bought, and, floating as if on air, reached the station. For a moment, I thought I might simply float all the way to Mogalthur, but there was no avoiding the train. By the next afternoon, I reached Mogalthur.

By the time I arrived home, everyone had already finished their meals. I suppose my people hadn’t expected I would leave as soon as I received the letter. Whatever the case, my father’s joy was visible on his dignified face. My mother, unable to contain her happiness, stayed by my side while I bathed, while I ate, endlessly chattering away with boundless, tireless words. I wondered, does my mother ever run out of things to say?

For two or three days, without a moment’s rest, my father went to Narsapur, running from cloth shops to goldsmiths’ houses as if he had wheels on his feet, buying things, having things made, instructing others to make arrangements, and, without telling me a word, managed everything himself as if he had a thousand hands and a thousand feet, making sure nothing was lacking and all arrangements were perfectly in place.

On the fourth day, Surya, having finished all his meals and other routines on time, arrived at Bhimavaram by dawn, accompanied by a handful of relatives and four or five bundles tied up with cloth. Going to attend a wedding is usually an occasion for pomp and merriment, but for this particular affair, it did not seem right to invite relatives. No sooner had the letter arrived than they all came running, preparing themselves as if something grand was about to happen— nothing could be more inappropriate. This whole procession of people tagging along was not to my liking in the least; in fact, I found it rather embarrassing. What would they even do there? How would these people spend three days with nothing to occupy themselves? I pondered this for a moment, chuckled to myself, and drifted off into my own world of thoughts, dreaming the sweetest of dreams, until we reached Bhimavaram. Just outside the town, my uncle’s clerks and servants were waiting to receive us, offering their greetings and escorting us into the village. From then on, everything that was supposed to happen proceeded in proper order, without a hitch.
Barrister Parvateesam
My Doubt.
To be honest, I had no idea what had actually happened. They said it would be three days, so I assumed that was the custom. I, for my part, thought it would be just three minutes!

While the priest was shouting, “Hey, why haven’t the couple come out yet?” my Saraswati rested her head on my shoulder, her cheeks blushing red, giggling quietly. I was thinking, “We’re the only ones here, so why does he keep saying ‘the couple’? What a madman!” I even considered saying, “Sir, if you ask this and that, you won’t get an answer, I say!” but I didn’t.

Well, let’s leave all that aside. On the fourth day, after feasting at the wedding banquet, thanks to my father-in-law’s influence, we all squeezed ourselves into the four carriages waiting at the doorstep and reached Mogalthur by evening. Immediately, they arranged all sorts of refreshments for us. The elders and two cook-brahmins together, without any delay or shortage, provided us with everything we needed, including water for washing our feet.

Again, without anyone telling us or doing anything special, they declared that three days had passed. The relatives who had come were very pleased—though I don’t know why—accepted the gifts we gave them, blessed us with, “May you be blessed with noble sons,” and went their separate ways.
As they were leaving, I wondered, “Why are they all in such a hurry to go?” Saraswati, trying to stifle her laughter, darted inside.

I overheard my people saying, “Another week or so.” Well, without any sense of time, not knowing day from night, even forgetting about lunch and other meals, we lived as if in another world. That very evening, my father decided that we should go to Bhimavaram, and from there, it would be convenient to travel to Madras. He made all the arrangements, gathered all the things needed for our new household, and warned me to get ready for the journey.
Startled, I told Saraswati about this, and by evening, we had everything packed and were ready for the trip.

chapters.title: A Turning Point
paragraphs: ...we set off.

We stayed in Bhimavaram for another two days. My mother-in-law, with all her affection, packed us off with gifts, delicacies, pickles, and all sorts of household utensils and supplies that might be needed. She even sent along, to assist not just me but also Saraswati, a trustworthy relative from her side—a woman who was alone and struggling financially. (A great soul, as the saying goes, “Like Panuganti’s kumkum box, filled with sacred ash!”)

My father-in-law, in his wisdom, suggested in many ways that it would be better for me to postpone my Madras practice for a while, to stay here and gain some experience first, and only then set up practice in Madras. He said this would be much more convenient and advantageous. But I did not like that idea. From the very beginning, I had heard from many that if one starts in the High Court itself, one develops a broad outlook, keen analytical skills, and the ability to impress even the most eminent judges with one’s arguments and expertise. Not only had I heard this, but even in my brief months of experience, I felt the same. I managed to convince my father-in-law of this and set off for Madras.

For a week or ten days after arriving in Madras, I had to make do in the small house I had previously rented. Though it was cramped and inconvenient, I managed to pass the time there until I was able to secure a slightly larger house.

Every day, I went to court punctually and also visited our seniors’ offices, diligently attending to all the work assigned to me. Our Narayana Murthy garu was very pleased to see my enthusiasm and dedication.
“Babu, I am curious to see how you will handle a case independently. Why don’t you take up a case on your own now?” he said one day, handing me an appeal.
“This will come up for hearing the day after tomorrow. Read it carefully and understand it thoroughly...”

“Go ahead. There’s a subtle point in this case. If you can grasp it, you’ll win. If not, the case is lost. Don’t ask me anything about it. I’ll be right beside you, listening to your argument. If you fail to bring up the point I have in mind, then and only then will I write it down on a slip of paper and hand it to you. After all, we mustn’t let our client lose the case, right?” he said with a smile.
He continued, “I’m confident you’ll understand this case properly and surely mention the point I have in mind. What do you say?”
