“What’s there to say no? I’ll certainly try. I’ve already picked up some of your ways of thinking, haven’t I? So I hope everything will go smoothly,” I replied, took my leave, and went back to my lodgings.
The next day, instead of going to his house, I met him directly at the court. The same happened on the third day. The hearing was scheduled for the sixth day.

For the first time in my life, I stood in a court—no less than the High Court—arguing before learned judges of great intellect. As I rose, adjusted my gown properly over my shoulders, and lifted my head to look at the judge, he fixed me with a sharp gaze, as if to ask, “Who is this young man?” I bowed my head in greeting, and as I turned towards the pleader’s bench, I noticed quite a few young men in the audience, seemingly there just to see me and hear my argument. I smiled, half visibly, half hidden, bowed my head slightly in their direction, and began my argument.

The entire courtroom fell silent. I spoke in English, fluently and without hesitation, without any awkward sentences, as if I had years of experience. Everyone sat watching me, listening intently. After about six hours, we reached the most complicated stage of the argument. Just as I had practiced, with some effort and a bit of nervousness, I presented the two key points, concluded my argument, turned to the judges, bowed respectfully again, and sat down.

Narayana Murthy was overjoyed. The other lawyers’ faces all bore expressions of “Well done!” The opposing counsel spent about ten minutes countering my argument, but even I could tell there was nothing interesting in his reply.

As I was coming out, Narayanamurthy garu placed his hand on my shoulder and walked a couple of steps with me, saying, “You spoke very well, my boy. You expressed everything I had in mind, and even better than I could have. I am very pleased. You will go far in life.” He patted my back and went on his way. I felt like bowing at his feet right there, but in the midst of that crowd, I couldn’t do it.
Two days later, the court delivered a clear and unequivocal verdict in favor of our client in the case I had argued. The judgment even included words of appreciation for me.

Thus, for a while, every now and then, Narayanamurthy garu not only encouraged me by entrusting me with cases, but also began to send me some appeals—cases from our side—directly to me. At first, I wondered who was spreading my fame and sending me these cases. Later, I learned that my father-in-law had made inquiries about me here, learned of my usefulness, and, with trust and affection, was quietly sending appeals from his circle and his friends’ circles my way.

So, whether at home or in court, I became increasingly absorbed in legal matters and law books, spending most of my time with clients. For our Saraswati, this was no entertainment at all; she began to show a bit of sulking and mild annoyance. Therefore, as a matter of duty, I started making it a point to finish work in the evening and take her for a carriage ride to the beach.

The first day, she seemed to enjoy it immensely. But after two or three days, she said, “What is this, dear? Why is it so crowded and bustling here? Isn’t there any place in this Madras where one can sit peacefully? Don’t these Madras people have homes and courtyards? And what’s with all this—people who come here don’t just sit for a while and go home, but men and women are all over each other, hugging and clinging as if they can’t breathe without one another! What are these kisses? What are these flirtations?” She asked all this with great astonishment.
It struck me that, ever since coming to Madras, I had never taken her to the beach before. Absent-mindedly, I walked a little further…
Barrister Parvateesam

Guiding her, close to the water? Seating her beside me, drawing her nearer with every word, wrapping my arm around her waist—whether she realized it or not—pulling her ever closer, gently stroking her hair, and, pretending to be a little bolder than usual, pressing her to my heart, I kissed her deeply. At first, she was startled, but by the time the kiss was over, she regained her senses, jerked away, and tried to move to the other side, glancing all around.
“What is this injustice, sir? What will people think if they see us? Or do you lose your mind when you see them?” she said, showing a hint of annoyance.
In reply, I caught her chin with one hand, lifted her face, and kissed her deeply once more. When she tried to escape again,

“Don’t worry, Saraswati. No one here cares about our business. Everyone’s hands are full with their own affairs, you know? Here, in the moonlight, in the thick darkness, in the gentle breeze, couples sitting by the sea, listening to the ocean’s song—there’s a kind of excitement and madness that comes over them here, which is different from what happens at home. Now do you understand why so many people come here, and why they behave this way? Hasn’t the saying ‘Desire is natural even among the wise’ ever occurred to you?” I said.
Saraswati, without a word, smiled softly, put her arms around my neck, and lowered her face close to mine.
At home, she had resolved not to study anymore, and when I tried four or five times to persuade her, she said,
“Oh, stop it! I said I’d tell you, didn’t I? Let’s see if you can keep it up for four days. If you don’t like it, Miss, I’ll find someone else to teach me.”
“Let’s leave Miss out of this. If you teach me, that’s enough. But when you’re teaching me textbooks, please, I beg you, don’t bring up anything but the subject matter,” she said.
Day by day, my practice was steadily flourishing. Once, even Prakashampantulu garu entrusted me with a criminal case…
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 505
He told me to handle the entire case under his supervision. I was eager to do it, but hesitated a little and could not answer immediately. Pantulu garu looked at me slowly and said,

“What’s this, Parvateesham? Why are you hesitating? You mustn’t be afraid. I know you’ll do this case very well. I’ll also come and sit right beside you. Don’t worry about anything. Read the whole case carefully. The entire matter hinges on a single point. If you can grasp that one thing, you’ll strike the drum and emerge victorious. I believe you alone can handle this case. Read it carefully,” he said, and personally placed all the relevant papers in my hands.

His words of praise filled me with pride. Gathering up the papers, I took leave of him and returned to my lodgings. For four days, I thought intensely about nothing but this case, without a break. On the fifth day, the trial arrived.

I had to argue the case on behalf of the accused. In the lower court, it was proved that he was guilty and he was sentenced. My argument was that the crime had not been proven against him in the lower court. The evidence against him was neither solid nor strong, and even the lower court had agreed to some extent. One man convinced the court that he had seen the accused committing the crime with his own eyes. On the strength of this single testimony, the court decided my client was guilty and imposed a harsh sentence. Now, I had to prove that the claim of having seen it directly was not credible. The examination of the other witnesses was complete. I believe I managed to convince the court that none of them had told the truth.

Now, I began to cross-examine the main witness, putting him in the dock. As before, he began to speak with unwavering confidence. I slowly approached him and, very gently, asked if I could borrow his spectacles for a moment. Making small talk, I put on his glasses myself and, pretending to look at some papers, paused for a moment.
“Tell me, sir, when you saw the accused enter the room earlier, and then quickly—”
Barrister Parvateesam
“You said you saw him come running out quickly to this side, didn’t you?” I asked.
“I did see him, sir,” replied the accused, sitting confidently in the dock.
“How far was that doorway from where you were standing?” I asked.
“I can’t say exactly, sir, but it must have been about fifteen or twenty feet away,” he replied.
“So, is that about the same distance as between you and the jury now?” I asked.
“Oh no, sir, it was much farther than this. I was just coming into the hall when I saw that man running from the far doorway. The moment I saw his face, I was frightened, sir,” he said.
“Was it really that clear to see?” I asked.
“It was, sir,” he replied again. Not stopping there, he added, “It happened right in front of my eyes—how could I not see it, sir?”

“True, my friend. That’s my mistake. How can I claim it wasn’t clear when you say you saw it so plainly?” I said. “But look here, the fourth person from the left in this jury is sitting there reading some book, not even listening to your testimony. Maybe the court officials haven’t noticed,” I said, as if it were something unrelated to the case.
“That’s exactly what I thought, sir. I was watching him too, wondering why he was sitting like that,” he said, breaking into a gentle smile.
“Oh, you noticed too! Then there’s no problem. By the way, poor fellow, I forgot to return your pair of glasses,” I said, handing them to him.
“That’s all right, sir,” he said, taking them.
“You may go now,” I said. For a moment, the entire court fell so silent that you could hear a pin drop. Then, all at once, the whole courtroom...

A sound as loud as a great sigh escaped me. The prosecution lawyers were utterly defeated, and I collapsed into my chair like a heap of dung. In a matter of moments, the case was concluded. Within two more days, the court would pronounce its verdict—guilty or not guilty.

While I was still being examined as a witness, our teacher made a face as sour as a tamarind, and, brimming with joy, slipped out of the courtroom. On the day the verdict was announced, he too kindly stayed to hear it, and lifted me up as though I were his own son.

“Well done, Parvatisham! Didn’t I tell you that day, you would win? See, my words have come true. Splendid! I’m so happy,” he said, and as he spoke, all the lawyers present rushed over, congratulated me, and shook my hand.

Floating on air, I went home, took off my gown and coat, settled into a chair, stretched out my legs, and recounted the entire tale to Saraswati with the pride of victory. Saraswati, in a burst of enthusiasm, came over to me on one leg, tried to do everything Prakasham had done, and in her excitement, stumbled into my lap and gave me a tight embrace.
A minute later, we heard the call, “Please hurry, the snacks and coffee are getting cold!”
No matter how solemn the atmosphere in court, the moment you return home, such little festivities are a source of boundless joy. It’s as if life itself is revived.

Not just at home, but even in court, amusing incidents occur from time to time. Once, I had to argue in a magistrate’s court on behalf of a criminal defendant. The accused was an elderly man, who, at first glance, appeared to be a person of great stature. He confided everything to me with touching candor. I agreed to take up his case. He was a wealthy man. The case was this: while boarding a first-class compartment at the railway station, he had, with great skill, snatched a watch and tried to make off with it, but was caught in the act. Before he was apprehended, he managed to pass the watch to someone else. That was the charge against him. I toiled hard to prove that he was not the criminal, and somehow...
I managed to convince the court officials. The court dismissed the case.
That evening, just as I was about to get up for dinner at eight o’clock, this gentleman appeared before me.
“Why have you come here now? Are you planning to commit another crime before you even get home?” I asked.
“No, sir! I will never do such a thing again. I can never forget the help you gave me that day. I cannot even pay you any fee, sir,” he said, folding his hands with deep respect.
“Well, what talk of fees now? We never discussed anything like that in the first place,” I replied.
“My intention is the same, sir. Still, I couldn’t forget your help, so I came to present you with a small token of gratitude,” he said.
“I don’t need any reward. It’s enough if you stay careful from now on. That itself is the best reward you can give me,” I said.
“No, sir, my heart won’t be satisfied unless you accept this from me,” he said, blushing and trembling, and tried to hand me a gold wristwatch.
I turned pale. “Why do I need this watch? When did I ever earn such a thing?” I asked.
“It’s been four days, sir. The watch is from the case earlier today,” he said.
I was dumbfounded. “How did you get this?” I asked.

“What I said is true, sir. I wouldn’t have got it from you, but thanks to your argument, not only did the court believe I hadn’t committed the theft, but even I was forced to believe it myself. I couldn’t contain my happiness. I couldn’t keep this stolen property with me any longer, so I’m giving it to you as a gift,” he said.
Suppressing a laugh, I thought, “If I quietly take this and go to the police, the stolen watch will be found with the barrister himself…”
“What are you saying?” I asked.

“Oh, my dear child, what words you speak! He would never do such a thing. Trust me, he’s come to his senses now. He won’t ever steal again,” my grandmother assured me. Without waiting for another word, the boy dashed away. The next day, I sent the item to the Awachi police by registered post.

A few days later, a sorrowful tale turned into an amusing incident. A senior barrister had to argue an important case in the Appellate Court. On the very same day, he also had a case scheduled in the Munsif Court, which was thirty miles away. He called his junior, explained the situation in detail, and said, “I am quite certain the court won’t take up our case for hearing today. I’ll go to the other town and be back within two hours. If, by chance, our case is called in my absence, politely request the court for an adjournment, explaining that I am away on urgent business and will return in two hours. Please convey this request to the court on my behalf.” With these instructions, the senior barrister set off.

Afterwards, the court called three or four cases, but for one reason or another, none could proceed—some party or the other was unprepared. Finally, the judge said, “We must take up the case of the barrister who has gone to the other town.” The client’s representative requested an adjournment for two hours, explaining the barrister’s absence. The judge, however, was as unyielding as fire—there was no way he would grant an adjournment. “Absolutely not,” he declared. “These senior advocates think themselves so important, as if all judges are in awe of them. If he does not appear in court this very moment, I shall have to dismiss the case,” he said, barely finishing his sentence when a clerk came running in and handed him a slip of paper.

The judge glanced at it and, utterly shocked, exclaimed, “Oh!” He slumped back in his chair, speechless for two minutes. The few people present were alarmed, wondering what had happened. At last, the judge recovered, stood up, and announced:

“Friends! I am deeply grieved to bring you tragic news. The barrister who was to argue before you today, along with another barrister who accompanied him, were hurrying back here when, on the way, their car met with an accident...”
Barrister Parvateesam
We had just received the tragic news that they had perished in the accident. “May Lord Parameshwara grant peace to their souls. We offer our condolences to their families,” someone said.

We all fell silent, motionless. Not a word escaped anyone’s lips. This news was immediately conveyed to their homes as well. Their relatives, anxious to learn the details, came running to the court. Gathering around, they asked for more information, but as we explained that the court had not yet received any further details and that we would inform them as soon as we knew more, the two deceased lawyers themselves strolled in, arm in arm, chatting merrily and laughing heartily.

A couple of us wondered, “How did they turn into ghosts so quickly?” and speculated whether ghosts, too, wore black coats, gowns, and turbans. While we were still pondering this, the two ‘dead’ lawyers, noticing the stunned and frozen atmosphere, paused their cheerful banter and asked anxiously, “What’s the matter, sir? What happened?” Looking at the faces around them, they waited for an answer, but no one could say a word.

“We beg you, first tell us truthfully—are you alive or dead? We’re dying here in suspense!” someone exclaimed. Judge garu, utterly bewildered, turned pale and stared at them, while the junior lawyers recounted the entire episode in detail, as if stringing pearls together. The two lawyers collapsed into their chairs and burst into such laughter that the whole courtroom echoed with it.
Just then, a police inspector came running in, saluted the judge, and stood at attention.
The judge said, “What is it now? Why have you come again?”

The inspector, flustered, replied, “There’s been a mistake, sir. This morning, around eleven o’clock, we saw these two lawyers leaving for the neighboring town. We also saw them return to Madras in a car about fifteen minutes ago. Within a quarter of an hour of their departure, news came from a nearby village that there had been a car accident and that two lawyers in black coats had died in it. Poor fellows, we thought the lawyers we saw were the ones who had passed away, so we reported it to the court and rushed to the scene of the accident.”

chapters.title: Public Life
paragraphs: “Except for those who wear crores worth of jewelry, these pleaders are nothing at all,” he declared, “so please forgive our mistake—I came running here in a hurry just to say that!”
We all burst out laughing. These half-dead lawyers dashed off to console the wives of those who were mourning for them.
If I begin to recount such stories, countless incidents from my meager experience come to mind.

Court affairs are proceeding quite satisfactorily. Everything is going along with great enthusiasm. Whenever I have some free time, I explain lessons to Saraswati—just enough to prepare her for her exams. I keep bringing her the books she needs and handing them over. She is diligently studying. Her studies are her business; my court work is mine. Thus, without interfering in each other’s affairs, we pass our days according to a timetable, meeting only when absolutely necessary—no, not what you’re thinking, only for meals and such—meeting at those times, and running our household without any mishaps.

As Saraswati’s exams approached, she devoted all her time to studying. I took up the responsibility of preparing meals, or, if I was also busy, we would get food from the hotel for both of us. No matter what happened, or how the meals arrived on time, there was no end to criticism—how the food came, whether it was on time, and so on. Amidst all this, Saraswati completed her exams, not just somehow, but quite satisfactorily. Exhausted and drained, she slept for two or three days straight.

Without a care in the world, during those days, I would occasionally take a break from my court work, sit beside her, and offer her fruit or drinks—she was so absorbed in her studies, she didn’t even notice. Be that as it may, on the fourth day, she woke up fresh and light, singing like a cuckoo, smiling like a flower, and appeared before me in the morning with a plate of fruit, singing me awake.
Apparently, the news had arrived that she had passed the exams with flying colors in both subjects. That evening, when I returned home, the celestial maiden—

I heard someone singing, as if from afar. Curious to know what was going on, I hurried over and was about to knock on the door when, lo and behold, someone flung it open with a dramatic flourish, grabbed my hand, pulled me into a tight embrace, and before I could wriggle free, I looked up to see who it was—was this a dream, or some Vaishnava illusion?—and there she was, shaking with laughter, giggling uncontrollably.

“Why are you staring at me so pale and bewildered? It’s me! Your Saraswati, your better half. Hurry up and get ready. I’ve decided to take you to the beach today, and my joy won’t be complete until I do. Why are you still gawking at me? I came first in my class in the recent exams! As a token of gratitude, I wanted to shower you with every possible honor, and here you are, blinking at me like an owl! Where did I find this husband, I wonder! No wonder they say men are rare and precious. Now, come on, quickly change out of those clothes.”
I was about to ask, “What’s all this?” when Saraswati herself barged in from behind.

For a week or ten days, I was utterly at her mercy, unable to think of anything, barely able to breathe, as she had me wrapped around her little finger and dragged me all over town. She paid no heed to my words or my affairs, much like a stubborn client who ignores a lawyer’s objections.

That evening, when I returned home, the newspapers were abuzz with the news that the next morning, a political leader—Gandhi, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi—would be arriving in Madras by the early train. While I was studying in Edinburgh during the Great War, I knew that he had specially organized the Indian Red Cross to aid the thousands of helpless Indian soldiers being slaughtered. For some months now, the papers had been reporting that he was vigorously organizing the national movement. Without telling Saraswati, I finished my morning chores early and hurried to Central Station.

Inside and outside the station, the crowds were packed so tightly that not even a grain of sand could fall to the ground. Volunteers were making heroic efforts to line everyone up in order. Somehow, I managed to slip through the crowd and, pretending to be a leader myself, slowly made my way inside. There, quite unexpectedly, I saw—at a meeting in Edinburgh—
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 513

After making me recite a few poems, my dear friend Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya, who had become quite close to me by then, exclaimed, “Hey! Parvateesham, so you’re here! Why didn’t you tell me? Had I known, I would have come straight to your house! Anyway, you’ve come at the perfect time. Come on!” Saying this, he grabbed me by the arm and led me forward, introducing me in rapid succession to two or three poets and a handful of political leaders. As he introduced me with such enthusiasm, they all seemed unsure of what status to assign me, and I, too, decided that I must surely be someone important. So, they let me proceed along with Gopalakrishnayya.

At about nine o’clock, with a great commotion, the mail train arrived at the station. The moment its sound was heard, nearly a hundred thousand people waiting inside and outside the station raised their voices in unison, shouting “Victory to Gandhi! Victory to Mother India!” The sound thundered to the skies. Inside the station, thousands upon thousands surged forward with such eagerness that it seemed as if they might throw themselves onto the train. The police and the volunteer guards stationed there had a truly herculean task in restraining the crowd.

In this tumult, to ensure that the guest of honor, Gandhiji, was not harmed, his foremost disciples and the tall, broad-shouldered Muslim brothers, Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali, seated Gandhiji upon their hands. With about a hundred people surrounding them and others clearing the way, they slowly carried him from where we stood to his car. Gandhiji, seeing the crowds, received their salutations with a gentle, divine smile, like a deity come to life. The people behind followed him out into the street. The car in which he sat started off slowly, and until it disappeared from sight, the crowds continued their jubilant cries. Along with the car, the throng marched noisily down the road.

Gopalakrishnayya, I, and three other poet friends stood there in the station, lost in thought. For about half an hour, the victorious shouts gradually faded, and in another moment, the entire city of Madras was enveloped in silence.
What we heard reached our ears, and by then we had come to our senses and stepped outside.
“Did you see that, Parvatisham? Did you see what public adoration and popularity really mean? Someday, we too must become like that,” he said.
I asked, “Is this ‘we’ you speak of in the plural or the singular?”
He laughed and replied, “Neither—it's the dual!”
With nothing more to say, we went upstairs and each went our separate ways.

As I was leaving, Gopalakrishnayya said, “Parvatisham! Will you come to the beach this evening? There, we can listen to Gandhi’s national address. If you come a bit early, we can have a chat. I really must speak with you.”

“Alright,” I agreed. By the time I slowly made my way back to my lodgings, the dinner hour had long passed. My wife, anxious and fretting, was standing at the street gate, peering down the road, wondering what had become of me—where I had gone, whether I’d missed dinner, even missed court hours. Only then did I realize how late I was. I hurriedly dashed through the gate in two quick strides, threw my arms around my frightened Saraswati, and led her inside, recounting everything that had happened.
She listened to the whole story and, with a sigh, exclaimed, “Oh dear! If only you had taken me along, I too could have seen that great man!”
I replied, “Would you really have been able to see him? In such a crowd, you wouldn’t have been able to stand at all. Never mind, let’s go to the meeting at the beach this evening.”
By then, she had calmed down and, pleased, hurried me off to bathe, while she went into the kitchen to prepare dinner.

That evening, we finished everything quickly and by five o’clock, we set off for the beach. At the station, there was such a crowd, such a crush, that I thought, “If it’s like this here, how will it be at the beach?” But as we reached the vast seashore, no matter how many people sat there, it never seemed like a crowd at all.

Wherever I looked, there was nothing but a sea of people—hundreds of thousands, it seemed, and nothing else caught the eye. I wondered if all of Madras’s population had gathered here. Somehow, weaving my way through the crowd—dodging those sitting, standing, and slowly making progress—I managed to move forward. Gopalakrishnayya garu, who appeared to be searching for us, spotted us from a distance and came up to me.

“Come, Parvateesham! I’ve been looking for you,” he said, placing his hand on my shoulder. Then, glancing at my wife, who was clinging to me for dear life, he added with a laugh, “You’ve brought this poor girl into this mob too? Is she your wife? You’re a lucky man!”

My wife greeted him with a respectful bow, which he acknowledged with a blessing. Then, gently guiding us away from the throng, he led us to the water’s edge, a little distance from the crowd. “Sit down, there’s still plenty of time before the meeting starts,” he said, settling himself first. We sat facing him. Though there were many people around, it felt as if we had found a little solitude within that mass of humanity.

For quite some time, Gopalakrishnayya, with a grave expression, spoke at length about the current political situation, the Gandhian movement, and the future that awaited us. “We must all join together and continue this movement with mutual support. We must endure many hardships and bear many difficulties. This is our trial by fire. But we must not falter. We must stand united, as one, and show the world what Andhras are—our commitment to action, our courage and valor—they have not faded, nor have they been forgotten. We must prove this, my friend,” he said.

Just then, from a distance, we heard the commotion announcing Gandhi’s arrival at the meeting. Our conversation ended abruptly, and Gopalakrishnayya led us slowly forward, right up near the dais. As he seated us comfortably, everyone around looked at us in surprise, wondering who we were.

That day’s speech is one I will never forget, not in this life or the next. Among tens of thousands—perhaps hundreds of thousands—of people, there was no sound but the collective breath of the crowd and the distant roar of the sea. Not another sound could be heard. Gandhi’s voice alone rang out, clear as a temple bell. Not a single syllable was lost...

The entire audience sat spellbound, listening without so much as a whisper. That day, I truly understood what it meant for a gathering to be under a spell. When his speech ended, not a single person present felt that it was over. It was as if everyone suddenly awoke from a trance. In unison, the crowd erupted into thunderous cheers and applause, swept away in ecstasy for two or three minutes. Amidst that uproar, it seemed even the roar of the ocean had forgotten itself and sat quietly, listening.

Before the applause had even died down, while the crowd was still in a frenzy, Gandhi was quietly escorted away and helped into a car. Only after he had left did people regain their senses, cease their clapping, and begin to exclaim in loud voices, “Oh my!” “What a speech!” “How wonderfully he spoke!” “How did he do it?” The entire seashore buzzed with such exclamations as people began to disperse towards their homes.
We both stood there, unmoving, until the crowd had thinned a little. Just then, Gopalakrishnayya came searching for us. “So, here you are!” he said, coming up to us.

“Parvateesham, how are you? He has made our duty clear. With Gandhi, there’s no room for thought or decision. Do you remember Tennyson’s words—‘Theirs not to reason why, theirs but to do and die’? That’s the warning! Gandhi, that divine destroyer, has put us in the same position. Now we must gird our loins, renounce everything, take up arms, and follow him. Come on, let’s go. Tomorrow, let’s meet here again and talk it over,” he declared, as if my reply was unnecessary, raising his head high, chest out, one hand behind his back, swinging his stick with the other, and striding away with great, dramatic steps.

The two of us looked at each other’s faces. Since there was no vehicle to be found, we resigned ourselves to walking home. All the way, Saraswati—who was usually so lively, always chattering, laughing, and making merry—walked beside me in utter silence, holding my hand, not uttering a word, right up to our doorstep. Even after we entered the house, she made no attempt at conversation.
This silence troubled me a little.
“What’s with this silent pose? Is it an ornament of error or a blemish?” I asked.

“I am neither an ornamented beauty nor a painted one. What you see on my face is the natural blush of a lotus in bloom, the blue of a fresh water-lily, the golden sheen of pure gold—believe me! This is not some cheap, painted decoration. I’m telling you the truth,” she said.
“Really! Well then, let me see properly,” I replied. Grabbing both her shoulders, I turned her to face me.

That evening, recalling Gopalakrishnayya’s suggestion, I went to the place where the meeting had been held the previous night. He was already there, waiting for me. Spotting me from afar, he approached with great delight, placed his hand on my shoulder, led me to the water’s edge, and made me sit beside him.

We spent several hours discussing various matters concerning the future of India—about Home Rule, Swaraj, Congress, and so on. In the end, we concluded that Gandhi’s path was indeed our only refuge. By then, it was quite late, so we both stood up and prepared to head home. I insisted repeatedly that he come to my house, but he politely declined. “I promise, I’ll come next time,” he said, deftly escaping the invitation.
“I’ll come, don’t worry! But you must settle your affairs quickly and enter the field as soon as possible—there’s no avoiding it,” he said as he left.

I walked home slowly, counting my steps, lost in thought. My wife was waiting for my return. Seeing my grave silence, she seemed a little worried, but didn’t rush to fuss over me. By the time I had washed my feet and changed my clothes, she called out, “Come, let’s eat,” and as soon as I heard her invitation, I forgot my silence and became my usual self again.

We finished our meal and the usual after-dinner banter quickly, set aside the silly songs and playful teasing, and began discussing what Gandhi had said yesterday. We debated some of the points Gopalakrishnayya had clarified today, critiqued them, and spoke as if we were great political leaders ourselves. Then I asked, “So, what do you say? What is it that we must do?” I turned to Saraswati for her opinion.

chapters.title: Politics
paragraphs: “Why do you ask me that? Why do you even have such a doubt? For me, there is only one path. That is the royal road—the very path shown by Gandhiji. There’s nothing left for us to think about. He has already thought of everything for us. Our job is not to think, but only to follow,” she declared, with great courage, without the slightest hesitation or shyness.
“Well then, let’s leave it to my own efforts,” I said, slowly leaning back on the bed. That devoted wife followed me.

For some months, without a moment’s rest, neglecting even my court cases, I wandered about like a man possessed. In villages and towns, at gatherings and meetings, I began to speak to the people about our country—its former glory, its present misery, and the administrative systems that had brought about this decline. I strove to awaken the people, to open their eyes. Day by day, my campaigning grew more intense. Old and young alike, in droves, flocked to these meetings. They began to listen with great enthusiasm, and their eager attention spurred us on even more. Not only did I neglect my household duties and my court work, but I even began to feel as though I was neglecting my own—

One day, I was giving a speech at a meeting in a hurry, when I began to feel a headache and feverish. By the time I returned home, Saraswati was not there. She had locked the door, assuming I wouldn’t return until ten at night, and had even taken the key with her. At a loss for what to do, I went to a hotel, had some coffee, and then spent time at a nearby friend’s house until nine o’clock. Then, I slowly made my way back to my lodgings. When I arrived, the lock was still firmly in place. I didn’t have the patience to go anywhere else, so I simply sat there.
After about half an hour, Saraswati came bustling in. She was startled to see me sitting on the steps, and rushed over to me, placing both her hands on my shoulders and peering into my face.
“Oh dear, what’s this? How long have you been sitting here? Why are you like this?” she asked, touching my cheek and forehead. “Oh no, you seem to have a fever!”
“All right, all right! First, open the door,” I said.
“Oh, my foolishness!” she exclaimed, hurriedly unlocking the door. After lighting the lamp, she came back to the porch, took me by the hand, and led me inside. She made me lie down on the bed.
“The moment you lie down, I’ll bring you some coffee,” she said, and dashed inside.

I didn’t even have the energy to protest, so I lay there in silence. True to her word, in five minutes she returned with a steaming cup of hot coffee and handed it to me. She sat beside me, her hand resting on me, gazing at my face with concern, not saying a word until I finished the coffee. As soon as I finished, she took the cup from my hand and said, “What a mistake I made! Poor thing, how long you must have been sitting here, suffering. I came late, thinking you wouldn’t be back until ten o’clock,” she said, bowing her head as if she’d committed some crime.
“It’s all right, never mind. But where did you go, anyway? You never mentioned it,” I said. She managed a faint smile without lifting her head.
“I am doing the same work as you,” she said. I was startled. Saraswati grabbed both my shoulders.
“What is this?” I asked anxiously.
“Nothing at all. Why are you getting so flustered? Lie down first. I’ll tell you,” she said, moving to the other side and making me lie down.
“Well then, start your lullaby,” I said.
“I’ll sing, but you mustn’t fall asleep. And don’t be in a hurry for anything else, either.”

“Just a few days after you started your campaign, some of the ladies from our Women’s Association came to me. They said that women, too, should not stay behind the men, but must come forward, spread awareness, and awaken all of womankind from this slumber. Only if women also join the political field and the struggle for self-rule alongside men, can our ideal be achieved. They said the responsibility to bring women into the sphere of action lies greatly upon you, as you are educated and a graduate. We greatly need the help of people like you. They insisted that I must join them. They didn’t even give me time to ask your permission. So, from that day, I have been going from village to village with them, carrying on the campaign,” she said.
I sat there, frozen, unable to reply, staring at her, pale as a ghost.

“Why are you staring at me like that? Do you think what I did was wrong? Was it a mistake? Say something quickly—your silence is very troubling. Tell me, am I doing something wrong? I am your better half, after all. If we both go our separate ways, how will that look? I never thought you’d be so narrow-minded. What do you say? What is your intention?” she asked, looking straight at me.
“Oh, you crazy woman! Don’t try to convince me with that whole lecture now. I have no patience to listen to it. I’m not at all saying that what you did was wrong. My...
I was delighted, thinking, “Is Saraswati really this lively, this grand? There seems to be no limit to my happiness.” Suddenly, she drew herself close to me...
“Wait, you have a fever, don’t you? I’ll go get you some medicine,” she said, and leapt off the bed in a hurry. I lay back, laughing to myself.

By the time she returned, my fever had subsided, but I was still feeling quite weak and didn’t venture outside. I had no mind for court work either. Torn between the urge to oversee the cooking and the anxiety about what I might need or how I was feeling, Saraswati fluttered back and forth between the kitchen and my room. Meanwhile, I managed to fall asleep for a while.
I must have slept until about eleven o’clock.

When I awoke, my wife was at my side. As I bathed and sat down for lunch, a letter arrived from home—my uncle had written. I have no idea how he found out, but he seemed to know my entire daily routine here. That’s why, rather sternly, he wrote that “it isn’t good for us to live so far apart; it would be better if you set up your practice in Narsapur or Bhimavaram, and you should make arrangements for that immediately.” That was the gist of his letter.

That afternoon, the two of us read my uncle’s letter two or three times, pondering separately and together about what our duty was. We spent the whole evening in heated discussion, weighing our options.

After some time, Saraswati said, “Given our current situation, it doesn’t seem possible to continue our plans here and also support your profession. So, let’s choose an auspicious day, set up our base in Narsapur or Bhimavaram, and continue our work from there. This campaign might be more needed in our own region. If we do this, even if it curtails our freedom a bit, your uncle will be somewhat satisfied, and the results of our efforts may be greater.”

Though I hadn’t fully made up my mind until then, I found myself agreeing with her. Now that we were of one mind, we said, “Jai Parameshwara!” and began making preparations to leave this place on an auspicious day.
Barrister Parvateesam

We resolved that it was absolutely necessary to raise the flag only after carefully considering the day. Here, after wrapping up all our activities, court affairs, and everything else, we managed to return home in less than a month. My mother and father were overjoyed. After a few days, we convened another small round-table meeting and decided that, from now on, we would set up our table right in the heart of Bhimavaram.

With that decision, one fine morning, we arrived in Bhimavaram, appearing before my mother-in-law and father-in-law without any prior notice. Both of them welcomed us with a mixture of joy and surprise. After two or three days of rest, my father-in-law, one day, began to inquire about my life in Madras, my practice there, and other such matters, one after another. So, like a string of pearls, I narrated everything that had happened, and I candidly explained the reason for my return as well. They were very pleased—not just because we had come, but also because they felt the public awareness campaign we had started in Madras was indeed a worthy endeavor. Hearing their approval, I too felt a renewed enthusiasm.

A couple of days later, I was delighted to discover that my father-in-law, without giving up his own practice, had also become involved in such activities. I was considering setting up house elsewhere, but my father-in-law would hear nothing of it. He insisted, quite forcefully, that I must stay right there with them. So, inevitably, I set up my board right next to his and began my domestic life there.

Unexpectedly, after four days, it became clear that my father-in-law had more or less retired from practice. However, as soon as another table appeared there, his former clients, unable to let him go, hoped that I would handle their cases instead. My father-in-law, agreeing with them, persuaded me to take on all those affairs. Thus, there was no escape from getting entangled in this game once again. Even there, I tried to keep things as manageable as possible and continued to participate in the public awareness campaign.
Saraswati, meanwhile, became completely independent and began devoting all her time to the campaign, both alongside her father and with the women’s association.
Our campaign grew day by day. Watching it unfold—

It was astonishing. In both villages and towns, no one quite knew what had awakened in the people, what fervor had gripped them, or what transformation had come about. Yet, without any clear hopes or desires, without knowing what consequences or results might follow, millions upon millions of people plunged into this movement. The haves relinquished all they possessed, and the have-nots, without a moment’s hesitation, were ready to embrace even greater deprivation. Those who once chanted “Victory to Lord Parameshwara!” seemed to have forgotten that phrase, and now, with the cry of “Victory to Gandhi!” on their lips, surged forward in droves. Witnessing this unprecedented upheaval—something no one had ever imagined—left the whole of India in a state of wonder, amazement, and shock.

Meanwhile, the hearts of the authorities began to race like runaway trains. Fear and trembling seized them all. Dreading how far this might go, they decided it would be best to nip it in the bud as soon as possible, and so they set their efforts in motion. But just as they began, they realized that what they had intended to suppress had already grown beyond their control, and they were forced to declare martial law. This only served to further inflame the people, who now became even more agitated and furious.

At this very moment, Gandhi’s words rang out: “The antidote to anger is not more anger, but peace. No matter how much injustice the authorities commit, no matter how much brute force they use, the people must remain calm. We must not cultivate a spirit of retaliation. However many blows we may suffer, however many lives we may lose, we must never abandon peace.” This exhortation worked wonders.

Among such a vast and diverse population, not a single person acted rashly or resorted to violence. No matter how tense the situation became, everyone moved with remarkable patience and without harboring any hatred. We who witnessed this were filled with amazement. We wondered where such immense strength had come from, how it had arisen from a single man’s words. If Gandhi, so endowed with this power, could put every one of his words into practice, and if the movement he had launched continued in this way, there was no doubt in our minds that Swaraj would be achieved within the very year he had promised.
Within just a few months of the movement’s inception, whether one had joined it or not, throughout the length and breadth of India—toward the authorities and the punishments they meted out...

The reverence and fear that had clung to authority for two or three centuries vanished in an instant. Both sides firmly believed that this was the first victory achieved in the non-violent struggle initiated by Gandhiji. Otherwise, how could it be that a simple, ordinary woman like Duvvuri Subbamma—a helpless widow—was brought to court by the police, accused of conspiring to overthrow the British Empire, upon which the sun never set? In a courtroom packed with people, surrounded by police, how could she, standing before the District Magistrate, boldly remove her veil, display her bald head, and address the Collector, “Both our heads are bald. Just because you’re wearing robes and sitting on that high seat doesn’t make you any more powerful than me. You can do nothing to me,” with such confidence?

The words she spoke sent a jolt through the hearts of the people. The courtroom trembled with a mix of fear and tears of joy as the crowd erupted in slogans: “Victory to Gandhi! Victory to Duvvuri Subbamma! Down with the foreign government!” Such scenes were enacted thousands of times. Our eyes and hearts were moved to tears. The officials’ hearts sank. When such scenes occurred daily, in every town, in countless numbers, the authorities lost their wits, became enraged, and began senseless acts of oppression. Every day, hundreds of people were arrested, declared guilty in court, and sent to jail. There, they were subjected to all kinds of tortures, and in turn, they staged satyagrahas resembling revolts. Because of such incidents, the authority of the officials became a laughingstock day by day.

Wherever you looked—on any street, at any crossroads, in any market square, inn, or temple—wherever people gathered, the only topics of conversation were: how many were punished that day, which leaders gave speeches, how the police tortured people, where fights broke out, and so on. No other kind of conversation reached the ears anymore. The police had no respite anywhere, no time even to sleep. Poor fellows, in this chaos, even my own uncle: in some village, he was arrested and by evening—

The news that Achyutaramaiah had been brought to Bhimavaram spread throughout the town. Before long, not only the entire population of the village but also people from neighboring villages—forty to fifty thousand strong—gathered around the police station. There was a great commotion as everyone clamored to see Achyutaramaiah. The police constables declared that it was not possible. “Let’s see why it’s not possible!” shouted the crowd, and all at once, they surged forward ten paces. The police were seized with fear. Some among the crowd tried to calm the others, urging them not to act rashly.

Just then, a police inspector rushed inside and brought Achyutaramaiah out to present him before the people. The crowd erupted in jubilant cheers. They shouted that Achyutaramaiah should be sent home for the night, and that they themselves would take responsibility for presenting him in court the next day. The police began to respond, but Achyutaramaiah stepped forward and said:

“It is not your duty to ask that I be sent home, nor is it their duty to send me. That would be against the law. What does it matter if I sleep at home or in the police station for this one night? Tomorrow, the judge will deliver his verdict in court, and if I am found to have acted unlawfully, I shall have to spend some months or years in prison anyway. That is when I must resign myself to a bed on the ground. You must not be hasty. You must remain calm. Remember, this is only the first step in our movement. Whether necessary or not—no, even if it is necessary—you must not give in to anger. Ours is a movement of peace. The very first principle we must hold to is that we rise above all attachment and aversion. Never, under any circumstances, must we forget this. Go home peacefully and sleep well. From tomorrow, one of you, or ten, or a hundred, must take my place and continue this struggle. Go now. The Lord is with us. Go on, then,” he said, folding his hands in salutation.
With that, the entire crowd dispersed in silence, without a murmur. “You have saved us, sir!” said the police, bowing once, and led Achyutaramaiah back inside.
Such scenes had become a part of our daily routine.

Now, with Achyutaramaiah having gone to jail, the court work increased so much that I could barely catch my breath. Even so, I continued my propaganda activities in between, whenever I could steal a moment. And then there was Saraswati—sometimes, even at night, she would not be at home; wherever you looked, there she was! Wherever there was a gathering, she would be there, speaking with the mesmerizing force of a modern-day Bhadrakali, inspiring, agitating, and stirring up the crowd. Watching her, I would be left astonished and envious, wondering why I was stuck running around courtrooms instead of matching her stride for stride. Was this my fate? The thought tormented me.

It’s true that, at least in court, I had earned a reputation for being clever, good-natured, and a just advocate. That reputation was well-deserved, too. Yet, my heart was never truly satisfied. This dissatisfaction only grew with each passing day. The main reason for it was the nagging feeling that what happened in court was not justice at all. Even back in Madras, during my early days practicing at the High Court, this thought would trouble me.
One day, emboldened, I said to Judge Jaddi, an I.C.S. officer, “Sir, it seems to me that there is more injustice than justice happening in these courts.”

He did not take offense. Instead, he smiled and replied, “What you say may well be true, Parvateesham! In these courts, we try to ensure that our judgments do not violate the laws and rules set by certain great men, but to say that what we deliver is pure justice or righteousness—that is difficult indeed.”
(We administer law, sir, not justice.) Hearing those words, I felt as if I ought to prostrate myself before him.
He laughed and said, “I don’t think you’ll be able to continue in this profession for long. Good luck and God bless you,” and patted me on the shoulder as he walked away.
While these thoughts weighed on me, I noticed that among my fellow lawyers, many of them...

The second reason, I believe, for my growing disinterest in this profession is the qualities, the rivalries, and the animosities that exist among those who practice it. In court, the lawyers for the plaintiff and the defendant may bark at each other like dogs, but once outside, they are expected to forget all enmity and resume their friendships. However, my own experience has often contradicted this expectation. Since my father-in-law had retired from active practice, for reasons unknown, a certain number of people developed a natural fondness for me. Because of this, within just a few months of my arrival in Bhimavaram, I began to receive more cases and better fees than others. I never considered this to be my own merit. I always attributed it to some stroke of luck or perhaps just chance. But among my fellow advocates, quite a few began to show signs of irritation towards me.

Once, both my court work and my outside engagements increased so much that I was unable to get up from bed for several days in a week. I could not attend to any work at all. I was suffering terribly from a persistent cough and fever. Somehow, by the grace of fate, I survived and recovered. I had to request adjournments for many important cases. In this situation, one day, a close acquaintance of my father-in-law—a very good friend and an important client, Raja Garu—came to see me early in the morning. He had a very important case pending in my hands, which had been delayed due to my illness. I assumed he had come to check on my health, given the circumstances.

After a while, he got up to take his leave. I too stood up and walked with him to the gate, saying, “Within two or three days, I’ll be back in court, and within a week or ten days, we’ll have your case finished. Everything is going in our favor. You need not have any doubts.”
“Very well,” he said, but instead of leaving, he stood there motionless for another moment.

“What is it, Raja Garu? It seems you came for something else as well. You seem to be hesitating with some doubt in your mind. Truly, you need have no doubts. Whatever your opinion may be, please tell me frankly—”

chapters.title: Final Chapter
paragraphs: Barrister Parvateesam

I said, “You may say so.” Even so, after a moment’s thought, he continued, “I have no doubts at all, sir. I have complete faith in you. But just yesterday, or perhaps the day before, another pleader in this very town—one with both name and clients—has been trying for a long time to bring me into his circle. Now, he has launched a new weapon. He told me that you are in very poor health, that you are suffering from advanced tuberculosis, and that you will not live more than two or three months. He suggested it would be wise for me to entrust all my cases to someone else before time runs out—in other words, to entrust them to him. I was shocked. I was stunned to realize that even such senior people could harbor such base thoughts. I was deeply troubled. I came to tell you all this, but I do not believe the health report he gave me about you, not even for a moment, sir.” With a respectful bow, he left without waiting for a reply.
I came inside and lay down for a long time, pondering the nature of mankind.

Two days after this incident, when I appeared in court, that senior pleader was astonished to see me. He even forgot to utter the usual, “Oh, are you well?” Within four or five days, our Raju’s case came up for hearing, and the verdict was in Raju’s favor. For that pleader, it was as if he had suffered a stroke.

As my court work increased, I began to feel a deep discouragement and disgust towards my profession. The corruption that occurs here, the mentality of the pleaders, the quarrelsome nature of the clients, the relentless desire to snatch even an inch of another’s property, the greed for a penny or a pie—whether for the plaintiff or the defendant—people appear in court, take a solemn oath before God, declaring, “I will tell the truth, I will not lie,” and then, without a trace of shame, make a profession of giving false testimony.

Watching the people I had taken as role models, I saw that, unsatisfied with the government salaries they received for their jobs, they secretly lined their pockets, conveniently forgetting the illegal activities they committed daily. Yet, if someone else were accused of those same crimes in court, these very men would, without a shred of hesitation, declare him guilty and sentence him with all the authority vested in them. Witnessing such scenes, I began to feel a deep aversion—not just towards the education I had acquired, or the money I earned, or the profession I practiced, or even my fellow Andhras, but towards the entire human race and this so-called civilization itself. The urge to abandon this profession grew stronger by the day.

Every day, the truth and appropriateness of Gandhiji’s call became clearer to me: he had urged all lawyers to leave the courts, all students to leave their schools, and dedicate their lives to the service of the nation and the attainment of self-rule. I gradually reduced my court work, spending more and more time idling away. Unable to bear the hypocrisy, my clients naturally drifted to other pleaders. During one such campaign, I myself could not escape arrest. The government, in its wisdom, decided that I should take a six-month “rest” in Rajahmundry jail. “The judges are compassionate, their orders must be obeyed, and I am grateful for their mercy,” I said, bowing respectfully as I stepped down from the dock. As I emerged from the cell, the crowd that had gathered erupted in cheers, while the officer presiding in the courtroom sat motionless, his head bowed in shame.

All those who had come to witness the proceedings followed me outside, accompanying me all the way to the jail. Like a new bride being sent to her in-laws’ house, they sent me off with tears of joy, performed my housewarming into the new abode, and then quietly dispersed on their own ways. The fear of going to jail vanished for everyone. In fact, not only did the fear disappear, but people became so emboldened that they would walk up to any police constable they saw and challenge him, “If you can, arrest me! Let’s see what you can do!” Those who had been to jail would return and regale others with tales of how pleasant jail life was, so much so that many began to wonder if it was all just a dream.

Those who claim to tell stories. Looking at it now, I feel that much of what they say is actually true. The reason is, nowadays, those sitting in jails are all highly educated people, men of property, and those accustomed to great earnings. Even after coming to jail, unable to forget or change their old habits, they started arranging for various comforts here and there. That is, despite knowing very well that it is forbidden to bring in all sorts of snacks, tea, coffee, cigarettes, and such into the jail walls, they somehow managed to get all the facilities they desired, one way or another.

One day, a funny incident occurred. Among us, the chief leader did not like any of these antics. One day, someone managed to get some excellent jalebis brought in, either from a nearby house or from somewhere else. Not only did they bring them in, but they also distributed them to everyone. The leader, without even questioning how these came here, nonchalantly took as many as he wanted and even praised those who had provided them.

The next day, under the pretext of some festival, a prominent man arranged for a feast for everyone, bringing in four or five varieties of snacks, coffee, and tea from a hotel. Our leader came and saw all these arrangements.
“This is all against the law. Who arranged this? How did all these things come here?” he asked rather sternly.
No one uttered a word. Everyone sat there pale and mute.
“Why is no one speaking?” he asked again, even more sharply.
Unable to keep quiet, I replied, “Well, I didn’t see it myself. But perhaps they came in the same way as yesterday’s jalebis did,” I said with great seriousness.
Everyone present burst out laughing. The leader was utterly...

In a fit of anger, he left without participating in the event. Such pastimes happened often, helping us forget our troubles. Besides these, every evening or night, during sessions of storytelling or political lectures, discussions would be held on scholarly topics by those well-versed in them. Thus, we lacked neither entertainment nor knowledge, and our days in jail passed pleasantly, without any sense of hardship.
Without my realizing it, six months slipped by in this manner. One morning, a police constable arrived and said,

“Sir, you are not permitted to stay here even a moment longer. You must kindly go home at once. The Superintendent has asked me to convey this to you,” he said, stamping his feet together, saluting smartly, and then left.
All my friends congratulated me and repeatedly wished, “May you soon return to jail!” I turned to leave for home, and as I was about to step out, I saw my father-in-law standing there, smiling.

“Well, Parvateesham, have you finished your first exam? Looks like you wrote it well! Come, let’s go,” he said, placing his hand on my shoulder. He seated me in the horse-cart waiting there, sat beside me, and took me home.

I chatted cheerfully along the way, dreaming that Saraswati would be waiting for me at the threshold. But when we reached home, only my mother-in-law was standing at the doorway. At that sight, my legs turned to water, my heart grew heavy, and my mind faltered. My father-in-law must have noticed all these changes on my face. With great sympathy, he gently placed his hand on my shoulder and said, “Saraswati too was arrested in the meantime. She was sentenced to three months. She’ll be back in a week. I didn’t tell you earlier, thinking you might already know.”
He spoke with such kindness.
“Ah, is that so? If you hadn’t told me, what would have been lost? I should have foreseen that things would turn out like this,” I said.

I got down from the cart and, without any further conversation, quietly went to my room. I managed, with some effort, to secure whatever lawful and unlawful amenities were necessary—such is prison life. The thought of how poor Saraswati was enduring all this filled me with unbearable sorrow. But then, remembering her courage and determination, I was filled with joy. Astonishing! Just one person’s words, and without distinction of caste, creed, gender, or age, an entire populace was swept up in a wave of emotion—how remarkable!

Day by day, the movement grew more intense. Police oppression and brutality were reaching new heights. Every day, hundreds and thousands of people were experiencing this suffering. Ten times as many, with fearless smiles, were marching to jail. Some were enduring lathi blows, their arms and legs broken, becoming disabled. Some even met with death. Yet, without fear or hesitation, without a thought of turning back, thousands and lakhs pressed forward. There was not a single empty spot in any jail. Hospitals were overflowing with the injured. As all of India surged forward in unison, the ruling authorities, terrified and bewildered, were at a loss as to how to stem or control this tide, this fervor. The officials, unable to think of any other recourse, unable to find a way to quell this storm, resorted to acts of tyranny. Men and women who landed in jail were subjected to all kinds of tortures. Not content with that, they sowed discord in our religion and caste system, inciting communal hatred, and even went so far as to groom leaders for a special political party to ensure this enmity would endure forever. The results were immediate. Everything they had hoped for, everything they had planned, came to pass. The hope that the whole of India would unite, that a renaissance would restore her ancient glory—

At a time when it seemed that peace was finally within reach, the poisonous seeds sown by the rulers had grown into monstrous trees, spreading their toxic fumes to all corners of the country. Everywhere one looked, religious riots and caste hatred were erupting, tearing society apart. For decades to come, the nation was left crippled, unable to rise, its back broken by these divisions.

Wherever Congress meetings, festivals, or processions began, there was no need for the police to bring lorries to disperse them. Members of the rival party would simply bring along a handful of their own thugs, and breaking up these gatherings became a regular practice. In every community, in every branch, and—why stop there—in every household, rifts deepened between fathers and sons, husbands and wives, brothers and sisters. The country was brought to the brink of utter disintegration. Those who led and encouraged this intolerable divisiveness were not the uneducated masses, but the so-called elders, the learned, the intellectuals.

No matter how dire or painful our circumstances, we must not forget our goal. We must reach our destination, come what may. The bugle calls of Congress leaders, declaring, “We shall surely succeed!” echoed with renewed vigor throughout the land. Campaigns and exhortations increased to keep the people’s courage and resolve from faltering. Gandhi began devising new and ever more ingenious strategies. Day by day, all respect for the authorities and the courts began to vanish. Whatever the officials said or did, Congressmen would twist the meaning and stir up trouble.

The third time I went to jail, the aforementioned Duvvuri Subbamma also arrived at that prison. Some friends from Pulla came to visit us, and in the midst of our conversations, music and poetry sessions began. In the women’s section, which was a little distance away from ours, Duvvuri Subbamma, upon hearing the music, came over to our section and asked, “Who is reciting those verses, my dear?”
One of my friends, observing her old-fashioned appearance, replied, “It’s the men here, madam—they’re the ones singing.”

"Is that so, my dear? Then it seems I was mistaken. How would a simpleton like me know any better? All I knew was this: these days, if men step into the working world, I assumed they’d end up in jail just like us. I never imagined they’d be wandering about here and there, singing silly songs and lullabies, living a life of comfort," she said, spinning around and walking away briskly.

That put a lid on everyone’s mouths. I thought even if you slashed their faces with a knife, not a drop of blood would come out. Without another word, without so much as a goodbye, they all quietly dispersed. Incidents like this happened every day.

In the past, lawyers and judges commanded a great deal of respect. Judges, in turn, showed affection, regard, and honor towards lawyers. Now, all that has vanished. Especially when the English occupy positions of authority, our lawyers are treated with even more neglect.

Once, a lawyer from Bezwada, a capable and genuine advocate like myself, had to go to a nearby town to argue a case before the sub-collector. After much effort, he finally reached the place, only to find the collector about to mount his bicycle and leave. Seeing the lawyer, the collector, with one foot already on the pedal, asked,
"Oh, have you come?"
"Yes, sir, I have a case before you today. I’ve come to argue it," replied the lawyer.
Mounting his bicycle, the collector said, "Well then, go ahead and argue. I have some work elsewhere, I’ll just go and come back."
"In that case, I’ll wait here until you return," said the pleader.
"No need for that, just present your arguments," said the collector.
"Then perhaps I’ll come another day," said the lawyer.
“There’s no need, sir. I told you I wouldn’t accept your argument,” he said, a little irritably.
This gentleman was quite flustered. “Telling me to argue with these walls in your absence is rather comical. I’m leaving now. Good day,” said the lawyer.
The Collector, now red with anger, declared, “If you don’t present your argument here and now, you’ll never get another chance to do so in this place.”
“That’s exactly my intention as well,” replied the lawyer, and left without another word.

This, my friends, is the impact of Gandhiji’s independence movement. Even in the High Court, our teacher Prakasham garu once pulled off a similar stunt. One time, a case came up—a rather trivial one, with about fifty plaintiffs. Prakasham garu accepted the brief for all of them and appeared in court to argue on their behalf. The judge, a very clever and experienced man, had already studied the case thoroughly and decided to have it disposed of quickly. Sitting on the bench, he asked Prakasham garu to present the plaintiffs’ case.
A few minutes into Prakasham garu’s opening,
“That’s enough, move on to the second point,” said the judge.
Prakasham garu began to repeat the same argument. After two minutes,
“That will do. Next case,” said the judge.

This happened seven or eight times. Finally, the judge, now a little exasperated, said, “What is your intention, sir? No matter how many times I ask, you keep repeating the same argument. If you have nothing more to say, shouldn’t you just stop?”
Prakasham garu, noticing the impatience the judge was displaying, responded with great calmness, as if he hadn’t noticed at all...

“Sir, there are fifty accused in this case. The same charge has been brought against all of them. Therefore, I have taken up the case on behalf of all fifty. So, my argument will be the same for all. If you would kindly have the patience to listen to at least one argument in full, neither of us would have any trouble. It appears that you have already read the case superficially, reached a decision, and are about to deliver a verdict without even hearing our side. Whether Your Lordships listen or not, I shall certainly present my argument on behalf of these fifty,” he began his plea.

The judges, having no alternative, resigned themselves to listen. Strangely enough, after hearing all the cases, the judge realized that his own opinion was mistaken, recognized the justice in the lawyer’s argument, and delivered a judgment in their favor.

In another High Court, an English judge, while presiding over proceedings, had brought along a puppy, which he kept on his lap, petting and playing with it as he sat. Observing this, the advocate stopped his argument mid-sentence and sat down in silence. Without lifting his head, still stroking the puppy on his lap, the judge asked, “Why are you sitting down? Is your argument finished?”
The advocate, without the slightest hesitation or nervousness, replied, “I am waiting until Your Lordship’s deliberations are complete, so that I may continue my argument.”
At this, the judge, embarrassed, lowered his head, immediately called for a servant, and ordered the puppy to be taken away. Then he said, “You may now continue your argument.”

The courage to rebuke such high-ranking English officials was, before the independence movement, possessed only by a rare few. At the mere mention of a ‘sahib’, people would tremble and scurry away to a safe distance. Only after the movement began did it become common to see such scenes every day, everywhere. This development...
Mokkapati Narasimha Shastri, 537 Unexpected, inspiring, and auspicious for the future.

Day by day, the movement was growing more intense. There was increasing negligence towards the British authorities. Protests were gaining strength. In these circumstances, everyone began to wonder how much longer this rule could last here. Those who still held power in their hands were encouraging the police force to commit all manner of atrocities; even if not directly encouraged, they turned a blind eye to the cruelties and injustices being perpetrated. The authorities pretended not to see the police’s misdeeds.

The police, emboldened, began to use threats, then lathi charges, then the deployment of tear gas, and after that, even guns and bayonets—all without fear. Many people were left crippled. Hundreds died on the spot. If ever a crowd larger than the police force gathered, the government would immediately call in the military. That was one level of oppression. But they devised an even more insidious tactic.

As if it weren’t enough to be troubled by our external enemies as described above, they stirred up even more powerful internal enemies among us. They recruited gangs of loafers—those who roamed the streets without work or purpose—and used them to disrupt Congress meetings, to pelt stones at speakers, and to cause all sorts of unspeakable riots. Worse still, they inflamed the caste and religious divisions within our own society, provoking such deep and lasting hatred among the people that nearly half of our population was split off and turned into a permanent enemy force against us. Even if the officials who created these divisions and their authority were to flee, the seeds of discord they sowed would continue to bear fruit in countless destructive ways.

They kept sending lakhs of people to jail. The accusations they made against these people were so laughable, and the way the prisoners treated the authorities with such contempt was so comical, that I must share one example.
Barrister Parvateesam

A blind Brahmin beggar, over sixty years old, was swept up in the fervor of the movement. Draped in some old khadi clothes that someone had donated out of charity, he would go about singing, “Give up liquor, sirs! Open your eyes!” and “We don’t want British rule!”—national songs, stirring songs—while begging for his food. This poor soul was accused of conspiring to overthrow the British Empire, upon which the sun never set, and was brought before the court.
Standing in the dock, the court clerk read out the charges against him in a loud, clear voice. The magistrate asked, “What have you to say in response to these charges?”

“Sir, I was born blind. I have no parents, no guardians, no one to care for me. I am a beggar, an orphan. Do you really believe, sir, that I am trying to overthrow the mighty British Empire? If you truly believe that, then I must say I am very proud to have grown so powerful! Even if you punish me, I can endure it. For me, it would be a pleasant experience; for you, perhaps, a painful one—think about that,” he replied.

For a moment, every heart in the gathered crowd throbbed as one. All around, cheers of joy echoed, and people wiped away tears of happiness as they quietly dispersed. The magistrate, head bowed, sentenced that blind and formidable rebel to six months of rigorous imprisonment.

Another incident of similar humor comes to mind. An elderly matron, well past fifty, was arrested for her enthusiastic participation in the movement and brought before the court. Without even questioning her, the magistrate said sternly,

“Wherever you brought this lady from, take her back there. Tell her to go home and mind her own business. Tell her not to step into politics. Tell her if she ever comes into this court again, she won’t get away with just words.”
Immediately, without even the blink of an eye, without a word—

Without a pause, she retorted, “Why should someone else tell me? I heard your words loud and clear, and I only came here to tell you what you asked me to say. I have no other business here.” With that, she spun around and, without another word, strode out. The police ran after her.

The magistrate was seized with such a furious rage that he almost leapt up, ready to thrash her then and there. But as the entire courtroom erupted in applause, he remembered his own dignity, hung his head, and slumped back into his chair, thoroughly deflated.

While all these strange and wonderful events were unfolding, movements sprang up everywhere: the campaign against paying taxes, the Salt Satyagraha, the agitation against giving toddy-tapping licenses or permits—one movement more fervent than the last. To suppress these, the authorities unleashed every possible form of repression, and as if that weren’t enough, they provoked our own people into internal strife and civil discord. Thus, the turmoil never ceased, and before we could catch our breath, the great world war itself broke out.

Our rulers began trying to enlist all our people into the war effort, while the Congress insisted that joining the army was in no way in the nation’s interest. The Justicites, Muslims, Loyalists, and various other groups, on the other hand, declared that all this was mere pretense, and that it was every man’s sacred duty to join the army. They launched a barrage of lectures, plays, bluffs, and bribes to drag people into the military.

In these circumstances, the English began to realize that ruling such a vast country from afar was becoming impossible. After countless obstacles, hardships, losses, and deaths, the English finally broke up our country, handed over a portion to us, and departed—leaving everyone bewildered.
As for us common Congress foot soldiers, we were left utterly at a loss, not knowing what to do, beset by all sorts of troubles and confusion.
Barrister Parvateesam

Watching the way things were going, for some days, Saraswati, Achyutaramaiah, and I spent our time expressing sympathy and offering occasional words of advice to those involved. Achyutaramaiah garu had completely retired from practice and entrusted all his work to me. Even before this movement began, I had developed a deep aversion and disinterest towards the court and the legal profession. I explained to my father-in-law that it was impossible for me to resume practice.

Returning home, my father came and advised me not to get involved in the movement any further, but instead to look after and improve whatever land and property we had. Considering the current situation, I decided that perhaps this was indeed my duty. So, Saraswati and I set off for Mogalturru.
Final Word

Be that as it may, I have at last managed to complete the third part of Parvatisham. I must insist that I have no personal gain in this endeavor. It all began, as fate would have it, on some auspicious but unplanned moment, when Chiranjeevi Puranam Subrahmanya Sharma casually made a suggestion, which I, half-hearing, half-ignoring, let slip by—only for Sri Narla Venkateswara Rao to turn it into a firm admonition in the guise of advice. “I cannot do it, sir!” I protested, but unable to refuse the words of friends, and unable to answer the thousands of kind-hearted, literature-loving friends who encouraged me, I found myself swept along by the momentum of that auspicious beginning and the force of Narla’s resolve. Thus, my efforts have, so far, met with success.

But it is not for me to judge; that is the prerogative of my discerning readers. With them, however, I seem to have a slight difference of opinion. Many have praised the work. Yet, some have remarked that the humor has diminished in the second part compared to the first, and even more so in the third part compared to the second. That may well be true. The answer to that lies in the second part—
Final Words
I have come to the end. I thought there was no need to always give the same answer at the end. Besides, I felt I should say a couple more words.

From the day Parvatisham set out in the boat, to the time when, having completed his education, become a householder, a renowned lawyer, a patriot, and a leader, he gave up everything—between these two points, nearly a Pushkaram, that is, twelve years, sped by in the blink of an eye. In this period, Parvatisham grew up immensely—not just physically, but also mentally and morally. He acquired a great deal of knowledge and learning. In his profession, he earned fame and reputation at lightning speed. He became a man of action, a tireless worker. He became a devotee, a thinker. He became a scholar, a man of wisdom. And not stopping there, he even began to display the qualities of a sage in the making. Therefore, should not the author too recognize this transformation and shape the narrative accordingly?

From the time he set out from Narsapur in the boat until he reached London, due to his uncivilized appearance, and later, because of his ignorant and bizarre antics, he was a figure of comedy. Everyone who saw him would burst out laughing. But by the time he reached London, with his natural intelligence, correcting his own mistakes, he learned to laugh at others. As his mind matured in this way, his sense of humor and understanding of comedy too inevitably grew.

Generally, when a person laughs, there is neither the time nor the inclination to ponder why he is laughing. Whether or not he has the time, he laughs without thinking. Among all the countless living beings created, only man can laugh. Not only can he laugh, but he also possesses the ability to reflect on why he is laughing—whether or not he uses this power, the fact remains that it exists within him.
Final Word

Truth be told, when a man sees the odd attire and language of another, he generally laughs—so says our school of rhetoric. But not only do we laugh at strange costumes and speech; we must also recognize that all manner of disarray, confusion, and thoughtless actions are equally sources of humor. Even when one laughs at these things knowingly, he often does so without pondering the reason. Yet, there is always a reason behind such laughter. Upon witnessing ignorance in another, a man unconsciously thinks, “I am so clever; would I ever behave so foolishly, wear such ridiculous clothes, or perform such senseless acts?”—and this pride, unbeknownst to him, prompts his laughter. He laughs for a moment and moves on, never giving it a second thought.

This, in essence, is to say that pride is the root of laughter—a view held by many Western philosophers, from Hazlitt to Anthony Ludovici. Later, as man becomes more thoughtful and introspective, all such pride fades away; he becomes wise, rises above the natural likes and dislikes of humanity, and, endowed with self-knowledge, laughs at the weaknesses of others with a sense of compassion, thinking, “Ah, poor fellow!” I believe this is the true doctrine. That is why, as Parvatisham grows, his mind matures, he cultivates thoughts beyond the reach of ordinary people, and for this reason, his humor becomes more refined and delicate. I have endeavored to shape him in this manner.
This is not the place for a more extensive discussion, so I trust that this explanation will satisfy the critics for now.
And finally, when the serialization began, my dear friend Purana Subrahmanya Sharma suggested that perhaps Narasimha Shastri could write two or three more parts—
Final Word

Once again, I express my gratitude to my friends who immediately understood my hints, encouraged me, and, at times, even compelled me to keep my pen moving—especially Sri Narla Venkateswara Rao, to whom I owe much. My heartfelt thanks also go to my dear daughter Kumari Kappagantu Rajarajeswari, who has been my right hand from the very beginning, and to young Indraganti Srikanta Sharma.
With renewed thanks, I offer them my blessings for long life, health, and prosperity, and now take my leave.
